[scan 12]

### Preface.

Before I give myself up to some more general reflections to which this biography prompts me, I wish to satisfy the need of my heart by expressing my heartfelt thanks to those who have supported me in it. Unfortunately they are not as many as I should have had to wish. How hard it is, after all, among us Germans to bring about a common effort, even should it be as good as effortless! Besides Hegel’s family, which had gradually handed over to me, with unconditional confidence, his entire scholarly and epistolary remains, I have only to thank Deacon *Binder* in Heidenheim, Professors *David Strauss* in Heilbronn, *Abegg* in Breslau, *Hinrichs* in Halle, *Sietze* in Treuenbrietzen, Baron *Boris d’Yxkull* in Livonia, and a man indispensable to the biographical interests of the present day, Herr *Varnhagen von Ense* in Berlin. All the others from whom I still expected contributions and to whom I had made my wish for them known have either had nothing to communicate or do not care to.

Unasked, on the other hand, Herr *Schwab* had the kindness to send me from Tübingen a copy of the letter in which Hegel declared himself ready to accept the post of house tutor that *Hölderlin* had found for him in Frankfurt am Main.

[p. IV]

It is to be hoped that through Herr Schwab we shall be more thoroughly informed about Hölderlin’s life than has hitherto been the case. I have therefore kept the section of the biography on Hegel’s relationship to Hölderlin shorter than I had originally intended. But even if Herr Schwab is of the opinion that the urge towards the *All* and the *One* in Hölderlin’s view of the world was first called forth by *Schelling*, I cannot convince myself of the correctness of this view. Schelling came to Tübingen only at Michaelmas 1790, and at first distinguished himself to the other students not as a philosophical mind but as a youth thoroughly schooled in the knowledge of Hebrew and precocious in his general culture, who came into closer contact with the older students, to whom Hegel and Hölderlin belonged, only through his participation in the political club of the Tübingen Stift. Yet as early as February 1791 Hölderlin wrote the Ἓν καὶ πᾶν into Hegel’s album as *his* motto. Hölderlin was most ardently devoted to the study of Greek literature and was at one with Hegel especially in his love of Sophocles. Humanity smiled upon him always and only through the *Hellenic ideal*; it was the sun of his life. With this Hellenism, however, there was joined in him a genuinely *Germanic* trait, the romantic conception of nature. The solitude of the forests and mountain heights suited him; light he all but deified, and he gladly fled from the changeful press of human affairs to “all-enduring” nature. The resolution of these two elements, namely, of contemplating *culture* in the ancient form of the Hellenic spirit and *nature* with all the enthusiastic longing, with the inwardness, of the Germanic heart, took in him the direction of an ecstatic, indeed daemonic, one-sided immersion in the unity of the All. Awakening from the enjoyment of its bliss

[p. V]

as from an intellectual intoxication, he shrank back before the determinacy and otherness of the actual. Certainly he felt the need not to take unity as a mere volatilization of differences. To this points his saying that one must grasp the Ἓν διαφέρον ἑαυτῷ; so too the letter to his half-brother, which places the *A Deo Principium* [From God the beginning] at its head. But his soft, poetic soul did not carry this work through. If we consider the remarkable document of Hegel’s addressed to Hölderlin, *Eleusis*, we can, I believe, infer from it how deeply this mystical moment was rooted in him as well. But he overcame its dangers through science, which Hölderlin indeed strove for but did not attain, and he went under in chaotic ferment, a ferment that in his case may have been occasioned individually, in its outbreak, by love for his *Diotima*, yet in so noble and rich a spirit was surely conditioned still more deeply.

I see Hölderlin, therefore, as the *prophetic* man who among the Tübingen students was the first to proclaim the “Sturm und Drang” of spirit toward totality and unity. He was the poetic forerunner of Schelling and Hegel. The *pantheistic* essence in him was certainly not first inoculated into him by Schelling, since it was properly and truly what constituted his individuality. Compare only the fact that Hölderlin was already celebrating the All and One at the beginning of the year 1791 with the other, that in Schelling’s essay *On the I* of 1795 nothing yet of the pantheism is contained, to which he began to pass over only later through his essay on the World Soul. In the sense in which one commonly speaks of Schelling’s pantheism, he first expressed it at all after 1800, in his two journals for speculative physics, in the *Bruno* and in the Yearbooks for Medicine; Hölderlin’s *Hyperion*, however, had already appeared in 1797.

[p. VI]

Hegel’s letters to *Schelling* I have had before me *not* in the *original*, only in a copy belonging to Hegel’s widow. From this the note of the date of Schelling’s replies is also taken. Schelling’s replies themselves have remained entirely unknown to me. He had them offered to me in December 1843 through Herr von *Henning* on condition of their complete printing. This courtesy I accepted with thanks, but regretted that I could no longer include the letters in the already completed biography, but only in the documentary appendix; yet even so, Herr von Schelling would put all friends of the history of our philosophical literature greatly in his debt.

To this I have remained without any answer.

On my personal relation to Hegel I already had to express myself in 1836 in the preface to my *Critique of Schleiermacher’s Doctrine of Faith*. I therefore recall only that I was indeed never an immediate pupil of Hegel’s, but yet came into contact with him and with the circle that had formed around him to such an extent that I was able to impress upon myself a sufficient idea of his personality and of his individual relation to Berlin. Oddly enough, I, his biographer, celebrated his *last* birthday with him. Private circumstances brought about my stay in Berlin in 1831, during the approach and the outbreak of the cholera. Hegel lived outside the Halle Gate, in the Grunow garden. Almost all his friends and acquaintances had gone away, fleeing from the destroying angel; such a shortage prevailed at the university that I even had to step in as guest opponent at the public disputation of the present Professor *Matthies* in Greifswald, and I still vividly remember how the copy of the theses for the disputation reached me through the city post quite pierced through and fumigated, as disinfected. Hegel, therefore, under such circumstances,

[p. VII]

had more leisure for me, and I associated with him and his family for some weeks at that time very cheerfully and happily. So it came about that I, as the guest of *Marheineke*, drove out with the latter and his wife also to Tivoli for the celebration of Hegel’s birthday. Who among us would have guessed how soon he was to be torn from us! I took leave of him amid nothing but humorous remarks about the cholera quarantine that awaited me on my journey to Halle before Wittenberg — and a few weeks later he himself had succumbed to this disease. When I too, in January 1832, fell sick unto death with cholera, the ironic thought sometimes flashed through my head that I was, after all, a far too faithful pupil of Hegel’s.

At Michaelmas 1833 I went from Halle here to Königsberg and was thereby removed from the livelier intercourse with the German Hegelians. A hundred miles of intervening space are an excellent means of making personal relations mythical. Just as we Königsbergers exist in Germany more as an idea to which one appeals, so too Germany becomes for us a very ideal object. This situation might appear disadvantageous for writing a biography whose locale is essentially Germany. But I believe that in it there also lies hidden the advantage of an unprejudiced criticism. Historiography requires the greatest familiarity with the content, but also a certain independence of it, which can be greatly facilitated by external isolation. This isolation is the peculiarity of my literary position. Hegel himself has expressed his conception of biography to the effect that he declares the specialities, the microscopic niceties, which intimate, daily and long-standing intercourse can afford knowledge of, to be subordinate, in that he says: “The interest of *biography* seems directly to stand opposed to a general purpose, but it itself has the historical world for its background,

[p. VIII]

in which the individual is entangled; even the subjectively original, humorous, etc., plays upon that content and heightens its interest thereby; what is merely cozy, however, has a different ground and interest from history.”

My local situation, however, has not only made my literary relations, so to speak, affectless, but has also placed me in a cultural circle in which the general foundations of the Kantian and Herbartian philosophy prevail with greater decisiveness and in wider extent than anywhere else. This circumstance compelled me quite immediately, more than others, to investigate the relation of these philosophies to the Hegelian. Hegel’s polemic against Kant has not, as it has so often been taken, the merely negative significance of a refuting, of an annihilating of the Kantian philosophy, but just as much the positive one of its further development and completion. This inner connection between Kant and Hegel I have set out in my *History of the Kantian Philosophy* and must appeal to it in this respect here. The relation of *Schelling’s* to Hegel I have brought up in the biography only from Hegel’s side. How it presents itself from Schelling’s side I have shown in my monograph on him, and may therefore also here make a presupposition. That Hegel’s Life was written precisely here in Königsberg, as it were under the eyes of Kant’s immortal manes, is therefore hardly a mere accident. Königsberg is not only for nature geographically, it is also historically for spirit a watershed.

With regard to the scientific criticism of Hegel himself I have refrained from all details, since for the biography it was more a matter of Hegel’s general image, and a more precise entering into his individual works would at once have led to an inexpedient prolixity. For me the

[p. IX]

reproduction of the more important works, especially of the still unknown essays of Hegel’s existing only in manuscript, had to be the main thing, and for the more specific appraisal of his system I can refer to the *Critical Elucidations* which I published on it in 1840, and in which I subjected in particular, besides his principles, the philosophy of history, the aesthetics and the philosophy of religion to a detailed analysis.

Nevertheless, to many there will be far too much philosophy in this biography. The great mass, even of the so-called educated, wants altogether no actual philosophy. It wants only ratiocination. If it condescends to read the life of a philosopher, it wants above all entertainment, interesting incidents, colorful character portraits, anecdotes, curiosities. But even Diogenes Laertius, that stockpile and storehouse of all the little stories and externalities of the ancient philosophers, could not avoid reporting not only on their writings but also on their doctrine, on their ideas. If one reads the history of a general, one will not be surprised to meet with the history of his campaigns. Is one to be astonished to find, in the history of a philosopher, the history of his philosophizing? And now especially in the history of a philosopher whose life was in itself so simple, so surveyable at a single glance, so German, so plain, so industrious, so without any piquant glitter of intrigues and secrets? Hegel did not yet belong to the race of philosophers which, on the stage on which it has put itself on show, lets the last remnant of character evaporate altogether in being, in *Bettina’s* expression, *thoroughly amiable* at work. He was still a man to whom, with stern earnestness, first and last the matter itself was what counted.

The greatest difficulty of my work lay in the peculiarity of Hegel’s basic nature, of having always developed scientifically,

[p. X]

*all-sidedly* and *gradually*. His producing was a quiet processing of his intelligence, a continual working on of his whole man. His biography therefore lacks the charm of great contrasts and passionate leaps, and is preserved from complete monotony only by the intensive significance of its hero. I therefore had to guard myself very much against the temptation to disturb this grand simplicity and to foist false transitions upon him.

The working out of Hegel’s biography was originally to fall to *Gans*, who had written his obituary for the Prussian State Gazette (reprinted in Gans’s *Miscellaneous Writings*, 1834, part II, pp. 242–252). Gans died, a loss as sudden as it was grave, to science as to life. Now in the autumn of 1839 the proposal of the biography was made to me. The sifting of Hegel’s significant written remains, the collecting of what belonged together but had been thrown together in confusion, the chronological determination of the papers, the copying of the more important ones, the research into circumstances often insignificant in themselves and yet indispensable, the correspondence on points of which I presumed a special knowledge in others, the weighing of so many personal considerations still reaching into the present, the keeping of a harmonious measure in the extent of the material — all this cost me so much time and effort that the appearance of this book was delayed much longer than I had at first thought. To be sure, I have lived through blissful hours in that rummaging, searching, discovering, combining and shaping. What consecration lies in everything that a great and good man accomplishes! How uplifting is the confidence of finding again, in everything that has proceeded from him, the trace of his powerful spirit, of his noble heart! Every new little leaf that I took in hand from the literary remains,

[p. XI]

I greeted devoutly as a new gold vein for penetrating deeper into the essence of the glorious man. Much, it is true, I at first overestimated in its substantive value. I even had first to get accustomed to the feeling that I possessed here in my room, crowded into a few chests, such precious relics! I had first to come to know yet other things of Hegel’s, in order to be able, as it surprised me, to assign to the individual item its proper place in his course of development. That initial relative overestimation, however, I needed, so as not to let my courage sink in mastering the material lying before me.

A Frenchman, *J. Willm*, wrote in 1836 in his *Essai sur la philosophie de Hegel*: “[French] Let us hope that a detailed biography soon, written without hatred as without favor, inspired solely by the desire to show all that so remarkable an individuality contains that is most characteristic, will initiate us into his most intimate life and will portray Hegel for us in all his aspects, both as man, and as sage, and as citizen. It is so sweet and so happy to love and to revere what one esteems and what one admires.”

Often have I recalled these words. But need I still assure you that I am far from the opinion that I had solved the task completely? That I made the work subjectively only in the sense of rendering yet another biography of Hegel’s, were it possible, superfluous; that the high responsibility constantly hovered before me which I have had in the first laying out of the matter, insofar as it must have an unavoidable after-effect for all future time; that I therefore *strove* to be exhaustive and conclusive, was necessary. But already the lack of so many documents which with time, as in the case of

[p. XII]

Schiller’s biography, may still come gradually to light, lets me even now see gaps that can be filled later. May my work then at least permit the easy filling-in! May the basic intuition that I bear of Hegel within me, and which has guided me in particulars, prove itself ever more! May also nothing be visible in my work of the processes that prepared it! When a bronze-founder sets up the statue of a hero, nothing more of the clay of the model, of the various pieces of metal united in the melting flux, of the thousand upon thousand chasing strokes, is to be seen on the smooth form. May Hegel’s image too in such a way have annihilated within itself all the crossings and traversings of my fantasy and reflection that were made for it.

Not without melancholy do I part from this work, though one must, after all, at some time let becoming also come to existence. For does it not seem as if we of today were only the gravediggers and monument-setters for the philosophers whom the second half of the last century bore, to die in the first of the present? *Kant* began in 1804 this *dying of the German philosophers*. Fichte, Jacobi, Solger, Reinhold, Krause, Schleiermacher, W. v. Humboldt, Fr. Schlegel, Herbart, Baader, Wagner, Windischmann, Fries and so many other lesser but in their place often irreplaceable teachers, or, like Erhard, sociable disseminators of philosophy, followed him. These men have now in turn been followed by the biographers. Fichte and Reinhold received worthy portrayals from their sons; Krause from his pupil Lindemann, Herbart from Hartenstein; W. v. Humboldt from his admirer Schlesier, etc.

Do we see successors for that harvest of death? Are we capable of likewise sending across into the second half of our century a holy host of thinkers? Do there live among our young men those whom Platonic enthusiasm and

[p. XIII]

Aristotelian blissful devotion to work has inspired the heart to immortal exertion for speculation? Do our young men perhaps dream of other wreaths, does the laurel beckon them on other paths, does the higher goal of the deed perhaps gleam for them as a lodestar, is it their ideal to actualize the ideals of those philosophers? Or are they to let themselves fall into indifference toward science and life and, after not seldom proclaiming themselves, with braggart haste, victors of the day, to be without sufficient strength for the future?

Strangely enough, in our days it is precisely the talents that seem unable to hold out properly. They quickly wear themselves out, become unfruitful after some promising blossoms, and begin to copy and repeat themselves just where, after the overcoming of the unripe and imperfect, one-sided and stormy attempts of youth, the period of vigorous and collected activity ought first to follow. Some, full of fine zeal, overhurry themselves in the run and must, like Constantin *Frantz*, in each next writing already partly take back their preceding one. Or they die quite early, like the highly gifted, noble youths Ferdinand *Weber* in Marburg, Philipp *Reidel* in Freiburg, who did not even live to see the printing of their work. Not to speak of those who, without posthumous fame as without fame, in a self-manufactured *premature renown*, through an ephemeral raising on the shield by some journal, take their fleeting tinsel wages for mere promises and improvise reforms, indeed revolutions of philosophy, of which this in its great world-historical course will never learn anything. These cavaliers of off-the-cuff speculation, staggering about in the labyrinth of their hypotheses, confuse the squabble of their tavern adventures with the earnest speech of legislative assemblies, and the din of a critical cudgel-fight with the tragic thunder of the battle.

[p. XIV]

*Schelling* is still one of the few who have lived through all the vicissitudes of our idealism in fresh actuality. Over how many graves his still ever vigorous eye gazes! Solitary he stands there. A Russian traveler once had a report printed in *Lewald’s Europa* that he had sought Schelling in Munich in vain. At last he had learned that the latter was staying, in order to be *alone*, at *Regensburg*. He traveled after him. But even in Regensburg, where he met Schelling, his dwelling remained a mystery to him. This seemed to me at that time genuinely Schellingian. Although I should guard against any public recognition of Schelling, since one of his more recent adherents in the Augsburg General Gazette has interpreted such utterances of mine as mere hypocrisy, I am nonetheless already too old a writer and have had too many similar experiences to let myself be determined by such petty considerations of prudence. So I do not deny that I then pictured to myself Regensburg, this ancient Roman Danube town, this city of the imperial diets, this city in which the Swabian Kepler died of hunger with his immortal work on the motion of the heavenly bodies, this city of old churches, medieval houses, this city which in its Catholicism is on the Danube what Cologne is on the Rhine: the inland German little Rome, this city before which, on the river hills of the stream, the Valhalla of German fame rises like a Doric temple — enough, that I pictured this city to myself as the most homogeneous residence for Schelling. So can fantasy err! Now Schelling lives with satisfaction in the modern, glittering Berlin and attends assemblies and balls. How mighty he appears outwardly in his present position, but how sublime he seemed to me then, in the dark, storm-laden Regensburg, wrestling a Herculean wrestle breast to breast, solitary, with the riddles of the universe. How it must have gripped him, when

[p. XV]

his only faithful *Steffens*, even at the toast on his birthday, voiced gloomy forebodings of death — Steffens, who, to make his biographer superfluous, is building himself in his Memoirs the spacious historical coffin.

But if the philosophers die too, philosophy does not die, for it is not a mere human affair, it is also God’s affair. The brooding of spirit over itself, the ever new exploration of the universe, the wish to cognize the essentiality of things, the constant making-present again of the eternal Ideas, which are the marrow of the world in its changing appearance: this commerce of spirit with itself and with nature, this urge of liberation from deception and semblance through the grasping of truth, can never disappear. As long as history rolls on, as long as religion exists, so long must philosophy also exist. Without religion spirit cannot exist — but without philosophy neither, and it is the most pernicious opinion to want to *maintain* religion in greater integrity by keeping philosophy, its exegesis, its transfiguration, *away* from it, or even being inclined to sacrifice it entirely to it. Begin as one will, one will not be able to deny spirit, once it has only overcome the rawness of nature and attained some leisure, the satisfaction through *culture*. Culture, however, means nothing other than thinking and determination of the will by thought, through the grasping of the universality and necessity of everything in its unity. Always, therefore, philosophers will rise again. There can never be a last system of philosophy.

Philosophy, however, has undeniably changed and extended its relation to actuality in such a way that it has sublated its former world-seclusion and world-estrangement. To this closer connection of knowing and acting, of theory and practice, which since Spinoza the

[p. XVI]

more distinguished philosophers have all more or less aspired to, Hegel has made a great advance especially by having made the difference between speculation and empiricism, the exclusive relation of a priori thinking to the so-called positive sciences, much clearer through his treatment of logic, and thereby much more identical. With him it is not so much of philosophy as quite simply of *science* that there is talk. Right away his first larger work, the *Phenomenology*, he called: *System of Science*. The Berlin Yearbooks were named: *Yearbooks for Scientific Criticism*, etc. In his naive professorial manner Hegel once expressed his aversion to all philosophy that issues in an abstract dialectic, in an ontological purism, in the words: “Those are the right philosophers who mean that in *essence* they have the true, and that if they keep saying essence, this is the inner and the right! I have no respect at all for their *essence-saying*; for it is precisely only an abstract reflection. To explicate the essence, however, is to make it appear as existence.”

Our age is bored not merely out of want of thoroughness with all philosophical investigations which do not go beyond the phenomenological and metaphysical to a more determinate cognition of nature and spirit. Certainly, *without epistemology, without metaphysics is philosophy impossible*. But it is not to remain standing with them, necessary as they are; from the empyrean of the abstract form of the Idea it is also to come to the Concept of the concrete existence of the Idea and prove itself in the *unity* of the Concept and its reality, for the Concept of the Idea is indeed no other than that of the unity of Concept and reality. Medieval scholasticism suffered from the excess of realitylessness; the later empiricism from the excess of conceptlessness; it is time that it prosper toward the *reconciliation*

[p. XVII]

of both abstractions, and because it is time for it, we see at present philosophy once again fall in the sharpest way into the one-sidedness of *abstract ontology and empiricism, theory and practice*. What is perishing seems, resisting its disappearance, to be victorious for a moment, as a drowning man is still lifted *above* the flood, which in the depths is already digging his grave. These one-sidednesses must therefore turn against the philosophy which relentlessly annihilates them. The relative necessity of their existence permits them, however, still before their downfall to indulge in the deceptive self-feeling of victory.

The abstract *ontology* we see in all those who want to sublate again the immediate unity of the Concept of thinking and being as the content of the logical Idea and to restore the former separation of logic and metaphysics, a separation which they consistently also drive again toward leading logic back into psychology and thereby to a merely subjective conception of the logical determinations. All of these have therefore written metaphysics, and one of them, *Braniß*, also already a logic. They are all now in embarrassment over their further progress, and we see least of all that their ontology had gained a lasting influence in the field of the real sciences, as they themselves naturally flattered themselves with such. They are all, because they cannot make clear to themselves the relation of subjective thinking to the absolute thought-determinations in the Hegelian system, opponents of it, but with considerate and sincere recognition of it, since it is impossible for them to overlook Hegel’s great achievements precisely in ontology.

The abstract *empiricism* has been so fortunate as to find in *Trendelenburg* a weighty representative. It agrees with abstract ontology in the separation of the

[p. XVIII]

Concept of thinking and being, but denies, what that does not, the possibility of *pure*, i.e. of nature and history abstracting thinking, and asserts *intuition* as the ground of cognition. Thinking has here merely a secondary position. However euphemistically one may now express oneself with regard to intuiting, in the end nothing remains but the old *dualism* of sensation and reflection, of being and thinking, of object and subject, of materialism and spiritualism; and then it cannot surprise us if the convenient and science-despairing removal, not dissolution, of dualism again takes place through the appeal to *faith*. That is surely a sign of the times, that a man so thoroughly at home in Aristotle could nevertheless have descended so far as to deny to the νοῦς the νόησις τῆς νοήσεως [thinking of thinking]. Against Hegel the abstract empiricism takes up preeminently the position of disputing the truth of his dialectical method, which the ontologists formally recognize, and of accusing him himself of the empiricism, the dependence on intuition, which he only artificially conceals. It holds pure thinking to be such as ventures to derive from itself being also in its real manifoldness, without troubling about it through the *mediation of intuiting*, not merely, no, even to produce it.

Abstract *theory* wants to give the *Concept of actuality*, while it yet abstracts from it as real. It has as its boldest representative the present *Schelling*, who calls his present philosophy an existential philosophy, but avoids the determinacy of the particular, the Concept of nature and of the state. He has therefore on the one hand an abstract ontology, his present modification of the Aristotelian principles, which he theologizes; on the other hand he has an abstract empiricism, his present philosophy of revelation,

[p. XIX]

in which he uncritically acknowledges the truth of the factual element of tradition and demands the necessity of faith. From the abstract ontology he is therefore distinguished by this empiricism; from the abstract empiricism by that ontology; from both negatively by his complete absence of method, positively by the postulate of an absolute will that is not bound to reason.

Abstract *practice* abstracts from the *historicity* of the actual, turns away from all metaphysics as a fruitless brooding, and throws itself at once upon the *need* and *enjoyment* of man, upon his heart and disposition. At the head of it stands Ludwig *Feuerbach*, whose philosophy of the future holds out nothing further than the agreement of sensibility and understanding for the *happiness* of the human individual, and which raises *tangibility* to the criterion of reality, to the absolute form of the true. Oh, how much more truthful is the doctrine of the man to whom this abstract practice otherwise is wont to pay homage, the doctrine of Spinoza, who said that we are virtuous if and because we are blessed, not blessed if and because we are virtuous, and who made the adequate cognition of the Idea the principle of practice!

*Feuerbach* is Schelling’s sharpest, most brilliant opponent, but agrees with him in this, that he evades the development of science into system, the organic carrying-through of cognition. He persists in the assertion of embryo-generalities and can therefore not exert on the further formation of philosophy the influence that one might have expected from the energy of the criticism with which he appeared. Like the present Schelling he does not enter more closely upon nature or the state. Because he begins at once with man as he goes and stands, and abhors the investigation of being, ability-to-be and ought-to-be, of the unprethinkable and the thought being, etc., as antediluvian phantasms,

[p. XX]

he appears more accessible, more practical, more humane, more domestic than Schelling, who delights precisely in the invention of occurrences in the *status absconditus* [hidden state] of the Godhead and with the mysterious mien of one initiated into the primeval-world processes understands how to captivate so many. This mythicizing theology, as a Christianity-affecting hypostasization of the Aristotelian causes, is for Feuerbach a mere fiction, in that he could say with Goethe’s Prometheus against the Schellingian God:

Here I sit, forming men / After my image, / A race that shall be like me, / To suffer, to weep, / To enjoy and to be glad, / And not to heed you, / Like me!

All four parties, abstract ontology as well as empiricism, theory as well as practice, agree therefore, because they scorn the cognition of the concrete and use it at most as an *example*, in being *abstract theologians*. They like best to set out reflections on the difference of faith and knowledge, revelation and reason, the divine and the human, the Christian and the natural, theology and speculation, doctrine of the Trinity and deism, transcendence and immanence, and the like, and do not get out of the frictions with the professional theologians. The only one of them who broke through abstraction here at least in one point was *Weisse* with his *Life of Jesus*. Abstract I call the theology of those parties because they have worked through no single theological science, and consequently behave theologically just as they do philosophically. Such abstractions are for themselves often completely true; they are not so, however, in the context of the totality of knowing; for in this they experience limitation by other determinations. Their inspiring unconditionality ceases. Because they are too general, they remain powerless, even if they piled Pelion upon

[p. XXI]

Ossa. Is it not remarkable how all four opponents of the Hegelian system agree also in this, in proclaiming *love*? The Hegelian philosophy could do this with the same right; it would not thereby contradict itself. But for science more is at stake than such edifying generalities. When one considers that Schelling and Feuerbach repel each other absolutely, one must still conclude that the love which they preach cannot well be the same; but we would know this only if they built up for us a state, an ethical commonwealth. Now they can, from their abstraction of love, treat the Hegelian state contemptuously, in that they miss love in it; but if it came to concrete determinations, the loftiness of that generality would soon be lost, as we recently experienced with the Concept of marriage.

The Hegelian philosophy has overcome the opposition of pure, i.e. abstract, thinking abstracting from intuiting, and of pure, i.e. abstract, intuition abstracting from thinking; it has in principle really overcome the opposition of reason and actuality, of theory and practice, of ideality and reality, of thinking and being, of subject and object, of the speculative and the empirical, of Idea and history, even if the carrying through of its method through all domains of knowing has made only an imperfect beginning, erroneous in many details. A hostile position against ontology or empiricism, against theory or practice is on the part of philosophy no longer possible at all, only on their part against philosophy, insofar as they still have antiquated representations of philosophizing in their heads and dream up beneath it an esoteric, wondrous procedure. Philosophy must not fall away again from its Concept as the simplest and last form of *science* in general.

[p. XXII]

Without predilection for any object it must traverse the universe with equal justice, for in the system of the All everything hangs together with everything. God is just as great a geometer as he is a good moralist. Hegel therefore had to produce an *Encyclopedia* of the philosophical sciences and successively work through all principal moments of his system, last of all the philosophy of history. His pupils, however, had at first to try their hand at the treatment of particular sciences, whereby the school was swept into the movement of the present and shared all its directions up to the extreme. In art it began romantic and ended hypermodern; in political life it appeared first aristocratic, up to the justification of English Toryism, then democratic, up to the utopian extravagance of French communism; in theology and church first orthodox, up to literalism, then heterodox, up to atheism. Only the person inexperienced in history can be astonished at the development of such extremes and fail to recognize their inner unity, which must behave negatively toward the directions, insofar as they as extremes lay claim to the rank of central principles.

Hegel’s philosophy is in principle too deep and in its design too comprehensive for it already to be completed. If its opponents regard it as already *perished*, that is an illusion with which they flatter themselves, in that they have indeed fallen prey to certain downfall through their one-sidedness. Were Hegel’s philosophy already dead, one would have to be astonished at the vehement polemic with which it is just now being fought by those who declare it to be defunct. A dead cause does not usually meet with such lively contradiction. Because the first epoch of its history is over, it does not yet follow that it is over with it. The downfall of the extremes which it brought forth out of itself in rapid growth

[p. XXIII]

is not a downfall of itself. On the contrary, it now enters into a second, more lasting, more substantive epoch, free of *school-egoism*, which will of course in time also lack neither extremes nor, still less, downfall, but which will have a more objective, calmer character and, after the wild waters of the critical tumult have run off downhill, will bring scientific detail work. As a man, when the world forsakes him, when false friends fall away, when all outward advantages of his situation collapse, when he has to renounce all glitter in whose vain splendor the lazy mass so gladly basks, can show in such isolation whether he has a substance in himself that lets him endure in misfortune and preserves his courage for continued striving, so the Hegelian philosophy has now to show this.

A true philosophy is the deed of a people. Only with it does it prove that it has carried through the process of culture in itself to its last depth and has intuited the Absolute in a form commensurate with its individual self-consciousness. Therefore the philosophy of a people must also speak its own language, because spirit can perceive the actual image of its peculiarity wholly only in its tones. As long as a people has not a philosophy of its own and so long as it does not produce it in its own language, it is not yet truly cultured, were it even, what agrees very well with this, very civilized. But for philosophy, insofar as it is philosophy, the peculiarity of national origin at the same time does not matter at all. Here the universality and necessity of its content and the completion of its proof alone have significance. Whether the true is cognized and pronounced by a Greek or a German, by a Frenchman or an Englishman, has for it itself, as truth, no weight. Every true philosophy is therefore, as national, at the same time a universally human one

[p. XXIV]

and, in the great course of humanity, an indispensable member. It has the capacity of absolute diffusibility through all peoples, and there comes for each the time when it must appropriate the genuine philosophy of the other peoples, if it wants to secure and further its own progress.

Once one has seen this, one will rightly appreciate the relation of the Hegelian philosophy to Germany as well as to foreign countries. It is a genuinely *German* philosophy, in which the Swabian profundity has united with the Prussian acuteness. An exclusively *Prussian* one it is not at all. The distrust of Germany toward it as a means of Prussian lust for dominion has vanished. The suspicion against it as a Prussian state philosophy has dissolved to such an extent that at present hardly anyone will let himself be induced by its study to render himself especially employable. But as German philosophy it is also above all things philosophy, and has thereby awakened the interest of foreign countries too. Strictly speaking, however, this is limited to *France*. In Italy the Curia makes the study of German philosophy impossible through its prohibition; in England people have too much to do practically to engage more specially in it; the *Times* mocked the attention which we devoted to Schelling’s struggle with the Hegelian school in Berlin and thought we were abstruse enthusiasts, for the whole difference between Hegel and Schelling consisted in the end in this, that the first is very obscure and the second still more obscure; in Scandinavia and Denmark German philosophy is accorded a very lively share, which is, however, of a more passive kind, a diligent learning, which through Ebbe Sam. *Bring* at Lund has even called forth an *Ordbok för att befordra Studerandet af Hegels Skrifter* [dictionary to promote the study of Hegel’s writings].

France, however, whatever one may have against it,

[p. XXV]

is that country in which, outside Germany, at present alone a deeper need of philosophy, a more comprehensive knowledge of its literature, an interest not merely learned or utilitarian but also arising from genuinely speculative impulse, prevails.

The French have not only extended the opposition of ideological sensualism and gnostic mysticism into many-membered, great schools; they have done more; they have begun to sublate it in a new direction, which during the Restoration period arose as the so-called eclectic school. At that time, when *Cousin* before an enthusiastic crowd of almost eight hundred young men in the halls of the Collegium du Plessis delivered his lectures on morals and its history; at that time, when the ministry through his dismissal created for him the highest popularity, the glowing devotion of the Parisian youth, the attention and esteem of all noble and liberal-minded; at that time, when he made energetic arrangements to renew the study of Platonic and Cartesian philosophy, the foundation was also first laid by him to a more intimate interaction between French and German philosophy. Whatever weaknesses Cousin may later have shown, this merit will remain to him. The *historical* study of philosophy has been powerfully stimulated by him and from him spread over all academies of France and over all branches of philosophy; *Schelling* and *Hegel* have become better known to the French through him in their connection with *Kant* and *Fichte* and been made into unavoidabilities for philosophical culture.

I do not wish to pursue this topic further here. Only one remark I must still add. Namely, among us Germans at present the relation of our philosophy to the French is in part again quite and utterly distorted. Some younger German writers, through a certain

[p. XXVI]

similarity of their situation, have fallen to renewing the invectives which *Voltaire*, *Diderot*, *d’Alembert* and others hurled against the corrupt theology of the previous century, still more against the moral corruption of the clergy. In that they mixed *Hegel’s* recognition of the courage and spirit of those men from his *History of Philosophy* into their utterances, they have aroused the idea as if Hegel, at bottom, if one only pursued his actual consequence, agreed completely with the *Système de la nature* [System of Nature] as the Bible of atheism. This is a great wrong done to Hegel. In that now that repristination called forth a reaction, one went so far in it as to condemn French philosophy in general again and to overlook the difference that exists between the present and that of the previous century. This is a great wrong done to *Cousin*, his opponent *Leroux*, *Lamennais*, *Bonald*, *Virey*, *Jouffroy*, *Damiron*, *Royer-Collard*, the younger *Bonnet*, *Matter* and so many others. With the dismissive phrases of shallowness and frivolity of the French one can get by only among the ignorant. I therefore lament that serious efforts to make the interchange between German and French philosophy livelier have been at once again condemned among us from the standpoint of a Gallomania. The Augsburg General Gazette has also made me the reproach of *flirting with the French* — because I defended Hegel against *Leroux*. Is that just? Is that a procedure such as befits so serious a concern as philosophy? Thus interaction is already flirtation? When *Schelling* wrote his all too well-known preface to Cousin’s preface, it should have surprised me little if he had been accused of a dalliance with the French, for he praised not only

[p. XXVII]

individual Frenchmen, he extolled not only the scientific seriousness of the French spirit, but set up the French in general as a model especially of philosophical presentation. And now does a pupil of the present Schelling reproach me, who attack a Frenchman, with flirting with the French? In a newspaper which announces to us every praise of Schelling among the French, every translation of one of his writings into French, at once as an event glorious for German philosophy, in a newspaper which even publishes at once Schelling’s letters of thanks to French scholars, such as his letter to *Stanislas Julien*, when the latter had sent him the *Tao-te-king* of *Lao-tseu*. I say this truly not out of envy, as the Augsburger might quickly interpret, for Julien has also presented his excellent book to me. Let us hope that the further development of the community of German and French striving for science can be held up neither by the Augsburg General Gazette nor by the suspicions of the hierarchical-fanatical priest party of southern France.

The Hegelian philosophy is in religious relation essentially *Protestant*. Protestantism I call that shape of religion which grounds the reconciliation of God and man through the certainty that the essence of human self-consciousness has divine self-consciousness for its content and therefore freedom for its form. In and for itself it would indeed be desirable that philosophy be treated first as a science like others, whose results as such concern neither the state nor the church. As little as mathematics is made answerable for it when it discovers a new curve, or zoology when it discovers a new animal, or medicine when it invents a new method of operation, etc., so little ought philosophy

[p. XXVIII]

to be made answerable to the state or the church for its researches; for philosophy too is, as science, independent and dependent on its own necessity. But one knows well how little such independence is granted to it and how the world, when a philosophy is spoken of, strives before all things after its political and ecclesiastical confession of faith, in order to be able to determine its interest for or against it according to the outcome of this. So the Hegelian philosophy too has been looked at for its religiosity, for its Christianity. The Cardinal Secretary Lambruschini declares it accordingly un-Christian; the benefice-rich but knowledge-poor Anglican archbishops declare it, in the darkness of their unphilosophical theology, in thick books to be a dangerous renewal of Brahmanic pantheism; the hierarchical Pietists declare it un-Christian, etc. And yet it has itself always been in the faith of being truly Christian and therefore of having had outside itself still much un-Christianity to combat. It has confessed itself Protestant and will always carry before Protestantism the oriflamme of freedom through the self-cognition and self-willing of the eternally true. For a time it seemed as if *Schelling* would take over this mission from it with greater success. But soon this opinion vanished, because Schelling abstracts too much from the ethical element of religious life and concerns himself too exclusively only with a dogmatics whose doctrine of the Trinity, Christology and Satanology is heretical and whose Concept of the church is negative against all existing churches — a postulate of the future.

The Catholic philosophy will now probably have become aware of its error in abusing Schelling’s authority for itself. *Günther’s Eurystheus and Herakles* has already made the beginning of carefully comparing the positive element of the Schellingian philosophy of revelation with the positive element of the Roman

[p. XXIX]

Church. Against Hegel the polemic of Catholicism has in the end become lachrymose. It has complained of the inhuman tone in which he spoke against Catholicism, and indecorously of the host as of an external thing that is presented for adoration. But I find that this polemic ignores the principal passage of Hegel’s which it would have had to refute. Hegel holds that in Catholicism, from the first and highest relation of man’s externality to God, all the other external, and thereby unfree, unspiritual and superstitious relations flow, and he then continues: “namely a *lay estate*, which receives the *knowledge* of divine truth, as well as the direction of *will* and *conscience*, from without and from another estate, which itself attains to the possession of that knowledge not in a spiritual manner alone, but essentially needs for it an external consecration. Further, the way of praying, in part merely moving the lips, in part spiritless in that the subject renounces the direct direction toward God and *asks* others *to pray* — the direction of devotion to miraculous images, even to bones, and the expectation of miracles through them — in general, justice through external works, a merit that is supposed to be acquired through actions, indeed can even first be transferred to others, etc. — All this binds the spirit under a *being-external-to-itself*, whereby its Concept is misconstrued and perverted in its innermost, and right and justice, ethical life and conscience, accountability and duty are corrupted at their root.”

“To such a principle and such a development of the unfreedom of spirit in the religious there corresponds only a legislation and constitution of legal and ethical unfreedom, and a condition of injustice and unethicality in the actual state. Consistently the Catholic

[p. XXX]

religion has been so loudly extolled as the one, and is still often extolled, by which alone the stability of governments is secured — in truth, of such governments as are bound up with institutions that rest on the unfreedom of the spirit that is supposed to be legally and ethically free, i.e. on institutions of injustice and a condition of ethical corruption and barbarism. These governments, however, do not know that in *fanaticism* they have the fearsome power which for so long, and only on the condition, does not turn against them that they remain captive under the bondage of injustice and immorality. But there is yet another power present in spirit; against that being-external-and-torn-asunder consciousness gathers itself into its inner free actuality; *worldly wisdom* awakens in the spirit of governments and of peoples, i.e. wisdom about what is right and rational *in and for itself* in actuality. Rightly has the production of thinking, and more precisely philosophy, been called worldly wisdom [*Weltweisheit*], for thinking makes the truth of spirit present, leads it into the world, and so frees it in its actuality and in itself.”

These golden words of Hegel’s are the soul of the political and ecclesiastical practice of his philosophy.

Protestantism, and with it Christianity, is at present rising again to a purer, higher shape. The ferment of this progress allows it, indeed, perhaps even allows Christianity, to appear for the moment as having perished. But it frees itself only from its ready-made forms, henceforth dead to it, and thereby gains, for the dead who wish to remain such and are so proud of their unchangeability, the look of instability. Catholicism presents itself again quite strong and stately, and enjoys on the part of governments an infinite delicacy of treatment. While, however, it extends in breadth,

[p. XXXI]

it loses so much the more in depth, and will have to learn by experience that the more intensive is indeed also the more extensive — an experience which history, however, requires time to make. For individuals this necessity is often tragic; they must hold out with resignation in the grim struggle of contradiction. The strength of Protestantism is only apparently threatened by the dissolution of its confessional differences, for it contains the adequate Concept of spirit, itself to be the living unity of truth and of its certainty. A whole people cannot lose its substance overnight. Individuals from it may fall into forgetfulness of the past, into an abstraction from the future unalterably conditioned by it. But a people, be it ever so fragmented within itself, artificially held apart, ever so alienated within itself against itself, ever so charmedly irresolute, is nonetheless an inner, solidary unity. It is so grown together with its nature, with its monuments, its memories, the tendencies handed to it by the world spirit, that, however one may try to push it out of its God-marked path, it is always turned back into it again, to fulfill its destiny. And so there is no need to fear that from the heaven of its history, beside a Lessing, Schiller, Goethe, Kant, Fichte, Hegel too should not shine down upon the German people for ever, blessed, as a holy constellation!

Königsberg, 18 March 1844.

*Karl Rosenkranz.*

### Book One.

[scan 48]

#### Ancestry.

Hegel’s ancestry is, to be sure, immediately a genuinely Swabian one, branching out on all sides into kinship with the Göritzes, the Schnepffs, the Gmelins, etc. But if we follow it back several centuries, the family chronicle leads us to *Carinthia*. A family Bible and a humorous family tree of the Hegel lineage, printed in folio for a wedding feast at Stuttgart on the 27th of August 1720, allow the genealogy to be surveyed in sufficient detail. The founder of the line emigrated for the sake of religion from Carinthia, which in the sixteenth century belonged, together with Graz and Styria, to Archduke Charles, the son of Emperor Ferdinand I (d. 1564) and brother of Emperor Maximilian II (d. 1576). The son of Archduke Charles was Ferdinand II, who later succeeded his childless cousin Matthias on the throne and died in 1637. This line of the Austrian imperial house was the most zealously Catholic, held fast to the statutes of the Council of Trent with grim literalness, and through its oppression of the Protestants occasioned numerous emigrations among them.

It was under this Charles, then, that the pewterer *Johannes Hegel* too, on account of his Protestant confession, turned as an exile from Carinthia to Swabia, for which reason the genealogical wedding poem mentioned above celebrates him with well-deserved praise. He settled in Württemberg at *Großbottwar*, carried on his trade, and knew how to make himself so much at home and so respected there that he was later elected burgomaster of the little town. From this Johannes the whole Hegel family in Württemberg descends. At times it has been very numerous

[p. 4]

and has always remained in the middle class of citizens. Its members were partly craftsmen, partly subaltern officials, but in particular also scholarchs and pastors. Even the pastor who baptized *Schiller* was, according to G. Schwab’s account, a Hegel. Four grandsons of that Johannes, brothers, received in 1643, under Emperor Ferdinand III, a coat of arms from the Count Palatine or Court Count Mattheus Deuring of Mittel-Woyerburg, on account of respectability, honesty, skill, good conduct and virtue. — At present no male descendant of that Johannes is said to be living in Württemberg any longer, and the philosopher *Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel* would thus be the one who transplanted his line from southern to northern Germany.

*Georg Ludwig Hegel*, born 1733, married *Maria Magdalena Fromme* on 29 September 1769. G. W. F. Hegel, born on 27 August 1770, was their eldest son. Among his godparents there was, remarkably enough, also a representative of his calling, the professor of philosophy *Breyer* of Erlangen. Hegel had besides only one sister, *Christiane*, who remained unmarried, and one brother, *Ludwig*, who devoted himself to the military profession, also took part in the Russian campaign, and died unmarried. Hegel’s father was at first secretary of the ducal revenue office, afterwards expedition councillor, and died on 14 January 1799. The mother was, for those times, a woman of much culture, who held her eldest son very dear because he learned so well, and in his fifth year herself taught him the first declension. She died in 1783 of a bilious fever, from which the father, the sister and Hegel himself were at the same time lying gravely ill. The memory of his mother was sacred to Hegel. As late as 20 September 1825 he wrote from Berlin to Christiane: “Today is the anniversary of the death of our mother, which I always keep in remembrance.”

#### Early Youth.

Stuttgart, Hegel’s birthplace, lies in a valley which nevertheless allows the eye a wide prospect and everywhere, above all in the direction of charming Cannstatt, opens up the most delightful walks.

[p. 5]

It is free of the confining constraint which in narrower valleys, surrounded by higher mountain ranges, so easily seizes us. As a capital it affords a view of the totality of human existence and awakens a feeling for the manifoldness of social pleasures. For Hegel, therefore, Stuttgart as a residence has undoubtedly become important in that it at once set against his deep, genuinely Swabian inwardness the counterweight of a direction outward. To the dreamy, ingenious being-within-itself, which so gladly intoxicates itself in the lovely forest solitude, in the secluded valleys of the Alb, there stood opposed at the same time the external breadth, the colorful social stir of the residence and of the court. To this was added the special circumstance that Stuttgart at precisely that time, as the history of *Schiller’s* youthful years shows, developed a deeper spiritual stirring not without a certain sharpness.

Hegel’s boyhood passed quietly and cheerfully, noticeable for nothing out of the ordinary. In his sixth year he had smallpox in its most malignant form. He was thought already lost, and was for several days completely blind. He always had a great inclination to vigorous jumping, but proved awkward and clumsy with the dancing master. In the parental home plain bourgeois comfort and order prevailed. Through the father’s official position many connections with persons of higher station were brought about, and court and politics were also brought early nearer to the children. In our Hegel there developed an all-sided attentiveness, which, quite unintentionally, out of pure drive for cognition, worked in the most various domains with almost equal progress. Brooding reflection sought to get on the track of the essence of things, while the receptiveness of the whole atmosphere led to a steady gathering of new knowledge. Of a poetic nature very early characteristic traits can be told, because such a nature aims at the individualization of all relations. In a thinker’s nature only one trait is characteristic, the reflective dissolving of everything given, so that it gains the appearance as if such a man engaged with something only in order to find out what it really is in itself. The higher universality of self-consciousness manifested itself in Hegel very early

[p. 6]

also in this, that in his writings he used forms of the Swabian stem-dialect only with the addition: “As we Swabians are wont to say.”

However much he was boy with boy, child with children, and loved above all, among his playmates, the friends *Leypold* and *Duttenhofer*, his drive for cognition nevertheless impelled him early to attach himself to older persons, namely to his teachers, whom he accompanied on walks or who also visited his father’s house. Especially favorable to him were, besides others still to be mentioned, the prelate *Abel*, professor at the academy in Stuttgart, later in Tübingen, and the prelate *Griesinger*, from whom he received his confirmation instruction and who also remained his father confessor.

#### Gymnasium.

In his fifth year Hegel attended a so-called Latin school. From his seventh year on he frequented the Gymnasium of his native city and thus remained in uninterrupted contact with the manifold stimulations of the residence. He was thereby preserved from those eccentricities of feeling and fantasy into which precisely the livelier and nobler natures in the Württemberg preparatory institutions for the university, the so-called *lower seminaries*, with their then still monastic arrangement, not seldom tended to fall. Hegel too had at first been meant for the lower seminaries, but the plan was given up, and the father sought to hasten the development of the boy, eager to learn, through private tutors. Among other things he sent the ten-year-old to Colonel *Duttenhofer*, to learn geometry and some astronomy from him. The colonel also took him out through the gate with other boys for field surveying.

At school Hegel was a veritable model pupil and received prizes in every class. On 6 July 1785, when his most beloved teacher *Löffler* died, he himself described the school career he had completed up to that moment in the following words: “I came in the autumn of 1777 to him (Löffler), when he was preceptor of the first lower class. I was thus also with him for the half-year 1778, and since in this year the late Herr Preceptor *Schäffner* had died,

[p. 7]

he advanced in the autumn with us one class further, so that I thus enjoyed his instruction the whole year 1778 and the greater part of 1779. When I left him for my uncle’s, Herr Prelate *Göriz’s* class, I nonetheless had private instruction with him the whole year. Likewise in 1783, when I was a novice in the 5th class under Herr Prof. Naß. In the first private instruction *Lebret* and *Autenrieth* also went along with me, in the second I was quite alone. In the first we construed Curtius, Aesop, the New Testament, namely on Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday from 11 to 12 and 2 to 3. In the second I construed Cicero *de senectute* [On Old Age], *Somnium Scipionis* [Scipio’s Dream], *Laelius de amicitia* [Laelius on Friendship], in Greek, in the New Testament, the epistles to the Thessalonians and that to the Romans, and some Hebrew in the Psalms. Finally also in Vida’s *Christiad*, of which I could recite much by heart.”

Löffler’s influence on Hegel was great in yet another respect. He gave him in 1778, namely, Wieland’s translation of *Shakespeare* with the words: “You do not understand it yet, but you will soon learn to understand it.” *The Merry Wives of Windsor* was the first piece that vividly appealed to the boy.

From 26 June 1785 to 7 January 1787 Hegel kept, now in German, now in the Latin language, a kind of *diary* in a proper quarto volume stitched together from draft paper. By no means is there a report for every day; for weeks, for months on end it records nothing. The greatest attention it devotes to the *progress in cognition* of the Gymnasium pupil; the contemplation of his further life runs along more by the way. A deep ethical feeling breaks through at times; of moral struggles, however, there is no trace. Nevertheless the diary is a proof that Hegel directed himself upon himself. In himself, to be sure, he found nothing special, and for lack of experiential material he used the diary for a time only for perfecting himself in writing Latin. Even the description of a conflagration, at which he was helpfully present with his father, was used by him only for a rhetorical showpiece. If, however, the admirably diligent youth supervised his studies with a certain pedantry and subjected even his methods of work to a careful

[p. 8]

criticism, as in a remarkable essay on so-called *excerpting* written in March 1786; if, sparing of time, he notes down that he had at times taken healthy exercise for an hour, there is yet no lack of testimonies, either, of how openly he gave himself over to the stimulations of life. He attends the court concerts and also takes pleasure in the beautiful girls whom he sees on that occasion. He visits the Catholic church, rejects the cult of the mass, but praises the sermon. A fine horse that is led across the street strikes him. At a social gathering he observes the diversity of interest and the different degree of it. The drunken peasants at the annual fair do not escape him. The Stuttgart superstition about the Furious Host [*das wüthende Heer*] provokes him to anger and scorn; he notes down with satisfaction that an evening concert at Herr von *Türkheim’s* and the escorting of the carriages with torches had given occasion for a renewal of the old delusion, and now exclaims: “*O tempora, o mores!* [O the times, O the customs!] It happened in 1785! Oh! Oh!”

As a prominent feature of these diary notes, Hegel’s ever recurring direction upon the *Concept of history* is to be regarded. Schröckh’s compendium has his great approval for this reason, that it does not stop merely at a nomenclature and chronology, does not merely recount battles in which a couple of hundred men hacked about, but because it also turns to the interests of culture. He is glad to get a concept, if at first an obscure and one-sided one, of *pragmatic* history. He wants to investigate which passions agitate men most violently. The reading of *Livy* makes an epoch for him. He arrives at the thought that something could be done for the *enlightenment of the common man*, but holds this to be very difficult, and makes himself in particular the objection that for such an undertaking he had not yet studied history *philosophically*. His judgment is determined very early, precisely in historical matters, and already in 1785 there occur in it utterances which set him in conflict with those of his teachers. Thus Professor *Offerdinger* had explained in class the sacrifice of a cock by Socrates to Aesculapius from the unconsciousness with which the poison had already filled Socrates. That was

[p. 9]

quite in the essence of the epoch of that time, which wanted to have Socrates free of all superstition. Hegel too was wholly gripped by the principle of Enlightenment and did not dare to deny away entirely the weakening of consciousness by the poison, but thought nonetheless that Socrates had, besides this cause, also reflected that, because it was the custom, he did not wish, by omitting this slight gift, quite to affront the rabble.

In the very conception, the reflection on contradiction appears characteristic, e.g. that every good has also its evil side, or that a man dies at the moment in which he is still bringing the spoon with soup to his mouth for his self-preservation. He makes it in particular a reproach to his age that it so often prides itself on the height of its culture and enlightenment and on account of its superstition disparages antiquity, while yet the belief in angels and devils is only a reproduction of the antique belief in demons, which the Enlightenment itself treats as illusion. And so one indeed no longer sacrifices immediately to the gods, but one makes gifts in Christianity, among Catholics and Lutherans, to the priests, in order to work through them upon God, which is an even greater superstition, an even greater folly.

Toward the female or, as he says, weaker sex the diligent pupil assumes a more indifferent attitude. He does not avoid it, any more than he excludes novels from his reading, since indeed he cannot at all tear himself loose from *Sophie’s Journey*. But neither does he exactly seek out female society. In general he holds it to be necessary, because only through it can the *dross* of social culture be cast off, for women, he thought, have the *monopoly* of praise and blame.

Anything that could be called an action or event does not occur at all in this diary. In December 1785 Hegel had exerted himself greatly for an examination, fell ill, got a large abscess on the neck, and had to let himself finally, after he had endured much pain, be operated on under the direction of the physician *Consbruch*. In his circle there appear, after Löffler’s death, chiefly the professors *Hopf* and *Cloß*. Löffler’s

[p. 10]

death was in fact for him, next to the death of his beloved mother, the most shattering event of his Gymnasium time, and he wrote about it in July 1785 in his diary: “Herr Preceptor *Löffler* was one of my most venerable teachers; especially in the lower Gymnasium I may boldly call him almost the most excellent. He was the most upright and most impartial man. To his pupils, to be useful to themselves and to the world, was his chief concern. He did not think so basely as others, who believe: now they have their bread and need study no further, if only they can carry on the eternal, yearly renewed classroom routine. No, not so thought the blessed man! He knew the worth of the sciences and the comfort which they afford one in various mishaps. How often, and how contented and cheerful, he sat with me in that beloved little room, and I with him. — Few knew his merits. It was a great misfortune for the man that he had to work so wholly beneath his sphere. And now he too has fallen asleep! But eternally shall I bear his memory unmoved in my heart.”

#### Reading, and His Method in It.

Hegel’s culture was, on the side of principle, one thoroughly of the *Enlightenment*, on the side of study one belonging thoroughly to *classical antiquity*. The language of the Greeks and Romans made up the marrow of the instruction at the Gymnasium. With *mathematics*, on the other hand, we find Hegel more occupied privately. But to the ancients too he devoted, besides school, great private diligence. Thus from the winter of 1786 to September 1787 he produced, in private instruction, a complete translation, still preserved, of the treatise of *Longinus*, *On the Sublime*. His immediate inclination was livelier toward Greek than toward Latin, for which reason he applied a greater exertion to the latter, in order not to remain behind in it. His manifold reading gave his Latin style a certain studied quality of expression; he liked himself in rare, less usual phrases.

[p. 11]

The ancient *authors* he held in very high esteem and laid out for himself a still extant *catalogue* of those which were in his possession. Not only the more significant are noted in it, but also such as do not exactly tend to lie within the pupil’s horizon. Quite in the manner of a librarian he gave, in various columns, first the complete title of the edition, then the place of printing and the year, finally the price the book had cost him. The money for such purchases he also took, according to his diary, from his *pocket money*. The auction of the library of his dear teacher Löffler led him especially into such temptation. Acquaintances such as that with the antiquarian bookseller *Betulius*, the closer attachment to the professors of the Gymnasium, the visit to and use of the ducal library had to nourish his literary sense and early procure it a great expansion.

For the domestic reading of the authors Hegel made careful *preparations*, which have in part been preserved. 1785, 31 October, he began the preparation for the *Psalms*; 1786, from 3 July on, he collected *unknown* words from the war songs of *Tyrtaeus*; 1786, 10 July, he began the preparation for the *Iliad*, 14 November for *Cicero’s* letters *ad Familiares* [to his friends]; 1787, from 1 June on, *Euripides* appeared; 1788 from May the *Ethics* of *Aristotle* and from 29 July the *Oedipus* at Colonus of *Sophocles*. Of other preparations still extant the time cannot be determined; thus a very detailed one on *Theocritus* may also fall in the later time of the Tübingen studies. The reading of *Sophocles* he continued uninterruptedly for some years. He also translated him into German and later, probably in consequence of his acquaintance with *Hölderlin*, tried to render metrically not only the dialogue but even the choruses, which, however, did not succeed particularly well. Most fully he occupied himself, as the translations still preserved show, with the *Antigone*, which for him represented most completely the beauty and depth of the Greek spirit. His enthusiasm for the sublimity and grace of the ethical pathos in this tragedy remained the same throughout his whole life. — From 5 April 1786 he translated the *Encheiridion* of Epictetus.

[p. 12]

To this he copied out the Greek text himself chapter by chapter, so that the preserved manuscript, in the alternation of Greek and German script, looks somewhat variegated. — There is also still extant, for a considerable part of *Thucydides*, the manuscript of a translation, which, however, in all probability falls only in the time when Hegel lived in Bern. — A translation of the *Agricola* of *Tacitus* has been lost.

This philological culture, although the center of the Gymnasium education, brought about nevertheless in Hegel no one-sided direction upon the linguistic and the antiquarian, but attained in him its true purpose, to open the sense for *humanity* and to learn to understand the state-founding and state-directing, the poetizing and thinking free human being. Early penetrated by the nobility and the beauty of Hellenism, Hegel was never able to acknowledge genuine Christianity in a form which excludes from itself the seriousness of antique serenity. The universality of his study of antiquity, moreover, enabled him not only to a deeper understanding, but also preserved him from a false deification of it.

In Hegel’s further reading it is noticeable that he read, very early, *literary periodicals*: the *Swabian Museum*, the *General German Library*, the *Library of the Fine Arts and Sciences*, etc. He gained thereby a *critical coolness*, which knows how to grasp an object from the most various sides, to judge it, and to take part for himself in it according to these various relations. What one calls, in the young, unseemly anticipation of a later standpoint, precocious cleverness, did not take place there. It was in fact the ripeness of early thoughtfulness. The naivety of his depth protected Hegel from all affectation, which was foreign to himself his whole life long and also disagreeable in others.

In his reading he now proceeded as follows. Everything that seemed to him noteworthy — and what did not seem so to him! — he wrote on a single leaf, which he marked above with the general rubric under which the particular content had to be subsumed. In the middle of the upper margin he then wrote in large letters, not seldom in Fraktur script,

[p. 13]

the catchword of the article. These leaves themselves he arranged again for himself in alphabetical order and was by means of this simple device in a position to use his excerpts at any moment. In all his moving about he always preserved these incunabula of his culture. They lie partly in folders, partly in slipcase boxes, on whose backs an orienting label is pasted.

One of the largest of these collections of excerpts concerns *philology and literary history*. In the Latin language there is treated here of the life, the writings and the editions of almost all antique authors, and the rarer ones too occur in it, as e.g. *Polyaenus’s* book on the stratagems of famous generals. Occasionally the extracts swell into little books; thus e.g. Brunk’s notes on Sophocles are copied out completely. — Another collection concerns *aesthetics*. In the articles Epic, Didactic Poem, Novel, etc., there appear here all the favorite writers of that time: *Rammler*, Dusch, Lessing, Wieland, *Engel*, *Eberhard* and others. Especially extensively are Dusch’s letters on the formation of taste and *Wieland’s* discussion of the Horatian epistles exploited. *Klopstock’s* odes are found for the most part copied out. A collection of *album maxims* of 1786 and of witty points of roguish humor, such as Hegel always loved, is also to be counted here. — A fragment attempts an analysis of the republican tragedy *Fiesko*. — *Gottsched’s* Kernel of German Grammar is almost wholly copied out, and even a *lexicon* of the idioms of the German language in its various dialects, evidently compiled by himself, is not lacking.

Another fairly rich division bears the title: *Experiences* and Physiognomy. — Here *Zimmermann* on Solitude, *Meiners’s* Letters on Switzerland, *Wünsch’s* Cosmological Conversations, *Rousseau’s* Confessions and *Nicolai’s* Travels in Germany have chiefly supplied the material. From the last in particular the whole characterization of the various German tribal physiognomies, the Bavarian, Brandenburg, Tyrolean, Viennese, etc., is extracted. Physiognomy was then the order of the day and formed in it, for all the play, yet a deeper element, for in order

[p. 14]

to grasp spirit rightly in its appearance, one had in the end to go into its essence as well.

Still other divisions are arranged according to the particular sciences. *Arithmetic*, *geometry* and *applied mathematics* are taken chiefly from Kästner’s writings; — Hegel’s school notebooks on geometry, mechanics and optics are moreover also still extant in very clean and orderly condition. — Among the leaves on physics there is found the *theory of colors* from Scheuchzer’s *Physica*, Zurich 1729, cut out. — For *psychology* Campe’s *Doctrine of the Soul for Children*, for *morals* Garve and Ferguson play a great role. In *pedagogy* long excerpts are devoted to the ideal of the *house tutor*, and *Schlözer’s Staatsanzeigen* [State Gazette] are extensively used. Many determinations of what is just and what is virtuous Hegel has set down categorically from Plato, Aristotle, Tacitus and Cicero in the original passages. — In the *philosophical* history an extract from *Meiners’s* History of Humanity is to be noted. — For *natural theology* as well as for *positive* theology the sources of the extracts are almost always the critical journals.

*Philosophy* has likewise a division of its own. Since the *connection* is too essential for philosophy, it would not go with the alphabetical dismemberment, and Hegel began to extend the excerpts to whole books. Thus Locke’s, Hume’s and Kant’s works are found extensively excerpted, though probably only from the academic time. The study of Kant’s *Critique of Reason*, at least, falls with certainty only in the year 1789. At the Gymnasium *Sulzer* seems to have been the guide for the *encyclopedic* survey, whose brief *Compendium of All the Sciences* was then very popular generally. — The first trace of a more explicit direction toward philosophy is found in a little notebook begun on 10 June 1785 with the title: *Definitions* of Various Objects. The first two definitions concern *superstition* and *beauty*, the third *philosophizing*, i.e. “to press on to the ground and inner constitution of human concepts and cognitions of the most important truths.” This

[p. 15]

definition is borrowed from a book of *Schröckh’s*! The following one, from *Mendelssohn’s Phaedo*, describes the concept of change: “a thing is called changed when, of two opposed determinations that can belong to it, the one ceases and the other begins to be actual.” *Logic* is defined as: “a compendium of the rules of thinking, abstracted from the history of humanity.” The concept of states is taken from *Cicero’s Somnium Scipionis*, ch. III, as: “*concilia coetusque hominum, jure sociati* [assemblies and gatherings of men, joined together by law].” etc. A great part of the definitions is taken from a now wholly obscure writer, *Rochau*.

#### Writings from the Gymnasium Years.

The unsparing immersion in everything worth knowing, the full devotion to the instruction offered, did not suppress Hegel’s spontaneity but was rather a work of it. The passive self-surrender in *learning* was only the reverse side of the restless self-activity dwelling in him. The greater this was, the more strictly did he subject himself to the *discipline* of taking foreign representations and thoughts into himself *unaltered* by his reflection.
