For this, *copying out* was for him the foremost means, of which he made use his whole life long. It is boundless what he appropriated in this way, and one hardly comprehends how he, since he never withdrew from society, was able to find the time for it. In later years he made, namely, from the *Morning Chronicle*, the *Reviews*, the *Courier*, the *Constitutionnel*, the *Journal des débats*, the Jena Literary Gazette, and still in Berlin from the *Morgenblatt* [Morning Paper] and its *Kunstblatt* [art supplement], such extracts. But *whole books* too he never ceased to excerpt as soon as they seemed to him important, and there are still extant, even from later times, his extracts from *Creuzer’s Symbolism*, from the first volume of *Schleiermacher’s Doctrine of Faith*, from *Haller’s Restoration of the Political Sciences*, from the writings of the Petersburg astronomer *Schubert*, etc., as monuments of his iron diligence. For the sake of precision he always added to the excerpt the *source*.

[p. 16]

Through the copying out he penetrated into the finest fibers of what was foreign and attained to being able to transpose himself into any, even the most individual standpoint and to speak its own terminology. In criticism he therefore understood so masterfully “to place himself within the circle of the opponent” and to develop his view *as if it were his own*. This power of self-surrender also drew upon him manifold misunderstanding, in that superficial and fleeting readers confused such objective incarnation of Hegel’s with himself and often charged him with what he was precisely combating.

To *style* he devoted great attention from early on, and what one is wont to call a good style, ease of expression, he possessed in his youth in high degree. Only later, in the struggle with the deepest Ideas, did the smoothly flowing stream vanish. The *striking* force, however, was at no time denied him. So comprehensive a reading and so careful an appropriation of it, manifold exercises at the Gymnasium, occupations such as the translation of *Longinus*, could hardly remain without fruit in this respect. At the Gymnasium there were exercises in oratory in the Latin language. From Hegel there is still left one such, *de utilitate poeseos* [on the usefulness of poetry], without date and without particular remarkableness. Besides, German essays were read aloud by the author in class, which was called *delivering* or *declaiming*. With this, however, it never wanted to succeed with Hegel. His whole life long the complaint renewed itself with him that his oral presentation was very defective, and the regret over it grew the stronger as the excellence of what was spoken itself could not be mistaken. Also in the Tübingen seminary testimonial Hegel was designated as: *orator haud magnus* [no great orator]. How often, therefore, was there not talk against his speech, and whoever knew nothing to say against his system at least disparaged his delivery. Hegel gesticulated much, but the bodily gesture as well as the movement of the voice did not coincide harmoniously enough with the content. In the one who can master presentation outwardly, *because he is finished with the matter*, no inhibition occurs between the inner and the utterance. His feeling, representing and thinking

[p. 17]

passes momentarily into his speaking. With Hegel there always remained in this process a residue, even when he had previously put the speech on paper. He *produced* the content *always anew* and could therefore, even for the moment, always make it only *relatively finished*. This struggle with presentation, to find the last, penetrating expression that leaves nothing behind, this unceasing seeking, this fullness of possibility, made it harder for him with the years, the richer his culture, the more many-sided his thinking, and the more conditioned his position by its greatness, not only speaking in general but also writing, and one can see in particular nothing more hacked up, nothing more struck out, continually rewritten, than a Hegelian draft of a letter from the Berlin period. If Lessing has it said of the art of the painter that the way from the head to the hand is so far, this can be said of Hegel of tongue and hand. His *handwriting* firmed up already in 1786 and shows an unhalting flow and great distinctness of the individual letters. To each its due is given in complete distinction. The connection has nothing blurring or fusing. Only in the *Jena* period does a frequent emending and abbreviating begin. Beside the powerful larger script appears a smaller one, also swaying up and down in the line, pressing the letters together and passing from the round stroke into a pointed form. *Most beautifully* Hegel wrote *French*. There are still some extracts from *Rousseau* extant which may very well be seen as calligraphy. — It would be ridiculous to see an *advantage* in the heaviness of Hegel’s oral diction, but it would at the same time be unjust not to find the ground of the momentary incongruity between content and expression in him, apart from the organism, also in his spirit, so hard to satisfy.

There are still left some works of Hegel’s from the Gymnasium time, which give an idea of how he shaped for himself the mass of thoughts which he took into himself through his extensive reading. The oldest, first product of Hegelian authorship at all is a declamation delivered, still before the beginning of the diary, on 30 May 1785: a *conversation* between

[p. 18]

*three*, namely Antonius, Octavius and Lepidus, concerning the triumvirate. The reading of Shakespeare is visible enough, but there is nonetheless in the simple dialogue, namely in the depiction of Octavius’s self-feeling, much originality, much naive decisiveness. The teacher judged this German piece of work with the following Latin words: “[Latin] You have rendered, quite skillfully and in conformity with Roman history, the characters of this triumvirate, and you join to the exposition a style commendable for accuracy and ease.” — Then there is found again only, from the year 1787, the 10th of August, an essay: *on the Religion of the Greeks and Romans*, which is very extensive and on the whole breathes the spirit of humanity of the age of that time. The conclusion presses *tolerance* toward dissenters, because to fall into errors is so easy and we would therefore seldom ascribe them to malice and ignorance. “This should make us attentive, as regards our inherited and propagated opinions, *to examine even those* against which no doubt, no suspicion ever came to our mind that they might perhaps be wholly false or only half true.” The teacher was quite well satisfied with the matter itself, but the delivery had to be censured: “[Latin] if to elocution there should be added eloquence of the body and firmness of voice, you would not stand badly at the lectern.” — On 7 August 1788 Hegel delivered a treatise: *on some characteristic differences of the ancient poets*, it must be added, *from our present ones*. The originality and simplicity of the ancients, their unreserved candor toward a public, was set forth with much delicacy. Hegel cited here for the first time the *Lessing* verses, which we find repeatedly in his papers during the Tübingen period, that the ancients

cold book-learning, which, with dead signs, / Merely presses itself into the brain,

did not know, but in all that they knew could also say:

How? Where? Why? they had learned it.

With this work too Professor Hopf was very satisfied, called it “[Latin] a specimen of his own prowess and a *happy omen of things to come*,” but did not fail to add the old complaint: “[Latin] see to it that the *declamation* corresponds to the composition.”

[p. 19]

On leaving the Gymnasium, in the autumn of 1788, Hegel delivered in the public assembly of teachers and pupils a farewell speech, in which he paid the institution a very fine compliment by *depicting the stunted condition of the arts and sciences under the Turks* and making from there the transition to how much better it is to be educated at the Stuttgart Gymnasium. The reverential and ceremonious manner with which he was wont, his whole life long, to make his debut on such occasions presents itself here already completely. The sincerity and thoroughness of his piety and of his, so to speak, official conscience satisfied itself only in a certain exhausting breadth. After he had shown here that the wretched condition of the arts and sciences among the Turks lay not in the lack of talent but in the lack of interest in their cultivation on the part of the state, he concluded:

“So great an influence, then, has education on the whole welfare of a state! How strikingly do we see in this nation the terrible consequences of its neglect. If we consider the natural capacities of the Turks and then the crudeness of their character and what they achieve in the sciences, *we*, by contrast, shall learn to recognize and duly appreciate our high good fortune that Providence let us be born in a state whose prince, convinced of the importance of education and of the general and widespread utility of the sciences, makes both the object of his especial high solicitude, and has founded for his glory also on this side lasting and unforgettable monuments, which a late posterity will still admire and bless. Of these excellent sentiments and this zeal for the welfare of the fatherland the most eloquent proof, and the one that concerns us most closely, is — the arrangements of this institute, at the foundation of which lies the sublime view of educating for the state, for its needs, useful and serviceable members. That the arrangements are perfected in every possible way and kept upright and flourishing for all time, this we have to thank, after *Karl*, above all you, most venerable men. These, your unremitting efforts, everyone to whom the happiness of his fatherland is important must revere with the most heartfelt gratitude.

[p. 20]

But especially have we at present, before all, the most pressing reasons to surrender our hearts wholly to the feelings of gratitude toward the high patrons and superintendents of this institute. Thanks to you for the inestimable and countless benefactions which have flowed to us from our tender age on, through your favor, in this house consecrated to the sciences and to education. Thanks especially for the most gracious reception into the higher institutions destined for our further culture, where under your wise guidance and beneficent supervision we shall continue and complete our career on a new path. Here it is a duty to render public and heartfelt thanks also to you, dearest teachers. Thanks to you for the instruction in everything that is worth knowing, for the guidance to everything that is good and noble. Thanks to you also for your paternal correction of our manifold faults. Forgive us, venerable leaders of our youth, our transgressions against your admonitions aimed at our best, whose wisdom the inexperienced youth does not always know how to appreciate.

You, however, best friends and fellow students, who are still engaged on the very course which we have in part gone in your company and have just now left behind, be assured that we are in part already now, too late for the past, learning to see what consequences every inattention to the warnings of our teachers and superiors has, to our disadvantage, and that we shall be ever more convinced of this truth with the growth of our experience and our riper knowledge. — The feeling of the importance of your vocation will give you ever new courage and gradually a love for your occupation, which will reward you through more manifold, more genuine and more lasting pleasure and happiness than the finest inventions of sensuality can ever afford. Let us together form the firm resolve, through diligence and good conduct, to make ourselves worthy of this solicitude and these benefactions. Thank with us the most gracious Being that it bestowed on our youth precisely these teachers and these educators. Let us ask Providence that it may bless and reward your efforts; may it ever strengthen your powers and health and

[p. 21]

let your years reach the farthest goal of human age. The glad consciousness of the much good accomplished and the tranquil looking back on the years that have passed — the reward of a life marked with deeds —, the pleasant fruits which from your efforts already in part ripen, which you will in part still see blossom, the blessings of all the upright, may they sweeten for *you* the burdens of the advancing years, and with the most cheerful serenity may you look toward the eternity that requites all.”

#### Hegel’s Peculiarities.

The history of a philosopher is the history of his *thinking*, the history of the formation of his system. What with other individuals appears, in an external breadth, in the entanglement of many persons and circumstances, as deeds — these are with him the thoughts. With Hegel the external course of life is extremely simple. There is little to say of it. He associated constantly with many good and noble people, but without coming into significant conflicts, into personally especially interesting relations. In Germany’s and Europe’s fate he took the most heartfelt part, but here too he was never a lever of events. As oral teacher, as writer, he brought forth in gradual growth one of the most extraordinary effects, without, however, as Fichte still did, occasioning thereby special catastrophes of his fate. In love without Abelardian romanticism, in politics without Baconian ambition, in religion without Spinozistic misfortune, in intercourse without Leibnizian absent-mindedness, in teaching without Fichtean collision, he remained, without noisy appearance, always dedicated to the strictest service of *science*. Since this constituted the *essence* of his *individuality*, he lacked, so to speak, for other spheres of impulse and of art, any occasion to lay stress on his individuality, on his self. Politics attracted him mightily, but a practical intervention in it remained for him, as deed, always remote.

When Hegel left Stuttgart, the type of his personality was already firmly stamped, and it has remained true to itself throughout his whole life.

[p. 22]

Even in the diction of his youthful attempts the attentive reader will not fail to notice some favorite turns of phrase and constructions which he constantly retained. Some things were, to be sure, set down in Berlin to Hegel as individual which were merely *Swabian* generally and which, so long as Hegel lived more in southern Germany, struck nobody as remarkable in him: that plain, bourgeois way of conducting oneself, that intuitive naivety, that meaningful way of speaking, that purely factual and honest intelligence. His true peculiarity was the highest energy of cognition in union with the greatest personal independence from himself, whereby he came to let other human beings and things too stand as independent of him and to treat them quite objectively. *To present* himself *as a philosopher*, to emphasize his study in particular, never occurred to him at all. At most he made fun of it with amiable irony. In intercourse, in immediate appearance, he was the whole *human being*. Depictions of the philosopher *as he ought to be*, a painting out of the loftiness of his sentiments, etc., bored him early on, and still shortly before his death (*Works*, vol. XVII, p. 231), he expressed himself on it to the effect that the old philosophers indeed still had to go back to the subjective. “But modern philosophy goes upon principles that are of a more concrete nature — and contain not merely an abstract foundation but also themselves the determination and development within themselves; hence such a depiction of the subject of philosophizing is idle, and exposed to a censure of another kind, at least to a Horatian jest about the sage who is happy, rich, indeed a king — except when catarrh afflicts him.” — Hegel therefore always and everywhere conformed to the prevailing custom and fashion. To want to show peculiarity in such things seemed to him not worth the trouble. With this way of thinking he soon made himself at home everywhere.

Accustomed to seek in philosophy the solution of the contradictions that tormented him, he remained reconciled with life and therefore also appeared in intercourse not *choosy*. With countless people from the most various classes of society he has had friendly ties. We have thus found him at the

[p. 23]

Gymnasium; we shall find him just so at the university and still in advanced age, where attaching oneself becomes more difficult. North German sensibility and pretension was foreign to his easygoing openness, and significant phenomena of the North German cast of mind, e.g. *Hamann* and *Solger*, he could comprehend only as *hypochondriac*. If, however, he did not avoid even the ordinary in social gatherings, he nonetheless made throughout the demand of sound human understanding, of ethical soundness, in general of genuine humanity. One has often wondered in Berlin that Hegel did not isolate himself more sharply and was also able to form lasting social relations with less significant people. But this judgment of insignificance is just quite a relative one, for *what is humanly attractive* lies surely not alone in scientific or artistic culture or even in high rank. And Hegel sought, precisely for intercourse outside himself, not philosophy as such, but congeniality, affection and gracious diversion. The straining up of personal relations, that exquisite *cult of individuality*, as it so often emerged with the sweet flattery of aristocratic friendships in the last third of the preceding century, and of which Hegel in his relation to *Hölderlin* had partly himself had experience, was irksome to him. He shrank from falling prey, even under the noblest form, to a frustrating aesthetic bliss.

He had two peculiarities. They were, however, themselves of a sociable kind. He *took snuff* heavily and played, from early youth on, in the paternal home, gladly *chess* and *cards*, in which he thus was in harmony with *Kant*. In earlier years he often played l’hombre and tarok, in Berlin usually whist. At Frankfurt in 1798 he wrote down the following remark on card playing itself: “Inclination to card playing is a main trait in the character of our time. *Understanding* and *passion* are the properties of the soul which are active in it. The former seeks out the rules and applies them as power of judgment at every moment. Hence people of deep reason and brilliant imagination are often bad players, not merely because they could not interest themselves in the game, but because their power of judgment is often not so practiced in the constant application of rules to daily life. Passion is

[p. 24]

what chiefly gives interest. For the cool player, who at the same time does not play out of greed for gain, card playing has interest especially from the side of understanding and power of judgment, as an exercise of them. Otherwise, however, besides the desire for gain, the alternation of passion in fear and hope is the circumstance that makes card playing so universal: a spirit that cannot possibly subsist together with tranquility of the heart, which has something sublime in itself, which all Greek works breathe amid all play of passion, and which, in the highest swing of passion, so long as man is still man and is not scourged by a demon, still shows itself mighty. This passionate, restless mood of spirit is what characterizes our age, and to it card playing too owes its diffusion. As in the interest of passion, so too in that activity of the understanding that occurs in it, even if it is found in the player alone, not a spark of an ingredient of reason is present. — Hence, even in an otherwise innocent game, nothing is more striking to us than to hear the name of God mentioned in relation to it. For much as we in general let Providence take part even in the smallest things, especially in such as seem to us to belong to the domain of chance (above all in games of hazard, where often the fortune of a not wicked, perhaps only misled man and his family hangs on a few cards), just so much does it strike us to be reminded of it in this connection.”

The same unassuming, yet, in its unconsciousness, all the more captivating inconspicuousness of his person, to which the inner emphasis was indeed not lacking, showed itself also in Hegel’s immediate surroundings, in the furnishing of his rooms. He was concerned there only for the practical. All arts of impressing thereby were despised by him. He did not at all think of such effect-seeking through a sterile nimbus. His simple writing table, with the picturesque disorder of his notebooks, letters and snuffboxes, has become world-famous for it.

We now accompany Hegel to the university. In *autumn* he went to Tübingen, in autumn to Bamberg, in autumn to Nuremberg, in autumn to Heidelberg, in autumn to Berlin and in autumn — he died; one of those strange traits of human fate for which one would gladly discover in individuality itself a

[p. 25]

ground, and would accordingly have to call Hegel a replete, harvesting nature of autumn.

#### The University of Tübingen.

Hegel, *consecrated to theology*, as the then current expression of the land went, attended the national university of Tübingen. He enjoyed the special advantage, as ducal *stipendiary*, of living entirely free of care and, as *Seminarist*, of being able to rejoice in an exemplary, more precise guidance of his studies. The theologian *Schnurrer*, d. 1822, issued to Hegel on 27 October 1788 the matriculation certificate, which, according to the usage of the time, contained the written undertaking, issued in lieu of an oath, concerning the police regulations of conduct, in 9 concisely drawn-up Latin provisions. According to Hegel’s still extant, very well transcribed lecture notebooks, he heard in 1788–89 with Schnurrer, who at that time gave a new impulse to exegesis, history of the Apostles and the first part of the Psalms; in the summer semester of 1789 with the same the second part of the Psalms and the Catholic epistles; with *Flatt* on Cicero *de natura Deorum* [On the Nature of the Gods]. In the winter semester of 1789–1790 he heard with *Rösler* history of philosophy and in the summer of 1790 with *Flatt*: metaphysics and natural theology. In the properly theological course of 1790–93 he heard almost only with *Storr*, a very worthy, very orthodox, but no less dry man, the Gospels of Luke, Matthew, John, the Epistle to the Romans and other epistles, and besides these dogmatics. — On his own he went through a course in *anatomy*. — For several years he was tormented by a tertian fever, which even forced him for a time to interrupt his academic studies. He spent several months of his recovery in the paternal house and occupied himself here, besides with his beloved Greek tragedians, chiefly with *botany*.

*Flatt*, who died only in 1821, is well to be noted as Hegel’s teacher, inasmuch as he belonged to the most acute and most liberal opponents of the Kantian system. The Wolffian logic

[p. 26]

had Hegel, as he himself relates (*Works*, vol. XVII, p. 364), already from his fourteenth year, the definitions of the *idea clara* [clear idea] already from his twelfth year, completely mastered. We find no evidence that he attended lectures on logic at the university. Yet this may rest on an accidental circumstance. *Ploucquet*, that is, the real logician and metaphysician, was indeed still alive, but perhaps no longer lectured, and died in 1790 — Ploucquet, the *calculator* in logic, the sharpest contrast to the later logician Hegel. If Flatt stood between the Wolffian and the Kantian philosophy and, together with a dying culture, also handed down the new one that emerged from it, so *Rösler*, the editor of the *Library of the Church Fathers*, whom, however, they let lecture on church history only once and only in a very compendious fashion, likewise stood between orthodoxy and heterodoxy, and must have been a not unwelcome teacher for the youth, already so deeply infected by the tendencies of the Enlightenment.

On the whole, however, Hegel found little satisfaction in the academic instruction, as emerges from a letter to *Schelling*. A great deal contributed to this, no doubt, the monastic character and the pedantry of the theological seminary, of the so-called *Stift*, beautifully situated on the Neckar. The students, who lived in this former Augustinian monastery under the special supervision of professors and Repetents, formed a peculiar world among the university students. In the town they were called the *Stiftler* [Stift students] or also, jokingly, from their strictly supervised dress, the *Black Ones*. During meals sermons were delivered, and the speaker got better fare. Hegel too had to preach. But not only was his pulpit delivery, according to his sister’s report, soft and halting, but his *sermons* themselves too seem to have been only *opera operata* [mere routine performances]. On 10 January 1792 he preached on Isaiah 61, 7 and 8; on the second Sunday after Trinity 1793 on Matthew V, 1–16; of the sermon on the Friday of Philip and James 1793 there exists only the detailed disposition on a theme without indication of the text, and finally, without text and date, a very carefully thought-out sermon on *placability*. There prevails in it the driest moral interpretation of Christianity, and the thoroughness with which the concepts of duty are set out is unable to compensate for the excessive

[p. 27]

sobriety, which is conventional only at the beginning and end and somewhat fades away.

To be sure, other work was also done in the Stift, but of this, together with the Repetent’s corrections, only the first one of *free choice*, from December 1788, has been preserved, and this is moreover a new edition, altered almost only in its theory, of the last school declamation of 7 August, with only an altered title: “*On some advantages which the reading of the ancient classical Greek and Roman writers affords us.*” Toward the end the following remarkable passage has been added: “From the series and the spirit of the surviving writings we can abstract a complete history of the culture of the Greeks and Romans, and many other phenomena, too, can thereby be set in a clearer light. To give an example, much in the culture, the habits, mores and customs of the *Israelite* people, which had and still have much influence on us, can thence be explained more naturally and made more comprehensible. For the human spirit was at all times in general *the same*, only that its development is variously modified by the diversity of circumstances. — Finally, since the works of the ancients, as has already been said, are so eminently serviceable for the acquisition of concepts, one sees what an appropriate preparation for the *study of philosophy* the reading of them is. One thereby brings along at any rate a stock of abstract concepts and an at least somewhat exercised power of thought, especially since for many parts of this science they contain at least the seed and the first grounds, which in more recent times have chiefly been set out more clearly, developed and more closely determined. The many contradictions of the ancient philosophers, especially in the speculation on the practical part of worldly wisdom, have at least lightened the labor of finding the *middle way* where the truth lies.”

[p. 28]

#### Student Life.

Of Hegel’s student days there have survived, among the year-mates with whom he lived together, a few traditions, themselves already dying out with them, which were communicated in the *Zeitung für die elegante Welt* [Newspaper for the Elegant World] of 1839, nos. 35–37, and from which the following is to be inserted here: “In the Stift there are at present circulating only a few recollections of Hegel (e.g. that he is said to have worked a great deal at night, and the like). Not even about the room which he occupied are there certain and consistent reports. One knows only that, prompted by Schelling, he moved for some time into the latter’s room. Hegel’s year-mates and fellow members of the Stift have now for the most part gone down into the grave. Only a few still live, scattered through all the districts of Swabia, as aged pastors. One of those year-mates, a ragged genius in the little town of Pfullingen not far from Tübingen, told me on what intimate terms he had stood with Hegel, how they had conversed daily with one another, how they, in order to make use of the morning hours, had agreed with one another to wake each other, and how he who had slept through the waking had had to give the other, as a punishment, his portion of cloister wine from the midday meal. In company Hegel had made himself a well-liked companion through his joviality. He had also not disdained to attend, now and then, merry carousals at which sacrifice was made to Bacchus. In general he had behaved somewhat in the manner of a genius, so that his morality had been better than his legality. As for Hegel’s scholarly course of formation, he had, especially at the beginning of his career in the Stift, worked little, done nothing at all for theology, at most read his Kant, but spent most of his time at the game of tarock. While at that time a society of young Kantians had formed in the Stift, Hegel had read Rousseau and in the realm of knowledge had undertaken only aimless forays. As a special curiosity he further adduced that Hegel had found great pleasure in the Book of Job, on account of its unregulated language of nature. An event, however, had completely transformed Hegel and had become the most secret mainspring of the great metamorphosis which from then on had taken place in him.

[p. 29]

For there prevails in the Stift the old custom of ranking within the individual year-groups. In Württemberg ranking is carried on into manhood. Except in China, in no country are so many examinations held and rankings made as in this one. The rankings are printed; they are the measure for later appointments. By his *locus* [rank] one measures the man. Hegel, then, at first third in his year-group, was later made fourth, partly on account of his disorderly manner of study, and into his place advanced the later Württemberg prelate *Märklin*. This demotion is said to have left in Hegel a lasting wound. He sought to conceal it, became reserved, and began to work with tremendous exertion. He spent whole weeks of nights on the sofa. — Hegel is said to have been the most enthusiastic orator of freedom and equality and, like all young minds at that time, to have raved about the ideas of the Revolution. One morning, on a Sunday, it was a fine clear spring morning, Hegel and Schelling, with a few more friends, are said to have gone to a meadow not far from Tübingen and to have erected a tree of liberty there. A tree of liberty! Was that not a prophetic word? In the East, where at that time the founder of Criticism had crushed dogmatism, the word of freedom had resounded; in the West it had emerged from the streams of blood that were shed for its sake, — and now the two founders of the absolute philosophy erect a tree of liberty.”

These mythical traditions are on the whole not incorrect if we compare them with what authentic sources contain about that time: *Hegel’s album*, a note of his sister, and an account, communicated by Herr Deacon Dr. *Binder* in Heidenheim, by Pastor *Fink* in Hohenmemmingen, Hegel’s most faithful comrade. In the album we find first of all the whole numerous group of *relatives*, the cousins, the female cousins, the godfathers and godmothers from the family of the *Göritzes*, *Reyscher*, etc. We gather from it, among other things, that the pursuit of the *English* language had been customary in this circle. — A second group is formed by the *good comrades*, of whom Hegel possessed a fairly large circle. One found nothing particularly spirited in him at that time. His boyhood acquaintances

[p. 30]

in Swabia were astonished when he later surprised them with his fame. That, it was said, we should never have thought of Hegel! — In the chivalric arts of the academy Hegel remained behind. He rode now and then. He drank along stoutly on occasion, especially during the summer of 1790. With his bosom comrade *Fink* he began fencing, but soon gave it up again. To a number of external hindrances, which the fever caused him for a long time, there came in addition a neglect of dress. However much, therefore, he liked to associate with young ladies, and however well liked he was among them on account of his disposition and mental liveliness, he was nonetheless but little successful with them. His sister expresses herself very well on this point when she says: “he here and there gave a preference, but aroused no hopes.” In this tone, then, are also composed most of the album entries of the female personnel. When it was possible, Hegel tried to arrange with the ladies a game of forfeits, in which a little kiss, too, from lovely lips had after all to fall to his share. All these circumstances combined to give him a somewhat morose, ponderous exterior, to make him appear older than he was. He therefore received in the Stift the nickname: *the old man*, or also simply: *the Old One*. On one of the album leaves his friend *Fallot* has painted him with bowed head, creeping along on crutches, and has written beneath: “God help the old man!”

But Hegel’s uprightness, honesty and gaiety made him very well liked among his comrades in the Stift as well as among other students in the town. The album leaves usually style him as *dearest brother* and express a genuine fervor for him. Also from later letters of these university friends, of a *Griesinger*, *Stäudlin* and others, the genuine fidelity of this feeling emerges. The county of *Mömpelgard* [Montbéliard] across the Rhine still belonged at that time to Württemberg, and was ceded to France only in the Peace of Lunéville. Hence students from Mömpelgard had at that time a free table in the Stift, through which they easily came into closer connection with the Stift students. They represented the *French* element, and Hegel associated with most of them, in particular with *Fallot* and

[p. 31]

*Billing* of Colmar. Also a German-Englishman, E. H. *Kaufmann*, has inscribed himself in English in the album; Hegel himself wrote beneath the names: departed on 16 August 1793 for North America. The album leaves in general naturally contain many an allusion no longer decipherable by us, and fluctuate in expression between great commonplaceness and sentimental exuberance. Some are characteristic through definite relations. Thus a M. *Sartorius* inscribed himself on 7 September 1791 with the following words:

“Friendship is a plant which, carefully tended, thrives in any soil. — You maintained recently that *botany* expected no further enlargements. Quickly enter the supplement in your Linnée — and remember, as botanist or non-botanist alike, your sincere friend.”

Other occasions were provided by *responding* [at disputations], by *the parting from the Stift*, by little *adventures*. For excursions into the surrounding country Hegel was always ready. The neighboring villages, the monastery of Neresheim, etc., were visited. Once he made with *Fink* and others, in particular a Mömpelgarder, without the *venia* [leave] of the Stift authorities, a pleasure ride to a village some hours distant. There the Mömpelgarder’s nag fell ill, so that it could not be got to move from the spot again. Hegel and Fink could well have reached Tübingen again on their horses in such a way that their absence from the Stift would not have been noticed and punished. But they preferred to stay with the comrade who had lost his nag until provision was made for a joint return home, and for this reason had to go for some hours into the Stift’s jail.

A special attention, if with great shyness, Hegel devoted in 1791 to the daughter of a deceased Tübingen professor of theology, *Hegelmeier*. She was called *Auguste* and lived with her mother in the house of a baker, who, as is customary in Swabia and the Palatinate, at the same time kept a wine tavern. She was very beautiful. Her mouth in particular is said to have been enchanting. A certain coquetry, the flatteringly sweet consciousness of being able to conquer hearts, only contributed to the heightening of her charms. She had every evening the task of going into the cellar,

[p. 32]

whereby, according to the arrangement of the house, the way led her through the baker’s tap-room. Hence her admirers gathered here, Hegel too, and sought to pay court to her here. Once they even brought it about that a ball was given for her. The university riding-master had three daughters, to whom attentions were also diligently paid. The father lent his garden house, in which there was a quite pretty dance floor, and where Auguste was now the celebrated queen. She died on 10 October 1840 at Karlsruhe as the wife of the vice-chancellor at the Baden High Court of Appeal in Mannheim, *Krippendorf*. Hence in the album not only is the great ball mentioned, but above all it says also: *V. A! Vive la belle Augustine pour toi seul!* [Long live the beautiful Augustine, for you alone!] etc. Hegel must have taken this first passionate interest in a girl very much to heart, for a friend, *Elsner*, wrote to him on 10 May 1791, “*as a warning*,” these words in the album: “What is a girl’s favor? First she broods our dearest hopes with a mother’s warmth; then, like an inconstant hen, she leaves the nest and surrenders her already germinating offspring to death and decay.”

A principal element, however, of the liveliest social intercourse became the *Revolution*. When it broke out, hardly anyone foresaw the course of its development. The bloody specter of terrorism did not yet disturb the devotion to the spectacle of seeing a state step into actuality out of the Idea of the state, out of the Concept of the powers essential for its existence, after it had stripped from itself the withered skin of a past that had become a lie, an injustice, by the act of a solemn renunciation. With infinite enthusiasm, with the purest heart, the noblest Germans turned to this truly philosophical spectacle. A Klopstock and a Schiller, a Kant and a Forster, a Baggesen and a Schlabrendorf, a Merk and a Jacobi, met in the glowing expectation of an *ethical rebirth* of Europe, now that the rights of mankind were decreed. Is it to be wondered at that, not far from the Rhine, from Strasbourg, young men fell into the most decided enthusiasm for the French Revolution, that through what happened in France they were also stirred to a critique of domestic

[p. 33]

conditions, to vague hopes for the further development of the same into higher forms? — There formed in the Stift a *political* club. The French *newspapers* were taken. Their news was devoured. Through an apothecary who was a member of the club, this passionate political, though harmless, interest was betrayed. Duke Karl himself came to Tübingen for the investigation. The ringleader, a Stift student, escaped in good time to Strasbourg. The Duke, however, was wise enough not to make much of the matter. The most zealous participants in the club were the Mömpelgarders, and that was too natural to hold greatly against them. In the case of the rest one recognized that the poetry of cosmopolitanism, which had already celebrated its breakthrough in *Schiller*, is only too well suited to youthful indefiniteness, and that the school of life itself, through its manifold conditionedness, best cures one of exaggerations. The excitement of the students was for a time still heightened by the circumstance that the émigré corps of Count *Mirabeau* lay in the neighboring *Rottenburg*. If one of this corps let himself be seen in Tübingen, he had much to suffer, especially from the Mömpelgarders. Frequent duels were the consequence. Indeed, when once a Republican captured by the émigrés escaped to Tübingen, he was kept hidden for several days in the Stift. That head of the club, a capable musician, arranged, under an unsuspicious pretext and name, a public concert, which supplied the means for being able to send the Republican secretly across the Rhine.

Hegel’s father was a decided aristocrat. The son found himself swept along by the current of the age and did not shrink from the most violent debates with his father on this point. In that club he, who already at the Gymnasium had read Rousseau so much and so gladly, and to whom at the university Kant and Plato offered no resistance in this direction, became not only one of the most decided participants but even a speaker. For what was genuine and great in the French Revolution Hegel from this time on always retained a tender reverence, even if the emptiness of mere declamation about freedom and equality, rights of man, welfare of the people, etc., soon became odious to him. In the album leaves

[p. 34]

we find almost all the notes struck which the enthusiasm for that gigantic event was bound to elicit in the young men. “*In tyrannos!*” [Against the tyrants!] rages one with *Hutten*, “Death to the rabble!” cries another, “*Vive la liberté!*” [Long live liberty!] a third, “*Vive Jean Jaques!*” [Long live Jean Jacques!] a fourth, “[French] And may the dreadful politics that claims an absolute power over hearts perish forever!” a fifth, “Fatherland and freedom!” a sixth, etc. On 5 October 1793 *Billing* of Colmar wrote: “[French] If there were a government of angels, they would govern themselves democratically.” As a symbol he added: “*liberté raisonnée!*” [*reasoned* liberty!]

For companionable intercourse *Fallot* and *Fink* were Hegel’s chief comrades in the Stift. The former wrote on 7 September 1791 on the back of the leaf on which he had drawn him on 12 February of the same year as an old man creeping along bent over: “[French] My dear friend, it is only some days since we have already committed many follies in love. I hope that you will always remember with pleasure the evenings that we spent together at the *baker’s*, drinking four-batz wine and eating butter-pretzels.” In *Fink’s* album Hegel wrote on 4 September 1790 these then popular trite verses:

“Happy is he who on his path / Has a friend at his side; / Thrice happy, though, is he / Whom his girl kisses ardently.”

On the back he wrote in the following year:

“Beautifully the last summer closed, more beautifully the present! / The motto of that was: / — Wine, of this: Love! / 7th Octbr. 91. / V. A!!!”

Many a vacation Hegel spent in Fink’s birthplace, Königsbronn, and Fink conversely in Hegel’s paternal house. After the separation from the seminary they saw each other again only once, when Fink was traveling through Frankfurt am Main while Hegel lived there as a house tutor; — the infinitely melancholy lot of so many youthful friendships! — Of famous men in Hegel’s

[p. 35]

album of that time may be mentioned *Matthisson*, who on 27 June 1793 inscribed himself in Tübingen with the Horatian: *Virtus recludens immeritis mori* [Virtue, opening the way to those who do not deserve to die] etc.

#### The Dissertation *pro magisterio*, 1790.

The Stift students pursue for two years a philosophical course, for three years a theological one. The former is customarily concluded with the acquisition of the philosophical doctoral degree. Hegel was, under *Storr’s* protectorate, on 27 September 1790, that is, in the twentieth year of his life, promoted *Magister of Philosophy* by the then dean of the Tübingen philosophical faculty, Professor of Philosophy and Mathematics Chr. Fr. *Pfleiderer*. The diploma is composed in quite ordinary terms: “[Latin] after the customary examinations have been held and public specimens of learning submitted.” These consisted in a dissertation: *de limite officiorum humanorum, seposita animorum immortalitate* [On the Limit of Human Duties, with the Immortality of Souls Set Aside]. *Sectio prior* [first section]. 4to, 28 pp. In August Hegel had publicly defended it under the presidency of the professor of practical eloquence and poetry, A. Fr. *Bök*. The occasion for precisely his theme Hegel had taken from the task which the curators of the Stolpian bequest had set a year earlier for a prize competition: “[Latin] Whether there are duties to which man cannot be shown to be bound by nature unless the immortality of souls is posited?” Hegel relates this himself in the *Proömium* [preface] and at the same time holds that such practical questions would always retain a great charm for men, even if it might seem as though they were already exhausted by the achievements of the philosophers. He wished to divide his investigation into two parts. In the first, which he treated in the dissertation, he asked: “[Latin] to what duties, and by what incentives, man can be impelled, even if he had no expectation of life, and this both when God is set aside and when God is posited?” In the second part, which he remained in debt for, he wished to indicate more closely the limits of duties and to examine: “[Latin] what that supreme element in the pursuit of virtue is which, without the sure hope of a perennial life of souls, would be deprived of every foundation of reason.”

[p. 36]

This treatise shows us, on the one hand, the study of the *Kantian* philosophy, on the other, the struggle with it and the attempt to get beyond its dualism. Hegel proceeds from the claim that in human nature *sensibility* and *reason* are, as it were, so grown together that both powers establish only a *single* subject: “[Latin] sensibility has so, as it were, grown together with reason that both forces constitute *one* subject.” Of *purely* moral actions there could therefore be no talk, but only of such as included within themselves incentives from sensibility. In the individual human being, however, various *stages* of ethical formation arise through the unequal relation of sensibility and reason, because man only gradually comes to subject sensibility wholly to the laws of reason. Let us now think of a man who *denies* the immortality of the soul *with complete conviction*, namely in such a way that he expects from our free actions after this life no *effect* whatever, either for good or for evil, and consequently abolishes between the present and the future, a this side and a beyond, all *moral connection*. Let us think, Hegel continues, of this man as of noble spirit, zealously concerned for the furtherance of his welfare and striving to lead a life worthy of reason. What *universal* purpose of life, in accord with his opinion, will such a man set before himself? — Since such a man thinks the consciousness and the memory of the past as one day vanishing completely for him, as if he had not lived this life at all, he lacks the desirable consolation of the constancy (*perpetuitas*) of life and of his sensation. The loss of it must appear the harder to him, and all the more so, the more vivid his consciousness, the more certain and long-lasting that foresight is in him. “[Latin] The use of what *is present* is subject to various vicissitudes, its degree depending partly on the power of man, partly on fortune, its duration uncertain, its outcome none for one who is to die.” On the one hand, therefore, he will also meet the utmost of human fate with a brave spirit, on the other devote the greater strength to the present moment of action. He will, further, with regard to the evils which are once for all inseparable from the human lot, be more cautious and in

[p. 37]

combating them more circumspect, in order to produce for himself, in the finite span of life, a *minimum of evil* and a *maximum of good*. He will consequently differ greatly from other men, who expect after this life immortality and the *greater* goods bound up with it, both in the estimation of the *quality* of goods and in the *manner and way* of striving after the greatest *quantity* of them.

The duties which such a man will derive in his ethics from the nature of man are: 1) duties of immediate *necessity* or of instinct; 2) of *pleasure*; 3) of *utility* and 4) of *perfection*, namely of beauty, greatness of soul, etc. Hegel goes through these various duties and shows that, although each of them can be thought without regard to God and immortality, the fulfilment of them nevertheless acquires a quite different charm if one thinks of them as the expression of the necessity of a *supreme will*, of an infinitely powerful, wise and good *God*, who manifests himself in the order and in the laws of nature and guides everything that happens with the most exact knowledge. Especially, Hegel thinks, do the duties of perfection gain from this standpoint, because man can behold the All *as a perfected whole*, and regard himself as a citizen in the realm of the greatest and best ruler, only with the presupposition of God.

The second part of the treatise, in which he wished to speak of the limit of the duties of one who does not believe in continuance after death, Hegel remained in debt for. As it stands, it expresses clearly enough the struggle with the worldview of that time, that of the Enlightenment. In *Kant’s* philosophy the Enlightenment had received its highest and systematic development. According to Kant man *needed* the belief in immortality and, in order to give this a content, the belief in a God who rewards the good in the beyond and punishes evil. Hegel denied neither God nor immortality, but wished to make the attempt to see whether, without that presupposition, *duties* must not nevertheless exist, *virtues* not nevertheless *be able to be practiced*? In moral respect he wished thus to make practical reason valid in complete disinterestedness as an *end in itself*. For the

[p. 38]

realization of its necessity he counted faith in God only among the *incentives* for doing what duty commands with still quite another fervor. For Hegel’s philosophical formation there was contained in this conception, undeniably, the important point that, in placing man *practically* wholly upon the *thing* itself, he took this step *theoretically* as well, and brought to consciousness the *disinterested mode of consideration* which proceeds wholly *objectively* and is satisfied with the determinations of the What. One must not want to hold something true because one wishes it. The *theoretical* indifference *to presuppose nothing* for the Concept is above all necessary to the philosopher, who is to cognize, without passion, without prejudice, without being bribed by authority or egoism, what is true in and for itself. Shallowness, to be sure, often enough takes such ataraxy of self-consciousness for coldness of heart and at once calls theoretical impartiality with regard to the Concept of God and of immortality atheism. This stage of purely objective courage, which for the time being leaves out of play the *relation* of a determination to God or to personal continuance, Hegel had to establish in himself first as the *specific pathos* of the one who philosophizes, and he expressed himself about it as clearly as energetically in the opening words of his dissertation: “[Latin] Whatever opinion one may cherish concerning the origin and ends of worldly things; whether one subjects them to divine providence or removes the Deity from their midst; whether one believes souls immortal or destined to perish with the body: yet in those things which are accomplished *in the very nature of things* and are perceived by the external and internal sense of all, no opinion will be able to change anything.”

#### Dissertation *pro candidatura examinis consistorialis*, 1793.

As a consequence of his study of philosophy on the one hand, of positive theology on the other, Hegel fell into a violent struggle with the whole culture of the age. The romanticism of orthodoxy, in its dead literalism, satisfied him as little as the moral narrowness of the Enlightenment. He studied the New Testament carefully in order, as it was later begun to be expressed, to separate the

[p. 39]

primitive Christianity from that shape which the following ages have developed out of it. He endeavored to separate the concept of *fetish-faith*, as he called it, from that of the *religion of reason*, and to unite both through imagination in a living *folk religion*, in the case of which latter the Hellenic conditions then chiefly hovered before him. The religion of reason as such he treated in the Kantian sense as an unattainable *ideal*. With great acuity he subjected the ecclesiastical form of public religion, like the moralizing form of private religion, to criticism, and in his outpourings scourged especially also the desolation of lifeless scholarship as well as the morally corrupting presumption of the splinter-judging moral police of the clergy. The dualism in which Hegel found himself placed by the fact that he fully recognized the entitlement of the Enlightenment to subjective freedom, but objectively had no satisfaction at all in the actuality ruled by it, was probably the reason why he chose as the subject of his *theological* treatise, which he had to deliver in the autumn of 1793 for the lawful completion of the candidates’ examination, a theme which let the ferment present in him come to expression not at all. For he wrote, in the manner of *Spittler* and *Plank*, with thorough research into sources which goes in the notes into the slightest details, a treatise:

*De ecclesiae Wirtembergicae renascentis calamitatibus* / [On the Calamities of the Württemberg Church in Its Rebirth]. / *Tubingae* [Tübingen], 80 pp., 4to.

He defended it in June. The date is not noted on the title. Eighteen appended theses relate, to the extent of one third, to the content of the dissertation, the others especially to the difference of *Protestantism* from *Catholicism*. The treatise itself is wholly devoted to the particular interest of the Württemberg church. The merits of Duke *Ulrich* and of the reformers *Melanchthon* and *Brentius* are developed with great precision. The state of philosophy in Württemberg at the time of the Reformation is described in § 12.

[p. 40]

#### Hegel, Hölderlin and Schelling.

Of the fellow students with whom Hegel stood in scholarly and friendly intercourse at the Stift, two must be especially singled out, *Hölderlin* and *Schelling*. However much Hegel was seized by the Enlightenment, he was just as little its unconditional worshipper. The breadth of his spirit harbored many worlds within it, whose struggle with one another quietly and lastingly prepared in him a higher intuition of all things. The intensity with which he had already at the Gymnasium in Stuttgart absorbed the essence of Greek antiquity, in particular the poetry of a Sophocles, itself formed an immediate reaction against the frosty, intuition-less, meager thing to which the intellectualism of the Enlightenment began to amount ever more visibly. In Hölderlin Hegel found the love of Greek antiquity concentrated to the extreme. Hölderlin’s one-sidedness set him at variance with Germany and the present incurably. Precisely the element from which, *composing poetry*, he drew forth the highest enchantment became for him *in life* the annihilating one. He was, of the same age as Hegel, born in 1770 at Neislingen in Swabia and was to study theology at Tübingen. The novel *Hyperion* he is said to have begun already at the Stift. Hegel formed an intimate friendship with him. On 12 Feb. 1791 Hölderlin wrote into Hegel’s album Goethe’s words: “Delight and love are the wings to great deeds”; and as a symbol: *“Ἓν καὶ πᾶν”* [One and All] — Hölderlin left Tübingen after the completion of his studies in order to go to Jena, where he became an enthusiastic listener of Fichte’s and inspired Hegel along with himself by his reports in letters.

With Hölderlin, Fink, Renz and other friends Hegel, according to reliable reports, read and discussed *Plato* (some of his translation attempts from Plato of that time are still extant), *Kant*, *Jacobi’s Woldemar* and *Allwill*, the *Letters on *Spinoza and *Hippel’s Life Stories in Ascending Line*. Hegel’s preference for Hippel’s humor is sufficiently known from his later judgments about it (e.g. *Aesthetics*, vol. II, p. 228 ff.). Into Hegel’s circle there entered in the autumn of 1790 Schelling. His father was at that time prelate and rector at Bebenhausen, later at Maulbronn (cf. Paulus, *Memorabilien*, p. 94). He brought the son himself to

[p. 41]

Tübingen into the Stift and described him on this occasion as a *praecox ingenium* [precocious mind]. In Swabia those who are discharged together from a lower seminary to a higher one, or in general, in the Stift too, are moved from one age-class into another, are called a *Promotion* [year-group], and the individuals who take part in it *Compromotionalen* [year-mates]. The first of such a year-group exerts a great influence on its members and thereby on others too. Although, therefore, Schelling was not yet fifteen years old at his entry into the Stift, his position as first in the year-group nevertheless opened to him that political club of which was told earlier. It was his knowledge of *Hebrew* above all on which, besides, his standing in the Stift rested. Hegel was five years older than Schelling and already Magister of Philosophy when the latter first came to Tübingen; they therefore stood at first far enough apart from each other. Only in that club did they meet, and political sympathy led them gradually also to a friendly and scholarly intercourse. That philosophy as such had at that time established a *direct* connection between them does not seem to have been the case. One must not transfer the relation of the Jena period to this earlier one. Up to now Hegel himself is the only authentic source on this mythical time of youth, and a closer picture of it can be attained scarcely even by conjecture. Thus it will strike anyone, e.g., how the word *Aether* signifies in Hegel as well as in Hölderlin an extreme of perfection, of blessed repose — yet neither need have taken it over from the other, but both can have drawn it from the same source, the Greek tragedians.

#### Hegel as House Tutor in Switzerland, Autumn 1793 to Autumn 1796.

After the completion of the course at Tübingen Hegel betook himself back to Stuttgart for a few weeks and associated in this time especially with the young jurist *Stäudlin*, who was also a friend of Hölderlin’s and was at that time, in a cosmopolitan sense,

[p. 42]

occupied with all sorts of journalistic plans. According to a letter of Stäudlin’s of 14 December 1793 from Stuttgart to Hegel, they took frequent walks to Cannstatt, where they seasoned the enjoyment of wine with jest and laughter. “These hours laughed through,” writes Stäudlin, “were so sweet that I am truly heartily grateful to you for them, dear Hegel. You are one of those honest ones who suit me entirely, and whom for that very reason I should like always to have at my side.” — Stäudlin had a servant, *Johann*, who by his original naïveté afforded them much amusement, so that they dubbed a certain sort of witticisms after him *Johannities*; e.g.:

*Stäudlin*: Johann, what is a verse?

*Johann*: A verse is when it begins at the front and stops again and then begins again at the front. —

*Stäudlin*: What then does your soul do after death?

*Johann*: It gets wings and flies straight to heaven.

*Stäudlin*: Johann, when your soul’s wing / Bears you one day to heaven, / No more your master’s cudgel / Beats dust from your jerkin; / When the angels then teach you / What a verse is in truth, / And all the spheres are astonished / At your Johannities, etc.

Hegel accepted a position as house tutor with Herr *Steiger* of Tschugg in *Bern*. Nothing more precise can be reported about this situation. In a passport from Bern Hegel is listed as: [French] governor *of the children* of our dear and loyal citizen Steiguer of Tschougg. How many children, however, and of what age he had to teach does not appear. — It is remarkable enough that *Kant, Fichte* and *Herbart* — the latter two in Switzerland also, Herbart even in Bern as well — were likewise house tutors. If such a relation leaves room for self-formation, it may well be suited to the further maturing of a deeper genius, namely through the necessity of constantly running through the elementary determinations of knowledge. However

[p. 43]

burdensome this occupation may appear, it nevertheless also preserves thoroughness. For the art of communication it is in any case beneficial. It demands simplicity and familiar liveliness without yet requiring the rhetorical measuredness of public lectures. — So much emerges from Hegel’s letters to Schelling, that his office did not leave him too much leisure. A poem of Hegel’s to Hölderlin also confirms this. He rejoices in it that the night grants him rest and removes the day’s irksome noise.

During the summer he usually stayed with the family of his employer in Tschugg above *Erlach*. In Bern itself he formed a friendly tie with a painter *Sonnenschein*. This painter had a lively wife and daughter. They played the clavier, sang, especially songs of Schiller, and also amused themselves with a game of Boston. A certain *Fleischmann*, with whom Hegel, as with Sonnenschein, later from Frankfurt still exchanged some letters, shared the harmless joys of the family. The content of the painter’s letters is for the most part the recollection of the joys of the evenings spent with Hegel. “Joy, fair spark of the gods!” he writes on 13 November 1797, “is sung often enough in your memory.”

Hegel had the good fortune to live continually in interesting cities; also the good fortune not to make too short stays in them, but to linger long enough to become thoroughly familiar with their conditions; but also the good fortune not to remain overlong in them, so that the local spirit with its leaden dominion could have crept up on him. Stuttgart, Tübingen, Bern, Frankfurt am Main, Jena, Bamberg, Nuremberg, Heidelberg, Berlin — what a series, indeed, of chosen cities, each of which is endowed with the most peculiar charms. But Hegel’s restlessness to intuit the Idea even in the most many-sided reality did not have enough of such a change of residence, and he made, whenever he could, journeys, up to a great age. And in this too his places of residence were fortunate, that they offered him easy opportunity for travel in all directions. Thus in May 1795 he also made from Bern an excursion to *Geneva*, of which, however, we know nothing more precise. At the end of July 1796 he made, with three Saxon house tutors, *Thomas*, *Stolde* and *Hohenbaum*,

[p. 44]

a journey on foot to the Bernese Alps, of which he kept a very exact diary, still preserved. Without any romanticism of illusion he applies himself in it to a strictly objective description. He gives what presents itself to him correctly and reliably, but without any individual poetry of sensation. One sees well that he undertook the wandering with the expectation of being quite deeply seized in his feeling by the giant mountain heads, etc., but the *masses of the rocks and of the ice* are unable to extort from him any tribute of admiration. Dead, dreary, without stimulus for the imagination, they appear to him. It is so — further he cannot feel anything in their presence. The *water*, on the other hand, with its lively play, carries him away to delight. His description of the fall of the Reichenbach is beautiful. The eternal becoming of a spectacle which remains the same in its outlines, this dialectical aspect of the phenomenon, fascinates him deeply. — Characteristic is the *all-sidedness* of his interest. Not only nature, which here indeed constantly steps into the foreground, occupies him in all its shapes, from the glacier colossus to the isolated crystal, from the forests to the grass and the flower, from the lake to the spring, but also man in struggle with nature and the diversity of human custom, of human ways of life. The diversity of color in dress strikes him, the diversity in foodstuffs; he notes what is brought from Italy for the Swiss cheese, describes the process of cheese-making, etc. Yet not only such an economic, mercantile and industrial glance does he show, he also brings out the universally human, as in a touching tale of a minstrel and his child. Against the *eudaemonistic* tendency of the physico-theology of that time he expresses himself with deepest indignation. In view of the primeval nature of the Alps and its ruthless shattering of the works of men it seems to him almost impossible to arrive at such representations. He accuses the age of serving therein *the idol of vanity and of selfishness* instead of the true God. The diremption, however, in which he then lived — not with the *historical Christ*, to be sure, but with *historical Christianity* — is mirrored in the contemptuous manner in which he speaks of the fantasy of Christianity

[p. 45]

and contrasts its *legend* with the Greek *myth* (as he *expressly writes*).

#### Theological and Historical Studies of the Swiss Period.

As is well known, Hegel used to say of Schelling that he had made his studies before the eyes of the public. He himself concealed his own and strove to hand over to publicity only more or less *artistically* elaborated works, the ripe results. The peculiar beauty of Schelling’s presentation therefore rests more on the charm of momentary excitement, improvisatory emotion, sudden invention, with all the merits and defects of these. The planful elaboration of a draft, the consistent working-through of an Idea, the dramatic entanglement and resolution of a theme, on the contrary, constitute the most proper beauty of Hegel’s writings. The specification of expression for the individual proceeds with him from the *Concept of the whole*, has an objectively plastic assurance, and is not merely a tone borne by a fleeting mood. In comparison with the graceful negligence and boldness of Schelling, Hegel’s works therefore have a more ponderous look. Because he proceeds artistically, he strives for a harmony of the particular with the universal. From the standpoint of the whole task he oversees the individual shaping and accompanies, entirely at home in the individual determinacies, each of his steps with critical care.

During his life as a house tutor in Switzerland Hegel emancipated himself entirely from the dead theology of Tübingen. The struggle was mighty and is reflected also in the unevenness of the style of his writings of that time, which is *alternately* fluent and light, then again broken up and gnarled. Sometimes, especially in exegetical attempts, he becomes, to the point of triviality, sensible and intelligible; then again, where dogmatic concepts are at issue, he becomes obscure, mystical, tangled, indeed a few times baroque. The *Idea* which moved Hegel through and through in this period was that of *love*.

[p. 46]

Already at the Stift he had come upon the idea of setting up an *analogy* of love with reason, although love was only an *empirical* principle. He found in the movement of love the *dialectical* element: to pass out of oneself into an other than oneself, to be by oneself in the other, and to return to oneself only in order to externalize oneself anew. The *absolute*, yet for the time being only individual and subjective actualization of the Idea of love he saw in Christ as the *God-man*. Love is to be *universal* in its essence. Through the *communities* of Christianity, Hegel thought at that time, it becomes a *particular* one, a love of *Christians for Christians* as ἅγιοι, as baptized persons among one another, a love which, in its direction toward God and Christ, leaves aside the infinite manifoldness of *worldly* life. In the enthusiasm for the imitation of the *poor* life of Jesus, Christian love seemed to Hegel to be in danger of becoming not only indifferent, but even *exclusive* toward the wealth of spirit in state, art and science. But Hegel did not want to see the powers of the world contemptuously cast away, as though carrying on their mischief outside the realm of love. Thus he found himself referred from the consideration of the *church* to that of the *state*. Hegel took state and church as independent *individuals*, who effect their unity with one another only through the form of a *contract*. The principal concept around which this investigation therefore turned with him was that of *positive* religion, as that form in which the Idea of religion presents itself *empirically* as appearance. The highest in man is regulated in it, according to its concrete determinacy, by the *authority* of the church. It is prescribed by it exactly how one must feel in order to be allowed to count as pious. Not only must the individual have from himself the certainty of being reconciled with God within himself; he must also *present* for others, in statutorily established observances and modes of expression, that it is so, and thereby be able to arouse in them, when they control him, the same certainty. This inference, this process, is unavoidable in a religion fixed as an ecclesiastical state. But Hegel did not want to tolerate such supervision of the individual in his religious life. It seemed to him to annihilate religion itself. The *control*

[p. 47]

should, in his view, fall only to the *state*, from the side of right, and relate not to conscience, to the inner life of man, but solely to his *deeds* as to his externalized inner life. It was not to judge the feelings and mien of another, and was to want to assess not by conjectures and subjective presuppositions, but solely by the *objective law*. Because Hegel thus concentrated religion in inwardness, because he wanted it withdrawn from the *police* inspection of a clerical authority, he had to pose for himself the problem of comparing the institutions of a positive religion in doctrine, morals and ceremonial with the concept of an *invisible church*.

The Hellenic philosophers had no need to trouble themselves about a theology sanctioned by synods, consistories and governments. In the Middle Ages, on the other hand, theology swallowed philosophy. When the latter tore itself free from ecclesiastical tutelage, it nevertheless retained, vis-à-vis the general consciousness, the obligation to justify the Concept of the Absolute posited by it in relation to the one valid in the church. *Descartes*, out of regard for his personal safety, still unconditionally submitted to the judgment of the *church*. *Spinoza*, on the other hand, vindicated philosophy for the *state*, which without freedom of thought, according to him, does not correspond to its Concept. He therefore subjected the concepts of revelation and inspiration, of miracle and prophecy, which Descartes had always evaded, to the sharpest critique of the understanding in his *Tractatus theologico-politicus*. *Leibniz* thereupon sought to show the *concordance* of faith and reason, to refute doubt concerning the rationality of the dogmas, to elucidate the mystery of the Trinity itself *per nova logica reperta* [by newly discovered logical means], and to reconcile the various confessions with one another. All skeptics and empiricists, Charron, Bayle, Locke, Hume, etc., as adherents of so-called *natural* religion, occupied themselves with the critique of Christianity; *Kant* made reason, as moral philosophy, the judge in matters of faith. *Fichte* gave a philosophical guide to the blessed life, asserting at the same time its agreement with primitive Christianity, whose exposition he ascribed to the *Johannine* Gospel, a hypothesis which, critically, is, as is well known, subject to the gravest doubts. *Schelling*

[p. 48]

sketched in 1803 a historical construction of Christianity and made, since his Erlangen epoch, desperate efforts to rationalize even the miracles. It is the necessity of spirit itself *not to tolerate a dualism between its religion and its philosophy*. In the individual philosophers this necessity comes to light only in a particular way. To the hierarchically minded theologians the salt of speculation has indeed often been inconvenient. They have regarded the philosophy of religion, speculative theology, as an unlawful encroachment upon their domain and have often branded it as a pernicious presumption. But divine reason is naturally stronger than such domineering conceit, and philosophy has, in spite of all the polemic of clerical arrogance, ever anew sought to reconcile self-consciousness in its faith with knowledge.

Hegel, trained academically as a theologian, could not at all escape the task of attaining the *unity of thinking* in faith and knowledge. What special theological studies he made in the literature in Switzerland cannot well be stated, because he rarely names a name in his papers. The theological journal *Memorabilien*, edited by *Paulus* at that time, the writings of *Mosheim*, the commentaries of *Hugo Grotius*, now and then the name of *Kant’s* and *Fichte’s*, *Spinoza’s Tractatus theologico-politicus*, *Marivaux’s* novels, of which he judged that they had dealt the main blow in France to monastic asceticism and its unnaturalness, *Forster’s* and others’ travel descriptions, together with the General *Jena* Literary Gazette, are the only things that can be cited.

Much in the papers of this period is *fragmentary*. Reflections on the mythology of the Greeks and Romans, on the condition of Christianity in the Roman Empire, etc., alternate with entirely practical remarks, e.g., that preachers should not occupy themselves with agriculture was an opinion of distinguished professors who held such a thing beneath their dignity and wanted to make university scholars of all pastors — not far removed from the prohibition against marrying. — Toward the concept of *Jewish* history from the theological standpoint he made many attempts and in doing so at times went into the smallest detail,

[p. 49]

particularly in the characterization of Abraham and Moses. In the development of Jewish history itself it seemed to him especially important that the people made the *transition from the pastoral life* to the *state* not without *foreign* influence and tied its independence to *general enmity*. He found, therefore, in the constitution of the Jews the *diremption with nature* carried through in such a way that they sought to compensate for their dependence on the law in the *self-will of a service* which was nothing but opposition to nature. “The fate of the Jewish people is the fate of *Macbeth*, who stepped out of nature itself, attached himself to alien beings, in their service had to trample down and murder everything holy in human nature, had to be forsaken by his gods (for they were gods, he was a servant) and shattered by his own faith.” — Hegel’s view of Jewish history was very unequal at different times. It repelled him as vehemently as it fascinated him, and tormented him throughout life as a gloomy riddle. Now, as in the *Phenomenology*, he ignored it; now, as in the *Philosophy of Right*, he moved it close to the Germanic spirit; now, as in the *Philosophy of Religion*, he coordinated it as the immediate form of the spiritual individuality of the Greeks and Romans; finally, in the *Philosophy of History*, he integrated it into the Persian Empire. In each of these respects there lies in the history of the Jews a justification, but only the summation of them all into unity can satisfy.

Hegel’s *dogmatic* reflections had for their object partly the concept of positive faith in general, partly the concept of reconciliation in particular. The group of concepts: guilt and punishment, law and fate, sin and forgiveness of sin, occupied him from all sides in the most earnest way. In these works Hegel’s philosophical genius emerged, half-unconsciously to himself, from its chrysalis. The young man, regarding himself as a theological Magister, still treated theology as the most essential element of his studies, while out of this soil the flower of philosophy had already raised its head. That *punishment* as such *does not improve*; that the peculiar element in the fate of Christ is the elevation above all fate, the guilt of innocence;

[p. 50]

that sin has no power against love; that the unity of the divine and the human is the essence of love, the truth of life; that the Lord’s Supper, like baptism, consists of *mystical* acts in which *more* is present than is seen and felt *with the senses*; that the forgiveness of sins is *fate reconciled through love*, not the abolition of the consciousness of guilt, not the negation of the punishment of sin — all these Concepts Hegel developed at that time with profound inwardness and austere dialectical force. A melancholy loftiness is poured out over these essays. His immersion in the *life of Christ* finally went so far with him that in the spring of 1795 he himself wrote one.

In the Catholic Middle Ages the life of Christ was, through the mediation of sculpture, painting and dramatic art in the Passion plays, *intuited* in the most proper sense of the word. Protestantism entirely abolished the plastic element in the Reformed cult; in the Lutheran it diminished it and transformed the theatrical objectivity into the musical-dramatic objectivity of the *oratorios*. The representation of the *history of Christ* was, on the whole, at first pushed into the background. The *dogmas* as such took precedence, and the Bible was rather the means of asserting the proof of their truth. Only after the Thirty Years’ War, only after the elaboration of Protestant dogmatics by an acute understanding, did people gradually go back to the Bible without apologetic, without polemical reference. They immersed themselves in the appearance of Christ for its own sake, not in order to attach to it a critique of the controversial doctrines. A mighty impulse of the heart sustained an intimate sociability, a real *intercourse* with Jesus (which name almost displaced the Greek one), and the Herrnhuters systematized it formally with the most fervent imagination. *Klopstock’s Messiah* had to have an infinite significance for this age; but the *understanding* soon confronted the image of the Redeemer created from the *imagination*, and began to examine the history of Christ according to its *probability*. Klopstock’s *Messiah* was completed in 1773, and the *Wolfenbüttel* Fragments, which made so great a breach for the criticism of the Gospels, first appeared in 1778. From that time there followed one another many writings which set themselves the development of the *purpose*, of the *plan*,

[p. 51]

of the *character* of Jesus. In Switzerland J. J. *Hess* published, from 1768, a *Life of Jesus*; *Lavater* went astray in 1783–86 into a re-poeticizing of Klopstock’s *Messiah*. *Parallels* between *Jesus* and *Socrates* came into vogue.

Hegel himself had, in the private lessons with his beloved preceptor Löffler, translated the Archbishop *Vida’s Christias* (first 1592) and learned much of it by heart. In Tübingen the parallel between Christ and Socrates occupied him keenly. Intoxicated with Greek antiquity, he was not disinclined not only to coordinate them, but even to give *Socrates* the preference in many respects.
