Thus he praised in the latter at that time that he had given occasion to no mystical ceremonies, that he had bound his pupils by no obligations toward his person, had not tied their fate to his own, and the like. In Switzerland such comparisons faded away. He made arrangements to bring the life of Jesus, step by step, to the most exact representation. He drew up schemata for a unification of the facts narrated in the different Gospels, partly scattered, partly divergent. He reflected on the miracle, conceded it to faith as a form of its cognition, but rejected it on the side of the understanding. Finally, from 9 May to 24 July 1795, he worked out a *Life of Jesus*, still completely extant, consisting of 19 sheets, and gathered into it his isolated preliminary studies. Hegel’s conception of Christ was here that of a pure, lofty, divine man, whose struggle is directed to the victory of virtue over vice, of truth over the lie, to the triumph of freedom and love over servitude and enmity. All miracles he therefore simply left out. After reporting on John the Baptist, he begins the history of Christ itself quite plainly with these words: “The place where he was born was a village, Bethlehem in Judaea. His parents were Joseph and Mary, who otherwise lived in Nazareth in Galilee, but had to travel to Bethlehem, the ancestral seat of Joseph’s family, in order to be entered in the list, etc.” Just as plainly he ends with the description of the burial of Christ and with the suicide of Judas.

The peculiarity of Hegel’s Gospel harmony consists, then, in the abstraction from everything miraculous in the physical sense.

[p. 52]

But precisely because this is not there at all, because it gives the understanding no offense whatever, is neither critically wrangled away by it nor depotentiated by explanations, the narrative nevertheless makes a great impression. Hegel wanted to represent Christ to himself in *full human actuality*, to set him before himself according to his spiritual soundness under test. He therefore observed all outward circumstances sharply, weighed with care all the psychological moments in Jesus’ relation to his disciples, and in the didactic passages employed in his expression wholly the *language of his time*, without, however, falling into the triviality of Bahrdt’s Bible in the popular tone. Rather, the language, which has for us admittedly become somewhat old-fashioned, breathes a naive loftiness, however dry it may sound at first in the words: virtue, character, love of duty, and the like. In the endeavor to dissolve the *content* of Christ’s words entirely into the form of a self-consciousness adequate to it, Hegel repeatedly made use of bold, indeed peculiar paraphrases. The thaumaturgic element put him in no embarrassment at all. The irritability with which the modern, sickly orthodoxy persecutes anyone who follows the example of Christ in his indifference toward miracles, bordering on disregard, was foreign to the age of Herder’s humanity at that time. One had no need to fear being taken for a non-Christian if one believed, to be sure, in the divinity of Christ, in a holy meaning of the miraculous matters narrated of him, but not in the factual truth of the miracles themselves. Moreover, Hegel did not merely mean to make things easy for himself by omitting the miracles from the life of Jesus, but also gave manifold account of himself concerning the relation of speculation to the Concept of miracle. About the *truth of miracles for the imagination*, he held, all were agreed. What mattered for the founding of the *highest science* was whether one had to proceed for it from a *history*, from an *authority*, from something not comprehended, or to ascribe to reason independence and necessity. With the attempt to explain the miracles exegetically or historically one already gives up the right of reason, because one thereby betrays, over against the defender of the miracle, an indecision in regard to the autonomy of reason.

Hegel has thus actually produced a life of Jesus, a coherent,

[p. 53]

history of Christ harmonizing in the tone of its expression with our culture. Yet with this historical-pragmatic work he did not yet rest content, but seems to have intended a still more detailed presentation of it. On the Sermon on the Mount, on this and that parable, there are excursuses which point to this. He also seems to have drafted introductions to the *Life of Jesus* several times; e.g.: “Jesus appeared not long before the last crisis, which brought on the ferment of the manifold elements of the Jewish fate. In this period of the development of this material, until it is gathered into a whole and until pure opposition, open war, arises, several partial outbreaks preceded the last act. People of common soul, but of strong passions, grasped the fate of the Jewish people only incompletely and were therefore not calm enough either to let themselves, suffering, be carried along by its waves without consciousness, or to await a further development in order to join to themselves, as would have been necessary, a greater power. They anticipated the whole and fell without honor and without effect. — Jesus fought not merely one part of the Jewish fate, because he was not entangled in another part of it, but *set himself against the whole*, was thus himself exalted above it and sought to raise his people above it. But such enmities as he sought to sublate can be *overcome* only by *bravery*, not *reconciled through love*. His sublime attempt, too, to overcome the whole of fate, therefore had to miscarry among his people, and he himself to become a sacrifice of it. Because Jesus had sided with no side of fate, his religion had to find so great an entrance — not indeed among his people, for this still possessed too much, but in the rest of the world — among human beings who had *no share any longer in fate*, who had nothing more at all to defend or to assert.”

Hegel’s *exegetical* labors from this epoch formed the strongest contrast to the dry method which prevailed at the Tübingen seminary. Here, under *Schnurrer*, penetration into the linguistic and perhaps also archaeological element had been the main thing in exegesis. The age sought to free itself from the interpretation, hitherto dominated by the symbolic books,

[p. 54]

and to find the *original* sense of the text through grammatical, lexical and cultural-historical mediation. In Hegel we see the direction toward cognition of the general *content* emerge. On the epistolary part of the New Testament he seems not to have bestowed thought at all, only on the historical. The working-out of the *Life of Jesus* was followed, likewise after many individual, aphoristic prolegomena, by a detailed *critique of the Concept of positive religion*, a manuscript almost 30 sheets strong, worked out, according to the date inscribed, between 20 November 1795 and 29 April 1796. The problem which already occupied Hegel at the seminary — how a *folk religion* is possible, how imagination and understanding are *equally* satisfied in it, how private religion is reconciled with the public, and how religion as church can be united with the right and the custom of the state — was taken up by him again in it. The deeper his love for the *historical Christ* was, the more embittered was he against the *dogmatics* of his time and against the many contradictions in the condition of the Church and of the clergy with the dogma of love. With regard to Christ he himself recalled *Plato’s* saying that, if virtue once appeared in person, everyone would have to love it. But against the captivity of reason under faith, against the pretension of theologians to withhold the examination of thought from their doctrinal edifices, against hierarchical presumption of every kind, against the avarice and ambition by which clergymen so often stain their conduct, he turned with shattering vehemence. In respect of the *popular power of diction* this work is the most accomplished that Hegel wrote.

The following chapters are found in it: 1) What is positive religion? 2) The Christian religion as positive. 3) Jesus speaks much of his own individual person. 4) Jesus speaks of himself as the Messiah. 5) Miracle as principle of obligation for the moral law. 6) On the disciples of Christ. 7) Their being sent out into the country. 8) Resurrection of Christ and the command after it to his disciples. 9) What is applicable in a small society is unjust in a state: community of goods and absolute equality of individuals. 10) The Lord’s Supper. 11) Zeal for propagation.

[p. 55]

12) The becoming-a-state of a moral and religious society. 13) Conflict of the Church with the State. 14) Contract of the Church with the State: representation and doctrine. 15) What form morality must take in a church. 16) Necessity of the rise of sects. 17) Comparison of Christianity with paganism.

Because of the difficulty of not going astray about the object of his critique, Hegel himself remarked by way of introduction: “When one writes about the Christian religion, one is always exposed to the danger of being accused of the error of forming an incorrect representation of its purpose and essence; and whatever one finds to object to in the representation one has formed of it, people are at once ready with the rejoinder that this does not touch the Christian religion, but only certain representations of it. If one asks to be shown the system of doctrine in which one may *reliably* find the pure system of the Christian religion, these gentlemen will all answer with *one* voice:

Do you not know my compendium, then?

But, gentlemen, your self-written compendia, or those you take as the basis of your system of faith, are themselves so different that one must ask you first to come to an agreement among yourselves before you pass off anything as not belonging to the Christian religion.”

The *psychological* side of his investigation Hegel pursued with extraordinary acuity, and he fought above all that practice which seeks to enforce a course of feelings it has prescribed as a necessary element of orthodoxy. “The necessary consequence of this, of *commanding feelings*, was and had to be *self-deception*: that one believed one had the prescribed feeling, believed one’s feeling agreed with what one had found described, whereas a feeling so artificially contrived could not equal the true, natural one either in strength or in worth. This self-deception can be his *false reassurance*, which sets a high value on these feelings wrought in the spiritual hothouse, thinks a great deal of itself on their account, and is therefore weak where strength would now be needed. If such a person notices this himself, he may fall into helplessness, anxiety, *distrust*

[p. 56]

*of himself*, a state of soul that is often driven to madness. Often, too, he falls into *despair* who, with all good will and all possible exertion, still believes he has not driven his feelings up to the height that is demanded of him. Since he finds himself in the field of feelings and can never arrive at a firm standard of his perfection, except perhaps through deceptions of the imagination, he will find himself in an *anxiety* which lacks strength and resolution and which finds some calm only in trust in the unbounded grace of the Godhead. Only a slight tension of the exaltation of the imagination, and this state too is transformed into *madness* and derangement. —

The most common effect is a species of the self-deception mentioned above, in that, *with all the wealth of spiritual feelings, one retains on the whole the same character*, and the ordinary man dwells *beside* the spiritual one, at most is fitted out by the latter with phrases and outward gestures, in trade and traffic is the ordinary man, but on Sundays, or among his brethren or before his prayer-book, quite another. It is often too harsh to accuse such a character of actual hypocrisy.”

The difficult problem of Christian communism Hegel judged, in respect of its historical shape, thus: “The maxim of *community of goods*, if it had been held to with all strictness, would have done little to further the spread of Christianity, and it was therefore early, wisely or under compulsion, abandoned to the extent that it was no longer demanded, as a condition of his admission, of one who wished to be taken into the society; but all the more were voluntary contributions to the treasury of the society urged as a means of buying oneself into heaven; whereby the clergy gained further in the sequel, in that they recommended this liberality toward themselves to the laity, but took good care not to squander their own acquired property, and so, in order to enrich themselves as the poor and needy, made the other half of mankind beggars. In the Catholic Church this enrichment of the monasteries, the clergy and the churches has been maintained, of which the poor

[p. 57]

receive little, and this little in such a way that begging is thereby maintained and, through an unnatural inversion of things, the vagrant idler who spends the night in the street is better off than the industrious working man. In the Protestant Church the occasional contribution of butter and eggs is given to the shepherd of souls voluntarily, as to a friend, if he wins the affection of his *flock*, not as a means of buying heaven; and in respect of alms, not even a poor Jewish beggar is driven away from the doors of the charitable.”

“In regard to *equality* among the first Christians — since the slave became the brother of his master, since humility, to raise oneself above no one, to esteem men not by honors and dignities, not by talents and other brilliant qualities, but by the strength of their faith, the feeling of one’s own unworthiness became the first law of a Christian — this *theory* has indeed been retained in its whole extent, but it is prudently added that it is so *in the eyes of heaven*, and hence in this earthly life no further notice is taken of it. The simple man who hears these principles of humility, of abhorrence of all pride and all vanity, set forth with touching eloquence by his bishop or superintendent, and sees the mien of edification with which the distinguished gentlemen and ladies listened to it in the congregation; the simple man who, after the sermon, were to approach his prelate together with the distinguished gentlemen and ladies familiarly, and hoped to find in them humble brothers and friends, would soon be able to read in their smiling or contemptuous mien that this is not to be taken so literally, that the real application of it is to be found only in *heaven*. When distinguished Christian prelates still today wash the feet of a number of poor people annually, that is not much more than a *comedy*, after which everything is left as it was, and which has also lost significance in that foot-washing, according to our customs, is no longer, as among the Jews, a daily act and courtesy toward guests, one usually performed only by slaves or servants. Whereas the annual plowing of the Chinese Emperor, however much it has sunk to a comedy, yet still

[p. 58]

has thereby an immediate significance for every spectator, that plowing the field is still a chief occupation of the greater part of his subjects.”

The negative sharpness of Hegel had its ground in the affirmative power dwelling within him. The penetrating gaze with which his understanding discovered contradictions of every kind had its condition in the unity, in whose depth he sought to resolve those dissonances into harmony. Over against the critical and skeptical spirit in him there stood one that was mystical in the good sense of the word, from which he rose above the standpoint of mere morality in religion. Thus there are still found some 12 sheets belonging together, in which the *founding of the community*, as an analysis of the origin and propagation of the *baptismal formula*, forms the subject. In this investigation Hegel wants to use the word *faith* only in the sense that it is to mean faith in the *divine*. Only he who has the divine in himself can believe in the divine. Only spirit can cognize spirit. “In that in which he believes he finds his own nature again, even if he has *not the consciousness* that this thing found would be his own nature. In every man himself is the light and the life. He is not illuminated by a light like a dark body that bears only a foreign gleam, but *his own fuel catches fire* and is a flame of its own.” — “When Jesus asked his disciples: Who do men say that the Son of Man is? his friends reported the opinions of the Jews, who, even while they transfigured him, still could not go out of actuality, but saw in him the individual. But when Peter had declared his faith in the *Son of Man, that he recognizes in him the Son of God*, Jesus pronounces him blessed, for the Father in heaven has *revealed* this to him. A revelation was not needed for a *mere* cognition of *divine* nature. A great part of Christians *learns* this cognition. Children are given conclusions from the miracles, etc., that Jesus is God. One cannot call this learning, this receiving of faith, a divine revelation. Command and cudgel do it here. ‘My Father in heaven has revealed it to you,’ i.e., the divine that is in you has recognized me as divine; you have understood my

[p. 59]

essence; it has echoed in yours.” — Similar analyses to those on baptism Hegel applied to the concept of the *resurrection* of Christ, entering at the same time into immortality. The main point for him here was the necessity that the element in which individuals, with all individual inequality, meet each other cannot be a symbol, not an allegory, not a merely *personified* being, but, in order to be loved, must be a *real personality*. Hence the resurrection of Jesus had been so important to the first Christians. The union of Christians was not merely an *assembly* of people who had similar representations, of persons who believe the same thing merely as holding it to be true; it was rather a *community*, a union in love and full of life. Yet the community as directed only to *love* was still imperfect, because it entailed an *impoverishment of culture*, an exclusion of many fine relations of political ethical life, an indifference toward many joyful bonds and high interests. Thus Hegel came here upon the *dualism* of state and church. He found the origin of the fanaticism of faith against the state, against individuality, against the manifoldness of life, in the restriction of love to itself, in its *flight from all forms, even though its spirit already stirred in them*. From the removal of inactive and undeveloped love from all fate Hegel at that time drew the resignation to the possibility of a sublation of the dualism on the part of the Church. “Between the extremes of friendship, of hatred and of indifference toward the world, between these extremes, which find themselves within the opposition of God and the world, of the divine and of life, the Christian Church has run through the circle forward and backward; but it is its fate that Church and state, divine service and life, piety and virtue, spiritual and worldly activity, can never melt together into one.”

Alongside his theological studies and in connection with them Hegel pursued *historical* ones. Already at the Gymnasium he had occupied himself eagerly with history. What pragmatic history actually is, he sought to answer for himself. Schröckh’s compendium pleased him because it was concerned to set aside the inessential, the spiritless

[p. 60]

and did not lay the main accent on battles, registers of names, etc. That he had not yet studied philosophy of history he noted expressly for himself; from Meiners’s history of culture he made an excerpt; he tried to analyze the passions which have been especially active in world history, etc. With careful consideration of the sources he wrote, in his candidate’s dissertation, the history of the Reformation of the Württemberg Church. The development of how Christ’s *fatelessness* at the same time brought about his *only fate* initiated him into the mystery of all history. In regard to church history he studied especially *Gibbon* and *Montesquieu*; of the ancients, with passion, *Thucydides*; fragments of a translation of the latter are still extant. *Raynal’s histoire des deux Indes*, *Hume’s History of England*, *Schiller’s* historical works he studied pre-eminently also for the *art of composition*, about which he made very interesting observations, and he even subjected Schiller’s periodology in his *Thirty Years’ War*, which had just then appeared, to a strict critique. Large, carefully laid-out tables are extant in which he set out chronologically, on the left, the history of the Papal States, on the right that of the German Empire, and in the middle between the two extremes the history of the various *Italian* states. On the spirit of the *Orientals*, on the *wailing women* of the ancients, on the legislation of *Lycurgus*, on the parties of the *Roman* Empire, on the *sequence* of revelations, on the incomprehensibility of the passion of *chivalrous gallantry* in the Middle Ages for the ancients, on the unbridled *imagination* of the women of the Middle Ages, on the striving for *security of property* in the modern states with neglect of the security and freedom of the person, on the *civil wars of Italy*, on the *publicity of the death penalty*, etc., Hegel expressed himself in ingenious aphorisms.

How ruminative he could often become, in such free outpourings of his self-study, toward the mastery of the given, may be shown by the following analysis as an example: “*Achilles* died, wounded by an arrow in the heel. He *could* just as well have been wounded at any other point of the body. The wound at

[p. 61]

that part was therefore the highest contingency. By the direction of the arrow it was thoroughly determined. But the one struck was, with regard to the remaining parts (to which, since it makes up a whole with them, it must necessarily be related), distinguished as the wounded *struck* part. This possibility of the others to be *able* to be wounded, and the opposed actuality of not *being* wounded; just as the actuality of the wounded state of the heel and its opposed possibility of also not being wounded, the Greeks unite in the imagination through a myth, Achilles’ immersion in the Lethe, according to which the unwounded parts at the same time *could* not be wounded, and the wounded part *alone* could only be wounded.” — A nature so deep and universal as Hegel’s was endowed with that tenderness, groping down into the finest nuances, which is necessary in order to penetrate to the ultimate grounds. The breadth of abstraction had as its counterpart in him the most thorough absorption in the most concrete. Hence Hegel also devoted to *style* a greater attention than may well seem to many. One can find in Hegel — as in any writer — certain small negligences, some provincialisms, and especially in more advanced age, when he had to struggle with a certain superfetation of representations and thoughts, overloaded periods; yet in the choice of expression as well as in the construction one will in the end have to yield to him, and often precisely where one was perhaps at first most inclined to improve him. Of the German authors *Kant* has also stylistically influenced him most strongly.

Hegel seems at that time to have gone about also with *practical* projects. The upheaval of all relations through the Revolution in France and the neighboring countries gave manifold occasion for such thoughts. Had not many a one of his fellow students — not merely the later peer of France, the theologian Reinhard — gone from the Tübingen Stift to Paris to play a role! How else should we explain that Hegel worked through the *financial constitution of Bern* down to the smallest detail, down to the highway toll, etc.? In Switzerland, moreover, often compelled to speak French, he also practiced himself in French

[p. 62]

*writing*. With preference he read the writings of Benjamin *Constant*, whom he did *not* fail to follow even into his last years of life. In his own manner he treated *political* matters in smaller essays, e.g. the change which arises in *military affairs* from the fact that the constitution of a state passes from the *monarchical* form to the republican.

#### Hegel’s Correspondence with Schelling.

The different standpoints which Hegel worked through in himself, and of which he set down in a multitude of aphorisms the monuments of reflection, followed one another in him without the appearance of external vehemence and violence. A development that broke off quickly, throwing itself from one extreme to the other, was not Hegel’s way; its basic form was *gradualness*. Slowly, and always only through an estrangement from himself, his system grew forth. Hegel’s productivity attached itself in its formation first critically to something *given*. But while it grasped the latter, his *own* genius also stepped forth. The externalization to what is alien was the service by means of which he freed himself from the bondage of his immediate depth. From such devotion and critique he then returned so much the more self-assured to himself. This holds especially of his relation to Schelling, which has often enough been distorted into a dependency, as if Hegel, without peculiar power, had merely hammered the poetry of Schelling’s philosophizing, with a flat understanding, into a dry prose. For as true as it is that Hegel owes to the Schellingian system a mighty impetus and has taken it up into himself in the most profound way, so true it is also that he has no less made Fichte’s, no less Kant’s, no less Spinoza’s, Plato’s and Aristotle’s system a living possession. He did not need to fear spoiling his own originality by the study of other originals, as weak natures often hold themselves instinctively aloof from the achievements of others, because acquaintance with them would make their own achievements superfluous. Schelling had the advantage over Hegel of the facility of freeing himself quickly from that which

[p. 63]

he had worked out, to separate it and hand it over to the public. Upon Hegel, who brooded more within himself, he made an extraordinary *impression* by his confident and glory-crowned appearance.

In the *Heidelberg Yearbooks Bachmann* in 1810, in a review of Hegel’s *Phenomenology*, compared for the first time Schelling with Plato, Hegel with Aristotle. Since that time this comparison has become stereotyped. It also has a certain truth, yet, like all such comparisons, not unconditionally. In particular it does not fit with regard to form. It would be hard to find in Schelling anything similar to Plato’s artistic closedness and careful execution; the dialogue *Bruno* remains too far behind Plato’s dramatic energy and stylistic peculiarity. Hegel’s compositions, on the other hand, differ from the Aristotelian precisely again through their dialectical course, which not merely keeps the whole in order, but lets the Concept unfold itself without interludes, a movement which lets the individual determinations appear, as it were, as acting. Schelling’s sanguine restlessness and combinatory boldness were indisputably necessary to create a breakthrough through the narrowness into which idealism had fallen through the subjective extreme; but Hegel’s thorough scholarship, self-denial, patience and critical coldness were no less necessary in order to bring forth determinate shapes from the chaotic tumult which followed that breakthrough. The presentient, postulatory element in Schelling had to make the attempt at verification through the considered, coherence-demanding element in Hegel. Schelling promised more than he performed; Hegel promised nothing, but performed all the more. Hegel, too, like every inventive head, carried about with him all manner of plans which have not come to execution. But he held back the utterance of such thoughts or gave them, when he did utter them, the form of generality. *One* can, he was wont to say in such a case, conceive the thought of a philosophical mathematics, etc. He did not announce with solemn pomp that he would make the great stroke.

Oddly enough, the opinion has also spread of holding Schelling poetic and modern in expression, Hegel abstruse and scholastic. The parallel between Plato and Aristotle has, according to a very common, groundless prejudice, raised the favor

[p. 64]

for the style of the former just as much as the disfavor for that of the latter. In fact, Schelling has gladly taken over enthusiastic turns of phrase from Plato and, where he lacked Concepts, has gladly cited the verses of old poets, namely in prefaces and smaller essays. But if one praises the poetic touch of these, it is wrong to forget that the figurative originality of Hegel is no less great in his armored prefaces, in his speeches and critiques. Were the talk, however, of the larger works, one would have to call, without hesitation, not Hegel but Schelling the *scholastic*. Not only is the expression with him often kept entirely in scholastic terminology, even down to the inclination toward Latin endings on already naturalized Latin words, but also the cut of the whole is entirely scholastic in problems and solutions, in propositions and proofs, in theories and verifications, demonstrations and corollaries — quite apart from the fact that at every moment one is torn out of the continuity of the development by remarks, parentheses, remarks on the remarks. One always senses the in itself ingenious spirit, but also the half-measure of its shaping, and Hegel with his dialectic is by far the *more modern spirit*. In *way of life*, on the other hand, Schelling is the more modern man. In science he wraps himself halfway in the gray gown of the scholastic; but when, as academic president, he does the honors at the birthday of a king or at the funeral ceremony for a Talleyrand, yes, then he shines with the most up-to-date elegance.

Schelling had taken his doctorate in Tübingen in 1792 with a dissertation on the third chapter of Genesis. In 1793 he had printed in the *Memorabilien*, a philosophical-theological journal edited by *Paulus*, Part V, pp. 1–68, an essay on myths, historical legends and philosophemes of the oldest world. Hegel had not been in contact with Schelling since his departure from Tübingen, but a notice of that essay which came to his attention occasioned him to write to Schelling from Bern on Christmas Eve 1794 as follows:

My dear fellow!

I would gladly have long since renewed with you the friendly connection in which we formerly stood with one another. This

[p. 65]

desire awoke again quite recently, in that I only lately read the notice of an essay by you in the Paulus *Memorabilien* and met you on your old way, clarifying important theological Concepts and helping little by little to put aside the old leaven. I can attest to you nothing other than a joyful sympathy over it. I believe the time has come when one should, in general, speak out more freely, in part indeed already does so, and is allowed to. Only my distance from the scenes of literary activity puts me out of the position of receiving, now and then, news of a matter which interests me so much, and you would oblige me greatly if you would be willing to give me news, partly of this, partly of your works, from time to time. I long very much for a situation — not in Tübingen — where I could make up for what I formerly neglected, and could myself lend a hand to the work now and then. I am not wholly idle, but my too heterogeneous and often interrupted occupation lets me come to nothing proper. By chance I spoke a few days ago here with the author of the letters in *Archenholz’s Minerva*, with which you are well acquainted, signed D., allegedly an Englishman. The author, however, is a Silesian and is called *Elsner*. He gave me news of some Württembergers in Paris, also of *Reinhard*, who has in the *Departement des affaires étrangères* a post of great importance. Elsner is still a young man, of whom one sees that he has worked much. He is living as a private scholar here this winter. — What is *Renz* doing, then? Has he buried his talent? I hope not. It would certainly be worth the trouble to induce or encourage him to collect his certainly thorough investigations on important subjects. This might perhaps compensate him for the vexation which he has had for a long time. I have some friends in Saxony who would be quite helpful to him toward further placing. If you do not consider him wholly disinclined, then encourage him to something of the sort, seek to overcome his modesty. In any case greet him on my account.

How do things look otherwise in Tübingen? Until a sort of *Reinhold* or *Fichte* sits there on a professorial chair, nothing real will come out. Nowhere, I believe, is so faithfully

[p. 66]

as there the old system propagated; and even if this has no influence on individual good heads, the matter nevertheless maintains itself in the greater part, in the mechanical heads. With regard to these it is very important what kind of system, what kind of spirit, a professor has, for through them this is for the most part set in circulation or properly kept therein.

Of other objections than *Storr’s* to *Kant’s* doctrine of religion I have not yet heard. But it will probably have experienced more of them already. Its influence, which for now admittedly is still quiet, will come to daylight only with time.

That Car— has been guillotined you will know? Do you still read French papers? If I remember rightly, I was told that they are forbidden in Württemberg. This trial is very important and has unveiled the whole infamy of the Robespierrots.

A thousand greetings to *Süßkind* and *Kapf*.

Your friend.

One more request. Could *Süßkind* not send me the pages from the *Oberdeutsche Zeitung* in which *Mauchart’s Repertorium* is reviewed? I would not know how to get hold of them here.

Schelling’s answer, on the eve of Epiphany 1795.

Hegel to Schelling; undated, 1795.

My dear fellow!

How much joy your letter has given me, I need not tell you at greater length. More than your faithful remembrance of your friends, only the course which your spirit had long since entered upon, and which it still continues to pursue, could interest me. Never have we become strangers to one another as friends. Still less are we strangers to one another with regard to that which constitutes the greatest interest of every rational person and to whose furtherance and spread he will seek, as far as lies within his powers, to contribute.

For some time I have taken up again the study of the *Kantian* philosophy, in order to learn to apply its important results to many an idea still commonplace among us, and

[p. 67]

to work these over in accordance with those. — With the newer endeavors to penetrate into deeper depths I am as yet as little acquainted as with the *Reinholdian* ones, since these speculations seem to me to be of greater significance only for theoretical reason than of great applicability to more general, usable Concepts. I therefore do not know these endeavors more closely with respect to their purpose; I only dimly surmise it. But that you did not communicate to me the sheets which you had printed, apprehension about the postage should surely not have deterred you from. Just give them to the mail coach, not to the letter post. They will be highly valuable to me.

What you tell me of the theological-Kantian — *si Diis placet* [if the gods please] — course of philosophy in Tübingen is not to be wondered at. *Orthodoxy is not to be shaken as long as its profession, bound up with worldly advantages, is interwoven with the whole of the state.* This interest is too strong for it to be given up soon, and it works without one being clearly conscious of it in its entirety. So long, then, it has on its side the whole, always most numerous troop of thoughtless followers or shouters without any higher interest. If this troop reads something that is contrary to its conviction (if one wants to do its word-mongering the honor of calling it that), and whose truth it perhaps feels, then it says: yes, it is probably true — goes to sleep on it, and in the morning one drinks one’s coffee and pours it out for others, as if nothing had happened. Besides, they put up with everything that is offered them and that keeps them in the system of routine. But I believe it would be interesting to disturb as much as possible, in their ant-like zeal, the theologians who bring up critical building material for the fortification of their Gothic temple, to make everything difficult for them, to whip them out of every corner of evasion until they find none more and must show their nakedness quite to the light of day. Among the building material which they carry off from the Kantian pyre in order to prevent the conflagration of dogmatics, they also probably always bring burning coals in with them, and facilitate the general spread of philosophical ideas. As to the mischief of which you write, and whose final act I can imagine accordingly, it is, however, indisputably

[p. 68]

Fichte who, by his *Critique of Revelation*, has opened door and hinge to it. He himself has made moderate use of it, but once his principles are firmly accepted, no goal or dam is any longer to be set for theological logic. He constructs from the holiness of God what he, by virtue of his moral nature, must and should do, and has thereby reintroduced the old manner in dogmatics of proving. It would perhaps be worth the trouble to elucidate this more closely. If I had time, I would seek to determine more closely how far we, *after the fortification of moral faith*, may now use the *legitimated Idea of God backwards*, e.g. in explaining the teleological relation, etc.; take it along even now from *ethicotheology* to *physicotheology*, and now hold sway there with it. This seems to me to be the course which one takes with the Idea of providence in general, as well as with miracles, and, like Fichte, with revelation, etc. Should I come to develop my opinion further, I will submit it to your critique, but beg indulgence in advance. My distance from many kinds of books and the restrictedness of my time do not permit me to work out many an idea which I carry about with me. I shall at least do no less than I can. I am convinced that only through continual shaking and jolting from all sides is an effect of importance finally to be hoped for. Something always sticks, and every contribution of the kind, even if it contains nothing new, has its merit, and communication and common labor encourages and strengthens. Let us often repeat your call: we will not remain behind!

What is *Renz* doing? There seems to be something distrustful in his character, which does not gladly communicate itself, works only for itself, holds others not worth the trouble of doing something for them, or holds the evil too incurable. Might your friendship urge him, urge him to activity, to polemicize against the theologians now living? The necessity, and that it is not superfluous, is evident from their very existence.

*Hölderlin* writes to me at times from Jena. I will make him reproaches on your account. He hears Fichte and speaks with enthusiasm of him as a Titan who for humanity

[p. 69]

fights, and whose sphere of action will certainly not remain within the walls of the lecture hall. From the fact that he does not write to you you must not infer coldness in friendship, for this has certainly not diminished with him, and his interest in cosmopolitan ideas is, as it seems to me, ever on the increase. May the Kingdom of God come, and may our hands not be idle in our lap!

An expression in your letter about the moral proof I do not quite understand, the one: “to know how to handle them so that the individual personal being springs forth.” Do you believe we do not actually reach so far? Farewell! Reason and freedom remain our watchword, and our point of union the *invisible church*.

Answer me very soon. Greet my friends.

H.

Schelling’s answer. Tübingen, the 4th of February 1795.

Hegel to Schelling. Bern, the 16th of April 1795.

My dear fellow!

The delay of my answer has its ground partly in all sorts of business, partly also in distractions, which were occasioned by the political festivals that were celebrated here. Every ten years the *conseil souverain* [sovereign council] and the members who may have retired in this time are replenished. How humanly things go on in this, how all the intrigues at princely courts through cousins and female cousins are nothing compared with the combinations which are made here, I cannot describe to you. The father appoints his son, or the son-in-law who brings the largest dowry, etc. To get to know an aristocratic constitution one must have spent such a winter here before Easter, at which the replenishment takes place.

Still more did the wish hinder me from a speedier answer, to write you a thorough judgment on your writing sent to me, for which I thank you very much, at least to show you that I have fully grasped your ideas. But I had not the time for a thorough study of them. Only so far as I have grasped the main ideas do I see in them a *completion* of *science*, which will give us the most fruitful results.

[p. 70]

I see in it the work of a head whose friendship I can be proud of, who will deliver his great contribution to the important revolution in the system of ideas of all Germany. To encourage you to carry out your system fully would be an insult, since an activity that has seized such a subject has no need of it. From the *Kantian* system and its highest completion I expect a revolution in Germany which will proceed from principles that are already present and need only to be worked over generally and applied to all previous knowledge. Always, to be sure, such an esoteric philosophy will remain; the Idea of God as the absolute I will belong under it. In studying the postulates of practical reason I had had presentiments of what you set out clearly to me in your last letter, what I found in your writing, and what *Fichte’s Foundation of the Science of Knowledge* will completely disclose to me. By the consequences that will result from this, many gentlemen will one day be put into amazement. One will grow dizzy at this highest height. But why has it taken so long to arrive at rating the dignity of man higher, at recognizing his faculty of freedom, which sets him in the same order of spirits? I believe there is no better sign of the times than this, that humanity is *presented as so worthy of respect before itself*. It is a proof that the nimbus around the heads of the oppressors and gods of the earth is vanishing. The philosophers prove this dignity, and the peoples will learn to feel it and will not demand their rights trodden into the dust, but themselves take them up again, appropriate them. Religion and politics have played under one blanket. The former has *taught* what despotism *wanted*: contempt for the human race, its incapacity for any good, to be anything through itself. With the spread of the ideas of how everything *ought* to be, the indolence of settled people, forever taking everything as it is, will vanish. The enlivening power of ideas, even if they should still have limitations in themselves, such as those of the fatherland, its constitution, etc., will elevate hearts, and they will learn to sacrifice themselves to them, since at present the spirit of the constitutions has made with self-interest a

[p. 71]

pact, on which it has founded its kingdom. I constantly call to myself from the *Courses of Life*: “Strive toward the sun, friends, so that the salvation of the human race may soon be ripe. What do the hindering leaves want, what the branches? *Fight your way through to the sun!* And if you grow weary, well and good, so much the better one sleeps!” — It occurs to me that this summer is your last in Tübingen. If you write a disputation of your own, I would ask you to send it to me as soon as possible. Also if you have anything else printed, then ask the bookseller *Cotta* to have it sent to me. — I am eager for the products of the Easter fair. *Fichte’s Science of Knowledge* I intend to study in the summer, when I shall in general have more leisure to carry out some ideas which I have been going about with for a long time; in which respect I lack the use of a library, which I would very much need. — *Schiller’s Horen*, first number, has given me great enjoyment. The essay *On the Aesthetic Education of the Human Race* is a masterpiece. — *Niethammer* announced at the beginning of the year a *philosophical journal*; has anything come of it? — *Hölderlin* writes to me often from Jena. He is quite enraptured with *Fichte*, of whom he expects great designs. How well it must do *Kant* to see the fruits of his labor already in such worthy successors. The harvest will one day be glorious. To *Süßkind* I give thanks for the friendly trouble he has undertaken for me. What is *Renz* doing? According to your remarks, his relation to his uncle is incomprehensible to me and takes from me the courage to turn to him. — What path is *Hauber* taking?

Farewell, my friend! I should like to see us gathered again someday, to communicate many things to one another, to hear from one another what could confirm our hopes.

Your H.

Schelling’s answer of 21 July 1795, from Tübingen.

Hegel to Schelling. Tschugg near Erlach, via Bern, the 30th of August 1795.

The gifts, my dearest friend, which you have sent me, as well as your letter, have caused me the liveliest joy and the

[p. 72]

fullest enjoyment, and I am obliged to you in the extreme for it. It is impossible for me to write you everything that I felt and thought thereby. Your first writing, the attempt to study Fichte’s *Foundation*, in part my own presentiments, have put me in a position to penetrate into your spirit and to follow its course, much more than I was able to do with your first writing, which however is now explained to me by your second. I was once on the point of making clear to myself in an essay what it could mean *to approach God*, and believed I would find in it the satisfaction of the postulate that practical reason commands the world of appearances, and of the remaining postulates. What hovered before me obscure and undeveloped, your writing has clarified for me most gloriously and satisfyingly. Thanks be to you for it, on my behalf; and everyone to whom the welfare of the sciences and the best of the world is at heart will thank you, if not now, then in time. What will stand in the way of being understood and of your endeavors finding entry will, I imagine, in general be this, that people will absolutely not want to give up their not-I. In the moral respect they fear illumination and the struggle into which their comfortable system of convenience may fall. In the theoretical sense they have indeed learned from Kant that the hitherto customary proof for immortality and the ontological one are not tenable (they held it to be the disclosure of an artificial deception, p. 17 of your writing), but they have not yet grasped that the failing of such adventures of reason and of its flying beyond the I is grounded in its very nature. Hence with them, too, e.g. also in their treatment of the attributes of God, nothing has been changed. Only the ground was laid differently. And this *attribute of God* is still, as the *Lebensläufer* [author of the *Courses of Life*] somewhere expresses it, the skeleton key with which these gentlemen unlock everything. If p. 103 of your writing does not open their understanding also about this (for even to draw these conclusions they are too sluggish, one must dictate everything to them *totidem verbis* [in so many words]), then they are *capita insanabilia* [incurable cases].

The reviewer of your first writing in the Tübingen learned gazette may be venerable in other respects, but to believe that he finds in it an objective principle as the highest,

[p. 73]

has indeed truly shown no profundity. It will probably be *Abel*. The wretched reviewer, however, in *Jacob’s Philosophical Annals* you have treated as he deserved. *Jacob* will probably want to become a knight, too, on the Fichtean philosophy, as *Eberhard* did on the Kantian, and their pompously announced journals will have the same fate.

The gloomy prospects which you show for philosophy in your letter have filled me with melancholy. Above the consequences which the misunderstanding of your principles could have for you, you are exalted. You have silently cast your word into infinite time. To be grinned at here and there, that, I know, you despise, but in regard to others, who recoil before the results, your writing is as good as not written at all. Your system will have the fate of all the systems of those men whose spirit has run ahead of the faith and the prejudices of their times. One has decried them and refuted them from out of their own system; meanwhile scientific culture went quietly its course, and fifty years later the crowd, which merely swims along with the stream of its time, has found with astonishment that the works which it came to know in polemics by hearsay as containing long since refuted errors, when it happens by chance to get sight of one itself, contain the ruling system of their times. A judgment occurs to me here that a Repetent passed on you last summer. He told me you were *too enlightened for this century*; in the next, perhaps, your principles would be in their place. With regard to you, this judgment seems to me insipid, but characteristic with regard to him who passed it and the whole large class of those who do not think it well done to raise themselves above the line of the enlightenment prevailing in their age, circle or state, above the general level, but have the comfortable hope that everything will come in time, and then there will be time enough left for them to take a step forward, or rather they have the hope that they will be pushed along too. Lift your legs yourselves, gentlemen!

The spirit which the previous government threatened to introduce was grounded in hypocrisy and timidity, a consequence of despotism,

[p. 74]

and itself in turn the father of hypocrisy; a spirit that must become dominant in every public constitution that has the chimerical notion of wanting to examine hearts and reins and to take virtue and piety as the standard for the estimation of merit and the distribution of offices. I feel most inwardly the lamentableness of such a condition, in which the state wants to descend into the holy depths of morality and to judge it. It is lamentable even when the state means well. Still infinitely sadder, when hypocrites get the office of judge into their hands, which must happen even if it had been well meant at the outset. This spirit seems to have had influence also on the supplementing of your Repetent institution, which, if it consisted of well-organized heads, could do real good.

Remarks on your writing you cannot expect from me. I am here only an apprentice. I am attempting to study Fichte’s *Foundation*. Allow me a remark which struck me, so that you may at least see the good will to satisfy your desire to have remarks communicated to you. In § 12 you ascribe to the I the attribute of being the *sole substance*. If substance and accident are reciprocal Concepts, then it seems to me that the Concept of substance would *not* be applicable to the *absolute* I; well enough to the *empirical* I, as it occurs in self-consciousness; but that you ascribe to this I, uniting the highest thesis and antithesis, *indivisibility*, which predicate could be attributed only to the absolute, not to the I as it occurs in self-consciousness, in which it occurs only as positing a *part* of its reality. — What I could write you about your disputation would be to attest to you my joy at the freer spirit of the higher criticism that weaves therein, which, as I expected no otherwise of you, unbribed by the venerableness of names, has the whole before its eyes and does not hold words sacred, — and to pay you compliments on your acumen and your scholarship. — I have found in it especially also a suspicion confirmed which I have long harbored, that it would perhaps have turned out more honorable for us and for humanity if some — be it which it may — through councils and creeds

[p. 75]

damned *heresy* had grown into the public system of faith, than that the orthodox system has kept the upper hand.

I am sorry for *Fichte*. Beer-glasses and student swords of the fatherland have therefore resisted the power of his spirit. Perhaps he would have accomplished more had he left them their coarseness and only set himself the task of training a quiet, chosen little band. But it is shameful all the same, his and *Schiller’s* treatment of would-be philosophers. My God, what men of the letter and slaves there still are among them!

*Niethammer’s Journal* I hope to receive any day now, and I look forward especially to your contributions. Your example and your efforts encourage me anew to follow after the cultivation of our times as far as possible. *Hölderlin*, as I hear, has been in Tübingen. Surely you have spent pleasant hours together. How much I wished to have been the third man there!

Of my own work it is not worth the trouble to speak. Perhaps I shall send you, in some time, the plan of something I intend to work out, in which I shall in time call upon you especially for friendly help as well, also in the field of church history, where I am very weak and where I can best seek counsel from you.

Since you will soon be leaving Tübingen, be so kind as to inform me soon of what you have in mind to undertake and of your future place of residence, as of all your fortunes. Above all spare your health, for the sake of your friends. Do not be too stingy with the time you have to spend on recreation. Greet my friends heartily. Next time I shall enclose a letter to Renz for you. It would delay the dispatch of this one. Meanwhile greet him heartily from me, if you write to him. Answer me soon. You cannot believe how good it does me, in my solitude, to hear something from you and other friends from time to time.

Your Hegel.

Letter from Schelling, January 1796, and Leipzig, 20 June 1796.

[p. 76]

#### Hegel’s Correspondence with Hölderlin.

From the letters of Hegel just communicated it already appears that Hegel had entered into a correspondence with Hölderlin immediately after the farewell from Tübingen, one which, however, as it seems, had come somewhat to a standstill. When Hölderlin had gone to Frankfurt am Main as a house tutor, he found there a situation in the same capacity for Hegel, of which he believed that it would be agreeable to him. He therefore wrote to him, and Hegel accepted the offer in the following letter, written from Tschugg near Erlach in 1796, undated, but according to other circumstances in the middle of the summer:

Dearest Hölderlin!

So I am granted, once more, the joy of hearing something from you again; from every line of your letter speaks your unalterable friendship for me; I cannot tell you how much joy it has given me, and still more the hope of soon seeing you myself and embracing you.

Without dwelling longer on this agreeable thought, let me speak directly of the main matter. Your wish alone to see me in the situation of which you write assures me that this relation cannot be other than advantageous for me; I therefore follow your call without hesitation and renounce other prospects that offered themselves to me. With pleasure I enter the excellent family in which I may hope that the share I shall take in the education of my future pupils will be of happy success; to fill their heads with words and concepts usually succeeds, to be sure, but upon the more essential matter, the formation of character, a house tutor will be able to have little influence if the spirit of the parents does not harmonize with his efforts. — With regard to the economic and other circumstances in the house it is indeed often a matter of prudence to explain oneself exactly about them in advance; but I believe I can dispense with this precaution here, and leave it to you to look after my interest, since you will also know best what is usual in Frankfurt in this respect and in what proportion the necessities of life and money stand to one another.

[p. 77]

Service in the house and free laundry I shall also be able to expect.

I refrain from asking you for explanations with regard to Herr *Gogel’s* wishes about the instruction and the special supervision of his children; the instruction at this age will still consist in such knowledge as belongs to all educated people — with regard to outward manners, as to the greater or lesser latitude which Herr Gogel wishes to allow to youthful liveliness, I shall learn his wishes best on the spot and be able to come to an understanding with him about it myself more fully than can be done by letters.

As for the journey, I foresee that its costs will not exceed 10 Karolins, and I wish that you would speak of it provisionally with Herr Gogel and, as you then find fitting, request him to send me a bill of exchange through you, — or, when I come to Frankfurt, to reimburse me the costs.

Much as I regret not being able to set out at once, it is nevertheless impossible for me to leave the house in which I am before about the end of the year, and to arrive in Frankfurt before the middle of January. Since you have once begun to interest yourself in this matter for me, I must still impose upon you to communicate the substance of my letter to Herr Gogel and at the same time to assure him of my esteem. He will, to be sure, see for himself that a part of what you may have said of me to inspire in him the confidence with which he honors me must be put down rather to the account of your friendship for me, or that one friend cannot always judge the other reliably; assure him, however, that I shall take every pains to deserve your recommendation. —

How much share in my quick resolution the longing for you has, how the image of our reunion, of the joyful future of being with you, would hover before my eyes during this interval — of that nothing — farewell.

Your Hegel.

[p. 78]

But this very image became so vivid in him that, full of the most ardent longing for his friend, he composed the following mystical poem in August 1796:

#### Eleusis.

#### *To Hölderlin.*

Around me, in me, dwells repose. The never weary care / Of busy men is sleeping. They grant freedom / And leisure to me. Thanks to you, my / Deliveress, O Night! — With veil of whitish mist / The moon enfolds the uncertain borders / Of the distant hills. Kindly the bright streak / Of the lake gleams over.

Memory puts far off the tedious noises of the day, / As if years lay between it and now. / Your image, my beloved, steps before me, / And the delight of days now fled. But soon it yields / To the sweeter hopes of meeting again.

Already I see painted the long-desired, fiery / Embrace’s scene; then the scene of questions, of the more secret, / The mutual searching-out / Of what in bearing, expression, cast of mind in the friend / Has changed here since that time; — the bliss of certainty / Of finding the old bond’s faith still firmer, riper, / The bond that no oath sealed: / *To live for free truth alone,* / *Peace with the statute* / *That rules opinion and feeling never, never to make!*

Now with more sluggish actuality negotiates the sense / That bore me lightly over mountains, rivers, to you. / But soon a sigh proclaims their discord, and with it / The dream of sweet fancies flees.

My eye lifts up to the eternal heaven’s vault, / To you, O shining star of night! / And of all wishes, of all hopes / Forgetting streams down from your eternity.

Sense loses itself in the beholding. / What I called mine vanishes. / I give myself up to the immeasurable. / I am in it, am all, am only it. / To the returning thought estranged, / It shudders before the infinite and, astonished, grasps / Not the depth of this beholding.

[p. 79]

To the senses fantasy brings the eternal near, / Weds it with shape. — Welcome, you, / Sublime spirits, lofty shades, / From whose brow perfection shines. / It does not terrify. I feel, it is my home too, / The splendor, the earnestness that flows about you.

Ha! if now the gates of your sanctuary sprang open, / O Ceres, you who were enthroned in Eleusis! / Drunk with inspiration I feel now / The shudders of your nearness, / Would understand your revelations. / I would interpret the lofty sense of the images, would hear / The hymns at the feast of the gods, / The lofty sayings of their council.

But your halls have fallen silent, O goddess! / Fled is the circle of the gods to Olympus, / Back from the desecrated altars, / Fled from the grave of profaned humanity / The genius of innocence that conjured them here. / The wisdom of your priests is silent. No sound of the holy consecrations / Has saved itself to us, and in vain seeks / The inquirer’s curiosity, more than love / Of wisdom. The seekers possess it, and despise you. / To master them, they dig for words / Into which your lofty sense was stamped. / In vain! A little dust and ashes only do they seize, / Wherein your life will never, nevermore return for them. / Yet amid mould and the soulless there too were pleased with themselves / The eternally dead, the easily contented! — In vain, there remained / No sign of your festivals, no trace of an image.

To the son of the consecration the fullness of the lofty teachings, / The depth of the unutterable feeling, was far too holy / For him to deem dry signs worthy of it. / Even thought does not grasp the soul, / Which, beyond time and space, sunk in a presentiment of the infinite, / Forgets itself and now to consciousness again / Awakes. Whoever would even speak of it to others, / Were he to speak with angels’ tongues, feels the poverty of words. / He shudders, having thought the holy so small, / Having made it so small through them, that speech seems sin to him / And that, trembling, he closes his mouth. / What the initiate thus forbade himself, a wise / Law forbade the poorer spirits: to make that not known,

[p. 80]

What they have seen, heard, felt in holy night. / That the din of their mischief not disturb even the better ones / In their devotion, their hollow word-lumber, / Not make him angry at the holy itself, that this not / Be so trodden in the mire that one even entrusted it / To memory, so that it not / Become the plaything and the ware of the sophist, / Which he sold by the obol, / The cloak of the eloquent hypocrite, or even / The rod already of the merry boy, and so empty / In the end become that it had only in the echo / Of foreign tongues the root of its life. / Jealously your sons, goddess, did not carry / Your honor to gaping-place and market; they kept it / In the inner sanctuary of the breast. / Hence you did not live upon their mouth. / Their life honored you. In their deeds you live still. / This night too I heard you, holy deity. / You the life of your children, too, often reveals to me, / You I often divine as the soul of their deeds! / You are the lofty sense, the faithful belief / That in a deity, even if everything perishes, does not waver.

#### Life as House Tutor in Frankfurt am Main, from New Year 1797 to the End of 1800.

What Hegel so keenly wished for in his letters to Schelling, a richer literary apparatus, greater leisure and inspiring intercourse with like-minded friends, was to fall to his lot in Frankfurt. In the autumn of 1796 he went from Bern first to Stuttgart, to see his family again. According to his sister’s report he was very withdrawn, almost gloomy, and thawed only in quite narrow circles into the cheerfulness that people had formerly so liked in him. In January 1797 he took up his post as house tutor in Frankfurt with the merchant *Gogel*, who lived on the Rossmarkt. His situation here must have been fairly comfortable. The painter *Sonnenschein* of Bern expressly mentions in his letters, with great satisfaction, having heard that he is doing so very well. But above all the less care-ridden, more leisured position of Hegel is evident from the great labors which he here went through

[p. 81]

In the same city which was the cradle of *Goethe’s poetry* the *Hegelian system of philosophy* too was to celebrate its actual birthplace.

If Hegel was a polyhistor at the Gymnasium, a republican at the seminary, a theologian and historian in Switzerland, then in Frankfurt the urge of his *speculative* talent matured also into the *resolve* to live for it alone. The *political* inclination he always retained, and never regarded his philosophy as something heterogeneous to it.

But Frankfurt granted him not only a scholarly leisure, it also created for him a *social* world which suited him in heart and spirit. Here he found his *Hölderlin*, whose unhappy catastrophe he was to witness here. Here he found *Sinclair*, who had likewise studied in Tübingen and strove with all his powers to overcome the subjectivism of idealism. Here he found the latter’s spirited friend *Zwilling*; the philosopher *Muhrbeck*, who later died in Greifswald. Here he came into contact with *Berger*, with *Erichson*, with *Erhard*. With *Molitor*, *Ebel* and *Vogt*, whom *Bettina’s* correspondence with Günderode presents to us so vividly, he had, despite Sinclair’s acquaintance with them, no personal relation. Sinclair expressly writes from Hamburg, on 16 August 1810, to Hegel: “*Molitor*, of whom I already spoke to you, I think, sends you his regards. Although you would not agree entirely, you would nevertheless find in him and in Nicolaus *Vogt* and *Ebel* here a very interesting company.”

In the same letter Sinclair gives closer information about *Zwilling*: “It would please me very much, he writes, if this bond of truth might yet strengthen that of our old friendship, for the others are no more, and of those who shared with us the view of truth you alone have remained to me. I must tell you, namely, that Zwilling fell at the battle of Wagram on the second day. He was squadron commander in the Hessen-Homburg hussars, was to become a major, and had the greatest prospects. He was known in the army as the most skillful and bravest officer and had carried out several coups on his own. In the battle he held the most dangerous place on the left wing,

[p. 82]

where his regiment lost two thirds of its officers and men. A canister shot burst at his side and wounded those standing around as well. Yet he lived a few minutes more, and when he had fallen from his horse and the hussars lifted him and carried him behind the front, he spoke with them to the last and said: they should just bury him in the earth, alive or dead, so that the enemy, should he advance, would find no further Austrian officer. He had foreseen his death, had made his will two days before, and on the evening of the first battle he said he would not survive the next day. In the night he fell upon the Saxons with his division, which alarmed the whole camp, almost produced a total rout, and compelled Napoleon himself to mount his horse. All these circumstances I have from the best sources.”

Sinclair lived with his mother in *Homburg* and held various appointments in the Hessian civil service. In philosophy he was at that time a Fichtean, but sought gradually to form a system of his own, which he published under the title *Truth and Certainty* in 1811 in three volumes, adding in 1813 a work on the treatment of physics from the standpoint of metaphysics. He was active as a poet too. With Erichson he published pseudonymously, as *Crisalin*, in 1803 a small collection of poems, *Faith and Poetry*, and soon afterward, in Schiller’s manner, a trilogy in three parts, *The Cevennes War*. He must be regarded as the one who, in contrast to the *classical Romanticism* of Hölderlin, became for Hegel the representative of *Christian Romanticism* standing immediately close to him. Through the *speculative* mysticism into which Hegel during his Swiss period had passed over from rationalism and Fichteanism, he had become very receptive to such materials of culture. Sinclair was also acquainted with Hegel’s family and held Christiane especially in high regard. He lived now in Frankfurt, now in Homburg, and took Hölderlin across to the latter place when he fell into his madness. Sinclair died suddenly of a stroke at the Congress of Vienna (see Varnhagen’s *Memoirs*, vol. V, p. 47).

That Hegel in his intercourse with Sinclair and Hölderlin in a

[p. 83]

situation that satisfied him completely in his heart could be *tempted* into poetic attempts is no wonder, although he could not make a verse. Hegel had the highest receptiveness for music not only in general, but also for the musical side of language; he was himself a master of prose, but to hear out the measure of the tones in *his own* presentation was unspeakably hard for him. So great is the difference between the most re-creative reproduction and production. We have already seen how Hegel’s elegy to Hölderlin, despite the simple iambic rhythm, has a multitude of hybrid passages. The remaining Frankfurt poetic attempts all show the struggle with the meter and the succumbing in it. In the language, however, there appears at the same time again so much that is strangely peculiar that we must form at least some closer idea of it. As a genuine Faust he then possessed a *poodle* and on 10 December 1798 made on it the following verses, ending with a *Fabula docet* [the moral of the fable], which were probably meant by his intention to be distichs:

He runs in wide circles out into the plain; we are his return;

He searches in the earth, he catches sight of me and already hops up at me again. Where does he stay?

Now he has met playmates. They tease, flee and seek one another;

He who just now chased is now a fugitive. But see, they now run too far.

Here! The word tears him loose from instinct and compels him to the master.

But a bitch draws him again to the right. Halt!

Back! He does not hear. The stick awaits you. I no longer see him.

Along the hedge he sneaks hither, the bad conscience delays his steps.

To me! You circle wide around me, fawn, he must —

Have you never yet *seen* what it means: Must? Here you see it. He cannot do otherwise.

You cry out because of the blows: obey the calling word of the master.

In most of these formally strange creations there prevails a shatteringly wistful strain. In exuberant enthusiasm everything wants to dissolve into light and sound. Thus he wrote on 12 December 1798, two days, that is, after that accurate description of the necessity of the poodle, an ode-like poem:

Your friends mourn, O nature! / You, thousand-shaped Proteus, / Your power of change has abandoned, / And a soulless husk

[p. 84]

Lies, the skin of the aged earth, / From whose pores once joy and soul played. / But upon the cloudless, / All-vaulting blue / Wanders in unfailing splendor / The eye of the world, / Smiles kindly at the bride, etc.

On 21 August 1800 he described a *moonlight bath*:

Against the stream’s pressing waves / I labored to maintain my place, / And, embraced by their surrounding coolness, / Strengthened in struggling against them, / I stepped dripping onto the bank. / But over there with drunken face / Luna pressed up through the vapors. / Does heating struggle redden her cheek above earth and mist, / Or does she blush virginally, exposing herself to the mortal race? / Down to us and our plains, trees, / She tenderly lays her rays upon, / For the immortals, not growing poorer, / Nor lower, give themselves to earth and live with her, etc.

He also sang of *spring* in would-be stanzas and interwove with his description the Cerealian myth. At least the beginning may stand here, because turns of phrase like that of a *threatening* of spring are too remarkable:

Spring threatens! To outer life, as the bud / Swells toward it, man too feels urged / To give himself up. / The sun grows, and loud and wild / Outward goes the striving of all the senses! — / Then you set yet within us an image, / A higher one than nature’s shapes, / To hold fast the inner that wants to flee.

Indeed the spirit shall unite with nature, / Yet not too rashly nor unconsecrated, / Thus your severity, high priestess, still parts / Those who already think themselves joined. / Only received by the mother as yours, / Only freed of guilt before the queen, / May love now glow forth transfigured from you, / Paying homage to you, only its happiness can bloom.

[p. 85]

The lofty brow, freed of the bandage’s covering, / Is now adorned by the diadem, forth / Wells under, over it the fullness of the locks, / Bright is the eye; high aloft in the chariot / Majestically the figure moves through the surging crowd, etc.

#### Political Studies.

From a residence city Hegel had come, out of the parental house, as that of an official, to an idyllic university town; from a patriarchal aristocracy of lineage in Bern he now came to a city of mercantile money-aristocracy. At the same time he moved closer again to the immediate scene of political development and found his participation in it thereby heightened. For the relations of acquisition and possession *England* in particular captivated him, partly, no doubt, following the general inclination which the previous century felt toward the study of its constitution as an ideal, and partly, too, no doubt, because in no country of Europe have the forms of acquisition and of property developed so many-sidedly as precisely in England, and this development is matched in personal relations by an equally rich manifold. With great suspense, as his excerpts from English newspapers prove, Hegel followed the parliamentary debates on the *poor-rate* as the alms with which the aristocracy of rank and of money hoped to appease the vehemence of the multitude without subsistence. — The reform of the *Prussian Landrecht*, too, interested him greatly. He wrote down many a remark on it, e.g. on the *prison system*: “The question has been raised whether the Spanish cloak and fiddle punishment has been abolished by the General Prussian Landrecht? It has been thought that, so long as the prisons in the country and even in most towns serve only to receive the prisoners and for the sensation of punishment, nothing would thereby be accomplished against the peasants and in particular against the lower class and the servants, but the purpose of punishment would be entirely missed, and the country would also lose a considerable quantity of workers, if the lesser corporal punishments might be restricted to *mere* imprisonment

[p. 86]

*Carmer’s* reply runs: ‘the corporal punishments — as hindrances to the ennoblement of morality in the lower classes of the people — to be put out of practice as far as possible, so that they would become dispensable through modification of the ordinary prison institutions. If arrest were made so severe by complete solitude and isolation from all communication with human beings, by cutting off accustomed needs and comforts, e.g. tobacco, by all manner of positions and postures repugnant to sensation yet not harmful to health, and by disagreeable, sour labors, etc., that its quality permitted a shorter duration and the propensity to sloth found no nourishment in it.’ — Is this not *Iroquois-like*, who devise torments for their captive enemies and with voluptuousness practice every new torture? The *moral voluptuousness* of punishing and of the intention of improvement is not much different from the voluptuousness of revenge, and, with the intention of ennoblement, very much at odds in displaying cruelty, for nothing brutalizes and makes so abominable as the sight of it. *Cutting off communication is just, for the criminal has isolated himself.* To regard and to command human beings with a cold understanding, now as laboring and producing beings, now as beings to be improved, becomes the worst tyranny, because the best of the whole as purpose is alien to them, if it is not just.”

All Hegel’s thoughts on the essence of civil society, on need and labor, on the division of labor and the wealth of the estates, poor relief and police, taxes, etc., finally concentrated in a glossing *commentary* on the German translation of *Stewart’s* political economy, which he wrote from 19 February to 16 May 1799 and which is still completely preserved. There occur in it many grand views into politics and history, many fine remarks. Stewart was still an adherent of the mercantile system. With noble pathos, with a wealth of interesting examples, Hegel combated what is dead in it, striving in the midst of competition and in the mechanism of labor as of commerce to rescue the heart of man.

Hegel had repeatedly occupied himself in Switzerland with *Kant’s Critique of Practical Reason*. An excerpt from it with some remarks, such as he had earlier made at the Stift also from

[p. 87]

the *Critique of Pure Reason*, has also been preserved. But when Kant in 1797 published his *Doctrine of Right* and *Doctrine of Virtue*, he subjected both works, together with the *Metaphysics of Morals*, from 10 August 1798 onward, to a strict study. He wished here to leave nothing uncomprehended, nothing undiscussed. After he had proceeded in his excerpt from the introductions to the particular, he set, in the individual points, quite simply his own concepts over against the Kantian concepts. He already strove here to unite the *legality* of positive right and the *morality* of the inwardness that knows itself as good or evil in a higher Concept, which he in these commentaries frequently called simply *life*, later *ethical life*. He protested against the suppression of *nature* in Kant and against the *dismemberment* of man into the casuistry arising from the absolutism of the concept of duty. Of the critique of the *Doctrine of Virtue* only little has remained, chiefly a smaller essay concerning its possibility and division, which connects with Kant’s attempts to find the *transition* from the *Doctrine of Right* to the *Doctrine of Virtue*. The commentary on the *Metaphysics of Morals* and on the *Doctrine of Right*, however, is still completely extant and, in its unconstrained vigor, filled with the whole charm of such unintentional productions, which one might compare to the drawings of visual artists. From the dualism of *state* and *church* he now sought to find his way out. Kant’s opinion he summed up in the following words: “Both, state and church, are to leave one another in peace and are none of one another’s business.” To this Hegel wrote: “How and to what extent is this separation possible? If the state has the principle of *property*, the law of the church is contrary to its law. Its law concerns throughout determinate rights, man being thought very *incompletely* as a *possessing* one, whereas in the church man is a *whole* and the purpose of the church, as the visible one, which acts and makes arrangements, goes toward giving him the feeling of this wholeness and maintaining it. Acting in the spirit of the church, man acts as a whole not only against individual laws of the state, but against the whole spirit of them, against *their whole*.
