Either the citizen is not in earnest about his relation to the state or not about that to the church, if he can remain calm in both

[p. 88]

The two extremes, *Jesuits* and *Quakers*, have sought to be in earnest about both and to unite them, the latter by not letting themselves in for anything of the state that would be contrary to the church (a determinate one, to be sure, which admits much that is of the state, makes into the ecclesiastical much that, because it is law, is not so); the former attempted, with thoroughgoing outward submission to its laws, to cheat the state, through the inwardness of their freedom of conscience, of all civic virtues. If the state wishes to cling firmly to its whole and by force to keep the overflowing church from its banks, it becomes inhuman and monstrous and will engender *fanaticism*, which, because it sees the individual human beings, the human relations, in the power of the state, shatters it in them and so shatters them along with it. — If, however, the principle of the state is *a complete whole, then church and state cannot possibly be different*. What to the latter is the thought, the ruling, is to the former precisely the same whole as a living one, presented by imagination. The whole of the church is only then a fragment when man in the whole is shattered into a particular *state-man* and a particular *church-man*.”

The significance of contemporary history in general, its relation to the future, occupied Hegel keenly, and he sought to gather his thoughts on it into more general points of view. Thus he portrayed the present *world crisis*: “The ever-growing contradiction between the unknown, which men seek unconsciously, and the life that is offered and permitted them and which they have made their own, the longing for life of those who have worked nature up into the Idea within themselves, contain the striving for mutual approach. The need of the former, in consciousness, concerning what holds them captive, and the desire to obtain the unknown, coincides with the need of the latter to pass over into life out of their Idea. These cannot live alone, and *alone is man always*, even if he has presented his nature before himself, has made this presentation his companion and enjoys himself in it. He must *also find what is presented as something living*. The situation of man, whom the age has driven into an inner world, can either, if he wishes to maintain himself in it, be only a perpetual

[p. 89]

death, or, if nature drives him to life, only a striving to sublate the negative of the existing world, in order to find himself in it, in order to be able to live. His suffering is bound up with consciousness of the limits on account of which he disdains life as it would be permitted to him. He wills his suffering, whereas the suffering of the man without reflection on his fate is without will, because he honors the negative, takes the limits in the form of their lawful and power-holding existence as unconquerable and his determinacies, like their contradictions, as absolute, and sacrifices himself and others to them, even when they violate his drives.”

“The sublation of that which with regard to nature is negative, with regard to will positive, is effected neither by force that one inflicts on one’s own fate nor by that which it experiences from outside. In both cases fate remains what it is. The determinacy, the limit, is not separated from life by *force*. Foreign force is a particular against a particular, the robbery of a property, a new suffering. *The enthusiasm of one who is bound is a moment fearful to himself*, in which he loses himself and finds his consciousness again only in what has been forgotten.”

“The feeling of the contradiction of nature with the existing life is the need that it be removed, and this it will be when *the existing life* has lost its power and all its dignity, when it has become pure negative. All appearances of this age show that satisfaction is no longer found in the old life. *It was a confinement to an orderly dominion over one’s property, a contemplation and enjoyment of one’s wholly subject small world; and then also a self-annihilation reconciling this confinement, and an elevation in the thought of heaven.* On the one hand the *need* of the age has attacked that property, on the other hand in *luxury* the limitation has been removed, and in both cases man has been made the master and *his power over actuality the highest*. Over this arid life of the understanding there has grown greater, on one side, the *bad conscience* of making one’s property, things, into the Absolute, and

[p. 90]

with it, on the other, the *suffering* of men. A better life has breathed upon this age. Its urge feeds on the deeds of great characters among individual men, on the movements of whole peoples, on the presentation of nature and of fate by poets. Through metaphysics the limitations receive their bounds and their necessity in the connection of the whole. The limited life as power can only then be attacked by a better one in a hostile way with power, when this too has become a power and has force to fear. As a particular against a particular, nature in its actual life is the only attack or refutation of the worse life, and such a thing cannot be the object of a deliberate activity. But the limited can be attacked through its own truth, which lies in it, and be brought into contradiction with this. It founds its dominion not on force (particular against particular), but rather on *universality*. This truth, the right which it lays claim to for itself, must be taken from it and given to that part of life which is demanded. This dignity of a universality, of a right, is what makes the demand of suffering (of the drives that come into contradiction with the existing life clothed with that honor) *so timid, as if going against conscience*. To the positive, to the existing, which is a negation of nature, its truth, that right shall be, is left. In the *German Empire* the power-holding universality as the source of all right has vanished, because it has isolated itself, made itself particular. Universality is therefore now present only as *thought*, no longer as *actuality*. About what *public opinion*, more brightly or more darkly, through *loss of confidence*, has decided, little is needed to make a clearer consciousness more general. And all existing rights have, after all, their ground only in this connection with the whole, which, because it has long since ceased to be, has let them all become particular.”

But Hegel did not stop at such general considerations; he expressed his sympathy in Germany’s fate in a very definite way by composing a *political pamphlet*, which he wrote in 1798 and whose title he changed in many ways. At first it was to be called:

[p. 91]

That the *Württemberg* magistrates must be elected by the people.

Then he put, for “people”: by the *citizens*; and at last he wrote:

On the Most Recent *Internal Conditions* of Württemberg, especially on the Constitution of the Magistracy.

A dedication: To the Württemberg People, he struck out later. Except for a few fragments this work is no longer extant. He wished to have it printed and communicated it to three friends in Stuttgart. These gave him some further hints for suitable alterations, strengthened his materials still more, but in the end advised omitting the printing, since the work would not only do no good, but rather, under the prevailing circumstances, do harm. One of these friends wrote from Stuttgart on 7 August the following:

“As long, moreover, as no other arrangements with regard to legislation are made, just as much comes out of many diets as if one were held once in 27 years. They are not much more than a new burden for the deceived people. The dismissal of the Estates, too, which you have set down quite generally, is likewise nothing less than arbitrary. — To be sure, dearest friend, our standing has sunk deep. The advocates of the great nation have given up the most sacred rights of humanity to the contempt and mockery of our enemies. I know no revenge that would be commensurate with their crime. Under these circumstances the publication of your essay would also be for us more an evil than a benefit.”

The principles of the work wavered between those of *Rousseau’s* politics, to which Hegel paid homage in Tübingen, and the *Platonic* politics of an ideal and a real estate, to which he turned in Frankfurt, and sought to reconcile unity and equality with the manifoldness of the particular in a new *organization of the Württemberg Estates*. The beautiful opening ran thus:

“It would be time, once, for the Württemberg people to emerge from its wavering between fear and hope, from its alternation of expectation and of disappointment in its expectation. I will not say that it would also be time,

[p. 92]

that everyone who, in a change of things or in the preservation of the old, wishes only his limited advantage or the advantage of his estate, asks only his vanity for counsel, — would give up those paltry wishes, let these petty cares go, and take upon his soul the care for the universal. For men of better wishes, of purer zeal, it would be especially time to hold before their indeterminate will the parts of the constitution that are founded on injustice, and to direct their activity toward the necessary change of such parts.”

“The calm contentment with the actual, the hopelessness, the patient submission to a fate too great, all-powerful, has passed over into hope, into expectation, into courage for something else. The image of better, more just times has come vividly into the souls of men, and a longing, a sighing for a purer, freer condition has stirred all hearts and set them at odds with actuality. The urge to break through the meager limits has fastened its hopes to every event, to every glimmer, even to outrages. Whence could the Württembergers expect more just help than from the assembly of their Estates? The postponement of the satisfaction of these hopes, time, can only purify that longing, but it will only strengthen the drive toward what remedies a true need, that longing will eat only the deeper into the hearts through the delay. It is no chance dizziness that passes. Call it a fever paroxysm, but it ends only with death, or when the sick matter has been sweated out. It is an effort of the still healthy force to drive out the evil.”

“Universal and deep is the feeling that the state-edifice, as it still exists now, is untenable. Universal is the anxiety that it will collapse and in its fall wound everyone. Shall, with that conviction in the heart, this fear become so powerful that one will leave it to chance what is overturned, what preserved, what may stand or what fall? Should one not wish to abandon the untenable itself? To examine with calm eye what belongs to the untenable? *Justice* is in this judgment the sole *standard*; the *courage* to *practice justice*,

[p. 93]

the *sole power* that can remove the tottering completely with honor and glory and bring about a secured condition. How blind are those who may believe that institutions, constitutions, laws that no longer agree with the customs, the needs, the opinion of men, from which the spirit has fled, will last longer; that forms in which understanding and feeling take no more interest are mighty enough to constitute longer the bond of a people! — All attempts to procure confidence for relations, parts of a constitution from which faith has departed, to whitewash the gravediggers with fine words, not only cover the ingenious inventors with shame, but prepare a far more terrible outbreak, in which revenge joins itself to the need of improvement and the ever deceived, oppressed multitude takes punishment too for the dishonesty. With the feeling of a tottering of things to do nothing else than to await calmly and blindly the collapse of the old edifice, broken open everywhere, attacked in its roots, and to let oneself be shattered by the falling timber, is just as much against all prudence as against honor.” —

“If a change is to take place, something must be changed. So bare a truth must be said for this reason, because *the anxiety that must* is distinguished from *the courage that wills* in that the men who are driven by the former do indeed feel and concede the necessity of a change, but, when a beginning is to be made, nevertheless show the weakness of wanting to keep everything in whose possession they find themselves; — like a spendthrift who is in the necessity of limiting his expenditures, but finds every article of his former needs, about whose curtailment one speaks to him, indispensable, wants to give up nothing, until at last his indispensable is taken from him as well as the dispensable. The spectacle of such weakness a people, Germans, must not give. After cold conviction that a change is necessary, they must now not be afraid to go into the particulars of the investigation, and what they find unjust, the abolition of it must he who suffers wrong demand,

[p. 94]

and he who is in unjust possession must voluntarily sacrifice it.”

“This strength, to be able to raise oneself above one’s small interest to justice, is presupposed in the following investigation as much as the honesty to will it and not merely to pretend it. Only too often there lies hidden behind the wishes and the zeal for the common good the reservation: *so far as it agrees with our interest*. Such a readiness to give the yes to all improvements takes fright, turns pale, as soon as a demand is once made upon this readiness itself. Far from this hypocrisy, let each individual, each estate, before he makes demands on others, before he seeks the cause of the evil *outside himself*, begin with himself, weigh his relations, his rights; and if he finds himself in possession of unequal rights, let him strive thereafter to put himself in equilibrium with the rest.”

#### Resumption of the Critique of Positive Religion.

The political studies gave way in 1799 and 1800 again to those on religion, in so far as Hegel took up again his old theme, the critique of the Concept of positive religion. It seems, however, as if he now treated this work with greater mildness, with acknowledgment of the necessity of the positive, especially on the side of the philosophy of religion. Indeed, it is possible that he developed *the Concept of religion*, with reference to his system of the whole of philosophy, on which he was working in these years, in a manuscript, of which some sheets marked with letters are still extant; the conclusion, completed in the middle of September 1800, reads as follows:

“Thinking life lifts out of shape, out of the mortal, the transient, the infinitely opposed, the mutually combating, the living, the free from passing away, the relation without the dead and self-killing of the manifoldness, not a unity, a thought relation, but all-living, all-powerful, infinite life, and calls it *God*. This elevation of man, not from the finite to the infinite — for these are only products

[p. 95]

of mere reflection, and as such their separation is absolute — but from finite life to infinite life, is *religion*. The infinite life one may call a *spirit*, in contrast to abstract multiplicity, for *spirit* is the living unity of the manifold in opposition, as its shape, not in opposition to the manifold as a dead, mere multiplicity separated from it, for then it would be the mere unity that is called *law* and is something merely thought, unliving. Spirit is animating law in union with the manifold, which is then something animated. If man posits this animated manifoldness as a multitude of many at once and yet in connection with the animating, then these individual lives become organs, the whole becomes an infinite All of life. If he posits *the infinite life as spirit of the whole at the same time outside himself*, because he himself is something limited, posits himself *at the same time outside himself*, the limited one, and raises himself to the living, unites himself most inwardly with it, *then he worships God*.”

“Although the manifold is no longer posited here as such, but at the same time occurs entirely in relation to the living spirit, as animated, as organ, thereby precisely something would still be excluded, and an incompleteness and an opposition would therefore remain, namely the *dead*. In other words: if the manifold is posited only as organ in relation, then the opposition itself is excluded, but life cannot be considered precisely as union, as relation alone, but must at the same time be considered as opposition. If I say: it is the connection of opposition and relation, then *this connection itself can again be isolated* and it can be objected that the non-connection stands opposed. I should have to express myself: *life is the connection of connection and of non-connection*. I.e. every expression is a product of reflection, and hence it can be shown of each, as of something posited, that by the very fact that something is posited another is at the same time not posited, is excluded. This being driven on without a point of rest must, however, be checked once and for all by not forgetting that in the living whole death, opposition, the understanding is *at the same time* posited, namely as a manifold that is living

[p. 96]

and as living can posit itself as a whole, whereby it is at the same time a part, i.e. one for which there is something dead, and which is itself dead for something else. This being-a-part of the living sublates itself in religion. The limited life raises itself to the infinite, and only because the finite itself is life does it bear within it the possibility of raising itself to infinite life. *Philosophy must for this very reason end with religion*, because the former is a thinking and therefore has an opposition, partly of the non-thinking, partly of the thinking and the thought. It has to point out the finitude in everything finite and by reason to demand the completion of it.”

From this abstract description of religion, which fixes upon the expression of liveliness, we must assume, up to the conclusion now to be communicated, a development which had got so far as to present the *cult* and to demonstrate for it the necessity of an objective center. “For all peoples it was the eastern region of the temple, and for the worshipers of an invisible God only this shapeless element of the determinate *space*, only a place. But this merely opposed, purely objective, merely spatial element need not remain necessarily in this incompleteness of complete objectivity; it can itself, as subsisting for itself, return through shape to its own subjectivity. Divine feeling, the infinite felt by the finite, is completed only by reflection’s coming in, lingering over it. A relation of the latter to feeling, however, is only a cognition of it as something subjective, only a consciousness of feeling, a separated reflection over the separated feeling. The pure spatial objectivity gives the point of union for many, and the shaped objectivity is at the same time, through the subjectivity bound up with it, not an actual but only a possible one. And with this, just as above the antinomy of time, the moment and the time of life, was posited as necessary, so also the objective antinomy with regard to the object is posited. The being that is infinite in the immeasurability of space is at the same time in determinate space, somewhat as in the line:

Whom the heaven of all heavens did not enclose, / He lies now in Mary’s lap.

[p. 97]

“In religious life his relation to objects, his acting as an animating of them, was shown, but reminded of his fate, by virtue of which he must let even the objective subsist as objective or even himself make living things into objects. It may be that *this making an object* must be *only for the moment*, that life removes itself from it again, frees itself from it, and leaves the suppressed to its own life and its resurrection. But it is necessary that it also retain for the objects the objectivity up to *complete annihilation*. With all the increased religious union shown by the completions so far, *hypocrisy* can still take place, namely through a particular *property* kept back for oneself. With the firm having of things man would not have fulfilled the — negatively expressed — condition of religion, namely to be free of absolute objectivity, to have raised himself above finite life. He would be incapable of union with infinite life, because he would still have retained something for himself, would still be engaged in a mastering, or entangled in a dependence. And therefore he gives from his property, whose necessity is his fate, as *sacrifice*; only some, for his fate is necessary and cannot be sublated. He annihilates a part also before the deity; from the annihilation of the remainder he removes the particularity, as much as possible, through communal sharing with friends, and by its being a purposeless superfluity. Through this *annihilating for the sake of annihilating* he makes good his otherwise particular relation of *purposive annihilating* and has at the same time completed the objectivity of the objects through an annihilation not related to itself, their complete relationlessness, death. Although the necessity of a *relating* annihilation of the objects remains, nevertheless this purposeless annihilating for the sake of annihilating occurs at times, which proves itself as the only religious one toward absolute objects.”

“It need only still be touched on briefly that the remaining external spatial surroundings, as a necessary boundary, may occupy themselves not so much with purposeless beauty itself as *by purposive beautification have to point to something else*, and that it is the essence of divine service to sublate the contemplative or thinking consideration of the objective God or

[p. 98]

rather to fuse with subjectivity in living joy: of song, of bodily movements, of a kind of subjective utterance which, like resounding speech, can become objective and beautiful through rule, becoming dance, of a manifold of activities, of the arrangement of presenting, of sacrificing, etc. This *plurality* of utterances and of the uttering also requires unity, order, which as a living thing is an orderer, a commander, a *priest*, who, when a needy outer life of men has separated itself very greatly, likewise becomes a *separated* one; not to mention further consequences and their completions.”

“This *more complete* union in religion, such an elevation of finite life to the infinite that as little finite, limited, i.e. purely objective or purely subjective, as possible remain, that every opposition arisen even in this elevation and completion be completed again, is *not absolutely necessary*. Religion is elevation of the finite to the infinite, and such an elevation is necessary, for the former is conditioned by the latter. But at what stage of opposition and union the determinate nature of a race of men remains standing is contingent with regard to the indeterminate nature. The most perfect completeness is possible among peoples whose life is as little as possible torn and sundered, i.e. among *happy* ones. More unhappy ones cannot reach those stages, but *must*, in the separation, be concerned for the preservation of a member of it, for *independence*. They must not lose this; their highest pride must be to maintain the separation firm and the One, whether one may now regard this from the side of subjectivity as independence, or from the other as an alien, remote, unattainable object. Both seem compatible side by side, however necessary it is that, *the stronger the separation*, the purer the I and the further at the same time the object is above and far from man; that, the greater and more secluded the inner, the greater and more secluded the outer, and, if the latter is posited as the independent, the more subjugated man must seem. But precisely this *being-ruled* by the over-great object is what is held fast as *relation*.

[p. 99]

It is contingent which side consciousness takes up, whether that of fearing a God who is infinitely exalted above the heaven of all heavens, above all connection and belonging, hovering over nature, overpowering; — or of setting oneself as pure I above the ruins of this body and the shining suns, above the thousand-times-thousand world-bodies, above the as many times new solar systems as there are of you all, you shining suns. If the separation is infinite, then the fixing of the subjective or the objective is indifferent, but the opposition remains, absolute finite against absolute infinite. The elevation of finite life to the infinite could be only an elevation *above* finite life. The infinite is (then) the most complete, in so far as it is opposed to totality, i.e. to the infinity of the finite, not in so far as this opposition would be sublated in beautiful union, but in so far as the union is sublated, and the opposition is a hovering of the I *above* all nature or the dependence, more correctly, relation to a being above all nature. This religion can be sublime and terribly sublime, but not beautifully human; and so the blessedness in which the I has everything, everything opposed, under its feet, is an appearance of the age, equivalent at bottom to that of depending on an alien being that cannot become man, or, if it did so, thus had become in time, in this union too would remain an absolutely particular, only an absolute One — the worthiest, noblest thing, if union with time were ignoble and base.”

On 14 September 1800.

#### The System.

While Hegel, to be sure, started out from quite determinate tasks, from concrete needs, in his formation he rose imperceptibly to the universal, to the investigation of principles. He had not approached science with the *intention* of inventing a system. The striving for such a thing arose in him quite gradually. One may well assume that the headlong rapid development of his younger friend Schelling gave him, for the

[p. 100]

concentration on the systematic a mighty impetus and spurred him on to silent rivalry. From the booksellers’ bills still extant by chance, which Hegel paid in Frankfurt, we see that he bought chiefly *Schelling’s* writings and *Greek classics* in the best, newest editions. In particular he must have studied *Plato* and *Sextus Empiricus* a great deal. Two points stood firm for him at once, in contrast to Schelling: the independence of the Concept of the *logical* and of *spirit*. From this peculiarity, however, a hard struggle was bound to arise for him over the relation of both Concepts to that of nature, in particular over against Schelling’s metamorphoses. Hegel differed from Schelling also in the manner of working. The latter took the subjective entanglement, the individual turbidity of the struggle upward to a higher standpoint, still into his products as well, which makes them infinitely alluring for softer natures inclined to the fantastic. Hegel, on the other hand, strove with manly strength to attain a plastic severity, an unfailing determinacy of expression.

There is no more skewed and shallower representation of Hegel’s philosophy than that which sees in it only *criticism* or only *logic*, perhaps with the further addition that Hegel’s logic is, to be sure, not that of a sound understanding but, since it identifies itself with metaphysics and declares the Concept to be the creative, that of a most adventurous, overwrought Neoplatonism, which presumes even to be speculative theology. Hegel’s system is rather the philosophy of *spirit* in the sense that with him the Concept of spirit alone first makes that of nature and of the Idea as logical *possible*. The expression Idea is, because it designates also the content of philosophy in general, admittedly one easily misunderstood. It belongs to the philosophical trade to learn to know the differences of its value. That Hegel developed the Concept of the Idea in its *abstract* form, which he called the *logical*, in and for itself (which Schelling did, to be sure, in a lemmatic and supplementary way, but never in the organic connection of all logical determinations), was for him the necessary consequence of his grasping the Concept precisely in its *most concrete* form, in that of spirit. This real-productive form, integrating all other forms *actu* [in act],

[p. 101]

form had to make the beginning with him, in the subjective history of his thinking, as the *last* that is also the first. Hence we see Hegel not at all, as one might expect from some depictions of his philosophy, occupied in his youthful period with a barren, logical schematism and mechanically subordinating to its categories the externally picked-up wealth of the universe, but we see a man of heart who, in an immense urge for knowledge, concerns himself with everything with a certain evenness of temper, yet to whom *history* in particular, as the work of spirit, and *religion*, as the most universal form of representation which the historically appearing spirit makes of its essence, go to the heart. From this the wrath, too, is comprehensible with which Hegel fought down within himself the external theology of the understanding, and the mystical trait which for a time fixed itself in him. With Hegel, therefore, everything was from the very start different than with Schelling. The partial community of terminology can deceive as little about their specific difference as the personal intercourse of many years in which they stood.

After Hegel had once emerged with decided consciousness from his theological narrowness and had recognized his vocation for speculation, he worked at philosophy always only as a *whole*, as a *system*. Of his first attempts, none of which he seems to have carried through to the end, we can form only an insufficient idea from a few Sibylline remains. So much emerges from them, that his speculation had at first a *theosophical* character, in which, however, the energy of dialectical thinking fell into grave discord with the pictorial quality of the Gnostic forms of intuition and soon compelled a purer, more logical form. There is still extant a significant fragment of such a work, which dealt with the *divine triangle*. This geometrizing manner of representation had been brought into currency again at that time by *Fr. Baader*, and Hegel went through this form too in the course of his formation. But since he wished to penetrate it with scientific earnestness, and not merely to delight in it with mystical play, he had to ruin it according to its geometrical determinacy, thus precisely according to the most peculiar characteristic

[p. 102]

of its form. His dialectical spirit was not satisfied with a *simple* triangle. To express the life of the Idea he constructed a *triangle of triangles*, which he let move through one another in such a way that each not merely became once an *extreme* and once a *middle* in general, but had also within itself, with each of its *sides*, to go through this process. But in order, in this hardness and crudity of intuition, to recognize nevertheless again the ideal softness of the unity, the fluidity of the distinctions represented as triangle and sides, he proceeded consistently to the further barbarism of expressing the totality as a *quadrangle* resting above the triangles and their process. The interesting thing about this fragment, which breaks off at the construction of the animal, consists chiefly in the energetic conflict of the woodenness of the form with the liveliness of the dialectic of the content. Hegel was bound to prove the impossibility of presenting the truth for cognition in any determinacy other than the logical, without violence and wild half-fantasy.

To that extent this work was perhaps for Hegel the most formidable and the most fruitful exertion. But with regard to content too it furthered him in that with it he began to penetrate speculatively the representation of the *Trinity* as the fundamental one of the Christian church. A closer acquaintance with the German mystics of the Middle Ages and their profound language supported him in this. Already at the close of the Swiss period there are found among Hegel’s papers excerpts of passages from *Meister Eckart* and *Tauler*, which he copied out of literary journals. But as he entered upon Gnosis, the *Concept* of spirit pressed upon him as that which, because it is the *total Concept*, fundamentally escapes all representing. *Love*, he thought, would be a more appropriate, more intelligible expression for the Concept of God, but *spirit* is deeper.

After such experiments Hegel seems to have raised himself to a comprehensive systematics carried out from beginning to end. There is extant a manuscript of 102 sheets, the beginning of which is missing. It begins with the Concept of abstract being, contains the whole logic, metaphysics and philosophy of nature

[p. 103]

up to the Concept of organic nature, which is not carried out. Then there is found on the same paper, in the same manner, some 30 sheets in extent, the *System of Ethical Life*. In these manuscripts we possess the oldest, most original shape of the Hegelian system. Philosophy was for him the *self-cognition* of the process of the Absolute, which, as pure *ideality*, is not affected by the *alternation* of the quantitative difference of becoming, which belongs to the finite. The distinction of the pure Idea, of nature and of spirit as the historical is sublated in the total totality of the absolute spirit present in them. If the Absolute is to be:

1) conceived according to its *purely ideal* being-in-itself, then no other determinations are possible for it than those of being and thinking *in general*. Apart from the *world*, as the appearance to which the Absolute externalizes itself just as eternally as it takes the same back again into simple unity with itself, it is only the *real possibility* of the universe and of its process. According to its true Concept, its actuality, the Absolute can be cognized only in the *free passage* through its realization and in the just as free taking-back of the same into itself. In that pure ideality it is indeed already totality, but only in itself. It is the *Concept* of the unity of the Concept and its reality, but only the Concept. It is abstract.

2) The realization of the unity of the Concept and its reality, the positing of the immediate unity of thinking and being as reality, is *nature*. The Idea as such is also identity of thinking and being, but in the form of thinking only; nature is the same identity, but in the form of being. In itself nature too is spirit, for it is the spirit which posits it as *its Other*, ϑάτερον, without this whole cognizing itself *for itself* as spirit. In nature the Absolute beholds itself; but because its cognizing remains in it only an external one, the intuition of ideality in real existence is also only for the cognizing spirit, not for nature.

3) But from nature spirit proceeds as *spirit for itself*, because it is its essence to produce cognizing as self-cognizing, but in nature cognizing *outside itself*

[p. 104]

and, in difference from itself, is not immediately identical with itself. In the difference from itself as nature, spirit is indeed realized *objectively*, but not as *spirit*, not in such a way that the objective existence would itself again be *subjectivity existing for itself*. The *simple doubling* of itself as nature therefore does not suffice; the *twofold doubling* must be posited. The absolute spirit must *unite* itself *immediately* with nature *as spirit, in order to sublate this unity* and to make itself, in nature as in itself, accord with its Concept. Thus cognizing becomes not merely life, as in nature, but, as *living*, a cognizing of cognizing, *history*. But as nature in its reality for spirit as *its otherness* is yet only an ideal opposition, so too the *becoming of spirit* in and for itself is a *semblance*, which consequently must likewise be *sublated* (religion). Spirit as finite, as appearing, cognizes itself in the absolute spirit, and the absolute spirit, free in and for itself from the process of becoming, cognizes itself in the historical spirit as itself. As little as nature is for spirit a foreign, impenetrable accident, so little is history.

These determinations make up the outline of the Hegelian philosophy. But however deeply and decisively they lay in the spirit of their originator, so slow, so gradual was nevertheless the process of formation in which he took possession of them. Our interest is to present to ourselves the particular moments of this gradualness, the quiet but for that reason no less energetic transformations of this formation, so far as that is still feasible. In general we may call this stage of the Hegelian systematics the *Platonic*. We meet Platonic views and turns in it everywhere; of a more definite influence of Aristotle nothing is yet to be noticed.

#### I. The Logical Idea.

Hegel at that time still called the sphere of the pure Idea also *theoretical* philosophy, and distinguished within it the logic of the *understanding* from that of reason, which latter he also called *metaphysics* in the proper sense.

The *logic* fell apart for him: 1) into the categories of *being*;

[p. 105]

2) into the Concept of *thinking*; 3) into the Concept of *proportion*, namely of being and thinking, i.e. of cognizing as method.

*Being* is, determined immediately in itself, *quality*. This determinacy sublates itself into the indeterminacy of its delimitation, into *quantity*, whose moments Hegel at that time posited as the numerical *one*, as the *plurality* of numerical ones and as the *allness* of the same. The determinacy in itself and the indeterminacy toward the outside are, however, only moments of *infinity*, which is the negation of one quality by another, the negation of one quantity by another, or finally the negation of quality by the alteration of its extensive or intensive quantity. Since, however, the process of quantitative alteration realizes itself only in the qualitative, the simple determinacy establishes itself again and again out of all quantitative alteration for itself. Infinity, which is only a progression from quantum to quantum or an extension of the quantum going into the indeterminate, must therefore be distinguished from that which is the *determinate unity* of determinacy and indeterminacy. The former Hegel already at that time called the *bad*, the latter the *true* infinity.

*Plato* uses, for the determinate unity of the determinate and the indeterminate, of the πέρας [limit] and of the ἄπειρον [the unlimited], the expression μέτρον [measure] in the *Philebus*. This Hegel first applied later on to designate the unity of quality and quantity. In no case, however, has he undertaken anything *unheard-of* with the development of this group of concepts, as ignorance has often declared about it, which would sooner suspect anything else in it than a connection of the concept-zealous Swabian with the fair-spoken Greek. Beside Plato’s influence the *Kantian* is here also still visible enough in Hegel. Yet he differed from Kant in that he placed the concept of quality before that of quantity and derived the concept of quantity dialectically from that of quality, whereas in the Kantian table of categories the categories were only placed *side by side*. Hegel had at that time already a perfect consciousness of the necessity of positing, as *beginning*, only the simple determinacy,

[p. 106]

which has its limit in itself. He said therefore, in reference to *Schelling*:

“The so-called construction of the Idea has produced, from the opposed activities, the *ideal* and the *real*, as the unity of both, absolutely only the limit. The ideal activity is absolutely equivalent to the unity. The *ambiguity* of this unity determines itself as the unity of the opposition in that, as unity of itself and of the real activity, i.e. of the plurality, it still remains outside itself as an unreunited unity and, over against it, the plurality; so that every such unity of opposites, as moment of the whole, just as also the whole, the highest Idea, absolutely remains only limit. To judge whether the unity is only limit or absolute unity: this results immediately from whether, outside of or after the unity, those posited in it as one are still *beings for themselves*. — Then the becoming-one remains only an *ought*, i.e. a beyond over against the unity of the limit, and both fall asunder. — The same is the case with the construction of matter from *opposed forces*, the attractive and repulsive force, of which the former designates the unity, the latter the plurality. — Since these moments are now represented as forces, one fixes them as absolute qualities and thereby makes them perfectly equal to one another, so that then only a difference of mere direction remains.”

As the second main moment of the Concept of being Hegel posited, under the name *relation*, the absolute determinations of reflection, namely *substantiality*, *causality* and *reciprocity*. These concepts had been worked over so many times since the Humean skepticism, which made causality the apple of discord of thinking, by Kant, Fichte, Jacobi and Schelling, that Hegel found least to alter here, and even with himself the original formulation, as he gave it here, has remained fairly the same through all the metamorphoses of his system. What distinguished him from those thinkers, however, was the *transition* which he made from the concept of the reversal of the active into the passive, of the passive into the active, as the opposition of substance against itself and dissolution of the opposition in itself, to the *Concept of the Concept* as the unity of the universal, the particular and the individual

[p. 107]

Reciprocity he also called *paralytic infinity*. Literally:

“What has arisen is infinity in a being-one of opposites, in which they are not posited as such at all and in which they are at the same time distinguished as ideal, the *dialectical* element of this relation, which, as *our reflection*, has to posit *itself* in its realization. Immediately, nothing here concerns us but what has thus arisen of necessity. As infinity is at rest in it, so we must, as it were, likewise bring our reflection to rest and only take what is there. Our reflection will become the reflection of this relation itself. The *universal* is not pure unity, but fulfilled, the self-equal being-one of the opposed; the *particular* is not a substance, but the distinct is something posited as sublated, being as non-being, etc.”

For the grasp of Hegel’s logic this transition has become *critical*, because it develops the connection of the Concept of being with that of thinking as one forming itself through itself. The *ontological* determinations have, in the *forward* direction, in the Concept as such their presupposition and are therefore in themselves *not unlogical*. The *Concept* for itself has, in the *backward* direction, in the determinations of being and essence its presupposition and is therefore in itself *not unontological*. The ordinary logic begins at once dogmatically with the positing of subject and predicate. The determinations of quality, quantity, etc., it takes up lemmatically. Hegel sought, on the contrary, to raise the Concept of reciprocity to that which constitutes the *bond* of the ontological and *logical* element. The distinctions of substance are not put into it by an understanding fundamentally external to it, as in Spinoza, or even dead properties indifferent to one another, such as the theologians in fact once spoke of as *resting* properties of God. If the difference of substance from itself is the one positing itself *actu* [in act], then the opposition of substance is not only the opposition against the opposition in itself, but also the opposition against itself. Both oppositions are consequently, as self-negation of the unity, just as much negated, and this negative identity is that of the

[p. 108]

Concept of the Concept. Substance as the universal distinguishes itself not only from itself or particularizes itself, but it distinguishes itself also from its distinction, refers itself back out of the distinction to itself as its principle, or is: *subject*. With this Concept the merely *real inherence* of the distinction as accident of substance ceases and becomes *ideal immanence*, in that the subject in its being-for-itself is not only *distinguished* from the distinctions as which it posits itself, but also *distinguishes* itself from itself as being for itself in the totality of its differences. It is not merely, say, a one, a fixed point; it is *individual*, although this expression does not suffice to exhaust the Concept of subjectivity, since for it individuality, as the being-for-itself of being-for-itself, constitutes itself only a *moment*. In this connection the concepts substance and subject stand *through themselves*. Formally this connection can be expressed thus: that through it the *unity* of metaphysics and logic is proved; only one must not represent this unity, as has happened, merely as the negation of metaphysics and logic, as if, namely, Hegel had neither a metaphysics nor a logic. In *Plato* the necessity of this connection appears in that he gives, in the Philebus, νοῦς as the principle of the μέτρον, the measure, however, containing the *active* opposition of warm and cold, swift and slow, high and low, etc. In *Aristotle*, however, the necessity of this connection is posited in that he demands, for the movement of essence, a beginning, which he traces back to the “for the sake of which,” to the *concept of purpose*.

Originally Hegel posited the Concept as the absolute form of thinking, as the ideal reflection of being, and indeed on the one hand as *determinate* Concept, i.e. as the fixation of the universal, particular or individual; on the other hand as *judgment*, and this again partly as the *being-for-itself of the predicate* and reflection of the subject into itself; partly as the *being-for-itself of the subject* and realization of the predicate, i.e. he developed first the singular, particular and universal judgment in connection with the categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive, but only then the positive, negative and infinite. His main thought in this was, once

[p. 109]

to subsume the subject under the predicate, the other time the predicate under the subject. Thus he tried, with a subtle obstinacy and not without constraint, the elevation of the infinite judgment from the significance of positing, as predicate, an *abstract negation* of the predicate, to *positive* determinacy: to grasp the non-being as the non-being of a predicate that is supposed to be according to the essence of the subject, and thereby to make the syllogistic form necessary in itself. For this reason the *modal* form of judgment does not occur at all in Hegel at that time. The *syllogism* itself was for him the relation of the predicates as opposed determinacies, sublated, however, in the ideality of the subject, just as the relation of the subjects as opposed, but in the reality of the predicates identical, identities, so that he distinguished the realization of the subject as *individual* and as *universal*, i.e. the hypothetical and the inductive syllogism.

Hegel treated these forms at that time only as *finite* and, to judge from the original manuscript, neither very elaborately nor, as has already been remarked before, without great harshness in the presentation. Only in the third main section of the logic, after the doctrine of being and of relation, in the Concept of *proportion*, did he become more far-reaching and the violence of the struggle disappear, at least in places. Proportion Hegel called at that time what he later termed *method*. The proportion was to present the *equality* of the universal and the individual as: *definition*, *division* and proof. The definition leads back to the *subsumption* of the syllogism, but must in turn go back from this to the *coordination* of the *members* and their subsumption under the universality of the *definitum*, thus to the *particularization* of the judgment. The definition determines the subject according to its universality. The distinction of the defined subject is the *division* of the same, i.e. the determination of the distinction which the universal, *as itself*, posits in the particularization of the subject. Up to this point, Hegel says expressly, the presentation is *our dialectical treatment*; but now there enters in the proof *the reflection of reality into itself*, the infinite circular course, which, he says, presents the *unity* of the individual with the particular and universal as a *totality* moving *within itself*,

[p. 110]

this, he says, being properly the *construction* and, as equality of reflection with itself at all points, *deduction*.

From here on Hegel now wished to present *cognizing* as equality of the form of reflection and of the content infinite in itself, under the name *metaphysics*. Literally:

“The logic ceases there where the relation ceases and its members fall apart as beings for themselves, in that cognizing, as the reflection into itself, becomes for itself its first moment, as the passive being-for-itself outside cognizing as the other moment, which *unfolds its reflection into itself*, the other of itself, and, as it itself, is the relation to an other. — It is no longer an other for us, but for itself, or it negates itself.”

The totality of the self-realizing reality of cognizing was now for Hegel: 1) the circular movement, returning into itself, of a *system of principles*; 2) *objectivity* and 3) *subjectivity*. — The system of principles contained properly a critique of the ordinary conception of the so-called laws of thought of identity and contradiction, of the excluded third and of the ground; entirely in the manner in which one also knows them from Hegel’s later presentations. The *necessity* of contradiction as a *moment* of the development of identity as that which distinguishes itself was here already especially urged. — What Hegel called *objectivity*, however, remained still very obscure. He understood by it the *monad* or *soul*, the *world* and the highest *being*. The fundamental thought which pervades this dialectically bold development, carried through with the utmost exertion, consists presumably in grasping objectivity as a reality free from the cognizing subject, determined in itself. It is therefore to be a *self-preserving* individuality or soul. The *ground* of everything is to be posited *monadically*, and the difference of the monads is to sublate itself in the *genus* as the ground of the individual souls. Since the genera themselves are different, they constitute as totality the *world*, which in turn sublates itself in the self-sameness of the *highest being* as its ground, insofar as the same has, in its unity, extinguished all differences

[p. 111]

and is the *creative* principle of the genera. — But this Concept too is to sublate itself again into that of *self-conscious subjectivity*. The genus of the genera is only the objective universality of everything particular and individual. Only the *universality that is for itself*, which posits itself in its individuality as universal, is that reality which is absolutely ideality.

One might say of this metaphysics also that it wanted to make the *Kantian* synthetic apperception of self-consciousness into truth pneumatologically, cosmologically and theologically. The Concept of the highest being Hegel posited as the in-itself, in which existence as the posited essence is yet taken back again into the unity *as not having been*. In order that the non-being of existence may be posited, its being must be posited; otherwise having-been is impossible. *Negation*, *without its constant being-negated*, without its being-posited-ideally, is, over against self-sameness, the *evil principle*, which *imagines itself* within itself. “The highest being has created the world, which for it is of ethereal transparency and clarity; but this is for itself dark.” Subjectivity alone sublates all indifference of difference, all half-relating, so that individuality is *absolutely* one with universality. In the unity of the genus with the individual the unity is only *in itself*, but neither for the individual nor for the genus. And not only does the individual have in another, but a genus too has in another genus, a *limit*. In the highest being the totality of genera and individuals is indeed posited as a *constantly* vanishing existence, but only in the I is infinity as simple, transparent to itself in all dimensions, attained. The I is: a) *theoretical* or consciousness, b) *practical*, *fulfilling itself with itself*. But thus subjectivity is only *formal*, because on the one hand it has in the objectivity *given* to consciousness, on the other in the postulate of what ought to be objective, a constant limit of existence. Hegel therefore distinguished from it already at that time c) the *absolute spirit*, as the *form of subjectivity absolute through the absoluteness of its content*, in which cognizing eternally, *without a beyond*

[p. 112]

of either theory or practice, moves in eternal equality with itself in such a way that the Concept of itself immediately turns over into reality, but reality has just as much only ideal existence. “For the monad, which has its beyond in the highest being as the absolute genus, self-preservation is only a *longing*, which aims to rescue individuality through the zero of infinity, to preserve individuality, with the stripping off of determinacy, as immortal, as absolute individuality.” In the absolute spirit the inequality with itself is only the distinguishing of equality from itself; it has no beginning outside itself, but, positing itself as its Other, it is infinity returning into itself. This Concept, which Hegel distinguishes *specifically* from Schelling and which he brought to light in the boldest, most paradoxical, indeed, it is not too much to say, most desperate turns, in violent struggle, was at that time frequently repeated by him in the following words: “This is the Idea of the absolute essence. It is this only as absolute *spirit*. It is this, that out of its relation to itself it becomes an Other to itself. *The relation to itself is for it*, i.e. for this relation itself, the *infinite*. *For us*, i.e. for cognizing, for the *spirit coming to itself*, it is otherness.”

#### II. Nature.

It is easy to notice that Hegel at that time still *mixed* into his presentation everywhere the *phenomenological* element, the relation of knowing consciousness to its cognizing. Now here, now there he reminds himself to distinguish the Concept of the in-itself from the determinacy of its appearing for cognizing. Later, after he had at the close of the Jena period completely overcome this Fichteanism through the independent working-out of the *Phenomenology*, he could set forth the moments of the system without such regard to the subjective process of cognizing in objectively free articulation. The logical Idea as such was for him at that time not yet the *concrete totality* either, but the absolute *spirit*, which proves itself as Idea, as nature, as history, for itself as the Absolute. The *existence* of nature he never, as one has probably misunderstood him, in a *causal manner*

[p. 113]

derived from a barren concept of the understanding, but always from the Concept of spirit, which, to be sure, thought of as without nature and history, coincides in content with the Concept of the Idea. At that time, literally, thus:

“This whole Idea of spirit is *only Idea*, or it itself is *its own first moment*. For spirit, as this movement of return into itself, has found itself in the in-itself, the content of cognizing, and is spirit only as this unity in its *Other* (so Hegel wrote at that time); it is only thus absolute spirit. But it is not itself absolute spirit, or has not cognized itself as absolute spirit. It is this *for us*, not for itself. Metaphysics is its becoming and it as Idea. It is absolute spirit, positing the other as itself, infinity returning into itself. But this return is again simple relation or infinity itself, and at its highest point it falls thus again back into its *first*, into its beginning.” — Hegel demands, therefore, that the circular course of spirit be not merely this *simple* one of cognizing, which in its moments *never forgets itself*, which is *not in all moments* of the circular course only as its reflection, only as Idea, but that spirit fold its infinity together into a dissolvable unity in itself, to which, finding itself in it as in an Other, it stand opposed as spirit — spirit which “returns from this falling-away of infinity as *victor over a spirit to itself* and has just as eternally *returned*. Only this *totality of return* is in itself and passes no more into another. Spirit is the Absolute, and its Idea is absolutely realized only when the moments of spirit themselves are this spirit, but then too there is no more *going-beyond-it*.”

Spirit, now, in that it beholds its Other as itself and posits the same, for its self-cognizing, as an Other in itself, is *nature*: “The simple spirit relating itself to itself is the *ether*, the absolute *matter*, and that it is the spirit which has found itself in its Other is the nature closed in itself and living. It is the first moment of the *self-realizing* spirit.” Nature is therefore the contradiction of its essence, namely, in itself absolute

[p. 114]

spirit to be. It is the becoming-other of itself, because the I does not exist in it. In the introduction to the Concept of nature Hegel gave himself great trouble, admittedly often with daring words, to distinguish the abstract determination of the *ideal* otherness of the simple Idea from the *real* otherness of the Idea as nature, and to show how, in the *totality* of the process of absolute spirit, the otherness of the same as nature, its externalization to real infinity, is yet only an *ideal* moment. The logical determinations exist, according to Hegel, in nature only as *sublated* in it. He expressed this at that time thus, that the progression from the Concept of spirit as pure Idea must be taken not only *logically* but also *metaphysically*. “In nature, as it is in itself, determinacy as the indifferent relation of a whole and its parts, of external determinacy by magnitude and of qualitative difference, just so the different relation of substantiality, of causal and reciprocal relation, as well as that which in turn has taken this up into indifference, the relation of a particular and universal, and a being-for-itself *this*, which is reflected into itself and posits this relation ideally as sublated in itself, — is wholly extinguished; and its existence as well as its ideality or its becoming absolute spirit is the metaphysical becoming, or the becoming of cognizing into self-cognizing. — In this way the *philosophical* way of regarding nature separates itself from the *common* one, which holds merely to those relations of unreflected infinity and for which nature consists of wholes and parts in quantitative differences and in causal relation, as well as in it as a multitude of *Thises*. This appearing or this manner of reality is posited in nature itself as ideal — or the appearing of nature is an appearing as spirit, the reality as that of a spirit. That it is spirit is not an inner. — Its essence in itself is that it is *living* nature, infinity reflected into itself, cognizing, and its matter or its absolute self-sameness is life. — It is, however, only a formal life, not a life cognizing itself, it is life in itself, but not *for itself*.”

“The whole of nature, it is said in the course, is the spirit that, as the

[p. 115]

*Other* of itself, presents itself. This determinacy of the Other is of a wholly different nature than the determinacy which is sublated in the Idea as such. Nature as the absolute spirit that is other to itself is perfectly living spirit, *not* presenting itself in *ideal* moments of the Idea, but the Idea expressing itself in the moments. The determinacy of spirit as one that is other to itself is solely the form of otherness, or of the opposition of the moments existing for themselves. It is spirit as itself, not spirit cognizing itself as absolute spirit; absolute self-reflection which is *not* itself this absolute self-reflection, which is *not for itself the unity of a doubled* cognizing finding itself. This unity, which in its universal determination is absolutely simple negative unity, the absolute pure nothing, the complete sublation rising out of the totality of the opposition and the self-sameness issuing from it, is that as which spirit does *not* posit itself in nature. It is not *real* in it *as absolute I*, and otherness itself as nature is therefore the universal determinacy of *asunderness*, the *element of quantity*, of non-negative but positive self-sameness, or subsistence, the *indifference* of relating-to-itself: an unfolding of all moments of spirit, which appear for themselves as individual, again not fixed and rigid, but each in itself presenting the absolute infinity and the circular course of the moments in itself, so that none rests and stands fast, but absolutely moves and changes, but so that *its becoming-other is the production of the opposed*, yet conversely just so it itself always proceeds from this in like manner, both in the universal element of subsistence, so that each at once is in its becoming-other and in its being at once perishes.”

Hegel was at that time in the *Platonic* stage of his formation, not only in the architectonic of his system, but also in the terminology, which inclines to a *mystically ideal pictoriality*, and in the execution of the philosophy of nature occasionally recalls quite specifically the *Timaeus*. With the *Schellingian* philosophy of nature the Hegelian has very little in common, properly only that which the former again with the then empirical natural science

[p. 116]

had in common in respect of its general results. With Schelling the center of his philosophy of nature remained the *dynamic* and chemical process. Hegel, however, directed himself *evenly* to the whole and began from the very start with *mechanics*. The transition from the Concept of spirit as *Idea* to real self-presentation as *nature* he made at that time through the Concept of the *ether*. He posited absolute spirit as ether, which not merely *permeates* everything, but is it itself. This ether, which has been recognized by empiricism, through *Encke* and *Hansen*, at least as a *resisting medium*, Hegel described with great fondness and with a poetry mystical, undeniably alluding to the Christian doctrine of the Logos.

“The ether is not the living God, but it is the first form of His reality as infinite elasticity, as the *absolute process of fermentation*, as the absolute unrest of self-sameness, just as much not to be as to be. The inequality of absolute spirit, in which it stands over against itself as its Other, goes back into its unity and rest with itself. It *speaks* itself out in itself, not in an Other, to itself, and is just so the *perception of its eternal word*, the absolute *melody and harmony of the universe*. The breaking forth of the articulated word is at the same time the reception of the tone in the soft, absolutely yielding infinity of the air. Spirit as ether cognizing itself therefore remains in its movement just as much rest, in its speaking-out just as much mute and closed. — What it lets shoot together within itself into shapes, of that it is just as much the fluid and transparent dissolution. This fullness and wealth cloud it as little as water is clouded by salts dissolved in it, and it is in general no such intermediate thing between day and night as the clouding is. — The contraction of the solidity of the ether is the first moment of the negative one, of the point, of the *star*, simple self-sameness sublating in itself all distinction, absolutely self-spreading light. The stars are only the *formal* expression of the Concept of infinity, an *absolute multiplicity*, just as their quantity is a boundless going-beyond. Their infinity is a negative beyond, a multiplicity of ones *without unity*, as well as a *to*-

[p. 117]

*talityless quantity*. — This infinite is in itself unreasonable, a sublimity as empty as its admiration is thoughtless. — The fixed stars are self-suns, not suns for one another. They can present the totality of the relation only as a system of geometrical figures and the system of numbers as constellations, whose points have ordered distances from one another. They are an immovable painting, a formal model, which in mute hieroglyphs represents an eternal past that has its present and its life only in the cognizing of this script.”

This non-admiration of the multitude of stars remained a constant trait of Hegel’s. As little as on his Swiss journey through the Alps he knew how to draw from the colossal rocks any other impression than the dry judgment: it is so; whereas he watched the dance of the waterfalls enraptured — so too his admiration of the reason of the heavens began only with the planetary system of our sun.

He divided at that time the whole philosophy of nature only into two parts: into the system of the *sun* and into that of the *earth*.

In the former he developed, with a much greater prolixity than he later did, the Concept of *space* and *time* as the moments of *movement*. In the solar system he distinguished, in which he constantly remained the same, *four* different *forms* of movement, namely: 1) the *central*, relating itself to itself as center; 2) the *axisless*, active digression; 3) that of *passive inherence*; and 4) that of *complete* movement, which both, like the central body, rotates about itself as center and at the same time revolves about the central body. Thus he determined the *solar*, *cometary*, *lunar* and *planetary* bodies in a wholly logical manner as a syllogism whose universal middle is the sun.

In the system of the earth he distinguished, as also later, mechanics, physics and organics. But since he had already anticipated cosmic mechanics in the Concept of the planetary system, he treats in mechanics only that form of movement which he later designated as the sphere of *finite* mechanics. He began at that time with the construction of the *body*,

[p. 118]

went then over to the Concept of *impact* and *fall*, and concluded with a very elaborate development of the *movement of projectiles, of the pendulum and of the lever*, which latter investigations have wholly disappeared from his later philosophy of nature.

The transition to *physics* he made through the Concept of the *process*, as he called, *sensu strictiori* [in the stricter sense], the *proper dialectic* which lies in the nature of the terrestrial bodies. The process fell apart for him into the *ideal* and the *real*. By the former he understood the *unity* of all processes in the earth as the universal individuality, which constantly extinguishes their differences in itself and just as much restores them from their dissolution. The qualitative moments of this process are nitrogen, oxygen, which he for the most part still called phlogiston, hydrogen and carbon gas. After the model of the *Platonic bond of analogy* in the *Timaeus*, Hegel wanted to connect the *extremes* through a *double middle*, from which each member relates itself to the other as each for itself to the extreme nearest it, and so the mediation of the same, through its connection with the other member, becomes the *unity of the extreme with the extreme*. Thus the sun and earth through the double middle of the comet and the moon; nitrogen and carbon gas through the double middle of hydrogen and oxygen gas; air and earth as elements through the double middle of water and fire; the atmosphere and the land through the double middle of the sea and the volcanoes; finally the extreme of metal and of clay through the double middle of salt and sulphur. All *moments* of the extreme and of the two sides of the middle form among themselves again a unity. The comet, hydrogen, water, the sea and salt are in themselves the same; just so the moon, oxygen, fire, the volcano and sulphur, etc.

From this process of the *physical elements* Hegel distinguished the *real* process as that of *finite chemism* and of the finite *chemical* elements. With obstinacy he insisted on taking the medley of the strata of fossils not merely *mechanically*, but rather on recognizing in it also an individualizing impulse of the earth. But since he introduced *mineralogy*, as the singularization of the earth, into physics

[p. 119]

he concluded it, to be sure, as later, with the Concept of the chemical process, but for organics it lacked the *geological* organism, which he later placed immediately before the vegetable and animal organism.

In the fundamental conception of nature Hegel therefore remained the same; but the treatment was at that time warmer, more enthusiastic, bolder, more poetical. With a creative urge the presentation flows on in unchecked continuity. Scarcely here and there in the manuscript is a slight dividing stroke or even a heading made. The expression has, particularly in the description of the ideal elementary process, together with great logical exactness, often a peculiar *wildness* that mirrors, as it were, the struggle of the elements in word and rhythm. If in *Schelling’s* attempts in the philosophy of nature one hypothesis crowds out the other, if the citations in and under the text seldom let the presentation come to a pure flow, and if the critique of the reporter, with its countless optative turns, at once makes every determinacy just posited problematic again: then one can conceive no greater contrast than the purely objective dialectic of Hegel, advancing with penetrating elaboration, to be sure often harsh and ungainly, indeed abstruse. Nothing is falser than to imagine that Hegel in the philosophy of nature leaned wholly and entirely on *Schelling*. With manifold agreement, his was a wholly different world, for whose elaboration and public presentation, however, he became, with the years, the more his positive knowledge widened, ever more cautious and circumspect. To give an idea of the pregnancy of his diction at that time in this field, let there stand here the description of the integration of the other elements in the fire process as a telluric power.

“Fire, as this process of the whole, insofar as it is rooted in the earth and this becomes *absolute brittleness*, must be in this as a part of it. That the moments are in it as *parts* is the manner of their indifference, according to which it is the whole of them as parts, i.e. as subsisting elements. Fire, as this process a part of the earth, is *points* of the same, which contract in it into this brittleness

[p. 120]

and drive them beyond crystallization up to combustibility, or rather in which the element of individuality does not open up as far as the crystallization of shape, but with its birth is driven into this tension by the water, and toward the thunderstorm, the comet in formation, becomes the *volcano*, the moon that remains in the earth. As the atmospheric and the satellites shape themselves in the air and throw down a solid residue from the blaze, so the volcano is the inverted brittle point formed in the earth, which passes *not* into an underground thunderstorm, but, its opposite, instead of into the neutrality of water, into neutral individuality, into *glass*. The combustion of the cloud is in general, on the side of the shape of the earth, the neutral, soluble water. It can well also present in itself the whole process and come even to the opposition, of a burnt-out earth, to the atmospheric or to the moon. But the seat of this side of the process is properly in the earth the *real* burning, the self-dissolving brittleness, in which the shaped sets itself against fluidity and, in its absolute desiccation consuming itself, breaks out into the flame and passes into burnt brittle matter, into the shapelessness of it. The moons and satellites cannot owe their origin to eruptions of volcanoes, but are rather atmosphericals, cometary nuclei, which have purified themselves of the cometary and have it on their earth, as the sea of the same, but remain in this relation always against it.”

With extraordinary care Hegel treated the mineralogical singularization of the universal individual of the earth: metallicity, brittleness, neutrality and earthiness proper. The individual kinds of stone and their transitions into one another he described at length and with a certain speculative elegance. From *granite*, as the unity of mica, quartz and feldspar, he proceeded through *lime* and *clay* to *basalt* as that turning-point at which the earthy makes itself immediately, through its own dissolution, into the *soil* of the organic. Here now the determinacy of the process was also to be shown in the individual bodies of the determinate system, how the moments of fire, air and earth are posited in them in the process, in

[p. 121]

which manner these elements, bound by them and ideal, attain to their freedom and become out of the opposition of the individual bodies. The *abstractions* of these are: *metal*, the combustible or *sulphur*, the neutral or *salt*; and the *earth*, which again is just as much simple metallicity as *silica*, neutral as *lime*. The earthy of the earths coincides with the combustible, the brittle of earth is *clay*. With particular attention the *diamond* is described: “*Silica*, the metal of the earths, comprehends, even if it is otherwise neutral, the disintegrating moments of the earth into simple unity and becomes, in that in its solidity it is not metallic but within the earthy, thereby itself brittle. That which is in itself brittle, combustible, like the *diamond*, does not belong to the silica family, in that it, not fluid but firm and shaped, has taken its individuality together into this high unity, up to transparency, up to the extinguishing of all inequality in itself or synthetic color, and even up to the regularity of fracture, of cleavage, and has simplified itself. Although through its individuality not belonging to the stones, it is as it were a center, which drives the earthy of the earths just so up to the highest unity, combustibility, as it on the other side so annihilates this brittleness, like *naphtha*, that it not only, like this, merely transparent and fluid, proceeds to shapelessness, but itself, having as it were the concrete water of crystallization in it, drives individuality out into the dimensions of shape, angles, surfaces and lines, and thus completely masters the brittleness through shape.” — For the determination of the difference of the metals Hegel posited *specific gravity* and shape, so that the division of the metals by relation to free fire, into non-oxidizable and oxidizable ones, falls outside it. *Oxidizability* is immediately the no-longer-preserving-itself of the metal and not cognizable in the metal as such. Metal being for itself divides itself only into the *continuous* and *brittle*. This *superficial* division becomes, however, already in the behavior toward the ideal process of oxygen in free fire another, and in it already it comes to light, as for instance in lead, how far the metallic fluidity only

[p. 122]

form or is essential. The form of continuity, of the passive relating itself to itself, is as it were the *dissimulation*, the restrained, which conceals what it is in movement. Just so is the specific gravity, which likewise is what is taken together into one of the whole Idea (tungsten), as it were the *obstinacy* of a *smallness*, which would be called character if the object were large, but is formally the same.”

Since Hegel distinguished the earth as the universal individual of its elementary processes and as the falling-asunder of the external medley of earths and stones, he explained the *articulation* of the earth as the result of an *absolutely past* process, of which it itself has remained behind as the *processless* image in this respect. “In that these formations of the earth-individuality present their moments, as a past becoming, indifferently alongside one another in the form of indifference, their differentiated relation to one another falls away at first as process. The differentiated relation is rather the paralyzed. By the nature of being moments they are cut off from one another, and just so there is lacking to them the ideal unity of Concepts, the intermixture of them in the process. That cut-offness admits their unity only as a *synthetic* unity, as an intermixture and merely external connection, which presents nothing of their absolute relation. But this, *the ground* of the *stratification* and of the external manner of their existence, must at the same time appear and be present in the separated itself, because *nature does not exist as pure Concept*, but in the indifference of the limit has its negative as a positive, just so toward the limited as indifferent and itself as such an existent. This limit, as existing unity of both, is their *passing over* into one another. — This passing-over is the vanishing of the one form, or that their opposite already appears in it itself. The manner of the passing-over, however, as limit, is at the same time not the externality of the intermixture of the opposed, the quantitative diminishing of the one and increasing of the other, but an independent forming or *change of form*. The rock passing over into another takes its continuity together and interrupts it or lets its own more concealed

[p. 123]

interruption enter more noticeably into existence. The increasing of its interrupting is, as interrupting, not a quantitative but a *qualitative* one. It forms itself into spheres or surfaces, small lumps, threads or into kidneys, the intermediate thing between the two, according as it passes over from the granular form or from the surface form. This passing-over, mixed with the intermixture, is at the same time determined in its formations as distinct from it. But it itself also has its limit.”

Although now Hegel acknowledged a becoming, or better a *having-become*, of the earth, he nevertheless did not want the *spatial* succession made the principle of a science of the formation of the earth, which with light effort transforms the *side-by-side* into a *succession* and calls this the *history* of the earth. The earth lacks, according to him, the taking-back of its multiplications into absolute universality. It is therefore, as *totality*, not the simplicity of its parts equal to the Concept, but their intermixedness. “The earth now presents only the *image* of that process without the process itself. Its fire is extinguished and *time* has no power over the formations, except the universal external one which it has over the individual as such, but not over them as universal, for their universality is the indifferent one. — The process itself is a *past*.
