To enliven it through time and to represent the moments of its image as a sequence does not engage the content of them itself, for time is the wholly empty process, an abstraction of it, for which the real moments of it are something absolutely particular, a content which is not the Idea of time itself. The articulating of the image into time brings in rather only the false semblance of comprehension, in that the arising and succession of the sequence do posit a relation, but an absolutely relationless one, in that what thus relates itself in time relates itself precisely not through its content, not through *what it is*, but in a wholly empty way, the content in this relating being the absolutely indifferent, and so in itself not as related.”

[p. 124]

#### III. Spirit.

Hegel at that time worked out the philosophy of spirit, before he arrived at the *Phenomenology*, only as a *System of Ethical Life*. In the announcement for the students he later called it *Natural Right*. In the lectures which he devoted in Jena to the *whole* system, *art and religion* were treated at the final *close* of ethics without any particular fullness, however many special works he had also devoted to the latter, as we have seen. *Anthropology and psychology* were still left entirely to one side. The philosophy of ethical life was, to be sure, not in principle, but certainly in the development of the particular, as highly *Platonizing*, extraordinarily different from its later shape. The Concepts of abstract *right* and of abstract *morality* were fused in it with the Concept of *ethical life* itself, which is quite natural insofar as Hegel’s energy had to see itself driven to treat precisely this latter Concept, with which he overcame the lifelessness of Kantian morality and the impracticality of Fichte’s politics, with a certain exclusiveness.

Hegel proceeded from the view that in absolute ethical life the *universal* and the *particular* of the will must be posited as an identity differentiated in itself, yet sublating the difference into absolute unity. The universal he also called, in the first draft of the system, *intuition*, the particular on the other hand *Concept*. From that identity he now inferred, for its real construction, the necessity of positing the universal as well as the particular for itself as moments in such a way that, first, the *subsumption* of the Concept under intuition, then that of intuition under the Concept, and finally the adequacy of intuition and Concept would be posited. Thus he obtained three parts, which he entitled, in the highest abstraction, as follows: 1) absolute ethical life according to the relation; 2) the *negative*, or crime, and 3) *absolute ethical life*. Apart from the abstractness of the expression, the division itself has, even in comparison with the later systematics, the undeniable advantage of greater simplicity.

The first part developed the *natural potency* of the ethical

[p. 125]

spirit. Hegel proceeded from the *practical feeling* which becomes a *determinate need*, the satisfaction of which engenders *enjoyment*. — As a means to the satisfaction of the need there arises *labor*, which by the *invention of the tool* seeks to ease the mechanical mastery of nature and to reduce the *physical* dependence of man on nature and on other men. The *absolute means* of man is *speech*, the tone filled with spirit. — Through the working-over of the inorganic, the particular is subsumed under the universal in a real manner. There arises *property*, the *exchange* of it, a universal form for representing its value, *money*. — The manifold relations of persons become determinate *contracts*, and the inner difference of willing becomes the difference of *lordship* and *bondage*, which in the *family* receives its organic shaping through the incorporation of the servant into it. “The indifference of the relation of lordship and bondage, in which personality and the abstraction of life are therefore one and the same, and which appears merely as an external relation, is the family. In it the totality of nature and everything previous is united; the whole previous particularity is posited in it as universal. It is the ideality: a) of external needs; b) of the sexual relation, as the natural difference posited in the individuals themselves, and c) of the relation of parents to children, or of reason that has stepped forth naturally, but as reason existing as nature.”

In opposition to the natural determinacy of spirit, the second part was to contain the presentation of the *inversion* of the positive relation, hence the subsumption of universality under particularity. This inversion is *crime*. In it the ideal side, *conscience*, is only something inward, not inward and outward at once, something subjective, not objective at once. Immediately the criminal, in what he apparently injures externally and as something alien to him, has just so injured and sublated himself ideally. To that extent the external deed is at once an inward one; the crime committed against the other is just so committed against himself. But the consciousness of this his own annihilation is a subjective, inward thing, or the *bad* conscience.

[p. 126]

It is to that extent incomplete and must also present itself externally as avenging *justice*. Because it is an inward, incomplete thing, it drives toward its totality. It betrays and reveals itself and works by itself until it sees this ideal counteraction or inversion externally before it, threatening its reality and as its enemy. Then it begins to be satisfied. Crime and avenging justice are, because the one is the opposite of the other, absolutely bound together, and justice, which subsumes the particular again under the universal, is the negation of the first negation. The sequence of stages of the criminal negation is: a) *natural annihilation*; b) *theft*, *robbery* and *subjugation*; c) *murder*, *revenge* and the *duel*, under which, as the wavering between murder and revenge, Hegel subsumed *war* as the absolute form of the duel. The first Concept, natural annihilation, was understood by him thus: “The wholly indeterminate, universal negation, which does not go to anything singular but is directed against the abstraction of what has been formed, is natural annihilation or *purposeless destruction*, devastation. Thus nature is turned against the formation which intelligence bestows upon it, as against its own producing of what is organized; and just as the element, the objective, is subsumed under intuition and life, so the element in turn subsumes the organized and individualized under itself and annihilates it, and this annihilation is devastation. So in the human race forming alternates with destroying. When forming has long enough encroached upon inorganic nature and determined its formlessness on all sides, then the suppressed indeterminacy breaks loose and the barbarism of destruction falls upon what has been formed, clears away and makes everything free and level and equal. In its greatest splendor devastation appears in the Orient, and a Genghis Khan and a Tamerlane, as the besoms of God, sweep whole continents quite clean. The Nordic barbarians who constantly fall upon the South are in the determinacy of the understanding. Their poor enjoyment, which they have formed into a slight manifold, has thereby a determinacy, and their devastating is not indifferent, purely for the sake of devastating. — Fanaticism

[p. 127]

of devastating is, because it is an absolute element and assumes the form of nature, outwardly insuperable, for difference and the determinate succumb to indifference and indeterminacy; but it has, like the negative in general, its negation within itself. The formless drives itself into indeterminacy, because it is after all not absolutely formless, so far into expansion, like a water bubble, until it bursts into infinitely small drops. It passes from its pure unity over into its opposite, absolute formlessness, into absolute multiplicity, and thereby becomes wholly formal form or absolute particularity, and with that the weakest. This progression of devastation to absolute devastation and to the absolute transition into its opposite is *fury*, which annihilates itself.”

The third part has *ethical life* itself, as it is perfectly in accordance with its Concept, for its object; for in the first totality, in the family, there is no absolute equality, but always still an insuperability of nature posited; in the negative, however, the highest is always only the annihilating of the one relation by the other. “In true ethical life the eyes of spirit and the bodily eyes coincide completely. By nature the man sees flesh of his flesh in the woman, by ethical life only spirit of his spirit in the ethical being and through it. Ethical life posits the *empirical* consciousness and the *absolute* in such an identity that the difference is only an ideal one, nothing in the reality of differentiation. In ethical life, then, the individual is in *an eternal manner*. His empirical being and doing is a thoroughly universal one, for it is not the individual that acts, but the universal, absolute spirit in him. The view of philosophy concerning the world and necessity, according to which all things are in God and there is no singularity, is perfectly realized for the empirical consciousness, in that every singularity of acting or thinking or being has its essence and significance wholly and solely in the *whole* and, insofar as its ground is thought, wholly and solely this is thought, and the individual knows and imagines no other; whereas the non-ethical empirical consciousness consists in this, that between the being-one of the universal and the particular, of which

[p. 128]

the former is the ground, it interposes some other singularity as ground. Here, on the contrary, the absolute identity, which was previously in nature and something inward, has stepped forth into consciousness. The intuition of this Idea of ethical life, however, the form in which it appears from the side of its particularity, is the *people*.”

Ethical life articulates itself: 1) into a *system of estates*, and is 2) government, the self-conscious movement of the whole.

The *estates* differ: a) as the *absolute estate*, which has for its content the production of the whole as ethical totality; b) as the estate of *rectitude*, which without individuality and in the particularity of its relations is without freedom; c) as the estate of crude ethical life, or the *peasant estate*. — Quite characteristic of the time in which Hegel elaborated his philosophy of right is it that he almost always has war in mind, the *danger of death*, still wholly abstracting from an *equal* obligation of *all* citizens to military service, indeed denies to the second estate, that of those engaged in trades and commerce, the *capacity for bravery*, whereas of the peasant estate he says: “On account of its totality it is capable also of bravery, and is able, in this labor and in the danger of death, to join the first estate.”

In the organism of the estates ethical totality appears in *repose*, but in reality movement is present, which seeks to subsume under the universal that which wants to posit itself for itself as difference. Insofar as this movement is posited as *cause*, as *power*, it is *constitution*. “A truly ethical totality must have entered into this separation, and the Concept of government must present itself as the wisdom of the constitution, so that the form and the consciousness are just as real as the absolute is in the form of identity and nature. The totality is only as the *unity of essence and form*, neither of which can be lacking. Crudeness in relation to constitution, in which nothing is separated, but against every singularity of determination immediately the whole as such moves, is formlessness and sublation of freedom; for this is in the form and in this, that the single part,

[p. 129]

a subordinate system of the whole organism, is self-active for itself in its determinacy.”

Hegel therefore divided government into the *absolute* and, as he called it, the *universal*, which moves in the individual potencies. By the former he properly understood *legislation*, the cognition of the substantial, which is manifestly the deed of the absolute estate, the estate of the free. Hegel, however, was not content with this, but went in his Platonism so far that he singled out from the first estate the *elders* and the *priests* as the lawgivers, in that, namely, *every* member of this estate is to become a priest in the transition from manhood into higher age. “From old age the self-constituting of individuality vanishes. From life it has lost the side of shape and reality, and on the threshold of death, which will take the individual absolutely up into the universal, it is already half dead. Through the loss of the real of the individuality of the particular, however, it alone is capable, outside of its estate, which is the shape and self-possession of its individuality, of being in indifference over all, and of preserving the whole in all its parts and through all. To the highest indifferent, to God and nature, to the priests and to the elders, the preservation of the whole alone can be tied, for every other form of reality is in difference.” Hegel holds that there is much talk of the *deception of the priests*, but that it is a quite absurd thought and impossible that a people *could be deceived*. The deception consists only in this, that the absolute consciousness, according to its existence, separates itself from the active, and that the individual now posits himself as *contingent* according to his singularity, insofar as he acts as this one, now as *necessary*, insofar as he *acts* and in acting attains the self-enjoyment of the universality of his essence. “A formal thought of absolute government is to be found in all systems of theory as well as of actuality, namely its *organic central power*, and indeed one that preserves the constitution. But first, such a thought, like *Fichte’s* ephorate, in its negative attitude is wholly formal and empty; then, all possible supervision over the

[p. 130]

governing in everything particular is ascribed to it; it is thus to be, commanding over everything, working *with superior power* and at the same time, as power, a nothing. It is only by *presupposing the difference of the estates*, and thus being truly the supreme one, that absolute government is not formal. If it does not presuppose it, the whole power of reality falls into one lump, however much that might otherwise ramify within itself, and the crudeness of this lump would have its equally crude and wisdomless power undivided at its apex. There would be no truly objective difference in it.”

The differences of government, insofar as it realizes the movement of the subsumption of the particular under the universal, were developed by Hegel as the system: 1) of *need*, 2) of *justice* and 3) of *education*; the last system, however, was left still very indeterminate.

In carrying out the first system he showed, through the inequality of *acquisition*, the necessity of the *inequality of possession*, hence also of *enjoyment*. “When inequality becomes the opposition of luxurious wealth and the deepest poverty, and thereby on both sides bestiality, contempt for everything high, sets in, then a people is dissolved. Government must therefore work to resist as far as possible the *fluctuation* in the value of *things*, especially as it too needs means for the maintenance of the first estate, further for the administrative officials, for the building and upkeep of roads, temples, etc., and hence itself perishes through such a dissolution. It can, however, thoroughly preserve ethical life only by letting the acquiring estate *constitute* itself *by itself for itself*, so that its law and right be not merely thought universality, but a living dependence, trust, esteem, a relation of individuality to individuality. Government is to reserve to itself only the *external* limitation of this organization. — This ethical life sublates the elementary, the pure mass, quantity. The rich man is immediately compelled to diminish the relation of domination and even the suspicion of it by letting all share in it — as the Athenian

[p. 131]

law demanded the defraying of the festivals by the richest man of the quarter.”

In the second section, in the system of justice, Hegel considered the *constitution of the state* in the narrower sense. “Ethical life as the living, self-subsistent spirit, which appears as a Briareus, with myriads of eyes, arms and other limbs, each of which is an absolute individual, is an absolutely universal; and in relation to the individual, every part of this universality, everything that belongs to it, appears as an object, as an end. It is, as such, something ideal for it.”

The ethical life of the *individual* consists of the *virtues*, as they appear in their *transience*. Ethical life as absolute is not the sum total, but the indifference of all virtues. It appears not as love *toward* fatherland and people and laws, but as the absolute life *in* the fatherland and *for* the people. It is absolute truth, culture and unselfishness, for in the eternal, wherein singularity is sublated and the alternation of all determinacies, there is nothing of one’s own, and every movement of ethical life is the highest beauty, freedom and blessedness. With infinite enthusiasm Hegel indulges in the praise of ethical life as of the divine, as it is without veil for immediate intuition, but he develops only the virtues of the *estates*; of *private* morality there is no mention.

Next he develops the *administration of justice* in civil and criminal law, the *lawsuit*, and once more *war* as a lawsuit between peoples in which *fate* is the judge. Of the formal difference of constitutions as monarchy, aristocracy and democracy he speaks only in passing, in a note, says that each of these forms may be capable of being unfree, and indicates the connection of each with religion. Of *bravery* he asserts, in the description of war, that it is adorned with the whole garland of the virtues. The manifold of relations in war, he says, lets the virtues, through empirical necessity, appear quickly without external or internal hypocrisy. “But with the relations the existence of the virtues too vanishes just as quickly, virtues which, because they

[p. 132]

have this haste of pursuing one another, are just as much without any relation to a determinate totality, the whole condition of a citizen, and thus just as much vices. The distress of war posits the highest abstinence, the highest wretchedness and appearance of avarice, and then of enjoyment, which is equally revelry, because it can have no regard for the morrow or for the whole of life and livelihood. Thrift and liberality become avarice and hardheartedness toward oneself and others, when the highest distress demands this restriction — and prodigality, for property is thrown away, as it can have no abiding, and the expenditure is wholly inappropriate to one’s own or another’s use and need. — The distress of war demands the highest exertions of the body, and complete formal conceptual unity of the spirit in mechanical labor, just as much as the highest servitude of external obedience.”

The organic principle of government is freedom, that the *governing* be also the governed. In the third system the universal is to be the absolute and, purely as such, the determining. In the first system it is the crude, merely quantitative, wisdomless universal; in the second the universality is the formal one of recognizing; it is cause. Here, in the third system, *education* is the formation of the people with annihilation of all semblance, and indeed: 1) as formation of the *talent* for art and science; 2) as *discipline* in the individual, as police. “The great discipline is the universal customs, the order and training for war and the testing of the individual’s truthfulness in it.” 3) A people goes through *generation* constantly beyond itself within itself, or brings forth out of itself objectively another: *colonization*.

Hegel first made the conclusion of the philosophy of spirit into the conclusion of the system of philosophy itself by seeking to demonstrate the necessity of philosophy in a people as the ideal *complement of war*. *Absolute labor* is death alone, he said, because it sublates determinate singularity, which is why *bravery* in the state brings the absolute *sacrifice*. Since, however, for those who in fighting do not die there remains the *abasement* of not having *died* and of having the self-enjoyment of their

[p. 133]

singularity, there remains only *speculation, as the absolute cognition of truth,* as the form in which the simple consciousness of the infinite is possible without the determinacy of individual self-subsistent life. “The absolute consciousness of the individuals of the people, the living spirit of it, must be pure, absolute consciousness, absolute spirit in form as well as in content, and the spirit of the people becomes spirit of the *natural and ethical universe*. Only so is the spirit absolutely returned into its absolute self-sameness, into the ether of its simple Idea, and the end of philosophy into its beginning.”

But this conclusion did not satisfy Hegel when he later came, in Jena, with his philosophy to oral communication. He elaborated further the Concept of the difference of constitutions and determined the estate of the free for monarchy as the *nobility*, insofar as it stands opposed to majesty in the mute *struggle bearing the form of obedience*. Especially, however, he elaborated, in a manner distinguished by its simplicity and intelligibility, the Concept of religious *cultus*, as that in which a people attains its highest self-enjoyment. He demanded that in *religion* the reality of the objective itself, and thereby also subjectivity and particularity, be posited as *sublated*. Were the latter to be retained as *negative freedom* in this highest region of universal rationality, perhaps even (as he remarked against *Schleiermacher’s* at that time epoch-making *Speeches on Religion*) as virtuosity, then it would not be taken seriously to let *spirit appear in a shape of spirit*, whereas it is the essence of religion that spirit be ashamed of none of its individuals, refuse to appear to none, and that each have the power over it to conjure it. The sublation of subjectivity, however, is not bare annihilation of it, but annihilation only of its *empirical* individuality and through it purification to the absolute enjoyment of its absolute essence. Because in religion the ideal shape of spirit is real, its real side however ideal, and because in it spirit appears for the individual, it has for him *first* the shape of an objective, which weaves and lives in the people as its spirit and is alive in all. In science

[p. 134]

spirit appears in objective shape, in the shape of being, and it is precisely the same that is also subjective. In *matter*, therefore, *knowing has nothing special over religion*. Its essence presses spirit together from the extension of empirical existence into the highest point of intension, and presents it objectively to intuiting and thinking, so that it enjoys itself and its own intuition and in this enjoyment is at the same time real, i.e. that it recognizes itself in the individual and the individual himself in it. Presenting itself *objectively* as totality of empirical existence, the *essence* of God has a *history* for spirit. His being-alive consists of events and deeds. The liveliest god of a people is its *national god*, in whom for the people not only its pure spirit, but at the same time its empirical existence, the untruth and insecurity of the same as a sum of singularities, appears *transfigured*. Because spirit in religion is not in the ideality of science but in relation to reality, it necessarily itself has a *bounded* shape, which, fixed for itself, constitutes in every religion its *positive* side. The *religious tradition* therefore expresses the twofold: on the one hand the *speculative Idea* of spirit, on the other the limitation taken from the *empirical* existence of the people, not the limitation of the Idea, such as art in general must exercise. Because, then, religion excludes science and art from itself, *insofar* as it is religion, it is a *doing* as complement of art and science, the *cultus*, which raises subjectivity and freedom to their highest enjoyment, in that, as divine service, it *sacrifices* to the great spirit a part of singularity and through this surrender sets the remaining property free. Through the reality of the annihilation of singularity in sacrifice the subject saves itself against the one-sidedness of *deception*, that its elevation is only in thoughts. This doing, the *irony* toward the mortal and useful doing of men, is *reconciliation*, the basic Idea of religion. Insofar as singularity wants to assert itself against rational universality, it becomes *sin*, *crime*. Here spirit reconciles itself only as *fate in punishment*. Reconciliation is exalted above punishment

[p. 135]

and therefore appears as just necessity. Since, now, reconciliation in general addresses itself only to spirit and cannot sublate the chain of determinate existence, *nothing* is *changed* by it in fate. Only the essence of the energy of the struggle with it, as the possibility of staking in it the entire compass of empirical existence, is also the possibility of reconciliation with fate, because spirit has torn itself away from fate through the ethicality of the struggle itself.

Religion must, as Hegel expressed himself in the then fashionable language of the philosophy of nature, appear world-historically according to the three universal dimensions of reason, within the *climatic* modification according to its empirical difference, in the following three forms: 1) in the form of *identity*, in original reconciledness of spirit and its real being in individuality; 2) in the form that spirit begins from the infinite difference of its identity and from it reconstructs a *relative* identity and reconciles itself; 3) this identity, subsumed under that first, absolute one, will posit the being-one of reason in a shape of spirit, and of that same reason in its real being or in individuality, as original and at the same time as its infinite opposition and its reconstruction.

In the first dimension, as original reconciliation, religion is *natural religion*. To the fantasy of its pantheism nature is in and for itself a spirit and holy. From no element has its god withdrawn. Individual individuals may have a curse lying upon them, but no universal of nature is forsaken by God. For individual moments the spirit may be angry with such peoples, but they are sure of his reconciliation. Dealing with life is a conversation with the gods, a reciprocal giving and receiving from them, and every external movement a meaningful word of fate. The *shapes of the gods* are able to be dissolved neither into actualities, nor into historical view, nor into thoughts. *The eternity of the ideals of a beautiful mythology* rests neither on their perfect artistic beauty, nor on the truth of the Ideas which they

[p. 136]

express, nor on the actuality to which they belong, but precisely on the identity of all this and the *inseparability* of the same.

But second, this beautiful world of gods must perish with the spirit that animates it and can remain only as a memento. The unity of spirit with its reality must tear apart. The ideal principle must constitute itself in the form of universality, the real settle itself as singularity, and nature between the two remain lying as a *desecrated corpse*. Spirit must leave its dwelling in living nature and rise against it as a potency. The ethical pain had to be infinite. The time of this pain had come when the Romans had shattered the living individuality of the peoples, thereby driven out their spirits, destroyed their ethical life, and spread over the isolation the universality of their dominion. At the time of this isolation, which found no reconciliation, and of this universality, which had no life, in this *tedium of the world*, when everywhere on the cultivated earth peace reigned, the original identity out of its being torn apart had to raise its eternal power above its pain and attain again to its own intuition, or the race of men had to go to ruin within itself. The first scene of the *appearance* of ethereal reason, reawakened in the world that had ceased to be nature, had to be that people which in the whole course of existence has been the *most rejected* of peoples, because in it the *pain* had to be deepest and its expression had to have a truth intelligible to the whole world.

*Christ* became the founder of a religion by giving expression, from the innermost depth, to the suffering of his whole time, and thereby raising above it the power of the divinity of spirit, the absolute certainty of reconciliation, which he bore in himself, and by his *confidence* awakening *the confidence of others*. The suffering of his time, to which nature had become unfaithful, he expressed in the absolute *contempt* of nature that had become *world*, and the absolute *confidence* of reconciliation in the *certainty* that he was *one with God*. — The contempt which he expressed toward the world,

[p. 137]

had necessarily, as his fate, to avenge itself on him through death, and this very death had to justify the contempt of the world and make it a fixed point. These two necessary elements had to become the hinge of the new religion: the de-deification of nature, hence the contempt of the world, and that in this infinite separation one man nevertheless bore in himself the confidence of being one with the Absolute. In this man the world was again reconciled with the spirit. Because the whole of nature had become ungodly, only the nature of this man could be divine, and nature be *consecrated* again only from him. But because the certainty of man of being ungodly saw divinity in him *alone*, and had to tie to his *personality* the becoming-one of individuality with the absolute spirit, his existence became the beginning of this religion itself. The most striking direction of this religion had to be, first, the contempt of the world and of the universal that existed as *state*, and the symbol of this contempt the *cross*, that which for this world, as the gallows, was the most ignominious and dishonoring. No more necessary and more significant signal of the absolute separation from actuality and of the war of extermination against it could be set up.

The other side of the infinite pain of this absolute separation was its reconciliation in the faith that *God* had appeared *in human form* and that human nature had thus reconciled itself with itself in this single shape as representative of the species. This single human shape expressed in its history the *whole* history of the empirical existence of the human race, as it had to, in order to be able to be the *national god of the race*. But it expressed this history at the same time only in that it was God’s. For the principle is, namely, infinite pain, absolute rupture of nature. Without this pain reconciliation has no meaning and no truth. In order that this potency of religion may be, it *must eternally produce* this pain, *in order to be able to reconcile eternally*. The empirical condition of the world, from which religion began, must through the struggle of this reconciling religion itself be sublated

[p. 138]

so that the world may really become happier and more reconciled, and religion thus sublate itself. It must therefore at the same time bear within itself the principle of arousing infinite suffering, in order to reconcile infinitely. It has the principle, the fate of the world, necessarily in the history of its God, who died the death of a criminal. The death of a criminal would itself be only something singular. The sight of death as universal necessity can arouse no infinite religious pain, but he who died on the cross is at the same time the God of this religion, and as such his history expresses the infinite suffering of de-deified nature. The divine had been thrust into the *commonness of life*, *the divine itself had died*. The thought that God himself was dead on earth expresses alone the feeling of this infinite pain; as likewise his reconciliation, that he *rose* from the grave. Through his life and death the God is abased, through his resurrection man has been deified. That infinite pain and this eternal reconciliation this religion cannot let depend on the contingent, empirical existence of individuals. It must constitute itself as a cultus, through which that pain is aroused and this reconciliation imparted. Natural religion must leave to *chance* how far the original reconciliation is alive in the individual. But the religion which aims at the *reconstruction* of indifferent harmony must, violently against nature, produce that infinite difference, in order to make possible that its reconciliation be the reconstructed one.

This has indeed happened in the Christian religion with consummate *wisdom*. Man is led through an infinite sum of *arranged conditions* to the pains of divine death and of the dying of all life, and out of this death is awakened again to becoming-one with the God-man, in whom the race is reconciled, by eating his body and drinking his blood, the most intimate kind of union, and sanctified. The history of God is the history of the whole race, and every individual goes through this entire history of the race. From the reconsecrated man onward

[p. 139]

the whole of nature too is made holy again, a temple of reawakened life. To everything the *new consecration* is given. The ruling power of the monarch is consecrated from religion: his scepter contains a piece of the holy cross. All land has been endowed with particular messengers of God and marked with their footprints. Each can boast of a holy history of its own of its reconciliation and has *individualized* the new consecration. To all particular doing and to all things of the highest and lowest doing consecration is given anew, which they had lost; — the old curse that lies upon everything is dissolved, the whole of nature taken into grace and its pain reconciled.

Through this reconstructed religion, to the form of the ideality of spirit, which can exist in natural religion alone, namely *art*, the other side has necessarily been added, the ideality of spirit under the *form of thinking*, and folk religion must contain the highest Ideas of speculation not merely as a *mythology*, but pronounced in the *form of Ideas*. It reveres the Absolute in the form of the *Trinity*, God as the *paternal principle*, the *absolute thought*; then his reality, him in his creation, the *eternal Son*, who however as divine reality has two sides, the one of his proper divinity, according to which the Son of God is God, the other the side of his singularity as world; finally the eternal identity of this world, of the objective, with the eternal thought, the *Holy Spirit*. Because religion proceeds from the infinite pain, the reconciliation of this pain has had to become at the same time, in the reconciled God, objectively this relation as *love*, and the divinity in which this love finds its happiness, the *Mother* of God herself.

In *Catholicism* this religion has become the *beautiful* religion. *Protestantism* has sublated the poetry of consecration, the individualization of sanctification, and poured the color of universality again over nature hallowed *as a fatherland*, and the religious fatherland and the appearance of the God again banished from one’s own fatherland into distant remoteness.

[p. 140]

It has transformed the infinite pain, the liveliness, confidence and peace of reconciliation into an infinite *longing*. It has impressed upon religion the whole character of *northern* subjectivity. Because it transformed the whole cycle of pain and its reconciliation into longing, the longing however into the thinking and knowing of reconciliation, because thus in it the violence and necessity with which the pain was aroused fell away, this form of religion, as infinite pain and its reconciliation, was given over to contingency and could pass over into the empirical reconciliation with the actuality of existence, and into an unmediated, undisturbed sinking into the commonness of empirical existence and everyday necessity. That religious elevation and the sanctification of empirical existence, the *Sabbath of the world*, has vanished, and life has become a common, unholy workday.

Although Hegel at that time, as emerges sufficiently from the foregoing communications, held Protestantism to be just as finite a form of Christianity as Catholicism, he nevertheless did not on that account, like many of his contemporaries, go over to Catholicism, but believed that out of Christianity, *through the mediation of philosophy*, a *third* form of religion would form itself. He said in this respect: “Because that beauty and sanctification has gone down, it can neither *return* nor be mourned, but only the *necessity of its passing away* be recognized, as well as the higher be divined, for which it has to prepare the way and which must step into its place. — It may, that is, seem, according to what has gone before, that the reconstruction takes place within the sphere of the opposition from which the pain proceeds, and that the whole previous religious form stands only in the potency of the *relative opposition*, for nature is sanctified, but not through a spirit of its own; it is reconciled, but remains for itself something unholy, as before. The consecration comes from something external. The whole spiritual sphere has not risen out of its own ground and soil. The infinite pain is permanent in the sanctification and the reconciliation itself a sigh toward heaven. — Now that

[p. 141]

Protestantism has stripped off the alien consecration, the spirit may dare to sanctify itself as spirit in its own shape and to establish the original reconciliation with itself in a *new religion*, into which the infinite pain and the whole gravity of its opposition are taken up, but which dissolves itself unclouded and pure, if, that is, there shall be a *free people* and reason shall have reborn its reality as an ethical spirit, which can have the boldness to take for itself its pure shape *on its own ground and out of its own majesty*. — Each individual is a blind link in the chain of absolute necessity, on which the world is further formed. Each individual can raise himself to dominion over a greater length of this chain only if he recognizes whither the great necessity wills, and from this cognition learns to speak the magic words that conjure up its shape. This cognition, to enclose within itself at once the whole energy of suffering and of the opposition which for a couple of thousand years has ruled the world and all the forms of its development, and to raise itself above it, only *philosophy* is able to give.”

Such was Hegel’s original system.

#### The Father’s Death and the Emergence from Obscurity.

In the midst of such occupations Hegel received a short but shattering letter from his sister, of 15 January 1799:

“Last night, hardly before 12 o’clock, Father died quite gently and peacefully. I am unable to write to you further. May God stand by me.”

Your Christiane.

The settlement of the estate required Hegel’s presence in Stuttgart. He left Frankfurt on 9 March and returned on 28 March. The property was so divided that the two brothers, the Magister Georg Wilhelm and the officer,

[p. 142]

Georg Ludwig, set aside for their sister, as compensation for the costs caused by them in their careers, the sum of 500 florins, and indeed of this the Magister 350, Ludwig however 150 florins. Hegel accordingly kept, according to the document still extant, for his share still 3154 florins, 24 kreuzer, 4 pfennigs. In possession of this fortune he now thought very vividly of entering the academic sphere, but, after his thorough manner, spent still a longer time in preparation for it.

In the autumn of 1800 he made an excursion to *Mainz*. The passport for it was issued to him by the chancellery of the city on 19 September. If one were to state, from such passport documents, even only Hegel’s height, it would look bad. In one passport he has 2 inches, in another 8, in one even 10! The one in question styles him *maître ès Arts* [Master of Arts] and describes him thus: “[French] aged 30 years, height 5 feet, 2 inches, hair and eyebrows brown, eyes gray, nose medium, mouth medium, chin round, forehead mediocre, face oval.”

Hegel had now put his external circumstances in order; he had fulfilled his obligations as house tutor; his works were ripening toward publication. His apprentice years were running out, his journeyman years were beginning. Hegel wanted to go to Jena, the philosophical Eldorado of the day, as if it went without saying. First, however, he wished for a wholly solitary rest, and wrote therefore to Schelling to ask his advice about it. He announced to him that he *too* had indeed had to create a *system*, but hoped nevertheless to meet him as a friend. He believed that Schelling, whose spirit and activity were just then in the fairest bloom, was of all his contemporaries the one most homogeneous with himself. So, after much pondering back and forth about his future, he sat down and wrote to him.

Frankfurt am Main, 2 November 1800.

“I think, dear Schelling, that a separation of several years cannot make me embarrassed to ask your kindness on account of a particular wish. My request concerns some addresses

[p. 143]

for *Bamberg*, where I wished to stay for some time. Since I at last find myself in a position to leave my previous circumstances, I am resolved to spend a time in an independent situation and to devote it to studies and works already begun. Before I dare to entrust myself to the literary hubbub of Jena, I want first to strengthen myself by a stay in a third place. Bamberg occurred to me all the more because I hoped to find you there. I hear you are back in Jena. In Bamberg I know no one, nor do I otherwise know how to obtain an address there, and I therefore take the liberty of asking you for this, as also for your good advice, in order to find an arrangement regarding board and lodging and the like. Equally agreeable it will be to me if you will open for me the way to some literary acquaintances. Should your local knowledge prefer another place, Erfurt, Eisenach, I ask for your advice. I seek cheap provisions, on account of my bodily condition a good beer, a few acquaintances, and would prefer a *Catholic* city to a Protestant one. I want to see that religion once from close by. Excuse my request on the ground of the lack of acquaintances who lie closer to me in this, and forgive my circumstantiality about such particularities to our old friendship. — Your great public course I have watched with admiration and joy. You will excuse me from either speaking of it humbly or wishing also to show myself to you. I avail myself of the middle word, that I hope that we shall find each other again as friends. — In my scientific formation, which began from the more subordinate needs of men, I had to be driven forward to science, and the ideal of youth had to transform itself into the form of reflection, into a *system* at the same time. I ask myself now, while I am still occupied with it, *what return to intervention in the life of men is to be found*? — Of all the men I see around me, I see only in you the one in whom I — also with regard to utterance and effect on the world — would like to find my friend, for I see that you have grasped man purely, that is, with your whole heart and without vanity. I look

[p. 144]

therefore also, with regard to myself, with such confidence upon you, that you recognize my unselfish endeavor, even if its sphere be lower, and could find a worth in it. In my wish and hope to meet you, I must, however far off that may be, know how to honor fate too and expect from its favor how we shall meet.

Farewell! I request an early reply from you. Remember me to our friend Berger.

Your friend H.

[scan 190]

### Book Two.

[scan 192]

#### Jena’s Literary Situation.

Hegel allowed himself to be persuaded to go straight from Frankfurt to Jena.

The actual literary ferment was already over here. *Fichte*, who had withdrawn on account of the charge of atheism, was already in Berlin. The *Schlegels’ Athenaeum*, this piquant periodical, which had accustomed the public to paradox, had already ceased publication. The Romantics had dispersed. *Novalis* had died in 1800 in Weißenfels and *Tieck* had moved away in the summer of the same year. *Schelling* finally, who had come as extraordinary professor from Leipzig, was at least no longer a novelty.

But the movement now went into breadth: Jena bristled with young men who wanted to make a career in philosophy. The example of Reinhold, Fichte, Schelling, their swift rise to fame, tempted powerfully, and against Fichte’s speculative audacity one could protect oneself by caution, against his disciplinary conflicts with the students by compliance. The lecture catalogues of the Jena university of that time drip with philosophy. They show a sample-card of the most manifold philosophical standpoints, from the dogmatically Wolffian to the romantic improvisations of the philosophy of nature. The old *Hennings* and *Ulrich* read on and on their logic and morals, but alongside came and went Privatdozenten, as pigeons fly in and out of a dovecote. Among them are quite forgotten names, like *Kistner*, *Vermehren*, etc., but also many who later surfaced again elsewhere, like *Schad*, *Fries*, *Krause*, Gruber, Ast, etc. Almost all these Privatdozenten announced, besides

[p. 148]

their favorite subject, in which they had made special studies, logic, because this course, as the one to be taken up by the studying youth according to custom, still offered the readiest prospect of fees. Yet it belonged, although now one man had a bent more for mathematics, another more for natural right, a third for psychology, already to etiquette to lecture also on *philosophy of nature* or *philosophical encyclopedia*. Not a few besides offered, to the gentlemen students, *if they wished it*, *desiderantibus* [to those desiring it], to impart also this and that, e.g. declaiming, disputing, and the like. As Hegel’s still remaining enrollment sheets show, the prices were moderate, 2 to 3 Laubthaler for the lecture course.

Moreover, most of them went about with projects for new *periodicals* or sought at least, also on account of the fee, to collaborate on one already existing.

The ambition, finally, to be appointed *professor*, in order to set oneself somewhat apart from the mass of Privatdozenten, was extraordinary. As is always the way of the world at German universities, this striving produced a competition which, through a craving for protecting acquaintances, through carping and the tale-bearing of little anecdotes, was often spiteful. When, therefore, *Bavaria* began to organize its educational institutions according to a new plan, it could draw from Jena a whole colony of scholars. *Niethammer*, *Paulus*, *Schelling*, Ast, and others went away. Those who remained behind looked after them with envy and strove to share the same fate as soon as possible.

Into this state of things Hegel entered in January 1801, one more Swabian among the many Swabians already gathered here.

#### The Difference between Fichte’s and Schelling’s System.

Once he had come to Jena, it was incumbent on Hegel to attest his philosophical physiognomy publicly. Since, now, the Kantian philosophy had been followed by Reinhold’s modification of it, this by Fichte’s *Science of Knowledge*, this by Schelling’s transcendental idealism, and Jena, from Wolffianism onward, all these

[p. 149]

phases of philosophy within itself, it was quite fitting that Hegel took as the subject of his first work, which he wrote in a few months, by July 1801, the *Difference* between Fichte’s and Schelling’s System. Since, as a literarily wholly unknown man of already riper age, he suddenly stepped among a crowd in which literary activity was universal, he had to indicate at least approximately the position he would take. It also urged him to see the deep culture won in silence enter into interaction with that of the day.

In March 1800 Schelling had published his *System of Transcendental Idealism*, which Hegel was still studying in Frankfurt. Schelling was in it still a Fichtean to the extent that he constructed *nature* wholly from the standpoint of the I. To be sure, it *was to be*, from the Concept of matter to that of teleology, the parallel of the development of the I from sensing to willing, but still it was not yet grasped for itself in its free objectivity. Schelling *wavered* constantly between idealism and realism and had therefore closed his system of that time with *artistic production*, because in this the freedom of the producing I and the necessity of the thing unite immediately as genius. Hegel now showed in Fichte’s philosophy the one-sidedness of grasping all objectivity only *subjectively* and therefore, in the concrete, especially in morals and politics, of falling apart into an endless aggregate of finitudes. He recognized Fichte’s system from the side of *philosophizing*, from the side of productive power, of the mastery of speculation, as an immortal work; as system itself, however, this philosophy did not satisfy him, because, as he proved at length, it reaches neither the Concept of nature nor that of ethical life and aesthetic culture; because it nowhere comprehends the object also in its positive self-subsistence against the subject, but only as a negative barrier, and therefore still less the Absolute as the identity of object and subject. Of Schelling’s philosophy he recognized that it *possesses* objectivity as the necessary, in itself self-subsistent correlate of subjectivity, as also the Concept of the sublation of this double one-sidedness in the Concept of the Absolute, but in a delicate manner he also made noticeable the defect that the

[p. 150]

Absolute is determined as yet only as the *point of indifference* of the objective and the subjective.

In the *introduction* and in the *appendix* of the book he appeared more decisively. The former gave an *exposition of the manifold forms which occur in present-day philosophizing*, an interesting critique of all the concepts around which the philosophical struggle of that time moved in respect of principle: need of philosophy, principle of philosophy as supreme first proposition, transcendent intuition, reflection as instrument of philosophizing, history of philosophy, etc. Each of these short essays brought long-considered determinations in pithy language. The Concept of the system as the self-organizing totality of knowledge, which cannot be derived merely demonstratively from a supreme, unproven first principle, and the necessity of the *union of the synthetic and analytic* method for speculation, were here especially emphasized.

The appendix occupied itself with *Reinhold* and *Bardili*. The former had at that time driven Kant’s thought, of making the critique of the faculty of cognition the condition of cognizing, to the absurd consequence of a *preliminary* philosophizing, of a beginning before the beginning, of a grounding before the ground. He had degraded the cognition of truth to a mere *tendency*. Against such asthenia Hegel turned with as much asperity as humor and remarked bluntly that the beginning must begin precisely with the beginning. *Bardili*, a cousin of Schelling’s, had at that time written a work he called *First Outline of Logic*, in which Reinhold saw a welcome relief for the speculative embarrassments into which he had again fallen. Reinhold was a noble, but too feminine a soul. He always had to have a man on whom he could rely, to whom he could cling. The fresh impertinence with which Bardili treated Kant and Fichte impressed him in turn, as Fichte had once impressed him in relation to Kant. He did not see that the Bardilian logic differed from the common one only through the attempt to carry through the opposition of the *One* and the *Many*. That Bardili again grasped thinking in the *independence*

[p. 151]

of its determinations from the phenomenological process of subjective intelligence, from the history of self-consciousness, was a real merit. Neither in Fichte nor in Schelling had the logical element come to recognition in accordance with its free independence. But Bardili was not the first, as he supposed, to take thinking as a *reckoning*. This turn of logic, in order to secure the immanent significance of its categories, had been there before him often enough, and he himself related quite naively in the preface to his *Logic* how it arose from reading the logics of Bilfinger and Ploucquet during a stay in the country at Easter vacation. That he renewed it at a time when quantitative difference and indifference were the order of the day, when the more and the less, the equating and unequating, dominated all the formulas of philosophizing, was not to be wondered at. In holding that the determinations of thinking have a worth for themselves, apart from their being thought in consciousness, Hegel agreed with Bardili; but he had to declare himself against him all the more vehemently because the latter, by identifying logic with the operation of reckoning, made it ossified again, perverted the dialectical fluidity of thinking into the deadness of number, into the dullness of the equating and unequating of the one and the many, and thus, despite the semblance of a higher, metaphysical flight, fell back in the end entirely into the most ordinary formalism. And yet — how often was the gossip to be renewed, as though Hegel owed his logic to the Bardilian one.

#### The Dissertation on the Orbits of the Planets.

Having provisionally marked out his literary position by his first work, Hegel next had, for his purposes, the preparation of a habilitation dissertation to attend to. The theme for it, an inquiry into the lawfulness of the distances of the planets from one another, he had long been carrying about with him. Extracts from Kant’s writings on mechanics and astronomy, from Kepler, Newton and others, are found among his papers much earlier. He wrote the

[p. 152]

dissertation first in German. Then he summarized it more briefly in Latin. These manuscripts and a heap of calculations belonging to them are still extant.

Hegel was deeply imbued with Kepler’s *Harmonia mundi*. That, as Kepler declared with presentient certainty, reason exists in the systematics of the heavenly bodies, was for him a thought which he would gladly have exhausted in its whole extent. He reproached philosophy with having done too little as yet for astronomy. The *confounding* of merely mathematical determinations with already physical ones, e.g. of lines and points with *forces*, seemed to him a chief ground of the *confusion* in the philosophy of nature, and *Newton* one of the weightiest authorities for it. He held that Kepler had already grasped the actual core of the matter with regard to celestial mechanics, and that Newton had only brought this content, given to him, *hypothetically* into mathematical formulas. This technical merit could not justify celebrating Newton, as so often happened, as the one who had *discovered* the true form of the motion of the heavenly bodies, the ellipse. Into the polemic against Newton’s hypothesis of the so-called *tangential force* Hegel put all his life long all the bitterness of an injured patriotism, for Kepler was not only a German but his countryman, a Swabian, whom, to be sure, the University of Tübingen had once likewise rejected from theological scruples, i.e. out of fear of the truth. Hegel was vexed that the Germans themselves, over the banal admiration of the Briton, put Kepler so much in the shade. Newton’s *Optics* too gave him an inexhaustible material for the reproach of not having properly separated mathematical determinations from physical ones; a polemic which in his case was heightened still further by his interest in Goethe’s theory of colors, and by which he made enemies of many natural scientists, who in return treated him as a scholastic who, with a great expenditure of sterile logic, was vainly endeavoring to bring to honor a few whims of Goethe and Schelling.

The dissertation was to develop *a priori* the Keplerian laws of the shape of the planetary orbit and of the speed of motion of the heavenly bodies. In this Hegel did not pay homage, as it were,

[p. 153]

in a hasty construing. He did not in the least despise the *so-called exact* sciences, but submitted rather to their instruction with the most willing perseverance, so that, as the numerous and extensive extracts still extant demonstrate, he left almost none of the more celebrated works of mathematicians, physicists and physiologists unstudied. Only when empiricism wanted to narrow the room of speculation and to deny it the recognition just as necessary for it, did he turn against it. Yet Hegel lacked, for the intuition of nature, that *primitive* certainty which distinguished him in the realm of the logical Idea and of spirit. His original education in mathematics and physics, too, was wholly Newtonian. His later idealism made it impossible for him to explain the motions of the heavenly bodies through determinations of *finite* mechanics, of *impact* and *fall*; impossible to assume two different forces which in perihelion and aphelion were to act in inverse measure to the velocity. The apple which is supposed to have helped the sleeping Newton to the cognition that in every smallest mechanical motion on the earth the same law of gravity rules as in the harmonious giant vortex of the heavenly bodies, he called the *astronomical fall of man*. He knew well, as Newton himself had declared, that his expressions, attraction, impulse, etc., *were* to have only a mathematical meaning. But how often is this not forgotten! Hegel now exalted Kepler precisely for this reason, because he had known how to preserve mathematical purity. Yet his exposition remained imperfect. The *conscientiousness* of his empirical, highly manifold knowledge, the anxiety not to let a mistake slip in detail, stood constantly in conflict with the *universalism* of his speculative conception and produced an undeniable heaviness and obscurity of expression. *Schelling* had no such scruple before problematic ventures, and by the poetry of his turns of phrase, by the divinatory gleam of great prospects, aroused a decided enthusiasm, which has always been lacking to Hegel in the field of the philosophy of nature.

The dissertation was to develop the relation of space and time,

[p. 154]

of square and cube, of straight line and curve, of circle and ellipse. It was to appear apologetically for Kepler, polemically against Newton. But the manner in which the Concept of being and thinking was brought into connection with that of number and geometrical figuration was in fact still very subjectively idealistic. The thought, then favored and pursued above all by H. *Schubart*, of regarding the series of the planets as a line of different degrees of cohesion was not forgotten either. Nevertheless, but for a small appendage which Hegel added at the end, on two pages, with a *Superest* [there remains], the treatise would have maintained an unchallenged standing as one of the most thorough of the natural philosophy of that time, to which *Schelling* himself appealed. But since the reprinting of the dissertation in Hegel’s collected works it has been attacked in so hostile a manner that we must dwell on it here for a moment. At the end, namely, Hegel came to speak of the distances of the planets from one another, whose regularity Kepler had discovered and which had repeatedly been brought up by *Kant*, *Lambert*, *Titius*, *Bode*. Hegel saw in the conjecture of a planet between Mars and Jupiter, and in the eager search for it by the astronomers, the proof that *experience* has of itself the drive to *agree with reason*. According to the proportion of 4, 7, 10, 16, 52, 100, there falls between 16 and 52 yet 28. For 16 Mars existed, for 52 Jupiter. Thus a corresponding planet was lacking for 28. Astronomy now relied on the a priori necessity that the planet corresponding to this member of the progression *must be found* and therefore went hunting for it. Now Hegel mentioned incidentally at the end of his treatise that in the Platonic *Timaeus* another series of numbers is given, according to which the Demiurge formed the universe: 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 16, 27. Were *this* progression the true order of nature, *then would* there be a great interspace between the fourth and fifth planets, and it would be evident that one could look for no planet there.

Hegel wrote his dissertation in the spring and summer of 1801, yet evidently cannot yet have known anything of Piazzi’s discovery of Ceres on 1 January 1801. Of the discovery of the

[p. 155]

Pallas by *Olbers* on 28 March 1802 could naturally be as little in question as that of Juno in 1804 or of Vesta in 1807. The outcry that was raised over the philosopher’s demonstrating the planet away from his professorial chair, while the astronomers, out of mischief, discovered it, is therefore a quite empty, boyish malicious joy.

The question is when Piazzi’s observation at Palermo became known in Jena. In Hegel’s lectures on the philosophy of nature there it did not remain disregarded. The vanity of wanting to have and know something *otherwise* speculatively than one must know it empirically never entered Hegel’s mind. The gap in the planetary system, like the hypotheses for filling it, he knew very well, so that acquaintance with those discoveries could only be gratifying to him. But his utterance was itself only a *hypothesis*, by which he, since the telescopes of the astronomers had already *sought* the planet missing according to calculation *so long in vain*, wanted to come to the aid of the *experience made up to then*, namely that between Mars and Jupiter there is a leap, hence to do anything but oppose it or deny it, rather to confirm it. On the condition that the Platonic progression were the truer, *would* the planet not yet found be sought in vain! — If, finally, empiricism had wanted to triumph completely, it would have had to discover only *one* planet. Instead of it there came to light, in due time, four little planets which one had not expected at all.

The task of deriving speculatively the relation of the distance and of the period of revolution of the planets Hegel pursued throughout his whole life without having arrived thereby at a decided result gratifying to him. His veneration for the genius of Kepler remained always the same, and even his renewal of the Pythagorean representation that the planets are ordered according to the laws of *musical* harmony he always mentioned with solemn admiration. In the Romantic reaction against the mechanism of the understanding, Newton was set over against Kepler and Goethe, just as in physiology and medicine one began to exalt Paracelsus, in speculation generally Jakob Böhme.

[p. 156]

#### Habilitation Disputation of 27 August 1801.

On 27 August, thus on his natural birthday, Hegel celebrated his second, academic one.

He appended to his dissertation theses which contained the most essential points of his system. Their formulation was in part *paradoxical*, which is not so much a reproach as a praise, for theses are meant to provoke the love of controversy, and must therefore arouse the itch of contradiction. The sequence of the theses shows a certain coherence; first logical ones are set down, then ones on the philosophy of nature. Thereupon follow critical ones on the Concept of philosophy in general, and lastly a few from practical philosophy. These theses, for whose oral defense Hegel wrote himself a slip, still preserved, with marginal glosses, are quite remarkable because they contain in part the main points at which people were accustomed to take offense at Hegel and which were always defended by him with tenacity. For this reason we must dwell on them somewhat longer.

I. [Latin] Contradiction is the rule of the true, non-contradiction the rule of the false. *Wolff* had said something perfectly true with his Concept of contradiction. He had expressed in this negative form the Concept of positive identity. It is impossible that a determination as such *for itself* can at the same time be the opposite one. Everything determinate is in its determinacy equal to itself, is the exclusion of its opposite. Concepts which contradict *themselves* must therefore be untrue. This truth Hegel never disputed, however often he has been misunderstood, but he combated the stopping short at it as an error. The Concept that something, in equality with itself, is *at the same time its opposite*, is just as true as that something, related only to itself, does not contradict itself. Identity, i.e. the relation to itself, is only a *moment* of the whole. The distinction, which as determinate distinction becomes the difference of the identical as of the *positive* and *negative*, is no less essential. True and false are moments of *cognizing*; good and evil moments of the *freedom* of the will, etc. The true has in the false, the good in the evil *its* opposition. The white color is not white, in that it itself

[p. 157]

would be immediately at the same time the black one — but it is the one which has in the black its contradiction, which is posited only through it itself. With the Concept of the true the Concept of the untrue is at the same time posited; the true is not that which would be without contradiction; but it itself is at the same time the positive negation of its negation, as *Spinoza* expressed it: [Latin] the true is the index of itself and of the false. The usual proposition of identity and of contradiction, that A = A and that A cannot be at the same time B and the negation of B, is, in its undialectical rigidity, the death of all deeper cognition. With it one remains far from a correct apprehension of everything negative, of pain, illness, evil, wickedness, error, etc. That a quality as such cannot be at the same time *not this* quality, that thus a wooden iron or iron wood are impossibilities, is quite right. But that the *same subject* cannot at the same time unite opposed determinations in itself is quite false. Even in the sphere of mechanical nature the contradiction of the centripetal and centrifugal force is sublated in bodies. If one understands Hegel, to be sure, as though *persistence* in contradiction counted for him as the Concept of the true, as though he did not know the Concept of the *dissolution* of contradiction, the *return* of identity out of the negativity of its opposition to itself, then one invents an absurdity for him. Hegel, however, was driven beyond the Wolffian law of thought by *Kant’s dialectic* in the *Critique of Pure Reason*; for Kant had shown at great length in the *antinomies* that with the mere not-contradicting oneself, contradicting oneself too can be demonstrated as *equally true*, in which relation Hegel said in the second section of his thesis: [Latin] contradiction is not the contradiction of the false.

II. [Latin] The syllogism is the principle of idealism. With this proposition Hegel’s *logical* direction stepped forth decisively. It was in itself only a consequence of the Kantian philosophy, which had designated anew the form of inference as that of *reason* itself. In the triplicity of the Kantian categories, in the thesis, antithesis and synthesis of the Fichtean deduction, in the identity and twofoldness of the Schellingian construction, the syllogism had always already lain at the ground. Hegel now raised science

[p. 158]

again to *consciousness* of the necessity of carrying this form through.

III. [Latin] The square is the law of nature, the triangle that of mind. This proposition was a consequence partly of *Baader’s* renewal of the mystical ternary, of which we have treated earlier, partly of Platonism, to which Hegel gave himself up in the original elaboration of his system. Plato had laid the bond of analogy, a : b = b : c, thus a = c, b = c, at the ground of the *elementary* process, so that air and water constitute the *broken middle* between the extremes of fire and earth, and air relates to fire as water to earth, thus air to water as fire to earth. Hegel sought constantly to hold fast to this thought, that in nature the difference presents itself in the form of a *double existence* of the diverse (*Works*, vol. XIV. 2, p. 251). Yet it can be demonstrated as a general determination at most for inorganic nature, and for the organic only in such cases where it refers to the inorganic. That the triad is the law of spirit is genuinely Platonic; the whole *Republic* has a triadic construction. Hegel referred the triplicity above all to the difference of the subject from the object in the identity of the subject.

IV. [Latin] In true arithmetic there is room neither for addition except of unity to the dyad, nor for subtraction except of the dyad from the triad, nor for the triad as sum, nor for unity as difference. This proposition too, which wants to set up the simplest formula for the different kinds of calculation, contains the germ of a chief endeavor of Hegel’s, in which he succeeded in breaking through as little as in the calculation of the orbits of the planets.

V. [Latin] As the magnet is a natural lever, so the gravity of the planets toward the sun is a natural pendulum. This parallel was entirely in the taste of the natural philosophy of that time and had at least the interest of the novelty of the comparison. With the expression *natural lever* for the *magnet*, *natural pendulum* for the *radius vector* of the *planet*, Hegel presumably wanted to designate the difference of their *immanent* motion from *finite* motion.

VI. [Latin] The Idea is the synthesis of the infinite and the finite, and all philosophy is in Ideas.

[p. 159]

VII. [Latin] Critical philosophy lacks Ideas and is an imperfect form of Skepticism.

VIII. [Latin] The matter of the postulate of reason, which critical philosophy presents, destroys that very philosophy, and is the principle of Spinozism.

IX. [Latin] The state of nature is not unjust, and for that reason one must emerge from it. If Hegel seems hereby to contradict *Hobbes*, that is not the case. Rather, he extends the well-known Hobbesian proposition. The *status naturae* [state of nature] is only the possibility of the opposed determinations of the just and the unjust. The will must give up its naturalness; it must determine itself. Only with this do right and wrong *arise*; — a Concept which Hegel likewise repeated all his life, especially against the presupposition of a primitive state of justice.

X. [Latin] The principle of moral science is reverence to be held toward fate.

XI. [Latin] Virtue excludes innocence, both of acting and of suffering.

XII. [Latin] Morality absolute in all respects is repugnant to virtue.

These paradoxes were all directed against the limitations in Kantian *morals*, in that Hegel sought to assert against them rather the *ancient* Concept of ethical life, of which there was already mention earlier and of which there will be mention again directly.

#### Lectures in Jena.

For a correct representation of the relation into which Hegel entered with Schelling as a Dozent, it will be expedient to state what lectures Schelling gave while Hegel taught together with him in Jena. The essential difference of the two philosophers, which runs through their whole striving, through their whole activity as writers, emerges characteristically in this: that Schelling develops more critically general, *principial* foundations, Hegel on the other hand more the elaboration of philosophy in the form of a cycle of *sciences*. For the sake of more exact characterization we shall also be unable to avoid citing the Latin expressions of their own in which absolute idealism proclaimed itself at that time. Schelling’s announcement in the lecture catalogue read in the winter of 1801: [Latin] In private lectures

[p. 160]

he will deliver from his own books the system of philosophy as a whole; having prefaced an introduction in which he will dispute about the *Idea* and the ends of true philosophy, he will also prepare an entrance for those who are only now approaching the study of philosophy. He will also institute a disputatorium, the plan of which he will indicate at greater length elsewhere. — In the summer of 1802: [Latin] Publicly he will deliver the principles of rightly conducting *academic studies*; privately, if other circumstances permit, he will also expound the system of philosophy as a whole. These were the well-known lectures on the method of academic study, which appeared later in print. — In the winter of 1802: [Latin] Privately 1) he will deliver the whole plan of speculative philosophy from that outline of his system which is inserted in the book: *Neue Zeitschrift für speculative Physik* [New Journal for Speculative Physics], Parts I, II; 2) he will deliver the philosophy of art, or *Aesthetics*, by that plan and method which he followed in the construction of philosophy as a whole, and which he will set forth at greater length elsewhere. — In the summer of 1803: [Latin] He will continue his public lectures on the plan of rightly conducting academic study at the beginning of the semester and bring them to an end. — For the winter of 1803: [Latin] Returning from his journey, he will announce his lectures. But he gave no further lectures in Jena, entering instead into Bavarian service.

Schelling’s delivery is said to have been captivating at that time. With personal confidence he combined rhetorical ease. Besides, his hearers were enthralled by the nimbus of a revolutionary in philosophy, which Schelling always knew how to spread over his public appearance. Against his brilliantly negligent, loftily indefinite manner (e.g. in the announcements cited: [Latin] he will set forth the plan at greater length *elsewhere*; if other *circumstances* permit, etc.) the plain manner of Hegel made a marked contrast. His exposition was that of a man who, abstracting wholly from himself, directed only to the matter, indeed by no means lacks the telling expression, but does lack the oratorical fullness which wins the hearer also externally, through the flow of diction, through the sonorous tone of the voice, through the liveliness of gesture. He gave on the average one private lecture course at the price of three Laubthalers, and besides a public lecture course, both usually four hours weekly.

In the winter of 1801, on his first appearance, he announced as

[p. 161]

a private lecture course: *Logic* and *Metaphysics*, in the afternoons from 3–4 o’clock, and had in it 11 hearers, among whom a brother of *Schelling’s*, *Troxler* and *Abeken* are recorded. — [Latin] Free of charge he will treat an *introduction* to philosophy and will conduct a philosophical disputatorium *jointly* with the most excellent Schelling. Nothing, however, seems to have come of this undertaking, any more than of the summer lectures of 1802, a time in which his literary labors claimed him wholly. — In the winter of 1802 he again announced *Logic* and *Metaphysics*, and indeed: [Latin] following the book to appear at the approaching fair. How far this was already possible for him, we know from his Frankfurt period, and, given our knowledge of that, it will not surprise us either that he wanted to lecture on *natural right* from dictations. — In the summer of 1803 he repeated this and wished besides to present the *whole* philosophy, referring once more to a compendium which he would publish with Cotta: [Latin] an outline of philosophy as a whole from the compendium to appear in the current summer (Tübingen, Cotta). — In the winter of 1803 he repeated this attempt from dictations under the title: *System of Speculative Philosophy*, and gave as particular parts of it: [Latin] a) Logic and Metaphysics, *or transcendental idealism*; b) philosophy of nature; c) of mind. — In the summer of 1804 he seems, perhaps for lack of hearers, not to have lectured. — In the winter of 1804 he repeated the presentation of the *whole system of philosophy* [Latin] from dictations: the whole science of philosophy, i.e. *speculative* philosophy (logic and metaphysics), of nature and of mind. The number of his hearers, among whom now also *Bachmann*, rose now to 30 and thereafter maintained itself between 20 and 30. — In the summer of 1805 he repeated, alongside *natural right*, this same lecture course, [Latin] from the book to appear during the summer. But the book again did not appear. — In the winter of 1805 he lectured for the first time on the *History of Philosophy*; besides this, *Realphilosophie* ([Latin] the philosophy of nature and of mind); finally, for the first time and never again, *pure mathematics* ([Latin] pure mathematics, and indeed arithmetic from the book: *Stahl’s*, professor in Jena, *Anfangsgründe der reinen Arithmetik* [Elements of Pure Arithmetic], 2nd ed.; geometry from the book: *Lorenz*, etc.). This lecture course actually came about, and Hegel’s successor in

[p. 162]

Berlin, *Gabler*, took part in it with much satisfaction. — In the summer of 1806 he again lectured on philosophy of nature and of spirit, but besides this on speculative philosophy, in which for the first time he presented the *Phenomenology* and the *Logic*, which he also announced again for the winter of 1806.

Since the summer of 1805 a Bremer by the name of *Suthmeier*, the Oldenburger von *Bommel*, the Hollander van *Ghert*, *Gabler* and the highly promising Thuringian *Zellmann*, who unfortunately died so soon afterwards, had formed the core of Hegel’s audience. As a curiosity it may still be mentioned that even in the last semester a modern Greek, Georg *Rhetorides* of Constantinople, attended Hegel.

#### Critical Journal of Philosophy, 1802–1803.

Hegel regarded himself at that time as essentially in agreement with Schelling. The latter seems to have held the same view with regard to Hegel. They therefore united to publish a journal. Schelling, however, took only a slight part in it and at the same time brought out his new *Journal for Speculative Physics*, so that the former journal appears almost wholly as Hegel’s work. To be sure, they did not sign their names to the individual essays, and thereby have given occasion for dispute over the authenticity of them; at that time, however, they probably wished to express with this peculiarity only the fervor with which they were resolved to represent the same cause. Schelling himself (vol.
