I, part 1, p. 124) called Hegel “a downright categorical man, who cannot bear the great fuss made over philosophy and just so straight out has an appetite even without that.” — The fair report of the *Stuttgart Allgemeine Zeitung* had, on the occasion of Hegel’s work on Fichte and Schelling, spread the news that “Schelling has *fetched* himself a vigorous champion from his native land and *through* him *makes known* to the astonished public that Fichte too stands far beneath his views.” Against such an insinuation Hegel, loc. cit., p. 120, found himself obliged, in order to preserve his independence, to say that with all circumlocutions and mitigations he could express nothing else than that

[p. 163]

the author of that report is a *liar*, “for which I declare him with these clear words.”

Hegel opened the journal with an introduction on the *essence of philosophical criticism* in general and its relation to the present state of philosophy in particular. — He combated therein the delusion of those who fix *different philosophies* alongside one another and forget that philosophy is only *One*. He combated the *craving for originality* of thinking, the shallowing of speculation by *false popularizing*, and justified philosophy when, in order to secure its determinacy as *appearing*, it throws the nullities of non-philosophy, which make the pretension of insinuating themselves to the public instead of it, back into their nothing. He concluded, p. XXIII: “If a multitude wanted to save itself from the danger of the struggle and of the manifestation of its inner nothingness by declaring the others merely a party, it would by that very fact have recognized these as something, and have denied itself that universality for which what is actually a party must be not a party but rather nothing at all, and thereby have avowed itself as a party, i.e. as nothing for true philosophy.”

Before we go through in detail the individual essays which Hegel supplied, we must pause for a moment to bring him before our minds in his peculiarity as a critic. Criticism, namely, is to relate the Idea that is in and for itself to the expression which it has received in a determinate, *singular* presentation. It is thereby compelled to compare such a work also with the standpoint which the consciousness of spirit has already attained concerning the Idea in general. Every criticism which fixes only one of these moments is one-sided. If only the singularity of a work is considered, there arises the *report* of its content, perhaps with the addition of a few glosses on the good or bad style, on this or that inaccuracy. — But if a work is taken only as one coordinated with similar works, according to the moment of particularity, there arises the *relation of rank*. Since every comparative can in turn be turned into a positive, the diplomatizing literary-historical manner indulges itself especially in this classifying of the

[p. 164]

authors. — If, finally, the individual work, without any regard to the culture of the time at hand, is at once related directly to the Idea as such, thus if the moment of universality is fixed, then the wrong will ensue of overlooking the *historical mediation*, from whose coherence the producing subject cannot after all tear himself absolutely loose, and of unconditionally either exalting or rejecting a work from this summit as the most faithful copy of the Idea. — True criticism demands the interpenetration of all these moments. It must not merely *say* that something is good or bad. It must develop an apodictic judgment that a work, *as such*, deserves this or that predicate. It must possess just as much the Concept of the Idea that is in and for itself as the Concept of the shape of the same that has already become past. In the Concept of the Idea it has at the same time the measure for progress into the future. It must therefore become a *productive reproduction*, which does not impose praise or blame on the work from without, but lets it *characterize itself*.

Hegel understood such characterization excellently, as Goethe too acknowledges in his correspondence with *Zelter*. In the energy with which, in his own words, he knew how “to place himself within the circle of the opponent,” in order to refute him through himself and not to attack him and be in the right where he simply is not, he was able to present the foreign view with the greatest vividness *positively*, a gift which, as already remarked once, became fateful for him insofar as cursory readers have often overlooked what in Hegel is merely the exposition of what is being judged and what is his own opinion. In this he had at his command many gifts which, to be sure, do not affect the *substantive punctum saliens* [salient point] and are more of a secondary nature, but without which criticism will not have its intended effect on the age. Hegel, namely, was all his life, so far as this was possible, well informed about the *statistics of literature*. He did not possess that self-adoring loftiness which holds it beneath its dignity to take notice of anything other than itself. Without knowledge of the so-called “circumstances and conditions,” in the critical treatment of literary phenomena it will easily be lacking in tact

[p. 165]

Besides this, however, Hegel had a sinewy wit, which appeared now as naive irony, now as cutting satire, now as absolute humor, in manifold turns, in an inexhaustibility of new and telling images. Never, however, did his superiority seduce him to a summary condemnation wholesale, to a neglect of the factual proof of his assertions. Down into his late age he observed exactness in citing and did not grudge the trouble of giving, as a guarantee for the reader, even the *page number*. Citing passages by itself, to be sure, makes a criticism so little a thorough one that it even serves to conceal its lack of thoroughness, because it gives the appearance that the critic has read the book. About nothing is complaint rightly made so much as about passages torn out of their context. Something quite different it is, however, when the critic has made himself master of the sense of the whole and then understands how to cite the telling passages.

First Hegel supplied in the *Journal*, I, 1, pp. 91–115, a little skirmish: “How *Common Sense* Takes Philosophy, Presented in the Works of Herr *Krug*.” — This review depicted the conduct of the abstract understanding in a concrete example. It also made Krug’s demand upon speculation, to deduce for him his *writing pen*, deservedly ridiculous, and thereby confirmed in Krug, because in fact he wrote still more than he thought, for life an insuperable grudge against the so-called philosophy of identity.

In the second number followed: “The Relation of *Skepticism* to Philosophy, Exposition of Its Different Modifications and Comparison of the Newest with the Ancient.” The newest was at that time that of Schulze, who, since he had caused such a stir with his *Aenesidemus*, had come forward with a thick, two-volume *critique of theoretical philosophy*. Hegel, who, like *Herbart*, had devoted a thorough study to *Sextus Empiricus*, showed the Schulzean wretchedness of perverting the *impartiality* of truth into the indifference of *partylessness*, and, in order to prepare no fate for itself, of wanting to have no determinate philosophy either. P. 3: “Upon political apragmosyne [abstention from public affairs], at the time when disturbances broke out in the state, the Athenian

[p. 166]

lawgiver had set death upon it; *philosophical apragmosyne*, not to take sides for itself but to be resolved beforehand to submit to whatever might be crowned by fate with victory and universality, is for itself afflicted with the death of speculative reason.” Hegel demonstrated convincingly that *genuine skepticism* constitutes a *moment* of every true philosophy, because such a philosophy is precisely neither dogmatism nor skepticism. P. 20: “This skepticism, which appears in its *pure explicit* shape in the *Parmenides*, is to be found *implicit* in every genuine philosophical system, for it is the free side of every philosophy. If in any proposition which expresses a cognition of reason, what is reflected in it, the Concepts contained in it, is isolated, and the manner in which they are connected is considered, it must show itself that these Concepts are at the same time sublated, or are united in such a way that they contradict one another; otherwise it would be no rational but an understanding-proposition.” P. 50: “Apart from the skepticism, however, which is one with philosophy, the skepticism separated from it can be a twofold one, either that it is not directed against reason, or that it is directed against it.” — With comprehensive learning Hegel developed that the *ancient* skepticism was far removed from the mental reservation of the *modern* kind, of holding sensory objectivity to be true, that it rather included within itself the doubt about the certainty of the categories with which it combated the dogmatic systems. Lastly Hegel chastised Schulze’s barbarous contempt for great natural gifts, which likewise stems from the bad empirical psychology that makes the soul, as it were, into a sack in which fancy, understanding and reason are merely to be found side by side. The effect of this understanding, as it resounds with its befogging, narcotic, oppressive tone here through four alphabets, is, he said, as if one were walking through a field of blooming henbane, whose stupefying fragrances no effort can withstand, and where one is stirred by no enlivening ray, not even in the form of a presentiment.

This treatise, which reached into the innermost of philosophy, was followed on pp. 75–112 by a lighter one: “*Rückert* and *Weiß*, or

[p. 167]

the Philosophy for which no Thinking and Knowing is Needed.” Hegel set here an example of the presumption, from which the suffering in the domain of the age stems, *of wanting nonetheless to have a philosophy without any philosophy*, in that the multitude is condemned to want it without being able to want it. Hegel passed here from his usual gravity to playful wit, to cheerful irony; where he could manage with pocket-pistol shots, he threw no bombs.

The first essay of the third number: “On the Relation of the *Philosophy of Nature to Philosophy in General*” fused the Schellingian tone with his own in a certain intentionality, because Hegel therein spoke for Schelling and himself at the same time, as indeed many interpolations and extensions may derive from the former himself. But after Schelling had already conducted his justification himself against the Jena *Literary Gazette*, against Eschenmeyer and against more trifling attacks and misunderstandings, it was more natural that Hegel, as a knight of speculation, entered the lists. The introduction of the essay was important only temporarily and not without sophistry. Hegel sought to apply the designation *philosophy of nature* to the whole of philosophy, of which *speculative physics or the theory of nature* is only a part, which one often confuses with it. All the more important and rich in content was the treatment of the following three particular points:

1) That up to now it has been a matter of keeping the I *outside the Absolute*. This expression of the philosophy of reflection of subjectivity, especially in its apex as Fichtean dogmatism, can count as the concentrated summation of the necessity that the Absolute be posited not only in the I, but that also the I be posited in the Absolute, i.e. that the infinite form be determined only as a *moment* of the Absolute, not as the Absolute itself. The cognizing subject is not to have the thing-in-itself over against it as an unknowable beyond, but to comprehend the Absolute as reality and, in the identity of the Concept with it, to distinguish itself from it. Dogmatism had always made the demand to have the Absolute *outside itself*; *absolute idealism*, on the contrary, recognizes neither in the I nor in nature a limit.

[p. 168]

2) “Because we,” said Hegel in his own and Schelling’s name, “do not even recognize as philosophy *a philosophy that is not already religion in its principle*, we reject a cognition of the Absolute which emerges from philosophy only as a *result*, which thinks God not in himself but in an empirical relation. For the very reason that for us the *spirit of ethical life and of philosophy* is *one and the same*, we reject a doctrine according to which the intellectual, like nature, is only a means of ethical life, and for that very reason would have to be in itself stripped of the inner essence of ethical life.” Hegel declared that religion without *historical* relation is unthinkable, that, as opposition in the form of appearance, only *paganism* and *Christianity* are possible, the former as an elevation of finitude to infinity, the latter as a becoming-finite of the infinite, as the becoming-man of God, but that a *unity of this double form* is necessary, whose *first appearance* is celebrated *in the form of speculation*, which proclaims the *absolute gospel*, inasmuch as Christianity is indeed the *way* to consummation, but not the *consummation* itself. Hegel therefore determined paganism as the *deification of nature*, whereas Christianity, through nature as the infinite *body of God*, beholds right into the innermost and the spirit *of God*. There reigns the cheerfulness of immediate *being-reconciled*, here the *pain of becoming-reconciled*; there the *symbol* rules, here *mysticism*, of which even Protestantism has not been able to rid itself. The task of the world is the union of the depth of Christian reconciliation with the beauty of the Greek world.

3) The polemic stirred up by *Reinhold*, *Bardili*, *Köppen*, *E. von Weiller*, *Salat* and others had accused the philosophy of nature also of *unethicality*, in that it perverted speculative physics into *naturalism*, the I of transcendental idealism into *egoism*, into solipsism. Against this Hegel directed the objection that narrow minds, in murky sentimentality, with a marrowless and powerless talk of morality from which all Idea of God had been removed, had first displaced religion and now sought to displace philosophy as well. But “from true ethical energy there must spring a philosophy that is wholly from

[p. 169]

pure reason and only in Ideas; that pushing forward of ethical life is, however, directed against reason and speculation. Ethical life in principle is the liberation of the soul from the foreign and material, elevation to being determined by pure reason without other admixture. The same purification of the soul is the *condition* for philosophy.” The loftily poetic conclusion of the treatise describes the wandering of the self-purifying soul to Eleusis and recalls Hegel’s elegy to Hölderlin.

The first number of the second volume of the *Journal*, 1802, pp. 1 to 188, gave a treatise: “*Faith and Knowledge, or the Philosophy of Reflection of Subjectivity in the Completeness* of Its Forms as Kantian, Jacobian and Fichtean Philosophy.” Hegel determined the relation of these in connection with the great form of the world spirit which had recognized itself therein, with the principle of the North, of *Protestantism*, in which beauty and truth present themselves in feelings and dispositions, in love and understanding. The *Kantian* philosophy holds, according to Hegel, to the *objectivity of the Concept*, even if this should happen in the end only in the form of postulating. The *Jacobian*, on the contrary, absorbs the Absolute wholly into the inwardness of the subject and volatilizes all shaping of consciousness into the longing for the infinite. The *Fichtean*, finally, *unites* the striving for objective determination of the Concept with the yearning of individuality. The critical reproduction of these three philosophies everywhere fused the apprehension of the characteristic universality with the freshness of the most immediate vividness, which knew how to take up the originality of their form precisely in its most decisive turns and thereby to set forth the *diremption* of reflection with itself. If we consider the splendor in which Jacobi then stood, Hegel’s courage too is to be acknowledged, with which he uncovered its shadow sides and ruthlessly opposed the unprincipled chatter of his kindred spirits in philosophy, Herder’s too. On the record he proved the sourness and injustice of Jacobi’s judgment of others. Relentlessly he pursued the *wanting-to-hold-fast of the finite*, the contamination of the elevation to the Absolute by the constant reflecting on itself even in the act of elevating. In the

[p. 170]

philosophy as in religion, he demanded with penetrating earnestness, *the subject is to give itself up*. P. 123: “The whole sphere of finitude, of self-being-something, of sensuousness, sinks in the true thinking and beholding of the eternal, which here becomes one; all the gnats of subjectivity burn up in this consuming fire, and even the *consciousness of this giving-up* and annihilating is annihilated; even among religious acts, in which faith is feeling and beholding, there are more or less pure and objective ones; as in song consciousness and subjectivity melt more into the objective harmony than they sublate themselves in silent prayer.”

Hegel wanted religion in its independence to be organized as a *community*, in which not the representing virtuosity of the priest, but, as in an objective work of art, *the spirit of God itself in all members of the totality* is to stir. In the preface to his work on the *Difference* Hegel had acknowledged the great significance which *Schleiermacher’s* immortal *Speeches on Religion* had for the age. But he saw in them at the same time the highest potentiation of the religious subjectivity, longing only for God, not sinking into him to absolute enjoyment, and the contradiction of this with the essence of religion, which frees the subject from reflection on itself. It is essential to adduce here the main passage of his critique of Schleiermacher, p. 135, because the later struggle of Hegel and his school with the Schleiermacherian theology relates to it as notes to the text. “In these speeches nature (in distinction, namely, from Jacobi’s ‘faith in the sensuous,’ beyond which Schleiermacher went) is annihilated as a collection of finite actualities and acknowledged as universe, whereby longing is brought back from its fleeing out beyond actuality toward an eternal beyond, the partition between the subject or cognizing and the absolute unattainable object is torn down, pain is reconciled in enjoyment, the endless striving, however, satisfied in beholding. But since the individual thereby casts its subjectivity from itself and the dogmatism of longing dissolves its opposite into idealism, this subject-objectivity of the intuition of the universe is to remain *nonetheless once more something particular*

[p. 171]

and *subjective*; the virtuosity of the religious artist is to be allowed to intermingle its subjectivity into the *tragic seriousness of religion* and, instead of veiling individuality either beneath the body of an objective presentation of great shapes and of their movement among one another, but of the movement of the universe in them, — as in the triumphant church of nature genius built in epics and tragedies; or, instead of taking from lyrical expression its subjective element by its being at the same time present in memory and appearing as universal speech, this subjective element is to constitute, in the presentation of *one’s own* intuition of the universe, as in the production of it in others, the essential vitality and truth, art without a work of art is to perennate, and the freedom of the highest intuition is to subsist in singularity and in the having of something particular for oneself. If the *priest* can only be an instrument and servant belonging to the community, who *sacrifices* himself to it and to himself, in order to do the limiting and objective element of religious intuition, and to whom all power and strength can accrue from the mature community only as to a *representative*, then it, *presenting itself as immature*, is to have the purpose and intention of letting the inner element of intuition be effected in itself by him as a virtuoso of edification and enthusiasm. To a subjective peculiarity of intuition (*idiot* a person is called, insofar as peculiarity is in him), instead of extirpating it and at least not acknowledging it, so much is to be conceded that it may *form the principle of a community of its own*.” Thus, Hegel thinks, there results, instead of an organic constitution, “instead of the true virtuosity of receiving its objectivity and reality in laws and in the body of a people and of a universal church,” not even a longing, but only a *seeking of longing*.

The metaphysics of subjectivity had, according to Hegel, in those three philosophies, by the positing-as-absolute of the individual moments of the totality and the working out of each of them into a system, brought the *formation* itself to an end and thereby immediately posited the external possibility that, p. 186: “The true philosophy, arising out of this formation and annihilating the absoluteness of its finitudes, with its whole wealth subjected to the totality

[p. 172]

presents itself at the same time as *completed appearance*, for as the consummation of fine art is through the consummation of mechanical skill, so too the rich appearance of philosophy is brought to an end through the *completeness of formation*, and this completeness has been run through.” This sublime consciousness of the world-historical significance and consummation of philosophy Hegel applied also to *religion*, inasmuch as philosophy too has to take up into itself the infinity of opposition, the *negation*, but *only as a moment*; a reflection which is filled with the whole force of his speculative-religious enthusiasm: “The pure Concept, however, or infinity as the abyss of nothingness in which all being sinks, must designate the infinite pain — which before was only *historical in formation* and as the feeling on which the religion of the new age rests, the feeling: *God himself is dead*, that which was, as it were, only empirically expressed in Pascal’s words: [French] nature is such that it *marks everywhere a lost God*, both in man and outside man — purely as a moment, but also not as more than a moment, of the highest Idea, and so give to what was perhaps also either the moral precept of a sacrifice of empirical being or the concept of formal abstraction a *philosophical* existence, and thus give to philosophy the Idea of *absolute freedom*, and with it absolute suffering or the *speculative Good Friday*, which otherwise was historical, and restore it itself in the whole truth and harshness of its godlessness, out of which *harshness* alone, because the cheerful, ungrounded and more individual character of dogmatic philosophies, as of nature-religions, must vanish, the highest totality in its whole seriousness and from its deepest ground, at once all-embracing, and in the most cheerful shape of its freedom can — and must — arise.”

In the two other — and last — numbers of the second volume Hegel wrote a great treatise: “On the Scientific Ways of Treating Natural Law, Its Place in Practical Philosophy, and Its Relation to the Positive Sciences of Right.” Here it was that he first let his own system emerge more definitely. First he gave a critique of the *empirical* and *formal* way of treating natural law and came

[p. 173]

above all to the Fichtean. Not only did he show the inadequacy of those methods, but also developed positively that Concept in which he sublated the dualism of the practical philosophy of *Kant* and *Fichte*. He recognized in these philosophies the greatness of wanting to carry through *morality* as the absolute principle, but that this had at the same time been impossible because of the finitude of subjectivity, and that therefore alongside morality *legality* had stepped. With this, the external compulsion of coercion had now returned in the place of the free self-determination of morality, and the *Fichtean state*, far from becoming the organic totality of the spirit of a people, had degenerated into the worst *police state*, in which the all-supervising Ephorate annihilates the freedom of private life and consequently makes just as little a truly public life possible. For the first time Hegel now introduced publicly the expression *ethical life* for that form of practical spirit in which, as in the *objective freedom of a people*, legality and morality are posited as immediately *identical*. In the *doctrine of right* of Kant and Fichte the *law* was satisfied, in the *doctrine of virtue* of Kant, in the doctrine of morals of Fichte, the *autonomy* of the moral subject. The *unity* was lacking. The *commonwealth* with its institutions remained for the moral subject a foreign world, in which it *took part*, with greater or lesser restriction, only, with which it was not in and for itself *identical* as with body of its body and spirit of its spirit. This duality Hegel broke through, aroused by the deepest instinct of the modern world, which advances irresistibly toward such a goal. The growing-together of the Hellenic citizen with his commonwealth, the immediate interest in its fate as in his own, the πολιτεύειν [civic life], the ancient self-consciousness of the sanctity of custom, the law become *individual pathos*, hovered before him as an ideal which in the modern states, to be sure, could realize the depth of unity only through the *monarchical* form of them.

This treatise with its ethical loftiness would be worthy of a lawgiver! If Hegel later in his *Outline of the Philosophy of Right and of the Political Sciences* developed all these Concepts more separately, with greater detail, in a more artful sys-

[p. 174]

tem, one must nonetheless maintain that the originality of its conception in this more youthful shape is more beautiful, fresher, indeed in part truer.

Often the Hegelian philosophy has been reproached with a *disparagement of the moral*. Now Hegel did indeed declare himself emphatically against seeing in morality the *only* absolute form of practical spirit simply, but from the *contempt* of it, as it became the fashion in the Romantic school and among some philosophers belonging to it, he constantly kept far away. The necessity of morality he constantly acknowledged. The name *Ethics* seemed to him most fitting for it, which he designated as a natural description of the virtues. Since science had already done justice to the Concept of the subjective side of practical spirit through *Kant* and *Fichte*, it had to turn to the objective. In *Herbart* too we see, some years later, how in practical philosophy he could no longer remain at the atomistics of the doctrine of virtues and duties, but pressed for an exhaustive unity of the practical *Ideas*. Hegel conceived the *individuality* of the individual as a *natural* limit, from which he must be freed through education. It is often overlooked, however, that the particularity of the individual counted for him as a negative only with regard to the truth of *cognizing* and *willing*. By no means was he an enemy of individuality where it is justified, where, as in everything aesthetic, it becomes a necessary condition. On the contrary, he acknowledged it here most definitely and defended it most vividly, as we have, e.g., just now seen him take the great natural gifts under his protection against Schulze’s flat contempt for them. That with the word individuality he did not want to see consecrated the pretension of arbitrary exceptions to the ethical law, not every abnormality of chance, not every caprice of feeble subjects — will anyone hold that against him? *Education* he always held very high and conceived it as the subduing of the accidental particularity of the individual, as discipline, as the *becoming* of ethical life. The positive side of it consisted for him in this, that the individual, nursed at the breast of universal ethical life, lives in its intuition at first as a foreign being, comprehends it more and more, and

[p. 175]

so passes over into the universal spirit. “The ethical life of the individual is a pulse-beat of the whole system and is itself the whole system.”

Of the *etymological* justification of the word *Sittlichkeit* [ethical life], for expressing in it equally the systematic character of the objective necessity that has become habit for a people and the unity of the individual’s subjective will with that necessity, Hegel had the most complete awareness, and he declared himself on it in vol. II, issue 3, p. 1: “We note here also an indication of language, which, though otherwise rejected, is perfectly justified by what precedes: that it lies, namely, in the nature of universal ethical life to be a universal, or *Sitten* [customs]; that the Greek word which designates ethical life, and the German, therefore express this its nature admirably; but that the most recent systems of ethical life, since they make a being-for-itself and singularity their principle, cannot fail to exhibit their relation to these words; and this inner indication proves itself so powerful that those systems, in order to designate *their* subject matter, could not misuse those words for it, but adopted the word *morality*, which to be sure points in the same direction by its origin, but, because it is more a word only just *made*, does not resist its bad meaning so immediately.”

The derivation of so-called natural right from individual subordinate powers, which one raised to validity for the whole, to the dignity of a principle, Hegel combated with sharp dialectic, in particular the *confusion* of the points of view in the *theory of punishment*. He wished punishment to be regarded as springing from freedom, as bearing respect and fear for it within itself, without regard to utility as without lust for revenge, and as, even while coercing, remaining within freedom. P. 60: “If, on the other hand, punishment is represented *only as coercion*, it is posited merely as a determinacy and as something utterly finite, as nothing that bears rationality within itself, and falls wholly under the common concept of a determinate thing against another, or of a commodity for which something else, namely the crime, is to be bought. The state, as judicial power, keeps a *market with determinacies that are called crimes*, and that are for sale to it

[p. 176]

against other determinacies, and the *code of laws* is the *price list*.”

No less did Hegel already at that time turn against the application of the category of the *contract*, which fits only *relative relations*, to absolute spheres. Issue 3, p. 19: “The form of such a subordinate relation as the contract is has forced its way into the absolute *majesty* of ethical totality, and, e.g., for *monarchy* the absolute universality of the center and the oneness of the particular in it has been conceived now according to the contract of authorization, as a relation of a supreme official of the state to the abstraction of the state, now according to the relation of the common contract in general, as a matter of two determinate parties, each of which needs the other, as a relation of reciprocal performance, and through such relations, which lie wholly within the finite, the Idea and absolute majesty have immediately been annihilated; just as it is also self-contradictory when, for the *law of nations*, the relation of absolutely self-subsistent and free peoples, which are ethical totalities, is to be determined according to the relation of civil contract, which goes immediately to the singularity and dependence of *subjects*.”

To cite this political view of Hegel here is necessary also for the reason that his *opponents*, when he began to become more influential, were so ready to have it believed that only Napoleon’s Caesarism, later his call to Berlin, had produced this conviction in him.

In the Concept of the organization of the *constitution* of the state Hegel was at that time, as we already know, strongly Platonizing. He distinguished, properly, only *two estates*, of which the one, the real, was to have as its content the sphere of *finite* interests, the other, the ideal, the interests of the *state as such*, the *producing of freedom in and for itself*. To be sure Hegel still distinguished a *third estate*, which, p. 71, “in the rawness of its non-formative labor has to do only with the earth as element, and whose labor has the whole of need before it in the immediate object without intermediate links, and so is itself a solid totality and indifference like an element.” But he held also that this estate must in part be reckoned with that of the non-free,

[p. 177]

whose labor goes to singularity and does not include the danger of death, but in part would help to increase the estate of the free in *mass*, in that it preserves its bodies and its spirit in the possibility of formal, absolute ethical life, of bravery and a violent death. In that Hegel joined Plato and Aristotle in holding that only the determinate *separation* of singularity and universality within the ethical totality could preserve ethical life itself, he admitted that the modern principle of *equality* had produced a *commingling* of both estates, and with it a sinking of the whole into the pettiness and listless indifference of *private life*, out of which one could emerge only through a *conscious recognition of the opposition and of the right of both estates*, through the constitution of a self-conscious *sacrifice* of what is, for ethical life, in and for itself inorganic. — To this separation he linked an intuition of history, carried out with splendid poetry, as a double process in which the *tragedy* of free self-sacrifice for the whole is identical with the *comedy* of the necessary fate of the finite, of going under; from which sublime comedy the other, common one must remain distinguished, whose entanglements are without fate and without true struggle, because in them the ethical nature is itself caught in the finite.

Not to the formlessness of *cosmopolitanism*, nor to the emptiness of the *rights of mankind* and the equal emptiness of a *state of nations* and a world republic, can the *absolute shape* of ethical life flee, but only the *most beautiful shape* of the purest and freest *individuality* is it able to bring forth out of itself, in that it sets the finite over against itself objectively, sacrifices it with consciousness, and thereby wards off the fate of the same from its freedom. Here, for the first time publicly, Hegel pronounced most decisively, p. 87, his Concept of the Absolute as spirit, as the absolute subject, in which all oppositions are contained *potentia* and *actu* [in potentiality and in act]. He separated himself in substance from *Schelling* when he said, p. 88: “Therefore, if the Absolute is this, that it intuits itself, and indeed as *itself*, and that absolute intuition and this

[p. 178]

self-cognition, that infinite expansion and this infinite taking-back of it into itself, are absolutely one, then, if both are real as attributes, spirit *is higher than nature*; for if the latter is the absolute self-intuiting and the actuality of the infinitely differentiated mediation and unfolding, then spirit, which in the taking-back of the universe into itself is the intuiting of itself as itself, or absolute cognition, is both the totality of this multiplicity, thrown asunder, *over which it reaches*, and also the absolute ideality of it, in which it annihilates this asunderness, and is reflected into itself as the unmediated point of unity of the infinite Concept.”

#### Didactic Modification of the System.

In Jena Hegel had at first presented his system in the whole abruptness of its original conception, but within a few years he was able to gain sufficient experience that such a form was not suited to academic lecturing. He had to feel keenly the need of a more *popular* presentation. The gulf between the deep spirit which unfolded itself in that system with the boldest abstraction, and the consciousness which the student brought directly into the lecture, was too great. Hegel therefore now reworked the philosophy of *nature* and of *spirit* into more accessible presentations, in that he no longer let the dialectical element step forth so formalistically for itself, but rather fuse more with the subject matter. He abandoned the solemn ideality with which he had formerly accompanied the logical side of the presentation step by step, set the principal determinations more categorically, and in the execution strove for what might be called a *genre-pictorial* clarification, which often issued also in a critique of the age, not merely in scientific but also in political and religious respect. In the lecture announcements of the Jena catalogue Hegel said that his lecture would take place *ex dictatis* [from dictation]. Perhaps this is meant only to say that he would not lecture from a printed compendium, as was then still almost universally customary, but from his own notebooks; for of paragraphs and the like there is in the manuscripts of this period still extant no trace

[p. 179]

of it, and with their pithy, rough-draft style they would besides have been poorly enough suited to it.

Hegel saw himself compelled, in the *introductions*, to set forth in an appealing manner the need of philosophy, its absolute justification and its connection with life and the positive sciences. He had to devote a more detailed discussion to those *transitions* which are alien to ordinary consciousness. Although therefore the division of the whole into the *triad* of Idea, nature and spirit remained unshakably the same, he nevertheless now, out of pedagogical consideration, changed a good deal in particulars. And the division itself he treated without pedantry. He held fast to the matter, to be sure, but with the numbers he was not exact. Of such modifications the following is the most remarkable, as a division in a lecture of the *whole* system:

1) The Logic, or the science of the Idea as such;

2) the philosophy of nature, or the realization of the Idea, which first creates for itself its body in nature;

3) ethical nature as real spirit;

4) religion as the resumption of the whole into one, as the return to the first simplicity of the Idea.

With such greater freedom of general presentation the terminology, too, altered in particulars. To be sure, it always retained the striving for precision and clarity, but also tried out experimentally the different sides of a concept against one another; thus he called, e.g., the Logic also simply idealism, also merely speculative Idea, or speculative philosophy, and the like. Nor were *favorite turns of phrase* lacking, such as the often recurring *transparency* of cognition as the ether of spirit. *Favorite concepts* there were also for him, which he presented with peculiar energy and with that transcendent pathos which gripped even the resisting mightily. In particular there belonged here the portrayal, ever repeated with rapture, of *Greek mythology* and of the *ethical spirit of a people*, whose individuals indeed have a hard task at its work, but which itself, in its deep seriousness, is through the freedom of its doing a cheerful play. Then he was inexhaustible

[p. 180]

in new images, in ingenious expressions, in ever sharper determinations of concepts.

Thus he once spoke of *genius*, the *inventive* spirit, namely first with regard to art, but then also in the general sense: “*Mnemosyne*, or the absolute Muse, art, takes over the side of presenting the shapes of spirit externally, as intuitable, visible and audible. This Muse is itself the universally expressing consciousness of the people. The artwork of mythology propagates itself in living tradition. As the generations themselves grow on in the liberation of their consciousness, so it grows on and purifies and ripens itself. This artwork is the common good, as much as the work of all. Each generation hands it on, beautified, to the next, or has worked on the liberation of absolute consciousness. Those who are called *geniuses* have acquired some particular skill in which they make the universal shapes of the people into their work, as others make something else. What they produce is not their invention, but the invention of the *whole* people, or the *finding* that the people has found its essence. What belongs to the artist as *such* is his formal activity, his particular skill in this kind of presentation, and for this itself he has been educated in the universal skill. He is, as it were, one who is among workers who build a stone arch whose scaffolding is present invisibly as Idea. Each sets a stone in place. The artist, too, in just this way. It befalls him by chance to be the last; in that he sets in the stone, the arch bears itself. He sees, as he sets in this stone, that the whole is One arch, says so, and passes for the inventor. Or as with workers who dig for a spring, the one whom it befalls to take away the last layer of earth has the same labor as the others — and the spring leaps up for him. — It is the same with a *state revolution*. We can think of the people as buried beneath the earth, over which a lake lies. Each believes he is working only for himself and for the preservation of the whole, in that he takes a piece of stone for himself from above and uses it for himself and for the universal underground structure. The tension of the air, of the universal element, begins to change;

[p. 181]

it makes them craving for water. Uneasily they do not know what they lack, and to help themselves they dig ever higher, in the belief that they are improving their underground condition. The crust becomes transparent. One catches sight of it, cries: Water! tears away the last layer, and the lake plunges in and *drowns* them, in that it *waters* them. — Thus the artwork is the work of all. There is one who completes it, who brings it to the light of day, in that he works on the last part of it, and he is the favorite of Mnemosyne. — If in our times, to be sure, the living world does not form the artwork in itself, the artist must transpose his imagination into a past world; he must *dream* himself a world, but the character of dreaming or of non-living being, of past-ness, is absolutely imprinted on his work as well.”

Of Hegel’s general remarks in his introductions — on the deception of the individual in setting himself against the universal necessity, in taking his relation to it for something contingent and not seeing in it, again, the doing of necessity itself; — on the dissolution of the opposition between slumbering, instinctive consciousness and awakened, critical consciousness through the movement of the world itself, with whose objectivity genuine philosophy cannot find itself in contradiction; — on the independence of philosophy, which for its grounding needs as little any other science as any foreign tool, etc.; — of such pedagogical-propaedeutic presentations the lectures printed after Hegel’s death give a sufficient picture, and it is therefore superfluous to cite anything from them, however valuable some things of this kind appear through the completeness of their presentation.

But we cannot refrain from mentioning more specifically one of these introductions, that to the lecture on the *whole* system, because it contains a very decided *polemic* against the degenerations of the *Schelling*ian *philosophy of nature*, which were then beginning to inundate philosophical literature. Besides, it brings important remarks on *terminology* in general, namely on carrying it through, as far as possible, wholly in the *mother tongue*. Hegel speaks first of how we make the study of philosophy harder for ourselves partly in that we make demands upon it

[p. 182]

which are not to be made upon it; partly in that we frighten ourselves off by the representation of demands which philosophy is said to make on us and which are too hard to fulfill. In religion, it is said, the true is indeed supposed to present itself to us, but for our culture faith in general has passed away; reason has grown strong, and its demand is that we do not believe what the true is, but know it; that we do not merely have it for intuition, but comprehend it. The truth of his individuality, which prescribes to him exactly the course of his existence, the individual recognizes well enough, but the consciousness of universal life he expects from philosophy. Here the hope seems to be deceived, when instead of the fullness of life, concepts, and, held against the wealth of the immediate world, the poorest abstractions appeared. But the Concept is itself the *mediator between itself and life*, in that it teaches us to find life in itself, the Concept in life. Of this, to be sure, only science itself can convince.

“There is indeed a *murky* intermediate thing between *feeling* and *science*, a speculative feeling or the Idea, which cannot free itself from fantasy and feeling and yet also is no longer merely fantasy and feeling. I mean *mysticism*, or rather the *Oriental*, just as much as the *Jakob Böhmean* attempts to present the Idea. Orientalism is exalted above mere beauty or above restricted configuration. It is the infinite, the formless that it strives to grasp in the fantasy of its images, but, driven by the infinite always beyond the image, it always again sublates its image, and attempts itself in a new one, which it equally lets vanish again. It is therefore only a *splendid rhetoric*, which always confesses the *impotence of the means*, namely of *images*, to present the essence. — The newer mysticism is of a *more dismal* and more painful kind. It descends with common, sensuous representations into the depths of the essence and struggles to master it and to bring it before its consciousness. But in the form of common *sensuous* representation the essence cannot be grasped. In whatever representation it may be grasped, the representation is *inadequate*. It is only with force

[p. 183]

adapted to it and must be torn apart just as violently. There presents itself only the struggle of an inner something that ferments within itself and cannot bring itself forth to the light of day and to clarity, feels its incapacity painfully and rolls about in twitchings and convulsions which can come to no resolution.”

“The *clear* element is the universal, the *Concept*, which is just as deep as it is extended in its revelation that conceals nothing.”

“For the *fixing* of concepts a means is at hand which on the one hand fulfills its purpose, but can also become more dangerous than the evil of conceptlessness itself, namely *philosophical terminology*, the words constituted for this purpose from foreign languages, from Latin and Greek. I do not know what lies in this, that, e.g., the expression *quantitative difference* seems *firmer* than when we say: *difference of magnitude*. Properly it belongs to the highest culture of a people *to say everything* in its language. The concepts that we designate with foreign words seem to us themselves to have *something foreign* about them, not to belong to us peculiarly and immediately. The elements of things seem to us not to be the *present* concepts with which we always deal and have to do and in which the commonest man expresses himself. *Being, non-being, one, many, quality, magnitude*, etc. are such pure essences with which we constantly *keep house* in ordinary life. Such forms seem to us, as it were, not worthy enough to grasp in them this high *beyond*, the Idea, the Absolute, and something foreign to be more suitable, because the Absolute, the *suprasensuous* world itself, is foreign to this common daily life in which we use those concepts. But what is *in itself* must not have this foreignness *for us*, and we must not give it this *foreign look through a foreign terminology*, but hold ourselves convinced that spirit itself *lives everywhere* and that it expresses its forms in our immediate vernacular. They occur in ordinary speech *mixed and enveloped in sheer concretes*, e.g., the tree is green. Tree and green are what rules representation. In ordinary life we do not reflect on the Is, do not lift out this *pure being*, do not make

[p. 184]

it our object, as philosophy does. But this *being* is present here and expressed. It is, to be sure, necessary to have recourse to foreign terminology when we do not find in our language the determinate designations of concepts. It is not usual for us to do violence to language and to form *new forms out of old words*. Our thinking is not yet properly at home in our language, does not command the language as it should, but we harbor here a blind reverence for what has been handed down.”

“This foreign terminology, which is used partly uselessly, partly in a perverse manner, becomes however a great evil in that it makes the concepts, which are in themselves *movement*, into something *firm* and *fixed*, whereby the spirit and the life of the matter itself vanishes and philosophy sinks down to an *empty formalism*, which nothing is easier than to acquire and to prattle in; to those, however, who do not understand this terminology it seems very hard and deep. Precisely this is the *seductive* aspect of such a terminology, that it is in fact very easy to master it. It is all the easier to speak in it because I can allow myself all possible senselessnesses and trivialities if I am not ashamed before myself to speak in a language to people who do not understand it.”

“You must therefore, in the study of philosophy, not take such terminology for the essence and have no reverence for it. It seemed very hard ten to twenty years ago, too, to work oneself into the Kantian terminology and to use the terminology of synthetic judgments *a priori*, synthetic unity of apperception, transcendent and transcendental, etc.; but such a flood rushes by as quickly as it came. Many take possession of this language, and the secret comes to light *that very common thoughts hide behind such a scarecrow of expression*. — I remark this chiefly on account of the present look of philosophy, namely of the philosophy of nature, with which much mischief is done in the *Schelling*ian terminology. *Schelling* has, to be sure, expressed a good sense and philosophical thoughts in these forms, but this in that he himself showed himself *in fact free* of this

[p. 185]

terminology, for in almost every succeeding presentation of his philosophy he has used a *new* one. But as this philosophy is now spoken of in the public, it is really only the *superficiality* of the thoughts that hides beneath it. Into the depth of this philosophy, as we see it in so many writings, I cannot introduce you, for it has no depth, and I say this so that you may *not let yourselves be overawed*, as if behind these thundering, hundredweight-heavy words a sense must necessarily lurk. — What alone can interest is to look at the amazement into which it puts the ignorant multitude. In fact, however, this present formalism can be taught in half an hour. Say, e.g., instead of: it is something *long*, it goes in the *length*, and this length is *magnetism*; instead of *broad*, it goes in the *breadth* and is *electricity*; instead of *thick*, bodily, it goes in the *third dimension*; instead of *pointed*, it is the *pole of contraction*; instead of: the fish is long, it stands under the *schema* of magnetism, etc., etc.”

After Hegel had expressed himself on this at still greater length, he declared that the emptiness of this presumption forced him to it, and continued:

“I tell you in advance that in the philosophical *system which I present* you will find nothing of this flood of formalism. When I speak of this terminology and its use, as it now rages, as I have spoken, I know very well, moreover, how to distinguish *Schelling’s ideas* from the use *that his pupils make of them*, and I honor *Schelling*’s genuine merit for philosophy just as much as I despise this formalism; and because I know *Schelling*’s philosophy, I know that its genuine Idea, which it awakens anew in our time, is independent of this formalism.”

In such introductions Hegel combated, then, not Schelling himself, to whom he rather held fast indestructibly his original friendship, but the devastation of thinking which his pupils had begun to wreak. He also turned against the *Romanticism* which was then seeking to establish itself in philosophy. He protested most emphatically against the notion

[p. 186]

as if philosophy by its nature existed only for *some chosen few*, as if it demanded a special *genius*, a peculiar organization. “It is briefly to be remarked that philosophy, as the *science of reason*, through the universal manner of its being, is by its very nature for *all*. Not all attain to it, but of that there is no question, any more than *all human beings* attain to being *princes*. *What is revolting*, that some human beings stand above others, lies solely in this, when it is asserted that, differing by nature, they were *beings of another kind*.”

With incorruptible sobriety he analyzed *enthusiasm*, which always makes assurances of *revelations of the Eternal and Holy*, but does not attain to determinacy of cognition. He rejected the appeal of such shallow enthusiasts to *Plato* with Plato himself, because Plato ascribes prophesying not to the sober-minded, but only to the sleeper, when the power of consciousness is fettered; or to the sick or to the enthusiast, who, however, does not know himself and whose words, uttered in divine frenzy, must first be interpreted by the sober-minded according to reason, as to what they mean; as indeed the Demiurges, too, mindful of the father’s commission to make the mortal race as good as possible, *in order that our bad side might be touched by something of the truth*, placed prophecy *in the liver*. — Hegel compared this heated being, which wishes to replace the lack of sense by vehement assurances of the deep significance of the words, with the flatness of the newer dramas, in which even the “outspread, flailing arms, the red countenance, the eyes staring into the blue, the twitching lips and chewing jaws” are supposed first to give emphasis to the *lean* word.

Since he presented philosophy in the element of free universality according to logical method, as the inner organization of reason; since he demanded of the philosophizing subject that by abstraction from all given determinacy it make itself into self-conscious emptiness, over against which the whole fullness of the universe at first stands; and since he also treated the *philosophy of nature* logically, he had in Jena from the side of Romanticism soon the

[p. 187]

prejudice against him that he failed to appreciate the *poetry of nature*. Because he went beyond Schelling in that he did not merely coordinate spirit with nature but rather posited it as the *absolutely universal*, he went on, to be sure, to speak for the *liberation* of spirit from bondage to nature, even of contempt for nature. But this *ethical* consideration is quite another than the scientific. Hegel said: “Indeed the individual spirit, as energy of character, can hold firm to itself and assert its individuality, let nature be what it will. His negative attitude toward nature, though it be something other than he, despises its power, and in this contempt he holds it remote from himself and himself free of it. And indeed the individual is great and free only to the extent that his contempt for nature is great.”

Already at that time encountering the prejudice against him, as if he meant this contempt not practically but theoretically, he declared, with an allusion to a passage in *Goethe*’s *Faust*: “Nature is a whole for the living and, if one will so name it, *poetic* intuition. Before it the manifold of nature passes by as a series of living beings and recognizes in the bush, in the air and in the water the brothers. For this poetic intuition of nature it is indeed an absolute whole, a living thing. But this livingness is in its configuration an individuality. Inwardly the living are the same, but they have an absolute externality of being toward one another. Each is for itself and their movement toward one another an absolutely contingent one. In this isolated livingness each steps against the other with equal right, and, in that the infinity of their singularity is their *destruction*, this itself is not justified in itself. Their intuition is a *sensitive pain*. The *ethical* individualities step out of nature. It is only an accessory being, a tool of theirs. Where it is *more*, where the ethical beings strive, as it were, to keep themselves low enough in their enjoyment — *idyll poetry* — there they themselves fall into that abasing sensitivity and into a restrictedness of life whose paltriness can interest only formally as presentation in general.”

[p. 188]

Carefully Hegel took account of all the misunderstandings that must arise from the speculative presentation, insofar as it contradicts the common-sense understanding, which indeed itself calls itself the rational one. *Nature*, e.g., is in the *totality of spirit* the *negative* moment, which is opposed both to the simple Idea and to spirit that is for itself. Nature is the otherness of the Idea, which is sublated by spirit through its freedom in it — by spirit, for which, as thinking itself, the Idea is in its ideality. This negativity has now been represented also by the *Gnostics* and by *Schelling* as a *going-forth* of the Idea out of itself, as a *falling-away* of it from itself. Now Hegel reminds us that in these representations one *can* make present to oneself what is right, if one *already knows* it at all; but that it is unskillful always to want already to possess the matter in these forms, because they express only an *occurrence*, an *indifference of relation*, while the Concept posits negation essentially only as a *moment*, but as *absolutely necessary*.

Thus Hegel sought to overcome as far as possible the primitive heaviness of his system, to round everything off more systematically within itself by simplification, and to make it more comprehensible through examples, indeed through references to the immediate present. Least of all was the fundamental shape of the *Logic* and *Metaphysics* altered. In the introductions, however, one sees the greatest effort to justify the undertaking in general. It was just odd, he thought, that the newer philosophy *despised* the Logic and that nonetheless the same was universally *demanded* of it, while those, to be sure, who still paid homage to the *old forms* of Logic were *just as little satisfied*, so that both parties had created no new Logic. “*Fichte*’s *Science of Knowledge* as well as *Schelling*’s *Transcendental Idealism* are both nothing other than attempts to present Logic or speculative philosophy purely for itself. *Fichte*, as is well known, proceeded from the great but *one-sided* standpoint of consciousness, of the I, of the subject, and this made a complete and free execution impossible for him. *Schelling* proceeds indeed from just this, indeed sublates this standpoint in the sequel, but, as far as speculative philosophy itself is concerned, in these attempts *consciousness seems not to have been present*

[p. 189]

that nothing else was at stake. *Schelling* in his later views of philosophy sets up the speculative Idea in general, *without development* in itself, and passes at once to the shape which it has as philosophy of nature.”

In one of the introductions to what he called speculative philosophy *sensu strictiori* [in the strictest sense], he first pointed out to philosophy in general the time of its appearing, namely that it appears in the *epochs of transition* in which the old ethical form of peoples is completely overcome by a new one, which indeed happens sooner among smaller peoples than among larger ones, especially the colossi of modern times. Here Hegel dwells for a moment on the portrayal of the *great man*, in which he himself was so great, and leads then, as became *stereotyped* with him, back through Alexander the Great by way of Aristotle as his educator into philosophy. “These sober-minded natures do nothing but pronounce the word, and the peoples will cling to them. The great spirits who are able to do this must, in order to be able to do it, be *purified* of all peculiarities of the preceding shape. If they wish to accomplish the work in *its* totality, they must also have grasped it in *their* whole totality. They perhaps seize it only at one end and bring it forward. But because nature wills the *whole*, it thrusts them from the *point* on which they had placed themselves, and sets other men there; and these too are one-sided, a sequence of individuals, until the whole work is accomplished. But if it is to have been the deed of *One* man, he must have recognized the whole and thereby have purified himself of all restrictedness. The terrors of the objective world, as well as all fetters of ethical actuality, and with these also all *foreign* supports for standing in this world, as well as all confidence in a firm bond in it, must have fallen from him, i.e., he must have been educated in the school of philosophy. From this he can raise up the still slumbering shape of a new ethical world to awakening and boldly enter into struggle with the old forms of the world spirit, as Jacob wrestled with God; sure that the forms which he *can* destroy are an obsolete shape and the new one is a new divine revelation.

[p. 190]

He can regard the whole existing human world as a material which he appropriates to himself, and out of which his great individuality forms its body; a material which, itself living, forms the more sluggish or more lively organs of this great figure. Thus, to cite the greatest example of the human being who wove his individuality into fate and gave it a new freedom, Alexander the Macedonian passed from the school of Aristotle to the conquest of the world.”

“In the lecture course on Logic and Metaphysics which I offer to present to you this winter, I shall take a propaedeutic regard to this character of philosophizing and begin from the *finite*, in order to go from it, namely insofar as it is previously annihilated, to the *infinite*. The lecture of philosophy formerly had the form of Logic and Metaphysics. I follow this form in my lecture, not so much because it has a long authority for itself as with regard to its serviceability.”

“Philosophy, namely, as the science of truth, has the infinite cognition or the cognition of the Absolute as its object. Over against this cognition, however, or *speculation*, stands finite cognition or *reflection*; not as if both were absolutely opposed to one another; finite cognition abstracts only from the absolute identity of that which in rational cognition is related to one another or posited as equal — and by this abstraction alone does it become finite cognition. In rational cognition or philosophy the *forms* of finite cognition are indeed also posited, but at the same time their finitude is annihilated by the fact that they are *related* to one another. — The object of a true Logic will therefore be this: to set up the *forms of finitude*, and indeed not gathered empirically, but as they emerge from reason, though, robbed of reason by the understanding, appear only in their finitude. — Then the strivings of the understanding must be presented, how it *imitates* reason in the production of an identity, but can bring forth only a *formal identity*. In order, however, to recognize the understanding as imitating, we must at the same time always hold up to it the archetype which it copies, the

[p. 191]

expression of reason itself. — Finally we must sublate the forms of the understanding themselves through *reason*, show what meaning and what content these finite forms of cognition have for reason. The cognition of reason, insofar as it belongs to Logic, will thus be only a *negative* cognition of it.”

“I believe that from this speculative side alone Logic can serve as an introduction to philosophy, insofar as it fixes the finite forms as such, in that it completely cognizes reflection and clears it out of the way, so that it lays no hindrances in the way of speculation and at the same time familiarizes it with the *image of the Absolute*, held up, as it were, in a *reflection*. According to this general concept of Logic I shall proceed in the following order, whose necessity will emerge in the science itself:

I. The *universal forms or laws or categories* of finitude, in objective as well as subjective respect, or abstracted from that: whether these forms are subjective or objective, to present them according to their finitude, as reflexes of the Absolute.

II. The *subjective* forms of finitude or finite thinking, the *understanding*, to consider in just the same way and in its stage-sequence through concepts, judgments and syllogisms. With regard to the latter it is to be remarked that, though the rational form expresses itself more clearly in them, and they are therefore also usually ascribed to reason as the rational thinking of reason, we take them here only as formal inferring, as belonging to the understanding.

III. Finally, the *sublation* of this finite cognition by *reason* must be shown. Here is the place to state the *speculative significance of the syllogisms*, in general the foundations of a scientific cognition. — To this *pure* Logic an *applied* one is customarily appended, but partly what is customarily treated here is too universal and trivial for it to deserve any attention; partly what of it is properly scientific will occur in the third part, rational cognition.”

“From this third part of Logic, namely the negative or annihilating side of reason, the transition to proper

[p. 192]

philosophy or to *Metaphysics* will be made. We have here above all to construct completely for ourselves the *principle* of all philosophy. From true cognition of it the conviction will emerge that *at all times* there has been only *One* and the same philosophy. I promise hereby, then, not only nothing new, but am concerned in my philosophical endeavors precisely with restoring the oldest of the old and freeing it from the misunderstanding in which the more recent times of unphilosophy have buried it. It is not long ago that even the mere concept of philosophy was invented anew in Germany, but its invention, too, is new only for our times.”

In the lecture on Metaphysics Hegel strove preeminently to develop ever more clearly the transition to Realphilosophie. He did this at that time in a wholly speculative-theological bearing. Even in the summer of 1806, in the lecture on Realphilosophie, he called the simple Idea the *night of the divine mystery*, from whose untroubled density nature and conscious spirit would be released to subsist for themselves. With his then still half theosophical conception of the absolute Idea Hegel would satisfy far more those who at present do not know how they are to unite in his work the *Concept of the absolute Idea* with the Concept of *absolute spirit* and the finitude of human self-consciousness with the *absoluteness of spirit*. He also called the immanent dialectic of the Absolute the *course of life of God*. The main point was that he dissolved the deadness of the concept of God as a fixed point, just as of fixed attributes, entirely. “The intuiting of God as of himself is the eternal *creating of the universe*, in which each point for itself, as relative totality, has its peculiar course of life. This diverging of the real, this being-posited of the manifold is the *goodness of God*. But the *singular* sublates itself also as singular and shows thereby its universality. This act is the *cognizing of intuiting*, the absolute turning point, the *justice of God*, which as absolute power turns out the negative side in the real and thereby converts it from its being-for-itself into the unity with everything else

[p. 193]

Insofar as God, as the *eternally self-identical* self-consciousness, is not immediately submerged in this double process of the universe as at once *resting and becoming*, insofar, then, as his re-creating of the created absolutely retains the character of ideality, he is the *eternal wisdom and blessedness*. Every relative totality, even the least, is blessed in its course of life. To this blessed being-within-itself relativity indeed does damage; but the *judgment* into which the singular is led cannot, precisely because the singular is restricted, judge abstractly. *God*, as judge of the world, must, because he is the absolutely universal totality, *break his heart*. He *cannot judge* it, he can *only have mercy* on it.” — Hegel also still liked, as was already indicated above at the first exposition of Metaphysics, to present the creation of the universe as the *pronouncing* of the absolute *Word* and the return of the universe into itself as the *perceiving* of it, so that nature and history became the *medium*, vanishing itself as otherness, between speaking and perceiving.

The *philosophy of nature* underwent more alterations than the Logic and Metaphysics. The division into *solar* and *terrestrial system* was abandoned and the whole divided into three parts, of which the first was called *Mechanics*, the second *Configuration* and *Chemism*, the third *Organics*. The details on this division *Michelet* has given in his edition of the second part of Hegel’s *Encyclopedia*, Preface, p. XX ff. Also the greater part of the Additions made there is borrowed from the notebook written from 1801 to 1805. The report communicated there, p. XVIII, that Hegel lectured on the philosophy of nature only once in Jena, is an error.

But Hegel made still greater alterations, particularly in the presentation, with the philosophy of *spirit*. As we have seen, he delivered it in Jena originally almost only within the restriction of the philosophy of right and of the state, to which core the remaining moments attached themselves only as an *extension of the beginning and end* and first began to expand more in the *Phenomenology*. Thus we find, e.g., that Hegel now in the introduction parallels fantasy with *free will*; with the tool

[p. 194]

*memory*; with cunning the *sign*, and so, insofar, begins to add the psychological incidentally to the practical. If bravery was formerly his goddess, now it is cunning. “Honor cunning, he cries, for it is the *femininity of the will*, the irony of brute power. Where this is not able to get at it with force *from the front*, there cunning with its wit seizes it *from the sides*. Cunning is not low slyness. It unites itself with the highest openness. The great conduct consists precisely in compelling others, through one’s own openness, to lay themselves open as they are in themselves; without all artifice of an intrigue they are outwitted by such openness.”

The Platonic element, which was so strongly accentuated in the first conception of Hegel’s Ethics, receded now more. The general division remained still fairly the same. In particulars, however, much inorganic accumulation of the material prevailed, which was often only roughly subsumed under a general category. First the I as theoretical and practical in general was treated, and the treatment concluded again with the family. — Secondly, *actual* spirit was developed as the *process of recognition*, and under this category property, contract, the law having force in making wills, in taxation and administration of justice. — Thirdly, under the title *Constitution*, first the Concept of the *state* in general as an *individuum* constituted by the will under a determinate natural conditionedness, and then the system of *estates* as of the spirit articulating itself, was gone through. The estates were here distinguished only into two, into the class of the *lower*, which have to do with the singularization of life, with its necessity, and into the class of the *public*, which have to do with the creation of the universal as universal. — Hegel thus began now from below, not, as earlier, from above. Each of these estates he characterized according to its dispositions and distinguished the former within itself: a) as the half-subterranean *peasant estate*; b) as the *trades* and c) *commercial estate*. In the estate of publicness, however, he distinguished: a) the *mechanical* man of business, or the official, who is essentially police; b) the *political* man of business or government official and c) the *soldier estate*. Of

[p. 195]

a national armament, and of a peasant estate befriending general culture through the mediation of school instruction, Hegel still had no inkling. Morality with its virtues he distributed throughout the whole. The conclusion he no longer made merely with the elevation of ethical life to religion through the preparation and overcoming of a fate, but he posited *art, religion and science* as the particular stages of the absolute self-liberation of spirit.

For the Concept of the *origin of the state* we already meet the so often repeated polemic of Hegel against the theory which lays a *contract* at its foundation. Ironically he remarked that the defenders of this theory always let the minority submit most obediently to the majority, and seem to forget how the individual, too, has the positive right to *run away*. Never, he said, had states been founded in this way, but only through the sublime *power* of great men. “Not through physical strength, for many are stronger than one, but the great man has something in his features which the others may call their lord. They obey him against their will. *Their immediate will is his will, but their conscious one is different.* The great man has the former on his side and they *must*, whether they will or not. This is the advantage of the great man, to know and to pronounce the absolute will. His power is therefore *necessary and just*, insofar as it constitutes and maintains the state as *this actual individuum*.” — From this standpoint Hegel seeks to make Machiavelli’s politics comprehensible, because, against the rawness with which in his fatherland every leader, every nobleman, every city maintained itself as sovereign, only tyrannical rule and the terror of death could have extirpated the immediate validity of the individual and have established the state. With deep bitterness Hegel added to this justification the remark: “The *Germans* have most abhorred such teachings, and *Machiavellism* expresses to them the most evil, because they just lie sick of the same disease and have died of it. Indifference of subjects toward their princes and of the latter, in turn, toward being princes, i.e., toward conducting themselves as princes

[p. 196]

makes that tyranny superfluous — for the willfulness of the princes has thereby become impotent.”

Further on Hegel speaks of the different forms of the state, depicts the beautiful life of the Hellenic democracy, but shows its defect in this, that the individual had simply renounced particularity, without knowing it as such, as *this* self, as the essence. “The higher diremption is thus that *each goes back completely into himself*, knows his *self* as such as the *essence*, to which willfulness comes, to be, separated from the existing universal, nevertheless absolute, to possess in his knowing his *Absolute immediately*. As an individual he lets the universal go free, has complete self-subsistence, gives up his actuality as outwardly existing and counts for himself only in his *knowing*. The free universal is the *point of individuality*. As free from knowing, as not constituted by it, as extreme of government it is an immediate, a *natural* one: it is the *hereditary monarch*. Here is the *firm, immediate knot of the whole*. The whole, however, is the middle of all, the free spirit, which, free from the completely fixed extremes, bears itself, independent of the knowing of the individuals as of the constitution of the regent. The spiritual bond is *public opinion* as the true legislative corps, as the immediate declaration of the general will, which lives in the execution of all commands. It is *now differently* governed and legislated in states whose constitution is formally still the same, and this changes gradually. — This hereditary monarchy is the *higher* principle of the more recent time, which the ancients did not know. According to it the *many* of the multitude stand over against the *One* individuum, the monarch; those are the fluid movement, this *alone* is the immediate, natural, i.e., *hither has nature fled*. It is the last remnant of it as *positive*; all other families are to be abandoned. Every other individuum counts *only as alienated, formed*, as that to which it has *made* itself; this alone is *born* to it, immediate will, absolute resolve to be: *We command*. The commonwealth, however, as a whole, is neither on the Many as individuals nor on the

[p. 197]

One bound, but is the indestructible body, closed within itself, bearing it and itself.”

In the presentation of the Concept of art, religion and science Hegel made the advance of freeing *art* from its connection with *mythology*, without however failing to recognize in natural religion the necessity of perfecting itself and its form through art. The advance from its Concept to that of religion he therefore already at that time made in such a way that he understood by the latter only the *revealed* as the *absolute*, which turns out *the depth of the essence, that God is the self-certain self of all*. Art generates the world as spiritual for intuition. “It is the Indian Bacchus, who is not the clear, self-knowing, but the *inspired* spirit, who envelops himself in sensation and image, beneath which the fearful is concealed.” In the *absolute religion* as the truth of art the non-correspondence of content and form is sublated, and spirit has the true representation of itself, to know itself as the absolute self, as universal actuality. Everyone in it raises himself to this intuition: “his nature, his station, sinks like a dream image, like an island appearing as a little cloud of vapor on the edge of the horizon. In his knowing himself as spirit he is equal to the prince, and counts before God as much as any other. He is the alienation of his *whole* sphere, of his whole existing world, not that alienation which is only form, *formation* of existence.”

The relation of absolute religion to the state Hegel now posited in this, that it, as *congregation* through the devotion of faith, which satisfies itself within itself, in its representations, is one side of *abstraction from the present*, while the state, however, has actuality only in present existence. Not inwardness, not reconciliation as a merely represented one, but the reality existing as deed, as manifest determinacy, counts for it. It must therefore subject the *Church*, insofar as it needs immediate actuality, under its *dominion*.
