State and Church are reconciled only when religion in the state has the actuality conformable to its Concept of spirit, and the state in the representation of faith about spirit finds the true concept of its existence, overarching all insecurity

[p. 198]

and instability of the individual as *absolute guarantee*, as absolute justification of world-fate. Without this *reconciliation* both are *imperfect*. “The state which subjects itself to the church is either abandoned and lost to the *fanaticism* which sacrifices the present to a represented beyond, — or the *rule of priests* would be introduced, which demands not the alienation of doing and existence in and for itself, but of the will as such in existence as such, and indeed not against the universal being-recognized but against an individual will as such.”

Religion is now indeed the thinking spirit, which however does not *think itself* and therefore still stands in inequality with itself. To sublate this is the deed of science. *Philosophy* sets up again the *immediacy*, the unity of the singular and universal, which exists in itself in the I, through the *mediation of the Concept*. —

#### Hegel’s Wastebook, 1803–1806.

With Schelling Hegel was together at Jena for two and a half years, from the beginning of the year 1801 to the summer of 1803. During the latter Schelling entered Bavarian service and went first to Würzburg. The *Critical Journal of Philosophy* had already ceased at the beginning of this year. Perhaps it was the relative solitude in speculative respect into which Hegel saw himself placed by Schelling’s departure that drove him to throw together, pell-mell, reflections of all kinds, excerpts from philosophical and natural-scientific books, notes of physical experiments he had made himself, in a small folio which he kept for this purpose.

The experiments concerned chiefly *Goethe’s theory of colors*. Hegel once drew himself, badly enough, lying on the floor and observing the play of colors of the light at his window.

The excerpts from *philosophical* writings concern chiefly *Eschenmayer*, *Köppen*, *Wagner*, but especially *Kayßler*; those from natural-scientific ones go to all domains of

[p. 199]

nature. They devote the greatest attention to the greatest as to the smallest things — the orbits of the planets, feldspar, galvanism, syphilis, peat, and so on — and are taken just as much from German as from French and English books. In these extracts Hegel behaved quite passively; to those of speculative content he sometimes added approving or contesting glosses. A multitude of remarks concerned the method of philosophy and the general ferment of the age.

If one takes these *critical Xenia*, hurled down in a momentary impulse, in the most uneven handwriting but with the whole power of original genius, by themselves, their beauty surprises. Between the rock-blocks of learned excerpts and book titles they spring up as thoughtful flowers. Each of these fragments is a small whole and, in its contingency, of the greatest determinacy of expression. Not only in content but also in turns of phrase many of them, though clarified to a higher perfection, passed over into the *Preface to the Phenomenology*. In them Hegel freed himself more and more from the *one-sided mysticism* into which the Schellingian philosophy was beginning to degenerate. The loose arbitrariness, the half-poetry with which people deceived themselves about their own ignorance, the naiveté bordering on impudence with which imitators of Schelling’s genius assured themselves of an absolute knowing of the Absolute while they served up senseless gibberish, found in him an incorruptible judge. His polemic against the *formlessness* of Jakob Böhme in particular was renewed. The content of this theosophist he knew how to value, but the persistence in his manner, the imitation of it, he condemned unconditionally as *barbarism*. When the counter-position to the culture he had received from the school of the Enlightenment arose in him, he himself passed through a mystical phase and tormented himself with such attempts as the triangle of triangles. Now he set against the dark splendid language of mysticism the clarity of cognition and the intelligibility of expression. The continual study of the ancients did not let him lapse into romantic slovenliness and wildness. Besides the philosophers he studied incessantly Homer and the tragedians, and the fragments contain many keen-eared remarks on *prosody and metrics*.

[p. 200]

A principal moment of these language-bold, spirit-spiced paradoxes is the thought that *philosophy* is now expected to replace the *loss of religion*. Speculation is supposed to afford not so much the thorough development of the Idea in the element of comprehending thinking as rather the edifying enjoyment of a half-sensuous, poetic intuition of the Absolute. Very remarkable appears herein a kind of phenomenological *Faustiad*, the depiction of which often has a certain gigantic singularity. It is not a consideration of Goethe’s *Faust* or of any other determinate poem, but a *Promethean confession*, which attached itself to the figure of Faust, “who found the bounds of humanity too narrow and with wild power thrust against them, to push them beyond actuality,” only as to the universal type of the Germans for the desperate struggle of the individual with the necessity that once and for all exists. What of torment cuts through the heart at not being able to grasp this world, into which we have come without being asked whether we wished to have a part in it; what of deception is devised to conceal from us the horrifying contradictions of existence; what of impotence of a faith there is whose God no longer performs miracles for the wretched one who calls upon him; what of self-accusation about the abuse of our freedom shoots through us with consuming remorse; what of wish pervades us to flee from entanglement with history aside into a fateless idyll — all this is expressed by Hegel with great but strange energy, until at last he finds in the thought of *resignation* that *the deception is a necessary moment of appearance* and that we can find the source of happiness only *in ourselves*. — Such a confession was not possible for him without himself being shaken to the depths by these feelings.

Finally we see in these fragments the *patriotic* struggle of Hegel too shining through in not a few utterances. Germany had gone politically to ruin. Over this political nullity Hegel raged with tremendous force, which now poured itself out in warm sympathy, now in piquant irony, but for the most part expressed itself in a wistfully sarcastic tone. All stirrings of the age reverberated in him; to everything he was attentive

[p. 201]

and even the smallest change of manners did not escape him in its significance for the whole. Never has the actuality of the rational been taken by Hegel as a stale contentment with everything existing just as it is; rather, the ought-to-be of reason against the ought-not-to-be of unreason in what exists he emphasized just as strongly, and in this polemic he was capable of the most sublime anger.

#### The Phenomenological Crisis of the System, up to 1807.

From the lecture catalogue of Jena we have seen above that Hegel for several years announced the appearance of a textbook with Cotta. It did not appear, however. In part external hindrances may have been to blame, but it is no less probable that the constant *reshaping* in which Hegel was engaged with the detail of his philosophy also caused him an inner hesitation. So it was for him indisputably also a great advance when in 1805–1806 he lectured for the first time on the *history of philosophy*. His great familiarity with it he had, no doubt, already sufficiently demonstrated in the treatises for the *Critical Journal*; but now he became aware, most determinately, of the *unity* of philosophy in all philosophies in the *continuum* of one great connection; now he worked through *world history* for the first time from the standpoint of absolute knowing; now he saw himself for the first time in his *historical* relation to the precedents that had gone before him. Publicly he expressed himself about *Schelling*, acknowledged his great merit with warmth, but criticized the merely *quantitative* distinction of the opposition of the Absolute in itself, as a bare indifference in which everything is only a predominance of the one or the other factor, no true distinction; he criticized the lack of *dialectic*, which in Plato, with whom Schelling moreover has much in common, is everywhere associated with the content, etc. These lectures on the history of philosophy Hegel did not essentially alter in his later lectures, as they are also printed, but only carried out more richly. That judgment about Schelling became stereotyped with him. It stands him in good stead,

[p. 202]

to have said the same, openly and publicly, already in Schelling’s lifetime at the beginning of this century. At the close of the lecture he then spoke those words, which have for some time since become so famous and so often used as a motto: “A *new epoch* has arisen in the world. It seems that the world spirit has now succeeded in shedding all alien, objective essence and in finally grasping itself as absolute spirit, and in generating from itself what becomes objective to it and retaining it, with calm, in its power. The struggle of finite self-consciousness with the absolute self-consciousness, which appeared to the former as outside it, ceases, etc.”

Yet another deed was necessary to let him become aware of his whole independence. This deed was the *Phenomenology of Spirit*. The whole of modern philosophy had sprung from the *Concept of self-consciousness*. With presaging confidence *Schelling* had added the objective idealism to the subjective, but the unity of subject and object was with him only a presupposition. Hegel sublated the Concept of self-consciousness not merely in that of the Absolute or of reason in general, but in the Concept of *spirit*, as a mere *moment*. But no less did he do this with the Concept of *substantiality*, which in various forms had recurred as the barrier of self-consciousness. He therefore developed, first in his *introductions* to the Logic and Metaphysics, the Concept of *experience*, which *consciousness makes of itself*. From this there arose, since 1804, the plan for the *Phenomenology*, into which he, however, deposited the soundest results of his studies of that time generally. Into this ideal history of consciousness he drew in the end all the content of empirically historical consciousness. *Fichte*, in the *Science of Knowledge*, had held only to the determinations of the theoretical, practical and teleological-aesthetic moment of consciousness. *Schelling* in the epochs of it, as he expounded them in the *System of Transcendental Idealism*, went already into the concrete content, into the Concept of nature, of history and of art.

This direction Hegel exhausted. He presented consciousness

[p. 203]

1) as it determines itself *for itself*; 2) how this determinacy relates to the essence of consciousness *that is in itself*; and 3) the necessity of *sublating* each of its shapes again and again, through the consequence of its development, until it has reached that one in which, as infinite reflection into itself, as being-for-itself, it *coincides* absolutely with the infinity of the content as its essence that is in itself, and consequently can make no further progress beyond itself. Hence the development of consciousness is *self-development*. Between its initial being-for-itself and the end — already immanent in this beginning and filled with the riches of the natural and spiritual universe — there exists from the outset an identical relation. This *compels* consciousness to leave each of its shapes, insofar as the same is still one-sided. Each has, so long as it is brought forth by consciousness as its essence, a relatively absolute worth. The absolutely absolute form, however, is reached only with the absoluteness of the content, when the movement, without possibility of a progress, can be only a recollective return into the series of shapes run through, or the free presentation of the Absolute in its unity with self-consciousness. The cognition of this process therefore constantly beholds not only the self-consciousness fixed on a determinate stage of its self-generation, the *particular* shape of knowing, but also the *lack* posited therein, which compels consciousness to look down on this particular shape in itself as one that *has been* and to make the attempt of another. Hereby there arises a *double semblance*. First, there seems to consciousness to be the *absolutely true* the determinacy within which it is just then dwelling, in which it finds its essence epoch by epoch. Second, however, in that through the all-sided unfolding of this standpoint its limitedness becomes manifest, while in its perishing the emergence of a new shape is at the same time contained, which consciousness once more greets with the trust of its reconciliation, the vanishing shape of consciousness is hereby posited as one that is indeed not absolutely, but yet *relatively untrue*. It seemed to be the absolutely true, but did not prove itself as such. Yet not only is the *semblance necessary*, but there exists also a free

[p. 204]

*limit* of progress, which cannot again be reduced to the significance of a surmountable *barrier*, and which shape of self-consciousness consequently cannot again pass over into another, higher one as its truth. This shape is that of *absolute knowing*, because in it the appearance of spirit becomes *equal* to its essence and, retrospectively, the *traversing* of the manifold shapes, which this last standpoint empirically sends ahead of itself as the condition of its existence, is justified. For in that progression of stages spirit did indeed make in each moment the experience of its actual essence. Each is in itself *totality*, and the going beyond the individual has not merely a negative but rather just as much a positive character. Hence Hegel called this science the *Phenomenology of Spirit*. The name *Phenomenology* was already native in German philosophy. *Kant*, in the *Metaphysical Foundations of Natural Science*, had so named the doctrine of the semblance that occurs in the apprehension of material motion through the senses. *Lambert* had earlier already, in his *New Organon*, so named the doctrine of semblance in cognizing and willing generally. The *first part* of the System of Science the Phenomenology of Spirit was, according to Hegel, to constitute insofar as it enlightens consciousness about its own nature and depicts its further formation up to the stage on which it comprehends itself as the absolutely comprehending, i.e. on which the difference between itself as being-for-itself and the content objective to it as its essence has become a free unity determining itself in itself.

The main points of the treatise were therefore the Concept 1) of consciousness, 2) of spirit and 3) of absolute knowing as the self-consciousness of absolute spirit. A science of consciousness one had possessed already since *Fichte*, but the Concept of spirit, in which subjectivity as well as substantiality are posited only as moments, as well as the Concept of the absoluteness of knowing as the self-knowing of absolute spirit, was the new, infinite advance that Hegel made. In the detailed presentation which he gave there are admittedly a multitude of *accidental offshoots*, which have rather a contemporary-historical significance, as indeed Hegel himself in old age called the Phenomenology his *voyages of discovery*.

[p. 205]

Within the *complete* system of philosophy, as it begins out of itself and closes in itself, the Concept of consciousness must naturally occur as a *moment* of the whole. Here the *further* relation which Hegel made at that time, of presenting consciousness as that which cognizes itself in nature, in ethical life, culture, morality and religion, is not necessary, because this content here no longer appears as an *object* of consciousness, but in pure, immanently dialectical form. Within the total system, therefore, only the determinations of consciousness as such can be posited: consciousness, self-consciousness and reason as self-conscious, as rationality. If the task is set of educating a given consciousness up to the standpoint from which it can enter into philosophy, which only as system is truly philosophy, then the science of the experience of consciousness, or the Phenomenology of Spirit, has to undertake this propaedeutic business. *Schelling* has recommended the *history of philosophy* for this purpose. It contains, however, the difficulty that in it already all the problems of cognition occur, not merely the subjective side of cognition. In his Phenomenology of that time Hegel went through the whole *breadth* of the *concrete* content of consciousness and *mingled* therein the critique of the philosophy of the day with *a philosophy of world history*. We perceive quite determinate references to Kant, Fichte and Schelling and see the turning points of history also appear in ever new formations. Stoicism and skepticism, e.g., belong world-historically to the transition of spirit from Greekdom to Romandom. This transition occurs again, from another side, in the downfall of the world of beautiful ethical life into that of the legal condition. And again in the transition from art-religion to revealed religion. — In the unhappy consciousness, into which Hegel lets skepticism pass over, there is already depicted the romantic yearning and brokenness, which in the estrangement of spirit recurs once more as faith, further as beautiful-souledness, and finally as the transition from revealed religion to absolute knowing.

This extensive treatment of the Phenomenology distinguishes

[p. 206]

itself, then, from the brief treatment in Hegel’s *Encyclopedia* by the interweaving of everything knowable, which must as it were pass the test of being able to endure as an object of consciousness. But it does not follow from this, as has been asserted, that Hegel later *abandoned* the Phenomenology entirely and that his system has a *double* beginning, the *phenomenological* one of 1807 and the *logical* one of 1812. The duality of the beginning lies in the difference between the beginning that the *philosophizing subject* makes, which only approaches speculation and, as Hegel jestingly says, must first be stood on its *head*, and that beginning which the Idea makes in and for itself as self-development, and in which the objective Concept of beginning in general, i.e. the identity of being and nothing, must be contained. The *orientation* of the subject about itself, the grasping of its singularity in its universality, the comprehending of reason as the universal identity of the self and of the universe objective to it, must just as much be present as a necessary and organic member of the system itself, and is only taken out of it for the *formation* of the subject. If this were not the case, a part of philosophy would exist outside philosophy. The usual introduction-mischief would show itself, which gathers up from all sides, in an unorganic way, this and that Concept. The pedagogical moment Hegel also expressed in the Preface to the Phenomenology in this way, that the world spirit — under which name, however, he understood not God but humanity in its totality — is to be regarded as the *individual* which raises itself step by step, through the mediation of its history, to absolute knowing.

The Phenomenology is the absolute watershed not only of two philosophies, but at the same time of two different worldviews in general, a consciousness which Hegel himself pronounced so energetically, especially on solemn occasions, in closing speeches to his lectures, in inaugural addresses of his professorships and in prefaces. The spirit of humanity paused in this work for a moment to *render account* to itself of what it had become up to then for its Concept. It reviewed its whole past and set itself up in Hegel its philosophical Dante

[p. 207]

who led consciousness out of the Infernum of naturalness, through the Purgatorium of the human ethical deed, up to the Paradise of religious reconciliation and scientific freedom. Hegel overcame therein the tedium of history. The progress of the same into the infinite has, in spite of its contradictions, pains, tears and martyrs, only the significance of a cheerful further shaping, because humanity has become aware of the *principle* of history and with it has won the Concept of the process in which it stands. What of concrete material Hegel drew into his history is therefore also not so wholly accidental as it might seem. The shapes drawn by him — of the unhappy consciousness, of pleasure and necessity; of the law of the heart and of the madness of self-conceit; of freedom and its terror; of virtue and the way of the world, etc. — have also already gradually become important categories, ethical powers. Hegel’s great gift of presentation expressed these antinomies with a pregnancy by which they had to become naturalized in literature.

For the presentation of the Phenomenology is a genuine work of art. What its Preface said of the *Concept of method*, that it must let the content move itself, must let it show itself in its self-shaping, this the work itself has accomplished in the real dialectic of the shapes of consciousness. With the sharpest determination of expression there is at the same time combined a lofty poetry, which in original images embodies even the most difficult up to an, as it were, microscopic distinctness. So plastic, so beautiful, so rounded, so free of all foreign admixture, of all ephemeral consideration, Hegel himself never again produced anything. It lay in this aesthetic perfection that the concretely historical phenomena which Hegel visibly spread beneath his general presentations appeared nevertheless only as the *classical symbols* of the Concept of the matter and as an intensive heightening of the color of the diction. E.g., in the description of the *unhappy consciousness* the opposition of the changeable appearance and the unchangeable essence is given; the diremption of self-consciousness into the extreme of the relation to itself according to its earthly neediness and into the extreme of the relation to the unchangeable.

[p. 208]

By the renunciation of property, marriage and self-decision, self-consciousness seeks to extirpate its changeability and to bring itself into contact with the Eternal, etc. All these determinations have in Hegel indisputably the hierarchy of the Christian Middle Ages as their background, but at the same time this particular substratum is so worked away and the universal essentiality of the matter so brought out that one has thereby comprehended the inner driving force of *every* hierarchy, as the religion of fear, for the absolute misfortune of spirit.

Thus it was indisputably *Sophocles*, and in particular his *Antigone*, that hovered before Hegel for the incomparable depiction of the human and divine law distributed to *man* and *woman*, but at the same time the presentation of the essence of masculinity and femininity in general has succeeded in it in the most splendid way.

Some of the shapes seem to be merely a paradox. The individuality which realizes itself as rational not merely theoretically or practically, but is real in and for itself, appears first as the *spiritual animal kingdom* or *deception* and the *matter itself*. Now, judging by the catchwords employed, it has quite the appearance as if Hegel here were merely the rogue who satirizes the pomposity of German scholars. But if one looks more closely, one discovers a shape of consciousness which must occur everywhere that individuality deceives itself and others by claiming that what matters to it in its producing or criticizing is not the enjoyment of its individuality but solely the *matter itself*. It is evident how the conditionedness of production and criticism by individual limitation must lead to the deception of concealing the individual interest behind the firm of the matter itself.

One of Hegel’s most extraordinary depictions, full of new intuitions, was the Concept of the dissolution of *culture* and of its realm of actuality. Culture he characterized as the validation of knowing as knowing, as *judging*, whose worth depends neither on *birth*, nor on *wealth*, nor on the *standing* of the individual in society, as birth or wealth or both these powers mediate it for him. Culture interests rather *through itself*. In the struggle

[p. 209]

of those different powers, in their threat against one another, in the flattery of the subjugated, in the praise of the universal state power as the *selfless* middle of all on the one hand, as the single *self* whose name has no equal on the other, there develops *language* as the existence of spirit. It becomes the tearing *judging* in which all those moments that are supposed to count as essence and actual members of the whole dissolve, and which is just as much this self-dissolving play with itself. This judging and speaking is therefore at this stage the true and unconquerable, all-overpowering thing, the element about which alone in this real world it is *truly* a matter. Each part of it comes therein to this, that its spirit is expressed, or that with spirit it is spoken of and said of it what it is. The *honest* consciousness takes each moment as an abiding essentiality. It is uncultivated thoughtlessness not to know that it does just as much the perverted. The *torn* consciousness, on the other hand, is the consciousness of perversion, and indeed of *absolute perversion*. The Concept is the ruling thing in it, which brings together the thoughts that lie far apart from honesty, and whose language is therefore *witty*. “The content of the speech of spirit about and concerning itself is thus the perversion of all concepts and realities, the universal deception of itself and of others, and the *shamelessness* of stating this deception is for that very reason the greatest *truth*.” — In this depiction Hegel has now indisputably once more had in view a determinate shape of the historical spirit, namely the French one before the Revolution. *Goethe’s* translation of *Diderot’s* dialogue, *Rameau’s Nephew*, produced from the manuscript in 1804, was bound to supply him for this chapter, just in time, the last building stones. The characterization, e.g., of the *espèces*, i.e. of the wretchednesses that are good in their kind, would probably otherwise have remained unwritten. But here too one would go astray if one wished to restrict the significance of this painting merely to that epoch, or even to let oneself be guided by *Gervinus*, who in the last volume of his *German Literary History* sharply censures Goethe for having translated *Rameau’s Nephew*, because one learns to know such things better from the records of tribunals and madhouses. That

[p. 210]

witty language of the torn, all-perverting consciousness enters again as the center of interest *always and everywhere* where culture, as the estrangement of spirit from everything given, leads it to *absolute vanity*, further also to the recognition of the same, and from this still further to the Concept of true reality. From the ancient world and the dissolution of its culture we need only recall, e.g., *Lucian* and the letters of the younger *Pliny*, in order to have there too the proof of the existence of this wit, which knows its own perversity better and expresses it more determinately than the honest consciousness standing over against it is able to do.

Hegel did, to be sure, give some Concepts another turn, some expressions another sense, than is immediately presumed in them. The *beautiful* soul, e.g., which in the last decades of the previous century played so great a role and which in the confessions of such a one, that *Goethe* wove into his *Wilhelm Meister*, reached the perfection of its literary shape, was presented by Hegel as evil, because it, holding the determinacy of acting away from itself as a defilement by worldliness, and revering its inactivity as purity and beauty, i.e. is vain, and permits itself to exclude from communion with itself, and to censure as unclean, the agents who engage in the particularization of circumstances and in the guilt of their alteration. In the end, however, it must recognize this very flight of its from actuality, its dread of acting, as deed and guilt, and in its hardness, in separating itself from the agents and condemning the same as evil, confess itself as evil.

There must still be mentioned the transition which Hegel made from the Concept of religion to that of absolute knowing, and from this to that of its realization in systematic science. Hegel distinguished here natural religion, art-religion and *revealed* religion. In the latter it is namely manifest that the *absolute essence* is, according to its Concept, self-consciousness. It is therefore also, from the side of its appearance, empirically intuited as a single human being whose *sensuous existence*, however, must first be sublated through death into one that *has been*, before it, according to its universal significance, in recollection

[p. 211]

can be understood. For, appearing as this determinate individual, the absolute essence seems to have only humbled itself, and only in spirit, *rising again*, is it recognized by it that here too, so to speak, the master shows himself in limitation. Yet through this mediation there now mixes into the thinking of the absolute essence the sensuousness of representation, so that the appearance of the same, as immediate presence, belongs to *past* and *distance*. The inadequacy of this representation to the Concept of the Absolute as something without duration is, to be sure, taken back again by the opposed one, but the *faith of the community* still always passes only from one representation to another; the unity of the representations remains an inner, presupposed one.

According to the *content*, i.e. in knowing the Absolute and in it itself as spirit, self-consciousness is now perfected. It *knows the truth*. Yet the *form* of this knowing is still imperfect, and it is only the sublation of this imperfection that remains to be done. Knowing as absolute must posit the unity of content and form as self-producing, and comprehend what religion represents as the course of a contingent *occurrence* as the eternal process of the absolute essence. Hegel has shown in the Phenomenology constantly, now the externalization of substance into subject, now the externalization of the subject into substance, so that the truth is the unity of this double process, without which the Absolute would indeed be *lonely*. Spirit, without being for itself as spirit in spirits, would be spirit only in itself. This solipsism history sublates, with which spirit enters into finitude, into all its contradiction and pain. But out of the Place of the Skull of death, out of the extremest estrangement, it returns in eternal rejuvenation again to itself, and out of the fullness of this realm of spirits there foams up to it, to be sure, not its immediate infinity, which is a groundlessly existing one, but that in which it enjoys itself, through doing and suffering, as true spirit.

The truth represented in revealed religion is purified, in the Concept of absolute knowing, of the deficiencies of the original representation, to cognition. Since now consciousness

[p. 212]

has thereby raised itself to the last possible standpoint, it must prove the Concept of the equality of its certainty and its truth as the *system of science* itself, for with itself, with the *metamorphoses* of its shapes, it is absolutely *finished*. From the lowest, from *sensuous certainty*, it has raised itself to the highest and most ideal, to the *absoluteness* of knowing. Every opposition of its self-consciousness, every deception, spirit has overcome. Every *moment* of its world-representation it has made into a *stage* of its development, and it has ceased to be a searching cognition. In this absolute spiritual essence the content of science is for self-consciousness just as much *universal self-consciousness*, just as it is for it all reality or *the essentiality that is in itself*, and just as it is itself therein at the same time this *single* self-consciousness.

In his lectures of that time Hegel expressed himself on this point as follows: “The Absolute is itself the element of this consciousness. In it, therefore, the Concepts are neither empty abstractions and thoughts moving beyond being — they have filled themselves with actual consciousness; nor alien essentialities and an objective in-itself or a being that would not be Concept — actuality has shown itself to it as its own spirit. For the sake of this certainty of itself in *being*, or since self-consciousness has formed itself into the element and substance of science, a *particular reflection* of it into itself is *superfluous*. It would have the significance that it did not immediately possess itself in the Concept, but would first still have to be reminded of this especially and to restore itself in it, as happens with representation, when it remembers that this is its representation. It therefore abandons itself freely to the nature and necessity of the Concept, certain of its own immediate presence therein, conscious of not standing in an alien power and therefore secure of not being led away from itself by it and lost in an unknown land. — There is therefore also no need to give the Concept at once the form of self-consciousness and to call it perhaps I, in order always to remember oneself in the object of its knowing. The nature of the Concept would thereby acquire the false look

[p. 213]

and the false significance of belonging to self-consciousness only insofar as the latter opposes itself to the objective manner, and it would thereby at the same time lose the immediate significance of being and of universality. Rather, for knowing as the unity of universal and single self-consciousness, this its element and essence itself is the object and content of its science, and must therefore be expressed in an objective manner. And so it is *being*. In it, as the simple, absolute Concept, it knows itself immediately as self-consciousness, so that it does not occur to it, in this being, to have expressed thereby something opposed to self-consciousness and to engage with it in a struggle, whereby it would first have to be decided whether it or this being would come off the worse, nor to occasion, through the acknowledgment of this being, a misunderstanding or even a danger for its independence. It has in its truth the certainty of itself, and calmly above this it therefore watches the free self-movement, as the being which appears *immediately* develops its essence, to be spirit, and presents itself as that which it is in itself. Insofar as self-consciousness as such mingles and interweaves itself into the movement of the object which it has in science, it stands at a stage on which it has grasped neither itself nor its object as spirit, and has not yet acquired the calm toward it, which it attains only when it can endure it in its freedom and independence because it is knowing spirit. — If, then, the consciousness that is only coming to science takes offense, at its content as it shows itself, at *being, nonbeing, unity*, etc., as if these essential forms of the content were empty, contentless, as if alien essences were designated with them that did not concern this living self-consciousness, then the consciousness that has been educated through science and has returned to it from the experience of the world distinguishes itself from that view in this, that it is *knowing*, i.e. that it has in those abstractions the significance of their universality, and that for it they are not abstract moments in the sense as if they, withdrawn from reality, carried on their business far from it, but are universal essences in which reality likewise,

[p. 214]

in being sublated, is preserved, and that it further comprehends these essences, their course and their whole, or has its self immediately in them and is at home in them.”

By virtue of such cognition Hegel could well assert, in the Preface to the *Phenomenology*, that the representations of philosophical *method* handed down up to him belonged to a *vanished* culture. If this should perhaps sound boastful or revolutionary, he knew himself to be far from such a tone. — He once actually lectured on the Phenomenology, which he had been preparing for publication since 1804, in the summer of 1806. Its printing had already begun, and the sheets were distributed individually to the auditors. However, the printing was completed only in 1807. Hegel’s abstract of the whole, which he made for the purpose of the lecture, is still extant. He linked the Phenomenology with the Logic in such a way that he took the former as an introduction to the latter and passed from the Concept of absolute knowing immediately to that of being. In the same half-year he also lectured on the philosophy of nature and of spirit as Realphilosophie, and here let the Phenomenology intervene significantly in the presentation of nature, in that he dealt with opinion, understanding and reason for the apprehension of nature. To opinion he coordinated, on the side of nature, the contingency of existence individuated in space and time; to the understanding the universal laws of nature; to reason life, the organic. It was a dialectical critique of the categories in which empirical as well as abstract-metaphysical natural science is accustomed to move. — The Phenomenology was Hegel’s last lecture in Jena. He concluded the lecture course on speculative philosophy on 18 September 1806 with the following words: “This, gentlemen, is speculative philosophy, so far as I have come in the development of it. Consider it as a beginning of philosophizing, which you will carry further. We stand in an important epoch of time, a ferment, in which spirit has made a jolt, has gone beyond its previous shape and gains a new one. The whole mass of previous representations, Concepts, the bonds of the world, are dissolved and collapse into themselves like a dream image. A new emergence of spirit is preparing. Philosophy has above all its appearance

[p. 215]

to greet and to acknowledge it, while others, powerlessly resisting it, cling to the past, and the majority unconsciously make up the mass of its appearing. Philosophy, however, has, recognizing it as the eternal, to render it its honor. Commending myself to your kind remembrance, I wish you pleasant holidays.”

#### Influence on the Students.

What came of the pleasant holidays which Hegel, in his earlier patriarchal manner, wished his auditorium, we shall soon see, but must first depict the social circumstances in which Hegel moved at Jena, and begin with the effect which he exercised on the students. Regardless of rhetorical elegance, matter-of-fact through and through, deeply stirred by the impulse of the present, ever striving onward and yet often quite dogmatic in expression, Hegel knew how to captivate the students by the intensity of his speculation. His voice had a similarity to his eye. The latter was large, but turned inward, and its brokenly gleaming gaze was of the deepest ideality, which momentarily was also, outwardly, of the most gripping power. The voice was somewhat broad, without sonorous ring, but through the apparent commonness there penetrated that lofty animation which the power of cognition generated, and which in moments in which the genius of humanity through him conjured his listeners left no one unmoved. The earnestness of the noble features had at first, if not something repellent, yet something restraining, but through the mildness and friendliness of the expression one was won again and drawn near. A peculiar smile revealed the purest benevolence, but at the same time there lay in it something harsh, indeed cutting, painful, or rather ironic. There was mirrored in him the tragic trait of the philosopher, of the hero who wrestles with the riddle of the world.

On the students as a mass Hegel had no influence at all. To these he was known only as a strange obscurity, and whoever wished to hear not merely the older professors but also to try it once with a younger lecturer went rather

[p. 216]

to *Fries*, who was striving upward at the same time as Hegel. All the more firmly did a small circle of adherents and admirers hold fast, whose enthusiasm rose extraordinarily especially in the last years of Hegel’s Jena sojourn. The Bremen man *Suthmeier* mentioned above preached especially the gospel of the Absolute and recruited listeners for Hegel, as others did the same for *Fries*, others for *Krause*. Suthmeier was a man of genius, but let himself fall into an unruly dissoluteness, and this way of life naturally did not contribute to refuting the prejudice that the philosophy of the Absolute was not only practically something useless but also, in ethical regard, positively dangerous. By his decided judgment, which was most striking in the negation of the customary, by a brusque confidence, he dominated many. Another listener of Hegel’s, a Thuringian, *Zellmann*, was far deeper, but consumptive, quiet, turned inward, and knew how to make himself count externally not at all. One day Suthmeier dragged a coarse fellow of homespun, bluntly natural common sense along into the lecture. After the hour the latter declared that he did not know at all what the talk was actually about here, whether of ducks or of geese. Thereupon the Hegelians made this mocking verse:

Whether of geese or of ducks / You ask, is the talk here? / Well! You must turn the question about, / And they are not missing there.

The much-named, much-praised Absolute was now, to be sure, for the majority something very dark, chaotic, at which they gazed more in amazement than understood in deed. The negative side of the opposition to the old, the previous, the insight into the untenability of what had inwardly already gone to ground, formed itself most clearly and strongly. If a student toiled at the Absolute to the point of hypochondria, the others consoled him with the saying that the breakthrough would surely come with him. The genuine disciples cherished the greatest esteem for the master and an almost idolatrous veneration for everything that issued from him. He appeared to them as a higher being, in comparison with whom everything of their own in their previous condition and all the knowledge of others was null

[p. 217]

and rejected. This veneration, so beneficial to youth, and exaggerating, extended to everything, even the slightest, that one could learn of the life and doings of the beloved man, to every trait, every manner of conduct and behavior, every utterance. Behind every word that one could catch outside the lectures a deeper significance, a higher truth was sought. Thus the bookseller *Frommann* once gave a midday meal to some famous scholars who had come on a visit, to which Hegel too was invited. When it drew to a close, the host made all kinds of apologies for his poor hospitality: the kitchen had collapsed on him, otherwise this and that more should have come forth. Hegel is said to have replied: “Just bring what you have. There is everything here to consume. We shall see to it that it meets its fate.” Such things people admired.

That Hegel took snuff one saw sufficiently in the lecture. Now, however, the great question was raised whether he also smoked, and there people found out how he had once been at *Niethammer’s* in company and had gone into the kitchen to light a clay pipe! — A student, about to go from Jena to Würzburg, took his leave of him. Hegel said to him: “I have a friend there too, *Schelling*.” Here, the enthusiasts now remarked, the word *friend* was meant to say something quite different from what it does otherwise in ordinary life. — The lecture course on the history of philosophy Hegel gave in the evening by candlelight, in the auditorium situated in the rear building of Eichstädt’s house. When now in the lecture one shape of speculation after the other emerged, only to submerge again, and when finally also, unforeseen by the listeners, the Schellingian system came in its turn, an elderly Mecklenburger leapt up after the conclusion of one lecture, when Hegel had already departed, and cried out with horror: “that is surely *death*, and so everything must pass away.” From this there arose now a lively discussion among the students, in which finally Suthmeier held forth and pathetically expounded: that was indeed death and must be death, but in this death was life, which, purified by it, would unfold ever more gloriously. — In a small university town

[p. 218]

insignificant incidents and utterances in themselves acquire a greater importance and remain longer in the memory, whereas in today’s larger university towns scarcely any anecdotes about the professors are possible any more. So the students busied themselves for weeks with the following *quid pro quo*. In the summer of 1806 Hegel lectured from 3 to 4 and from 5 to 6. Once he had slept a little after dinner, woke, heard the clock strike, believed it was three, hurried off and appeared before the listeners of the theologian *Augusti*, who lectured in the same auditorium. He began his lecture at once, until one of the listeners, with much trouble, made him aware of his error and that it was only two o’clock. In the meantime Augusti too had come, heard someone speaking at the door of the auditorium, listened, recognized Hegel’s voice and now withdrew again, because he believed that he had erred and come an hour late. When then at 3 o’clock Hegel’s listeners assembled, he said: “Gentlemen, of the experiences of consciousness about itself the first is the truth, or rather untruth, of sensuous certainty. At this we have stopped, and I myself made a special experience of it an hour ago.” But from the brief smile with which he accompanied these words he passed at once back to his accustomed philosophical earnestness. How he for his part stood toward individual listeners who came personally closer to him is shown perhaps best partly by the weighty letter which he wrote to *Zellmann* (*Works*, vol. XVII, 627), partly by the manner and way in which pupils expressed themselves to him in letters. *Van Ghert*’s attachment, whose manner of love we shall come to know later, is known. Several letters from Hegel to him are printed. But there are also still letters from other, otherwise unknown pupils extant. Thus a certain *Lange* went from Jena to Heidelberg and wrote from here, under 4 December 1805, in the expectation that Hegel might perhaps be called there:

Most revered of my teachers!

“With more rapture I should like to say to you orally at this moment here in Heidelberg how warmly, how strongly my heart beats for you, how greatly I revere you as him who gave to my spirit power and to my

[p. 219]

life firmness, as I now rejoice to be able to converse with you in writing. Only your presence could complete my joy at being in Heidelberg,” etc. In the course of the letter Lange relates how little he was satisfied by *Fries*, how greatly, on the other hand, by *Daub*, who knows Hegel’s writings and is keenly interested in him: “Daub’s lecture is the most gripping I have ever heard. There he stands, his gaze toward heaven, his head leaning somewhat on his hand, and speaks now with an inwardness, with a warmth, that carries one away. If one examines more closely, everything is full of spirit and life,” etc. — Another listener, *Held*, later a professor in Bavaria, tried it at Würzburg with the *Wagner*ian philosophy, saw through its deficiencies, however, soon enough, and wrote a report about it to Hegel, in order to hear from him whether he perhaps did Wagner an injustice. This critique does not belong further here, but for the characterization of the personal relationship to Hegel let the following words of the letter stand here; Held namely mentions the glorious hours which he had lived in Hegel’s proximity, and continues: “And in truth I learn to value these precious hours ever more, especially since I left Professor Wagner’s lectures so unsatisfied. Quite different was the path on which you led us to truth, and to a quite different, higher, more glorious goal should we have come on it, as I can easily guess from what I had the good fortune to hear from you. Wagner’s philosophy seems to me on the whole only a superficial one, or really no system at all, which has merely the semblance of depth. His fluent delivery, his surprising views and applications, bribed me during the lectures themselves, but now that I coldly restudy the whole, I miss exceedingly much in it,” etc.

In Jena it was the custom to bring the prorector, entering and departing every half-year, a festive music, which then also extended to this or that docent who happened to be celebrated. This honor was also once bestowed on Hegel, in February 1806. He was surprised and spoke some lofty and solemn words, yet in part dark to the students, on the significance of science, for whose esteem and recognition he took the honor paid to him.

[p. 220]

#### Honors and Professorship.

Among the natural scientists Hegel had many friends at that time. He pursued the study of nature with great zeal, heard physiology with *Ackermann* in Jena, who was later transferred to Heidelberg, botanized with *Schelver*, conversed about chemistry with his friend and countryman *Seebeck*, immersed himself with *Kastner*, who was especially fond of him, in the science of medicine, and made a geognostic journey to the Harz, on which he got as far as Westphalia and Göttingen. On 30 January 1804 the *Jena Mineralogical Society* appointed him unanimously its assessor; the natural-scientific society of Westphalia at *Bröckhausen*, on 1 August of the same year, its ordinary member; the physical society in *Heidelberg*, on 1 January 1807, its honorary member.

When now toward the end of 1804 it was a matter of appointing Fries professor in Jena, one could not, without being unjust, pass over Hegel. He also made, on 29 September, a petition to the Weimar ministry, in which he referred to his numerous audience from the winter of 1803/4 and then argued that he was the *oldest* of the Privatdozents, and consequently, through the distinction conferred on others before him by the highest authorities, had to fear the possibility of being restricted in his activity. — So he was then granted, in February 1805, an *extraordinary professorship*. As a stipendiary of Tübingen he had to apply to the Stuttgart consistory for permission to accept it, and received this on 6 July 1805: *salvo regressu cum omnibus effectibus in patriam* [with the right of return to the homeland with all his effects]. — When he was later appointed at Nuremberg he omitted this, and thereby lost his Württemberg citizenship.

On 1 July 1806 he drew for the first and for the last time, with all sorts of deductions, his first salary, of 100 thalers.

#### Social Circle.

In his comfortably sociable accessibility Hegel remained true to himself in Jena too. He found here many countrymen, among whom for the earlier time *Schelling*, for the latter *Niethammer* stood foremost in

[p. 221]

his company. Schelling went, as already mentioned, in the summer of 1803 to Würzburg. Up to the publication of the Phenomenology Hegel wrote to him a few more times, but there is only a single letter still extant, of 16 November 1803, which however can at the same time best introduce us to Hegel’s whole situation.

“I write to you since I have heard that you have now arrived at your fixed place and post, and first acknowledge to you the receipt of your letter, written to me from Stuttgart shortly before your departure for Munich.

How much your appointment, which is at the same time in every respect very honorable, has pleased me, I need not tell you. Jena, *tantis viris orba* [bereft of such great men], has missed you especially, and even among the common people your loss was held to be the most significant, just as the people that does not call itself common seemed to wish to possess you again.

You still owe me a report on the many remarkable things you have seen on your journey. I hope especially that you will not withhold from me not only how you found this whole New Bavarian spirit in activity, but also how it stands with our friends, both in Salzburg and my special ones in Munich, and with this whole clan. As far as one can tell, the tone of the latter toward you seems to be about to soften for the time being, and so the transition to an opposite one to be preparing itself.

As for the conditions here, you will receive sufficient information through the Jenaers migrating to Würzburg. Without doubt the lot of these emigrants is as opposed as their direction. *Loder* has told it for certain that he has a loss of 1000 thalers in fees this year. There are only 35 medical students in Halle, who anyhow attend lectures meagerly, since they must make the whole course over again in Berlin — all circumstances that could be known beforehand. The others derive no good prognostic from this. Into which little brooks your philosophical stream is divided here you will have heard. I too have taken up lecturing again and get along with it better than before. — The *Literaturzeitung* now to appear will be just as common a

[p. 222]

institute as the preceding one and any other. *Goethe* was concerned with nothing further. Since *Eichstädt* offered himself and money, the whole matter was knocked down to him without more ado, so that Jena might have a Literaturzeitung.

Among the new phenomena belongs that *Ritter* has been requested by the students to lecture on galvanism. He has applied to the philosophical faculty and awaits an answer from the courts. *Fernow* could find no auditorium large enough for those who registered. It is said that he reads Kantian definitions off to them.

Of literary novelties nothing has come before my eyes except a worthless piece by *Kotzebue*, expectorations of a diarrhea which he let out while still in Germany. It is the old song of Goethe and the Schlegels. — *Goethe* is going very much for the real and for apparatus. Not only did he get *Schelver* to set up a botanical cabinet, but a physiological one is also being established, and from *Ritter* he immediately demanded the plan for a galvanic apparatus.

The Weimar theater has as yet nothing new to show. *Schiller* is said to be working on *William Tell*.

Here you have a letter full of novelties and details. The whole crisis of this age seems altogether at this moment to show a manifold individual fuss, even though the basic elements have already separated and for that very reason each seems busied with setting itself in possession of what belongs to each by nature out of the collapse of the universal. And when the operation is over, those too who have no eyes and those who do not want to have any will have to look at the damage by force and be greatly astonished.”

“Farewell and preserve your friendship

Your Hegel.”

How Hegel stood toward *Goethe* and *Schiller* is evident from their correspondence. Hegel’s depth was not for a moment misjudged by them, but expressed itself for them, especially for Goethe, to whom actual speculation remained rather foreign, in an incomprehensible manner. Goethe (in the letters to Schiller) wished,

[p. 223]

that *Fernow* might give Hegel some of his superficial lightness, and that Hegel in return might give Fernow some of his substance. According to notes still extant, of 27 November and 15 December 1803, Goethe requested from Hegel a review of a book, in a sense which they were to discuss orally. The book is not named. But there still exists in manuscript a critique by Hegel of the second edition of *Herder’s God*, Gotha 1800, which sets out the difference between it and the first edition with mild sharpness. This work Goethe probably wished Hegel to review for the new Jena *Literaturzeitung*.

On 27 June 1806 *Goethe* wrote to Hegel the following lines, which perhaps refer to the salary granted to the latter:

“Regard the enclosed, my dear Herr Doctor, at least as a proof that I have not ceased to work for you quietly. I could indeed have wished to announce more, but in such cases much is gained for the future if only a beginning has once been made. I, who wish you to fare right well, and to see you again healthy and cheerful.”

With *Gries*, who had begun to transplant the fairest blossoms of Romance poetry onto German soil, Hegel stood on cordial terms of intercourse; with the *Schlegels*, however, he had no closer relationship. A lecture course which *Friedrich Schlegel* gave on transcendental philosophy soon enough came to an end again, as Hegel himself relates (*Works*, vol. XVII, p. 351): “he was finished with his course in six weeks, not exactly to the satisfaction of his hearers, who had expected and paid for a half-year one.” It is ridiculous when it has been asserted more than once that Hegel borrowed his *method* from Friedrich Schlegel! As if the general thought that scientific construction must contain a triplicity of moments and present the content objectively were already the Concept of that method, already that dialectic to which Hegel, through the preface to the *Phenomenology* and through the *Phenomenology* itself, had indeed already drawn attention, but for which he could break a path only through his system of the *Logic*.

In mentioning Friedrich Schlegel it may well be most fittingly inserted here how the *conversion* to *Catholicism* was also at that time urged upon Hegel. In this form

[p. 224]

Romanticism not infrequently miscarried. A friend of Hegel’s, *Möller*, who had gone from Jena to *Münster*, wrote him from there on 24 November 1804 an affectionate letter, in which he says that, whereas Hegel, as *Ritter* had told him, was occupied intensively with physics, he himself, since they last saw each other, had thrown himself into theology, had become Catholic, and now found himself, outwardly and inwardly, in the purest peace. Since Protestantism, he says, love had grown cold in the world, and lukewarmness and indifference had taken the place of religion and the fear of God. In a series of mystical propositions, half Taulerian, half philosophy of nature, he then sketches his profession of faith, recommends to Hegel for his conversion the book of *Augustine*, *de vera religione* [on true religion], and is so zealous that he promises to lend it to him, should he be unable to get it!

In almost all who came somewhat closer to him personally and were not already prejudiced against him, Hegel aroused enthusiasm for himself. To give a quite glaring example of how far this rapturous affection sometimes went, let the beginning of a letter from *Hufnagel* in Frankfurt am Main, of 4 May 1803, stand here: “To your friendship and love I owe so many enjoyments, when we still wandered in the body before one another, but you afford me such fair enjoyments even now in absence. Only that *your* and *your* — or, if it does not sound too proud, our *Schelling’s heavenly manner* is too precious for me, the son of earth.” Etc.

With his countrymen Hegel lived in the best accord. When *Paulus* prepared his edition of *Spinoza*, he went through the French translations for him, as he himself says (*Works*, vol. XV, p. 371). But with others, too, he lived in friendly intercourse, as with *Knebel* and his wife, who often cheered him by her beautiful singing. Most intimately, however, was he bound to *Niethammer* and his wife, a bond of friendship which, strengthened between them by many a fate-trial happily withstood, remained unchanged until Hegel’s death. Niethammer was to him the most *reliable adviser* in all his affairs, from whom he had no secret, and who, by virtue of the influential position which he later assumed at Munich, could always extend to him a provident affection, often with success.

[p. 225]

#### Projects.

Already since the second year of his stay in Jena Hegel had wanted, as we have seen, to publish his system. *Schelling longed* greatly for it, as *Kastner*, who had visited him on his journey to Heidelberg, related in a letter to Hegel of 15 November 1805. But for a long time nothing came of it, until at last, under the greatest external hindrances, the bookseller *Göbhardt* in Bamberg took over the *Phenomenology* as the first part of the system. As so many of Hegel’s friends now went first to Bavaria, then to Baden, while in Jena itself the prospect of a thriving career remained meager, Hegel too threw himself into the hope of coming to *Heidelberg*, where *Schelver*, *Kastner*, *Ackermann*, *Thibaut* and *Daub* took a lively interest in it. This interest, however, availed little against the dominion which the minister von *Reizenstein* and the court councillor *Voss* exercised over all the affairs of the university. Besides, as *Kastner* intimates in a letter, there was the difficulty that in Karlsruhe people were prejudiced against the new philosophy, because they did not quite trust it not to destroy religion, which they regarded as the so-called prop of the state. Hegel turned to *Voss*. The draft of his letter is printed in *Works*, vol. XVII, p. 473. We learn from it not only how Hegel himself regarded his activity in Jena — how, just as Luther had made the *Bible* speak German and Voss *Homer*, he wished to teach *philosophy to speak German* — but also that he wished to lecture on *aesthetics* in the sense of the French *Cours de litérature*. Voss excused himself on account of the limitation of the funds, saying that he could do nothing for him. His answer of 24 August 1805 concluded: “May the genius of Germany bless your resolve to lead philosophy back from the clouds again to friendly intercourse with well-spoken children of men. It seems to me that an inward understanding and feeling is not even possible apart from the familiar language of the heart, and that our rich primal language has, for the finest and most tender stirrings of the spirit, either culture or supple formability. An Olympian in shepherd’s guise

[p. 226]

would work greater wonders than through superhuman apparitions.”

For several years, as he relates in a letter to *Niethammer*, Hegel carried the project of translating from the French the *Physiology* of *Richerand*, a pupil of Bichat. To be sure, he added, there were no German views in it.

But what occupied him most vividly was the plan of publishing a *critical journal*, perhaps, as one flattered oneself after the cessation of the journal of the *Studies*, through the mediation of *Daub* and *Creuzer* and others, with the support of the Karlsruhe government. With *Schelver*, *Kastner*, but above all with *Niethammer*, he discussed the tendency and arrangement of the journal. Against the prevailing reviewing racket it was to constitute an opposition. Not the *external* completeness of the various fields and of the *mass* of their writings, but completeness in the truly *important* was to determine the selection. Just as little was the *prolixity of detail* of a special science to be entered into, but rather what is *generally* of interest to be brought out of each. The critique itself was to refrain from the reviewer’s air of being always still cleverer than something already very clever, and above all to give an *analysis of the content*, because this alone can produce for the public a closer acquaintance with the matter, and the mere approving or rejecting notice of writings profits as little as the discussion of *personal* relations or, as Hegel called it, the *dialogue with the author*. In the case of more comprehensive works, the *maxims* from which their composition proceeds were in particular to be subjected to a critique. The *ancient literature*, because it in any case has the interest of every cultivated person on its side, as does *aesthetic* culture generally, was to enjoy careful consideration; everything half-hearted and vain was to be certain without circumlocution of annihilation, and the turbidity of the fermentation of that time to find no indulgence. The protest against the spiritlessness of the merely customary, however, was not to adopt the manner of a certain philosophical scientificity which, instead of being application and transition of the abstract Ideas to the determinate content and the

[p. 227]

actual sciences, *which is what is at present at stake*, is rather, “for the most part empty formalism, an immature brew of half-grasped notions, shallow and mostly even silly conceits, and an ignorance of philosophy itself as well as of the sciences, such as — to designate more precisely what I mean — the *Windischmann*, *Görres*, and also for the most part the *Steffens* way of doing things, as well as the specimens which the Jena *Literaturzeitung* gave, especially at its beginning. To this raw forest torrent, which threatens to confound reason and science, whose manners and principles *Schelling*, after having partly propounded and employed them, now solemnly begins to renounce — a scientific critique has chiefly to oppose itself.” The draft which Hegel worked out for such a journal, and the editorship of which he would very gladly have taken over, is printed under the title *Maxims of the Journal of German Literature*, *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 393–399. It concludes with the words: “It will begin with July 1807.” But it remained with the prospectus. The public conditions of a time stirred by war were too unfavorable to such undertakings.

#### The Jena Catastrophe, Autumn 1806.

The marches of the Prussian troops through Jena and their reviews on public squares had given Hegel occasion to express himself on the future of the Prussian army. He promised himself little from it, and unfortunately his expectations were confirmed. Jena’s fate in those days is so well known in all its particulars that a more detailed treatment of it, although Hegel’s numerous letters to Niethammer from this time would furnish varied material, may be omitted. When the French, pressing in before the battle, began to break into the houses and to plunder, Hegel held out against the onslaught in his lodgings for quite a while. He gave the soldiers to eat and drink what he had. When some, of an appearance to commit the worst, threatened him, he luckily noticed the cross of the Legion of Honor on the breast of one of them, pointed to it and said, he hoped from a man honored with this badge, even for

[p. 228]

a simple German scholar, an honorable treatment; whereupon the soldiers calmed down somewhat and contented themselves with a bottle of wine. When the storming in grew ever worse and more dangerous, when the fire that had broken out spread, Hegel put the last manuscript of the *Phenomenology*, to be sent off to Bamberg, in his pocket, left his books and papers to their fate, and on 14 October found refuge in the house of the prorector *Gabler*, whose son, later Hegel’s successor in Berlin, procured for him in the topmost story an empty little student’s room for a temporary abode. In Gabler’s house an officer of higher rank had taken up his quarters, whereby the house was protected. After the battle Napoleon at once had the unopposed fire that was spreading checked and restored order to some extent, whereupon Hegel at once returned to his lodgings. Here he found everything thrown into confusion by the soldiers. Paper, pen, penknife had been taken from him. He had to run about among his friends in order to be able to write a letter, called the war in one of them the Gottseibeiuns [the Devil], and said that no one had pictured it to himself as so bad.

*Gans*, in his obituary of Hegel in the Prussian *Staatszeitung*, said — and from there it has often been repeated — that Hegel completed the *Phenomenology of Spirit* under the thunder of the cannon of the battle of Jena. This is not incorrect in so far as Hegel, in order to keep punctually the peremptory deadline stipulated with the bookseller for the delivery of the manuscript, was just about to send off the last sheets. One sees from his letters to *Niethammer*, who was employed in Bamberg, his boundless anxiety over the *ruin* of his whole laborious work in these unquiet times. He did not know whether the manuscript he had sent off had arrived; nor what fate Bamberg might perhaps have; nor whether he would receive from the publisher, in such circumstances, a payment for his work, however urgently he needed it. Finally he was in fact at his wits’ end. After the plundering of the town he had, in the proper sense of the word, not a penny, and turned also for this ever more painful embarrassment to Niethammer, who proved himself once more a prompt friend and

[p. 229]

sent him a draft payable in Jena, which at least put an end to the momentary need.

It is attractive to observe how in the letters to Niethammer, out of the tangle of news about a thousand personal circumstances, about the condition of houses and gardens, about the well-being of beloved people, about the misprints in the *Phenomenology*, about the uncertain course of the post, etc., Hegel’s interest in *Napoleon* breaks through. Even *before* the battle he wrote to Niethammer as follows:

“Jena, Monday, 13 October 1806, on the day when Jena was occupied by the French and the Emperor Napoleon entered its walls.”

“What anxiety I must feel for the consignments of manuscript sent off earlier, last Wednesday and Friday, you will see from the date. — Yesterday evening toward sunset I saw the shots of the French patrols both from the Gempenbachthal and from W.; the Prussians were driven out of the latter in the night. The firing lasted till after 12 o’clock, and today between 8 and 9 o’clock the French skirmishers, and an hour later the regular troops, entered. This hour was an hour of anguish, particularly through the people’s ignorance of the right which everyone has, according to the Emperor’s own will, even against these light troops, not to comply with their demands but calmly to give them what is necessary. Through clumsy conduct and neglected caution many have been put into embarrassment. Your sister-in-law, however, as well as the Döderlein house, has got off with the fright and remained unharmed. She now has 12 officers quartered on her. The *Emperor* — *this world soul* — I saw riding out through the town to reconnoiter. — It is indeed a wonderful feeling to see such an individual, who, concentrated here on one point, sitting on a horse, reaches out over the world and rules it. To the Prussians, to be sure, no better prognosis could be given — but from Thursday to Monday such advances are possible only to this extraordinary man, whom it is not possible not to admire.”

“But perhaps, if I have come through well today, I have

[p. 230]

suffered as much as or more than others. From the whole external aspect I must doubt whether my manuscript, which left on Wednesday and Friday, has arrived. My loss would indeed be far too great. My other acquaintances have suffered nothing; am I to be the only one? — God knows with what heavy heart I still venture this consignment, yet I do not doubt that behind the army's back the post circulates freely. — As I did earlier, all now wish the French army good fortune, which, given the quite monstrous difference of its leaders and of its common soldiers from those of its enemies, cannot fail it. Thus our region will soon be freed of this flood.”

“Frau Court Councillor Voigt told me that she will not let the postilion depart until early tomorrow morning, and I have spoken to her about asking, from the general staff, which is lodged in her house, a safe conduct, which will not be refused. Thus, I hope, God will still deliver my scribblings to you by the deadline. — As soon as you learn how to send me some money, I beg you most earnestly to do so. I shall shortly have absolute need of it.”

“At night at 11 o’clock, in District Commissioner Hellfeld’s house, where I now lodge and from which I look on at the rows of fires of the French battalions, which they have made out of the butchers’ stalls, junk booths and the like over the whole market square.

Your Hegel.”

#### Newspaper Editorship in Bamberg, 1807–1808.

As from 1805 the conditions in Jena became ever more confining, ever more devoid of prospects, Hegel had, as has already been told, hoped in Heidelberg for a professorship and perhaps, through journalism, for a further influence on German literature. Jena appeared to him, in his own expression in a letter, like a cloister. Its science, and even its view of art, were one-sided. This period had been necessary, but it was over; the school had run its course; its activity was splintered and flung out into the living world. The wealth of spirit and of life had

[p. 231]

not touched the seclusion of the school, but neither had the school touched it. Interests had ruled of which in Germany, Jena and Weimar excepted, no one knew anything. Books were regarded here as generally accepted of which scarcely a hundred copies had come before the public. Heidelberg seemed to be more advantageously situated than Jena for bringing political confusion and the vanity of a superficial knowing back to order and letting the power of science pass over also into actuality.

Since, however, no position for Hegel was made possible in Heidelberg, he had to think of something else, and toward the spring of 1806 Niethammer proposed to him the editorship of the *newspaper* appearing in Bamberg, which was actually in the possession of the court bursar *Schneiderbanger*. But Hegel was to edit not only the newspaper but also to enter into a *partnership* with its owner. The inventory of the composing room, the printing shop, the counting house, the editorial equipment, the stock of paper, wood, etc., was to be handed back by Hegel at the expiry of the contract in the same condition in which it stood at the time of the takeover, which date was stipulated for 1 July 1807. Specifically, to be sure, he was to attend to the *editorship* of the newspaper; but with the newspaper establishment there was also connected a *book trade and publishing house*. The staff for this was to be kept at common expense, and profit and loss from the undertakings were likewise to be shared.

When Niethammer made the first proposal for this business, Hegel declared at once that he could regard it not as something definitive but only as something transitory for him, until he had found a situation more suited to his aspiration, and said among other things on 20 February 1806: “The business itself will interest me, since, as you know, I follow the events of the world with curiosity, and from this side I should sooner have to fear it than to be put off by it. I hope also to be able soon to find my way into it. What tone and character, moreover, can be brought into the newspaper is to be seen on the spot. One may regard our newspapers, almost all of them, as worse than the French, and it would be interesting to bring a newspaper of this sort closer to the latter, without however giving up that which the German chiefly

[p. 232]

demands, a sort of pedantry and impartiality of the news, to give up.”

After Hegel had actually concluded the contract, he went to Bamberg between February and March — for the time cannot be determined exactly — of 1807, a place which, being quite Catholic, attracted him in many ways. His friend Niethammer and his wife, whom he held in high reverence and whom he was accustomed in his letters to call simply the *best woman*, still lived here, though already on the point of being transferred to Munich. *Paulus*, too, was still here, before he moved to Nuremberg. Hegel could, moreover, satisfy a long-cherished wish, to observe Catholicism once at close quarters. Finally, Bamberg was then still enlivened, as a prince-episcopal residence, by a multitude of *court festivities*. A *French theater* played here constantly, and Hegel thereby had occasion to come to know the classical theater of the French, and not only that but also its classical performers, such as *Talma*, in the best way.

He edited the newspaper for only one year, until the autumn of 1808. When *Gans*, in the obituary already cited, asserts that Hegel supplied the newspaper with spirited essays penetrating deeply into the politics of the day, this is an error. A careful examination of the six quarto volumes filling the annual runs of the newspaper for 1806 and 1807 shows no trace of leading, or as one then said, reasoning articles. In Hegel’s intention they may initially have lain, to judge from the remark communicated above, but Napoleon’s preponderance made them impossible. In a time in which so much happened, the simple, as faithful and coherent as possible presentation of the most important events was, under the given circumstances, the only thing to which one had to confine oneself. In a solemn announcement the newspaper, to be sure, also once promises to pay homage to the *Ideas* of the *true*, the *good* and the *beautiful* and to strive for a *noble style*, but with this customary booksellers’ puffing Hegel had nothing to do. In that clear and graphic reporting of the most noteworthy facts, such as one must always wish as the basis for judging the state of the world, the newspaper distinguished itself. Should one, however, single out anything in particular

[p. 233]

about it, it would be only perhaps the warm interest which shines forth from it for the personal greatness of Napoleon, for the fate of Prussia and its throne, which was decided precisely in these years, and for all advances in the domain of art and science.

Hegel might, judging by the irony with which he mocks his business to *Knebel*, especially also over his duty of being the best-informed, fall under the appearance of having taken the matter too lightly; but in fact he sought, according to letters still extant, to encourage his acquaintances throughout all Germany and to have them support him with news. Most of them, however, excused themselves, partly by their not knowing anything, partly by the dangerousness of such a correspondence. Several letters of Hegel to Knebel with this request, of 30 August 1807, 21 November 1807, 14 October 1808 (cf. Knebel’s *Literary Remains and Correspondence*, edited by *Varnhagen von Ense* and Mundt, vol. II, pp. 445–453), may serve us as an example. Knebel’s enthusiasm for the Greeks and Romans, his antique evenness of temper in life, his serene resignation, had bound him closely to Hegel. From those letters, in which roguish allusions to the *rock-cellar beer* as the Bamberg Hippocrene are standing, we perceive the amiably humorous tone which they had established between them. From Knebel’s still unprinted letters to Hegel we wish to bring forward here only those passages which serve for a closer characterization of the newspaper business. On 10 September 1807 Knebel wrote: “What you demand of me, perhaps only in jest, is altogether not my line.
