Nor do these parts seem to me at all the place for political news. *Lies* there are enough, which we collect partly from elsewhere, partly content ourselves with our own invention. But they are mostly of somewhat meager substance and fly with the word out of the mouth, so that one would truly not care to read them printed a second time.” — Later Knebel teases Hegel once about the fact that he wants to make him a communication of a sermon, which was *not bad*. But then it occurs to him that Hegel never showed any particular taste for sermons, and that political news would be dearer to him, which, however, are almost as rare as

[p. 234]

*good sermons*. Hegel suggested that Knebel’s Karl might at least become his correspondent and practice himself in the *objective* style which is called newspaper writing. Despite Knebel’s polite refusal to give news, Hegel nevertheless learned through him fairly everything that went on of some significance in Weimar and Jena. Thus among other things he told him on 7 October 1808 how *Napoleon* with *Alexander* of Russia had driven through the streets of Erfurt: “All eyes were fixed on the great emperors, and especially on Napoleon, who by the sight of a great, thinking, ever-active man, although in simple guise, enthused the whole crowd. One also admired the graciousness and condescension of the Emperor Alexander, so that one could say without exaggeration that one saw together in one carriage all that the world can show of the lofty and amiable in crowned form.” After a mention of the theater, where *la mort de César* [the death of Caesar] was given, of the illumination of the city and of the ball, Knebel continues: “What I can still report to you in this connection, not as a newspaper article, is that the great Napoleon has won the hearts of all men among us, and especially of the most intelligent, in a way which is quite independent of his greatness and power, and concerns the man even more than the emperor. In his features, together with a certain expression of melancholy, which according to Aristotle is the foundation of every great character, people have found marked not only the traits of a lofty spirit but a true greatness of heart, which the great events and exertions of his life could not extinguish. In short, one is enthusiastically disposed toward the great man. With our *Goethe* he has already conversed a couple of times for rather a long while, and perhaps has thereby also given German monarchs the example that they need not shrink from recognizing and honoring their most excellent men.”

We cannot leave Knebel’s letters without returning for a moment from politics to philosophy. The publication of the *Phenomenology* was awaited by Hegel’s friends with impatience. The bookseller *Frommann* communicated it to some in sheets. When Knebel got to read the preface through *Seebeck*, he wrote to Hegel: “I have your deeply thinking

[p. 235]

spirit with admiration. What remains to me, and, as it seems, also to some friends, as a wish is that you had at times laid the fine net of your thoughts, which in places shines forth quite clear and lovely, more sensibly graspable before our dim eyes. Truly, we hold you for one of the first thinkers of our time, but we should like you to have given still more bodily shape to the spiritual power. What I say here is perhaps rash, perhaps not sufficiently supported by reasons, but you must forgive my poetic wish if I should like to see the serious drawn over also into the province of the beautiful — without, for that reason, just into a Lucretian didactic poem. Your similes are excellent, like your thoughts.”

Since the appearance of the *Phenomenology* the criticism of *Schelling* began to grow sharper, particularly on the part of his own countrymen, as the letters of *Paulus*, *Seebeck* and others to Hegel show. One now had a positive achievement of philosophy, to which one could apply, as to a new measuring rod, his works. On Schelling’s *inaugural address* in the Munich Academy of Arts Knebel wrote to Hegel on 27 November 1807: “Herr Schelling’s inaugural address I had already read, and, I cannot deny it, wished that he, with a less gigantic striving after the impossible, had taught us more about the matter. *Art* and *poetry* are now also two words with which one has grown accustomed to pronounce the impossible. Yet one finds the matter almost everywhere. It is not all so new as one sometimes thinks, etc.”

#### Critique of the German Constitution, 1806–1808.

Although Hegel could give his newspaper no leading articles, or rather was not permitted to, the political impulse nevertheless fermented mightily in him, and there arose in him, especially as his business constantly forced him in this direction, the thought of a work in which he wanted to develop in detail the condition of Germany and to lay before the public the plan of a new constitution of it. A large part of this work he worked out. But the sudden transition from Bamberg to Nuremberg in November 1808, the

[p. 236]

resumption of specifically philosophical studies, but above all the unfavorableness of the time then for the publication of such writings, may have let the work stall again. Hegel wanted to become, as it were, the *Machiavelli of Germany*. If this sounds quite un-German according to the usual conception of politics which one is accustomed to connect with the name of Machiavelli, let it be recalled that *Fichte*, on whose patriotism surely no doubt rests, was pressed onto the same path and zealously devoted himself to the study of Machiavelli. It was the infinite need of *unity* which prompted both philosophers to this. Three or four times Hegel rewrote the opening of his book, but in these alterations the first words always remained the same, namely:

#### “*Germany is no longer a state!*”

The *Empire* was *supposed*, to be sure, to be a state, but was not. A French writer had called this unwieldy body *a constituted anarchy*. Hegel had still grown up in Württemberg with the representation of the German Empire, and the knowledge of its constitution was still immediately familiar to him. The impossibility that so badly organized a mass could hold its own against the onset of a unanimous people inspired for its freedom was long clear to him, and yet he choked on the thought that Germany as Germany, as a political whole, should cease to be. The fear that it might have the fate of Italy, perhaps a still worse one, moved him deeply. As also appears from the letter of 23 January 1807 to his pupil *Zellmann*, the French power impressed him enormously. The French, he says, had put off the life of habit; the fear of death for the individual had vanished among them; politics as such seemed unable to set the Germans in motion; it was another question if *religion* came into play with them.

Hegel asked in his work whether the downfall of the German Empire must be ascribed to a lack of *bravery*, of *personal courage*. This opinion, he answered himself, is refuted by history, which on the contrary, everywhere — even in the imperial army — gloriously confirms the martial efficiency of *individuals*,

[p. 237]

Consequently the misfortune must be laid to the charge of the fragmentation of Germany and the bad leadership of the soldiers.

He asked further whether that downfall might perhaps have sprung from a *national bankruptcy*. This, he thought, was just as little the case, for, with all the bad management of the individual states, Germany did not yet know all those important problems which in other states arise from a *national debt*, the treatment of which occupies the most distinguished minds and in which even small errors could draw the most dreadful consequences after them.

Finally he asked whether perhaps a *lack* of ethical life, of *culture*, of *religiosity* could be the cause of the weakness. This, he replied, could least of all be said. Not in the *individuals*, then, but in the *mechanism of the whole* must the *corruption* lie.

This corruption Hegel now found in the fact that the German Empire still wanted to move in the *forms of the medieval feudal state*, in which the vassal as a relative sovereign had to furnish to his sovereign the contingent conditioned by treaty, the latter thus being more or less dependent on the good will of his liege man. In *actuality*, however, feudalism had long since vanished; the petty princes had in fact become sovereigns and their dependence on the Empire a mere semblance. The *conduct of war* had been entirely altered by the ever more extended use of *gunpowder*, because thereby the form of the engagement as a *duel* of the individual with the individual was sublated and the movement of the individual as a *member of a mass* had become necessary, and consequently the motley composition of an army from many kinds of contingents with different uniforms, armament, etc., had become a contradiction against the absolute instrument of death, against gunpowder. — In *financial* respect, however, the Middle Ages had still in many cases had the form of contribution in *naturalistic fashion*, whereas the modern age throughout had made the *power of money*, as the universal value of *all* things and as the *most mobile* medium, the center in this domain. — In respect, finally, of *culture* and *religion*, in the Middle Ages the

[p. 238]

latter had been of political importance and had therefore also dominated culture. From this conception the German Empire had never been able to detach itself; almost all wars had acquired a religious tinge with it; the difference of confessions had always, even against the express provisions of treaties, become a source of civil advantages or disadvantages, less of the Catholic among Protestants than of the Protestant among Catholics. In actuality, on the other hand, the thought was already firmly established of putting the state as such into no direct connection with religion and of leaving it entirely, with the exception of its supervision in a moral respect, free to itself; *there must be no state religion*.

The greatest hindrance of the Germans, he said, was their *pedantry in being in the right*. In itself, to be sure, the *awe* before right was something venerable and a noble trait of the Germans; but they too often remained standing at the *formalism* of the positive existence of a right, without subjecting the content, whether it be rational or irrational, to a critique. The *Fiat justitia aut pereat mundus* [let justice be done, or let the world perish] was genuinely German. With such pedantism the *endless supervision* of all spheres was connected, which engendered a quite *useless prolixity* of the conduct of business and a *helpless lack of independence* in individuals.

Hegel was now of the view that politics must above all take the direction of the *concentration of the power of Germany outward*, in order to be able to protect itself against the encroachments of other nations. Here he believed he could take the following measures. The army, although a composite one, must nevertheless be *uniformly trained*. Every prince should become the *born general* of his contingent of troops. Likewise the various states should form a *federal treasury*, which for its part must be indifferent to the manner in which the individual state wanted to raise the taxes for this purpose, for the main thing must remain to be able constantly to dispose of a great sum. For the *foreign* affairs a *central place*, say Mainz, would have to be fixed, in which all the federal states would have a common government. — The internal affairs of each state, however — *property*, *custom*, *education*

[p. 239]

*religion*, would have to be given free to their own peculiar development. The citizens would have to *administer* their *particular* affairs *themselves*, because only thereby could the boundless shapelessness of the internal constitution of the states diminish and the energy gathering them together outward increase. —

The first time that Hegel did a purely political work, he took the constitution of Württemberg as his subject; now that of the whole of Germany, and came with his proposals pretty much to what the *German Confederation* later wished in part to realize. The relation of Germany to the foreign powers he carried through completely in his work and immersed himself in doing so in a philosophical analysis of modern European history generally. He possessed a very detailed and minute exact knowledge of all the relations of the German Empire, which to follow him into is not the place here. But now that the general Idea from which he proceeded has been stated, some communications about the organization of the constitution of Germany may be given as perfectly intelligible.

The German Empire, he said, had been annihilated by France. “Only the memory of a former bond still leaves a semblance of union, just as the fallen fruits can still be recognized as having belonged to their tree by the fact that they lie beneath its crown, but the place beneath it, even a shadow which touches them, does not save them from putrefaction and the power of the elements to which they now belong.”

The health of a state, Hegel thought, reveals itself not so much in the *calm of peace* as in the *movement of war*, because in the latter the strength of the cohesion of all with the whole appears, how much the state has set itself up to be able to demand of them, and how much that is worth which they may do for it from their own impulse and heart. “Thus in the war with the French Republic Germany has experienced in itself how it is no longer a state, and has become aware of its political condition both in the war itself and in the peace which ended this war and whose palpable results are: the loss of some of the fairest German lands, of some millions of its inhabitants, a burden of debt on the southern

[p. 240]

half heavier than on the northern, which prolongs the misery of war far into the peace; and that besides those who have come under the rule of the conquerors and at the same time of foreign laws and customs, many states will lose what is their highest good, *to be states of their own*.”

“But what the inner causes, the spirit of these results may be, of which they are only the outer and necessary appearances — for such a reflection peace is suited, just as this reflection is in itself worthy of everyone who does not surrender himself to what happens but cognizes the events and their necessity, and by such cognition distinguishes himself from those who see only caprice and chance, for the sake of their vanity, by which they persuade themselves that they would have conducted everything that has happened more cleverly and more happily.”

“The thoughts which this work contains can, in their public utterance, have no other purpose or effect than to further the understanding of what is, and with it the calmer view, as well as a tempered bearing of it in actual contact and in words. For it is not what is that makes us impetuous and suffering, but that it is *not as it ought to be*. But if we cognize that it is as it must be, i.e. not according to caprice and chance, then we cognize also that it ought to be so.”

“Above all, the advancing time has probably afflicted the Germans with the vice of bitterly censuring what has happened. In an eternal contradiction between what they demand and what does not happen according to their demand, they appear not merely fault-finding but, when they speak merely of their concepts, untruthful and dishonest, because they put necessity into their concepts of right and duties, but nothing happens according to this necessity, and they are themselves so accustomed to this, partly that their words always contradict their deeds, partly to make of the events something quite other than they are and to twist the explanation of them according to certain concepts. But whoever wished to come to know what is wont to happen in Germany by the concepts of what ought to happen, namely by the laws of the state, would err to the highest degree; for the

[p. 241]

dissolution of the state is recognized chiefly by the fact that everything goes otherwise than the laws. Equally he would err if the color taken from these laws appeared to him truly the ground and cause of them, for precisely because of their concepts the Germans appear so dishonest as not to confess anything as it is, nor to give it out for more or less than actually lies in the power of the matter.”

From such a condition Hegel drew the conclusion that those among us are always at an advantage who are able to adapt words and concepts to one another *by force*. — The German Empire, he said, had gone to ruin because it had *isolated* itself in the fate of the world. It was not enough that a multitude of men should unite for the purpose of *defending* themselves; they must also have the intention of *resisting*. In word the latter too had been the purpose of the German Empire, but not in deed. The manifoldness of customs, culture, of the forms of the administration of justice, of the systems of taxation, of the constitution as the manner of the union of power in one center, finally of religion itself, could never be an obstacle to a state’s asserting itself as a unity outward, as history sufficiently confirms. “According to the theories of the state, to be sure, which in our times have been set up partly by would-be philosophers and teachers of the rights of humanity, partly realized in monstrous political experiments, everything else, only the most important — language, culture, customs and religion — excepted, is subjected to the immediate activity of the supreme power of the state and determined by it, so that all these sides, down to their smallest threads, are drawn in by it. That the supreme power of the state must bear the highest supervision over the internal relations of a people and over their organizations determined by chance and old caprice; that these may not hinder the main activity of the state, but that it must above all things secure the latter for itself and for this purpose must not spare the subordinate systems of rights and privileges, goes without saying; but it is a great advantage of the old states of Europe that, in that the power of the state is secured for its needs and its course, it leaves to the citizens’ own activity, in the particulars of the administration of justice, of the administration

[p. 242]

etc., a free scope, partly in regard to the filling of the officials needed therein, partly to the dispatch of current business and the administration of the laws and customs. In view of the size of the present states, *the reality of the ideal*, according to which every free man is to have a share in the deliberation and determination of general affairs, is *altogether impossible*. The power of the state must concentrate in one center, both for the execution as government and for the decision on it. If this center is secured in itself by the reverence of the peoples and sanctified in its immutability in the person of the monarch determined by a law of nature and by birth, then a power of the state, without fear and jealousy, can freely leave to the subordinate systems and bodies a large part of the relations which arise in society, and their preservation according to the law, and every estate, every town, every commune, etc., can enjoy the freedom of doing and carrying out itself whatever lies within its district.”

After this exposition Hegel goes through the sequence of the *peace treaties* which Germany had entered into with other powers, in order to show how through lack of unity it had lost ever more in territory as in sovereignty. “A country one half of which in war either beats itself about among itself, or gives up the general defense and by neutrality abandons the other to the enemy, must be torn to pieces in war and dismembered in peace; because the strength of a country consists neither in the number of its inhabitants and warriors, nor in its fertility, nor in its size, but solely in the manner in which, by a rational union of the parts into one power of the state, all this can be used for the great work of common defense.”

Hegel called the German Empire a *state of thought*, in which the *paralysis* of the transition from the Concept into reality was *organized*, so that *caprice*, under the *semblance of some right*, can *at every stage* of the execution of the resolutions set itself against them destructively. “A general ordinance is made. It is to be carried out and, in case of refusal,

[p. 243]

legal proceedings are to be taken. If the refusal to comply is not brought to court, the execution remains lying undone in itself. If it is brought to court, the judgment can be prevented. If it comes about, it is not obeyed. This thought-thing of a resolution, however, is to be carried out and a penalty imposed. Thus the order for the compulsory execution is given. This order again is not executed. So a resolution must follow against those who do not execute, to compel them to execute. This again is not obeyed; so it must be decreed that the penalty shall be inflicted on those who do not inflict it on him who does not inflict it, etc. This is the dry history of how one stage after another, which is to put a law into operation, is made into a thought-thing.”

Hereupon Hegel goes more closely into the critique of the military, financial and judicial organization of the German Empire, urges the lack of a proper distinction of the general power of the state from the particular interests, and in the course of this pours out his anger also against the extreme of the modern police state and its hierarchy of officials. “In the more recent theories, in part carried out, the basic prejudice is that a state is a machine with a single spring, which imparts the movement to all the rest of the infinite wheelwork. From the supreme power of the state all the institutions which the essence of a society brings with it are to proceed, to be regulated, commanded, supervised, directed. *The pedantic mania for determining all detail, the unfree jealousy of any arranging and administering of their own by the estates, corporations, etc., this ignoble carping at all doing of their own by the citizens* that would have no relation to the power of the state but only to some general matter, has been clothed in the garb of principles of reason, according to which not a single heller of the common expenditure, which in a country of 20, 30 millions is made for the poor, may be spent without its having been first, not permitted, but commanded, controlled, inspected by the supreme government. In the care for education the appointment of every village schoolmaster, the expenditure of every penny for a windowpane of the village school, as

[p. 244]

also of the village council room, the appointment of every gate clerk and court bailiff, of every village judge, is to be a direct emanation of the supreme government; in the whole state every morsel from the soil that produces it to the mouth is to be conducted along a line which has been examined, calculated, rectified and commanded through state and law and government.” — What sort of leathern, spiritless life will be engendered in such a modern state, in which “everything is regulated from above down — as the French Republic has made itself — is, if this tone of the pedantry of ruling can persist, to be learned only in the future; but what life and what aridity prevail in another, equally regulated state, in the Prussian, strikes everyone who enters the first village of it, who sees its complete lack of scientific or artistic genius, or does not regard its strength by the ephemeral energy to which a single genius has known how to force it up for a time.”

Hegel sums up the main problem thus: “That the state is a thought-thing lies in this, that as a state it has no power, but that the power is in the hands of the individuals, and to recognize the power reciprocally by electoral capitulations and peace treaties, and so to make it legal — this has been, since the relation of the state to the individuals became an object of treaties, the general tendency of the political character of Germany. In the working-out from crudeness to culture it came down to which of the two, the universal, the state, or the individuals, would gain the upper hand. In most European countries the state has carried off the victory completely, in some in an incomplete manner, in none, with the pretension of being a state, so imperfectly as in Germany. The condition of *barbarism* consists, namely, in this, that *a multitude is a people without at the same time being a state*, that the state and the individuals exist in opposition and in a separation. The ruler is, as a personality, power of the state, and the safeguard against his personality is again only opposition of personality. In a cultivated state there stand between the personality of the monarch and the individuals the laws, or universality. — The contradiction that the state is the supreme

[p. 245]

power and that the individuals are not crushed by it is resolved by *the power of the laws*. It is this disbelief in the power of the laws that springs from lack of wisdom, that wavers between the necessity of giving the state the highest power and the fear that the individual may be crushed by it.”

To be sure, Hegel thought, Germany would attain free legality only with great difficulty. “If all parts would gain by Germany’s becoming one state, and if, in accordance with the general culture, this need were also deeply and definitely felt, such an event has nevertheless never been the fruit of deliberation, but of force. The common mass of the German people, together with its estates, which know of nothing else but the separation of the German peoples and to which the union of them is something quite alien, would have to be gathered into one mass by the power of a conqueror, and would have to be compelled to regard themselves as belonging to Germany. This Theseus would have to have magnanimity, to concede to the people which he had created out of scattered little peoples a share in what concerns all; character enough, in order to be rewarded, even if not with ingratitude, like Theseus, to be willing to bear, through the direction of the power of the state which he would hold in his hands, the hatred which Richelieu and other great men drew upon themselves, who shattered the particularities and peculiarities of men.”

Since it was said above that Hegel with this work had wanted to become the *Machiavelli* of Germany, a few words of his about him may find room here. In his extensive discussion of Italy he finally says of him: “Machiavelli’s work remains a great testimony which he gave to his time and to his own faith, that the fate of a people hastening toward its downfall can be saved by genius. Remarkable, too, amid the misunderstanding and hatred against Machiavelli’s *Prince*, is the particular fate of this work, that out of a kind of instinct a future monarch, whose whole life has most clearly expressed the dissolution of the German state into independent states, made his school exercise on this Machiavelli and set moral set-pieces against him, the emptiness of which he himself has demonstrated, both by his manner of acting and expressly in

[p. 246]

his writings, in that in the preface to the *History of the First Silesian War* he denies to the treaties of states their binding force when they no longer conform to the best interest of a state. — Otherwise, however, the more cunning public, which could not leave the genius in Machiavelli’s works unnoticed and at the same time thought too morally to approve his principles, but meaning well wished to rescue him himself, has cleared up this contradiction honestly and subtly enough to the effect that Machiavelli had not been in earnest about it, but that the whole is a persiflage, an irony, and one cannot help paying compliments to this irony-scenting public on its subtlety.”

#### Transition to the Rectorship in Nuremberg, Late Autumn 1808.

The southern German states to the west, Baden, Württemberg, Bavaria, were, as parts of the Confederation of the Rhine, swept along by the mighty current of the French spirit to the desire and the necessity of great changes. Above all, this need was felt in Bavaria, and here again especially in the educational system. Two almost opposed elements were here dominant, the monastic-scholastic and the principle of utility. It therefore came down to providing for further progress between the extreme of the Middle Ages and of the modern age, of monkhood and of the Enlightenment, through the mediation of the study of ancient literature and language. To have initiated this step in principle is *Niethammer’s* great merit, partly through his work on the dispute between philanthropism and humanism, partly through the draft of a *Normativ* [set of regulations] for the educational institutions of Bavaria. Bavaria wanted to ascend from the general elementary schools through Realinstitute [schools for modern, practical subjects], Gymnasien and Lyceen to the universities and academies. In Nuremberg a *Realinstitut* was established, at the head of which stood *Schubert*, to whom *Schweigger*, *Erhardt*, *Kanne* and others were joined as colleagues. The Aegidien Gymnasium had until then enjoyed the direction of a veteran, L. *Schenk*, and was now, according to the latest instructions, as one expressed oneself then in Bavaria, to be *reorganized*. The rector of a Gymnasium was always to be a philosopher and

[p. 247]

to impart the instruction in philosophy as well as in religion; — a determination which, however, was properly realized only in Nuremberg, only by Hegel.

In May 1808 Niethammer, who had been called to Munich as Supreme Councillor for Studies, had first conceived the thought that such a position might perhaps suit Hegel, but he ventured, as though such a proposal might, so to speak, offend him as a demotion, to inquire of him about it only timidly at first. On the contrary, Hegel’s fullest assent followed, so that *Paulus* too, who had been transferred from Würzburg to Nuremberg as district school councillor, now took an interest in his appointment. The prospect of coming out of a precarious situation, out of an activity undertaken from the outset as merely interim, into a regular appointment, and indeed into one that would again connect him dutifully with science — this prospect was so agreeable to Hegel that almost until his arrival in Nuremberg he could not believe at all in the actuality of his new position. Paulus and Niethammer had to urge him repeatedly, since the issuing of his letter of appointment was somewhat delayed, though the appointment had already been decreed, finally to set out for Nuremberg, which then happened in the course of November 1808.

It is now very easy to say that the speculative Pegasus was here, out of necessity, harnessed to the school cart, and that, for lack of a university auditorium, Hegel contented himself with Gymnasium pupils. Yet although the activity of the lecture chair was unquestionably the most suitable for Hegel, as he indeed also turned back to it again from the Gymnasium, that judgment in its generality is nevertheless extremely one-sided. In a time in which Napoleon suppressed all freer development of the German universities because they seemed dangerous to him in particular, one still found at the Gymnasium the readiest room for more energetic action. What could Fichte, Schelling and Steffens, after all, accomplish from 1808 to 1813 precisely as university teachers? Besides, Hegel’s position at the Gymnasium was by no means foreign to his individuality. Already in his boyhood years we could observe a pedagogical tic in him. For eight years he had been a house tutor. Thus we may not regard his rectorship at the Aegidien Gymnasium merely as a refuge

[p. 248]

of necessity, but must regard it at the same time as a business which he undertook with inner gladness, as this also expresses itself in all the letters he wrote from Nuremberg. The university he indeed always keeps in view there; now his thoughts fall on Tübingen, now on Heidelberg, now on Berlin, now on Holland, according as his friends opened other perspectives to him with their wishes and hopes, but he constantly shows contentment with his provisional situation.

But more still. The rectorship, after all, contained the express stipulation of the *teaching of philosophy* and was thus, from this side, an office *homogeneous* to him. The opinion, however, that the training of the Gymnasium youth was a kind of degradation of the philosopher, forgets to take into account that Hegel, for his part, *owes* much to the Gymnasium for his philosophy. He knew nothing of that false genius which thinks itself too good to engage with the ordinary consciousness and to make itself clear to it. Behind such aristocratic airs there often hides the unconscious apprehension of how it would come to light, with determinacy and clarity, that admired profundities are in fact often highly trivial truths or even absurdities. Hegel had no need of such a fear, and with his system at the Gymnasium he made, so to speak, the *test of intelligibility*. He had to extend still further the mediation between the unphilosophical and the speculatively formed consciousness, which he had already taken more and more into account as an academic teacher. He had to determine the distinctions more sharply, bring out the essential more expressively, set aside all merely ingenious glitter, which with him too sometimes took on a mystical coloring, and, what had incidentally always been his endeavor, apply himself in terminology as much as possible to *Germanness*. Without the school of the Nuremberg Gymnasium Hegel’s depth would probably not have attained so great a clarity as it did; in this pedagogical discipline, however, he worked off all *mysterious Romanticism* and also won, through his own deed, the conviction that philosophy is absolutely *teachable*. And so this transition

[p. 249]

to the rectorship was not merely something external, but also something inwardly necessary for Hegel.

#### Hegel as Educator.

He devoted himself to his office with the fullest dedication, with untiring zeal. In *philosophy and religion* he gave instruction in all the classes. In each he altered the presentation, not only in general but, when the individuality of the pupils seemed to demand it, also in the different grades of teaching. As the numerous notebooks still left behind show, he at the beginning rewrote his lecture thoroughly for each half-year, until from the year 1812 on only partial alterations occurred. He dictated paragraphs and explained them, sharply, penetratingly, but without great outward liveliness. He did not, to be sure, read off what he said, but he had the papers lying before him and looked straight ahead, scattering snuff liberally to the right and left. The pupils had to copy out the dictation once more in a clean hand. The oral explanation they likewise had to try to take down in writing. From time to time Hegel called upon one pupil or another to read out his transcript, partly to keep attention to the lecture in suspense, partly to provide a check on what had been written down. This transcript too he sometimes had them write out fair. At the beginning of every hour he called upon someone to repeat briefly, orally, the lecture of the last hour. Anyone might ask him questions if he had not rightly understood something. In his good-naturedness Hegel permitted them to interrupt him himself in the lecture, and often a large part of the hour went to giving information in answer to such requests, although Hegel knew how to bring the questions under general points of view which he held in connection with the main subject. At times he also had a Latin exercise written on philosophical matters.

His friendliness and mildness won him unconditional trust, but one must not suppose that only this side showed itself in him. Even when he addressed the senior pupils — which flattered their self-esteem — with *Herr*, he had thereby the intention of educating them, through this form, toward that manliness

[p. 250]

along with the rest, which one does not care to miss even in a youth: toward consciousness of the responsibility of action. To approach him fully, one first had to break through a certain partition, and only diligence and ethical conduct actually succeeded in doing this. The thought that Hegel had formerly lectured on philosophy to students, that he was a celebrated author and stood in literary as well as personal intercourse with many celebrated men, tremendously impressed the pupils. But also the deep seriousness which shone through enduringly in everything Hegel said and did, the objective gravity that surrounded him, held the pupils in great reverence of him. The many-sidedness of his culture supported this impression. When teachers fell ill for a short time, he not infrequently took over their hours, and the pupils were especially surprised when he continued the instruction without more ado not only in Greek and other subjects, but also in differential and integral calculus. What he said to them on chance occasions that was out of the ordinary stuck deep. Thus he once spoke about Indian and romantic poetry when *Herder’s Cid* and the *Sakontala* were acquired for the Gymnasium library, and recommended those books, which were then also read enthusiastically. If a pupil wished to engage more closely with philosophy and asked him to name writings for the purpose, he usually referred him to *Kant* and *Plato* and warned against distraction in the reading of the popular philosophers. One must only not want to understand everything *at once*, but take time for it, read on, and count on the explanation through the further connection, etc. Polemic he avoided altogether; at most he let fall once an amusing little word about the *tedious boredom* of *Wolff’s Metaphysics*. — In the mechanical side of the conduct of business he was on the one hand painful to the point of scrupulosity, but on the other hand he also passed over much with the greatest naïveté, declaring it summarily to be *external*. Only in genuine matters of discipline was he strict to the point of inexorability. To deliver great speeches out of season, in which so many a director seeks his strength, he did not like. The art of emotional appeal was denied him, and even when he wanted for once to shake hearts, the side of the understanding stood out the more. The *playing at being students* he absolutely could not

[p. 251]

endure, pursued all such utterances with bitter censure, and also inveighed — naturally not without taking much snuff in the process — against the indecent habit of *smoking*. — The graduating pupils he had come to him, in order to lay the seriousness of their step privately to their hearts and to give them hints for their conduct at the university, which proved their worth to most.

The Gymnasium flourished gaily under his direction, as was also publicly acknowledged at its twenty-fifth jubilee, when Hegel was already in the Prussian service. There was only one point which from 1811 on produced for a time a certain ill humor against him. The reaction, namely, against the French oppression became ever more general, ever more energetic, especially after the Russian campaign. The teachers of the Gymnasium not only did not resist this spirit of vengeance, but, so far as this was legally possible, gave it support. Hegel as rector bore the greatest responsibility here and kept himself, on the whole, outwardly indifferent. In the town, especially among the teaching staff, he was held to be a friend of the French. How this is to be understood, and whether Hegel, who, like thousands already at that time with him, *admired Napoleon*, was in fact unpatriotic, we shall, after the draft for a new constitution of Germany communicated earlier, probably be able to set right without further apology. Among the Gymnasium pupils an association formed, which met at a simple symposium, read aloud German essays on topics of its own choosing, and afterwards discussed them. Hegel learned of this. He had some members of the association come to him, requested some essays, praised their scientific striving, but proposed that they should rather read Homer cursorily, as extra work, in a class of the Gymnasium under his supervision. They did not indeed dare to contradict him, and read, but without proper gladness, and continued the meetings of the association henceforth *secretly* outside the gate in country inns. — Hegel set extraordinary store by *respect for religion*. The Catholic pupils of the Gymnasium were required, according to the instructions of the government, to attend Mass *daily*, the Protestants to hear the sermon in the Aegidien church on *Sundays*, and at the half-yearly

[p. 252]

reports the confirmed pupils were asked whether in the course of the semester they had partaken of Holy Communion?

Otherwise Hegel lived quietly for himself. In hat and gray frock coat, with a good deal of white linen put on, decent but without any trace of particular care for his attire, he appeared year in, year out. One saw him little in public places. Only at the Museum was he to be found every evening, for even though he no longer wrote a newspaper, he was before as after a passionate newspaper reader. Before his marriage he associated especially with *Paulus*, as long as the latter was in Nuremberg, and with *Seebeck*, who had likewise come here from Jena. In the latter’s discoveries Hegel took the liveliest part, just as Seebeck, according to the letters of his still extant, always hastened to acquaint Hegel immediately and in the most exact detail with everything important in his work. With the teachers of the Realinstitut as well as with the professors of nearby Erlangen he stood outwardly on friendly terms. Inwardly, however, there was, among *Schubert, Kanne, Schweigger* and Hegel in particular, too wide a divergence for the connection to have been able to assume the character of any intimacy.

Hegel’s services the government recognized partly through supplements to his salary, partly by conferring on him in 1813 also the office of a *school councillor* at the city commissariat in Nuremberg, in which capacity he also had to examine candidates for the teaching profession in philosophy, which he always did with the greatest humanity, usually taking the material from the history of philosophy.

We possess, fortunately, from Hegel himself an account of his conduct of the rectorship as instructive as it is charming, in the five speeches which he delivered at the *distributions of prizes* ordered by the government and at the *dismissal* connected with them of those leaving for the university. They are printed in the *Works*, vol. XVI, pp. 133–199. There ought, however, to be prefixed to them as an introduction the speech which Hegel delivered on 10 July 1809 to his predecessor in office, the Magister Leonhard *Schenk*, at his fiftieth jubilee of service, and which stands printed in the “Notice” that the librarian *Kiefhaber* of Nuremberg published of it in 1809 in quarto, pp. 25–30.

[p. 253]

If from certain quarters so much weight is laid on the fact that Hegel wrote no morality, and in particular no pedagogy, this is one of those odious insinuations which believe they have thereby proved the truth of a philosophy to be a lie, in that they suspect it of ethical impotence. Hegel indeed turned against moral vanity, against refined Pharisaism, never against morality itself; religion, however, he did place higher still than morality. The fact that there exists from Hegel neither a textbook of morals nor one of pedagogy is perfectly true; but does there follow from it, perhaps, what people have meant to infer, namely that the Concept of morality and of education is ignored or even annihilated by Hegel? As an answer in this respect one could point to Hegel’s philosophy of right and of the state, in which those concepts are treated systematically; but into the bargain we still have those speeches which set forth Hegel’s pedagogical and well-considered views on all sides. The first, of 29 September 1809, speaks about the reform of the Aegidien Gymnasium in general and then discusses the concept of the Gymnasium as an institution of instruction whose peculiar basis is the *study of the ancients and of the grammar* of their language. In the second speech, on 14 September 1810, he develops the concept of *discipline*, proceeding from a number of particulars, the religious instruction, the military exercises for the upper class ordered by the government, private diligence, etc., and then rising to the concept of ethical formation in its connection with the scientific. On 2 September 1811 he presented the *school* as the *mean* between *family life* and *public* life. On 2 September 1813 he recommended the study of the ancients chiefly from the side that it helps to preserve the *wholeness* of the human being, while our age forces us to one-sidedness of calling, to fragmentation of our doing. Finally, on 30 August 1815, he characterized the difficult situation in which we are placed by the powerful *struggle of the new with the old*, in that the youth is easily drawn by it into a ferment in which it, without having laid a sound ground within itself, can all too soon be abandoned to ruin in an empty formalism.

[p. 254]

Hegel censures sharply the all-too-early participation of children in the distractions and amusements of adults; the art of appearing to advantage as well, he says, comes quite of itself if only culture has prepared something worthy of appearing.

As emerges from his correspondence with Niethammer, Hegel at that time wanted to write a *pedagogy of the state*. Among his posthumous papers, however, there is nothing relating to such an undertaking. Pedagogy, moreover, he took less subjectively, as the influence of the self-conscious moral and didactic virtuosity of one individual upon other individuals, than objectively, as the animation of the individual by the spirit of his family, his school, his estate, his people, his church — and it was perhaps in this sense that he wanted to develop pedagogy as pedagogy of the state. The Gymnasium director *Fr. Kapp* of Hamm had those speeches of Hegel’s reprinted in 1835, analyzed systematically, under the title: *G. W. Fr. Hegel as Gymnasium Director*. With this, however, there must be compared the review of this work by L. v. J. in the Munich *Gelehrte Anzeigen*, 1837, Nos. 184–86, from which it follows, officially as it were, that Hegel did many things still better than Kapp, in spite of his enthusiasm, had conjectured in many respects.

#### The Philosophical Propaedeutic, 1808–1812.

The words of the Bavarian Normative, already quite modernly lithographed, which were authoritative for Hegel as a teacher of philosophy, ran as follows:

“It must always be kept in view, as the chief point of view, that in this part of the Gymnasium course of study the essential task is to guide the pupils to *speculative* thinking, and therefore to lead them by graduated exercise to the point at which they may be ripe for the systematic study of philosophy, with which the university instruction begins.”

“Insofar as the graduated sequence of the philosophical preparatory study indicated in the above course of instruction (namely, to lead the contemplative study of the Ideas, in the genetic method, from the erotematic presentation to the acroamatic) may seem set too high for a

[p. 255]

portion of the Gymnasium pupils, the following order may also be substituted for it:

1) In the *lower class* the beginning of the exercise of speculative thinking can be made with the formal part of philosophy, namely with *logic*. Here attention is then to be paid chiefly to logical technique and a sufficient acquaintance with the logical laws, whereby on the one side (formally) there is opportunity enough to exercise the acuteness of the young, but on the other side (materially) the technical skill is also acquired in scientific logic which is presupposed in the other philosophical sciences. In this respect it may even be beneficial to exercise the pupils also in the logical calculus of *Lambert and Ploucquet*.

2) After this exercise on the formal object of speculative thinking, *cosmology* (according to the old division of philosophy) can be chosen, in the *lower middle class*, as the first material object of the speculative exercise of thinking, in order now to lead the young man, with his speculative thinking, to philosophizing about the world first out of himself. Since *natural theology* attaches itself to it at more than one point, the latter is to be combined with cosmology in the same course of instruction. — The *Kantian critiques* of the cosmological and physico-theological proofs for the existence of God can be used by the teachers in both respects.

3) In the *upper middle class* the young man can then, with his philosophizing, be led back into himself and *psychology* chosen as the second material chief object of the speculative exercise of thinking. The *ethical* and *juridical* concepts attach themselves to this of their own accord, and the same course of instruction extends also over these latter. — For the first part of this course the psychological writings of *Carus* are chiefly to be used; for the latter the *Kantian* writings suffice provisionally.

4) In the *upper class* of the Gymnasium, finally, the objects of speculative thinking treated singly before are put together in a *philosophical encyclopedia*.”

These regulative determinations one must know in order to judge

[p. 256]

what Hegel, through their modifications, made of them in an independent manner. He arranged the course of instruction for himself, namely, thus:

1) *Lower class*: The basic concepts of right, of morals and religion, because this material is not only immediately familiar to children but also interesting.

2) *Middle class*: a) Psychology, chiefly as phenomenology of spirit, in order to introduce the Concept of thinking as the activity of the subject, of the individual consciousness, and b) Logic, this, however, in such a way that the ontological determinations were presented more extensively, the syllogistic ones more briefly. As a rule Hegel here gave, as an appendix, great attention to the Kantian *antinomies*, in that he rightly regarded them as the chief turning points of all reflection.

3) *Upper class*. Here Hegel presented, following the Normative, the encyclopedia, but in such a way that he touched more cursorily on those points which had already found their disposal in the earlier instruction, and treated more thoroughly those which had come to speech only scantily or not at all. The syllogistic was therefore developed more extensively; the basic concepts of natural science stepped forth; the phenomenology expanded into the doctrine of spirit in general; in the ethical domain the Concept of the state was grasped more determinately, and finally, beside religion, art and, in religion, the difference of the various forms of religion was brought out.

On this course of instruction and the method of his presentation Hegel justified himself, in consequence of a request from Niethammer, in a letter, very important for his pedagogical views, of 23 October 1812 (*Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 333–348), which met with his fullest approval. The Propaedeutic itself is printed (*Works*, vol. XVIII). For Hegel’s philosophical further formation this lecture was in formal respect a decided gain, because it compelled him to weigh every word exactly for the ease of understanding and to unite the greatest possible brevity with the greatest possible determinacy. But also with regard to the content he was successful. Hegel there himself ran through, namely, all those attempts with which one afterwards sought to save oneself from the sublation of the qualitative distinction between the metaphysical and logical categories

[p. 257]

The most important of these turns was probably the following articulation given in the propaedeutic encyclopedia:

1) Ontological logic:

a) Being,

b) Essence: α) Essence in itself,

β) Proposition,

γ) Ground and the grounded.

c) Actuality.

2) Subjective logic as the science of Concept, judgment and syllogism.

3) Doctrine of the Idea:

a) Life,

b) Cognizing and willing,

c) Knowing as system.

Compared with his earlier metaphysics and logic we see here the advance that Hegel no longer let the determinations of reflection of essence, which he had placed in Jena at the head of metaphysics under the title “System of Principles,” precede the Concept of essence; and likewise no longer let the Concept of the Concept itself precede the Concept of actuality (substantiality, causality and reciprocity), but follow it as its ideal principle. In the more specific treatment the transition from the Concept of the *syllogism* to the Concept of the *end* was made by him. The Concept of the end was entirely lacking in his original metaphysics as an express category. He now called it *process*, perhaps in order to approach with this word the Aristotelian concept of entelechy. Thus he succeeded in developing the Concept of objectivity as the proper opposition to subjectivity, as *realization of the Concept*. Finally, there also vanished the name *proportion*, not quite suitable for the Concept of the dialectical method, which Hegel still used in 1806.

Above all he gained a more comprehensive and deeper cognition of the doctrine of the *Concept, judgment and syllogism*, which he had never presented at the university with particular fullness, but now worked through on all sides, seeking to make every determination vivid through examples and to confirm it.

From the still extant manuscripts of the Propaedeutic there can be seen

[p. 258]

the constantly renewed re-examination and again differently turned presentation of these moments, as well as the iron diligence directed upon them.

In another respect too it was no insignificant advance that Hegel, in the Concept of subjective spirit, got ever more positively free of the one-sided conception of it merely as *consciousness*, in that he also delved into the cognition of those determinations which, proceeding from the philosophy of nature, had been greatly neglected out of contempt for empirical psychology. Hegel too had until then presented them rather in passing in the introductions to the philosophy of spirit; now, however, he saw himself obliged to set out, with precise determinacy and in connection, the Concept of intuition, imagination, memory, language, etc. As a favor of fate it must here further be regarded that through *Schubert, Kanne* and others at the Realinstitut the *magical* life of the soul and the *night side of nature* were already at that time brought forward with so great an interest, and Hegel was thereby in a manner compelled to go into it and to investigate the true element in this sphere also. Remarkably enough, Schubert and Hegel were at that time, in an analogous position, in the same city, so near one another, while afterwards the opposition present in them developed to the most cutting extreme at Munich and Berlin.

#### Hegel’s Marriage, Autumn 1811.

In the contemplation of a human life, insight into the individual harmony of such a life, cognition of its peculiar lawfulness, is of inexhaustible charm. Having grasped it, we have become, as it were, sure of the fate of this individual, and feel the reins of the rule governing within him delivered into our hands. In Hegel the most striking characteristic trait that has become noticeable to us is the quiet *gradualness*, the *organic ripeness*. In blasé characters we often observe the *tendency* to the deed; they often bubble over with velleity and appear to us in such moments capable of the greatest. But if it is to come to the actuality of the deed, then the impotence becomes manifest. They shrink

[p. 259]

back dispiritedly and hide their powerlessness to take the last step behind the dazzling sophistry of their many-sided culture, behind a fortress of “necessary considerations.” The sturdy nature, on the other hand, shows its power precisely in the moment of decision; the accomplishing does not *fail* it, though its earlier calm could often evoke the appearance of lesser strength. The blasé man must in the end reveal his impotence, the man gathered within himself, naive, substantial, immediately self-certain, his power of victory. Hegel was such a nature, persistently progressive and surprising in fact without much noise of announcement, and so his entrance into marriage also gladdens us. At forty years old he stood here almost as much already on the boundary as when, near thirty, he became Privatdozent. But he did not stop here; he had the courage to sublate the boundary and to pass over into a new sphere with the fullest consciousness of the significance of his doing. Hegel loved with a force and purity, with an inwardness and tenderness such as only the deepest heart is capable of. His consort was the living reflection of the loveliness hidden in himself, of spirited grace, of the beauty of his disposition. The philosophers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries still paid homage to the scholastic type of celibacy: Bruno, Campanella, Descartes, Spinoza, Malebranche, Leibniz, Wolff, Locke, Hume, Kant. The last-named was in Germany the last of those bachelors and of their bad theory of marriage. Fichte was again the first world-historical philosopher who married. After him we see Schelling, Herbart, Krause, Wagner, Troxler and even Catholics such as F. v. Baader, all of them wedded. Hegel seemed, as said, almost already fallen prey to celibacy, which grieved the heart of his sister especially, who for that reason also felt an indescribable joy at his marriage.

Hegel, the philosopher, who in science had finished with the whole past of our race, married out of a many-branched family which harbors within itself a wealth of historical memories. Hegel, the simple bourgeois man, married a patrician woman, a young noblewoman; Hegel, the man of critique, the hero of the Concept, married a woman whose innermost being was so soft, so ethereal, so full of the most restless mobility,

[p. 260]

so full of flight of fancy. But precisely this difference was reconciled in the depth of both spouses; or rather, their marriage was the ever self-renewing reconciliation of these elements. He found in her, she in him, always what they needed for a reciprocal action that completes and mutually rejuvenates. *Marie von Tucher*, of one of the oldest and best-known Nuremberg families, it was whose beauty, rare culture and amiability bound our rector to an eternal union with her. Such an ardor and loftiness of feeling did this love arouse in him that he, once more becoming wholly a youth, composed the following verses to *Marie* on 13 April 1811:

Step with me upon the mountain heights, / Tear yourself loose from the clouds; / Let us stand here in the ether / In the colorless lap of light.

What opinion has poured into the mind, / Half from truth, half from delusion mixed: / The lifeless mists have dissolved, / The breath of love of life has wiped them away.

That valley of narrow nothingness down there, / Of vain toil that rewards with toil, / Bound in dull sense to desire —, / Never has your heart dwelt in it.

Out of the valley-night a higher yearning raised you, / From within there opened to you / The light of the good and the beautiful, / You took your course to the morning hill.

The splendor of the sun reddens its airs, / Indeterminate presentiment weaves / Itself, after teaching and knowing, into the fragrances / Toward the image in which longing lives.

But from it no heart beats across; / As it receives the tones of longing, / Echo sends them back soullessly — / Upon itself it remains confined.

The feelings that revel in longing / Are a flattering breath brought to the self,

[p. 261]

In the vapor the soul must wither, / Poisonous wind is this sacrificial smoke.

Behold the altar here on mountain heights, / On which the phoenix dies in the flame, / To rise again in eternal youth, / Which only his ashes win for him.

Upon itself his thinking was turned, / Had saved itself up for its own, / Now shall the point of his existence melt away, / And the pain of the sacrifice became hard for him.

But feeling an immortal striving / It drives him beyond himself: / Let earthly nature tremble, / He carries it out in flames.

Fall, then, narrow bonds that divide us, / Only a sacrifice is the heart’s purchase, / To widen me to you, you to me, / Go up in fire, what isolates us!

For life is only reciprocal life, / Which love creates in love; / Given over to the kindred soul, / The heart opens itself in its strength.

If spirit steps onto free mountain heights, / It holds nothing back of its own; / If I live to see myself in you, you yourself in me, / Thus we enjoy the bliss of heaven!

And when he had now received the firm promise, he burst jubilantly into the strings on 17 April 1811:

#### To Marie.

You mine! Such a heart I may call mine! / In your glance / To recognize love’s glance returned, / O rapture, highest bliss!

How I love you, I may say it now, / What in pressed breast

[p. 262]

So long secretly has beaten toward you, / Let it become — I may now — loud joy!

Yet poor word, the rapture of love, / As it drives and presses within / Across to the heart — to express — / Your power is limited.

I could, nightingale, envy you / For the power of your throat, / Yet nature has the language only of sufferings, / Grudgingly, made so eloquent.

Yet if through speech she to the mouth / Of love’s blessedness / Gave no power to express, for the bond / Of lovers she bestows

On it a more inward sign: / The kiss is the deeper language / In which souls reach one another, / My heart flows over into yours.

Hegel’s reverence for marriage, and the happiness he found in it, were religious in the strictest sense of the word. Hegel distinguished the absolute satisfaction of destiny from the peace which, beyond all finitude, cannot be touched by the alternation of fortune and misfortune. Ethical freedom as such was for him the first thing; how one fares in one’s *circumstances* came with him only long afterward, and he therefore also demanded strict obedience to duty, without much reflecting this way and that. On such points it occasionally came, in his time as a betrothed man, to misunderstandings and discussions, which served to disclose the innermost of his individuality. We hold it to be no profanation of his love if we make clear by an example how tenderly and at the same time how wisely he conducted himself in such cases, because, besides, it is only in this way possible for us to gain an insight into this innermost sanctuary of his own feeling and disposition. A conversation about the

[p. 263]

happiness of marriage had once agitated the lovers greatly and let very different views come forth. Hegel wrote to his bride:

“I have written to you in thought almost the whole night through! — It was not about this or that single circumstance between us that my thoughts turned, but necessarily about the whole thought: shall we then make ourselves unhappy? — It cried out from the depths of my soul: this cannot, this shall not and may not be! — It will not be!

But what I have long been saying to you presents itself to me as a result: marriage is essentially a religious bond; love, for its completion, needs a still higher moment than it is in itself and for itself alone. What perfect satisfaction means, being wholly happy, is completed only by religion and the sense of duty, for only therein do all the particularizations of the temporal self step aside which can cause disturbance in actuality, which remains something imperfect and cannot be taken as the last thing, but in which that should lie which is called earthly happiness.

Had we not spoken definitely of it the evening before, or settled that we would call contentment what we are sure of attaining with one another; — said to ourselves: ‘there is a *blessed* contentment which, considered without illusion, is more than all that is called being happy.’ — When I (to my sister) wrote the words: ‘You see from this how happy I can be for all the rest of my life with her (Marie), and how happy such a gain of a love, for which I hardly any longer made myself hope in the world, already makes me,’ — I added, as though this happy feeling and its expression had been too much against what we had spoken, still: ‘*insofar as* happiness lies in the determination of my life.’ I do not mean that this should have hurt you! — I remind you further, dear Marie, that your deeper sense, the formation of your higher self within you, has taught you this too, that in not superficial dispositions a feeling of melancholy also attaches itself to every feeling of happiness! I remind you moreover that you promised me, for whatever of unbelief in contentment might still remain in my heart, to be my healer, that is, the reconciler of my true inner being with the

[p. 264]

manner in which I am toward the actual and for the actual — too often; that this point of view gives your vocation a higher side; that I credit you with the strength for it; that this strength must lie in *our* love; — your love for me, my love for you — so expressed in particular — bring in a distinction which would separate *our* love; and love is only *ours*, only this unity, only this bond; turn away from reflection in this distinction and let us hold fast to this One, which alone can be my strength, my new delight in life; let this trust lie at the ground of everything, and everything will truly be good.

— Ah! I could still write so much, also about my perhaps merely hypochondriacal pedantry, with which I so insisted on the difference between contentment and happiness — which again is so useless — that I have sworn to you and to myself, within myself, that your happiness shall be the dearest thing to me that I have. — There is also much that passes away only by one’s not touching it, forgets itself and is undone.”

On the same subject Hegel wrote, in another note, these words, most characteristic of his disposition: “I have hurt you with some of what I say. This pains me. I have hurt you in that I seemed to reject, as principles of your way of thinking and acting, moral views which I must reject. — On this I now say to you only this, that I reject these views on the one hand insofar as they abolish the distinction between what the heart likes and what pleases it, and duty, or rather remove the latter altogether and destroy morality. But just as much — and this is the chief matter between us — I ask you to believe me that, insofar as those views have this consequence, I do not ascribe them to *you*, not to your self, that I regard them as lying only in your reflection, that you do not think them in their consequence, nor know and survey them, — that they serve you to excuse others (to justify is something else, — for what one can excuse in others one does not therefore hold permitted to oneself; — but what one can justify is right for everyone, and for us too.)

[p. 265]

With regard to me and to the manner of my declaration, do not forget that when I condemn maxims I too easily lose from sight the manner in which they actually are in the particular individual — here in you — and that they come before my eyes in their universality, in their consequence, thus too gravely, which you do not think, — still much less that they would be contained therein for you. At the same time you yourself know that, even if character and the maxims of insight are different, it is not indifferent which maxims insight and judgment have; but I know just as well that maxims, when they contradict the character, are still more indifferent in a feminine being than in men.

Finally you know that there are wicked men who torment their wives only so that, from the wives’ conduct under it, their — the wives’ — patience and love may come constantly before the men’s view. I believe I am not so wicked; but if so lovable a being as you are is never to be hurt, I could almost not be sorry for it where I have hurt you, for I feel that through the deeper intuition into your being which I have thereby gained, the inwardness and thoroughness of my love for you has been increased still more. Console yourself, therefore, also with this, that whatever unloving and unsoft may have lain in my replies disappears completely in that I feel and recognize you ever more deeply, through and through, as lovable, loving and full of love.

I must go to my lesson. Farewell — dearest, dearest, gracious Marie.

Your Wilhelm.”

The confidence of the lovers has crowned a twenty-year marriage with the happiest outcome. The wedding was celebrated on 16 September 1811. All friends and acquaintances took the heartiest part in it. *Gabler*, since he could not be personally present, sent a poem. The happy Hegel wrote to *Niethammer*: “When one has found an office and a wife whom one loves, one is actually finished with life.” — Two

[p. 266]

boys, the elder *Karl*, the younger *Immanuel*, were to heighten the happiness of the spouses.

Hegel embraced his *whole household* with a lovingly watchful care. Nothing of ingenious negligence is to be seen here, nothing of vexation over the unavoidable contact with the petty side of life. The economic affairs were handled by him with prudence, but without anxiety as without levity. Like *Schiller* he kept, after old Swabian custom, a *household calendar* in quarto format interleaved with paper. In it he conscientiously entered all expenditures for lodging, clothing, firewood, servants’ wages, furniture, amusements, wine, etc., with the exception of those relating to the kitchen. After the closing of the monthly account and the correction of the stereotyped expenditures, it was totted up how much, in Hegel’s standing phrase, remained in the *purse*. For the children a *little box for saving* was set up, after the old custom. One might say of Hegel that he was so ingenious that he could allow himself to be a Philistine too. That rendering of accounts he kept up with his own hand until his death. From the calendars kept in Berlin it also becomes evident, among other things, how often he returned the lecture fee in cash to students. Travel-penny, honor-penny and emergency-penny, as our forefathers used to say, he always kept in order. For solemn surprises of his own people on their birthdays he himself took the tenderest care.

In the household he aimed at expediency and solidity of arrangement. Elegance came only after that. In the manner of living there reigned an unpretentious frugality, which, however, in its simple decorum never had to shrink from a stranger’s glance. Unless the confinements or illnesses of his wife made it necessary, he liked to keep only one maid for service, and even in Berlin, risen to prosperity at the summit of his fame, nothing of grandeur was to be noticed in him. His dwelling was beautifully situated, but he had no anteroom, no servant; one stepped directly from the hall into his friendly room.

What he loved was to make small excursions with his family, on which he recovered from his labors. So he also drove

[p. 267]

once with his wife from Nuremberg to Munich on a visit to the *Niethammers*, who also visited him again in Nuremberg, just as the common bond of friendship was still further strengthened by godparenthoods and the like. It was an infinite joy for Hegel that he could have his *sister* with him for a time in Nuremberg. The modern nuisance of constantly having to *refresh* oneself, and, because one has not previously wearied oneself at all by work, of making a serious business out of the art of so-called recreation, was wholly foreign to him.

#### Hegel’s Relation to Those Striving alongside Him at the Time.

The position which Hegel occupies in the history of German philosophy came to appearance in his life too, outwardly, in quite a plastic manner. If he was in fact the centralizing philosopher, as which he stands at the close of his life and still more after it, he also had to take up into himself personally the whole breadth of the differences which he sublated into unity through his deed of thought, and, *without his seeking it*, to come into the most many-sided contact. Until he appeared again as an academic teacher in Heidelberg, he had alongside him, of those striving at the same time with him, the following three groups: first, the strict adherents of Schelling; second, those Schellingians who sought to distinguish themselves independently from Schelling; third, those who were beginning to incline over from Schelling or Fichte to Hegel himself. The first, such as Ast, *Kanne*, *Görres* and others, remained for the most part in philosophy at the standpoint of Schelling’s transcendental idealism and at most rose to the mysticism of the same in his treatise on freedom, through which he had wished to create a counterweight against Hegel’s *Phenomenology*. — The second sought to fill in the deficiencies and gaps of Schelling’s philosophizing in various ways: *Steffens* and *Oken* by a more determinate entering into nature; *Stutzmann* by a more comprehensive philosophy of history; *Klein* by a more exact systematics, etc. Above all, however, there emerged the need of a proper *logic and metaphysics*, which through *Krause, Klein, Mehmel*,

[p. 268]

*Wagner*, and later also through *Troxler*, sought satisfaction. *Wagner*, like Schelling and Hegel likewise a Swabian, wanted to unite the *logical* with the *mathematical* and thereby to produce a new popular, tetradically divided table of categories as a new *Organon*; an experiment which, however, remained of slight effect in very restricted circles. — Toward Hegel himself finally there wavered over those who, though satisfied neither by Schelling nor by the works of his more independent pupils, yet also did not find in themselves strength enough to strike out on a path of their own. But they only first *wavered* over to him because the *Phenomenology*, namely its preface, had indeed gripped them deeply and filled them with great trust in Hegel, but, since this was to be the *first part of the system*, they did not rightly know how they were to imagine the continuation. Since now Hegel’s *Logic* appeared only between 1812 and 16, the natural consequence of this interval was that they partly lived on, stagnating, in expectation of it, and partly sought eclectically to fuse Schellingian philosophemes with the impulse received through the *Phenomenology*, which the noble *Berger* especially undertook.

Herbart’s philosophy was at that time little noticed. His local isolation in Königsberg, as well as the late publication of his larger systematic works, contributed not a little to such neglect. From Hegel’s posthumous papers it is not evident whether he ever read a book by Herbart, much as he was accustomed to take cognizance of all interesting appearances of literature in all fields. Nor in the letters of others to Hegel is Herbart ever mentioned, although one might suppose that his call from Göttingen to Königsberg must at least have offered an external occasion for it. When Hegel was already living in Berlin, Herbart visited him on a journey, without this personal contact, however, having had further consequences.

On the other hand we meet Hegel again in reciprocal action with philosophizers whose memory has almost already vanished from our literature and of whom, above all, *Sinclair*, whose outward circumstances have already come up above, must be named. While Hegel still lived in Jena, Sinclair sought to bring his poetic

[p. 269]

attempts closer, through him, to Wieland, Schiller and Goethe, in which he was also helpful to him. Hegel’s judgment on these poems came to this, that they were not plastic enough, which gave occasion among the friends to various discussions. As a curiosity, in how later events are often foreshadowed in earlier ones, it is to be noted that Sinclair, in one of his letters, of 25 April 1806 from Homburg, mentions Hegel’s wish to obtain an appointment in Berlin in case Fichte should be allowed to go from Erlangen to Göttingen. Sinclair named to him the cabinet councillor *Beyme* and the minister von *Schulenburg* as those to whom he would have to turn, but thought that Göttingen would treat philosophy in a stepmotherly way and that Fichte would not be called there. — On 16 August 1810 Sinclair offered Hegel the post of rector and *Adjuncti Ministerii* [assistant minister] in Homburg, because the situation of the region might perhaps suit him better. Later he proposed to him *Gießen* and his own efforts on its behalf. Hegel, however, did not accept these offers, thankful as he was for Sinclair’s loyal friendship in them.

The latter was in a high degree eager about the *Phenomenology*. *Bachmann* had reviewed it with enthusiasm in 1810 in the *Heidelberg Yearbooks*, and had thereby, as Hegel acknowledged with thanks in a letter to *van Ghert* and another to his sister, rendered him an essential service, because such reproductive reviews were with us once for all the only way to insinuate to the public the existence of a work. Sinclair wrote, among other things: “I know the book so far only from a piece of the Heidelberg Journal, in which the continuation of a review is contained. From this, however, I already conclude that it is masterly and that you have said things about the essence of philosophy which had not been said before. About the whole I cannot yet judge, — but so much I already see, that your work has gone deeper than hitherto, and that I, insofar as I regard it as free thoughts on the subject, find it exemplary. Your view will certainly work very beneficially against the spirit of today’s fashionable philosophy, for nothing seems to me more unworthy of the German sense of truth, which has from of old revealed itself in thoroughness of inquiry and in honest expression, than the charlatanry

[p. 270]

of Schelling and his associates, which is nothing but absence of method and unproven chatter, hypocritically hiding behind a silly enthusiasm.”

Hegel wrote excellent letters, but was a bad letter-writer if by a good one is understood him who answers quickly and easily. He often let people wait long, and in later years was accustomed to postpone letters that were not urgent until the holiday seasons. And because in personal relations he became the more scrupulous the older he grew, he usually wrote, as soon as he went into anything more thoroughly, a *draft*. To this circumstance we owe several of his replies, also to Sinclair, since Hegel’s other letters to the latter have unfortunately been lost through an unlucky accident. In 1810 Hegel wrote to Sinclair:

“I have, to be sure, great reproaches to make to myself for the negligence with which I did not reply sooner to your friendly invitation, which I received from you some years ago in Bamberg; all the more gratifying was it to me to see from your recent letter that this silence did not vex you and that you preserve the same sentiments toward me, and moreover remain true to philosophy and live, and continue to live, quite earnestly in it.
