The more immediate occasion you had for writing to me, namely to open and offer me the prospect of a position near you, I acknowledge with hearty thanks. I am professor of the philosophical preparatory sciences at the local Gymnasium and rector, and have besides the hope of coming in time to a university; in this I have what is personally the most excellent thing to me, a fixed career, and otherwise, at least for the most part, an official occupation connected with my study. If I threw away these advantages, or gave them up for greater ones, I should again bring a disturbance into my outward doing, which would set me back for a time. It would indeed be nice if we lived near one another, recapitulated everything together, drove ourselves through new things with one another. Do come once to visit our old Nuremberg. Your situation presumably permits you more readily to make an excursion than mine does me. I do not know whether you have already seen our regions, Franconia, and our Bavarian condition

[p. 271]

close up; it always has its curiosities. In the meantime, until I speak with you in person, I await your philosophical work. You have made a capable beginning, as in the earlier career with three tragedies, so in the philosophical one with three volumes. I look forward to it with great expectation, to see whether you are still the obstinate Fichtean and what role the progress to infinity plays in it. That you want to have it printed at your own expense — against that I would by all means advise you, if it were still time and if I had any advice to give you about it; you can only suffer considerable damage by it. I am sending you, finally, a copy of a beginning of my own, which I made some years ago. See for yourself what you want to make of it; it is a concrete side of spirit that is dealt with in it; the science itself is still to follow. How will your free, not to say anarchistic nature receive the Spanish boots in which I let spirit move? —

Yet I see that you, too, find fault with the want of method in the twaddle that is supposed to be philosophical, which is the order of the day — or was, for it seems to be running out by now. I am a schoolman who has to teach philosophy, and perhaps hold for that very reason that philosophy, as well as geometry, must become a regular edifice, one that is teachable, as well as the latter. But the knowledge of mathematics and philosophy is one thing, and the mathematically inventive, procreative talent, like the philosophical, another. My sphere is to invent that scientific form or to work on its elaboration.

The hero’s death that your friend *Zwilling* died has moved me greatly. To your lady mother, who has the kindness to remember me, I ask you to convey my most respectful regards. Also *Molitor*, who was once so obliging as to send me an essay of his on history, which I, however, in my usual dilatoriness, left unanswered, and for which I can only apologize, I ask you to greet likewise, as well as *Hölderlin*. Greet for me also the high Feldberg and Alken, toward which I looked across so often and so gladly from unhappy Frankfurt, because I knew you at its foot. Farewell!”

[p. 272]

In the spring of 1811 Sinclair sent his work to Hegel. He proceeded from *doubt* as the middle hovering between certainty and uncertainty, between truth and untruth. The mediation of these opposites remained subjective with him, in that he carried the relation of the I to itself, to things and to God through a multitude of determinations, which were regarded by him merely as moments of cognition. Sinclair relapsed into Fichteanism. He took into his system nature in all its manifoldness, and likewise will, art and religion; but in this universality he remained without genuine objectivity, inasmuch as he did not sublate the Concept of the I itself. His investigation of the particular was acute, original, pervaded by the deepest earnestness of striving and by high general culture; but it fell apart into countless differences which, to be sure, were all *related* to the I, but with it attained only a *formal identity*. Hegel’s *Phenomenology* therefore satisfied him extraordinarily through its Preface; all polemic against the want of method in philosophizing corresponded perfectly to his search for the right method. Of the book itself, however, he could appropriate only the beginning, up to the Concept of self-consciousness. What came further was enigmatic to him in its grounding, and he hoped, since the *Phenomenology* could have only the character of an isagoge [introduction], to gain more insight from the further execution of the system. The *beginning* of philosophy caused him great difficulty. In his opinion *doubt* led immediately out of *life* into science, and just so back out of science into life. On this important point Hegel wrote him the following interesting lines:

“I see well that I have a hard position against you, since in you I have to do not only with a philosopher but also with a jurist, who leads me through the course of procedure, its exceptions, cautions and *vitiorum* [defects]. I must see how I get on. Provisionally, however, I rejoice first at the friendly reception which my reply has found with you. I at least wanted to make a beginning of fulfilling your desire, and, however incomplete

[p. 273]

what I said about it was, I nevertheless see that it has had the result that you have set up very interesting and goal-directed viewpoints, the discussion of which would admittedly require a more extensive elaboration. Yet you yourself concede that my epistolary explanations may be of a fragmentary and desultory kind, in the manner of a touching, yet more intensive conversation; and this is the more agreeable to me as you do not thereby think the oral dispensable, and as I wish not to weaken the desire for a personal reunion thereby, but rather to heighten it.

We have begun with the beginning, as is fitting, and thereby conducted ourselves methodically enough. But I hold in general that, however much trouble the beginning in philosophy is wont to cause, and rightly causes, one should on the other side not make so much of it either. Foolishly, non-philosophers above all demand a beginning that is an Absolute, against which they cannot at once prattle, an irrefutable *primum*; — foolishly, or rather cunningly — for they would have to have been dropped very hard on their heads if they did not know in advance, with absolute certainty, that one can bring them nothing against which they could not bark and bring in the wisdom of their soundly reasoning understanding; and it would show little prudence in a philosopher if he let himself be deceived or seduced into wanting honestly to make such a beginning. For the beginning, precisely because it is beginning, is imperfect. Pythagoras demanded four years of silence from his pupils. At least the philosopher has the right to demand of the reader so long a silence of his own thoughts until he has gone through the whole. He can assure him in advance that what he finds to object to, he himself knows longer and better; that he will himself let it arise in its time and appear at its necessary place; that his whole philosophy itself is nothing other than a combating, refutation and annihilation of the beginning. — I agree with you entirely, to be sure, that one may not begin at random, but that the beginning is essentially the beginning of philosophy. I therefore demand for the beginning even more than you, namely, that it be itself already philosophy in deed and fact

[p. 274]

and avow itself as such, hence more than merely the need of philosophy, but also *no more* than that which it can be as the *beginning* of philosophy. Those who right at the beginning have the Idea of philosophy itself, the Absolute and our Lord God in all his glory, are admittedly poorly informed. *Doubt*, I grant you, is a great and worthy beginning. But can one not charge it with the *vitium subreptionis* [fault of surreption], that its treatment gives itself out as only the philosophical need and yet is already itself a philosophizing? Charge, that the analysis of doubt in its *premiers élemens* [first elements], whereby a contradiction presents itself in it — in that it poses innocently, as if it were not yet philosophizing — really only wants to smuggle in the philosophizing? But smuggling in is forbidden by imperial decrees, and a court of justice would have to recognize in that unprejudiced doing itself already a *métaphysique* or *idéologie* and, moreover, condemn the philosopher for smuggling and for the *vitium subreptionis*, and that by right. — In another respect you grant that you take up doubt first as a fact, and I too hold that the beginning can have only the form of a fact, or better of an *immediate*; for precisely for that reason it is beginning, because it is not yet *progress*. Only progression brings about something of the kind that is no longer immediate, but mediated through another. Doubt, however, according to its *content*, is rather the opposite of all fact or immediacy. It is already far more than a beginning, the *media res* [middle of the matter] between beginning and end. I do not know whether this is not at once a *vitium sub- et obreptionis*?

Yet I break off here, in order to thank you for the friendly sentiments which the close of your letter contains. As for my wishes, I have none beyond the thought that you have. My sole and last goal is to be a teacher at a university. Some hope was held out to me at Erlangen. The senate there proposed me, but with us nothing comes to pass. Here I have a salary of 1200 florins and something over. Here we have so far not got out of organizing and formalism. These present noisy circumstances of the age, what do they give, where all money is turned to other

[p. 275]

needs, by way of hope that much can be expended on the sciences, above all on philosophy and metaphysics? Even if a ministry has an interest in having good jurists, physicians, perhaps also good theologians — for the reason that in their professional life they find themselves so greatly hindered by mediocrity — how few know that the study of philosophy constitutes the genuine foundation of all theoretical and practical culture? At Gießen the post is filled. Philosophy in any case counts as something outlived. For a professor of philosophy one deems him capable who is outlived and has learned nothing proper, has qualified himself for nothing better. The house tutors of the ministers are wont to be promoted to such posts.”

Against the reproach of a *vitium subreptionis* Sinclair sought to defend himself in his letters, but hoped, since the correspondence on his controversy with Hegel seemed too prolix, all the more for a personal meeting with him. The war that soon afterwards broke out again, however, tore him into its confusion, and after its end he died unexpectedly quickly at the Congress of Vienna. Now his lofty and earnest striving is already forgotten!

In relation to Sinclair it had therefore been especially the Concept of method that was at issue; in the correspondence with others other viewpoints appeared. Hegel got into a correspondence, in particular, with *Windischmann* and *Thaden*, who contrasted with one another to the utmost, all the more so the less probable it is that the one letter-writer knew anything of the existence of the oppositional correspondence. In esteem and enthusiasm for Hegel the two men stood equal, but in their views it is impossible to contradict each other more glaringly. How Hegel for his part conducted himself toward these extremes can be seen only incompletely, because for that an insight into his answers would necessarily be required, which, a few drafts excepted, can be inferred only defectively from the reports of the letter-writers themselves. The one of these correspondences arose in 1810, the other in 1815; the one extended to the founding of the Berlin Yearbooks, the other to the appearance of the *Philosophy of Right*; the one

[p. 276]

had as its basis Catholicism and medicine; the other Protestantism and political economy.

From Aschaffenburg, where he lived as a physician, *Windischmann* first wrote to Hegel on 27 April 1810. He felt very depressed at that time; a hypochondriac mood had taken possession of him; he wanted to throw off his whole former life and begin an entirely new one. The *Phenomenology* had shaken him too in his innermost being, and he wrote to Hegel about it: “The study of your System of Science has convinced me that this work will one day, when the time of understanding comes, be regarded as the elementary book of the liberation of man, as the key to the new Gospel of which Lessing prophesied. You understand, of course, what I mean to say by this. But recognize also what this work is to me, and that few have felt it so deeply. I wanted to say this aloud and publicly, and could only hint at it, since the admission of my *whole* review in the Jena Literary Gazette was denied me, etc.”

Windischmann therefore attached himself to Hegel and invited him to visit him at Aschaffenburg. He wanted to write a work on *magic* and to present in it the *enchantment* of man by nature, as well as his *disenchantment* through culture, the permeation and transfiguration of nature by spirit. But as often as he set about it, he was seized with great fear, in the foresight that he would have to do in it with the most singular and most disreputable thing in man, and asked Hegel what he should do. The latter advised him to let the whole matter lie for the time being, which advice Windischmann also found sound. Later, however, he pursued this direction with constant reference to the Roman Catholic Church and its exorcistic doctrine of the sacraments. As he expounded in a special writing on the connection of *religion* with *medicine*, he wanted to reawaken in the physician the *priest*, a tendency that has gradually been developed within German Catholicism up to the monkish extreme. Like *Schubert*, *Eschenmayer*, *Passavant*, *Ennemoser*, Windischmann saw in somnambulism a *higher* state, freer in spirit, and, like them, he traced

[p. 277]

in the oldest traditions of the peoples the remains of that original, *paradisal* wisdom which man is supposed to have possessed before the Fall. In his letters to Hegel he always showed him the greatest love and veneration, especially since he had been appointed professor at Bonn. Their *confessional difference* he touched upon only with great delicacy, and consoled himself about this point, so important to him, always with the thought that Hegel, so far as he understood him, nevertheless believed in the *personal Christ*. In the notes to his translation of de *Maistre’s Evening Hours* he expressed himself hopefully about this, and felt himself particularly gladdened by Hegel’s review of *Göschel’s Aphorisms on Absolute Knowing and Not-Knowing*, because that belief seemed to him unquestionably expressed in it.

There was something soft in Windischmann, almost mawkishly beautiful-souled. On 17 October 1825, for example, he closed a letter with these words: “May I tell you that I remember you daily in my prayer? It is indeed the best that we can do for one another. Include me, then, a little in the inner closet of your heart, which is hidden from many, but to me not at all unknown.” — Hegel tolerated this pietistic Catholicism with friendly forbearance and showed Windischmann all manner of kindness. But when the latter’s *Philosophy in the Progress of World History* came out, Hegel believed he discovered in it a kind of plagiarism from his lectures on the philosophy of history, and expressed himself bitterly about it publicly in his lecture course. Against this Windischmann sought, in a letter of 1 August 1829, to defend himself at length and candidly, and without giving up his friendship. As early as 1813, he said, he had gone quite the same way; he had already had 23 sheets of a work, which several friends had also seen, printed, but had withdrawn them again because the further elaboration did not satisfy him; often already he had marveled at the great agreement that prevailed between his ideas and Hegel’s, even down to the expression, which, however, was perfectly comprehensible to him in men who pursue objective truth, and the like.

Quite different was Hegel’s relation to *Thaden*, estate owner of *Syndruphof* and Danish house-bailiff in *Flensburg*.

[p. 278]

He is one of those remarkable men in Angeln who are really peasants, but at the same time *philosophers*, and about whom *Steffens* in his *Memoirs*, V, 272 ff., gives interesting closer information; *Hülsen*, *Müller* and even *Berger* also belong to this circle; for the wider philosophical connection compare *Rosenkranz*, *Geschichte der Kantischen Philosophie* [History of the Kantian Philosophy], p. 421 ff. Instead of Windischmann’s inclination to lose himself in a mystical turbidity and to take the dreamy bliss of ecstatic states for the highest clarity, we meet here a sharp, bright thinking, which rather succumbs to the danger of abstract intellectualism. Instead of Roman churchliness we meet a self-confident Protestantism, which will not believe without knowing what and why it believes. Instead of the passive weapon of prayer there appears the vigor of seizing action; instead of the tendency to make social relations churchly and to subject them to obedience to priestly command, rather the direction toward political maturity and a manly independence certain of itself; finally, instead of the predilection for ingenious but mystical expressions, a striving for the widest possible popular dissemination of science, for clarity and Germanness of presentation. It was therefore above all the *Logic* that struck home with Thaden and seemed to him to realize the long-sought *philosophy without epithet*. He wrote about it, among other things, on 27 August 1815: “Your Logic is the book of books, a perfected masterpiece of the human spirit — and yet, as it seems, little known, and at least publicly not yet appreciated at its true worth by any single writer. The three known reviews are partly simple-minded, partly worthless — and since *Windischmann* too, the highly cultivated, has condemned himself by the very judgment of the Lord, the Jena Literary Gazette will also bring little of consequence to light on this subject. The next consequence of this will be that this book will be known and understood only when our children are as old as we are — meanwhile the great and the mighty go on in their caprice. This mischief would be considerably curbed if your doctrine could be still more widely disseminated. As your cause now stands, you are probably in danger that the continuation will no longer be printed

[p. 279]

because the publisher cannot even cover the printing costs. — It seems to me therefore useful and necessary, in accordance with the above presupposition, that you let the practical part of your *Logic* appear in another form. I therefore propose to publish a *journal* under the title: *Journal of Practical Philosophy*, and to continue in it in the manner begun.”

Immediately before his departure from Nuremberg for Heidelberg, Hegel answered this proposal, which was further motivated at length by the fact of the general contempt for everything speculative, according to a draft of the letter still extant, as follows:

“As I first return the friendly and hearty greeting, just as friendly and hearty, which you, my very highly esteemed sir, already offered me a year ago, the next thing must be to say something about the fact that I have let this reply wait so long. Seek the cause in nothing other than in the desire not to answer your friendly sympathy with my philosophical endeavors with a letter, so to speak, empty of deeds.

It has been most gratifying to me, who have lived very cut off from literary connection and believed I had carried on my philosophical authorship virtually in solitude, to hear from so distant a region a voice that bears witness to so warm an interest in me. On receiving your letter I congratulated myself that what I have printed was not merely a business between me and my publisher, and that it had found a spirit that it addressed, who even shows me useful counsels and ways to make what I have worked out better known and more effective in a more generally useful form. Having put myself in a position now to complete the third part of my *Logic*, I wanted to report this to you when it had come to public appearance. This happened at the beginning of summer, and thus one of your wishes was fulfilled. Since then other prospects have attached themselves to it, whose decisive development I wanted to await in order to give you a report of them. I received a call to Heidelberg, which I accepted, and hence could no longer enter upon a call to Berlin, which arrived somewhat later,

[p. 280]

just as I must also decline an appointment to Erlangen made since then by my government hitherto.

I see from this that the need for philosophy is again drawing closer also to the higher authorities, and that I too have not been forgotten. A teaching post at a university is the situation that I have long again wished for. Such a position is, according to our customs, the almost indispensable condition for procuring entry and dissemination for a philosophy, just as it also affords the only kind of living conversation face to face, which for its part exerts on the form of writing a quite different influence than mere representation, and I promise myself from this side a greater possibility of achieving something more satisfactory in writings.”

Let it be permitted, in order to conclude here the depiction of the relation between Hegel and Thaden, to anticipate the course of time somewhat. Thaden’s enthusiasm for Hegel reached its peak when the latter published the *Encyclopedia* and reviewed the Proceedings of the Württemberg Estates in the *Heidelberg Yearbooks*. But from here on he gradually became more dissatisfied and could not reconcile himself especially with many points of the *Philosophy of Right*, because through it, and above all through the defense of primogeniture contained in it, he believed the cause of political progress too greatly endangered. He therefore played the candid, sharp censor of Hegel and expressed himself with manly bluntness. Thus he wrote, for example, on 26 April 1818: “What is your friend *Schelling* doing? He was in his time a capable worker in the vineyard of the Lord. Is he already so weary that he can no longer pronounce himself on your philosophy, or really on philosophy? — The greatest misfortune for a philosopher is arrogance. Has he too been seized by this sickness?” — Thaden believed he could discover in Hegel the author of several critiques in the Vienna Yearbooks, on *Fries*, *Schopenhauer* and others, but was entirely mistaken in this. He made proposals for reviews, plans for the popularization of speculation, warned against this and that, demanded prudence of conduct, recognition of Voss’s polemic against crypto-Catholicism, and showed much desire for a moral-pedagogical supervision of the philosopher.

[p. 281]

On account of *Ancillon* he wrote, for example, on 22 January 1820: “Ancillon must not be criticized by you, not even mentioned in a note, 1) because he lives with you under one roof; 2) because he has more influence than you; and 3) because he is beneath all criticism.” — And on account of *Schleiermacher* he admonished: “Do not fall out with Schleiermacher; it would certainly greatly harm your good cause. I hear that the young people who attend your lectures quarrel violently with those who attend Schleiermacher’s; do what you can to damp these wanton quarrels. For the good and the clever must in our days hold together even more closely than in Luther’s times, as our opponents do, from the mystical enthusiast to the solid Jesuit; otherwise for a long time not merely the best but everything is lost.”

With another of these North German peasant philosophers, with *Berger* in *Seekamp* near Kiel, who died as professor at Kiel, Hegel had stood since the Frankfurt period in friendly relation. Berger behaved not merely critically, like Thaden, but went productively into the whole of science, as the extensive work left by him, *Grundzüge der Wissenschaft* [Outlines of Science], creditably proves. He brought it, however, only to a syncretism of Kantian and Schellingian speculation; to the latter he paid homage more in the science of nature, to the former more in that of the practical and religious. In the Concept of the universal he was not abstract, and in that of the individual not concrete enough. In presentation he united the flow of Steffensian fluency of speech with the visible effort toward the determinacy and genetic sequence of Hegelian dialectic. But here too only a half-measure resulted, which constantly attracts, because it rests on thorough knowledge and earnest striving, but in spite of all deliberateness and elegance soon wearies, because one does not see oneself truly advanced. Berger’s writings, however great the respect they deserve, are therefore, just like Sinclair’s, forgotten. The *Phenomenology* had deeply gripped him too. There lived in Berger something enthusiastic, a longing for the ethical improvement of the human race, a passionate humanity, a lay priestliness in the noblest sense of the word, such as is often peculiar to cultivated North Germans

[p. 282]

and also expresses itself with emphasis in Berger’s letters to Hegel. Thus he called out to him: “And now, in peace and friendship, therefore to philosophy, which is the highest and holiest muse of us all, and which as such also gives to friendship itself its eternal and highest consecration, as indeed friendship has wholly in *truth* its essence and the sole fresh source of its life.” —

That philosopher among those striving alongside him who in fact constitutes, in every respect, the middle term between Schelling and Hegel, *Solger*, came into contact with Hegel only when the latter became his colleague in Berlin. Remarkably enough, Solger, as we shall hear later, himself proposed him, and died already after Hegel had been in Berlin only a year.

Of his pupils whom he had had in Jena, it was a foreigner, the Netherlander *van Ghert*, who was to gladden him in Nuremberg with proofs of the most faithful attachment, and also further to devote to him all manner of kindnesses with ever the same disposition. Van Ghert had become *Advocat en commis by hët Ministerie van Eeredienst en Binnenlandsche Saken* [advocate and clerk at the Ministry of Worship and Interior Affairs] and later obtained a not insignificant position at Brussels. When he heard of the consequences of the battle of Jena and of the fate of Hegel thereby partly conditioned, he wrote to him from Amsterdam on 4 Aug. 1809:

#### Most honored sir and friend,

“Penetrated with the holiest feeling of respect and friendship, I venture to send you these lines. A sad piece of news from Heidelberg concerning your circumstances has so utterly cast me down that I can think of you only weeping — and since everything that concerns you interests me more than the whole world, I may no longer hesitate to inquire after your present situation.

It is reported to me, namely, that you are utterly ruined, that for this reason you have been obliged to write the Bamberg Newspaper and that you have now had to accept a conrectorship there. Not believing that the best men of Germany take so little interest in science that they would let true philosophers starve, or give them posts,

[p. 283]

which are suited only for meager heads, I really do not know what I am to make of the above-mentioned news. — On the other hand, I cannot comprehend either how it comes about that the second part of your divine *Phenomenology*, together with the philosophy of nature, does not appear. — However that may be, fear has mastered me, and I shall have no rest until you have the kindness to honor me with a letter from yourself. — If you are really as unfortunate as the reports say, then I could at times be of assistance to you in my fatherland. The universities will soon be reorganized, and if you should perhaps have a mind to become professor in Holland, where, however, up to now at least, the lectures are held in Latin, then I would spare no trouble to see to it that you obtained a good post. — I am *Doctor juris* [doctor of law] and *Commis* [clerk] at the Ministry *van Eeredienst* [of Worship] in Amsterdam. The minister, whom I know very well and who does a good deal on my representation, will call several professors, and so I could always propose you. — The annual salary is 4000 Dutch florins.

Although I must confess that up to now it looks very gloomy and nocturnal in my fatherland, and that one does not find even the slightest need of philosophy, I still hope that this may soon improve and that my countrymen may leave the low standpoint on which they have stood for so long. Up to now, to be sure, philosophy is still an abomination to them, and they call reasonable only those who mock at it. Above all they vent their fury against the Germans, or however they name everything, against the Kantian philosophy, of which they know nothing but a few poor fragmentary translations. — Spinoza, who was always an atheist, one may now at least praise without being branded a heretic, and enlightenment has already infected many.

If it is true, as I have been assured, that you do not have your books republished because the payment of the German booksellers is too low, then have the kindness to write me how much you demand per sheet, and I shall see whether the German bookseller *Brockhaus* in the Industrial Office of this city can meet your demand. He has a very good correspondence and seems to pay quite a lot for books

[p. 284]

He has published the *Divina Commedia* [Divine Comedy] by *Dante*, translated, *ni fallor* [if I am not mistaken], by *Kiesewetter*. — Do you know this man, and do you think he is in a position to translate the book? In the hope that you will not take this letter amiss and will soon honor me with your answer, I have the honor to commend myself to your dear friendship.”

Van Ghert occupied himself much with animal magnetism and also communicated to Hegel diaries of his cures. He also presented to him in Nuremberg a beautiful edition of Jakob Böhme in two folio volumes. Hegel urged him to investigate whether he could not turn up some manuscripts of Spinoza’s, but apart from the manuscript of the Hebrew grammar he found nothing more. The most interesting of Van Ghert’s letters to Hegel is printed in the latter’s *Works*, vol. XVI, pp. 475–83.

#### The Logic, 1812–1816.

Around Nuremberg, alongside the avenues, a deep moat runs everywhere. Behind the moat rise the mighty walls, interrupted from time to time by still mightier towers. If one enters the city, this contrast appears again everywhere and takes on the most manifold shapes. Straight and crooked, broad and narrow streets, high-lying and low-lying quarters of the town, dwarfed and again gigantic buildings alternate with one another. Here such a compression of the houses that one can see the sky only upward, there again the widest view onto the flat plain, from which, however, the proud castle rises once more. In the houses themselves this character repeats itself. Firmly joined, massive, they have outside so many projections at the gable, so many balcony-like protrusions; inside, by contrast, so many cozy nooks and galleries, that such a house is again a world for itself. The whole city has in the highest degree the character of contemplative sensibility. In the midst of a flat field it refreshes by its architectural elevation and depression. Of Roman origin, it makes up almost the geographical center of Germany, up to which on the one hand the transplanting of Slavic farmers advanced, while on the other hand the core of the Frankish

[p. 285]

stock bordered here. This stock has something choleric, which passes over into the light-blooded; with its zest for life and briskness there is united here the imitative docility of the Slav, to which Nuremberg owes much success in its industrial undertakings. The social bustle of present-day Nuremberg Hegel described in a humorous letter to Knebel in 1810, loc. cit. In this central city of inland Germany Hegel completed his *Logic*, which in the element of the purest abstraction piled up the tower-buildings of the eternal categories. The preface to the first volume is signed in March 1812, that to the third in July 1816.

This work now took the place of the second part of the *System of Science*, of which he had given the *Phenomenology* as the first, but was, for philosophy, apart from the Concept of the formation of consciousness, itself the first moment of the whole. Through the *Logic* the *Phenomenology* therefore itself first became rightly intelligible, because the former presented pure knowing in itself, not, like the latter, knowing in relation, and gave an extensive example of the method which Hegel had demanded as the only right one. He had gained the conviction that, while all the other sciences had progressed, logic and metaphysics had remained comparatively behind. Indeed, what formerly was called metaphysics had been rooted out root and branch and had vanished from the ranks of the sciences. As remarkable as it would be if for a people, for example, the science of its constitutional law had become useless, it would be at least as remarkable if a people lost its metaphysics. He compared the strange spectacle of seeing a *cultivated people without metaphysics* to a temple otherwise variously adorned, but without a Holy of Holies. With the *ignoring* of the thoroughgoing change which spirit has accomplished in itself, it is by now beginning to give out in the scientific sphere as well; the ferment, however, in which it is chiefly a matter for spirit of acquiring and asserting the principle in its undeveloped intensity, makes way for the higher demand that it become science. Thus in the logical sphere too one must begin *from the start*. As the kernel of the science of the same he set forth the *immanent* development of the *Concept*, its *ideal* movement, the absolute method of

[p. 286]

knowing and at the same time the immanent soul of the content itself. On this self-constructing path alone, he asserted, is philosophy capable of being objective, demonstrated science. The development of all natural and spiritual life rests solely on the nature of the *pure essentialities* that make up the content of logic. The content that is missed in the logical forms is nothing other than a firm foundation and concretion of these abstract determinations, and such a substantial essence is wont to be sought for them outside. But logical reason is itself the substantial, and it is not the fault of the object of logic if it is supposed to be devoid of content, but solely of the manner in which it is grasped. As *science*, truth is pure self-developing self-consciousness and has the shape of the self, that the in-and-for-itself-being is the known *Concept*, but the Concept as such is the *in-and-for-itself-being*.

This objective thinking is, then, according to Hegel, the *content* of pure science. It is therefore so little formal, it so little lacks matter for an actual and true cognition, that its content is rather solely the *absolutely true* as the *absolute form* itself. Logic is accordingly to be conceived as the *system of pure reason*, as the realm of pure thought. This realm is the truth as it is *without veil* in and for itself. One can therefore express oneself so, Hegel meant, that this content is the *presentation of God* as he is in his *eternal essence* before the creation of nature and of a finite spirit.

The *theologians* took this elevation of the Logic into a speculative theology very ill of Hegel. They have been astonished that the Concept of God, if one abstracts from nature and history, should coincide with the Concept of the logical Idea. They have quite overlooked that Hegel does not assert that the Concept of God in this abstraction is the complete, *final* Concept of God, but that he has rather always set up, beyond this, the Concept of *absolute spirit* as the also absolute Concept of God. Hegel is, however, perfectly right in saying that for God, in so far as he does not reveal himself in a nature and a world of spirits, no other determinations remain than those absolute

[p. 287]

abstractions of being, of essence and of the Concept. The theologians themselves confirm this when in pure theology they treat of the being, the essence, the infinity, the substantiality, the power, the teleology of God. But in that Hegel asserted the absoluteness of the logical determinations and claimed for the Concept of the Logos the same dignity of the Idea as for its forms, nature and spirit, he also threw the *logicians* into astonishment, who to be sure were wont to declaim on the indispensability of their science, but at the same time to regard its determinations only as *forms of our subjective intelligence*, and who recoiled unwillingly from the demand to grasp the Concept as an in itself absolute self-subsistence, as an αὐτοκίνησις [self-movement]. The *real sciences*, finally, fell into the misunderstanding as if Hegel made light of the particularity of their content, as if he were concerned only with the *logical element* in it. They saw in many of his utterances, in which he depicts the *dialectic* of the Concept as the moment on which scientific truth absolutely depends, a sacrifice of the *specific wealth* of nature and of spirit. Such a bare negation of the concrete never entered Hegel’s mind; to be sure, according to him the logical sublates itself into nature, as nature into spirit, which then again in its thinking grasps the simple logical categories for itself, but nature and spirit do not *volatilize* themselves into the logical with him. Against nature and against spirit the logical is to be asserted only as absolute *form*, although for itself, as *content*, it does not lack absoluteness and by virtue of its necessity stands entirely on a par with the concrete in the narrower sense.

From the standpoint of the particular sciences one could therefore least of all find one’s way in Hegel’s *Logic*, because one would not at once think the beginning, the *Concept of being as such*, but kept looking behind this absolute abstraction for a particular substantiality, *a being*. Being was supposed at once to be again a something, *an existent*. From this side one therefore busied oneself with the Logic in the usual way, by complaining of its *terminology*, which was said to be so abstruse and unusual, just as it had earlier been done with the Kantian *Critique*

[p. 288]

This comfort, of being able to reject philosophy on account of its bad, unclear expression, betrayed, in Hegel’s case too, really only the ignorance of the accusers, for Hegel had left his terminology either *entirely German*, following the track which our language had already entered in the fourteenth century in the speculative, as when he spoke of *essence* and the like, or else he had modeled his German designations on *Greek* patterns in *Plato* and Aristotle; for *being-for-itself*, *being-other*, *being-in-and-for-itself*, *self-identity*, etc., are all in accordance with ancient usage, only that this was often still much bolder, as the τὸ τι ἦν εἶναι and the ἐντελέχεια of Aristotle notoriously show; (the adverb ἐντελεχῶς occurs only once in Plato, *de legg.* 10, p. 905).

The spiritlessness in the usual treatment of logic lies, according to Hegel, especially in this, that its determinations hold in unmoved fixity and are brought only into *external relation* with one another. He said: “Because in judgments and inferences the operations are chiefly reduced to and grounded on the *quantitative* aspect of the determinations, everything rests on an external difference, on mere comparison, and becomes a wholly analytic procedure and conceptless calculating. The deriving of the so-called rules and laws, of inferring above all, is not much better than a fiddling with little rods of unequal length in order to sort them according to their size and combine them — like the playful occupation of children of searching together from variously cut-up pictures the fitting pieces. — One has therefore not without justice equated this thinking with reckoning and reckoning again with this thinking. In arithmetic numbers are taken as the conceptless, which has no meaning beyond its equality and inequality, i.e. beyond its wholly external relation, and which is a thought neither in itself nor in its relation. When it is mechanically calculated that three quarters multiplied by two thirds makes a half, this operation contains about as much and as little thought as the calculation of whether in a figure this or that kind of inference can take place.”

He therefore showed that only the consciousness of the form of the

[p. 289]

inner self-movement of the content, of which he had set up an example in the Concept of consciousness itself in the *Phenomenology of Spirit*, on a concrete object, could overcome the deadness of formal logic. The only thing, in order to gain *scientific progress* — and to the quite *simple* insight into which one must essentially strive — was the cognition of the logical proposition that the negative is just as much positive, or that what contradicts itself does not resolve itself into null, into the abstract nothing, but essentially only into the negation of its *particular* content, or that such a negation is not all negation but the *negation of the determinate thing* which resolves itself, hence *determinate* negation; that thus in the result there is essentially contained that from which it results; — which is really a tautology, for otherwise it would be an immediate, not a result. Since what results, the negation, is *determinate* negation, it has a *content*. It is a new Concept, but the higher, richer Concept than the preceding; for it has become richer by the negation or opposite of the latter; it contains it, then, but also more than it, and is the unity of it and of its opposite. On this path the system of Concepts has in general to form itself and to complete itself in an unstoppable, pure course, taking in nothing from without.

“How could I suppose,” Hegel exclaimed in the Introduction, “that the *method* which I have followed in this system of logic — or rather which this system follows in itself — is not still capable of much perfecting, of much elaboration in detail, yet I know at the same time that it is the *only true* one. This is evident of itself from the fact that it is nothing different from its object and content; — for it is the content in itself, the *dialectic* which it has in itself, which moves it forward. It is clear that no presentations can count as scientific which do not follow the course of this method and are not in accord with its simple rhythm, for it is the course of the thing itself.”

Kant’s great merit in having grasped the categories as necessary determinations of self-consciousness and contradiction as a necessary moment of dialectical reason,

[p. 290]

Hegel recognized in its whole extent, but he wanted partly to free the categories from the *restricted*, subjective conception, partly to let the Concept of contradiction count not merely in the *negative* sense that reason cannot get beyond it, but rather in the sense that it, as sublating itself, is only a *moment* of the affirmative unity. He therefore, to be sure, fixed being and the Concept as the *in themselves inseparable moments* of the logical and accordingly even divided Logic into the *objective* and *subjective*, into the *ontological* and *ideological*, but at the same time he made it noticeable that between the determinations of being and those of the *Concept* there exists a middle sphere, that of the *relation* of the simple differences of being, the sphere of the *determinations of reflection* or of *essence*, which one could indeed reckon to objective logic, because the Concept of the *subject* does not yet emerge in it, which, however, is no longer immediate being but *being shining in itself*, mediation. This Concept was indisputably the most original in the whole Hegelian Logic, which through it was actually articulated trichotomously. The determinations of 1) *being* are immediate and immediately *passing over* into one another; quality into quantity, quantity through the return to quality into measure; measure, however, through the indifference of quality and quantity as its factors 2) into *essence*, whose determinations have sense only as in *relation* to one another, like identity and difference, content and form, cause and effect, while 3) the determinations of the *Concept*, as the unity of immediacy and mediation, are *developing* or such as those in which every moment is at the same time totality. The universal divides itself into the particular, and this realizes itself as the individual, which therefore in its being-for-itself is totality, the self-subsistent, *object*. The Concept, however, in unity with its reality, is the Concept of the *Idea*.

Hegel foresaw the difficulties which the Concept of being as the beginning of the Logic would present. He reminded that the Phenomenology concludes with the Concept of pure knowing, and that insofar the beginning in the Logic with the Concept of the beginning is only objectively, not subjectively, an immediate. “As *pure* knowing is to mean nothing but knowing as such, so too pure

[p. 291]

being is to mean nothing but *being* in general; *being*, nothing else, without any further determination and fulfillment. — Here being is represented as the beginning, as having arisen through mediation, and indeed through that which is at the same time a sublating of itself; with the presupposition of pure knowing as the result of finite knowing, of consciousness. But if no presupposition is to be made, if the beginning itself is to be taken *immediately*, then it is determined only by this, that it is to be the beginning of logic, of thinking for itself. Only the *resolution*, which one can also regard as an arbitrary choice, namely that one wants to consider *thinking as such*, is at hand. Thus the beginning must be an *absolute* or, what is here equivalent, an *abstract* beginning; it may *presuppose nothing*, must be mediated by nothing, nor have a ground; it is rather itself to be the ground of the whole science.”

The ambiguity of the concept of *ground* for the beginning, insofar as the beginning must sublate itself, did not escape Hegel. He expressed himself explicitly about it also in this respect, that the Concept integrating all other Concepts, thus also that of the Idea as only as yet logical, is that of *absolute spirit*. Nature and spirit are not subordinated to the logical as to something higher, although pure thinking, i.e. thinking that abstracts from nature and history and moves within itself, can alone *within itself* become certain of the truth. Hegel says: “One must concede that the going forward is a *going back into the ground*, to the *original and true*, on which that with which the beginning is made depends and by which it is in fact *produced*. Thus consciousness on its way from immediacy, with which it begins, is led back to absolute knowing as its innermost truth. This last, the ground, is then also that from which the first proceeds, which at first appeared as an immediate. — Thus still more is the *absolute spirit*, which proves to be the concrete and last, highest truth of all being, recognized as at the end of the development freely externalizing itself and releasing itself into the shape of an *immediate being*, — resolving itself to the *creation of its world*, which contains all that which fell into the development that preceded that result, and which through this inverted position

[p. 292]

with its beginning is transformed into something dependent on the result as principle. The essential thing for science is not so much that a purely immediate be the beginning, but that the *whole be a circle* within itself, in which the first becomes also the last and the last also the first.”

Special pains to discuss his relation to *Kant* and to determine the relation of the logical to the real Hegel took in the Introduction to the doctrine of the Concept. He insisted on the *independence* of logic, but not in order to annihilate nature and spirit in it, but rather to release the *independence of nature and of spirit, in their unity* with the logical as such, from the latter. “The pure determinations of being, essence and Concept constitute, to be sure, also the foundation and the inner simple framework of the forms of spirit; spirit as *intuiting*, just as *sensory consciousness*, is in the determinacy of immediate being, just as spirit as *representing*, as well as *perceiving consciousness*, has raised itself from being to the stage of essence or of reflection. But these concrete shapes concern logical science as little as the concrete forms which the logical determinations assume in nature, and which would be *space and time*, then space and time filling themselves as *inorganic* nature and the *organic* nature. Just so is the Concept here too not to be regarded as the act of self-conscious understanding, not as the *subjective understanding*, but the Concept in and for itself, which constitutes just as much a *stage* of nature as *of spirit*. Life, or organic nature, is that stage of nature on which the Concept emerges, but as blind, not grasping itself, i.e. not thinking Concept; as such it pertains only to spirit. But of that unspiritual as well as of this spiritual shape of the Concept its logical form is independent.”

In order, however, to cut off here too the misunderstanding as if nature and spirit were a merely formal translation of the logical Idea, an empty *repetition* of it, he remarked expressly: “Since it is first of all *logic* here, not science in general, whose relation to truth is under discussion, it must further be conceded that the latter, as the *formal science*, cannot

[p. 293]

also contain, and should not contain, that reality which is the content of further parts of philosophy, of the *sciences of nature* and of spirit. These concrete sciences do indeed come forth in a more real form than logic, but at the same time not so that they turn back again to that reality which consciousness, raised above its appearance to science, has given up, or even return to the use of forms such as the categories and determinations of reflection are, whose finitude and untruth have presented themselves in logic. Rather logic shows the elevation of the Idea to the stage from which it becomes the creator of nature and passes over to the form of a *concrete immediacy*, whose Concept, however, also breaks up this shape again in order to become itself, as *concrete spirit*. Over against these concrete sciences, which, however, have the logical as their inner former and retain it, as they had it as their pre-former, logic itself is indeed the *formal* science, but the science of the *absolute form*, which in itself is totality, and contains the *pure Idea of truth* itself. This absolute form has in itself its content or reality.” — Since now Hegel at the close of the Logic expressed himself in such a way that the transition of the Idea to its otherness, nature, is to be thought as a free release, in which it, absolutely sure of itself, rests in itself, this aroused the double misunderstanding, partly of taking the Idea again only as an abstract Concept and forgetting its inner unity with the real, partly of confusing the logical Idea with absolute spirit in and for itself, whereas it must indeed be grasped as absolute spirit, but *as it is only in the determinacy of pure thinking*. Hegel spoke of the *divine* Concept and called it the *creative*, because to the Concept of an unworldly, preworldly, extraworldly God in fact no other predicates belong than those of the pure Idea, just as, indeed — were it necessary to furnish such proofs — the Johannine doctrine of the Logos rests on this representation. Hegel, who was so far from all Gnosticism, had to let himself be charged with a deification of the Concept, a *logotheism*, as if his Concept of God did not go beyond the abstract form of the logical; Hegel, who was so far from all empty rationalism

[p. 294]

because he recognized reason as the archeus immanent in all concrete reality, had to let himself be reproached after his death that *with the purely rational one can never get at actuality*, a reproach that had to surprise especially coming from a standpoint which had formerly taught word for word: “Nothing is outside reason, and everything is in it.”

Hardly was the first part of the *Logic* out when Hegel, from neighboring Erlangen, at once had to hear all the cavilings about the unthinkable contradictions of the *identity of being and nonbeing*, etc., which were to accompany him from then on to his end, and which, however thoughtlessly they are often made, still count today as the weightiest instances for the rejection of his philosophy. In Erlangen, namely, there was a countryman of his, the professor of mathematics *Pfaff*, an original, witty, learned and acute man, who found himself provoked by Hegel’s utterances on *Newton* in regard to the differential calculus. A humorous correspondence arose between him and Hegel. Pfaff saw postulates everywhere in the Logic, missed the proof, fished out for himself from the dialectical flow, for secure hold, individual definitions, and charged Hegel with mixing too much *pictorial imagery* into his presentation. Pfaff’s letters lie before us in part, Hegel’s answers not. Pfaff prefixed Latin salutations to his letters, e.g.:

“[Latin] To the philosopher, the mathematician most hostile to him, greeting.” Or: “[Latin] To the philosopher, discoverer of the new intelligible world, the mathematician, incapable and most eager for knowledge, many greetings,” etc.

With obstinate understanding Pfaff analyzed the most particular detail. He conceded to Hegel, half ironically, that he was right in the same, provided one thought just what he wanted to have been thought. But the connection of the individual Concepts, e.g. of being and nonbeing in becoming, appeared to him arbitrary; he missed here the *How* of the unity, because he sought it not as an immanent further determination of the Concepts themselves, but as a construction of thinking consciousness, as a *subjective synthesis*. That the philosopher cannot develop the negative of the particular determinations without the Concept of the *totality circling in itself* appeared to him as a *circulus in demonstrando* [circle in demonstration]: “One starts from a point,

[p. 295]

presupposes things, operations, which after all occur only afterwards; if everything is therefore to be right, one must come back again to the point from which one started. That you must move in a circle, not in a straight line like mathematics, not like a comet in the parabola, but like the planets as blessed gods in a returning figure, I infer also from the fact that you need language, while the mathematician is quite mute. — Now *ignoscite* [pardon me], that I again proceed quite mathematically. It is quite wholesome that there are people who are never converted by the philosophers. Considered mathematically, *all* are in the wrong when they want to prove anything. But whoever has once got the knack of it has got it. Kant was certainly a Kantian.” — For all his pride in the self-evidence of his science, Pfaff nevertheless took the study of logic quite seriously and let nothing pass that seemed questionable to him. Manifold offense was given him also by the expressions *Reflexion* and *Speculation*. “Latin again, from optics. Do tell me the Greek expressions. To speculate comes from *speculum*, mirror; the mirroring thinking; surely not *mirror-fencing*? On this your letter contains significant hints: ‘Apart from my thoughts there is nothing in the matter, and my thoughts are apart from the matter nothing.’ Since there are only *two* here, matter and thought, then, if sunlight is reflected through the moon to the earth, so that *three* belong to reflecting, the gate and door are shut to all *reflecting*. Instruct me exactly on this. It seems to me: *here lies the dog buried*. You say quite figuratively in the letter: ‘Speculative thinking just knocks about with such things; it needs them as one needs bread, in order to consume it.’ Perhaps an example from the *Logic*, p. 26, which has tormented me greatly.”

Pfaff probably meant the well-known example of the hundred thalers from Kant’s *Critique of Pure Reason*, extending over from p. 25 to p. 26.

#### Move from Nuremberg to Heidelberg, Autumn 1816.

The longing to attain an academic career once more had gradually risen very high in Hegel. With tense

[p. 296]

attention he listened in every direction where an opportunity might perhaps offer itself. In July 1816, that is, in the same month in which he published the last volume of the *Logic*, he was charged with proposing, in a rector’s report, candidates from among his own teaching staff for the filling of the *philological professorship at Erlangen*; among that staff he did in fact possess a capable philologist, the later Professor *Heller*. Hegel put himself, too, on the list of candidates, in order to take over, *alongside* the lecturing in philosophy, that in philology until the professorship of the latter could be filled otherwise. He did this in half despair, merely to be woven back somehow into university life at all. In fact the government also accepted his offer.

Then, however, he received a call from *Heidelberg* as professor of *philosophy*. His old friends, *Schelver* and *Thibaut*, his scientific admirers, such as *Creuzer* and *Daub*, the latter of whom was just then rector of the university, rejoiced unanimously over it in their letters. It is a saddening but only too true confession that the promotion to a professorship, a call, as it is usually termed, is commonly bound up with so many petty intrigues, wretched rivalries, narrow considerations on the part of governments, and finally pecuniary circumstances, that the joy of the friends, when for once everything has gone so purely, worthily and swiftly, positively hurts. Alas, what is right so often appears as the exception! *Daub* wrote on 30 July 1816:

“In a letter received yesterday from Karlsruhe, the commission, highly gratifying to me and to your friends here, has fallen to me of asking you whether you would be inclined to accept the post of a full professor of philosophy at the university here? The salary consists in 1300 florins, 6 Malter of grain and 9 Malter of spelt. That is, admittedly, little, but unfortunately I know that for the present no more can be granted, and so my hope of an affirmative answer to the above question would be very weak if I could not point to an experience, gained over several years on several of my colleagues and on myself, that the government, when professors with diligence and some

[p. 297]

applause, has gradually increased their salaries considerably, and will do so in the future as well. Now, however, Heidelberg would, in you, if you accepted the call, have a philosopher for the first time since the founding of the university (Spinoza was once called here, but in vain). Diligence the philosopher brings with him, and the philosopher who is called Hegel brings with him much else besides, of which, to be sure, the fewest here and everywhere have as yet any inkling, and which cannot be won through mere diligence. Applause will not be lacking, if only they at last get to hear a philosopher as well. On this, venerable man, and on your nobility of mind, in the interest of science and for its revival — it is indeed now, at the German universities, as if petrified and turned to wood — my hopes are founded. I write, therefore, as if we had both long been known to each other; but I do know you too, and truly not since yesterday, nor merely from the titles and prefaces to your works, or even only from the reviews with which you have been besmirched. — I hasten, so that this letter may still go off by the post today, and I beg you to excuse kindly my writing, which is hasty in any case.

Should I live to see you belong to the University of Heidelberg, which I love as my foster-mother and shall love to the end of my life, then a pure and refreshing ray of light will have fallen into my life. With truly sincere respect

Your most devoted Daub.”

In that same fateful month of July, Fr. v. *Raumer* had also come through Nuremberg and had conversed with Hegel about *the teaching of philosophy at universities*, from which arose the essay on this subject that is printed in *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 349–56. Through this contact Hegel’s earlier orientation toward Berlin was now stirred up again. Fr. v. Raumer, Link, Solger, Niebuhr and others took an interest in it, and Hegel was in fact proposed for *Fichte’s* professorship, which was still unfilled. On the part of the Ministry of the Interior, however, there was a certain misgiving.

[p. 298]

The minister *Schuckmann* had it written to Hegel, namely, under the 15th of August of the same year:

“From a letter of Herr Privy State Councillor *Niebuhr* the Ministry of the Interior has learned that you wish to be appointed at the university here. The teaching post of philosophy is also vacant, and in view of the reputation and esteem which you have acquired through your philosophical writings, the Ministry will gladly take you into consideration in filling this post. It believes, however, that for the benefit of the institution and of yourself it must first remove a misgiving, which is laid openly before you, as an honest man, for examination and reply. Since you, namely, have by now not given academic lectures for a considerable number of years, and were also not for long an academic teacher before, doubt has been raised from several quarters whether the skill to deliver a lively and penetrating lecture on your science is still fully at your command, which, as you yourself will be convinced, is so very necessary, because precisely for this science now, when the wretched bustle of bread-studies is noticeable everywhere, the spirit of the young people must especially be aroused and guided by a lively delivery. In reliance on your own insight into the duties of a teacher of philosophy and into the needs of science, the Ministry therefore leaves it to you to examine yourself whether you hold yourself fully qualified to satisfy the obligations to be undertaken here, and awaits your declaration in order to decide the further course thereupon.”

This misgiving of the Prussian government and the relations already entered into with Heidelberg determined Hegel to go to Heidelberg, although on 31 August the professorship of philology at Erlangen, too, was definitively offered him. The particulars of the negotiations that took place on this account, concerning increase of salary, lodging and lectures, can be gathered from the correspondence conducted with Daub about it, *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 483–90. With reference to Schuckmann’s letter Hegel said to Daub on 29 August: “If I can answer that my imperfect and timid beginning at Jena was followed by an eight-year

[p. 299]

year study and growing familiar with my thoughts, and an eight-year practice at the Gymnasium — an opportunity, perhaps more effective, because of the relation to the students, for the liberation of delivery than the academic lectern itself — then my chief reply will be that I already see myself engaged at Heidelberg.”

#### Activity in Heidelberg.

Having fallen ill through a premature confinement, Hegel’s wife was at first still detained in Nuremberg, and he had to travel alone. On the way he visited in *Würzburg*, which pleased him extraordinarily, an old friend, *Lichtenthaler*. In the letter to his wife he calls him by that venerable name itself, without, however, the nature of his relation to him becoming clearer. On the 19th of October he arrived in Heidelberg and from then on wrote almost daily to his wife, since he felt lonely after all and was plagued by the most violent longing to see wife and children with him before the onset of the worse winter weather. His countryman Professor *Eschenmayer*, a brother of that very man who later became so fanatical an opponent of the Hegelian philosophy, was most kindly helpful to him in setting up house, and Hegel therefore overflows, in his housekeeping reports on the purchase of firewood and the like, with grateful praise of him.

No less kindly was he received by *Paulus* with his wife and daughter. It was now the third time that he had met with him in the same city. The church councillor’s wife was an excellent, humorous woman, who was constantly having her fun of native wit with Hegel, and always wrote him interesting, lively letters and notes, nursed him in Heidelberg when he fell somewhat unwell, played cards with him, talked over his affairs with him — in short, behaved as a true friend. In her letters, which also express with vigorous frankness the liveliest participation in the political conditions of Germany, she always calls her husband, Paulus, with half-comical pathos the *Lord*, and herself always signs as “the *faithful Faithfulness*.” She knows right well how to jibe at the absoluteness of the gentlemen philosophers

[p. 300]

and only once is she wholly content with the Professor: that he, like her, loves the *forfaits* [crimes] at the theater. Hegel’s plan of going to Berlin was an abomination to her, since she was so very fond of him, and she remarked that she did not see what he wanted in a city where one drinks wine out of thimbles!

With Voss Hegel did at first indeed enter again into a relationship, but without consequence. With *Thibaut* and *Schelver*, however, he renewed his old friendly relationship. With *Daub* the relation was indeed spiritually deep, but personally not really intimate. They did not come together as much as one might perhaps have expected, and saw each other more only on general occasions. All the more did Hegel sympathize, in an individual way, with *Creuzer*.

Hegel remarked in his letters to his wife that in Heidelberg it was every man for himself and God for us all. There was no fuss and bustle in societies, but a quiet, “dear life.” The confinement of the family to itself was in fact also what he liked best. Intimacy of intercourse could arise only as a consequence of habit; he was therefore quite content and found himself oppressed by nothing. At first, to be sure, he had been dismayed by the small number of listeners. On 29 October he wrote: “Yesterday I began my lectures, but the number of listeners, to be sure, does not look so brilliant as had been represented and promised. I was, if not perplexed and impatient, at least astonished not to find it as it had been made out. For one lecture course I had only 4 listeners. Paulus, however, consoled me that he too had lectured for only 4 and 5.” This changed, however, within a few days, and he had in the one lecture course, the Encyclopedia, some twenty, in the other, History of Philosophy, some thirty listeners. He now consoled himself: “In the first half-year, at the first appearance, one must for the time being be content if one can only produce oneself. The students must first grow warm with one.” — His lectures on the history of philosophy he opened with a fine, hope-proud *address*, in which, after the long bloody struggles of the peoples, he greeted with priestly devotion the dawn of a new day, of a higher liberation of spirit.

[p. 301]

The beauty of the nature around Heidelberg delighted Hegel, and he mentioned it repeatedly in his letters. What *strolling* means, his wife would only now learn. He lived on the Friedrichsstraße in the suburb, if one turns left from the main street, coming from the city proper, out toward the Riesenstein, the last house on the right. Here Hegel often stood at the window, looking out at the mountains and chestnut woods swimming in haze, lost in Socratic musing — while the mass of the students on that account held him to be not particularly diligent. Although he attracted many irresistibly, most of them, after the manner of youth, nevertheless went shyly around him. Some drew nearer to him and accompanied him on his walks, he who, as always, went about in gray trousers and gray frock coat. During the summer of 1817 he was so lost in his thoughts that he often quite forgot the external. Thus he once went across the square to the university building after a heavy rain had softened the ground. A shoe stayed behind in the mud. But he walked on, without noticing, in his absorption, this defect.

As regards his lectures, he made, in relation to Jena, the further advance of arriving at the particular presentation of the philosophy of subjective spirit, or, as he was accustomed to call it in the announcement, of *anthropology and psychology*, and of *aesthetics*, for whose development Heidelberg’s natural charm, the *Boisserée* gallery of paintings then still located there, and the interesting architectural monuments and sculptural works scattered so numerously throughout the whole surrounding country did in fact offer a very fitting stimulus. Let us recall here that Hegel wrote to Voss at Heidelberg in 1805 that he wished to teach aesthetics here.

The students who came closer to him here were, right at the outset, *Carové*, then *d’Yxkull*, and, toward the end of his stay, *Hinrichs*. The first of these was already at that time occupied, under *Schelver’s* guidance, with animal magnetism. He was a Rhinelander, by his special study a jurist, by confession a Catholic, but wished to help bring about a reshaping of Catholicism from scientific principles, and therefore later attacked, in a well-known work, the fundamental law of

[p. 302]

ecclesiastical Romanism: *nulla extra ecclesiam salus* [no salvation outside the church]. We shall meet him again in Berlin.

The Baron *Boris d’Yxkull* is an Estonian, whose estates lie in the neighborhood of Riga. As a captain of horse guards he had taken part in the Russian campaign against France and, feeling sickly from the after-effects of the hardships he had suffered, longed for a deeper refreshment of the spirit through scientific culture. Without having yet read anything of Hegel, he formed the idea of him that he could learn through him, in a short time, the quintessence of human knowledge. He came to Heidelberg in the spring of 1817. He himself tells: “Hardly had I arrived when my first business, after I had looked around a little, was to visit the man of whose personality I had sketched the most fantastic pictures. With carefully studied phrases — for I was well aware of my complete lack of scientific training — I went, not without timidity but outwardly confident, to the Professor, and found, to my no small astonishment, a quite plain and simple man, who spoke rather heavily and brought forth nothing significant. Unsatisfied by this impression, though secretly attracted by Hegel’s friendly reception and a certain trait of kindly and yet ironical politeness, after I had enrolled for the Professor’s lecture courses I went to the first bookseller I came across, bought the works of Hegel’s that had already appeared, and sat down in the evening comfortably in my sofa corner to read them through. But the more I read, and the more attentive I tried to become in reading, the less I understood what I read, so that, after I had tormented myself for a couple of hours with a single sentence without being able to understand anything of it, I laid the book aside out of sorts, yet attended the lectures out of curiosity. In honesty, however, I had to tell myself that I did not understand my own notebooks and that I lacked all preliminary knowledge for these sciences. In my distress I now went again to Hegel, who, after he had patiently heard me, kindly set me right and advised me to take various *privatissima* [private tutorials]: Latin reading, the rudiments of algebra, natural science and geography. This went on for half a year, hard as it came to a man of twenty-six. Now I presented myself for the third time to Hegel, who

[p. 303]

received me, indeed, very kindly, and could not help smiling when I told him of my propaedeutic criss-cross and zigzag forays. His counsels were now more definite, his sympathy livelier, and I attended his lecture courses with some profit. A *conversatorium* of Doctor *Hinrichs*, in which disputants from all four faculties gathered and in which the explanation of the *Phenomenology of Spirit* formed the guiding thread, supported me. Occasionally, in the following two semesters, I saw Hegel at my place; more often I was at his, and accompanied him on solitary walks. He often told me that our over-clever age could be satisfied by method alone, because it tames thought and leads it to the matter. Religion was divined philosophy, philosophy nothing other than conscious religion; both sought, only by different paths, the same thing, namely God. I should never trust a philosophy that was either immoral or irreligious. He also complained at times of not being understood, repeated that logical knowledge was now concluded and that everyone now had to clear up in his own discipline, since there was only too much material already, but the logical relation and elaboration were still lacking; that only the conceit of immaturity, the obstinacy of the one-sided understanding, the hollowness and lachrymosity of sanctimonious sham blessedness, as well as the narrow-hearted egoism of privileged obscurantism, could resist the dawning day.”

After this Heidelberg period Boris d’Yxkull led a grand traveling life. Now he stood among the ruins of Ephesus, now on the snowfields of Sweden, now he was in Paris, now in Rome; everywhere a copy of Hegel’s *Logic* accompanied him, which is therefore certainly the most widely traveled of all logics. His interesting letters to Hegel, in particular from Petersburg and Paris, brought the philosopher well-outlined contours of the current world-fate and silhouettes from the highest regions of society. Excellently suited to Yxkull, therefore, was the traveling philosopher of Germany, Franz v. *Baader*, with whom he entered into lively oral as well as written intercourse, and whose personal acquaintance with Hegel he arranged during a stay in Berlin. Before this time, when Baader went to Russia, Hegel had indeed written about him to Boris d’Yxkull: “A prophet, they say, does not count

[p. 304]

much in his fatherland, I had thought that in Russia he would count. It does not yet seem so. They look quite past him. Such a prophetic person, perhaps just because he is held in low esteem, can be partly less suspect, partly more effective, than another who is clear about himself and about thoughts, as about men and circumstances, and who is thereby, among other things, also more honest toward himself and others.” — As a true friend of Baader, Yxkull always sought to put him in a better light with Hegel, which he also succeeded in doing to a certain degree.

Hegel remained in an unfailingly friendly relationship with d’Yxkull, who also invited him to visit him in Estonia, and sought also, as far as his insight reached, to stand by him with his counsel in many entanglements, which Yxkull accepted with thanks and with success. To cheer him up, when he threatened to become hypochondriac over his humanistic tendencies of culture, Hegel would also jest at times. Europe, he remarked, had already become a kind of cage (*Käficht*), in which only two *espèces* [species] of men seemed to move freely: the one, who himself belongs with heart and soul to the lockers-up; the other, who under the great wire vault seeks out a spot where he has neither for nor against its wires to act or react. If once the inner is in dissonance with the outer circumstances, it finds itself either aggrieved or unhappy, or else, if it cannot truly reconcile itself with the state of things, then its more advantageous resolve is to live for itself, call it what one will, in good Epicurean fashion or otherwise, and to remain a private person for oneself, a position which is at once that of a spectator and even that of the possibility of great effectiveness.

But he also worked in earnest against the melancholy of his Russian pupil and friend. Thus he wrote to him, e.g., on 28 November 1821: “You are so fortunate as to have a fatherland that occupies so great a place in the domain of world history and that without doubt has a still much higher determination. The other modern states, it might seem, have already more or less reached the goal of their development; perhaps several have the culminating point of it already behind them, and their condition has become stationary; Russia

[p. 305]

on the other hand, perhaps already the strongest power among the rest, bears in its bosom an immense possibility of development of its intensive nature. You have the personal good fortune, through your birth, your means, your talents and knowledge, and services already rendered, to have the nearer prospect of occupying in this colossal edifice a position that is not merely subordinate.”

Besides Carové and d’Yxkull, *Hinrichs*, born at Jever in East Frisia, came into a closer relation with Hegel while still at Heidelberg. He was then studying law. When Hegel lectured on natural law, he went at first more out of curiosity, found himself now attracted, now repelled, but imperceptibly got ever more into the subject and soon gave himself up to a thorough and enthusiastic study of the Hegelian writings. When Hegel, in the summer of 1818, set as the theme of a prize essay for the students of the philosophical faculty a discussion of the relation of the Platonic Idea to the Aristotelian entelechy, Hinrichs submitted a work on it. It became the occasion of the personal acquaintance of Hinrichs and Hegel, which, however, because the latter was already on the point of leaving for Berlin, turned out only brief and fleeting at that time. Hinrichs habilitated in May 1820 at Heidelberg as Privatdozent of philosophy. Hegel’s letters to Hinrichs, of which the first, concerning the art of scientific-literary composition, is especially important, stand in *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 508–17.

#### The Encyclopedia.

It was in Heidelberg, then, that Hegel for the first time came forward with the whole of his philosophy, which was also very necessary on this account alone, in order to protect the third part of his *Logic* from crass misunderstanding. For use in his lectures he had printed the exposition of the *Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences* which he had given from Michaelmas 1816 to Easter 1817. His notebooks from the Gymnasium offered him, as the comparison with the Propaedeutic shows, the best basis for it, except that he could now, alongside the clarity gained, again allow himself a higher form. In the preface he declared himself very decidedly, on the one hand, against the imposing and the unhinged in the

[p. 306]
