philosophy, on the other hand against the lack of thoughts, the shallowness of skepticism, the immediacy of knowing that remains standing in feeling. Neither the setting out on adventures of thought nor the vanity of emptiness of Ideas, which had made a mockery of German earnestness long enough and wearied its deeper philosophical need, but only *proving*, as it was formerly called, could advance: the *method*, which, as he hoped, would yet be recognized as the only true one, because identical with the content. — This first edition of the *Encyclopedia* still contains wholly the creative breath of the first production. The later editions have become much more detailed in the elaboration of particulars, but especially in polemical and apologetic remarks; yet in order to have Hegel’s system in its concentrated totality, as it came forth with the whole force of its primitive appearance, one will always have to return to this first edition and therefore also have to reprint it.

#### Contributions to the Heidelberg Yearbooks.

In the *Heidelberg Yearbooks of Literature* Hegel took over the *editorship* of the philosophical and philological department. He himself first contributed, in the volume for 1817, Nos. 1 and 2, a notice of the third volume of *Jacobi’s* collected works, which had appeared in 1816. We recall here how at the beginning of the century he had subjected Jacobi’s philosophizing to a severe censure. In Jacobi’s dispute with *Schelling* he had taken no part. Many a good friend stimulated him to it, and one of them remarked that Jacobi’s lachrymosity was as great as the maliciousness of Schelling, who, moreover, was erecting the gallows for his victim out of foreign wood, out of the writings of Hegel and Fr. Schlegel. But the passionateness of this dispute did not suit Hegel, and even now he declared that the passion of the time was to be regarded as past, though the matter it concerned must not be regarded as a past one, but rather retained for speculation always a great interest. He took back nothing of what he had censured in Jacobi in 1802, but on the contrary repeated much, such as the misunderstanding of Spinoza and of the philosophy of nature, the ingenious manner as a surrogate for the

[p. 307]

speculative form, the poverty and narrowness of the standpoint of beautiful individuality fixed as absolute, the lack of objectivity of the Concepts, etc., but he treated all these points mildly and brought out as the real problem the relation of substance and subject, of necessity and freedom.

What he had already developed at length in his *Logic*, he declared here expressly, namely that the attribute of thinking *in abstracto* does not yet suffice to vindicate for the Concept of substance as such the character of personality, because, although the negation of the finite is the point of departure for the Concept of substance, from it itself there is no transition to the individual, to individuation. With the greatest decisiveness and in quite clear words he too declared himself for *personality, freedom and immortality*. He conceded to Jacobi complete right in conceiving *the Absolute as spirit, as personal*; the unphilosophical, which he had to contradict, he found only in this, that Jacobi wanted to hold fast this content in the formlessness of immediate knowing and to exclude from it the mediation of insight into its necessity. In this respect he said: “God is no dead, but a *living God*; he is still more than the living one, he is *spirit and eternal love*, and is this solely through the fact that his *being* is not the *abstract*, but the distinguishing that moves within itself, and a cognizing of himself in the person distinguished by him, and his essence is the *immediate*, that is, *existent*, unity only insofar as it eternally *leads* that eternal mediation *back* to unity, and this leading back is itself this unity, the unity of life, of self-feeling, of personality, of knowing of itself.”

Jacobi understood the Concept of the *proof of the existence of God* as if the knowing and the being of God himself were thereby to be made into a *dependent* one, grounded in an other, which was later called Hegel’s pantheism, as if the self-cognizing of God in man excluded God’s self-knowing of himself. Hegel recalled in reply: “Since God is (for cognition) the result, this mediation itself explains itself, on the contrary, as sublating itself through itself. What is the *last* is cognized as the *first*; the end is the *purpose*; through its being found as the purpose, and indeed as the absolute purpose, this product

[p. 308]

is declared, rather, to be the immediate, first mover. This progression to a result is hereby just as much the going back into itself, the counter-thrust against itself; it is what was stated before as the eternal nature of spirit, as of the working final purpose that brings itself forth.” — Hegel therefore approved Jacobi’s polemic against the mere ought-to-be, the assertion of the conviction that the subjective Concept without objectivity is an empty semblance, just as spiritless as a mere being without the Concept, without having its ought-to-be within itself and being in conformity with it. “The consciousness that God is, that freedom is, that immortality is, is something quite other than the postulate that these Ideas merely *ought to be*; that theoretical side makes up the complement to the ought.” Finally he remarked at the close that Jacobi, according to the description he gives of *Hamann*, must find himself just as much in harmony with a cognizing “which is only a consciousness of *coincidence*, and a *knowing* of the Ideas of personality, freedom and God, not in the category of *incomprehensible* mysteries and miracles.”

The conciliatory manner in which Hegel expressed himself about Jacobi, and acknowledged the lovingness of his heart, won him many friends. Jacobi himself came to Heidelberg, and the philosophers sank, moved, upon each other’s breast. “Jacobi’s noble soul,” Hegel himself related of this scene, “knew no grudge.” Jacobi’s poetic admirer, too, *Jean Paul*, came to Heidelberg in the summer of 1818. He thought especially highly of Hegel’s wife, who, however, to his great regret, was just then, on account of her ill health, at the baths of *Schwalbach*.

Quite other consequences than those pleasant ones were to follow from the second critique, which Hegel incorporated into the *Heidelberg Yearbooks*, 1817, Nos. 66–68 and 73–77, on the printed proceedings in the assembly of the *estates of the Kingdom of Württemberg* in the years 1815 and 1816. How deeply he had already earlier penetrated the constitution of his fatherland, with how lively a participation he had followed its development, how much he had stirred the fate of Germany in his heart and in general had always turned to politics with the most extensive, world-embracing sense, we already know. The critique itself, therefore, can not only not surprise us, but must on the contrary appear to us as a natural tribute of Hegel’s patriotism

[p. 309]

The old imperial constitution had fallen, and now a new positive form of state was to come about. King *Friedrich* of Württemberg wished to give his land, in accordance with the provisions of the Act of the Congress of Vienna, a constitutional constitution.

“The promise, said Hegel, could be fulfilled in a way which might be held the most prudent, indeed even be passed off as the most just, but which would have been the *most perfidious counsel* that ministers could have given. If the princes of the new realms had wished to deceive their peoples quite thoroughly and to acquire honor, so to speak, before God and men, they would have given back to their peoples the so-called old constitutions; — honor *before God and the world* — for, after so many public voices, and in particular also after the history before us, one might think that the peoples would have streamed into the churches and sung loud Te Deums. — In place of Machiavelli’s name the princes would have earned the glory of the fine politics of the *Augustuses and Tiberiuses*, who likewise let the forms of the preceding condition, that of a republic at that time, continue, while this thing was no longer and irrevocably could no longer be, — a continuing and a deception, into which their Romans entered, and through which the establishment of a rational, monarchical condition, whose Concept the Romans had not yet found, became impossible. This politics might lie the nearer to our princes if they compared, from the experience of the last twenty-five years, the dangers and terrors that have attached themselves to the creation of new constitutions and of an actuality proceeding from thought, with the danger-free rest and nullity into which the institutions of the former constitutions of estates had brought themselves down; if they further connected with this already existing nullity the reflection how the Roman institutions, which Augustus and Tiberius let continue, had wholly lost the little sense and consistency which they might still seem to have in a German imperial fief.”

“King Friedrich showed himself exalted above the temptation of this deception. He summoned the heads of the princely and comital families of his realm and a selection from the rest of its nobility, likewise a number of popular deputies chosen by the burghers, for the 15th of March 1815, and the history

[p. 310]

of these proceedings opens with the ever-great scene that the king, in full assembly of these his estates of the realm, first delivered from the throne a speech to them, in which he, after he had first expressed what had already been done, namely that the previously so different parts of the country and subjects had been united into an inseparable whole, the difference of religious confession and of estate in civil respect had vanished, the public burdens for all been brought into an equal proportion, and thus all become *citizens of one state* — finally declared that he was laying the keystone to the edifice of the state, *in that he gave his people a constitution*.”

“There can well be no greater worldly spectacle on earth than that a monarch adds to the state power, which is at first wholly in his hands, a further one, and indeed *the foundation*, in that he takes his people into it as an essentially cooperating constituent. If one otherwise sees the great work of a state constitution, indeed most other acts of government, come about only in a series of fragmented actions and chance events, without overview and publicity, and the *public* appearance of princeliness and majesty had gradually restricted itself to *birthday celebrations or wedding festivals*; one may be tempted, at that scene, where the appearance of majesty corresponds so well to the inner content of its act, to linger for a moment as at a beneficent, sublime and strengthening intuition. But it would be equally near at hand to think that one must excuse oneself for such a moment of lingering. For the occasions in which we have become accustomed to see princely representation, the emptiness and inactivity of the former assembly of the state, the German Imperial Diet, in general the nullity and unactuality of public life, have made such a vexation against acts of this kind, a moral and hypochondriacal private conceit against the public and against the appearance of majesty, into the prevailing mood, that the mention of it, and perhaps the view that such an appearance is capable of stirring magnanimous feelings, ran the danger of being taken for anything rather than earnestness, scarcely even for good-naturedness, and of being judged rather as courtly folly and servile blindness and intentionality

[p. 311]

Our political deadness is incapable of becoming glad of such scenes, and thoroughness turns away from them, as mere externalities, to the substance of the matter and to one’s own thoughts about it.”

This substance Hegel found in the basic provisions of the constitutional charter, according to which the following rights were to be made actual: participation of the people in legislation; the right of tax approval; the old church property; accountability for the state expenditures; personal freedom; responsibility of state officials; the right of emigration; the continued activity of the estates.

The points of view for the further development of these provisions he perceived, on the one hand, in the efforts of the government to subdue the power and the pretensions of the aristocratic middle member and to win for the state its rights against it, on the other, in the efforts of the third estate, which often calls itself the people as well, against this same intermediary power, at times also against the government itself, to win and wrest for itself civic rights.

The assembled estates of the land, however, sought, by majority, to preserve as far as possible the particularity of precisely these *privileges* against the changes which the introduction of those rights made necessary and which were not possible without relative *sacrifice* of historically transmitted, hitherto existing *positive* rights. The *good, old right* was always praised by them; necessary modifications — necessary they called, however, only those made in their interest — they did not want to oppose; the *cause of the people* was to be theirs. Hegel attacked this opposition, in which he saw a *deception of the people*, without circumlocution. He pursued the sophistry of the loyal- and patriotic-sounding turns of phrase into their most secret hiding-places. The passive neutrality of the estates, who, instead of active intervention in the state and instead of concern for its honor abroad, preferred to cause the government endless embarrassments internally out of self-seeking egoism, he attacked no less mercilessly; even now they had forgotten nothing and learned nothing; the people was the *whole*, to which they too belonged, which they still refused to grasp; otherwise by people in a more determinate sense the *middle class* was to be understood; in the indeterminate sense it was the *mass of the many*. With implacable hatred, indeed with true wrath, he pursued the *scribes*, by whom the people

[p. 312]

were wholly excluded from the self-administration of justice and compelled, even in the pettiest acts, to costs and to the most circumstantial dependence. He saw herein chiefly the ground of the nullity to which the magistracies had sunk, so that the government had been obliged to draw the posts of town and village administration into its sphere. He therefore wished for a *corporate* life of the communes and estates once more, in order to awaken the *sense of state*, already developed in the higher spheres, in the lower ones as well. The condition merely of age and property, as also in France, of being *elector and eligible*, did not suffice for the true representation of essential interests. It was abstract, without objective content. A man who was 25 years old and possessed real property of 200 florins, who could thus be an elector, and otherwise belonged to no estate, to no particular circle of the political whole, was in the eyes of the people simply *nothing*.

Finally Hegel also scourged the *financial misconduct* practiced by the old estates, in that they had always had themselves paid in the most lavish way for the smallest business, indeed for obvious doing-nothing. Enough: he believed the Württemberg estates had done precisely the reverse of what the French Revolution wanted, namely to create a state out of reason. They had, on the contrary, a sense only for the *historical*, no matter whether it was rational or irrational; they did not engage in the *critique of content* and in this respect liked expressly to speak of the pernicious *poison* of the French principles.

Among the people this review, whose introduction in particular is a masterpiece, found so much response that the publisher of a periodical, the *Württemberg People’s Friend*, prevailed upon Hegel to have a special reprint made of it, as the most thorough manifesto against the *old-righters*, as one expressed it at that time, for greater circulation and more beneficial effect. Which also happened. It is now reprinted again in *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 219–360. This is the critique, as thorough as it is outspoken, on account of which narrow-hearted aristocrats have decried Hegel as a servile, because he defended the reason and popular character of the royal will against their egoism!

[scan 358]

### Book Three.

[scan 360]

#### Move to Prussia.

In Heidelberg Hegel found himself, to be sure, quite content too. But since, with the resumed academic activity, his self-esteem rose, and he sensed the possibility of an ever increasing recognition of his philosophy, Heidelberg appeared to him in this respect not too favorable. The splendor of nature in which this university is embedded, and which entices in all directions to interesting excursions, allures the students to manifold distractions. Even if they are not idle, it is nevertheless more positive science, exclusive specialist learning, than philosophy, with which they busy themselves. A cheerful, realistic sense makes up, once and for all, the basic mood of this university, and Heidelberg has therefore not yet been able to make a name for itself in philosophy. Those who taught philosophy here for some years were mediocrities; those who rose above the ordinary, like Fries and others, soon sought to get away again. If one wished to put this hurrying away also down to the slight salary of the philosophers there, one could still not ascribe it to the circumstance that it lay with the delivery of the philosophers, as if this had not had enough openness to the world and oratorically captivating energy. For in this respect neither *Fries* at Jena nor *Hillebrand* at Giessen was complained of, and yet they left Heidelberg. Even *Daub*, who achieved the extraordinary in delivery, gathered in properly speculative lecture courses only a small public around him, even in the most frequented periods of the university. Hegel made, in spite of his outwardly not immediately appealing delivery, through

[p. 316]

the originality of his whole being, incomparably more of an epoch than his predecessors.

From Berlin one had not lost sight of him, and soon recognized how powerfully he made an impact at Heidelberg despite the prejudices prevailing here against speculation. It was seen that the Gymnasium teaching had not brought him down as a lecturer, but had rather developed him toward greater intelligibility. And in Hegel’s soul too the representation of Berlin, of which, indeed, as we have seen from his correspondence with Sinclair, he had already thought in 1805, had become so lively that already from the beginning of the year 1818 he began to regard himself in Heidelberg as a stranger. *Berlin sand*, he remarked, was a more receptive sphere for philosophy than Heidelberg’s romantic surroundings.

Hegel was thus, from the true-German stock of the Swabians, through Switzerland, through Franconia, Saxony, Bavaria, Baden, nevertheless still to arrive at the state which, by its national origin from Germanized Slavdom, by its dynasty from the Swabian Zollerns, after the wars of liberation added to the old border against Russia the polar counter-border against France. Such a not yet rounded-off state seeks to subject its neighbors ideally, first of all from within, through a superiority of culture. Instinctively it feels out the elements still lacking to it and seeks to appropriate them when they exist outside it in already finished form. Whole masses of such ferments of culture Prussia had taken up into itself in the last century, especially French ones, from the Reformed who fled for the sake of their faith to the ingenious atheists of the Regency. In the assimilation of significant individuals this central colonizing continues at present.

We have heard earlier how low Prussia was ranked by Hegel at the time of the Jena catastrophe. He saw in it only the officials’ state, in whose spiritless mechanism all deeper interest in art and science had died out. But how Prussia had changed since that period! How it had come to self-consciousness precisely through it! How it looked about, to let nothing escape it, to promote its spiritual rebirth, well knowing that the material would follow of itself! How

[p. 317]

had Berlin in particular received, through the founding of the university, the spiritual centralization which it so greatly needed! The posture of an academy is necessarily always too aristocratic for it to be capable of exercising a popular effect; through the university, however, such an effect has been attained, and science has been mediated with the common consciousness, with public opinion, in Berlin. One can in this respect follow, in the series of the lectern notabilities of Berlin, the history of its present process of culture.

Prussia, protected by no natural frontiers except toward the north by the Baltic; in its extensive and intricate periphery touching directly the most various nations, cultures and constitutions; a state half conquering, half expanding through inheritance and purchase; formerly filled with the decided preponderance of a Protestant population, since the Peace of Paris also with the counterweight of a considerable Catholic one; can maintain an independent position only through the restless progress of its spiritual development. Science therefore has for it yet another significance than for states which see themselves secured by their natural situation, by the national or ecclesiastical unity of their population, or by great material resources. With the abandonment of science Prussia would abandon itself, for it is through and through an artificial, a made state, which can attain unity only through the mediation of culture, of self-conscious reason. (Cf. Rosenkranz, *History of the Kantian Philosophy*, p. 99 ff.) From this is explained the great significance which it had to have for Prussia to receive, through *Kant*, the philosophy corresponding to it, a philosophy which is theoretically critique, practically the imperative of ought and of postulating. Or, conversely, one may say that the Prussian state out of its essence has brought forth this sober and action-hungry philosophy as its Concept. Since the Hegelian philosophy is in truth the *completion* of the Kantian, there results from this the higher necessity which brought about Hegel’s call to Prussia and the rapid taking root of his philosophy in it.

What many liked to regard merely as the satisfaction of a favorite wish

[p. 318]

of the Ministry of *Altenstein* was at bottom the work of the progressive tendency of the Prussian spirit, and a philosopher who had himself emerged from Prussia, *Solger*, it was who especially fixed the attention of the minister of education upon Hegel. Moreover, Altenstein was in fact imbued with the most sincere veneration for Hegel. All his numerous letters to Hegel breathe heartfelt confidence, thorough esteem, and express in the most beautiful way an unfeigned enthusiasm for science. On 26 December 1817 he wrote to Hegel to offer him Fichte’s professorship anew, and Hegel, according to a letter of 24 January 1818, entered into it at once. Who knows what perspectives were still being conjured up before his mighty spirit! Who knows whether he did not hold out to himself the prospect of entering the government itself! The practical drive was always great in him, as in *Kant and Fichte*, and we have read in his correspondence with Schelling the remarkable passage already stressed, in which as a youth he asks what hope there is, alongside the occupation with theoretical works, of intervening in the life of men? At least there is found in his letter of resignation to the Grand Ducal Baden Ministry a passage which hardly admits of another interpretation and which is regarded by him as the real motive of his departure from Baden. It runs thus: “It must be for him above all of the greatest importance to have the prospect, with more opportunity as age advances further, of being able to pass from the *precarious function of teaching philosophy at a university* to another activity and to be made use of.”

The negotiations with Berlin came to an end in March 1818. Hegel was to receive a salary of 2000 thalers and 1000 thalers moving expenses; besides this, one wished to take into account any possible concern for his subsistence, which for the time being was held to be well secured: “Should, however, a ground for it develop in future, the Ministry values the gain of so deep a thinker and academic teacher, equipped with thorough science and animated by so earnest and right a striving, too highly not to be glad to contribute everything that may be necessary for the facilitation of your stay here. For the present it wishes nothing

[p. 319]

more than the desire of so many who have long been waiting for the filling of the chair of philosophy to see it quite soon fully satisfied.” — This benevolence soon proved itself faithful. The Ministry supported Hegel constantly in an extraordinary way, now through considerable remunerations, now through splendid travel money, and also entered most kindly into the greatest possible realization of other wishes of his, e.g. to see *Carové* and later L. v. *Henning* appointed as Repetents for his lectures.

With this relation to a larger state there developed in Hegel an elasticity that made him young again. The most cheerful confidence pervaded him. All the letters which he wrote in this regard during the summer of 1818 to his wife, who was at the baths at Schwalbach, are pervaded by the greatest predilection for Berlin. Everything he interprets for the best. He quickly finds his way into the peculiarities of Berlin. Everything satisfies him, and the boldest hopes for his activity spread out with a comfortable smile. The sister of the Minister Altenstein herself undertook the care of his first domestic arrangements. Hegel lived at first in the *Leipziger* Straße, later on the Spree, opposite the garden of Monbijou, having escaped the crass world-din in the nearby center of the main streets, and yet near enough to it, and entertained by an outlook as varied as it was charming over the river and the garden of Monbijou, at No. 4 on the *Kupfergraben*, which has become as world-famous through him as *Sanssouci* through its royal philosopher.

This is the true course of Hegel’s call to Berlin, which, as one sees from it, was anything but made suddenly, but had rather ripened gradually over years. Concerning the views that prevailed in Berlin at that time on this matter, we possess a significant utterance of *Solger’s* to Tieck of 26 April 1818 (*Nachgelassene Schriften* [Posthumous Writings], I, 619): “My lecture courses are now also under way again, but the listeners again only few. I am eager to see what effect Hegel’s presence will make. Certainly many believe that his appointment is disagreeable to me, and *yet I proposed him first*, and can assure you in general that, if I expect anything from him, it is only a greater

[p. 320]

revival of the sense for philosophy, hence something good. When I still stood beside Fichte, I had ten times as many listeners as now. I revere Hegel very much and agree with him in many respects most strikingly. In dialectic we have both, independently of one another, taken almost the same path, at least attacked the matter quite from the same and indeed new side. Whether in much else that is peculiar to me he would understand me just as well, I do not know. I should like to let thinking again pass quite into life, etc.”

But however great the expectation of Solger, of the Ministry and of many in Berlin regarding Hegel’s activity was, his appearance here too was nevertheless noiseless, without pomp and fuss, and only gradually did he press on to irresistibility. Solger wrote on 22 November 1818 to Tieck: “I was eager to see what impression the good Hegel would make here. No one speaks of him, for he is quiet and diligent. It would need only for the dullest echoer to have come here, of the sort they would only too gladly have one of, and a great din would be raised and the students be directed to his lecture courses for the salvation and rescue of their souls.”

#### Berlin and Philosophy.

The peculiar atmosphere of the local spirit into which Hegel had now entered is that of a thoroughgoing critical fragmentation. Berlin is the city of *absolute reflection*, which *unrest of thinking* is connected with the not yet culminated development of the Prussian state and of its capital itself. In Berlin nothing naive, nothing immediate exists, but everything as something produced only by reflection. A peculiar sharpness of understanding pervades here all classes of society and imparts to them also in the practical sphere a great mobility and briskness. The Berliner quickly recognizes the extremes and is, for the surface of acting, readily decisive. But with reflection an inclination to an *ironic attitude* is also bound up, the danger of which, of passing over into *boredom*, into *inactivity*, the Berliner can in the end overcome only through a striving toward the overcoming of reflection. He must therefore *cultivate himself*, and

[p. 321]

this he does too, with restless diligence, in every direction. He concerns himself about everything, even the remote; everything he appropriates; and nothing new happens under the sun that his reflection does not seize upon. Precisely for this reason, however, he always needs *new materials of culture*. Reflection is indeed always ready to take in materials, but it itself produces none and after every assimilation feels ever new hunger. From this side it appears, in the extreme, as a Moloch whose arms of fire let every fresh life burn itself out. And since a city is naturally more many-sided and stronger than an individual, such a one must be prepared for this: that, as soon as one has *comprehended* him, one will forget him, perhaps disdain him, however eagerly one had at first gone to meet him as a new object. Once one has grasped the material of culture that he can offer, has, so to speak, solved his riddle, one will subject him himself to sharp criticism and give him the at first humbling feeling of being not himself, as it seemed, the all-sided whole, but only a fragment and moment of it. Whoever comes to Berlin from outside will perhaps enter through triumphal arches, but it will not last long before he has to listen to Saturnian verses.

That unrest of reflection drives one, however, of itself to philosophy, because it is philosophy that sublates the *dualism* of reflecting. Only in speculative insight do all the contradictions vanish which reflection turns over and over and in whose press it maintains itself only through the dexterity of leaping ever from one to another — which the Berlin intelligence, often to the great danger of character, admittedly understands masterfully. *Religion* likewise contains the reconciliation of all contradictions, but in a form which belongs to the *heart*, as is still actually the case, e.g., in *Vienna*. In Berlin, by contrast, even piety is permeated by reflection. Faith is not unreflective surrender, but strives to give itself an intelligible account of the truth of its content.

Through the university Berlin had from now on the opportunity to do justice, in an orderly course of study, to the drive immanent in reflection to perfect itself in speculation; it

[p. 322]

could now also educate itself speculatively. *Fichte* was the first who introduced it into the school of purest abstraction and reflection, but he did not satisfy the need for a rounding-off of science. To that extent *Schleiermacher* became more significant for the Berliners, as on the one hand he extended himself more into the breadth of the individual sciences, lecturing on dialectic, psychology, ethics, aesthetics, the history of philosophy, and on the other devoted an excellent activity to the cognition of faith and the further formation of Protestantism. Schleiermacher had formed for himself in Berlin a quite peculiar congregation, belonging to the whole city, to all estates and ages, which in his sermons and lectures satisfied the need to bring reflection upon its faith into clarity, to trace the shape of its religious self-consciousness in pure outlines. In his genuinely North German personal reserve, which, with constant *reservation* of its *individuality*, opened itself in most active industry on all sides, Schleiermacher was the most complete opposite of Hegel, *a living work of art of reflection that had become nature*. But precisely because in him everything was reflection, he could indeed furnish the truly plastic expression of the deeper Berlinism, *but not lift it above itself*. — *Solger*, finally, was by nature befriended with this critical spirit of Berlin. He was born in Schwedt, had studied in Halle, heard Fichte in Berlin, lectured in Frankfurt on the Oder, and was called as professor to Berlin in 1811, where he died on 25 October 1819, and thus worked together with Hegel for only a single year; Hegel, ten years later, expressed himself at length about him, Hegel’s *Works*, vol. XVI. Solger is the *last* of the *intermediate figures* that stand midway between *Schelling* and Hegel. What in the endeavors of *Wagner*, *Krause*, *Stutzmann*, *Klein*, *Troxler*, *Sinclair*, *Schleiermacher* appeared in the most various directions as an experiment of speculation found in Solger’s philosophizing a final conclusion. He concentrated the transition to Hegel. Solger occupied himself preferably with dialectic, with ethics as politics, with aesthetics and philosophy of religion, thus precisely with the domains of cognition for which Schelling’s philosophy had indeed given the greatest stimulus, but, when

[p. 323]

it is a question of systematic consistency, had brought about no thoroughgoing transformation. The philosophy of nature, as the science most promoted by Schelling’s school, Solger did not exclude precisely on purpose, but he devoted to it just as little a deliberate study.

In a multitude of particulars, namely in politics, coinciding with Hegel, he differed from him first of all in that he wished to present dialectic as *dialogue*. The need to improve the method of speculation led him back to the *social* form of philosophizing, which, with the back and forth of question and answer, precedes in the history of thinking the discovery of the Concept’s own dialectic. Solger wanted to attain a greater objectivity of cognition through the dramatic opposition of *reflecting* subjectivities. Hegel, on the other hand, demanded of the subject that, in order to know speculatively, it abstract from its subjectivity absolutely and by this act make the same into the pure, reflection-free vessel of the Concept, which must bear in itself the necessity of its differentiation from other concepts as well as that of its connection with them. This independence of the Idea to be cognized from the subject that cognizes it he called the *self-movement of the Concept*. Solger felt himself never satisfied by his dialogical works of art, because the highest demand for unity of truth and certainty lived in him and the form of conversation cannot fully satisfy it. To him, therefore, because it brought into the dialogical presentation the act of the *elevation of consciousness* from reflection to speculation, Hegel’s method appeared as one that removes itself too far from universal human consciousness and wants to let nothing count but *speculation in general*. This never occurred to Hegel, however often it was reproached to him; only in *science*, and here rightly, did he make speculative cognition count as the absolutely true; outside it he fully recognized immediate certainty or the reassurance of authority. Solger wrote in the *Nachlass*, I, 702: “Into another error fall, on the other hand, the *stricter* philosophers, among whom I now reckon especially Hegel, however highly I must esteem him for his great knowledge

[p. 324]

and his clear insight into the various scientific metamorphoses of the faculty of thought. These, namely, recognize higher speculative thinking as a wholly different kind from the common, but hold it, in its lawfulness and universality, to be the only thing actual, and everything else, even cognition from experience, insofar as it cannot be traced back entirely to these laws, to be a deceptive and in every respect null fragmentation of the same.” This is merely a misunderstanding on Solger’s part, since Hegel has never denied the necessity of the empirical as such, but has just as much shown how, through its contradiction with itself, it presses on to the universality and necessity of the determinations themselves.

With Solger’s incompleteness of the dialectical process toward independence it is further connected that he lets logical precision still mingle with fancy and representation, which appears especially from his religio-philosophical considerations. Solger knew how to handle the subtlest abstractions with fluency. The concepts of being and cognizing, of being and non-being, occupied him in part in distinct, excellent treatises. But then representations such as creation, love, sacrifice and others again gave him much to do. His seriousness of research and his classical culture prevented him from being satisfied superficially. He studied, e.g., ancient mythology at length for the sake of the philosophy of religion.

To say in a word what placed him between Schelling and Hegel, this was *irony*, i.e. the manner in which he determined the *negative*. According to Schelling, the Absolute *is supposed* not to be thought without negation of itself as the positive, but he takes the negative only as an unfortunate accident, as an occurrence that should not have occurred, coming in from outside. Solger sought to grasp the negative already as the self-determination of the Absolute, but he did not succeed in apprehending it in its identity with the positive, in its immanent freedom, and so he remained at the mystical concept of *sacrifice*, that God, in order to create the world, makes himself into nothing.

With Solger Hegel indeed had no further intercourse, but they stood in thorough mutual esteem on friendly terms with one another.

[p. 325]

Hegel had wished to alternate with Solger, according to semesters, in the delivery of the individual subjects. About this a note of Solger’s to Hegel is still extant, in which, after expressing his lively joy that through Hegel the philosophy of nature would now also be represented, of which he did not have knowledge enough, he finally said: “Might I succeed in winning your friendship! I will make no long preliminaries about the inward and deep veneration that your writings have always inspired in me. I have attempted the work in my own way and by another path, and would wish that this too might not wholly displease you. Perhaps it is possible that we work not only in concord but also in agreement, and this good fortune I should prize the more highly as one is so little accustomed to it.

With all my heart

Yours.”

With *Schleiermacher* Hegel could not get on well. He met in him a personality which brought him close again to the circle of Schlegel’s Romanticism, though greatly mitigated by Jacobian yearning and tenderness. Still it is at any rate a proof of the ethical energy of both men that between them, given their so wholly opposed manner, and given the inclination of the Berlin atmosphere to foster such quarrels between celebrities in order to exploit them for the advancement of mediocrities, it never came to a public scandal. At a midday meal they did, to be sure, once in 1819, on account of *de Wette*, come to sharp blows. But Schleiermacher conducted himself with his frankness and wrote, attaching it to an external piece of information which he had promised Hegel at table, a few days afterward:

“In order not to forget the one over the other, most worthy Herr Colleague. The agent of the house of Hesse in Bordeaux is named Rebstock and lives at Alexanderplatz No. 4.

Incidentally, I really must be very much obliged to you that you at once answered the rude word which ought not to have escaped me the other day, for by that you have at least softened the sting which the vehemence that took me by surprise, in

[p. 326]

left behind in me. I should like, soon, if it so turns out, that we could continue the disputation where it stood before those improper words fell. For I esteem you far too much not to wish to come to an understanding with you about a subject which in our present situation is of such great importance.”

Schleiermacher.

Hegel replied to this:

“I thank you, most worthy Herr Colleague, first of all for the address of the wine dealer’s given in your note received yesterday; — then for the remark which, in removing a recent unpleasant occurrence between us, at the same time mediates the reply that proceeded from my agitation, and leaves in me only a decided increase of my esteem for you. — It is, as you remark, the present importance of the subject which tempted me in company to bring on a disputation which to continue with you, and to bring to a reconciliation of our views, can be nothing other than interesting.”

For all their inner tension, both, fully conscious of their independence, at last through their truly Attic urbanity managed, without ever dissembling, to hold their antipathy down on public occasions, indeed once even took a slide together arm in arm at Tivoli. Only in the pupils of both men did the contradiction of their views become an element of real hostility. *Gans* (*Rückblicke*, 1836, p. 252) gives as the real ground of Hegel’s harshness toward Schleiermacher that the latter, with all the means at his command, thwarted Hegel’s admission to the *Academy*. Gans mentions that Hegel, at the proposal to invite Schleiermacher to join the Berlin Yearbooks, flared up violently and declared that this meant driving himself out — which exclusion was only the counter-exclusion to that of Hegel from the Academy, for which it was alleged that an Academy could admit no philosopher who founds a school, because this would arouse strife, as indeed

[p. 327]

Fichte too had remained excluded; — which naturally was only a pretext.

Hegel’s chief influence on Berlin in the philosophical respect was now that he literally took it to school and taught it his system with naive rigidity. The peculiarity of Berlin described above favored this *discipline*, as Hegel himself liked to call it, extraordinarily, because the Berliner is indeed very pliable and in need of culture, but as yet little self-creative. He demands, through this condition, as it were, to be mastered, and gladly tolerates it if one only knows how to proceed with spirit and to give him nourishment. Hence Berlin too cannot take in contrasts enough, lest the sameness of a single direction produce an altogether intolerable flatness. So it was then a piece of good fortune for the cheerful city that to the Schleiermacherian element, with its versatile mobility, the Hegelian element, with its solid, articulated systematics and its urge for method, was opposed. But for Hegel and his school too it was a great favor of fate that Schleiermacher’s learning, spirit, wit, standing, popular power did not let them rise too quickly and made them work continually. Or rather, what we call a piece of good fortune was, taken from a higher standpoint, the necessity of the German spirit to place the classical representatives of the north-eastern culture in immediate relation to that of the south-west, in order thereby to initiate the deeper and more all-sided reconciliation of the German spirit with itself. Many Swiss, Swabians, Silesians, Pomeranians, Frisians and Saxons then heard Hegel and Schleiermacher with equal zeal.

#### Inaugural Address in Berlin.

On 22 October 1818 Hegel opened his lectures at Berlin with an address to his hearers which, as far as philosophy itself is concerned, was for the most part a verbal repetition of the one held two years earlier at Heidelberg. He added, however, some passages which concerned Prussia, Berlin and the critical philosophy that harmonizes with the Enlightenment in respect of the not-knowing of the divine.

[p. 328]

All the pompous turns which the later so-called Hegelianism was wont to take concerning the connection of the Hegelian philosophy with the “world-historical” determination of the Prussian state are already contained in germ in this address. Berlin pride must after all have something infectious. Hegel, otherwise indeed always manly but never power-drunk, opined: “At this university, the *university of the center*, philosophy, the center of all culture of spirit and of all science and truth, must also find its place and preeminent cultivation.” — The Germans were once more — even if without the express reminder of the Jews contained in the earlier Heidelberg address — praised as the *chosen people of God in philosophy*. “This science has taken refuge with the Germans and lives on in them alone. To us the safekeeping of this holy light is entrusted, and it is our calling to tend and nourish it and to take care that the highest that man can possess, the self-consciousness of his essence, not be extinguished and perish.”

The *Kantian* philosophy, the originally Prussian one, to which Hegel owed his own philosophy in the most essential points and whose perfecter he can with justice be called, was handled harshly by him: “In the end the so-called critical philosophy has given this not-knowing of the eternal and divine a good conscience, by assuring that it has *proved* that nothing can be known of the eternal and divine. This supposed cognition has even arrogated to itself the name of *philosophy*, etc.” He, on the contrary, promised a philosophy which would have *substance* and invoked the spirit of *youth* in doing so, for “it is still unbiased by the negative spirit of vanity, by the insubstantiality of a merely critical endeavor. A still healthy heart still has the courage to demand truth, and it is the realm of truth in which philosophy is at home, which it builds and in which we become partakers through its study. What in life is true, great and divine is so through the Idea: the aim of philosophy is to grasp it in its true shape and universality.”

[p. 329]

#### The Scientific Examination Commission.

In June 1820 the ministry appointed Hegel a full member of the Royal Scientific Examination Commission of the Province of Brandenburg. In this capacity he had partly to examine orally in philosophy young men, both as candidates for the teaching profession and also, under the arrangement then still in existence, with a view to their fitness for admission to the university, partly to go through and evaluate the minutes of the Gymnasia on the examination of the school-leaving candidates and the German essays written by these. Since Hegel himself had been rector of a Gymnasium long enough, he possessed indeed the most complete qualification for such an office, which was moreover suited to procure for him, beyond the circle of his immediate hearers, what one is wont to call influence. But the office was for him a false position insofar as his spirit, at an already advanced age, in the need to be able to complete important works gradually, in the full feeling of philosophical teaching power, found itself thereby, if only in part, set back again into a sphere which he had been so glad to be able to leave on the transition to Heidelberg. He therefore asked the ministry after some years to be willing to relieve him again of this office, which robbed him of so much time, which also happened in 1822.

In the assessment of the pupils’ work Hegel was very mild. He did not want one to demand of youth already what is self-thought, but rather to look to a clear and tasteful reproduction of what had come up in the circle of Gymnasium instruction, since the work of the school-leaving candidates had in particular also the purpose of making the higher authorities acquainted with the condition of the Gymnasia. Often he praised the good disposition in the essays, censured it when at many Gymnasia much was said of Christ or even of the Devil, polemicized against pupils’ praising the constitutions of Athens and Rome as models for a present-day statesman, warned against thoughtless rhetoric, and extended his criticism even to the handwriting and the format of the work. The correction by the teachers he assessed each time. Hegel

[p. 330]

was scrupulous in all such matters. He even wrote his judgments first in rough draft — a model Prussian official.

Connected with this occupation is a letter which Hegel addressed, at the beginning of the year 1823, on 7 February, to the ministry of education: *on the teaching of philosophy at Gymnasia*; *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 357–367. He complained in it greatly of the slight preparation with which so many young people came to the university, of their complete lack of knowledge and of culture. He must, he said, for himself and his colleagues be *alarmed*, considering that they were after all not merely to *train* such people for service but, according to the purpose of the universities, to educate them scientifically. Hence, he thought, an instruction of some *two hours* weekly in *formal logic* and *empirical psychology* in the yearly course of the Gymnasia for the Prima would be beneficial in bringing about a greater universality of the scientific sense. In such propaedeutic instruction in philosophy the point was not the so popular thinking for oneself, but that the forms of thinking and the determinate concepts be retained in *memory*, because without such fixation there is nothing there for spirit.

In the Prussian Gymnasia this procedure is now also followed, after *Herbart*, in 1821, in the appendix to the second edition of his *Textbook of Introduction to Philosophy*, had expressed himself similarly. The school-leaving candidates have to pass an examination in the so-called philosophical propaedeutic. Whether this is to the benefit or the harm of philosophy is not to be investigated here. In any case it is of value to see philosophy represented, at least, in the Gymnasia as well, as a branch of teaching alongside the others. The pupil thereby receives, even if he learned nothing, still symbolically the representation that the state deems philosophy necessary for universal culture.

#### The Philosophy of Right and Demagogy.

The first larger literary work which Hegel undertook at Berlin was the working up of his philosophy of right and of the state. The edition of it for the book trade was indeed

[p. 331]

made only in the year 1821, but the preface was already concluded on 25 June 1820. As to content, we find in it again the essentials of Hegel’s earlier political convictions, only neatly set out in paragraphs as regards form. The definite advances that can be singled out were the following. The Concept of *morality*, which earlier had been accidentally absorbed into the other concepts, is made independent, as the middle between the abstract right of the individual and the concrete right of the state, into the *essence* of the whole sphere of the objective will. Individual personal right forms the beginning as the immediate *being* of the will that objectifies itself. The negation of this objectivity, indifferent to the welfare, the intention, the conscience of others, is that subjectivity which, from its opinion, itself judges the quality of its willing, the relation of the same to its universality and necessity, which is in and for itself and ought to be. The negation, however, of this abstract inwardness as well as of that abstract externality is, according to Hegel, to be *ethical life*, whose moments he distinguished as the family, civil society and the state proper. This separation and positing of the Concept of *civil society* as the element opposed to the natural piety and inwardness of the family, through the culture of the understanding and the manifoldness of interests, was a great insight of Hegel’s. The *state* itself, as the unity of nature and culture, raises itself, according to him, above the plurality of families as above the egoism of cultivating and enjoying, to the Concept of *freedom as its end in itself*, to which the circles of the families as of society are subordinated. In the state itself he distinguished inner sovereignty from the outer, and grounded through the latter the transition of the *single* state into *world history*, of whose immense whole it is itself only a small member. The conception of the philosophy of history was here thus in its principle *Kantian*, namely to regard it from the Idea of the state.

Had these *Elements of the Philosophy of Right* now appeared, as *Thaden* wished, in a purely systematic form, they would perhaps indeed have been studied still more, but less discussed; now they are more discussed than studied. Hegel

[p. 332]

added, namely, to the text a multitude of remarks in which he entered upon questions of the day. Roman law as subsidiary in relation to that which a state has created for itself; the indeterminate and accidental in singular scrupulousness, when man is not held by the spirit and consciousness of an ethical community; the relation of state and church, that the latter, namely as an institution for the teaching of a faith, must be subordinated to the state as the self-conscious ethical substance, and the necessity of hereditary princely right were treated in a sharp and emphatic tone.

Already at the end of the last century and at the beginning of this one, Hegel had exchanged the seductive indeterminacy of the representations of people, of freedom and equality in general, for the more determinate concepts of the state, of articulation by estates and of an all-sidedly provident government. For the necessity of the hereditariness of monarchy as one of the deepest determinations of modern state life he had even been enthusiastic in Jena. One must therefore, in recollection of this, put aside the notion that Hegel first trimmed his Concept of the state to the interests of the Prussian government by a self-conscious defection from his philosophy. He conceded nothing of ethical autonomy. He demanded that a people give itself its laws, and declared it ridiculous, a disgrace, if one did not hold it ripe for this. He demanded the justice of the peace, publicity of the administration of justice and trial by jury, the administrative independence of communes and corporations. Finally he demanded popular representation and the two-chamber system, publicity of the proceedings of legislation, and freedom of the press for the formation of a truly public opinion. Hegel was at that time, under *Hardenberg*, convinced that all these concepts, in which he recognized the eternal reason of the state in general, constituted also the soul of the Prussian one. In a letter to the state chancellor, with which he sent him a copy of his philosophy of right, he expressed this belief quite decidedly. The Congress of Verona had not yet organized any reaction of the governments against the strivings of the peoples toward *self-government*; no one in Prussia yet doubted that sooner or later a popular representation

[p. 333]

for all Germany would come, and Hegel, having lived so long in smaller states, found himself quite captivated by the larger perspectives of Prussia.

Yet we must admit that in many respects his philosophical state had not even risen to the height to which Prussia had already advanced in its legislation. Against *Haller’s* tendency in the political sciences he had, to be sure, taken a decided stand. The thought that a state should be conceived only from the standpoint of private law, land and people only as the possession of a prince, governing only as a patriarchal conduct, and the laws not as the expression of the universal necessity of a spirit of a people, outraged him to his innermost, and he expressed this outrage in a well-known sharp remark to the *Philosophy of Right*, definitely enough to clear him of all suspicion of ever having inclined to the side of this so-called Restoration, in truth however, in relation to what exists, a revolution of political science. Just as energetically he declared himself against the *merely historical* conception of right, against the opinion as if it were a kind of spiritual vegetation. He granted every people the absolute authority to give itself laws and to raise practical reason, in individual forms appropriate to it, to the universal norm. The *Roman* law was therefore by him not at all revered as the *summum bonum* of legislation, and he liked to illuminate its shadow sides, in particular its law of the family, in glaring light. But in spite of such genuinely liberal views he nevertheless remained behind Prussia’s positive legislation on some points through earlier habituation. Of such a democracy harmonious with monarchy as the municipal ordinance of Prussia, i.e. of such a Concept of the political community, there are in him only beginnings, not elaborations. He still held fast to the two-chamber system and with it, in Anglican fashion, to a nobility of birth and entail, which for Prussia had already been legally antiquated, and against which he himself turned later, in 1831, in the critique of the English Reform Bill. That he never could rightly comprehend Prussia’s national system of defense has been remarked by us already more than once; he still always made the military into a

[p. 334]

particular estate of valor. Prussia carefully distinguishes between the estate which belongs to civil society through the culture of the individual, and that which falls to the individual through the mediation of election for political representation and legislation. It seems never to have become quite clear to Hegel that a Prussian province is neither a small state within the larger, nor merely quantitatively a French department or Russian government, but the state itself in a peculiar tribal individualization that is nevertheless concretely identical with the whole. What he did grasp quite correctly of Prussia was its relation to science, that Prussia could maintain and further develop itself only in free alliance with it.

But not only did he write remarks to the text, but also a *preface*, and in this he left behind a sting long and deeply felt. The year 1819 had, through Kotzebue’s murder, revealed the fanaticism to which the conceptless enthusiasm of German youth for the political rebirth of the fatherland had risen. The eccentricities of the Wartburg Festival, which occurred in the evening at the kindling of the customary October fires, neither resolved nor approved by the committee, had transferred the misgivings of the governments from the circles of youth to others as well, in particular to those of the teachers themselves. Hegel was hostile to this activity. His aversion to every secret league-making was sincere, and just as sincere his contempt for a thoughtless enthusiasm, his anger against a merely subjective politics which heated itself with the abstractions of people, freedom, brotherhood, unity and with similar generalities, for the reverse side of these representations, in flowery, phrase-laden declamations. His polemic against the abstract making of states out of thoughtless feelings was here precisely the reverse of that which he had conducted in 1817 against the historical particularism and monopolism of the Württemberg Estates. Then he combated an abstract past, now an abstract future. Certainly he was right, against the insightless insisting on an ideal, against an indeterminate ought and an often associated unmotivated contempt of what exists, to assert *the reason already present*

[p. 335]

*also in empirical actuality* and in this respect to impress respect for the historical.

But through two things he spoiled for himself the beneficial effects of his polemic, justified according to the Concept of the state. First, through the easy misunderstandability of the canon which he set up for politics in the preface to the *Philosophy of Right* with the notorious words: “What is actual is rational; what is rational is actual.” — He himself was compelled, later, in the second edition of his *Encyclopedia*, to give the explanation that by actuality he did not understand the merely empirical existence, mixed with chance and so also with the bad and with what ought not to be, but the existence identical with the Concept of reason. For if the actual is taken in the sense of subsuming under it the common appearance, the immediate reality, there is no question that the same can also be highly *unreasonable*. Reason is, to be sure, in and for itself and is the universal necessity, but in appearance chance claims for nature, and arbitrariness for history as the freedom of the individual, an undeniable right, so that the absoluteness of reason appears at the same time in the form of the relative; the relative, however, has a side in itself according to which it is not yet what it is to be, or no longer is what it should be. According to the common way in which philosophical matters are apprehended, there is therefore preached in that paradox of Hegel’s an absolute political quietism which, adopted as a maxim, could bring the greatest danger to a state still in full motion, such as the Prussian. Not wholly without reason, therefore, frightened by those words, all who had Prussia’s future before their eyes turned away mistrustfully from Hegel as a man whose politics was too narrow and too dependent on reference to Prussia as he just found it.

The second point that alienated hearts from him in that *preface* was that he not only spoke out against the demagogic tendency in general, but also wove into his polemic the name of a man whose colleague he had been as Privatdozent in Jena and whose successor in the teaching post he had been at Heidelberg. He called *Fries* the “commander of all shallowness” and rejected in

[p. 336]

the bitterest terms his enthusiasm for the fatherland, public spirit, friendship — as the “mush of the heart.” — These utterances would better have been left unsaid. And Hegel has had to pay dearly enough for them. An antipathy against him, rising to implacability, settled in all who belonged to the Kantian, the Jacobian, the de Wette–Schleiermacher and the national tendency. The greater Hegel’s standing in Berlin became, the more significantly he began really to intervene, also personally, in the learned officialdom, the more violent became the reaction against him, and we may not shirk the duty of reporting the most important part of the friction of that time. In the Halle *General Literary Gazette*, February 1822, No. 40, pp. 316–17, a critique of Hegel’s *Philosophy of Right* ended by communicating the passage adduced by Hegel himself as proof of his judgment on Fries, which reads: “In the people in which genuine public spirit reigned, life would come from below, from the people, to every business of public affairs; to every single work of popular education and of national service living associations would dedicate themselves, inviolably united by the holy chain of friendship.” — To this that review made the remark: “We admit that an interpretation inclined to the worst might find these words questionable; meanwhile they permit an innocuous one, even approved by the author, if he stands by his words quoted above about public opinion, p. 323. Is this, in the healthy sense, not genuine public spirit? Why, then, deliberately choose the bad interpretation and cast suspicion on the words? Herr Fries, so far as we know, has no happy lot, and the author’s conduct toward him resembles the scorn and deliberate insult of an already bowed man. Such conduct is *not noble*, yet the reviewer will keep silent the true name and leave its choice to the thinking reader.”

Since Hegel, in his objective cast of mind, had in fact not thought of a personal insult, he was quite beside himself. He copied out for himself the conclusion of the review and in his vexation went so far as to demand, in a lengthy letter, protection from the ministry of education against this denunciation, as

[p. 337]

he called it. He was so weak as to find it abominable that a Prussian official could be so suspected in a paper supported by the munificence of the Prussian government and appearing in Prussia itself. He assured them that he had thought not in the least of Fries as a private man, only of his pernicious principles. Indeed, he wished to furnish the ministry, in that critique of a party which believed itself privileged and was accustomed to take the big word, an example of where *too great a freedom of the press* could lead!

Now the minister *Altenstein* had, on 24 August 1821, said to Hegel with regard to his *Philosophy of Right*: “By insisting, in this work as in your lectures generally, with the seriousness that befits science, on grasping what is present and actual, and on comprehending the rational in nature and history, you give philosophy, as it seems to me, the only right position toward actuality, and thus it will succeed most surely in preserving your hearers from the pernicious conceit which rejects what exists *without having cognized it* and, particularly in regard to the state, takes pleasure in the arbitrary setting up of ideals empty of content.” — When Hegel now made that demand, *Altenstein* was indeed timid enough to recommend to the editorship of the Halle Literary Gazette a stricter censorship of the reviews to be taken into the paper, *under threat of the withdrawal* of the authorization granted to it, in case of non-observance. “To this, however,” Altenstein wrote to Hegel on 26 July, “the ministry has had to confine itself, since it fully recognized the correctness of your conviction that, if you wish to seek satisfaction for the personal attack directed against you in the review in question, you have to turn to the *courts*, or, in regard to the *public*, to make a *declaration* to it.”

Apart from this aberration of Hegel’s, of mixing the power of the state into literature, his *Philosophy of Right*, especially as a lecture course, had an extraordinarily beneficent effect. The simple thought that the human spirit in so many thousands of years cannot have produced in the existing states merely what is perverse and inhuman, that therefore a *merely negative* stance toward

[p. 338]

actuality as given is not the right one, and that it therefore does not come down to the bare postulating of other conditions — this simple thought worked on many with a magically reconciling power. The spirited conception of the particular elements of the organism of the state which Hegel gave created a quite different picture of the state from what the subjective generalities of Burschenschaft politics could have offered. One found oneself agreeably surprised to encounter in the present already more freedom and practical reason than the yearning pathos of exuberant speeches had led one to expect. Many young men who, as a result of the Burschenschaft investigations begun since 1817, still more since 1819, came to Berlin and became Hegel’s hearers, began to owe to him a truly new life, and formed quite properly the core of his following, to which the broader mass attached itself only gradually. Quite a number of names of upright, now esteemed men could be mentioned here who stood in such a relation to Hegel and for whom he was untiringly active, with a paternal heart, with sacrifices of every kind, indeed with personal danger.

His benevolence here may well have let itself be carried away even to the border of the adventurous. Only a small example of it shall be told. One of his hearers was, on account of political connections, in the prison of the Stadtvogtei, whose rear side faces out onto the Spree. Friends of the prisoner had opened an understanding with him, and since they, as the investigation also showed, rightly held him innocent, they sought to prove their sympathy to him by going in a boat at midnight under the window of his prison and trying to converse with him. Once it succeeded, and the friends, likewise hearers of Hegel’s, knew how to present the matter to him in such a way that he too resolved to take part in a trip. Very easily a bullet from the sentry could have spared the converter of demagogues all further efforts. Also Hegel seems to have been overcome on the water by the feeling of the strange situation. When the boat, namely, halted before the window, the conversation was to begin and, out of caution, be conducted in Latin. Hegel, however, limited himself to a few innocent generalities and asked, e.g., the prisoner: “*num me vides?*” [do you see me?]

[p. 339]

Since one could almost have reached him one’s hand, this question was somewhat comical and did not fail to arouse great hilarity, in which Hegel joined on the return trip with Socratic jest.

#### Defense of Goethe’s Theory of Colors.

The great interest which Hegel took in Goethe’s theory of colors, and constantly proved through exact work of his own, especially on the observations on the physiological colors made by Government Councillor *Schulze* and communicated to him in Nuremberg as an experiment (about which there is still extant a manuscript that seems to have been intended for print), was noted by Goethe with great pleasure. A reinforcement of his cause through a mightily burgeoning philosophy, through the accession and speculative interpretation of a philosopher like Hegel, the latter’s influence precisely in Berlin, the attempts of a pupil of Hegel’s, Herr v. *Henning*, to devote to the exposition of Goethe’s theory of colors a standing special lecture — all this could only be welcome to Goethe. Of the manner of the exchange between him and Hegel the letters of both printed in Hegel’s *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 501–508, can give an idea, although these are not all the letters exchanged between them. One sees from them that Goethe laid great value on Hegel’s assent, but also how happy it made Hegel to be recognized in his endeavors for it by a Goethe whose writings he was accustomed to read incessantly.

Goethe had sent him, at the beginning of summer 1821, a drinking glass which illustrated the chief moments of his doctrine, with the following inscription in his own hand:

#### To the Absolute

#### commends itself

#### most warmly

#### for friendly reception

#### the primal phenomenon.

In a still unprinted letter, to which the printed one of Goethe’s of 13 April 1821 is the answer, Hegel thanked with

[p. 340]

humorous solemnity. Wine, he said, had always been a great ally of the philosophy of nature, because it proves to the world so clearly that spirit is in nature too. But so instructive a wineglass as the one presented to him by Goethe was a true world-goblet, in which the black Ahriman serves the bright Ormuzd as the foil of revelation. The ancients too had not forgotten to give the mystical Dionysus a cup among his symbols.

From then on Goethe and Hegel remained again in constant, if not too copious, intercourse. They recommended young men to one another, e.g. Goethe his commentator *Schubart*, who afterward became so violent an opponent of Hegel. Later the Berlin Yearbooks gave occasion for several communications. Such letters of Goethe’s were among Hegel’s highest joys, and one can tell from the crumpled, brittle papers how much they have been looked at, how often they may have been triumphantly shown to dear acquaintances. *Zelter* was a chief intermediary of all literary, artistic and higher social stirrings of life between Berlin and Weimar.

The unity of Hegelian speculation and Goethean poetry became a veritable dogma of the Hegelian school. The poet was explained by means of the philosopher, the philosopher was verified, documented by means of the poet, as *Göschel* in particular has done, who then, to be sure, added the Bible to both. The accident that the birthdays of the two men adjoin one another gave their spiritual kinship quite a mystical sheen, and gave the more poetic comrades of the Weimar–Berlin circle much happy song-matter for encomiastic verses. So greatly did Hegel interest himself in everything that concerned Goethe and, in the scientific relation, his theory of colors, that he copied out from the *curriculum vitae* which *Schopenhauer* submitted to the philosophical faculty at Berlin the whole detailed account which the latter had given in it of his relation to Goethe with regard to his investigations on seeing and on colors.

[p. 341]

#### Polemic against the Theology of Feeling.

Had Hegel with his *Philosophy of Right* attacked the principle of subjectivity in the political respect, he was soon to come to do the same in the religious relation, an attack which, however, drew upon him infinitely more odium, slander, suspicion and embitterment. The theologians persecuted him from here on under the then dreaded nickname of a pantheist. The occasion was given by *Hinrichs*. He had asked Hegel to write for his book, *On Religion in Its Inner Relation to Science*, a commendatory preface, which Hegel also did, after a preceding correspondence, in April 1822. This foreword is also reprinted in Hegel’s *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 279–304. The wrath over the attack by the Halle Literary Gazette still churned on in him, and that preface was still written under the dominion of this affect, whereby it has in part received a great beauty of the most pithy language of anger. It strove for the proof that in general, and thus not for religion either, may *feeling as principle* be taken; still less could science itself, thus also theology, be *grounded* by feeling. Hegel showed first how the course of philosophy had to bring it about that feeling acquired the *significance* of a principle. The understanding, namely, had dissolved cognition into pure finitudes, whence the deeper need had fled to feeling, in order to restore in its simplicity the unity and wholeness lost in the splintering of reflection. This was the *justification of feeling*. But precisely here the turning point enters, namely the confusion of this *form* with the *content* itself. Feeling is the form of the immediate existence of spirit; consequently there lies in it as such no determination at all, but this comes to it only through the content mediated elsewhere. This could accordingly necessarily be an infinitely varied one, not only in the positive, healthy and good, but just as much in the negative, morbid and evil. If one says, then, that theology must proceed from feeling, *everything depends on the difference of the*

[p. 342]

*position*: whether feeling is to count only as the first, *initial* form of the content, or whether it is to count as substantial principle, as the *absolutely first*. If one asserts the latter, this is the way to screw up all possible *subjective notions* to the rank of scientific determinations, and door and gate are opened to the arbitrariness of determining. Spirit, which through thinking purifies itself to universality and necessity as its essence, is thereby put into contradiction with itself.

In thus turning against the theology of feeling in general, he also attacked, although he did not name the name, the particular modification which *Schleiermacher* in 1821 had given to feeling for the working out of dogmatics. We have seen earlier how Hegel already in 1802 judged the principle of Schleiermacher’s religiosity and churchliness. Even before Schleiermacher’s book appeared he had written to Daub that the enterprise reminded him of the Xenion:

Long enough can one pay with counters, / But in the end — then one must draw the purse after all.

Schleiermacher had entitled his book: *The Christian Faith, Presented in Coherent Connection according to the Principles of the Evangelical Church*. The principles, however, came back only to the presupposition that science consists in reflection on the particular condition of pious feeling. They had thus no objective character. Not revelation as fact; not the doctrine of the church as symbol; not the Bible as primitive holy tradition; not spirit in the necessity and universality of its essence, but the *empirical subject* was to be raised to principle.

Precisely this standpoint, in and for itself inadequate, is indeed in Schleiermacher what is great, and a necessary consequence to which the principle of subjectivity had to come. If, therefore, well-meaning but uninsightful followers of Schleiermacher have tried everything possible to cover up, by sophistical turns, the complete dissolution of all historical content in him; if they have persuaded themselves that revelation, the doctrine of the church, biblical tradition occupy in him a rank of principle

[p. 343]

whereas in him they are in truth only moments subordinated to his subjectivity, which he draws in very contingently as *confirmation* of his feeling, but not as ground of the *statements* of his pious stirrings, and which therefore also, gathered up from all sides, he has printed only below the text as remarks, as notes: so have they diminished the man, while they supposed they were making him greater by such distortions. One must not confuse the preacher Schleiermacher with the dogmatician; one must not confound the excellent *inconsistencies* within his dogmatics with its principle itself. Schleiermacher’s peculiarity lies, for one thing, in this, that he had made himself free of everything externally historical. Precisely thereby he was inwardly at one with Hegel, however much he came into conflict with him over the merely psychological mediation of the content of dogmatics.

The Protestant church has, to be sure, never had the principle of making the statements of a pious feeling its principle. That here the feeling of a Schleiermacher, of so spirited, deeply religious a man, furnished the material of the description, and that this circumstance made good again much that the principle as such spoiled, remains in the end only an accident. That which Schleiermacher called the *connection* was merely a *psychological analysis*. He found himself, in reflection on himself, among many other states *also* as a subject with stirrings which he called pious, to distinguish them from others, because they made themselves noticeable through the dualism of evil and good in relation to the universal world-connection. Evil he found as an existence posited through him, the good as one posited through him only insofar as he at the same time came upon, in his consciousness, the representation of Christ as that which had given his feeling the direction toward it, had made the decision for it possible. This Christ, however, his Lord and Master, worked in him actually only as an ideal.

Consistently he could have described only this dualistic state of sin and grace, but not the state that could be given to him not at all in his own experience, only in abstraction from it, hence only in pure *thinking*, the state

[p. 344]

of the feeling still untouched by the opposition of good and evil.
