For in the actuality of his pious feeling he found only the *krasis* [blend] of good and evil, with the relatively greater or lesser prominence of the one against the other, which quantitative difference he felt as the at the same time qualitative one of blessedness or damnation. From his own standpoint he had therefore to admit to himself that his conception of the essence of God in itself was no longer taken from feeling as such, but through an artificial act of reflection upon it. And as it fared with him with this unity, so also with the opposite one, the *actual sublatedness* of the opposition of sin and grace, which according to him does not occur empirically at all. Consequently this state too again cannot be felt, only *thought*. Because Schleiermacher could make no experience of the sensations which theology describes in the dogmas of *eschatology*, there remained to him here only analogical inferences of the understanding, and everything that he said of the dogmas of immortality, resurrection and the last judgment turned out therefore very thin and indeterminate; an indeterminacy which smacked entirely of the philosophy of the Enlightenment of the eighteenth century.

The complete lack of connection, finally, of his dogmatics — if by scientific connection one understands the inner, independent, not contrived interlocking of the determinations as such — showed itself at the end in quite a visible way. He treated there, namely, the dogma of the *Trinity* as a formal *collective proposition* to sum up the diversity of the statements of pious feeling into an aggregate unity. As little as he thereby did justice to the Concept of the matter, he was nonetheless here true to his principle. Most of his followers, in the endeavor to stamp him a model saint of orthodoxy, have vied to deprive him of even this greatness, and have left his acute critique of the doctrine of the Trinity unfruitful. Through their interpretations modeled on Calov, Quenstedt, Gerhard they have contrived to introduce into this necessary result of the principle of subjectivity a false objectivity. To be sure, Schleiermacher had, in the second edition of his immortal work, the highest product of sentimental rationalism, through what he could produce in the reciprocal brokenness of

[p. 345]

feeling and of reflection, already himself prepared such a confusion.

Since feeling as such is in itself indeterminate, the question arises by what it is determined and how it acquires a specific content. Strictly speaking, in Schleiermacher this content can relate only to his relationship *to Christ as the Redeemer*, and only through reflection does he go beyond this relation to the thought of *God*. Every feeling is to be *pious* in which, together with the particular worldly content, a relation to God is posited. The relation belongs factually to the human being. The subject, however, to which it is directed, is indeed, according to its essence, incomprehensible and unknown to the human being, yet is nevertheless supposed to count as the absolute, and therefore the feeling of the relation to it too is supposed to be a feeling of *dependence*, of a dependence which through the absoluteness of its content itself becomes absolute. The being-determined of the human being by God is, according to Schleiermacher, not *unity* with God, only relation.

If one calls these basic features of Schleiermacher’s doctrine of faith to mind, it becomes clear that Hegel’s opposition to it was by no means one prompted by personal motives, but was in fact one that sprang from the innermost core of his system. While Schleiermacher used thinking only as an instrument for bringing his feeling to expression, while he was concerned to expel philosophy from theology, Hegel held fast to the view that thinking is the principle of all science, and hence of theology too. “Whatever,” he said, “there is more in this science, or deserves to be more in it, than the general knowledge of religion, belonging to every member of any culture, this it has in common with philosophy.” — The followers of Schleiermacher in their polemic have often done Hegel an injustice by the assertion that he denied that religion could exist in the form of feeling. This absurdity never occurred to him; what seemed necessary to him, however, was the struggle against fixing this form. The intensity of feeling is supposed to unfold itself into objectivity, into a determinate representation of faith, into a breadth of religious acts, into a cult, into a science, which is basically impossible if one is to remain with sensation as the *exclusively true* form of

[p. 346]

religion.

Great men have the power to express what matters in a striking manner which gives *offense*. Woe to him through whom offense comes! This woe they must enjoy in fullest measure. But, says the same mouth, offense *must come*. Had Hegel given offense to the politics of subjectivity by his paradox of the rationality of the actual, so he now gave it to the theology of subjectivity by declaring the feeling of dependence to be the truly animal one and remarking sarcastically that, insofar as the feeling of absolute dependence is supposed to constitute the essence of Christianity, *the dog would be the best Christian*. This remark aroused a storm. A Privatdozent of the Berlin University, von *Keyserlingk*, wrote in 1824 a philosophy of religion and gave lectures on it, expressly against this remark, which Schleiermacher’s friends and followers, for all their otherwise tender-heartedness, never forgave Hegel. But as it usually goes with such remarks: in the original context in which they arose with their author, they indeed have all the energy, yet not at all the venomous sting which afterwards, in their fragmentary isolation, often seems to be their only point. That passage, which has become memorable, reads thus: “Even that that natural feeling is a feeling of the divine does not lie in feeling as natural. The divine is only in and for spirit, and spirit is this, as was said above, not by being a natural life, but a reborn one. If feeling is to constitute the fundamental determination of the essence of the human being, he is put on a level with the animal, for what is peculiar to the animal is that what its determination is, it has in feeling and lives in accordance with feeling. If religion in the human being is grounded only on a feeling, it has, rightly, no further determination than *the feeling of its dependence*, and so the dog would be the best Christian, for it bears this most strongly within itself and lives chiefly in this feeling. The dog too has feelings of redemption, when its hunger is satisfied by a bone. But spirit in religion has rather its liberation and the feeling of its divine freedom; only the free spirit has religion, and can have religion

[p. 347]

; what is bound in religion is the natural feeling of the heart, the particular subjectivity; what becomes free in it, and precisely thereby becomes so, is spirit. In the worst religions, and these are those in which servitude, and with it superstition, is most powerful, there is for the human being, in the elevation to God, the place where he feels, intuits and enjoys his freedom, infinity, universality, i.e. the higher, which stems not from feeling as such, but from spirit.”

Religion frees the human being from the burden of his self; but it frees him also from the delusion of having in God a being alien to him over against himself. To let oneself be determined by God is just as much as to let oneself be determined by one’s own essence, not contingent but necessary. Theologians like so much to speak of the *warmth* of the heart. But religion is not merely a warming of the individuality, which in its particularity still holds itself outside God; rather it is the absolute fire in which the heart, insofar as it is, by Christ’s own designation, the principle of the natural feelings, is burned up, and the spirit rises from such annihilation of what in it is void to unity with God as the Holy Spirit. We are accustomed to find theologians contradicting themselves even more than the philosophers. They often preach so beautifully of reconciliation with God, of the unity of human beings with God and thereby with one another. But if, with the union of the divine and the human, the seriousness and the truth of Christianity are to be made actual, they hastily declare this striving a pantheistic aberration, see in it the overthrow of state and church, and transform reverence for the divine into a terrorism of fear.

#### Hegel’s Interest in Art.

Berlin’s art treasures, its art exhibitions of every kind, stimulated Hegel’s love of art to the highest degree. For music he was passionately taken; for painting he possessed an innate eye. In poetry he was at home everywhere, and for architecture and sculpture he had at least the most open receptiveness,

[p. 348]

which he constantly sought to develop. It is truly ridiculous still to find Hegel presented here and there as a philosopher who was only a dry, abstruse logician, without any sense for works of the imagination. This conception is so untrue that, on the contrary, among the philosophers who distinguished themselves as *founders of systems*, Hegel stands thus far as the only one who has penetrated *the whole domain of art* with a distinctive spirit. Foreign nations have been juster in their judgment in this respect than the Germans. The French translator of Hegel’s *Aesthetics*, Bénard, says in his preface, p. V: [French] “We shall say, without fearing that we be accused of letting ourselves be carried away into exaggeration by a false enthusiasm: no philosopher has developed with as much depth and breadth the idea of art; none has determined and characterized the principal epochs of its history with the same precision; none, finally, has presented a classification and a theory of the arts that is more capable of satisfying the philosophical spirit of our century. — Moreover, the system set apart, one will find in abundance in this book original views, new insights, just appreciations, judgments of lofty import.”

What made Hegel stand out especially as a philosopher of art was the ability to engage with individual works of art of every kind with a determinate judgment. This ability was, to be sure, connected with his view of art in general, insofar as he left rather to one side the *metaphysics of the beautiful*, with which *Solger* had still occupied himself preeminently, and turned instead predominantly to art and its history. The closer discussion of the deficiencies that arose thereby: of the one-sidednesses which, even for a correct appreciation of the historical, resulted from the neglect of the pure Idea of the beautiful; of the forcedness with which he always wanted to bring the Concept of the sublime, of satire, of the romantic, etc., into connection only with determinate ideal forms and particular arts — this critique does not belong here. He has worked into his *Aesthetics* the soundest judgments on almost all the more important artists and works of art. Since in his lectures he now often mingled in as examples the immediate Berlin art world, its theater, its picture exhibitions

[p. 349]

etc., he gave the public thereby a great impulse, which, reacting upon him, created for him too an uncommon popularity.

More and more, therefore, did the earnest-cheerful occupation with art take up a large place in Hegel’s life. The aesthetic interest was at that time the only public one in Berlin. A political one did not exist. The melodramatic tension of police investigations was no political pathos, and the planned ecclesiastical policy, which in the capital of the Prussian state served as a kind of surrogate for the lack of political culture, was still in a state of attempts, which took on a more decided shape only from 1827. In time this excess of aesthetic bustle will vanish in Berlin too; religious culture has already known how to subordinate it to itself. But until the July Revolution the enjoyments of art were in fact the sole common center of Berlin society, and even such spirited, worldly-wise, patriotically cosmopolitan minds as *Rahel* furnish the proof of the then universal dominion of art. *Schleiermacher’s* Aesthetics too confirms what has been said in an interesting way and may quite properly be regarded as a product of the individual Berlin view of art, for Hegel had already brought his own with him from Heidelberg and only then inoculated the Berliners with it. If, however, the aesthetic element pushes back other substantial interests, if it is deliberately nourished in order to abstract from them, there is always connected with it much insipidity and sluggishness, much self-complacency and aimless craving for distraction. Looking and listening, enjoying and criticizing, becomes in the end a contentless, unmanly life of the Sybarite, which can corrupt even more capable natures. Until 1827 Berlin, a few quickly passing earnest fits aside, had produced in journalism, since the ceasing of Nicolai’s critical journal and of Gedicke’s Berlin Monthly, nothing but loose, light entertainment papers in which theater, concerts, poems, pictures, and anecdotal gossip about artists were the main thing. When Hegel now came to Berlin, he had the heroic labor of his life behind him. Sure of the depth, he took harmless delight in the light, graceful play of a beautiful superficiality. And he did more.

[p. 350]

By the unmistakable solidity of his participation he brought a greater earnestness into the aesthetic Epicureanism. His many-sided, reliable learning, his mature taste gave new points of view, necessitated new comparisons, forced a more scientific bearing. To be sure, much of this higher earnestness too soon became, unavoidably, an insufferable mannerism, in that a determinate Hegelianizing art criticism arose, which in judgment often fell into the most tasteless silliness and in tone into the most unnatural affectation, into a dialectical pedantry that presented the simplest things by the oddest detours. Yet to this shadow side of a precious, would-be speculative grasping of art there stood opposed also the light side of a really deeper penetration into the essence of the beautiful and of a happier mastery of the historical material. *Hotho* is, of the Berlin Hegelians, the one who presents this light side most purely in his lectures and writings, and who has therefore also rightly become the editor of Hegel’s *Aesthetics*. For the approximation of the system to the interests of the theater, *Rötscher* has then been especially active.

With the zest of a youth, with luxuriant delight, Hegel threw himself into the manifold nourishment which Berlin offered his sense of art. With unceasing and lasting pleasure he attended concerts, theater, galleries and exhibitions. Among the female singers he revered *Milder*, that unforgettable performer of Gluck’s and Mozart’s music, with the purest fervor. But even the mediocre he sought to find tolerable, and was inexhaustible in winning from it still some value from some side. In his good nature he condescended a couple of times so far as to take part in Berlin’s critical local papers. On Schiller’s *Wallenstein*, on Raupach’s *Converts*, he had articles inserted in 1825 in the Berlin *Schnellpost* (reprinted in the seventeenth volume of the collected works). Hegel’s thoroughness had to satisfy itself even in such things. His posthumous papers contain many small traces of the more exact account which he gave himself of such more ephemeral enjoyments. For the history of the visual arts he made himself

[p. 351]

especially from the Kunstblatt of the *Morgenblatt*, constantly long excerpts.

Let it be permitted, by way of illustration, to communicate one such private analysis, which in him on the one hand, in the detail, verges on the brooding, but on the other never sinks into it, and instead suddenly expands again to the most grandiose broad vistas. In 1820 he had visited the art exhibition at Dresden and wrote down the following about it:

“At this year’s art exhibition in Dresden were the four latest works of *Kügelgen*, bust-pictures in portrait size and format, of Christ, John the Baptist and the Evangelist, and of the Prodigal Son.

The portrait size and its format are indeed suitable for a head of Christ, but what a portrait is supposed to say of the others is not to be seen, still less of the Prodigal Son and John the Evangelist, of whom the former at least is no saint. — The manner of their expression and character is, moreover, itself portrait-like, insofar as they express not so much characters, physiognomies of another people, another time, another world, self-contained, distinctive figures, but show *the keynote of modern facial formation*: the gaze, especially the mouth and its whole surroundings, contains an elaboration — the technical is not meant — of the muscles, in that modern reflection, spiritual activity, sensation, — much having thought, having spoken, etc. — brings into these lower parts of the face (which among the ancients the beard in any case mostly covered) the tone of a manifoldly moved and thoroughly worked-through, in many directions and relations gone-through, self-restraining, considered and expressed demeanor. Where among the ancients there is no beard, in young and female figures, the form of the masseters is simple, round, and so the whole surroundings of the mouth, not only in momentary rest but so that one sees: this part has rested throughout the whole existence. The modern portraits, of a Dürer, Holbein, have a part of their excellence in this spirited diligence, which into the smallest part brings the reflex of a thinking, active, much-occupied life. Opposed to it stands the grandeur of the formation

[p. 352]

of the ancients, just as the simple, pure quality of Raphaelesque figures.

In John the Evangelist, but especially in the Prodigal Son, the expression in this state of contrition appears as a state, as a historical situation, as something momentary — and in the groundwork of the physiognomy one sees that it is capable of wholly other states, of happiness, etc., and that that expression can be only a passing one. In the case of a penitent, praying, kneeling Magdalene, also by a young artist, a sensitive woman made the remark that the penance had not penetrated her and that, when she had stood up, she could be again what she was before. In Correggio’s Magdalene this eternal depth and pious meditation of a noble soul is rather the fundamental essence, and that she has been frivolous lies behind the whole character of her spirit. One knows it rather only from elsewhere, historically. This side is the momentary, a fault that is transitory, something past.

This constitutes a chief difference of the great masters: the eternal, *imperishable*, in an expression that pervades the *whole*, so that nothing before and after, nothing other can be in this character. Correggio’s Saint Francis, etc., they *are* only this, through and through and always, what they are here and now. It is no situation. The situation gives not the content but the form of a heightened, more distinct expression, — or merely of the utterance of what they are in everything, through and through, and always.”

In what way Hegel then knew how to interweave such reflections, with a popular turn, into his lectures is shown, for the present case, by the *Aesthetics*, vol. III, pp. 79, 106.

#### Sociability.

To grasp rightly Hegel’s peculiarly sociable position in Berlin, we must once more return to the character, described earlier, of this city: that it is one only striving toward the grand, but by no means one already truly grand. At present, when through a railway network, also to the sea on two sides,

[p. 353]

toward Stettin and Hamburg, it has been brought closer, much may already have changed, and the habit of a larger scale of things, such as is at home in Paris and still more in London, may be in the process of coming to be. At that time, however, Berlin’s struggle for satiety was still far more conspicuous. To be publicly exposed to such a culture-craving world is a hard test. The individual must in this situation be at least in general finished with himself, in order to withstand the infallible manifold assaults, for the famous man is supposed to put himself eternally on stage for his visitors and in every conversation with any company to signal his peculiarity. He must be sure that every utterance of his, even the smallest, will be watched for, and that in being carried further it will be unconsciously, arbitrarily altered, now for the better, now for the worse. As an admirer, everyone wants to appropriate a little piece of the admired greatness; as an adversary, he wants to belittle this very greatness, which seems to him a false one, and on contact with it to gather new materials for the refutation of the prejudice. Now our modern life is in itself already so infinitely composite that, in the imposed cult of countless petty trivialities, it has the power to dwarf even mighty spirits, and the genius must always, in revolutionizing counter-thrusts against the conventional paltrinesses and stereotyped trivialities of opinion, create anew for itself free space, divine unconditionedness. The *universality* lying in the essence of philosophy is altogether made to expand this polypragmosyne, this scattering pygmy restlessness, into a destructive immoderation. Every science, every interest has for philosophy a legitimate point of connection, and even the insignificant person finds for himself a pretext, at least apparently cogent, to clear for himself access to the philosopher. The philosopher may not be a man of personal authority; he may give honor only to truth, without any personal regard. But for just this reason others like to make him an authority for themselves, for it seems that with it a final thing, impersonal, impartial reason, is attained. The philosopher in such a situation is left only the choice between a strict seclusion within himself and a many-sided expansion. The former position, almost to hypochondriacal

[p. 354]

irritability, had *Solger* taken; the second Hegel took, whose sociable nature, which had everywhere, wherever he lived, acquired for him numerous acquaintances, indeed friends, proved itself in Berlin too. And indeed he took this position without reflection, *without any intention*. No man could be further than he from artificial plans of life. In company he simply let himself go, and worked precisely through this harmlessness so enchantingly upon the calculating Berliners. The social relations into which he fell made themselves gradually of their own accord, and he pursued no tendency of society in an exclusive manner. Thus one acquaintance spun itself onto the other, one circle wound itself into the other, finally to a manifoldness already hard to survey, which to take in as a whole and to examine in its shadings scarcely occurred to him. From the letters to his family one can already gain an approximate idea of the manifold social contacts in which he finally stood. The necessary sickness of such a position in the world is the struggle with *being overrun*. Occasionally the demands became exceedingly strong, not to say fantastic. Not only was he to help others to enter into already existing positions, no, he was even to stamp professorships out of the ground for them. And not only Prussians, not only Germans, even foreigners turned to him with such proposals. The assurance of studying his philosophy or wanting to study it sufficed many as legitimation for laying their wishes before him. With an infinite bonhomie Hegel went into all such demands as far as was at all possible; many he had to oppose. Thus, e.g., a Hungarian called upon him to make it possible for him to study in Berlin for some years; he had first sucked in great prejudices against his philosophy at the University of Tübingen, but acquaintance with his writings themselves had given him a more favorable idea, and, in order to establish himself firmly in his system, he had begun to learn Hegel’s books *by heart*. Hegel may well have thought that this heroic act betrayed indeed much gift of admiration but less speculative talent; enough, he wrote to the Hungarian very politely that he was not

[p. 355]

in a position to create for him in Berlin a post according to his wishes.

Berlin sociability, moreover, still had at that time much that was unconstrained and open:

They sat and drank at the tea table / And spoke much of love, / The gentlemen, they were aesthetic, / The ladies of tender feeling.

Since the July Revolution this life-loving carefreeness has given way to a significant inner tension, whose characterization does not belong here. The biting, *caustic* quality, however, which makes up a basic trait of Berlinism and in the previous century received its first higher formation through the encyclopedist social circle of Frederick the Great, asserted itself also in Hegel’s time, at that time however with a predominantly smiling mien. How far Hegel entered on this cheerful, witty side into the Berlin manner is attested by a remarkable product which stands printed under the title: *Who Thinks Abstractly?* in his *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 400–405. What a strange, unique mixture of metaphysics, jest, satire, cuttingest satire, indeed shattering humor, which bursts forth in the observation of how a common old woman, when the severed head of a murderer was laid in the sunshine on the scaffold, exclaimed: how beautifully God’s sun of grace shines on Binder’s head! With this essay Hegel wanted to amuse a company, and in this respect the course he takes in it is very attractive. At first he is still the professor; he wants to instruct, but he wants also to remove the suspicion as if abstract thinking were at home only with philosophers. He begins by making himself clear through examples. The sentimental fair Leipzig women who wreathed with roses and violets the wheel on which a criminal had been broken think abstractly; that old woman who looks to God’s sun of grace, which she deems *worthy* to shine on the murderer’s head, thinks concretely. The market woman who, because the buyer has found her eggs rotten, scolds her and, by all the categories, very coarsely carried out by Hegel, leaves not a good thread on her, thinks abstractly. So it goes now in a compressed train onward, until, to sudden surprise, the essay breaks off abruptly as follows:

[p. 356]

“In the Austrian case the soldier may be beaten; he is therefore a canaille; for what has the passive right to be beaten is a canaille. Thus the common soldier counts for the officer as this abstraction of a beatable subject, with whom a gentleman who has uniform and sword-knot must have dealings, and that is enough to make one give oneself over to the devil.”

Yet Hegel wholly lacked the peculiar coquetry which in general characterizes the Berliner, down to Nante Strumpf, often with great charm; Swabian naïveté made such conduct quite impossible for him. The purest clarification of this element inclining toward the frivolous was *irony*, in the shape in which earlier a born Berliner, Ludwig *Tieck*, and later in intensive concentration *Heine* developed it. In no city would Heine perhaps have been so much read, so well understood, so much imitated in poems, and, what is most important, so much lived after, as precisely in Berlin, where thousands of young people could at that time have expressed their ethical confession in Heine’s words:

Sometimes it happened that I subdued / My sinful desire; / But when I did not succeed — / I had nonetheless much *plaisir*!

This element, whose frivolizing often rested on deep needs, played about Hegel indeed. He also grasped it in individual remarks, now tolerantly as jest and nonsense, now with indignation as immorality, but much — indeed, as *Hotho* himself concedes in his masterly characterization of Hegel in the *Preliminary Studies for Life and Art*, 1835, p. 394 — the most proper thing in it, what one might call, with an expression of Schelling’s mythology, the hunger for essence, escaped him. His substantial unaffectedness protected him quite immediately from the dangers to which reflective people are most exposed in this peculiarly coquettish element. This naïveté was the magical atmosphere which drew the Berlin youths, the yearning, inwardly broken, self-sundered North German natures, so omnipotently to Hegel, and over the years made him of itself the ever more decided center of a great circle, whose

[p. 357]

members rested in him as in a final one. What he said and how he did it counted as a conclusion altogether worthy of applause and imitation. There was even no lack of those who endeavored to copy him in gesticulating and speaking. Hegel’s great, already matured inwardness, which from earlier dangers of shipwreck had arrived in port, could not only endure the constant washing up of the tide of the day, but required rather, as a counterpoise to its intensity, a lighter, airier fare, and the philosopher was therefore quite right, when he emerged from the depths into the world of Concepts, to entertain himself, like other people, with the news of the day, with town stories, and the like.

In the infinite breadth of Berlin society the material for this was naturally rich enough. Even relationships simple in themselves harbor in Berlin more disposition to entanglement. Above all, there hovers over the so-called higher Berlin society a something that can best be compressed into the admittedly inadequate, yet essence-containing formula: what will, or would, one say of it at *court*! This often quite unconscious squinting toward the king, toward the ministers and their councillors, is unquestionably the only key to so many idiosyncrasies and inconsistencies of the finer Berlin world. Hegel stood fortunately enough in this respect, insofar as he lived in the encouraging consciousness of being on the best terms with State Chancellor *Hardenberg*, with Minister *Altenstein* and Kamptz, and thus of feeling no kind of *gêne* toward those above. To be sure, he also had to atone for this favor in that people gradually regarded him quite formally as a man whose intercession, especially through the mediation of his intimate friend, the Privy Senior Government Councillor J. *Schulze*, must have infallible appointability as its consequence. Egoism from then on poisoned many personal approaches to him. The urge of the Germans to come to Prussia, which appeared to them as a Canaan of science, where for it the milk of honor and the honey of considerable salary flowed in streams, became very strong, and a hundredfold Hegel was approached orally and in writing to help toward that and to intercede in this sense, on occasion, with His Excellency, Minister Altenstein.

[p. 358]

The amiability that Hegel had especially for the Berliners lay not only in the urbanity peculiar to him, which at the same time remained far from all elegant superficiality; not only in the easy-goingness with which he engaged with all and with everything, but also especially in his openness, in not wanting to seem more than he was. For *the art of advantageous seeming and appearing* is very highly developed in Berlin. Hegel’s free, harmless nature therefore seemed to the Berliners a great benefaction, and with noble instinct they sunned themselves in this probity and unfeignedness. *Laube* has in his *New Travel Novellas*, vol. I, 1837, pp. 373–417, furnished a genre picture, Hegel in Berlin, in which, to be sure, many characteristic traits of the philosopher are put together. If he, however, thinks that the great world *impressed* Hegel, when he applies to him the contrast of the literarily withdrawn Swabian Magister and the supple man of breeding, this judgment is mistaken. Hegel, as a Stuttgarter, was a born native of a royal residence city, had always lived in the best society and also enough among the nobility for it to be impermissible to place him in such a light. A natural heaviness of speech one must not caricature into awkwardness of expression, nor a plainness and simplicity of behavior formed in the burgher manner into gawky timidity. Power of every kind, whether it appeared as dominion or wealth, as talent and culture, or as the magic of beauty, Hegel took great pleasure in, because as a vigorous human being he loved everything energetic. But precisely because he himself felt the god in his bosom, submission to mere externalities, a homage to conventional splendors, was impossible for him. In his Gymnasium addresses, *Works*, vol. XVI, p. 197, there is a passage which fits his manner of being as its best elucidation, in saying: “Much harm has certainly been done in modern education by the principle that children should be taught early also worldly sociability, and to that end be introduced into society, that is: into the amusements and distractions of adults, or such things be prepared for them in the manner of adults. Experience refutes this thought, for it shows rather that people who had laid a solid inner ground, and

[p. 359]

were besides otherwise brought up in good manners, soon also got the hang of the habit of outward demeanor and conduct in the world, that distinguished men of the world have come even from the most confined monastic life, and that, on the other hand, people who were brought up in this externality of life also never arrived at any inner core. It takes little reflection to find this comprehensible; in order to appear with competence and advantage, the inner ground must have been tended and strongly cultivated.”

Hegel took extraordinary pleasure in the society of Berlin women, just as they in turn with predilection cherished and cared for the good, jesting Professor. He could not refrain from expressing his veneration to them from time to time also in verse, *quand même*. Thus on 31 March 1824 he wrote to a lady the following farewell stanza:

Three sisters, kindness, cheerfulness, understanding, / You have chosen as your Fates; / They are the ones who weave the bond of your life. / No one, even if born at Sans-souci, / Is free from sorrow, yet the strong hand / To conquer it those Horae also extend; / And let those who devoted themselves to their grace / Be everywhere attended by love and friendship.

#### In friendly remembrance / Prof. *Hegel*.

If educated women are unquestionably entitled to the most telling judgment on the social significance of a man, it will be welcome to insert here such a judgment from Berlin, which depicts for us Hegel in his relation to women. “Hegel was the friend of our house, which he often honored with his visit; besides, he was a faithful friend of the uncle, with whom he was wont to converse gladly and often. Conversation with me, however, like that with most ladies in our social circle, could be limited only to general social interests, and it was precisely the rare, amiable quality of the humane philosopher that he understood how to adapt himself, downward and upward, to every peculiarity of his surroundings,

[p. 360]

without ever making it in the least perceptible. Not a trace of pedantry mingled in the conversation when he spoke with the artist about the higher purposes of art, set before the financier a nobler tendency of his field than any that man had ever thought of, etc. With the tender mother he knew how to converse cozily about education, to say to the elegant lady something agreeable about the choice of toilette, in which he — incidentally — understood himself so particularly well that a newly chosen parure hardly escaped his attention, and he used always to choose with care the occasional toilette presents for his wife himself. To the thrifty housewife he gave not only his praise for a savory dish, but entered into all the details of its preparation, whereby he could then with humor sometimes appear as a zealous gastronome, which he by no means was, since in his house a noble simplicity prevailed in this too, as it was indeed in all respects pleasing and elevating to observe him as husband, father and householder. Adored by the children, deified by his wife, who, twenty-two years younger than he, clung to him not merely with the tenderness of a wife but with filial veneration, one saw him active in even-tempered helpfulness, endeavoring to let it go as well as possible with his guests in his surroundings. The conversation at table was mostly of such a kind that each of those present could take part in it, actively or at least silently. He himself did not speak without external difficulty. His organ was not favorable to speech; his expression neither light nor elegant; the Swabian dialect had remained with him; he always accompanied speech with movement of the arms and hands. Once one had, however, reconciled oneself to these externalities, the refrain of what one heard through them was usually so full of content, so thoughtful, or also so strikingly witty, that one found nothing to fault in the form either. At play he was positively amiable, one might say condescending toward his fellow players; always in the same humor in winning and losing, the smiling anger became the dear philosopher exquisitely when at whist he reproved his partner for bad play. He made use for this of certain standing expressions and phrases, which even in

[p. 361]

their triviality received sense and significance through him. He gladly teased good-naturedly those whom he especially loved. Thus Professor *Gans*, as a great favorite of his, was often the object of his jesting reproofs when during play he began to tell something and thereby turned his attention from the game. ‘There he chatters and chatters and pays no attention!’ he would then call out, scolding cheerfully. When he had nonetheless won the game, and the opponent perhaps claimed the *honneurs*, which could no longer help him, he would usually say with a malicious smile: ‘You can tie those to your leg now’ — an idiom which in similar cases is still used by those who have heard it from him.”

With regard to Hegel’s language, a sensible remark of Professor *Sietze*, communicated in manuscript, may here still be inserted: “The evident difficulty in Hegel’s language I could explain to myself only by his thinking, as it were, in nouns, so that on considering an object the relations appeared to him as if like figures that entered into action with one another and whose actions he then had first to translate into words. Quite peculiarly there figured here certain favorite constructions, e.g. the one formed after the French: It is in — that *c’est y, que* —. In consequence of such a peculiarity Hegel had occasionally to pull himself together in order not to write grammatically incorrectly. Not as though the rules were at all lacking to him, but because he first translated the content of his thoughts, *so that every language appeared to him as it were as a foreign one*. How masterfully he could speak again when he directed his attention precisely to that cannot serve here as a refutation, as little as e.g. *Chamisso’s* masterly poems serve to refute the fact that he spoke German and French equally awkwardly.”

But not only the friendly side must one weigh in Hegel’s social relations, but also the harsh one, his decisiveness, obstinacy, contrariness, his *tyranny*, as the Berliners were wont to call it. The mechanism of Berlin life makes it, to be sure, itself necessary to possess, in a public position, the power of determinacy, if one does not want to become the

[p. 362]

plaything of the parties and see one’s effectiveness paralyzed by them, indeed even, with the greatest talent, reduced to insignificance. Thus with Hegel too the cheerful surface of a variegated life of enjoyment, the intimate intercourse with the closer friends, such as Privy Councillor *Schulze*, Professor *Marheineke*, *Gans*, *Hotho*, the painter *Rösel*, the banker *Bloch*, *Beer*, the painter and fellow countryman *Xeller*, Court Councillor *Förster*, Dr. *Sietze*, etc., had a serious, often gloomy reverse side, and even with the friends the tough, strict character sometimes clashed hard. Against those who stood opposed to him in sheer contradiction he was adamant, and only in the best mood was he able to persuade himself to be together personally even with them. He had a great power of wrath and fury, and where he once believed he had to hate, there he did it quite thoroughly. So too in scolding he was fearful. Whom he seized, that man’s bones soon shook, and sometimes he set someone right, who did not expect it, like a schoolboy, so that such a person and those perhaps present were startled. Yet he was not stubborn to the point of implacability. Only he had to have gone first, with many a man, from a relationship good in itself but external, precisely through such a violence of opposition, in order to come to a warmer participation.

#### Travels.

The decade before the July Revolution was thus a carefree, life-loving one. The Restoration believed everything terrible done away with, relied on the spying eye of the police, on the walls of the prisons, on the bayonets of the soldiers and the scissors of the censorship. With cheerfulness one devoted oneself to the present, since even the fate-laden Corsican had died on St. Helena, in which art unfolded its magical illusions more than ever and nourished the finest sensualism — until suddenly and unexpectedly the thunder of the cannons at Paris, Antwerp and Warsaw boomed in the softened ears. Berlin, until then wholly sunk in its aesthetic life of enjoyment, had through its geographical position, moreover, the advantage of convenient travel in all directions, and could do nothing better than to prevent as far as possible the pettiness of interests and

[p. 363]

of tone, which in times sated with peace usually arise, through a broader worldview, through knowledge of other standards. Hegel had been scarcely a year in Berlin when the desire to travel seized him too, and he, despite advancing age, became more vigorous at it with every year.

Small excursions aside, he traveled in the autumn of 1819 with his family to the island of *Rügen*; in 1820 he toured, with his family and with *Förster*, *Dresden* and Saxon Switzerland; in 1822 he went to the *Netherlands*; in 1824 to *Vienna*; in 1826 to *Paris*; in 1829 via Weimar and Jena to *Carlsbad* and *Prague*.

Involuntarily one is reminded here that *Kant*, in the northeasternmost corner of German culture, although he was a very great geographer, did not travel at all; that *Fichte* and *Herbart*, both essentially North German, moved through Germany in the *diagonal*; that *Schelling*, essentially South German, until now at least always circled round in the *central* interior; that the central German *Krause* then was the first who crossed the borders of Germany, who went to Paris and Rome, until Hegel finally was on the best way to extend himself in all directions.

Of manifold places of residence he had, as we have seen, never been lacking, but *traveling for the sake of traveling* — not, as with Leibniz, on account of business — he engaged in properly only in Berlin. The reports of his journeys to the Netherlands, Vienna and Paris, which he wrote to his wife and which are printed in *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 544–624, present to us in their compressed way a fine picture of Hegel’s personality in its immediate, systemless energy, and are from this side especially priceless documents. All the wealth of his interest and of his feeling lays itself bare here, although we must think that much that also occupied him he did not let flow into the communication, because it belonged to domains which lie too far from the feminine heart. Thus he himself states that in Paris he intentionally held back the political reflections which pressed upon him, as unsuitable for his wife.

Hegel traveled indeed for recreation, but recreation in the sense of a sauntering idleness was to him after all a side matter.

[p. 364]

The exact apprehension of the great and beautiful that there is in the world was recreation to him. He had, as we already know of him from his Bernese Alpine journey, an eye and ear for everything, and little escaped him; even about the toilette of the ladies in Paris and Vienna he reported to his wife. *Nature* delighted him especially in the shape of *lovely wealth*. The view from the Nollendorf height, from the Schlossberg near Teplitz onto the Bohemian and Silesian mountains, that onto the Danube valley near Vienna, onto the luxuriantly green meadows of the Netherlands with their contentedly well-fed cattle, from Montmorency and from Montmartre onto the garden-like cultivated surroundings of Paris, delighted him. In such views light was his caressed element. How he praised the full moon which at Duran in Bohemia, together with two candles, gilded for him the paper on which he wrote. Only on the barren steppes of the Lüneburg Heath did the beautiful sunshine actually grieve him, having to shine on such dreary land. In Hesse he remarks from the mail coach the beautiful rising of the morning star and continues, reminded of Swabia, very touchingly: “Now we saw another physiognomy of nature than hitherto, no longer the unfruitful or fruitful plains, but beautiful oak woods, hills, the gentle slopes with fields of grain, the valleys with meadows — in short, a native nature.”

With the people we see him almost always content. Only where he notices mannerism and affectation does he grumble a little. Even the Rhine-touring of the students, who with the green knapsack and the tobacco pipe in the mouth entered Cologne Cathedral, this “student-tobacco-pipe society,” does not quite suit his mind. Otherwise it is usually said of his traveling companions that they were decent, honest, sensible, respectable people and that he got on well with them. If he comes into closer contact with someone and such a person proves friendly to him, he receives besides the predicate of a *dear, upright, faithful* human being, as in Cologne Frau *Horn* and Herr *Wallraff*, when they showed him their art objects. Against no one has he a preconceived thought. He therefore also visits all his colleagues in the specialty, however much they may differ from him in system: *Snell* in Giessen, *Suabedissen* in Marburg, *Windischmann* in Bonn, *Rembold*

[p. 365]

in Vienna, the latter of whom was later forced by the intrigues and persecutions of the Jesuits to give up his teaching post at the university. Yet again he consorts not only with the philosophers but with all scholars, as they happen to come his way. In Magdeburg he does not fail to visit *Carnot*, who was confined there, and enjoys his friendly reception by this hero of the Revolution, of the Empire, and of science.

What, however, shines forth before everything else on these journeys is the passionate interest in art, for whose satisfaction he proceeded with iron conscientiousness, so that he himself speaks of his *art affairs* and indeed arranges himself according to definite plans, e.g. in Prague according to one drafted for him by *Hirt*. There the churches are walked around and through, pictures looked at, theaters visited. Scarcely arrived in Vienna, he sits half an hour later already in the Italian opera, which for him, on account of the pure passion of tone, on account of the immediate freedom of the singers from everything else save their art, became a supreme musical enjoyment. In Bohemia he travels merely on account of a picture to an old castle, Karlstein; in Braunschweig he lingers merely on account of paintings recommended to him. In the Netherlands he makes a detour in order to come by way of Breda to see a work there by *Michel Angelo*, a mausoleum, about which he is quite beside himself. His short descriptions of such works are on closer consideration highly lasting and concentrate the peculiar quality of the matter often in one all-exhausting word. Hegel’s inventiveness in language comes to light thereby often, also in the comic, as when he speaks of *Deutschinnen* [female Germans], of *Altdeutschicis* [old-German-isms], and the like. Occasionally, in order to be quite brief and pointed, he becomes for a couple of lines quite wordy. Thus in describing the imperial castle in Prague he means merely to make a parenthesis, but piles therein predicate upon predicate: “But picture to yourself under it a modern palace, not such an angular, crooked and indefinissable, uninhabitable, shapeless, windowless, five-cornered, misshapen thing, like the castle of Nuremberg.” — Most extensive are his theater descriptions, mingled with interesting remarks also about the public,

[p. 366]

which is comprehensible from what was said earlier about the whole period.

He possessed a happy, annoyance-free receptivity, so that no sentimentality disturbed him. He also praises in the Italian singers that their voice is *free of yearning*, that nothing meek, unsatisfied rings out from it. The *grandeur* of things, e.g. in Paris, often *overwhelmed* him. Yet the softness also lying in his nature shows through at times in tender traits, especially with regard to his family. Occasionally past and future press involuntarily into the enjoyment-rich present. Thus he remarks, when passing through Menehould des Islettes by the windmill of Valmy, la Lune: “Memories of my youth, which took the greatest interest in it.” — When he, in company with *Raumer*, touched on the universities of Liège, Leuven and Ghent on the return journey from France, it had to occur to him again how his friend *van Ghert*, by whom he was received in Brussels in the most loving way, once in gloomy days had striven to prepare for him a place in the Netherlands. To this was linked for him the jestingly thrown-out reference to the future, p. 619: “We have looked around at these universities as at a future resting place, when the *priests in Berlin* quite spoil the Kupfergraben for me; the Curia in *Rome* would in any case be a more honorable opponent.”

The summit of self-conscious zest for life was for him Vienna. The paternal spirit of his ancestors who had once emigrated from Austria smiled at him here rosily in the nature- and art-beautiful Phaeacian city. Paris *occupied* him more. The Revolution and Napoleon, these great intuitions of his earlier years, came near to him everywhere here. Even the grandiose slaughterhouse, he remarks, Paris owes to Napoleon! There lay in Hegel a sympathy for the French mediated by his whole youth history, even if in Liège he answered a Frenchman, Baron de Reiffenberg, who demanded *une explication succincte de son système* [a succinct explanation of his system], very naively: *Monsieur, cela ne s’explique pas, surtout en Français* [Sir, that cannot be explained, least of all in French]. — In the long run, had he not been so happy in Berlin and so proud of his Prussian professorship, the Netherlands would perhaps have appealed to him most. The robust and powerfully

[p. 367]

beautiful quality of the figures, the picturesqueness of the costumes, the solidity of the way of life, the piety of custom, the free comfort of demeanor, the multitude of public works of art and the almost complete disappearance of nature in art, or rather the being-produced of nature by art, insofar as the soil has even been wrested from the sea and canals instead of rivers traverse the land: all this appealed to his mind extraordinarily and had for him something of the Hellenic spirit. One may compare, to find this judgment justified, the excellent depiction which he left in the *Aesthetics* of the Netherlands and its art.

The last larger tour that he made was in 1829 to Bohemia. He visited on it the eighty-year-old youth *Goethe* in Weimar, and, when he was drinking the Sprudel for some days in Carlsbad, met unexpectedly with *Schelling*. That this meeting in particular was very remarkable to him is evident from the fact that he writes about it both to *Daub* and to *Förster* (*Works*, vol. XVII, p. 538), how he had spent five days with Schelling in *old, stout friendship*. The only closer information about this meeting of the two philosophers, which first through Schelling’s well-known dismissive remarks about his friend since 1834 acquired a greater interest, is found in a letter of Hegel’s to his wife from Carlsbad, Friday, the 4th of September:

“Yesterday evening I had an encounter with an old acquaintance — with Schelling — who likewise arrived here a few days ago, alone like me, in order to go through the cure, as I am not. He is, by the way, very healthy and strong; the use of the Sprudel is only a preventive with him. We are both pleased about this and together as old stout friends. This afternoon we took a walk together, and then in the coffeehouse read officially the capture of Adrianople in the Austrian Observer and spent the evening together. And so for today the day’s work is concluded with these lines to you and with remembrance of you all. — Sunday: yesterday I was initiated with Sprudel-drinking, dined with Schelling at noon, and climbed the Dreikreuzberg.”

[p. 368]

#### Cousin and Hegel.

To this encounter with Schelling we may well best attach quite directly Hegel’s relation to Cousin, since Cousin became the organ through which the dispute for hegemony in German philosophy between Schelling and Hegel was first publicly played into their personal relation.

Cousin, a French philosopher of the Scottish school, had in 1817 and 1818, as the companion of a distinguished man, a son of the Duke of Montebello, made a journey to Germany. On it he stayed several weeks in Heidelberg and associated eagerly with Hegel, so that a friendly relationship was founded between the two men. In 1821 he dedicated to Hegel and Schelling, as *Amicis et magistris, philosophiae praesentis ducibus* [friends and teachers, leaders of present philosophy], the fourth part of his edition of Proclus, and to Hegel again in 1826, in his translation of Plato, the *Gorgias*.

In 1824 he was again on a journey in Germany. Suddenly, on the basis of wholly indefinite suspicions, he was, at the request of the Prussian government, arrested as politically suspect at Dresden and taken to prison in Berlin. Scarcely did Hegel learn of this incident when he at once, under the 4th of November, addressed to the Minister of the Interior and of Police, von *Schuckmann*, a detailed letter in which he interceded vigorously for the release of the French philosopher. He said therein among other things: “In the years 1817 and 1818 Professor Cousin from Paris, on the two journeys which he then made to Germany, sought me out also in Heidelberg. In the intercourse which I carried on with him during his stay of several weeks in the summer of the first-named year, I came to know him then, and indeed only from this side, as a man who was very seriously interested in the sciences and in particular in his and my common field, and had above all the eager endeavor to acquaint himself with the manner in which philosophy is pursued in Germany,

[p. 369]

with the utmost exactness. Such an impulse, which I find especially estimable in a Frenchman, further the thoroughness with which he entered into our more abstruse way of pursuing philosophy, and which I could not fail to recognize also in his lectures, delivered at the Paris university and communicated to me, as well as his character, which appeared to me upright and mild, have, as I may well say, awakened in me a lively, respectful, friendly interest in him. In the six years that have since elapsed I have had no further communication from him, and have learned only by hearsay that he has been suspended in one of his teaching posts, though left in the other. In his leisure, and at the same time to secure his subsistence, he has partly undertaken literary works, in the *Journal des savans* and in the *Archives litéraires*. Partly he has arranged a new edition of Descartes’s works, begun a translation of Plato, and, on the basis of a comparison of the Paris manuscripts, undertaken an edition of the works of Proclus, of which he has done me the honor, together with Schelling, of dedicating the fourth volume to me. I could not help being surprised, but also had to regret, to hear that such an exertion (of which I — I confess it — could hold myself capable only out of a sense of duty) has plunged him into a long-lasting illness and weakness.” — Now Hegel comes to the point that he had met him by chance a few weeks before in Dresden and renewed the old friendly relationship with him, on which account the incident of Cousin’s arrest had been all the more surprising to him, and he could only believe that some error was at work in it. He therefore had the urgent wish to see Cousin and speak with him, and asked for permission to do so.

On this intercession, on the mediation of the French legation, and on his word of honor, Cousin was set free. He now stayed some time longer in Berlin, where he lived in the most friendly intercourse, and the most philosophically fruitful for him, with Hegel and several of his pupils, *Gans*, *Hotho*, v. *Henning*, *Michelet*. From this time on he entered into correspondence with Hegel. In 1826 he was the most amiable and attentive friend to Hegel in Paris, making his stay there as pleasant and instructive as possible, about which Hegel in his letters to his

[p. 370]

wife expresses himself in the most satisfied and grateful way. This relationship was not disturbed as long as Hegel lived, not even after the July Revolution and after Cousin had become a peer and entered the ministry.

In his occupation with the Greek philosophers Cousin soon asked Hegel’s counsel on this point, soon on that. Of *Hotho’s* transcripts of Hegel’s *History of Philosophy* and *Philosophy of History* he had copies sent to Paris. Most earnestly he hoped — but in vain — for a critique by Hegel of his *Fragmens philosophiques*, which might make him better known in Germany; a wish which *Schelling* fulfilled for him, if only in 1833, in the Bavarian Annals. In his letters to Hegel Cousin never expresses himself otherwise than with the greatest modesty and tender esteem. Now he calls him solemnly: *Seigneur* [Lord], now: *mon maître* [my master]; now: *chèr Hegel* [dear Hegel], etc. In scientific respect he himself describes his conduct once very well, when he says: “[French] I await your Encyclopedia. I shall always *catch* something from it, and shall try to adjust to my own size *some scraps of your great thoughts*.” — On 1 August 1826 he wrote: “[French] *I want to form myself*, Hegel; I therefore need, as much for my conduct as for my publication, austere advice, and I expect it from you. In this respect you owe me from time to time a serious letter.” Of the goal that he had set himself he says: “[French] I told it strongly to our excellent friend *Schelling*, and I believe I wrote it also to Dr. Gans; it is not a matter of creating here in a hothouse an artificial interest for foreign speculation; no, it is a matter of implanting in the entrails of the country fertile germs, which develop there naturally and according to the primitive virtues of the soil; it is a matter of impressing upon France a French movement, which may then go forward of itself. — This being settled, speak, speak, my friend, my ears and my soul are open to you. If you have not the time to write to me, dictate to d’Henning, Hotho, Michelet, Gans, Förster some German pages in Latin characters; or, like the Emperor Napoleon, have your thought drafted and correct the draft, and send it to me. It is not a matter of paying compliments, but of giving loyal advice.” — Cousin was concerned, in his own expression, with winning a “*position forte et élevée*” [strong and lofty position]. On 7 April

[p. 371]

1828 he wrote to Hegel about it: “[French] I have made up my mind. No, I do not want to enter into affairs; my career is philosophy, teaching, public instruction. I declared it once for all to my friends, and I shall maintain my resolution. I have begun in my country a philosophical movement that is not without importance; I want in time to attach my name to it, that is my whole ambition. I have that one; I have no other. I desire in time to consolidate, broaden, improve my position in public instruction, but only in public instruction. What do you say to it, Hegel?”

What Hegel answered to this we do not know, since his letters to Cousin are not available to us. If we mention further that Cousin always praises Hegel’s letters as *excellens* [excellent] and *aimables* [amiable], the quotations given may well suffice to give an adequate idea, in scientific respect, of the correspondence of the two philosophers; for what else is said in it about politics, about notabilities, about Cousin’s prospects and his position toward the parties before and after the July Revolution, we have no right to communicate, however interesting it might be to the French in particular. But the purely factual report so far may also be sufficient to let the reader himself judge in what manner Cousin in 1833, in the preface to the second edition of his Fragments, described his relation to Hegel. According to the German translation of this preface, which has become best known among us, Cousin’s own words run, after he has assured us that he learned *German* with unspeakable effort, spent two years *deciphering Kant’s* Critiques in the *Latin* translation by *Born*, and had become more attentive to Germany through the reputation of the *philosophy of nature*, p. 36, as follows: “The new philosophy at that time still stirred and divided Germany as in the days of its origin. The great name of *Schelling* resounded in all the schools; here praised, there almost execrated, it called forth everywhere that passionate interest, that contest of fiery eulogies and violent attacks, in short that which we call by one word fame. I did not see Schelling this time; but instead of him I found, without seeking him — as if by chance — *Hegel* in Heidelberg. With him I began in Germany and with him I also ended.”

[p. 372]

“At that time, by the way, Hegel was still far from being the celebrated man whom I have since found again in Berlin, where he drew all eyes upon himself and stood at the head of a numerous and zealous school. Hegel had as yet no other reputation than that of an outstanding pupil of Schelling. He had published little-read books, and his lectures were scarcely beginning to make him more famous. The *Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences* appeared just then, and I received one of the first copies of it. This was a book bristling entirely with formulas, of rather scholastic appearance, and written in a language too little clear, especially for me. Hegel understood not much more French than I did German, and, immersed in his studies, neither at one with himself nor sure of his fame, he associated with almost no one and was also, to say it outright, not of extraordinary amiability. I cannot comprehend how it was possible for a still wholly unknown young man to interest him; but within the space of an hour he belonged to me as I to him, and this friendship of ours, put to the test more than once, did not belie itself to the last moment. From the first conversation on my judgment of him was formed; I grasped the whole compass of his spirit, I felt that I stood before a man superior to me, and when, from Heidelberg, I continued my journey through Germany, I carried the news of him everywhere, prophesied him, as it were, and said on my return to France to my friends: Gentlemen, I have found a man of genius.”

“The impression that Hegel left in me was deep, but confused. In the following year (1818) I went to Munich to seek out the author of the system himself. Hardly can two men be more unlike than I found the pupil and the master here. Hegel only with difficulty, and rarely, lets fall deep, somewhat enigmatic words; his vigorous diction, yet embarrassed in expression, his rigid countenance, his clouded brow — seem to be the image of thought turned back into itself. Schelling is thought unfolding itself; his speech is, like his glance, full of light and life: he possesses an innate eloquence. I spent an entire

[p. 373]

month with him and *Jacobi* at Munich in 1818, and only here did I begin to see a little more clearly in the philosophy of nature.”

What is one to say to this account! If fame, reputation, amiability of demeanor, facility of speech are the categories by which Cousin estimates the worth of a philosopher; if Cousin so little comprehended Hegel that at the very moment when the latter was completing his system as a totality with the publication of his *Encyclopedia*, he asserts of him that he was not yet clear with himself; if Cousin, finally, is vain enough to imagine to the French that he, as a prophet, had first made Hegel famous even in *Germany* — then, to be sure, such a relation becomes comprehensible. To describe what metamorphosis took place in Cousin from 1828 to 1833, we will leave to the French.

#### The Philosophy of History and the Orient.

In the winter semester of 1822–23 Hegel lectured for the first time on *philosophy of history*, and he gave this course for the last time, namely for the fifth time, in the semester of 1830–31. By no means is he the first who taught philosophy of history at the German universities. When he was still teaching in Jena, such attempts were made there by several. *Fichte’s Characteristics of the Present Age* was in fact also a philosophy of history. Best of all it was taught by *Stutzmann* in Erlangen. Yet for more recent times Hegel has indeed the merit of having brought the speculative treatment of universal history at the universities to a livelier stimulation. An *exact* science philosophy of history can never be. For if by it is understood the cognition of the *laws* that govern the development of the human spirit, then physical geography, psychology and practical philosophy are the true sciences with which it is concerned. The last has also to set out the *Concept of happening*, in which respect Hegel quite rightly made the conclusion of his practical philosophy with the Concept of history.

If, on the other hand, philosophy of history is understood as the cognition

[p. 374]

of the necessity in the particular course of the deeds and fortunes of peoples, then such a consideration is at once dependent also on the *erudition* and the *reproductive talent* of the individual, and not merely on the consequences of pure thinking. The limit of the development cannot here be drawn solely from the immanent determinacy of the matter; the so-called ingenious mixes with the logical derivation. If one has transferred the laws of biological periodicity to the history of spirit, distinguishing with *Herder* an age of childhood and youth, of manhood and old age, or, more abstractly, with *Krause* a period of germination, growth and ripening, then such a transference is contrary to the Concept of spirit as *genus*, for in this lies the *infinite* progressivity, so that, while everything possible does indeed become actual, possibility itself is never exhausted by all realizing, but, seemingly arrived at the abyss of the yawning boredom of an eternal sameness, is suddenly surprised again with discoveries and inventions that suffice for centuries to arouse new interest. *Krause* imagined that our planet would physically die out and that one day on it an old man would die alone as the most consummate human being; a poetically shuddersome but empty abstraction.

In his *Philosophy of Right* Hegel had presented world history as the domain into which the dialectic of the particular spirits of peoples passes of itself. It was to him the *tribunal*, in which they divest themselves of their one-sidedness through struggle with one another. The moment of right of this sphere, however, since no people recognizes another as judge over it, he had made into the atomistic standpoint of merely personal right. But above the many peoples stands the spirit of humanity, which precisely out of them and their struggles struggles forth to birth. Among the peoples there must therefore develop a *custom of humanity*, which they hold sacred, even if it is only a right of custom, a determination of public opinion. To be sure, this right too, like positive right fixed by definite treaties, can be violated by the arbitrariness of the individual peoples. Nevertheless it can exist as a true *power*, which the particular spirit of a people shrinks from offending and whose Nemesis it

[p. 375]

fears. That already Christianity in an ideal manner and world trade in a real manner compel the peoples ever more toward mutual recognition and toward the formation of a universal custom is clear. *Kant*, whom *Fichte* followed in this, therefore went beyond the concept of the law of nations, at the close of his philosophy of right, to that of *cosmopolitan right*, which in Hegel remained included in the Concept of world history.

In this, however, Hegel was in agreement with Kant, that he conceived the philosophy of history in such a way that the *state* gave it the form of its development. If pupils of Hegel have presented the philosophy of history as the conclusion of the whole system, as the crown of the tree, this is not in Hegel’s sense, who did indeed take account of religion, art and science as well, but only insofar as they are connected with the particular system of ethical life which we call the state of a people. *Deeds* are possible only in the domain of objective spirit. Hegel therefore placed the Concept of world history exactly in the middle between the Concept of objective and that of absolute spirit, because action and its unavoidable limitedness dissolves in the region of the absoluteness of spirit. In the order of the complete edition of his works, too, the *Philosophy of History* follows as the ninth volume upon the eighth, which contains the *Philosophy of Right*. One must only not understand Hegel so abstractly as if he, because he posits the absoluteness of spirit in art, religion and science *as* absoluteness, had held right and ethical life not to be in themselves absolute, holy and divine. Because the state counted for him as the form of the *determinate* development of objective freedom, he therefore concerned himself in the Introduction exclusively with its Concept, and said expressly with regard to art, religion and science: “We cannot have the intention of considering these three shapes more closely here; they have had to be named only because they are on the same ground as the object that we have to develop. The shape which is our purpose is the *state*. This gives us to recognize that what is in and for itself shows itself in history, and indeed on the ground of the present interests of men, within the world of appearance of spirit; in this world of appearance there is carried out

[p. 376]

the absolute final end. — — That the substantial now counts in actual doing and in the disposition of men, is present, and maintains itself, that is what we call the *state*.” Hence Hegel also concluded his lectures, according to the first edition, with the words: “The development of the principle of spirit is the true *theodicy*, for it is the insight that spirit can free itself only in the element of spirit, and that what has happened and happens every day comes not only from God, but is God’s own work.”

These lectures won for Hegel, similarly to those of Kant on geography for him, a great popularity with the mixed public, which on the average, to be sure, still has such strange representations of philosophy as a study-bound, world-remote monstrosity in its head that it is quite astonished when the philosopher too shows, in actuality and in apt language, a so-called sound judgment about world interests and world events. To the understanding of the lectures there attached itself, to be sure, as is wont not to fail, also a misunderstanding. Hegel could hold only to the universal, to the *decisive* peoples, deeds and individuals, and finally said himself: “We have considered only the progress of the Concept, and have had to renounce the charm of depicting more closely the good fortune, the periods of bloom of peoples, the beauty of the characters of individuals, the interest of their fate in suffering and joy. Philosophy has to do only with the splendor of the Idea, which is mirrored in world history.” Such utterances were interpreted to him as if *individuality* were in and for itself *indifferent* to him. For the necessity of the whole the contribution of the individual, even of the most powerful human being, is of course only his doing, which vanishes as a nothing in the all-sided mediation of the doing of all. But from this it is to be inferred neither that the *plastic* individuals, in whom spirits of peoples and epochs of history sum themselves up and concentrate, do not retain their peculiar dignity, because they have had to both work and suffer the most; nor that to the *humblest, most nameless individual* there does not accrue, on the part of his humanity, the same respect as to those heroes worked out into visible ideals.

[p. 377]

As for the first misunderstanding, that Hegel sacrificed the *freedom* of individuals to the abstraction of his *world spirit* and disregarded the rights of individuality and degraded them to a soulless organ, it is refuted not only by individual determinate utterances of Hegel’s, such as the one cited above, but also by the energy with which he himself knew how to depict and celebrate the peculiarity of a Socrates, Pericles, Alexander, Caesar, Luther. As for the second, however, the *contempt* for the men who live and die without fame, it would not only be altogether unphilosophical, but would also contradict thoroughly the Concept which the Hegelian philosophy sets up of the absolute dignity of man, even of the criminal. But of course — what Hegel already complained of orally — one can now no longer even read. In these lectures he says, as truly as beautifully: “The religiosity, the ethical life of a limited life — of a shepherd, of a peasant, in its concentrated inwardness and confinement to few and quite simple relations of life, has *infinite worth* and *the same worth* as the religiosity and ethical life of a cultivated cognition, and of an existence rich in the extent of relations and actions. This inner center, this simple region of subjective freedom, the hearth of willing, resolving and doing, the abstract content of conscience, that in which the guilt and worth of the individual is enclosed, remains untouched and is wholly removed from the loud noise of world history, and from the changes that are not merely external and temporal but also those which the absolute necessity of the Concept of freedom itself brings with it. In general, however, this is to be held fast, that what in the world is entitled to be noble and glorious *also* has something higher above it.”

For Hegel his philosophy of history was a deep need. It was an advance in his extensive development, the last of his works, with which he in a way returned to a content that had so vividly occupied him in the last third of his *Phenomenology*. He was therefore also so taken up by the work, much as it suited him, that he neglected his correspondence on its account even more than usual. On

[p. 378]

22 December 1822 he wrote, among other things, to Herr *Düboc* in Hamburg:

“Long since I ought to have answered your several friendly letters, honored friend, and I deserve reproaches on that account. But I have been so very busy, and have my head so full, that I have not been able to get to the few lines which would have been needed above all with regard to that matter. In this I am the opposite of a man of business; what for him is easy and expeditious at every moment is often impossible for me for many weeks — to write a few lines to a good friend. There is of course no lack of the half hour in which it could be settled; but when the man of business has finished a matter, it is so far out of his head that he can go straight on to another, and to another letter. I, however, must absolutely first wait for the time when I have my head free in order to be able to go at it; so long as it does not quite burn my fingers, in a time when interests of thought are going around in my head, I put off such things from one day to the next, so long as an excuse still offers itself that no real damage lies in the delay. — My lectures on the philosophy of world history give me a great deal to do. I am for the moment still, in quartos and octavo volumes, amid Indian and Chinese matters. But it is a very interesting and pleasurable business to let the peoples of the world pass in review; but I do not yet know rightly how I am to get through them down to this our latest time by Easter.”

Through these lectures Hegel nourished, even more than through those on the philosophy of religion and aesthetics, an interest in the study of the *Orient*, and supported in this the poetic strivings of *Goethe*, *Rückert*, *Platen*, *Hammer*, whose Hafiz poems, ghazals, qasidas and maqamas suited admirably the encroaching slackness and sensual softness of the age. Hegel, to be sure, for himself *made up for* what he had until then partly let escape him of the Orient. With true enthusiasm and accustomed persistence he plunged into the study of the Oriental cultures, in particular of Indian philosophy and Persian mysticism, the latter of which appealed to him infinitely, because it

[p. 379]

volatilized the subject into a mere accident of the substance with affirmative self-feeling, and made earnest of pantheism without reserve, without constraint, without gloom or unwillingness to sacrifice. Not as if he had found in the sublime verses of a *Dschellaledin Rumi* a complete counter-image of his philosophy, and, with his admiration of that mysticism, which at that time indeed even theologians such as *Tholuck* shared with him, had himself professed pantheism; — on the contrary he persisted stubbornly in reproaching the Orient with the *lack of subjective freedom*. But the carefree cheerfulness with which the Persian poet gives himself up as individual to the universal, and the truth with which he divests himself to the substance; that breadth of intuition and this sincerity of surrender to the All and the One, did him good against modern self-torment, against hypochondriac vanity, against the hypocritical sanctimony which, toward God, while it submits to him as Lord and adores him as love, yet holds fast in its desolate being-for-itself, against the tearfulness of the most self-complacent narrowness, which is unhappy enough to revere its biblical counterfeitings and its spiritless servitude as the most genuine Christianity and to persecute everyone who thinks otherwise.

In the case of many a Goethe-Hegelian, Hegel’s descriptions of the splendor and the devastating *frenzy* of the Orient unfortunately became partly phrase, to which no real study supplied a basis, partly a poetry running into the wild, which, beside *Goethe’s West-östlicher Divan* or even beside the Oriental originals, with its blasé, coquettish love of the cupbearer and its dull-audacious familiarity with Allah, looked like a complete caricature.
