The *Berliner Musenalmanach* of 1830 already contained the first orgies of this contrived pantheism, which in the end wasted away raving of an Indomania senseless in content and tasteless in form.

#### The School and Its Encomiastics.

Imperceptibly Hegel had attained, in Berlin, indeed in Prussia, to great power. It became the fashion to hear him. Men of all ranks attended his lectures. Students from all parts of Germany, from all European nations, in particular Poles, but also

[p. 380]

Modern Greeks and Scandinavians, sat at his feet and listened to his magical words, which he brought forth, rummaging in papers on the lectern, coughing, taking snuff, repeating himself, not without laboriousness. The depth of the content penetrated the spirits and made them blaze up in the purest enthusiasm. That self-interest too, with calculating ulterior motives, went into Hegel’s lecture courses goes without saying. One saw, as already recalled above, in Hegelianizing, or in the semblance of it, a means of eligibility for appointment. One hoped thereby to recommend oneself decidedly not only with Hegel but further also with the ministerial councillors and the minister himself. But in the majority the enthusiasm was pure, and in it the Berlin university lived through one of its most beautiful epochs.

It has indeed been said that Hegel had *made* a school in Berlin. He had become pupil-hungry.

With the great receptiveness of Berlin for the production of schools, however, the matter made itself of its own accord, because the *creator of a system*, in his productivity, in the security with which he rests on his talent, in the consciousness which he gains of himself as of a universal *historical necessity*, must act as absolutely attractive for the becoming, the undetermined and the striving. For the great crowd, for the egoism of disposition and the mediocrity of talent, however, it is always only the representation of the practical influence of the public position and of the favor of the government, of the authority of a man, that sets the last seal. Several circumstances combined to make this presupposition, more than is desirable for a philosopher, valid for Hegel. Several commissions which he carried out for the Ministry of Education, such as his opinion on instruction in philosophy at the Gymnasien; his membership in the Berlin scientific examination commission; an opinion which he drew up on *Esser’s*, another on *Calker’s Logic*, and on still other submissions of the ministry; the obstinacy with which he opposed in the faculty the admissibility of Dr. *Beneke* to the *venia legendi* and to an extraordinary professorship; the decisiveness with which he conversely defended in the faculty those of his own pupils whom he held to be ripe, like Dr. *Boumann*; the conferral of the faculty prize

[p. 381]

on the theme set by him, *de Idealismo* [on idealism], to the Hegelian Mußmann: all these things worked toward producing the opinion that, in order to be promoted to a teaching post in Prussia, one absolutely had to give oneself at least a Hegelian tinge, if one could not or would not get as far as a real Hegelianism. Hegel himself gradually grew accustomed to the notion that for speculative culture salvation was in fact to be found only within his philosophy. There began among the Berlin Hegelians the wretched fashion of taunting every peculiarity as a *bad particularity*, and, with a precocious pretension, of constructing every fresh phenomenon appearing outside the so-called school as already long present in the system, so that no one could any longer save himself from the fate of being “shown up as a moment.”

Apart, namely, from the Berlin of that time’s need to be schooled, the Hegelian philosophy had, more than other philosophies, the capacity to give a school work to do and to connect in the most many-sided way with other studies. First of all it possessed an elaborated *logic*, which made one familiar with all possible abstract categories, so that one learned to see through easily works from this side that had been undertaken without such a consciousness of the nature and the worth of the categories. Then it possessed a *history of philosophy*, which had its kernel in developing the Hegelian system as the *last* result of the entire history of philosophy. All *standpoints* which speculative cognition had ever taken up were to be contained within it itself as *necessary moments* of its conceptual articulation. It therefore seemed unassailable. Every standpoint that attempted an attack from outside was, as it were, already refuted beforehand by the fact that one had comprehended it itself, and indeed according to its organic genesis, whereas it appeared, accordingly, apart from this connection even much more imperfect than in the system itself. Finally, however, it offered through its *encyclopedic many-sidedness* points of connection to all particular directions of science. Even if the pupil renounced the ability to change anything *in principle*, there still remained to him the possibility of proving himself in the speculative apprehension and penetration of a particular

[p. 382]

material, of earning merit for its development and thereby furthering philosophy itself. The theologian, jurist, natural scientist, linguist, politician, historian, aesthetician, all were drawn into the great *collaboration*. The *master needed the journeymen*, and the journeymen had the prospect of becoming masters themselves in their fields. This lively philosophical zeal, which in *Marheineke*, *Vatke*, *Sietze*, *Gans*, *Hotho*, *Saling*, *Pohl*, *Göschel*, *Mußmann*, *Kapp*, *Hinrichs*, *Michelet*, *Poley*, M. *Veit*, the *Benarys*, *Rötscher* and others threw itself with a lust for conquest upon the special sciences, had as its consequence a significant, by no means yet completed transformation of them. Hegel’s friendliness not only, but also his earnestness, his admonishing to work, the strictness of his own demands and his own example of unremitting toil spurred to the work, and in a much higher degree than had been the case in the two preceding schools of philosophy in Germany, the Kantian and the Schellingian, there took place at that time a *unity* of striving and achieving.

Among the pupils themselves three groups soon separated from one another: the *sober*, the *exalted* and the *empty*.

The first were the quiet but deep minds who took up the new philosophy with lasting earnestness and proceeded from it gradually and without noise to the working-up of particular sciences.

The second, the exalted, were less scientific, but more *poetic*. The conception of world history in Hegel, his philosophy of art, the peculiarly poetic expression that more often broke through his dialectic, his rare gift of demonstrating the essence of the Idea in the world of appearance, all this enchanted them. Their imagination received new materials through him. In Goethean *forms* they began to versify Hegelian *formulas* and to celebrate in Hegel now a new Socrates, now an Alexander of the realm of spirit, now a speculatively world-creating Brahma. With time one heated and heightened oneself in such encomiastics up to the height at which one revered in Hegel, not indistinctly, a philosophical redeemer of the world.

The majority of the pupils was of course the group of the empty

[p. 383]

which was especially suited to the hasty re-teaching of what had been quickly learned, a race sprouting up very fruitfully out of the critical Berlin soil itself. These pupils were the originally wholly individualityless, who received a hold, a shape, only through contact with the magic wand of the system. With their reflection they in fact always reached exactly only as far as Hegel had just then thought ahead for them. With the greatest narrowness they combined, however, as is always the case with such subjects, the greatest arrogance about their philosophical culture. From sheer lack of positive knowledge these empty ones nevertheless sometimes undertook modifications of the system and then imagined that they, since they were after all already standing on his shoulders, could see far beyond the old gentleman. If they then condescended perhaps even occasionally to want to instruct him about his errors and deficiencies, he reacted in later time with vehemence and only now began to become really domineering.

These didactic-mad pupils were it above all who, by their presumption no less than by a superficial dialectic, by a heap of stereotyped commonplaces and lack of all true productivity, helped to bring the Hegelian school into discredit with the public, among which many pretty anecdotes about this *Hegelery* circulated. The opposition therefore found itself very satisfied when the *Gruppe* of that time in 1831 published his comedy against the school: *The Winds, or Quite Absolute Construction of More Recent World History, Poetized through Oberon’s Horn, by Absolutus von Hegelingen*. *Zelter* wrote about it on 20 May 1831 to *Goethe*: “A *bad* book has appeared against Hegel. It is called: *The Winds* — vapors of a slack stomach. I had been told it was witty, and I have tortured myself through some forty pages, but fell asleep. A stale imitation of *Oberon’s* and *Titania’s* golden wedding, as thin as thread, and meant maliciously. *Hegel* has looked at it too, and my judgment seemed consoling to him. Hegel is a very upright man, and I believe that he is also a worthy scholar.”

And yet, after the shadow side of the matter has thus not been concealed, it must be said that even this faction of the

[p. 384]

schoolified, agreed with the two others in feeling itself a participant in a great world-historical transformation, and in being uplifted by this pathos also in a substantial way. Through the young *heads* not only, but also through the young *hearts*, a *new life* trembled. The cognition that the negative is a determination immanent in the Absolute itself and, only on this ground, also sublated by it; the cognition of the necessity of pain for spirit, but also of the power of spirit to *endure contradiction*, to overcome it, to emerge as victor from all, even the hardest struggles, to reconciliation with itself; the certainty that the enjoyment of the absolutely true is possible already in this present, and that actuality is full also of the divine, if one only has the eyes and ears of spirit to see and to hear it — this certainty became the principle of the intellectual and ethical *rebirth* of many men who had been gravely sick with languishing sentimentality, with beautiful-souled bliss, with the unbelieving superstition, condemned even by the Church itself as a mortal sin, of being unable to become free from evil and baseness; with despair of knowing the truth and of finding any satisfaction in a life that was, for it, devoid of the Concept. This *ethical force*, with which Hegel gripped the hearts and led them back to trust in spirit, is indeed often wholly overlooked in the estimation of him, but in fact was of no less importance than the properly scientific effect which he exercised. *Kapp’s* confessions in his chaotic writings of that time present the lacerated state of the heart and its process of healing through speculative purification and self-liberation most vividly. A rich gleaning for the portrayal of such conditions could be gathered from the poems which the enthusiasm-drunk pupils addressed to him on festive occasions, in particular at Hegel’s *birthday celebration*. Foremost among the thyrsus-wavers were Heinrich *Stieglitz*, Moriz *Veit* and Karl *Werder*, who administered the high mass of such a glorification in the most glowing words. Here only a few examples. *Stieglitz* sang:

[p. 385]

What convulsively, in deepest quaking of the heart, / Has struggled through amid pain and joy, / The sting from which millions of lives / Have bled away, themselves scarcely aware, / The double battle that from the beginning rent / The human breast between deed and striving — / You, mighty one, have split its hydra head, / Have shaped deed and willing also as One.

Or also:

If the new day is to appear, / The old must go under, / And *opining* goes to the grave, / And *knowing* wants to arise.

Or in a genuinely Hegelian turn:

When spirit, split upon matter, / With mighty resistance / Strives to preserve itself, / What it has known as its self:

Then begin those torments / That only the strong one overcomes, / Until before the bright sunbeams / All mist succumbs.

When out of the press of this struggle, / Through the soul’s flame-death, / Victorious he has emerged / Into freedom’s dawn:

Then may from a thousand abysses, / Closely massed for resistance, / All powers league together, / No power defeats him more!

Very characteristic of the expectations which the school may have had of Hegel’s stay in France for the fate of his philosophy and for a deeper, more spiritual union of Germany with France through it, was a poem by Moriz *Veit*, in which he called out to him on his birthday:

[p. 386]

Westward! Though a thousand bolts / Roll themselves before the dark path, / Boldly loose the seals of earth, / Destroy deceit and vain delusion. / Up, spread your sun-wings, / Bright swan of the azure sea, / Your eternal compass is the limit, / Your swelling sail the thought.

— — — — — —

Light, light! cries the enraptured Frank, / As you draw near to him, and your thought.

O you, who have joined North and South / Through depth of spirit and power, / To whom from the Orient’s remotest tidings / The world spirit still audibly echoes, / You have found for yourself in the West / The spirit’s enduring shape — / Around you gather the best, / The noblest of the people in the West.

Many a turn of phrase, trodden all too flat only later, was in its first freshness still something quite different from what it presented itself as later in its worn-out threadbareness, like the comparison with Plato and Aristotle. Thus, e.g., for 27 August 1820 a pupil sang to him:

Now with graver mind we unroll sacred writings, / Only the consecrated may approach you, the consecrated. / Plato, more divine, to you, and Aristotle, master, / You who called down philosophy from heaven, / You who founded the realm of spirit, not to the threshold / Fast-bound; everywhere it holds sway with free power. / If Hellas knows you no more, you are hospitably received / By the Germanic spirit that now rules in the world. / As you began the building, now the dome rests closed: / Worthy of you the third dared only Hegel to be.

Such utterances, whose rain of flowers showered Hegel for a decade, prove to us the almost deifying devotion of the pupils. Differently, but likewise with the most heartfelt veneration, friends expressed themselves. Among these the painter *Rösel* is especially to be singled out

[p. 387]

whose amiable humor knew at all times how to spread the merriest mood through teasing fun, through the most cheerful inventions, and, for the celebration of Hegel’s birthday, each time to devise wittily something especially witty and cozy, of which many a beautiful document still exists in writing.

But as everything in the world has its epoch, so too the Hegelian birthday celebration in the year 1826 found its highest point of splendor, and a longer poem in distichs presented to him on that occasion, *The New Hercules*, by *Förster*, became the maximum of grateful, admiring expression of esteem and love. *Gans* and *Werder*, the latter of whom spoke of the *categories* of the Hegelian Logic as of *new gods*, addressed Hegel solemnly in the name of a large number of admirers, and he replied, deeply moved, extempore, pithily and with dignity, to the following effect in its main content: “that in living on one also necessarily experiences *no longer* seeing oneself with or at the head of the younger, but perceiving over against them a relation of age to youth; this moment had now come for him.”

At this celebration Hegel’s family happened to be away in Nuremberg with relatives. To this circumstance we owe a description of the festival by Hegel himself. On 29 August 1826 he wrote, after other utterances not belonging here: “It is thus about my birthday that I have to tell. Your remembrance sent to me, which Frau Aimée — quite prettily — prepared behind my back, like the writings of the boys, has delighted me heartily, and I have greeted and kissed you most inwardly in the image of the soul on that occasion. However early Frau Aimée got up and was concerned to bring yours first before my eyes, she had nevertheless not got up early enough. For we had already begun to celebrate this birthday of mine from its very first origin, at midnight, at 12 o’clock. At Herr *Bloch’s* I was at a whist, which, much prolonged, and at a supper likewise prolonged, brought on the whistling-in of the 27th by the night watchman, which was answered and outdone by the clinking of glasses. Your health was heartily clinked to as well, preeminently by me and by all (the Zelters were there), but especially by Rösel.

[p. 388]

“In the morning, however, various congratulators, dear faithful souls and friends, besides several letters with poems. Then a business conference, during which a visit turned up at my place — who do you think? — His Excellency Herr Privy Councillor von Kamptz himself in his own person. At noon I kept quiet and only clinked and drank with you most inwardly at the appointed time, saving myself for the evening. For then great honor, joy and proofs of love were in store for me. In a new locale, Unter den Linden, which was being inaugurated for the first time, a great supper, so elaborate that it would have deserved to be described to you, like the most complete, exquisite dinner. *Förster* the arranger, *Gans*, *Hülsen*, *Hotho*, *Rösel*, *Zelter* etc., about 20 persons. Then a deputation of 20 students entered, presented me with a precious beaker of silver (as the silver merchant heard that it was for me, he too contributed his own share, since he had been a hearer of mine) on a velvet cushion, together with a number of bound poems. Many others were still presented orally; Rösel too his, who had already sent me the same in the morning with an antique gift (a little mosaic marble tablet from Pompeii), in short, so that it was hard work to bring it to an end before midnight. That the students brought music and fanfare goes without saying. The company kept them, as it were, for the meal. Among the company of guests there was one whom I did not know. It was Professor *Wichmann*. It was disclosed to me that to him my bust (the much-discussed one, which Rauch could not get to) had been entrusted. Next week — the current one I still have to lecture — I shall sit for him. To my mother-in-law I shall have the honor of sending a copy in due time. If you want to surprise her, then tell her nothing of it. I too could have surprised you with it, but you know, I for my part do not love surprises — and I had to tell you of the honor and love that befell me on my birthday (a flower vase of crystal from Herr v. Hülsen not to be forgotten). So at midnight we linked my birthday with Goethe’s, the 28th.

Yesterday I slept until 11 o’clock and restored myself somewhat; not so much from the physical fatigues as from the

[p. 389]

deep emotions of my heart, and even upon getting up I received again a poem, a morning greeting from Dr. Stieglitz. You cannot believe what heartfelt, deeply felt testimonies of confidence, of love and of esteem I experience from the dear friends — older and younger. It is a day — rewarding for the many toils of life.

Now I have to ward off that too much of the good is done. To the public it looks different when, in the circle of friends, the mouth too could be taken too full.

Now live heartily well, wherever this letter may find you.”

Your faithful

man and father.

H.

Let us add further that Hegel was named, through van Ghert’s mediation, honorary member of the Royal Society *Concordia* at Brussels under President Schuermans; that in 1830 a *medal* was struck on him by the students, and that in 1831, the year of his death, he was decorated by the King with an *order*, on which latter distinction the minister v. *Altenstein*, highly pleased about it, congratulated Hegel in a very affectionate letter: so we have together everything of well-deserved honors that fell to Hegel’s lot in Berlin chiefly; for of smaller proofs of friendship and veneration he was in the end almost constantly, as it were, enveloped as by a silken net.

#### The Founding of the Berlin Yearbooks for Criticism.

It was mentioned above that Berlin in our century, up to the year 1827, lacked a worthy representation of literary criticism. This deficiency, for a capital in which an academy of sciences and a great university were found, Hegel recognized very soon, and he therefore addressed to the ministry of education a detailed letter on the *establishment of a critical journal* (*Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 368–90). In general he remained in it true to the principles which we have already come to know from him in 1802 in the essay on the *essence of philosophical criticism*

[p. 390]

with which he opened the journal edited by him and *Schelling*, as well as in the draft of the *maxims of a German Journal of Literature* written in 1806. He wanted to direct criticism to the progress of the sciences, to the *content*. It was not to serve to prop up mediocrity or to put on show the superiority of a reviewer over an author. It is therefore not necessary, after what was said earlier, to go into these ideas at greater length here. Hegel now wanted, however, to realize them in such a way that the journal, like the Paris *Journal des Savans*, should be a *state institution*, in that he hoped to give the enterprise greater weight by such a position. In order now, on the one hand, to preclude that the institute as such should have to answer jointly for the detailed character of the judgments in respect of their substance — for he conceded the obligation as regards the propriety and dignity of the tone — but, on the other hand, that the criticisms might take on the *odious character* of having been composed in a *contrived manner* in the sense of the government, all anonymity was to be banished. The Hegelian circle perceived in the *banditry* of anonymity, as *Gans* was wont to express himself, rightly the curse of our critical literature. The countless meannesses that are otherwise connected with this secrecy Hegel passed over for the time being, and held only to this, that the giving of names should obtain for the critic his *independence* in his judgment from the government, as well as that of the institute from him. His remaining proposals went practically down to the smallest, down to the setting out of the course of business, of the publisher, of the printing, of the paper.

The realization of this plan was, however, met with too many obstacles on the part of the state, so that Hegel had already as good as given it up. The need for it naturally not only remained but increased. Then a chance meeting of *Gans* and *Cotta* in a Paris salon in 1826 brought about the serious resumption of it, but as a *private enterprise* independent of the state. Gans has told at length the founding of the Berlin Yearbooks for scientific criticism in his *Rückblicke* [Retrospects], pp. 215–56. We can pick out from it here only the moment relating to Hegel. Gans

[p. 391]

arranged the essentials with Cotta in Stuttgart, and reports on his conversation with Hegel about the successes obtained: “The day after I had arrived in Berlin I betook myself at once to Hegel and found him in a green dressing gown with a black, cap-like bonnet, just taking a pinch from his snuffbox with one hand, with the other searching for something in papers which were piled up in disorder before him.

Well, are you at last back again? he said to me smilingly. We have been expecting you for a month; Privy Councillor *Schulze* believed you would not come back at all, and would not take up at all the professorship for which you applied.

One does not, after all, run away just because one arrives somewhat later, I replied, and that I come late has a good reason. For I am arriving not alone, but with a great Berlin literary gazette.

That may be a fine literary gazette for me; where on earth did you pick up the fellow who wants to undertake it?

He is by no means a bad man; it is Cotta, whose acquaintance I made in Paris, and with whom I have almost concluded the matter in Stuttgart.

Well, Cotta. Has he not yet forgotten the *Horen*, and the bad business which one makes with certain things in the second year, after they seemed to start well in the first? But Cotta understands the matter better than we all, and if he has begun something, we can surely entrust ourselves to his direction. Did he make you the proposal?

No, actually I to him. I thought that a university like the Berlin one could not remain much longer without a literary gazette, and that the arbitrariness and the merely negative which prevails in the previous undertakings of the kind demanded that such a thing be carried on in a positive way from a great center.

So I too thought, and for that reason addressed to the high ministry already years ago a paper, to which, however, up to now no resolution has followed. If one does not wish to take it up there, we can do it among ourselves. Only see to your professorship first. Of the other we shall speak further.”

[p. 392]

Gans then relates further how *Varnhagen von Ense*, through his fine tact, his extensive knowledge of literature, his industry and skilful presentation, became, next to Hegel, the most powerful support of the new enterprise. We must here, following a written communication of Varnhagen’s, characterize more closely his relation to Hegel. He says: “I saw Hegel fairly often, but our intercourse remained limited, since I was neither his hearer nor his companion in social matters. *Rahel* was very attentive to him, and liked to hear him speak, also acknowledged the full greatness of spirit in him; but when he visited us he mostly brought his wife with him, who then fell wholly to Rahel’s share, while Hegel was willing to talk politics with me, or was entangled, through Ludwig *Robert* (whose beautiful wife, his countrywoman, Hegel highly revered), in vexatious and fruitless disputes, and was pressed to admit that he was, after all, fundamentally less than Fichte. Hegel recognized Rahel as a clever, thinking woman, and treated her as such, but the real essence of her spirit he can hardly have known. I myself was on the best of terms with Hegel. A few lonely evenings in my room led to confidential confessions about things which he always avoided in larger conversation. Also at the founding of the Berlin Yearbooks for scientific criticism, in which much passion was aroused, our frictions had no consequences. I had often to hold my own against him, and this all the more vigorously as I was in the company the only one who was not hampered by personal relations or considerations, and so almost always and alone had to take over the opposition. But Hegel, when the Yearbooks were already under way, became ever more difficult, more tyrannical, and conducted himself in the sessions so strangely that the whole company felt that it could not go on so and that the matter must come to a standstill — then the role fell to me again to oppose him in the name of all and to indicate to the revered man that he too had to observe his limits. This was a violent struggle, conducted on both sides with bitter sharpness, a personal quarrel with accusations and reproaches. But nothing dishonorable occurred, nothing that would have injured esteem. During the supper following the session there continued

[p. 393]

the ill humor and the echo of the quarrel continued; the other guests present were more friendly with Hegel than I was, but in the matter more on my side. But when we rose from table, I stepped up to Hegel and said: “We must not part for the night like this! You have said hard things to me, I have said hard things to you, but nothing that was not to be accepted. Is there still need of the assurance that my esteem for you is unchanged? Here is my hand. Let us part reconciled!” — He not only clasped it, but we embraced one another heartily, and tears stood in his eyes. He had not expected this turn. Since then we have had no more quarrels.”

Next to Hegel and Varnhagen, those who took part in the editing of the Yearbooks were chiefly the theologian *Marheineke*, the physiologist *Schultze*, the philologists *Böckh* and *Bopp*, and the aesthetician *Hotho*. The general conduct of business was undertaken at first by *Gans*; after him by Leopold von *Henning*, who carried it out, with indestructible perseverance, through all the conflicts of the passions and also through all the metamorphoses of science, in a spirit equally active, conciliatory and administrative, technically and consistently.

For a great interest, the founding of a journal is always an important event. It is a second birth of that interest for the world. The interest becomes hospitably accessible to all, and thereby acquires a certain power even over those who until then ignored or despised it, for they must be prepared to fall to the public judgment of the journal. Although now the Yearbooks, as the original composition of their editorial board at once showed, by no means made Hegel’s philosophy their exclusive subject, it was nevertheless quite natural that under the given circumstances their principle should unfold itself especially in the domain of philosophy and theology. The undertaking also at once aroused not only great attention but also violent resistance, and even the abolition of anonymity was regarded by the opposition as a means of pressing Hegelians into service. *Börne* in particular, in an essay of his own (reprinted in the *Works*, III. 51 — 67), cast suspicion on the Yearbooks as a dangerous instrument of the Prussian government for working upon minds in the interest of its peculiar tendencies.

[p. 394]

A certain stiffness clung to the undertaking at the outset. The presentation of new members, the notification of the public of their admission, the conferences of the society, the appraisal of the papers received by two referees and the collective verdict of the conference, the critical suppers in the *Café national*, and the appointment of a general secretary were, to be sure, in themselves praiseworthy forms, directed to *publicity* and *impartiality*, but as they were handled, not without ponderousness, not without a certain pretension. The original provision, to read the reviews received aloud in the sessions of the society, was even not without impossibility. Yet this somewhat ceremonious procedure was still better than the formlessness and haphazardness of the editing that crept in later, and during which, as *Gans* already remarked, all the principles on which the institute had been founded were gradually contradicted in fact. Even anonymity, and with it bad personality, reappeared. It is the misfortune of critical periodicals to go on living beyond the hour of their death and yet not to want to rise again through a new birth.

It is not the place here to pursue further the fortunes of the Yearbooks, which through all inner changes at least always preserved the dignity of science; but for Hegel himself it is to be remarked that through the Yearbooks an entirely new *increase* of *importunities* arose. In the most comprehensive sense he was now, who already passed for the *philosopher of the state*, also the *fashionable philosopher*, and was to pronounce his beneficial magic blessing on everything in literature. Not only was he to promote young men who were making their literary debut in their advancement with the ministry; he was, from now on, by a review of their writings, to bring them to prominence with the public as well. And not only younger men approached him with such expectations, but also older ones, who had been in connection with him from earlier times. From all places and corners came writings whose authors took the liberty of sending to the *master of the newest*, or, as one used to say, as it were officially, of the *present philosophy*, a copy of their first or latest work with the most humble request to excuse leniently the imperfection of their labor.

[p. 395]

So much for the beginning. Further they assure him that they are concerned only with the *cause*; they know indeed how *little leisure* the much-occupied man has left, but they wish only to give him a small token of their unbounded gratitude, devotion and sincere, unchangeable veneration. So much for the middle. Transition to the end. *Should* the most deeply esteemed, much-solicited man nevertheless be able to resolve of his own accord to give *his judgment* in the Yearbooks of their feeble attempt, were it ever so brief, nothing would be more important to them and more rewarding for them. End: or should he be wholly prevented from it, he would surely transfer the criticism to a suitable collaborator of the Yearbooks, in any case be able to occasion it, and, if it turned out favorable, take the opportunity to direct the attention of the Privy Councillor Schulze or of the Minister to it.

This became the almost stereotyped content of an exceedingly great number of letters. Not only from persons of philosophical culture was Hegel overwhelmed with the sending of books and with personal recommendations, but also from the side of the so-called positive sciences and from other acquaintance. Since, understandably, he had neither time nor inclination to engage himself in all these interests, although on the average he took them into consideration with the greatest benevolence as far as he could, the consequence was that many, when their writings were reviewed either not at all or otherwise than they had wished and expected, drew from it a bitterness against Hegel which later, especially after his death, often vented itself in the most passionate utterances against him and his system. Not only did the joys and sorrows of such a patronage multiply with the years, but there also arose, through the reviews which he himself gave in the Yearbooks, epistolary polemics against him, which by no means spared him, but rather gave him hard things to hear, in a theological respect especially, so that with the Yearbooks there arose in him an unrest and tension, a weighing look about him and taking of considerations, even a sourness of tone, from which the ten preceding years had been free.

To be sure, he saw his philosophy and its language extending to a *European* breadth. In Paris he had in the then *Cousin*, the French philosopher of the state,

[p. 396]

sympathy for himself. In the Netherlands lived his faithful friend van *Ghert*, who in Brussels together with Dr. *Brouwer* founded the philosophical journal *Athenäum* and in Liège brought about the establishment of a philosophical college, a comprehensive institution of study, at which Professor *Seber* expounded Hegel’s philosophy. At The Hague Dr. *Kiehl* published a periodical devoted to it in the Dutch language; in Kiel, later in Copenhagen, *Heiberg*, who had come to know Hegel personally in Berlin. In Finland the professors *Tengström*, *Sundwall* and *Laurell* taught Hegelian philosophy in the Swedish language, etc. Such an extension abroad, and the closely gathered and enthusiastic admirers scattered all through Germany, in Berlin even, let him look toward the future of his philosophy into a great perspective. But in this perspective lay at the same time the prospect of the immeasurable struggle that was to come, and which, through an organ like the Yearbooks, could only gain in extent and sharpness.

If one surveys these many letters, one first gets the proper intuition and feeling of the weight which Hegel at that time put into the scales of culture. The younger *Fichte*, to whom, at his habilitation, he had been opponent on the Neoplatonic philosophy in Berlin, wished that he would express himself on his preliminary school of theology. *Weiße* sought instruction about his disagreement with him. *Feuerbach* stormed, in a detailed discussion, against all theologification of the system, with boldly modest speech. *Göschel* pressed for a more determinate biblification of the exposition of the philosophy of religion and dissented from Hegel with regard to the judgment on the quarrels of that day between the Pietists and Rationalists at Halle, in the respect that he declared it an abstraction to eliminate the personality of the contestants entirely from the judgment of the matter. *Leo* found in Hegel, in the most precarious time of his life, a well-meaning, truly fatherly adviser. In his letters he opened to him his whole, volcanically agitated heart and always kept the most grateful recognition of him. Rust reported on Bavarian conditions. *Weinholtz*, A. *Peters*, v. *Ravenstein*, *Günther*, v. *Keyserlingk*, etc., down to completely obscure and insignificant people, approached him with their concerns.

Here one already sees in miniature all the dissensions which

[p. 397]

later became great crises in the development of the Hegelian system and of his school. Whether the logical Idea is the absolute form or the absolute content of the system; whether the world spirit is God or God is distinguished by him from it for himself; whether Christianity is already the absolute religion or whether this is only the faith that also knows itself philosophically, etc. — all these questions were already voiced in those polite letters.

The responsibility which one imputed to him more and more, the longer it went on, bordered in Berlin often on the ridiculous. Hegel himself related how one day a man had come to him and made vehement representations to him about the dangerous consequences of his philosophy, because his son, who had attended a few courses of lectures with Hegel, or at least enrolled for them, had lost himself in an idle, spendthrift life of smoking taverns. That, said Hegel with a half-melancholy smile, I am now supposed to answer for as well!

#### Hegel’s Contributions to the Berlin Yearbooks.

Hegel devoted to the Yearbooks not only the liveliest participation in their editing, through conscientious attendance at their sessions and exact reporting on the reviews received that fell within his field, but he also remained an indefatigable collaborator, and thereby kept the interest of the younger men awake as well, which is so easily diminished by the remark that persons are often the most inclined to abandon and give up again enterprises and institutions founded by themselves.

In 1827 he first wrote a critical treatise on the treatise in which W. v. *Humboldt* had examined the Indian religious system which, under the name of the *Bhagavatgita*, is set forth as an episode in the epic Mahabharata. Hegel occupied himself much in Berlin with the study of the Orient, but for all the objective apprehension natural to him was not wholly free from the preconceived polemical thought of showing that the older literature of the Orient is by no means so absolute a compendium of divine wisdom as it has often been passed off for, and then that the Indian Orient is quite properly *pantheistic*, that

[p. 398]

pantheism is yet far removed from the *hylozoism* with which one often labels it with that name. In a note of thanks W. v. *Humboldt* expressed himself very flatteringly to Hegel about his work; to others, to be sure, otherwise. In the writings of *Gentz’*, edited by G. *Schlesier*, V. 298, there is found, namely, the following letter from him about it:

“Hegel is certainly a deep and rare head, but that a philosophy of this kind should strike deep roots I cannot conceive. I at least, as far as I have tried so far, have not been able to make friends with it in any way. The obscurity of the exposition may do him much harm. It is not stimulating, nor, like that of Kant and Fichte, colossal and sublime like the darkness of the grave, but arises from visible helplessness. It is as if language had not broken through for the author. For even where he treats quite ordinary things he is anything but light and noble. It may lie in a great lack of imagination. Nevertheless I should not like to deny the philosophy its worth. The public seems to me to divide, with regard to Hegel, into two classes: those who adhere to him unconditionally, and those who, as around a rugged cornerstone, wisely steer clear of him. He belongs, moreover, not to those philosophers who want to leave their effect merely to their ideas; he makes a school, and makes it with intent. The Yearbooks, too, have arisen from this. I have even, for that reason, joined the society with deliberate purpose, in order to indicate that one should not take it so. For the rest I associate with Hegel and stand outwardly on very good terms with him. Inwardly I have great and true respect for his ability and his talent, without failing to recognize the defects reproved above. The long review of me I can approve least of all. It mixes philosophy and fable, the genuine and the spurious, the primeval and the modern — what kind of philosophical history can that yield? The whole review, moreover, is directed against me too, though concealed, and proceeds plainly from the conviction that I am anything rather than a philosopher. I do not believe, however, that this makes me partial against it.”

A second work of Hegel’s in 1828 concerned *Solger’s* posthumous writings and correspondence. He discharged in it all that he had had on his heart about the

[p. 399]

*romantic school* since Jena. The irony of the two Schlegels; Tieck’s whim of leading the theater, in its arrangement, back to the monotony of Shakespeare’s age; the confusion of a richly imaged, fermenting, turbid mysticism with a truly dialectical philosophy clear in its Concepts; the looseness of artistic composition among the Romantics, their aberration into dry monstrosities and miracles; all this was scourged by him just as unmercifully as he praised Solger’s speculative talent and solid learning and explained his endeavor to make the Concept of irony the central point of his metaphysics as arising from a truly philosophical need.

A similar work to that on Solger he made in the same year on *Hamann*, whose writings, collected in Munich by *Roth* and published in Berlin, were then drawing attention anew. Hegel endeavored to set apart the various elements of this magical nature, because from the mixture of them, from their transference onto one another, arises the confusion in the judgment on Hamann. He followed the process which Hamann’s formation had taken and distinguished in him the period of a wild, worldly disorderly way of life; of an ascetically gloomy rebirth, of zealot tyranny toward his friends; finally, amid many persisting, never resolved contradictions, the period of a scientific, tolerant, amicably many-sided intercourse. He showed that Hamann had grasped the deepest problems *with presentiment*, but that such a fantastic-subjective concentration was still very far from a *developed*, systematic philosophy. He honored in Hamann, with whom he incidentally shared the same birthday, the 27th of August, the genius and the opposition of his firm, biblically grounded faith to the indeterminacy of the Enlightenment of that time in religious matters, but he did not spare him the inconsistencies into which the bristling contrariness of his nature, his aimless reading and an overdriven delight in symbolic expression had often led him. Over this criticism Hegel at once fell into a lively dispute with one of his pupils, with *Sietze*, who

[p. 400]

in his Prussian legal history appeared against him and undertook to portray Hamann as the *prophet* of Prussia.

One of Hegel’s most remarkable, and certainly most successful, critiques was, however, in 1829, his review of the *Aphorisms* on Absolute Knowing and Not-Knowing by G....l, i.e., by the Justizrath *Göschel*, who then still lived in Naumburg and was entirely unknown to Hegel personally. Göschel had endeavored to make the dialectical abstractions of *Hinrichs’* work on religion in its inner relation to science fruitful by presenting the different standpoints developed in it not only in a more comprehensible form, but also by relating them to definite facts of philosophy and of Christianity. He demonstrated, for example, how little, quite contrary to the current opinion then spread by the theology of feeling, the philosophy of *Jacobi* harmonizes with biblical and ecclesiastically positive Christianity. The reverse, however — that, likewise against the view then prevailing, the speculative philosophy, decried as pantheistic or even as atheistic, truly agrees with Christianity — Göschel knew how to make very plausible with his advocate-like talent as an apologist. Very many cultivated people still have the opinion that philosophy *cannot* agree with Christianity, and therefore hold the negative stance of a philosophy toward Christianity to be already the proof that it is a genuine, solid philosophy, just as, conversely, they distrust a philosophy as soon as it professes harmony with the essence of Christianity. What astonishment it therefore aroused when Hegel, in a detailed review, reckoned the Christianity of his philosophy, demonstrated by Göschel, in all seriousness very much to his credit, and, with full *consciousness of the evil semblance* that he thereby gave to the multitude, amicably pressed the author’s hand for his justification before the whole public. For us, who have come to know Hegel’s relation to theology from its first beginnings, there is nothing surprising in the fact that Hegel was convinced that in his speculation he stood with the essence of the Christian faith not merely in no contradiction, but rather in affirmative unity. For the great public, however, the representation of such a unity

[p. 401]

was something quite new, incredible. In part people began to doubt the sincerity of Hegel’s assurance, in part, if they meant him well, to declare him senile, a man who, out of impotence to carry through his own principles, was defecting from them unconsciously. The worst consequence was also actually this, that those who, even in philosophy, ultimately want not knowing but only faith, and therefore seek in philosophy only the proof of the impotence of knowing and the necessity of faith, began from this time on to undertake all sorts of dialectical trifling with the Christian dogmas and often to hold their theological crudities already for unauthorized results of Hegelian speculation.

Connected with such theological endeavors there stood at this time, in Hegel, a work which he elaborated as a lecture course and which is printed as an appendix to his *Philosophy of Religion*, on the *Proofs for the Existence of God*. He gave in it a presentation and critique of the cosmological, ontological and teleological proofs for the existence of God, and thereby indirectly a *speculative theology*. With regard to Hegel’s religious conviction this work is therefore very important, because through it it can be decided most unambiguously that he accepted a *personal* God. The expression personality is, to be sure, inconvenient and for many contains the representation of a limitedness, of a spatio-temporal finitude. In so far it would be desirable to avoid it altogether for science and to say subject instead of person. If it is asked whether, according to Hegel, the *world* as such is *immediately* the Absolute, or whether the Absolute is distinguished from the world as an existence perennially posited by it and perennially sublated, whether it exists as an *eternal subject*, being for itself and knowing its being-for-itself, the first question must be answered in the negative, the second in the affirmative. “God is activity, free activity, relating itself to itself, remaining with itself; it is the basic determination in the Concept or also in every representation of God, to be He Himself, as the *mediation* of Himself with Himself. If God is determined only as *Creator*, then His activity is taken only as an *outgoing* activity, expanding out of itself, as *intuitive* producing,

[p. 402]

without return to itself.” — The creation of the world lies, according to Hegel, certainly in the determination of God; precisely because He creates the world, He is not conditioned in His essence by it. The world is, as a necessary determination to which His freedom resolves itself, as eternal as He, but its becoming in Him is not His becoming through it, because He, as without beginning, cannot *become* at all. To be activity is not mere becoming. God does not *happen*, He *is*.

It is striking how much this work, which was composed for the most part by Hegel himself, and was not merely, like the *Philosophy of Religion*, written down from his delivery, has been neglected in the many disputes of more recent times about the relation of Hegelian speculation to the Concept of religion. In particular Hegel also demonstrated how one should not think the freedom of God over against the world as an *arbitrary* legislation for it, because such a legislation would in fact be nothing else than the assumption of *unreason* in God. With this endeavor, to renew the arguments for the existence of God, which had been antiquated as products of scholasticism by the Kantian critique of pure reason, in a purified shape freed from the rigid opposition of the Concept of being and of thinking, Hegel completed his relation to *Kant*, his affirmative building out of the foundation laid by him. It seems to us as if Hegel’s language, too, showed in these freer expositions many entirely new beauties. It is circumspectly popular, pithy, sharp, and in the drawing of determinate shapes of religiosity full of fresh, striking features.

The more the Berlin Yearbooks now developed into a propaganda for the Hegelian doctrine, the greater the circle soon became of those who joined them as collaborators, and the more many-sided, the more determinate, the opposition became thereby into which the Hegelian philosophy came with other philosophies and tendencies, the more violent the attack on it now also became. Not only in journals was the battle fought; not only in them was the accusation of ignorance, of the pernicious character of Hegelianism raised, and there discharged itself, under the form of scientific attack, often also envy, hatred, calumny,

[p. 403]

malice and stupidity, but the pamphlets too, those rockets of our literature, began their play. The Berlin pupils urged the master to take up the quarrel himself as well, because in their expositions one could always maintain that they had not understood him fully, or had even misunderstood him. They wished gladly to appeal to his authentic refutation and hoped, too, that the pithy manner of the *Old Man*, as they were wont in loving familiarity to call Hegel among themselves, would have the effect of silencing the barking against his philosophy for a considerable while.

Very unwillingly Hegel resolved to comply with this request. At last, however, he believed he owed it to the cause that his silence should not be regarded as an admission of the accusations raised so loudly and so decidedly, which denounced his philosophy as dangerous to state and church, or even as proof of embarrassment, and to oppose something to them. So he took up some of the pamphlets in several articles written with great sharpness, but grew weary of the *tedious business*, as he himself described it. He joked that he, *si parva magnis componere fas est* [if one may compare small things with great], could compare himself with Frederick the Great, who, *vis à vis* Cossacks and Pandours, had complained of having to scuffle with such rabble — a witty remark which the literary Philistines never forgave him, but always carried after him as proof of a boundless self-conceit. Hegel showed in this critique of his opponents a great virtuosity in the popular analysis of the most abstract Concepts such as being, nothing, becoming, one, many, and the like, an analysis which is not unimportant for his relation to the later Schellingian philosophy. Schelling, namely, always takes the Concept of the abstraction being in the sense of the most absolute concretum, of the substance existing through itself; the mere εἶναι and the τό τι ἦν εἶναι are taken together by him, and he struggles with all his might against taking the Concept of being as such for that which still lacks all particular determinateness of content. He takes it as the sum total of all reality and must therefore also make his division of philosophy into negative and positive through the separation of essence and its existence. This distinction

[p. 404]

is quite consistent in him. It is for him the only possibility of not falling back into Spinozism, which determines substance only as existing and as the self-concept of its existence. Hegel expressed himself very clearly that he sharply distinguishes the abstract Concept of being from concrete being, but also that in the latter being as such, the dry Is, of course is not lacking. In the manner of dispatching his opponents Hegel showed a magnificent *schoolmasterliness*. He did not weary of marking up for them their errors of thought in due form, as in an exercise. He lampooned their ignorance and ineptitude. He derided their Galimathias, which was supposed to be witty, their presumption, swollen into chivalry. Most strongly he scourged the hypocritical pietism which, although it is constrained to regard him as an unchristian, yet out of Christian love wants to *pray* for the salvation of his soul, and the ingratitude of this very pietism, which had visibly received from him himself its culture and the weapons with which it combated him.

There is no need to tell at length that Hegel did not attain his purpose at all with these critiques. Such defenses must expect their effect at another place. On the contrary, the anonymous and the named whom he pursued with his polemic nourished the bitterest rancor against him, which, especially after his death, has not ceased to heap up spiteful insinuations against him in bitter language.

It is very interesting to see how Hegel in 1831, in his last two critiques, was still to come into contact with the elements which after his death turned so energetically against his philosophy, the *Schellingian* and the *Herbartian*, so that he appeared in this too as a complete man, and in his unexpected dying as nonetheless justified. He still anticipated the nearest future of his philosophy. He subjected, namely, first *Görres’* lectures on *world history* to an exact examination, in order to demonstrate the untenable and senseless in the *number mysticism* on which Görres builds his periods. But he also uncovered the *unhistorical* in the *primeval history* of the human race much embellished by Görres. The Habelites and Cainites, the Hamites, Semites and Japhetides, which

[p. 405]

Görres lets play a great role, he unhesitatingly called “nebulosities.” He developed emphatically the difference between thinking comprehension, which proceeds to universal and factually necessary determinations, and a fantasizing which is, to be sure, brilliant, but chaotic.

With this critique he thus provoked against himself the hierarchical-mythical element. The other element to which he dedicated his *last* critique was indirectly the Herbartian philosophy. A pupil of Herbart’s, an East Prussian, *Ohlert*, had sent Hegel a work on *Idealrealism* with the request for his judgment of it. Hegel found in it a capable thinking, although still entangled in many imperfections, which seemed to him worthy of a closer and encouraging review. What, however, occurs in this Idealrealism about experience, about the Concept of contradiction, about the simplicity of quality and of the real essence, about the plurality of essences, rests chiefly on Herbartian foundations, and Hegel had thus, with this critique, given his judgment on the main points of the Herbartian metaphysics, which, taken scientifically, not politico-ecclesiastically, was to exert a much more significant reaction against his system than the Schellingian post-philosophy.

#### Second Edition of the Philosophical Encyclopedia.

In 1827 Hegel had to arrange for a second edition of his *Encyclopedia*, which was followed by a third after three years. Second editions are equally agreeable to authors and publishers. They count as the best proof of the worth, of the necessity, of a book. They are the factual critique for the great public. With scientific works, however, the drawback is that the progress of science usually calls forth the wish, the need, for alterations and, when these are made, a certain duality of earlier and later conception and an inequality of execution and even of tone easily arises through them. This fate the Hegelian Encyclopedia has experienced sufficiently. Hegel himself recognized the awkwardness of partial reworking. He wrote to *Daub*, who in

[p. 406]

Heidelberg took care of the proofs: “The rest I have sought to make more determinate and, as far as it goes, clearer; but what is not altered is the chief defect, that the content no longer corresponds to the title Encyclopedia, that the detail is not more restricted and the whole, on the other hand, kept more perspicuous.” And once more: “The endeavor, as it were the miserliness, to let stand as much as possible, is repaid in turn by the greater toil imposed of seeking out turns of phrase by which the alterations do least damage to the words of the text. You will now have a few sheets of the philosophy of nature in your hands; I have made essential alterations in it, but have not been able to prevent myself from going too far, here and there, into a detail which in turn is not commensurate with the character that the whole should have.”

To the need of those who are only just entering philosophy, Hegel wanted to give special consideration by a new introduction, but spoiled this intention at once by a title incomprehensible to the multitude, in that he headed it: *On the Position of Thought toward Objectivity*. He gave in it an outline of the principles of empiricism, of the Wolffian metaphysics, of criticism and of immediate knowing, i.e., of Cartesianism, of Jacobism and of Schellingianism, in so far as in the latter its principle of cognition, immediate intuition, is reflected upon. This introduction, in part also historically conceived, caused all the more confusion as it was bound to raise the question how it was related to the *Phenomenology*, which had previously taken on the isagogic function. The good thing about it, however, was that many learned from it the little which, in the dispute with Hegel, they brought forward in journals and pamphlets about Wolffian and Kantian philosophy. — To the philosophy of nature and philosophy of spirit Hegel now gave an incomparably greater fullness, and in numerous remarks gave a more closely entering consideration to all the objections and misunderstandings directed against his philosophy and against philosophy in general.

In particular, however, he took pains in the preface to shed closer light on all the accusations which were raised against him from the side of the theologians and to express as comprehensibly as possible the peculiar task of philosophy in regard to religion. He made to the so-called pious and to the theologians especially the reproach,

[p. 407]

of comprehending the speculative thoughts incorrectly *as spiritual facts*, and, without any suspicion of such falsification, of combating and decrying these Concepts, first distorted by themselves and not present at all in this way in philosophy. In particular he subjected some utterances of *Tholuck’s* to a brief and penetrating critique, because in this “inspired representative of the pietistic standpoint” he recognized on the one hand the deep feeling, but could at the same time show in him how this feeling does not at all protect him, in thinking, against the most one-sided understanding. He proved to him that in his dogmatics he fundamentally stands not at all so far from the theology of the Enlightenment so much abhorred by him, in that he, e.g., holds the dogma of the *Trinity* not at all as the foundation of our Christian faith, but for a mere scholastic *framework*. This polemic brought Hegel into the reputation of wanting to be even more orthodox than Tholuck, and not a few journals did not hesitate to scent, behind the patronage of the dogma of the Trinity, a crypto-Catholicism.

This opinion was further favored by another circumstance. Hegel expressed, namely, in the same preface a decided inclination toward the *Gnosis* of the knight Franz von *Baader*, and recognized on this occasion also the speculative depth of Jakob *Böhme*, Baader’s favorite. These utterances at once made him appear to the great public entirely in the light of the earlier Romanticism, which he himself had combated in its aberrations; the *Göttingen* learned notices made use especially of his praise of Böhme as a mighty spirit, as the rightly so-called *philosophus Teutonicus*, to bring him into the reputation of the unintelligible eccentricity of anti-rational mysticism. “Is it to be expected,” they exclaimed, “that such a philosophy, which expresses itself thus in the manner of Jakob Böhme, will exert on the heads of those who do not already wholly understand it — and among hundreds who want to penetrate into it, it would hardly succeed with one — any other effect than to turn these heads, and to produce in them the conceit that they have risen to the standpoint of absolute knowing, when the definitions, so hard to understand, with their new terminology float before them like billowing mist?” How many thousand times have these words been repeated in similar turn! (See H. A. *Oppermann*: the

[p. 408]

Göttingen learned notices, p. 238 — 48.) It was in vain that Hegel stated the *difference* of his philosophy from that Gnosis definitely enough, in so far as the latter seeks out the essence of the Idea in forms of representation and shows it as contained therein, whereas pure, systematic philosophy has behind it this *mythical and mystical ferment*, whose particular shapes are capable of an infinite multiplication. Hegel’s personal acquaintance with Baader was, as has already been related, brought about in Berlin by Baron Boris d’Yxkull. Baader now also took a friendlier position toward Hegel and let him know this, in his manner, by the fact that of his pamphlets he dedicated the one on dogmatics to *Marheineke* and wished to dedicate another work to Hegel, to which, however, it did not come. He wrote to him from Munich on 30 September 1830:

“I allow myself the preliminary announcement that my next work, Lectures on *J. Böhm’s Mysterium magnum*, dedicated to you, will appear within 2 or 3 months. — G. R. *Schelling*, who cannot get rid of his old or younger philosophemes, and therefore cannot go forward either, goes into breadth. His young philosophy of nature was a vigorous and juicy roast of game; but now he serves it up as a ragout, boiled with all sorts of ingredients, Christian ones too. — The devil is loose everywhere, and because they despised the Idea in its heavenly shape, they must now tremble before its hellish caricature.”

“Respect and devotion.”

Franz Baader.

However carefully Hegel in that preface to the Encyclopedia, and through all its paragraphs, sought to ward off the distorted conception of philosophy, the groundless prejudice against it and its thoughtless condemnation, this effort, as the still more armored preface to the third edition of the book showed, availed him nothing. Rather the vehemence of the theological opposition against him increased, the more the idea forced itself on people that Hegel at the end might really be right and that, as a philosopher, he could find himself in agreement with true Christianity. The theologians like, to be sure, to pass summary judgment on philosophy; they

[p. 409]

consider it an insult not to be held for philosophers as well in return. That philosophy should be able to see what is true in religion they do not concede, but seek to secure for themselves here the privilege of determination, as if it required a quite special, mysterious process, possible only to a graduated theologian, to know God in spirit and in truth.

#### Hegel’s Rectorship and the Celebration of the Augsburg Confession, 1830.

History appears from below, regarded from the details, as contingent, but from above as necessary in the universal concatenation of things. The French struck their *July Revolution* in the same year in which the German Protestants celebrated the memory of a chief act of the Reformation, the presentation of the confession of faith of the Lutherans at Augsburg on the 25th of June. In this world-critical year Hegel now enjoyed the honor of the rectorship of the Berlin University, and as such had to deliver the academic festal oration for that commemorative celebration.

This was, for the Prussian state, not without difficulty, in so far as it had made the *Union* of the Reformed and Lutherans the progressive principle of its church development. The Augsburg Confession is the foremost symbolic book of the *Lutherans*. If now, to be sure, in Prussia, through the princely house of the Hohenzollern, which had passed from the Lutheran church to the Reformed, the Augsburg Confession was always regarded in the sense that the determinations contained in it agreed in essentials with those of the Reformed church, it could nevertheless not be denied that with a solemn re-recognition of the *Augustana*, the principle of the union of the Protestants into a general *evangelical* church, which at the celebration of the Reformation festival of 1817 had seized hearts with such mighty enthusiasm, seemed to be contradicted and to be opposed to the Reformed. For the exclusive Lutherans the turn lay near, to resist the Union now with separatistic obstinacy — which also happened. This movement took its beginning through *Scheibel* from Silesia. For the exclusive Reformed, on the other hand, the concern had to arise

[p. 410]

that they would be impaired, that the evangelical united church would be made one-sided again into a Lutheran one, and that the Union itself would thus be made only a vehicle for craftily taking from them their religious peculiarity and for asserting that this was found in Lutheranism more perfectly, united with qualities they lack. This reaction took its beginning chiefly from the Reformed *Rhenish* congregations. Many theologians therefore took offense at that celebration, such as v. *Cöln* and D. *Schulze* in Breslau, who, though they did not exclude themselves, nevertheless published express reservations with regard to the restriction which could arise for the Reformed from such a celebration recalling the confessional differences.

Hegel as festal orator was in the fortunate case of being, from his youth, a Lutheran with his whole soul, as he declared very definitely on several occasions, also from the lecturer’s chair, especially in regard to the Lord’s Supper. When his family was in Nuremberg in the summer of 1826, he wrote repeated exhortations to his sons to look quite carefully at all the sights. They should surely also visit the *old* fortress and have *Wallenstein’s Stone* shown to them. Nuremberg had held itself bravely in the hot struggle with the Catholics. There our fathers had fought chivalrously for the *truth and freedom of faith*. This old Nuremberg fortress was, he said, an “inestimable pearl in our history.”

Despite this Lutheran inwardness, deeply inherent in him through his upbringing, Hegel in his oration avoided everything that could have emphasized Lutheranism as a particularity and put in the shade in the least the confession of faith or the church constitution of the Reformed. How could he indeed have done otherwise, since at the beginning of the century he had recognized in the Protestantism as well as the Catholicism of the past only one-sided forms of Christianity, which were to be sublated into a higher unity by means of philosophy, so that the objective intuition of Catholicism and the subjective inwardness and longing of Protestantism would melt together into the absolute freedom of self-consciousness.

On the other hand, he emphasized the relation of the Reformation to Romanism

[p. 411]

with great emphasis. Against its work-righteous Pelagianism he praised the Augsburg Confession, on account of the *sola fides justificat* [faith alone justifies], as indeed the *Magna Charta of Protestantism*. He depicted the corruption of the Church through *papistic Catholicism* in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and the *tyranny* with which the Church kept down all independence of science and impaired the minds in the freedom of faith. He depicted the demoralization of life through the *destruction of the family* by means of celibacy, through the *destruction of productive industry* by means of the deification of poverty and idleness and stupid work-righteousness, through the *destruction of conscientiousness* by means of a dull, immature obedience which in its thoughtlessness leaves the responsibility for its doing to the priests, finally through the *destruction of the state*, not only by means of the contempt and condemnation of marriage, of property and of thinking self-certainty, but also through the non-recognition of true princely sovereignty. With enthusiasm he raised up, on the contrary, Protestantism as the restorer of the ethical life of family life, of civic probity, of conscientiousness and freedom of conscience, of the unity of the divine and the human, as this expresses itself, according to him, especially also in the fact that the *prince* of a Protestant state is at the same time the *supreme bishop* of his church. With emphasis he rejected the unhappy error that one could suppose a state to be thoroughly constituted without having brought faith in God, as the innermost principle of all thinking, doing and letting be, to its truth.

If this oration will always remain a fine monument of Hegel’s genuinely Protestant disposition, he had as rector yet another occasion to interest himself in the promotion of the religious formation of the students. Negotiations were namely conducted between the ministry and the senate of the university about all sorts of buildings, partly on account of the Royal Theater, partly on account of a roof repair of the university building. On this occasion the senate drew attention to the *lack of a university church for Berlin*, and Hegel took up the

[p. 412]

cause with all his might. If no church could yet be built, then, he said, one should for the time being grant a prayer hall. Most universities of Germany, Hegel observed, were founded in times when the satisfaction of the religious need pressed itself with such immediate necessity that it could in no way be overlooked and put aside. Mostly endowed from monastery estates, they were provided at their origin with a church of their own. Such an endowment had come of itself. But if the founding of new universities, the Berlin one too, had taken its beginning rather from material arrangements, and a church was no longer reckoned among what is urgently necessary, the need nonetheless persisted no less, and one must therefore hold that the need of divine service at the university had not been mistaken and excluded, but its satisfaction only postponed. Now, since the university had grown to a number of 1800 students, it formed, with the families of the more than 100 lecturers, a not inconsiderable congregation. The students, for the most part strangers, found a place in the churches only by chance and with inconvenience, and this circumstance often kept them from attending divine service. The position of students in life, between need of guidance and spiritual independence, demanded also a peculiar consideration for the satisfaction of their religious need. If, then, a particular church belonged already to the *decorum* of a university, it was in our times just as important to counteract a neglect, indeed oblivion, of religious awakening and instruction as to preserve the young, when a religious impulse makes itself felt in them, from surrender to a feeble-minded and occasionally fanatical and malignant direction of religiosity. — Certainly one can only wish the Berlin university good fortune, in the interest of religion, that it has received no such separate church. Could one guarantee a university always a *Schleiermacher* as academic preacher, which he was at Halle, the proposal would rather be to be accepted. Otherwise, however, it is only of benefit when the student visits various churches, hears various preachers, and as a stranger nonetheless in the house of God feels the community of faith of a congregation to which

[p. 413]

he has otherwise no personal relation.

For the rest, Hegel conducted himself in his rectorship with all the gravity which he liked to put into such relations. In the world he saw at that time, with a beneficent illusion, the real counterpart of his Concepts. He was too modest to put the slightest value on himself as an individual; but in the respect for his rectorial dignity he deceived himself so far as to hold the university of the present Prussian state still for a formal *corporation* in the autonomous sense, and said in the inaugural address for this office: [Latin] “We are governed by laws; for the talent and arbitrary will of one man there is neither need nor place! This literary university enjoys its own firmness and spontaneous health.”

All the virtues of firmness, circumspection, punctuality, formed in the Nuremberg Gymnasium rectorship, sufficient for a painfully conscientious conduct of office, he developed in full measure. While he presided over the rectorship, he had the infinite satisfaction that no student had had to be brought to inquiry on account of demagogic intrigues. A false alarm had once frightened him. Immediately after the July Revolution a student had gone about for eight days with a *French cockade* on his cap, frank and free, in Berlin’s streets, and had even paid visits at the city jail. He was brought to inquiry. Hegel’s awkward suspense over this incident was resolved, however, in the ridiculousness, proved to evidence, that the student, in order to behave quite patriotically, quite anti-Gallic, had rather meant to wear the *Märkisch cockade*!

His valedictory address on leaving the rectorship, in which he himself related this yokel’s tale, Hegel could not hold publicly, because he was extremely unwell. His grateful devotion to his colleagues, and their cooperation in his business, went on this occasion to the boundless.

#### Critique of the English Reform Bill, 1831.

Hegel had so entirely settled into Prussia, in comfort, that this state, so often decried and mocked, of schools and

[p. 414]

barracks appeared to him in a quite different light than he himself had earlier regarded it. He felt so at home in it, so happy, that he also became unaccustomed to constitutionalism and found in the monarchical principle as such, even without popular representation, without budget, without free press, without publicity, the salvation of states. There lies in age the need of order and quiet, the need to secure the future and to educate the young according to determinate principles for it. Power as power, to keep down the bad self-will, the petty passions, the vanity of knowing better, the purposeless mania for innovation, became an idol to him. So it came about that his political views became ever more conservative. The people counted for him again, as once in the opposition to sansculottism, as the indeterminate, atomistic multitude; the granting of taxes by the estates appeared to him as a wrong if the government could thereby be restricted in its means; electoral representation became to him a matter of the chance of unreason; the French, whom he had liked so well in Paris in 1826, he now scolded as frivolous, as aimlessly restless.

In such a mood the event of the July Revolution shook him in the most dreadful way. There is a lack of larger written documents to portray more exactly Hegel’s state of mind at this time, but one can certainly compare it with that of *Niebuhr*, even if Hegel was calmer, more composed and not so tormented by the representation of a brutalizing war and military despotism as the Roman historian. The reflections, however, which Niebuhr has interwoven in his letters from 4 August 1830 to 19 December 1830 (*Biographical Notices*, vol. III, pp. 259 — 282), can certainly in part also be regarded as genuinely Hegelian. P. 260: “I lamented the ordinances, because they introduced an abominable disorder, but that they would succeed *for now* I did not doubt. To be sure, only for now; in the long run it could not last, and in a couple of years even the dynasty might well fall; namely, if the priests make it too mad.” — “My utterances about the coming future, its savagery, the scaring away of all the sciences and Muses, will be explained by posterity as the view of an unprejudiced contemporary;

[p. 415]

now, however, they will arouse the cry of the blinded. The fewest know where they want to go; they set out and run, like strollers who want to take some exercise, off into the distance: they stand wholly under the influence of declamations and fantastic thoughts; among them are noble people and even significant writers.” — P. 267: “Peculiar is the absence of every and any joyfulness, hope and illusion in these revolutions, in the French in particular, compared with 1789 — Everything has old features and is outlived; the old Lafayette, who still dreams himself in the old times, stands there like a ghost. There is far more consciousness than then; the low rabble wants to provide for its immediate advantage. The forms are indifferent only to a few young fantasts. It is very possible that a dissolution as in South America may occur even in France. The merchant class, however heartily it detests the priests, would only too gladly undo the revolution. I held it for impossible, because I knew the higher estates to be wholly intent on their advantage and far from all dreams. That these would not give themselves up to the bullets could be expected, and so it has turned out: they have let the rabble loose, which in Paris has conducted itself not merely heroically but, for a rabble, admirably.” — P. 270: “That we in Germany in particular are hastening in flight toward barbarism is my firm conviction, and much better it does not stand in France. That devastation too threatens us, as two hundred years ago, is to me unfortunately just as clear, and the end of the song will be despotism on the ruins. Within fifty years, and probably far sooner, there will be in all Europe, at least on the continent, no trace of free institutions and of freedom of the press.”

These apprehensions of a Niebuhr we wished to recall here, for, much as Hegel differed from him in his opinion on Roman history, he was nevertheless in agreement with him in this gloomy conception of the July Revolution, which Niebuhr as late as the 4th of July had held to be impossible.
