Since he, as only a statesman can do, pursued the reading of newspapers to the most extended compass, there stood at his disposal, for the substantiation of his views, always an enormous mass of facts. The most dreadful of all

[p. 416]

symptoms of impending further revolutions, also outside France, was to him the disrespect, the *awelessness* before all authority; the *courage from below* upward, the arguing and disobeying, was stronger, he said, than the courage from above, the commanding and keeping in order. Everywhere he now scented demagogic insolence. He copied out for himself from German, French and English newspapers turns of phrase in which he believed he saw the betrayal of such a disposition mirrored. When in the French Chambers the *raison publique* was distinguished from the *opinion publique*, he called the former, with horror, an “unheard-of category.” — When the people of Baden thought that a law on the murder of princes was just as superfluous among us Germans as, among the Athenians, Solon had not cared to set up any law against the murder of parents, he asserted that behind it there lurked “a demagogic trick.” Altogether, he thought, the princes were now only an *object of intrigue*. Since now several of his Berlin friends and pupils, *Gans* in particular, thought otherwise and were quite enthusiastic for the July Revolution and its possible consequences, it came about from then on to vehement, often vexatious conversations. And when the *Belgian* Revolution too could not, as was first expected, be damped down, he was quite beside himself. In an already printed letter to *Göschel* of 13 December 1830 he complained, on account of those struggles, that all those who defended the *substantial* rights of the state, of religion, were at once decried as servile and as informers. “Yet at present,” he confesses, “the enormous political interest has swallowed up all others — a crisis in which everything that was otherwise valid seems to be made problematic.”

If one considers that his youth lived through the first French Revolution, that his manhood saw Napoleon’s colossal wars, that since the Restoration he had attained the enjoyment of a happy leisure, and that from everywhere the rewarding successes of his honest, many years’ striving had begun to come toward him, it is no wonder that, like Niebuhr, he found the darkening of the political horizon and the prospect of new revolutions and wars of peoples most repugnant. Indeed he even fell ill again of the same illness with which, as a student in Tübingen,

[p. 417]

he had struggled; toward the end of the year 1830 he had the intermittent fever for three months.

Nevertheless, on calmer consideration he did not fail to recognize the necessity of the July Revolution. He conceived France as the state in which the political and the religious conscience are not yet identical with one another. The latter, as still essentially Catholic, is unfree, the former free. Since now religion is the innermost unity of man, comprehending everything under itself, there must also arise the striving to subordinate everything to it. Hence, in France religion seeks to master the state. But since the principle of the state has already reached a higher stage of culture than religion in the form of the Catholic church, the former must not only react against such subordination but also *be victorious in the reaction*. After some time, however, the revolution will find itself again on the same standpoint, because with it religion has not been changed, and consequently a new revolution must be brought about by the repeated breach of ecclesiastical unfreedom with political freedom. The knot at which France is toiling away is therefore this: *to want to carry through a revolution of the state without a reformation of the church*. Besides this, Hegel put what is peculiar in the course of the French crisis also in the relation of the *hommes de principes* and the *hommes d’état*, in the relation of the formal freedom of subjective self-determination and the necessity of a government that is directed to the concrete and particular. He explained by this the phenomenon that men of the opposition, as soon as they enter the ministry, turn about and govern just like those previously attacked by them, because they only now notice what a difference there is between abstract principles of equality, freedom, rights of man, and concrete, individual determinations. This conception of the *status quo* in France Hegel also expressed from the lecturer’s chair, in the philosophy of religion and philosophy of history, and then thought that Germany is much happier, partly because with it not only is the worldly conscience not distinguished from the religious, but also for the self-determination of the many, for the need of a self-conscious participation in the whole of the state and in

[p. 418]

its laws, the vitality of a concrete content had been preserved, in testimony of which he cited in particular the Prussian Municipal Ordinance.

When the *Reform Bill* then came up for discussion in England, he was seized by the most tormenting representations, which disturbed him day and night. He saw in it, namely, a *departure* from the *principle of England*, from *merely positive* right. Hegel was wholly for the Bill as an unavoidable measure demanded by justice and equity. But precisely because here sound common sense could grasp and set forth so clearly the infinite disproportion between right merely historically given and right rationally necessary, the danger for England seemed to him only the greater, because all its freedom had for its content less what is truly human than only peculiar privileges, *special* liberties.

He wrote, to give himself relief, a great essay on the Reform Bill, which he had inserted in the then still so-called Prussian State Gazette, 1831, Nos. 115–118; reprinted in *Works*, vol. XVII, pp. 425–76. He singled out for censure in England: the weakness of the monarchical principle against Parliament; the ostentation and garrulousness of political declamation, in contrast to which he praised a few brief but insightful utterances of a Wellington; the bad condition of the shapeless private law, and very strongly *the gruesome treatment of Ireland*. With an admirable expertness in detail he depicted the acts of violence which the landlords permit themselves, the feudal crudity of the hunting rights, the distress of the common people, the oppressive abuse of the tithe, the arrogance of the rich ecclesiastical prebendaries. Most bitterly he reproved the self-interest and *venality* in elections so widespread in England, although he also had to tell himself, in turn, that the insignificance of the individual and his material indemnification for the impossibility of securing a decisive share for himself mitigated much of this corruption in actuality.

The refrain of this extensive exposition was for him, on the one hand, for England the hopelessness of how it was to emerge from these tangled and sad conditions, on the other the praise of Germany

[p. 419]

particularly Prussia, showing how here the great and wise sense of the princes and a quiet reflection since the Thirty Years’ War had made quite different, more humane and more rational institutions, whereby, however, he painted England’s shadow side in colors too black, Germany’s light side in colors too brilliant.

One feels in the essay, solid as it is, and interesting as the turn was of opposing, in political respect, the blind admiration of England and the blind contempt of Germany, nevertheless already a morbid ill-humor.

#### Hegel’s Last Birthday Celebration.

To such political agitation there came now in 1831 also the demonic sickness of *cholera*. Hegel’s family moved outside the city, at the Kreuzberg, in the Grunow garden, into the upper story of a pleasant garden house, the so-called Little Castle. Communication with the city was reduced as much as possible. As soon as the holidays had begun, his solicitous wife would have it no other way than that Hegel too must move entirely into the garden, where he then lived quite comfortably amid studies, friendly visits, games of chess with his sons, little walks, and hearty persiflating scolding at the petty uprisings of those days in the German cities.

This shutting-out from the city was the reason that Hegel’s birthday in 1831 was celebrated in one of the spacious halls of the pleasure resort *Tivoli*, situated near the Kreuzberg, by the friends still present in Berlin (for most of them had gone away because of the cholera). At a cheerful meal *Rösel* developed his splendid humor to the full; *Zelter* was inexhaustible in communicating interesting judgments and *bons mots* of Goethe’s. The painter *Xeller* seasoned with his Swabian good-naturedness and his inward smile the enjoyment of the witticisms that were made; *Marheineke* spread over the whole a wholesome dignity which, with ironic tolerance, only furthered the joviality; Hegel’s sons sympathized with the women in a quiet and joyful emotion. Hardly had coffee been taken after the champagne when a terrible thunderstorm rose up, which

[p. 420]

determined most of them to a swift departure; Hegel too hurried to his nearby dwelling.

To bring his whole mood in this period vividly before us, there remains a very interesting document. *Heinrich Stieglitz*, since, owing to an accident, he could not be present at the festival, sent Hegel, in old affectionate custom, a *midnight greeting*, in which he eloquently depicted the dangers of the time, the threatening prospect of a general anarchy, and called Hegel to the struggle against those unleashed from Russia’s steppes to the shore of the Seine. He concluded his apostrophe:

Keep watch, you prince of spirits! / Truly, the hour will come / When it matters that even the master / With his god-hallowed mouth

Name aloud the word, the right one, / In which alone the magic dwells / That hollow semblance part / From the essence where spirit is enthroned.

To this Hegel replied the next day with the following verses, metrically, as usual, unpronounceable:

Welcome to me the friend’s greetings! / Not greeting only, demand for resolutions / To word-deed, to conjure / The many, friends themselves too, who rise up into madness.

Yet what is the crime of those you accuse, / Only that each wants to hear himself, wants to speak foremost; / So the word, to ward off the evil, / Would itself be only a means to increase this mischief still further.

And should it come, as it has long urged me, to strike out at last, / Then your call would be a pledge to venture it yet, / With hope that spirits may still strike back in answer to it, / And that it not die away in empty laments, / That they carry it to the people, to the work!

#### *Hegel.*

#### From the Little Castle on the Kreuzberg.

[p. 421]

#### The Literary Testament.

During the summer Hegel had begun to prepare a new edition of his *Logic* and had finished the first part, in which the introduction was carried further and the chapter on the Concept of the infinitely great and the infinitely small was very much completed, with definite reference to the doctrines of the most famous mathematicians. On 7 November he concluded the Preface, in which he expressed himself as clearly as possible about his Concept of the logical, and at the end voiced the apprehension whether in a time so politically agitated, so carried away by the surface of the day, there would still be room left for earnestness with the passionless stillness of thinking cognition. An infinite melancholy steals through these last lines.

Many a gloomy thing had drawn near him. The Minister von *Altenstein*, so highly revered by him, had lost in the course of the year 1830 his only beloved sister, and Hegel had expressed to him his sympathy in a rather long printed letter. As late as 1 September 1831, still from the Grunow garden house, he had called out to his highly esteemed friend *Heinrich Beer*, on the loss of a hopeful son, a few consoling words which faithfully mirror his deep and composed heart, without any inkling how soon he himself was to become the object of such laments, such consolations.

Because of the lectures he had moved back into the city, in which cholera had already broken out. He spoke, as it seemed, with still more fire than usual, and swept everything along.

Now an unpleasant incident occurred. *Gans*, returned from a journey, made the posting of his winter courses on the university’s bulletin board with an addendum in which he recommended to the students of jurisprudence Hegel’s lectures on the subjects pertaining thereto as very useful. At this Hegel was incensed, as at a guardianship of which he, after all, had no need whatever. He demanded in a note to Gans, with angry vehemence, the immediate withdrawal of a notice which compromised him with the students as with the lecturers, with fellow students

[p. 422]

and colleagues, since he did not know at all how he came to be recommended. He scolded Gans’s procedure as improprieties and clumsinesses, and declared that he wished to settle the matter in this way only out of friendly consideration. The whole note, the last words Hegel wrote at all, is a *single* period (printed in Dorow’s *Memoirs and Letters*, 1840, p. 142).

#### Hegel’s Death.

Quite suddenly, to everyone unexpectedly, on Leibniz’s death day, on 14 November 1831, at a quarter past five in the afternoon, Hegel died in his dwelling on the Kupfergraben of cholera, in its most concentrated and therefore, in its outward symptoms, less terrible form. His wife wrote about it to Hegel’s sister *Christiane* a rather long letter, from which only what belongs to the world is to be taken here.

“I will compose myself and tell you briefly how everything came about. My blessed beloved husband felt unwell from Sunday forenoon on, after he had still breakfasted quite cheerfully with us, complained of stomach pain and nausea, *without* any *dietary error* or *chill* having preceded. He had begun his lectures with full vigor and cheerfulness on the Thursday before, had still examined on Saturday, and had invited some dear friends for Sunday noon. I had them told this and devoted myself entirely to his care. The physician came by a fortunate chance at once, prescribed — but none of us found anything alarming in his condition. His stomach pain was bearable. First vomiting without, then with bile set in. He had already had similar attacks more often. He spent the night in the greatest restlessness. I sat at his bed, wrapped him in the bedclothes when he sat up in bed and tossed about, although he repeatedly asked me in the friendliest way to lie down and leave him alone with his impatience. His stomach pain was not so much violent, ‘but so wretched, like toothache, one cannot lie quietly in one place.’ — Monday morning he wanted to get up. We brought him into the adjoining sitting room, but

[p. 423]

his weakness was so great that on the way to the sofa he almost sank down. I had his bedstead set close beside it. We lifted him into warmed bedclothes. He complained only of weakness. All pain, all nausea was gone, so that he said: ‘Would to God I had had only one such quiet hour last night.’ He told me he needed rest, I should accept no visitors. If I wished to take his pulse, he lovingly took my hand, as if to say, leave this concern of your own. — The physician was there early in the morning, prescribed, as the day before, a mustard poultice over the abdomen (I had put leeches on him the evening before). In the forenoon hiccups set in, with difficulties in urinating. But for all that he lay quite gently, always in the same warmth and perspiration, always in full consciousness, and, as it seemed to me, without apprehension of danger. A second physician, Dr. *Horn*, was called in. A mustard poultice over the whole body, flannel cloths dipped in chamomile decoction over it. All this did not disturb or trouble him. At 3 o’clock a chest cramp set in, then again a gentle sleep; but over the left side of the face an icy coldness spread. The hands turned blue and cool. We knelt at his bed and listened to his breath. It was the slumbering-over of a transfigured one!

Let me break off. Now you know everything. Weep with me, but also thank God with me for this painless, gentle, blessed end. And now say, would you have recognized in all this even a *single* symptom of cholera? With horror I had to learn that the physicians, Medical Councillor *Barez* and Privy Councillor *Horn*, had recognized it as such, and indeed as the kind that without outward symptoms destroys the innermost life in the most violent manner. *How* he looked inside they did not see.

Although Hegel was reported to the Commission as having contracted cholera (which sealed the beloved corpse for me in my sitting room, where I had demanded that it should remain, and fumigated and disinfected everything), none of our friends was afraid, not even the most timid. All hurried to me in their grief. Some of them had seen him only the days before in the most cheerful good health, had still heard him on Thursday and Friday in his lectures, where with special vigor and fire

[p. 424]

he had delighted his listeners, so that he even said to me: ‘Today it has become particularly easy for me.’ Many could hardly compose themselves. During his illness, which lasted from Sunday at 11 o’clock until Monday at 5 o’clock, his dearest friends knew and suspected nothing from afar. None saw him any more, except Privy Councillor *Schulze*, whom in my anguish of heart I called to his dying. His heavenly calm and his blessed falling asleep were disturbed by no outward unrest, by no loud lament. With restrained tears and oppressed hearts we were, softly and quietly, seeming as calm as possible, occupied with him, until we were listening to his last sleep, in which the passing into death could not be distinguished. We could only kneel down and pray.

Through the most active mediation of our friends it was granted, as the first and only exception, out of regard for the personality of the transfigured one, after unspeakable struggles, through higher intercession, that he was not brought on the cholera hearse, not already after 24 hours, by night and fog, to the cholera cemetery. He now rests at the place which he had chosen and had designated as his own at Solger’s burial, next to Fichte and near Solger. Yesterday, Wednesday, at 3 o’clock in the afternoon, was his solemn funeral. The professors and students from all faculties, his older and younger pupils, assembled first in the great hall of the Aula. Here his faithful friend, the present Rector *Marheineke*, delivered a speech to the moved assembly. Thereupon the immeasurably long procession of students, who, because they were not allowed to accompany him with burning torches, carried torches wound with crape, and an innumerable line of carriages proceeded to the house of mourning, where they joined the four-horse hearse. My poor, deeply shaken sons drove after the beloved corpse with Marheineke and Privy Councillor Schulze. From the gate on, a chorus was struck up by the students. At the grave Court Councillor *Förster* delivered a speech, *Marheineke*, as clergyman, the blessing.”

Hegel’s only sister *Christiane* was severely stricken by this news of the death of her faithful brother Wilhelm, whom she had last seen in Nuremberg and whose course of fame she had followed with the most tender sympathy. She had never

[p. 425]

married. One of her warmest suitors, Gotthold, she had believed herself obliged to refuse, from perhaps too painful considerations. He had died unmarried, far from her, without ever having given up his love for her. From that time a deep grief gnawed at her life, which soon made itself known in certain agitations, eccentricities, and first broke out more decisively in Nuremberg in 1815. Hegel took pains to bring her to greater calm.

Judging by a silhouette, she looked very much like him. Her heart was deep. She made many excerpts from books, wrote down sermons for herself, took a lively interest in the Württemberg Chamber debates, and composed many poems, partly riddles, partly occasional verses; some of them, in which she buries her love earthly in order to lift it over into the eternal heaven of memory, are truly beautiful. In her poems she loved, like her brother, the Schillerian tone. For many years she was governess at the castle of *Jarthausen* in the house of the von *Berlichingens*. Later Hegel too provided for her to the best of his powers. The most zealous paternal sympathy was devoted to her by a relative, Pastor *Göritz* at Aalen. The last eight years she lived by herself alone and had a maidservant. A brother of the philosopher *Schelling*, Medical Councillor *Schelling*, took pains in the most honest way for years to alleviate her condition, and tried to cure it also with several bath cures. In November 1831, even before the news of her brother’s death arrived, she fell into the fixed idea that all the physicians had directed magnets and electrical machines against her. She now dressed fantastically, in order to counter the influence of these supposed attempts upon her life. Several times she tried to kill herself, to leap out of the window, to open a vein. The death of her brother she received at first quite quietly, apparently almost without sympathy, but a few hours later she broke into violent and long weeping.

Then for weeks she became outwardly quite rational and calm; but with this behavior she only wanted to deceive the attention of her surroundings. On 2 February 1832 she did not return from a walk. She had cast herself into the floods of the Nagold, was soon found, and on 4 February was decently buried in the churchyard at *Calw*. No one will be able to picture this noble, deeply religious being to himself without inward melancholy.

[p. 426]

The only sister of a sage celebrated by the world, dying in the capital of a great state surrounded by his family, dies in mental derangement, with broken heart, the lonely death by her own hand!

The general impression, however, which Hegel’s death made we cannot bring before ourselves more vividly than through a letter from *Varnhagen* von Ense to Ludwig *Robert*, from Berlin, of 16 November 1831:

“On receipt of this sheet the hard tidings of Hegel’s unexpectedly swift decease will already have reached you too and certainly struck you deeply. The notice in the State Gazette says falsely that he was struck by apoplexy. The announcement on the part of the widow names no illness. But it was cholera, the most fully developed, the most unconquerable cholera, which, already on the wane, has insidiously snatched away this dear victim too! Hegel had from the beginning a deep dread and anxiety of the fearsome monster, which he later seemed to have overcome and then became too bold. Thus on the day before his falling ill he did not deny himself the enjoyment of grapes, which acted chillingly on his bowels; other detrimental influences may have prepared his body for the evil already. It set in with the strongest violence and swiftest course. Yet he had no inkling of his approaching death and fell asleep, as the widow’s announcement says, painlessly, gently and blissfully. It is fine that he did not suffer! So his death was as happy as death can possibly be. Of undiminished spirit, in vigorous activity, at the height of fame and of influence, surrounded on all sides by great successes, content with his situation, cheerfully attracted by social life, taking a friendly part in all the offerings of the capital, he departed from the midst of these satisfactions without regret and pain, for the significance and name of his illness remained unknown to him, and the slumbering consciousness was allowed to dream of recovery.

But a dreadful gap has been torn for us! It yawns unfillably, ever larger on us, the longer one looks at it. He was really the cornerstone of the university here. On him rested the scientific character of the whole, in him the whole had its stability,

[p. 427]

its support. From all sides collapse now threatens. Such a combination of the deepest universal thinking and the most immense knowledge in all empirical domains of cognition is now absolutely lacking; what is still there is individual, for itself, must first seek out the higher relation and will rarely find it. Everyone feels, too, even the adversaries, what is lost with him. The whole city is stunned by the blow, it is as if the shock of this fall resonated in every crudest consciousness. The numerous friends and disciples want to despair. Gans met me yesterday with weeping eyes, and then shed hot tears at my house, vying with Rahel, giving free vent to his lamentation. The fall has gripped me deeply; I continually feel its upheaval and am almost sick from it; yet my feeling arises more from the general outlines of what has happened than from an immediate personal relation of it to me. With the greatest veneration, on the friendliest terms and in the most intimate companionship, the closest nearness between us nevertheless did not exist. We saw and felt ourselves also all too often as opponents, and indeed as such as hope for no reconciliation through the struggle and therefore prefer to avoid it. Even in the last time I had a discord with him on account of Fichte’s memory; the rigid tenacity which Fichte had against his opponents was Hegel’s too; but I shall in future perhaps have to defend the latter against a successor just as I last defended Fichte against Hegel.

Strange! Fichte died here of typhus, Hegel of cholera, both on great political weather-divides, whose most dubious trials they were removed from in good time.”

*Zelter* too reported on 16 November 1831 to *Goethe*: “They are just now about to put the good Hegel under the earth, who died the day before yesterday suddenly of cholera. On Friday evening he was still with me at my house and lectured the following day still. — Thus one learns the worth of men when they are gone. As a companion Hegel may not have found approval; we liked best to play a little game of whist together, which he played well and calmly. — A young woman said not long ago in the presence of other women: she had never yet heard a really significant word from Hegel’s mouth. After a pause

[p. 428]

I answered: that might well be possible; for it was his trade to speak to men.”

The grief of the Hegelian pupils throughout Germany and beyond was very great, and they felt themselves, since they especially venerated in Hegel the scientific master as much as they loved the noble and childlike man, for the moment bound in an enthusiastic unity, which also expressed itself in many poems, which were published in part in journals, in part sent to the family as tokens of mourning, and of one of which the conclusion may stand here as conclusion:

And when specters stir again, / Which long ago you banished into the night, / When it matters to sweep the temple clean / That you turned to the service of light: / Then let your spirit with its wingbeats / Be for us the pledge of certain victory, / But you, drink on in blessed clarity, / A prince of spirits, the cup of eternal truth.

[scan 474]

### Documents.

[scan 476]

I.

#### Hegel’s Diary from His Gymnasium Years.

1785. Sunday, the 26th of June.

At the morning service Herr *Regier*, preacher at the collegiate church, preached. He read out the *Augsburg Confession*, and first of all its preamble; then came the sermon. Even if I had retained nothing else, my historical knowledge would still have been increased. For I learned that the Augsburg Confession was presented on 25 June 1530, that Württemberg was reformed on 2 February 1535, and that in 1599 the evangelical religion was confirmed by the Treaty of Prague. They received the name of Protestants from the protestation against the harsh imperial decree at Speyer in 1529. It also comes to my mind that Luther died on 18 February 1546, and that the Elector of Saxony, John the Wise, was totally defeated and taken prisoner on 24 April 1547.

Monday, the 27th of June. No *world history* has pleased me better than *Schröckh’s*. He avoids the tedium of the many names of a special history, yet narrates all the principal events, but wisely leaves out altogether the many kings, the wars in which often a couple of hundred men scuffled, and the like, and combines what is most excellent, the instructive, with history. In the same way he everywhere carefully records the state of the learned and of the sciences. — Today there was *convent*. At the Gymnasium, namely, the professors meet every month, deliberate on the affairs concerning the 6th and 7th classes, and at the same time punish the transgressors of the Gymnasium laws. The *primi*, as *capita repraesentativa* [representative heads] of the year-group, as the Rector called us, had to appear. They were, from the seventh class: *Cammerer*, *proveteranus*, son of a court physician; *Duttenhofer*, *veteranus primus*, son of a game dealer, *specialissimus*; *Vischer*, *novitius primus*, son of a revenue-office secretary;

[p. 432]

from the sixth class: *Boger*, *veteranus primus*, son of a lieutenant-colonel; *Hegel*, *novitius primus*.

Nothing further was put to us than that we were earnestly admonished to warn our comrades not to get involved in wretched, dissolute gambling and other societies. For a society of young people has come to light, males of 16–17, females of 11–12 years. It is known under the name of the *Doggengesellschaft* [Mastiff Society], *Laplanders*, etc. The gentlemen take the young ladies out walking there and ruin themselves and their time in a wretched way.

Tuesday, the 28th of June. I made the remark *what different impressions one and the same object can make on different persons*. Namely, it was told that a woman of my acquaintance had happily been delivered. My father, as an erstwhile husband, was heartily pleased at it; J. B., as a grown woman who had already attended such events, even more, and said besides that there is no greater joy than when a woman has a happy delivery. But at the same time a fine horse was ridden past. B. and I stood at the windows. B., about 21 years old, a fellow, asked at once whose it was, while that joyful news was being brought, which he heard rather with indifference. I sprang to him, not particularly moved by the happy delivery, and gave him my approval that it was a really fine horse. — As I was eating cherries with much appetite and delighting myself splendidly and counting myself happy, someone else, admittedly older than I, looked on with indifference and said: in youth one believes one could not possibly pass a cherry-woman without one’s (as we Swabians say) mouth watering for them; in older years, however, one can almost let a whole spring roll past without longing for it likewise. I thought thereupon the for me rather painful, but yet wisest saying: that in youth, when from irrepressible craving one would surely put one’s health into bad circumstances, one *cannot* eat so much, in old age one does not *care* to.

Wednesday, the 29th of June. Dear me, dear me! Bad news from Hohenheim. These peasants, they are accursed people, have smashed all the windows of the Duke’s castle at Scharnhausen. — It was a holiday today. But I did not go to church, but went walking in the Bopserwald with *Duttenhofer* and *Autenrieth*.

Thursday, the 30th of June. There was a sultry heat today and it had the appearance as if there would be a thunderstorm, but it cleared away

[p. 433]

— I also played once again today my favorite *chess*, and although I am a poor player, I nevertheless won it both times. I never play according to a plan, as should actually be done, but at the beginning only at random, which however is a great fault. The further playing and the position of the pieces must then determine the plan according to which I shall play on. But I will endeavor next time to make this one each time right at the beginning and to follow it through the whole game. — I said so much about chess only *in fugam vacui* [to flee a void], so that the last day of this month might not remain empty.

Friday, the 1st of July. For a long time I had been pondering what a *pragmatic history* is. Today I have obtained an idea of it, though a rather obscure and one-sided one. A pragmatic history is, I believe, when one does not merely narrate facts, but also develops the character of a famous man, of a whole nation, its customs, usages, religion and the various changes and deviations of these items from other peoples; traces the decline and the rise of great empires; shows what this or that event or change of state has had for consequences for the constitution of the nation, for its character, etc., and the like.

Saturday, the 2nd of July. Why did *Socrates* have a cock sacrificed to Aesculapius before his end? asked Professor Offerdinger in a *Hebdomadarium* [weekly exercise]. After citing various opinions he said: he held that Socrates, through the effect of the poison, was no longer conscious of himself. I hold, besides this cause, also that he thought, since it was the custom, he did not wish, by omitting this slight gift, to affront the rabble altogether.

Sunday, the 3rd of July. On the way back from a walk we set up, I especially (that self-love must come into play at once!), the proposition: “*every good has its bad side* (often less, often more, in proportion to the good) and applied this proposition at every step. R., who was also along, went around another corner than we. It was farther. As we saw him come toward us, we waited. Now one said: what good this waiting and stopping on the way has in itself, he did not see. We answered: if we had run on, one of us might have fallen or had a not good thought. — Quite stoic!

Monday, the 4th of July. On the walk Professor *Cloß* examined me on various subjects, especially on the course of

[p. 434]

the sun or rather the inclination of the earth, whereby the seasons arise. Among other things I put the question: *why it is hotter in July and August than in June*, when the sun is yet nearest to us? That the heat in our atmosphere arises through the rebounding of the sun’s rays is known. Professor *Cloß* gave me the following explanation: In June and sooner the sun, as it were, excites and irritates, through its taction and ignition, the fire-particles near the surface of the earth. These now in turn irritate those lying beside them and so go on, as it were, in a chain to the center of the earth. In July and August most of them may now be irritated. In these months, then, the greatest heat is thrown back from the earth into the atmosphere and it is therefore hottest.

Tuesday, the 5th of July. I *bought* from the library of the late Preceptor *Löffler*, my most faithful teacher and guide, the following *books*: 1. Greek: *Aristoteles de moribus* [Aristotle on morals]; *Demosthenis oratio de corona* [Demosthenes’ oration on the crown]; *Isocratis opera omnia* [the complete works of Isocrates]; 2. Latin: a. prose: *Ciceronis opera philosophica* [Cicero’s philosophical works]; *A. Gellii noctes Atticae* [Aulus Gellius’s Attic Nights]; *Vellejus Paterculus*; *Diodorus Siculus*; b. poetic: *Plautus*; *Catullus*, *Tibullus*, *Propertius*; *Gallus*, *Claudianus* and *Ausonius*; *Hieronymus Vida*; *Virgilius Christianus*; *Sannazarius*.

Wednesday, the 6th of July. Preceptor *Löffler* was one of my most venerable teachers; especially in the lower Gymnasium I may boldly call him almost the most excellent.

Thursday, the 7th of July. He was the most upright and impartial man. His chief concern was to be useful to his pupils, to himself and to the world. He did not think so basely as others who believe: now they have their bread and need study no further, if only they can keep up the eternal class routine renewed every year. No, the blessed man did not think so. He knew the worth of the sciences and the comfort which they afford one in various mishaps. How often and how contentedly and cheerfully he sat with me in that beloved little room, and I with him! — Few knew his merits. It was a great misfortune for the man that he had to work so entirely beneath his sphere. And now he too has fallen asleep! But forever shall I bear his memory unremoved in my heart. — This I must still add, that he made me a present of 8 volumes of Shakespeare’s plays as early as 1778.

Friday, the 8th of July. As a general trait I have in the

[p. 435]

character of the *female sex* (some men too are certainly not free from it) found the complete violation of the verses of Horace, which read thus:

[Latin] In adversity it hopes, *in prosperity it fears* / A change of lot, the well-prepared / Heart.

Saturday, the 9th of July. If ever superstition has hatched a terrible adventure, stupid beneath all human reason, it is certainly the so-called *Muthesheer* (Valiant Host). Last Sunday night at 1 or 2 o’clock many people claimed to have seen it, even, *pudendum dictu* [shameful to say], people from whom one expects more enlightenment and who hold public offices. This old woman claims to have seen a fiery wagon with human beings, that one something else again. Commonly it is said that it is the devil in a fiery wagon. An angel of God flies ahead and calls to everyone: out of the way, the Valiant Host is coming! Whoever does not obey this divine call is dragged off by Herr Devil into his residence.

Sunday, the 10th of July. But to come back to the Valiant Host, various persons have been named to me who have seen or heard it (it is namely an abominable clatter). Some days afterward it turned out that it — oh shame, shame! — was coaches! Herr von *Türkheim* namely gave a concert, which was very well attended and lasted till 1 or 2 o’clock. In order then not to let the guests grope home in the darkness, he had them taken home with coaches and torches. And that was this Valiant Host. Ha, ha, ha! *O tempora, o mores!* [O the times, O the customs!] Happened in the year 1785. Oh, oh!

Monday, the 11th of July. On this occasion the following anecdote also occurred. Townspeople came to the main guard and told of that incident and at the same time asked the commanding officer to have a watch kept whether the Valiant Host would come again. The lieutenant thereupon ordered a watch to be kept. The soldier, who perhaps had not yet heard anything of it, asked: if it comes, does Your Honor, Lieutenant, command that I should halt it? — Yes, yes, said the lieutenant, just halt it. — But it stayed away.

Tuesday, the 12th of July. A similar story happened recently. Four women were driving from the turnpike house on the Ludwigsburg road to here, whereby one passes the gallows. It was at 12 o’clock at night. At the little turnpike house a mounted post-boy *without a head* had now come to them and kept riding with them, now beside, now before, now

[p. 436]

behind the coach. The coachman wanted to evade him, but the post-boy always followed, until at last he vanished at the gate. That, however, rested on the testimony of 5 or 6 persons. — Only some days afterward an officer declared that he had come at just the same place and at the same time upon a coach and ridden along with it, but had not wanted to go in through this gate, and had therefore ridden away from them by another way. He said at the same time that he had not been able to understand why the coachman had always wanted to evade him.

Wednesday, the 13th of July. I was today for the first time in the *ducal library*. Every Wednesday and Saturday from 2–5 it is open to everyone to visit it. In a large room where one waits there stands a long table with pen and paper. The book one wants one writes, next to one’s name, on a slip of paper and gives it to the attendant, who then brings the book over. I asked, because other books were not there, for *Batteux’s Introduction to the Belles Lettres* and read the section on the epopee.

Thursday, the 14th of July. Professors *Abel* and *Hopf* honored our society the day before yesterday with a visit. We went walking with them, where they entertained us especially about *Vienna*.

Friday, the 15th of July. I went walking with Professor *Cloß*. We read in *Mendelssohn’s Phaedo*, only as it were the preparation or introduction, namely the character of *Socrates*. Anytus, Melitus and Crito were the three monsters who procured his death from the timorous senate and the hotheaded rabble.

Saturday, the 16th of July. Town Clerk *Kläpfel* died today, when one already believed him on the way back to recovery.

Tuesday, the 19th of July. Likewise Government Councillor and Privy Cabinet Secretary *Schmidlin* died today of a stroke, as he was about to take the spoon in hand to eat. *Leypold*, a good friend of mine, is one of his grandsons.

Wednesday, the 20th of July. I was today again at the library and asked for *Dusch’s Letters on the Formation of Taste*, but either they were not there or they could not be found. I did not get them, and so read again in the *Rammler*. — I also played chess twice with Herr *Riedrer*, in which I won every time.

Thursday, the 21st of July. I went walking with Herr *Cloß*. As we were crossing the moat, the great bell was being tolled for the burial of Government Councillor Schmidlin. At the same time they began with

[p. 437]

trombones from the town tower — *moles propinqua nubibus arduis* [a mass rising near the lofty clouds] — to blow a dirge. The dull, solemn, slow tone of the bell and the sad sound of the *trombones* made such a sublime impression on me, which I cannot describe, as I at the same time sometimes saw the coaches from afar and thought of the laments of the bereaved.

Friday, the 22nd of July. I went walking again with Professor *Cloß*; he examined me on the *regular and irregular solids*.

The doctrine of these occupies Hegel at length in his diary up to 25 July. On the 29th a new epoch enters it, with *writing in Latin*.

Friday, the 29th of July. [Latin] For the sake of exercising style and acquiring strength it seems not inappropriate to write down a certain *well-known story* in the Latin idiom. I have therefore resolved to run briefly through *Roman affairs* and to taste them, at least with the tips of my lips. The city, founded by Romulus, the first king of the Romulidae, had *kings* from the beginning. When the last of them grew arrogant and curtailed the rights of the people, the citizens preferred another form of government, etc.

Saturday, the 30th of July. [Latin] I am indeed often wont to wonder at the wonderful fortunes of things. The *Offices* of Cicero and the *Dialogues* are in my hands, printed in 1582. Before a space of two years had elapsed, marveling at the age of the book, which it had endured, I reckoned with myself that two hundred years had rolled by since that book was printed. Reflecting then with myself that so many hands, which were diligently kept busy in producing the printing of the book, and the men by whose counsels those hands were directed, are now pressed down by the oblivion of posterity, I know not what I should say? Those men, had they remained alive, would surely have grieved, if they had learned that after death the memory of themselves, the memory of their virtues, the memory of their good deeds would fall away from the minds of men. Now, however, I do not doubt that these men feel quite otherwise.

Sunday, the 31st of July. [Latin] For lack of any other material, I shall narrate in a few words the calamities of *Adrastus*. Adrastus, son of the king of Phrygia, etc.

Monday, the 1st of August. [Latin] Reflecting rather often with myself on the difficulty of the Greek language, I have found, roughly, these causes. The Greeks, easily the most learned, the most polished, the bravest of their contemporaries, learned the letters of the barbarians only sparingly; with barbarian peoples, whom as rude they despised, they had little intercourse. The languages of oppressed peoples the victors either destroyed

[p. 438]

[Latin] and brought in their own, or allowed them to creep about only among the common people. In this rudeness of languages they cultivated and enlarged their native tongue all the more. From this arose the very great wealth of Greek letters, which causes the foreigner a great many difficulties.

Wednesday, the 3rd of August. [Latin] The unlimited liberty of the form of their states added a great heap. Since supreme power was for the most part subject to the people, whoever strove to have any weight or to accomplish anything had to do nothing rather than court popular favor, and so carry through his plans. It did not long escape the more sagacious that the people could be led to anything by eloquence of speech. All the more diligently did they apply themselves to it, and shaped the language to elegance and charm.

Thursday, the 4th of August. [Latin] To this is added the multitude, elegance and ornament of the *particles*. The rhythm of the Greeks, however, we are in our time certainly unable to imitate, since it has been utterly corrupted by the use of the worst words.

Sunday, the 7th of August. [Latin] Today for the first time I attended the divine service of the *Catholics* and the sacred oration which *Werkmeister* preached. The *Mass*, as they call it, was not yet finished when I arrived; it displeased me exceedingly, *as it would any sane man*. After a hymn had been sung, the oration itself followed, which pleased me so much that I resolved to attend this preacher more often. Its whole aim was to make the minds of the uncultivated, who rigidly retain harsh antiquity, milder and more loving towards other Christians, even though these differ from their own doctrines. Not a single word was heard from which that lamentable discord of the Christians could have been discerned.

Monday, the 8th of August. [Latin] It must surely not be passed over in silence in this narration of events that today, under God’s auspices, we began the most excellent histories of *Livy* in the class of the Reverend Professor *Cless*. The most reverend professor touched on the life of Livy, of which indeed little has come down to us. What I learned I shall record in a few words. Livy of Padua flourished under Augustus, etc.

Sunday, the 21st of August. [Latin] Today I again attended the sacred rites of the *Catholics*. *Majer* expounded the Catechism, and this exposition pleased me wonderfully both by the venerable learning of the expositor and by its very great perspicuity. Before noon a minister of divine things, recently co-opted and called, gave a public oration on virtue, and I greatly regretted not having been present at it.

Monday, the 22nd of August. [Latin] I too have often reflected by myself, and have also found in books things worthy of being weighed, *which is the most violent perturbation of the mind*, the one that has brought the most calamities upon men, cities,

[p. 439]

states, kingdoms? Let us see, therefore, what the desire for honor, the love of gold, pride, envy, despair, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge have brought about.

Tuesday, the 23rd of August. [Latin] Beyond doubt the *desire for honor* has brought the greatest public disasters, allied with the lust for dominion. What drove *Alexander* the Great to wage a most deadly war against Darius, by whom he had never been harmed? What *Timur*, king of Persia, who with Tartar victors, with victorious arms and immense glory ranged over Asia far and wide? What so many most distinguished leaders of the Romans, whom to enumerate would be a task of immense labor? Has not this commotion sent upon academic youth the most deadly contests, which they call *duels*, which have cut the threads of so many flourishing youths, so many only consolations and joys of parents?

Wednesday, the 24th of August. [Latin] Among barbarous and rude peoples is there any other impulse of virtue besides honor and love of fatherland, parents, wives, children? The same is established concerning our ancestors, that they laid waste immense stretches of fields and farmlands and sent to the dead an infinite number of men, in order to acquire a name for themselves not only through their neighborhood but through all Germany. So far on the desire for honor. Let us return to other things.

Here there follows in the diary an interruption until December. Hegel himself relates the cause. He had exerted himself for an examination with his health already impaired and got a swelling on the neck, which the physician Conspruch and the surgeon Mohrstadt cured.

[Latin] The 5th day before the Ides of December. I have resolved to resume now this diary, interrupted for a long interval of time by the examination held by us on the day before the Nones and on the Nones of September themselves, and most of all by the illness, both grave and lasting, which seized me, and to renew my former studies by *exercising my style*. It will therefore be pleasing to run briefly through the history of that time.

Some days before the examination, already somewhat wearied by ill health, I nevertheless did not restrain myself from going to that examination, though my teachers and others dissuaded me. That having happily been completed, I did not go beyond the threshold of our house again. Seized by a violent illness, I was nevertheless rescued by the diligence of the physician and by medicines promptly applied. I swelled greatly in the neck on the left side, all the poison and corruption of the disease having collected there. After long and much torment from this swelling, relief was brought by the art of the surgeon *Mohrstadt* and the physician *Conspruch*, of whom the former, having cut open the tumor, inflicted a wound two thumb-widths wide, so that a foul abundance of pus and blood

[p. 440]

flowed out for almost three days; which, by the diligence of the surgeon and frequent bandaging, closed up within about thirty days; for from the cutting of the wound, on the 6th day before the Nones of October, I attended the Gymnasium again on the day before the Calends of November.

[Latin] The 4th day before the Ides of December. While these things were being done with me, many other things worthy of memory happened apart from me. A most dear friend of mine was taken from us to Tübingen, one dedicated to theology, I think *J. F. Duttenhofer*. At the same span of time died that most celebrated man, the greatest ornament of our fatherland, *Moser*, who wrote so many books, as many as a human lifetime does not suffice to read through, who lived a life tossed about by so many and so various (chances). Died, distinguished in dignity and in other things which it is not fitting to relate here, *Hochsteter*. Died finally that man, illustrious in birth and wealth, *de Herzberg*.

[Latin] The 3rd day before the Ides of December. My little library too has meanwhile been increased by some books. For I bought some time ago: 1. *Livy*, from my own treasury, at the expense of four florins; 2. *Ernesti’s* Ciceronian Key [*Clavis Ciceroniana*], for a thaler; 3. *Cicero’s* Letters to Atticus, for ten kreuzer; 4. *Campe’s* Theophron, in the vernacular, for twenty-six kreuzer; 5. *Home’s* art of criticism, translated from English into the vernacular by Meinhard, for one florin and forty-five kreuzer; 6. *Seneca’s* philosophical works for fifteen kreuzer.

[Latin] The day before the Ides of December. A question having arisen today among us, whether *repetition is better than preparation* or the latter than the former, my judgment has always been that it is best for either to be joined with the other. If, however, one of the two should be lacking to the other, I for my part would hold that repetition should be preferred to preparation. For when we have prepared, we understand the matter, so to speak, only by half, and we draw out either not the whole sense or a perverse one. But when taught by the preceptor, we perceive the whole, just and genuine sense, which, repeated, is implanted in the mind almost for ever. But when we have prepared, the force of the words having been taken falsely, what the teacher has explained does not stick long unless it is repeated, and soon vanishes. Noble visitors being present today at Stuttgart, *public music* of voices, strings and horns was arranged.

[Latin] On the Ides of December itself. Today the solemn inspection of the morals and studies of the auditors of the sixth class was held, which they call *percursum*, Durchgang [passage]. Yesterday the seventh class was being examined.

[Latin] The 19th day before the Calends of January. *The annual fair* began yesterday, at which things to be given to children on the festal day on which the nativity of Christ is recalled are offered for sale. Yesterday especially, the day on which men from the country are present in greatest numbers, you could see them reeling with wine and revelling through the streets, each of whom had bought shoes or other things either for himself or for his wife or for his children; you could see

[p. 441]

countless disputes being waged here, wares being haggled over there, and many other things. — We had a holiday on these two days, of which I spent the first half in transacting business, the remaining time I devoted to leisure, jests, running about and walks. The burden now lies upon me of praying auspicious things for each of the professors on the Calends of Janus, in which task the old Latin poets, especially of the Middle Ages, provide and have provided excellent help.

[Latin] The 18th day before the Calends of January. For this winter semester I am pleased now, with my most venerable teacher and patron Herr *Hopf* especially as adviser, to take up Latin things and to work on these especially. But I vacillate and am drawn in various directions as to which classical author I should use above all. There occurred to me *Cicero’s Tusculan Questions*, which I resolved both to make German and to illustrate. But, such is juvenile inconstancy, my plan now displeases me, if less on account of the obscurity and difficulty of the Latinity, which is very far from this work, than on account of philosophy and eloquence, which, as he himself says, it seemed best to employ here.

[Latin] The 17th day before the Calends of January. It was night and, with a tranquil mind, I was sitting over a certain little book when the sound of bells, that a house in our city was *burning*, terrified us. Alas, what fear seized all! As the fire was already gaining strength, I and my father went to the aid of a certain house in the neighborhood. There you could see the house blazing all over with fire and almost already consumed by the conflagration. When we had come to that house, the flame began to die down and a little later almost to vanish, and the smoke to be borne far up to the stars. What more? Scarcely an hour had passed when the flame was extinguished, half the house consumed.

[Latin] The 16th day before the Calends of January. The cause, however, which started the fire, they vary six hundred times. Most narrate that it was lead, as they say, poured in. But here too others differ. Yet what would the review of so many rumors accomplish? Most agree, however, that the follies and trifles of the preceptor’s daughter, most unworthy of her age and station, were the cause of the fire; who, while she wished to save a certain bed, was badly burned in hair, face and clothing.

[Latin] The 12th day before the Calends of January. It was the winter solstice today and the feast day of St. *Thomas*. Now that we have borne the heaviest time of the year, this at least consoles, that now the days will be increased more and more in future. A small *concert of voices and strings* was also arranged in our house, at which Colonel *de Rau*, who lives in the upper part of our house, was present; when he departed there came Secretary *Moser* and his wife, Secretary *Günzler* and his wife, and Herr *Zoror*, brother of the two wives.

[p. 442]

[Latin] The 11th day before the Calends of January. Long since, indeed, before I was entangled in a grave illness, I began, so far as my modest talent allows, to explain the evils and goods that followed from the perturbations of the mind. Those of honor I have already set out. That many good things too followed, no one will deny, if the man who was seized by that desire sought honor from good deeds. Wherever indeed the deeds are most upright, the plans, however, if adopted through honor, you would call less upright. For right deeds, when they are accomplished from *virtue*, not from desire for one’s own gain, *are most of all to be praised*.

[Latin] The 10th day before the Calends of January. Let us now begin with the *desire for gold and wealth*, which is either sordid avarice or a dishonoring desire of acquiring money by injustice. But if the former, which I have called avarice, has taken hold of the mind, it harms others less than himself. He is the most unhappy of men, etc. The description concludes finally with the remark that the miser must also be faithless and cruel toward his own family and servants; [Latin] *yet the greatest fraud, if he is a prince’s minister*, is against the master to whom he has bound himself even by *oath* to be faithful.

[Latin] The 8th day before the Calends of January. Sunday. A day festal for our most blessed *Savior* has arisen today, on which, as is the custom, I too was favored by my father with most splendid gifts; of which, although many are most welcome, the most pleasant and useful is *Scheller’s Lexicon*, whose excellence I have already myself often perceived by use.

[Latin] On the Calends of January itself, 1786. The new year has thus dawned under the auspices of GOD. In the midst of these days I bought for myself also *Scheller’s precepts* of good Latin style, above all the Ciceronian.

[Latin] The 3rd day before the Ides of February, 1786. Let us now return to these our earlier exercises for practicing style, interrupted for a long interval of time, since today is the fifty-ninth birthday of our Most Serene Lord *the Duke*. By what chance I know not, I attended no sermon in which Chapter IX of the Wisdom of Solomon was expounded. In the afternoon I heard in the Gymnasium an oration of Professor *Schmidt*, which dealt with the merits of our Duke toward *literary affairs of Württemberg* and indeed expounded the excellences in which he had deserved well of the *University of Tübingen*; then those toward our *Gymnasium*, afterwards toward the *cloister schools*; there followed the *trivial schools* and those they call *German* ones; these were succeeded by the splendid institution of the *Academy*, at first indeed military, afterwards, the scope of this institution having been enlarged, also literary; he added finally also an institution for providing for the weaker sex, which they call a *school*, école. He closed the whole oration with ardent vows and prayers for the welfare of our Duke and his consort, now traveling.

[p. 443]

Although Hegel, with this survey of all the educational institutions then existing in Württemberg, made a new start at practicing and improving his Latin style incessantly through the stimulus of a diary, he must nevertheless either have lacked stimulating material for entries or have seen his zeal satisfied by adequate success. From now on there occur only a few more general reflections in the Latin language. One of them, from March 1786, contains the rough draft of a Latin speech on *sociability*, which he wished to deliver at the Gymnasium in the course of the summer, when the turn for such rhetorical exercise should come to him. He aims thereby to proceed as scholastically correct as possible in the arrangement and to bring in, in the execution, all the traditional ornamental phrases and transitional turns held to be Ciceronian. It would be tiresome to communicate the whole; but some points, on the advantage which association with older persons offers, on the necessity of observing the social forms, on the limits of sociability and on *association with the weaker sex*, are too characteristic of Hegel himself for them not to deserve being extracted. Moreover the Latin is really only rough-draft Latin:

“[Latin] First, then, and foremost, there accrues to those who converse with their elders the advantage that they procure for themselves the knowledge of many things. To this is added, above all, a knowledge which no one, whether he labors with some fruit for the welfare of others or does not wish to commit himself properly to the world, [can lack] without the greatest detriment — this is the knowledge of men. Let us add — a thing which in our times and customs especially cannot be dispensed with — that he will most easily learn certain rites and the art of commending oneself by outward appearance and form who has long been versed among polished and cultivated men and manners; worn, so to speak, by long familiarity with the world. For he who does not shine on the outward side is believed to labor under the same dullness of mind. — Since, then, so many benefits flow from just intercourse with other men, it is necessary that from a perverse and excessive [intercourse], if one may so say, many evils spring forth. These are: a. dissipation and distraction of the mind; b. loss of time; c. alienation and distaste for everything that requires a more serious mind, and for solitude. — I come now to the intercourse of the *weaker sex*, a reef on which many, and the most distinguished in spirit, have miserably perished. What then is to be done? Must one abstain wholly from any commerce with them? We are born, as I said, under the law that we cultivate commerce and intercourse. *But are women not human beings?* Who will contend this? We must therefore use them. But it is asked what and how great calamities

[p. 444]

follow? Is that intercourse devoid of all advantages? Far from it! On the contrary, if you use it rightly, it will offer you the greatest. For he who, as surely each of you both wants and would want, desires to be fortunate among the men who now inhabit the globe, must cast off, so to speak: *Schlacken* [dross], which nowhere can be done better and more diligently than in the society of these women. *For they have the monopoly of praise and of infamy!*”

An important reflection is contained in another passage of the diary from the same month. Hegel compares therein the religion of heathenism with the ordinary Christian faith. Since the writers of the ancients were such a rich source of intellectual and ethical culture for him, he took offense at the disparaging manner in which many treated the ancients on account of their religion. He found that what is charged against them as *superstition* is not alien to those themselves who made such reproaches. He convinced himself that the belief in *angels and devils* is only a repetition of the antique *belief in demons*. He abhorred the consequences which must result from such a representation for the *freedom of man*. He recognized the divine dignity of man in this, that he is himself responsible for his good and evil deeds.

[Latin] The 5th day before the Ides of March, 1786. Often, as I think about our enlightened times, it also occurs to my mind that reproaches and *mockeries* are often hurled by us against the various errors of the pagans and in general against the customs of all the ancients and the opinions confirmed by antiquity. What now recurs to my mind concerning them I shall commit to the pen in a few words. In the explanation of the history of the Gods and of mythology as a whole I heard, when the ancients were being mocked, about their superstition, since they believed that two genii presided over them, one good, the other evil; that these meet in perpetual conflict; and that if the good overcame the evil, things are well thought and done by man; if on the contrary the evil conquered and dominated man, depraved things both occur to the mind and the man breaks forth into wickedly done acts. Deliberating whether the opinion of our own age were the same, I found that very many assign all things well thought and done to divine powers, wickedly done to the powers of the devil. Everyone will see that these opinions of the two ages differ little from one another. Add that, although one devil is said always to lie in wait for the whole human race and for each single one, yet this increases the similarity, that one upright man is believed to have one or more angels, guardians of his life and morals, who withdraw from wicked men. If perchance some man of the common people has committed something against the laws, they think to wash away his guilt in some part by this, that they say God withdrew from him and permitted that he should fall,

[p. 445]

But that is the providence of divine goodness. It is indeed, but it would conflict with the design by which He formed men. For He willed that there should not be lacking in the chain of the universe of things a certain link, which should stand between the beasts — who, compelled by the iron bonds of instinct and lacking the liberty [to decide] whether they choose good or evil, do nothing by their own counsel — and that ethereal race of angels, who, alien to all evil, accomplish only what is right. There was left therefore to man the middle place between these, to whose entire discretion it is given whether he choose good or evil.

I have seen many of the Christians deride a like error. For the pagans believed that the wrath of the Gods is appeased by fasts, and by food and drink set before God. Let us refer this to our own times. In many rites I have seen the same superstition still persist, as in funeral rites and others among the more enlightened Lutherans. But among the Catholics it flourishes entire to this day. In this alone they differ. The pagans set their own foods before the Gods themselves; if the priests devoured them, they thought they had been eaten by the Gods. Today it is not so. For these superstitious little men hand over money, victuals and other things to the priests and thereby hunt after the favor of God. But what greater, what more horrible superstition or folly has there been?

On 18 March there follows a moral reflection on *anger*, which Hegel does not wish to admit even in regard to infamous deeds: [Latin] it is not necessary to be carried away into anger; it is enough to *grieve* over crimes and to bear them with distress. Finally on 22 March he concludes: [Latin] if anyone has learned so far to command *himself* that he is moved to anger by nothing, let him be *permitted* to be angry at crimes! — Immediately afterward he writes: “All human beings have the intention of making themselves *happy*, with a few rare exceptions who, in order to make others happy, possessed so much sublimity of soul as to *sacrifice themselves*. Yet these, I believe, have not sacrificed true blessedness, but only temporal advantages, temporal happiness, also life. These therefore make no exception here.” —

Then there follows, without beginning and end, a fragment on *enlightenment* through science and art, from which the following remarks must not be passed over: “To make a draft of an *enlightenment of the common man* I hold partly for most, even the most learned people, very difficult, partly however also *especially for me* much harder, since I have in general *not yet studied history philosophically* and thoroughly. Otherwise I believe that this enlightenment of the common man has always oriented itself according to the *religion of its time*. — With regard to the sciences and arts I am therefore of the opinion that they flourished first in the Orient and then migrated from there more and more toward the West.

[p. 446]

Much as one nowadays, *at least in respect of philosophy*, rightly avoids the *great praise* of the learning of the *Egyptians*, so much at least remains certain, that in regard to the mechanical and the fine arts they brought themselves to such a degree of perfection that even now the ruins of their works of art are admired; and it is very probable that the great and extensive practical knowledge had also already been brought into a more exact theory.” —

Nothing further is found from the year 1786. With the first days of the next year he sets about a diary once more, but keeps it up for only a week. All the more necessary will be the communication of this self-portrayal. Apart perhaps from a still more decided independence, no change is to be found in his nature. The striving for scientific cultivation is always in the foreground; alongside it, however, reflection also seizes upon whatever of interest the general life presents; of himself he thinks least. His one pervasive peculiarity is the selflessness of the most objective cast of mind.

On 1 January 1787. At present I am in the first year in the seventh class of the local Gymnasium. My chief concerns are still the languages, and indeed really Greek and Latin. Besides that I work now and then a little in mathematics. Apart from the public lessons I attend a lecture course with Professor *Hopf*, in which we devote 3 hours to *Longinus* and one hour to the *Duties* of *Cicero*. Of the manner in which we read them it is unnecessary to say anything. Some time I also give to the working out of small essays and to *writing down my thoughts*. On Sundays I work mostly at *spherical trigonometry*, and in part I devote them to good friends. Remaining quarter-hours I really fill out with reading and excerpting *Heyne’s* excursuses to his *Virgil*. In the forenoon I began to go through a little of the spherical trigonometry that I had copied out of *Lorentzen’s* Mathematics. But I was soon interrupted by visits that came to wish a happy New Year, and afterwards I had to go out on like errands. In the afternoon I meant only to read a little in *Sophie’s Journey*, but I could never tear myself away from it until the evening, when I went to the *concert*. For it is the custom that every New Year deputies from Esslingen present the Duke, under the title of *protection money*, with 100 ducats, whereupon each time a concert is arranged in the Academy. Of this one could, to be sure, hear little because of

[p. 447]

the din of the many listeners, but the time was nevertheless made very pleasantly short for me by my speaking there with good friends whom I had not seen for a long time. The *sight of beautiful girls* also contributed not a little to our conversation.

Tuesday, the 2nd of January. As usual; in the evening I excerpted from Heyne’s excursuses.

Wednesday, the 3rd of January. This night there was a total *lunar eclipse*. Professor *Hopf* equipped some telescopes at the Gymnasium for observation, from the new apparatus of instruments. Some came, but the completely overcast sky did not let one see the least thing. The Rector, illuminated [tipsy], told us among other things: he too, as a Gymnasium pupil, had been an observer with others and had gone *stellatum* by night. They had only been roaming about. Town philistines came along, who wanted to haul them in. The Gymnasium pupils said: they had gone *stellatum*. Oh, said the soldiers, they should lie in their beds by night and go *stellatum* by day.

Thursday, the 4th of January. 1–2 I visited *Haug*, son of the court instrument-maker here, where I saw a clock that played excellently in the tone of a transverse flute. — 4–5 and 6–7 I excerpted from Heyne’s excursuses; otherwise everything went as usual.

Friday, the 5th of January. From 9 to 10 I excerpted from a part of the *Allgemeine Deutsche Bibliothek* [General German Library] the *editions of Demosthenes*. From 10 to 11 I visited *Griesinger*, the son of the consistory councillor. There I saw the *Atlas coelestis* [celestial atlas] of *Mayer* and the whole library of the consistory councillor; I also borrowed from it the second part of *Kästner’s* Mathematics. In the afternoon I read and excerpted from a part of the *Allgemeine Deutsche Bibliothek*. 5–6 there was a lecture course on Longinus, on account of the holiday on the following day. After dinner I read in Kästner’s Mathematics.

Saturday, the 6th of January. The forenoon until half past ten I devoted to trigonometry. Afterwards I visited Professor *Hopf* on account of an obscure passage in Kästner’s Mathematics (II, 1765, p. 159). I was of the opinion that the poles of a circle always stand a quadrant away from all points of the circumference of the circle. But from that it would follow that only great circles of a sphere could have poles. Professor *Hopf* himself accepted this proposition. Only afterwards, however, did the error occur to me, and then I helped myself. — In the afternoon I visited *Steinkopf*, who renders his grandfather, the antiquary *Betulius*, who is beginning to grow old, quite good service everywhere

[p. 448]

and bears the greatest part of his many burdensome labors. — In the evening we played the *geographical card game*, which is almost the same as tarok, except that the latter has more variety and penalties; the former also has no tarocs, no Skiß, no Bagatt. — After dinner I studied spherical trigonometry, which no longer seems to me as hard as it appeared as long as I had not yet done anything in it.

Sunday, the 7th of January. Forenoon trigonometry. After dinner the beautiful sky enticed me to go for a walk. I followed the attraction and took myself a healthy exercise of several hours. On the way I met countless pedestrians, riders, and travelers in carriages. In the evening I visited *Leypold* in the Academy. All the remaining time, in the afternoon and after supper, I devoted to trigonometry.

II.

#### Writings from the Gymnasium Years.

1. On Excipiring. 2. Conversation among Three. 3. On the Religion of the Greeks and Romans. 4. On Some Characteristic Differences of the Ancient Poets.

#### *On Excipiring.*

March 1786.

“Since the so-called excipiring, the writing down of a theme in a language other than the one in which the theme is composed, is on the one hand vigorously defended and retained by many, partly teachers, partly others, and on the other hand rejected and banished by just as many, I will, so far as my insight extends, examine the grounds that are usually advanced in its defense.

A. I have heard some say that one attains by it an easy and flowing style, since many young people in translations, for which they have leisure, overreach themselves and become bombastic. This ground may have some probability for many. And certainly one does not easily fall into bombast in excipiring. But consider whether this so-called flowing Latin, whether it is really *such flowing* Latin. I understand by this a rhythmical and periodic

[p. 449]

style, wholly according to nature, which does not fall into the contrived and the bombastic. Now survey all the rules of a rhythmical, periodic, and simple manner of writing, and consider whether even the most practiced can observe them in excipiring. Consider the complete dissimilarity of German and other languages; in the excipiation one will for the most part find German constructions, connectives, and the very same sequence of sentences in the excipired language. — But what is to blame, then, that young people fall into the craving to write bombastic Latin? Among many causes this is perhaps to be noted as the original source, namely the manner in which one reads the most excellent writings of the ancients. By virtue of this one should believe that they are of use for nothing except to learn their language from them, and to learn their language again for nothing further except that one simply knows it. For one takes account quite solely and merely of the words and phrases, not at all of their spirit and nature. Of subject matter there is no talk at all. If one now reads such an author, there are many who diligently work up every phrase, be it from a writer who is an orator, a historian, or a philosopher; he may write naturally, artificially, obscurely, etc. Everything is mixed together. A rhetorical phrase by which a subject, for the sake of clarity, for the sake of antithesis, in order to derive a proof from it, has been circumscribed, is then brought into a historical, trifling matter. So it stands in Livy IV, 3, where Canuleius wants to represent quite clearly the unfair and unjust conduct of the patricians toward the plebeians, since these are just like those Roman citizens, the circumlocution for “fellow citizen”: [Latin] that we are their fellow citizens, and, though we do not have the same means, inhabit the same fatherland; and, shortly before: [Latin] unworthy that you should dwell with them in the same city within the same walls. Just so the rhetorical circumlocution for “they begrudge you life”: [Latin] they would take from you a share of this light, if they could; they are indignant that you breathe, that you utter a voice, that you have the forms of men — and so many thousand others. Now it has been said that these phrases are beautiful. The young people are praised when they bring in many of them in the next exercise, and now they think of nothing more than to circumscribe each single word by the greatest phrase. Whether it stands in the right or the wrong place, that is not looked to, but one measures it by length. The biggest are the best, and so arise bombast and fustian. The natural and genuine in the language is entirely neglected.

B. One acquires by it a facility, so that words and expressions become familiar and occur quickly. But the question is whether by such hurrying the reflection and the choice of words

[p. 450]

are not rather hindered. With familiar words it indeed takes not much reflection. But with less familiar ones, I believe, it does. If one does not yet have the phrase or the word and the dictating goes on, one should hurry too. But one cannot, one falters, and — either one leaves a blank space, or one becomes unwilling, and in unwillingness one is notoriously incapable of reflection. But if with difficult texts one leaves no gap at all, then the excipiation is either good or bad. If it is good, then one has certainly acquired this facility not through excipiring, but through frequent reading of the source itself and slow composing. If it is mediocre or bad, then tell me, to what use is such a wretched scribbling mania? There are people who know how to answer all questions, if only these answers consist of words, be they false, shallow, or hasty, or even absurd. So it is in excipiring, whereas I far prefer to the above those who answer, to be sure, not at once, but all the more circumspectly and cleverly. Just so a little slowness in composing pleases me better than a great haste in excipiring. By the former our style and the whole facility in a language become riper, more considered, and more in keeping with its spirit. And through circumspect practice one attains to a greater speed, and finally to one such as the best excipist, who from the very beginning never worked slowly, will never reach. And this consists in this: *writing quickly and at the same time well*.

C. From excipiring, it is said, one can judge the strength in a language. Now the question is what kind of strength one understands by that. Can one see critical strength from it? Let us here look at *Gesner’s* explanation of *criticism* and then judge, not whether one acquires a strength in it through excipiring, but only whether it lets itself be seen from it?
