For he explains it as a faculty of judging, which one obtains through the longest intercourse with the ancients, not only what the sense of the words is, but chiefly whether a whole book, a whole treatise, a formula, indeed even a single word really comes from the ancient to whom it is ascribed. One sees at once that this facility has not the slightest similarity to excipiring and cannot be judged from it. A good critic will indeed always use the words and expressions that actually express what is dictated, but he who has excipiring done is commonly a bad critic or none at all, and can prefer to such an excipiation a worse but more phrase-rich one. Yet this case really does not belong here, for a critic is

[p. 451]

no boy, and no youth any more. No, they are mostly grown men, and these one will hopefully not judge by excipiring. — Just as little, I believe, will one be able to judge the strength that one has acquired through *philosophical study of languages*, or the strength that one has attained in a language for the sake of its true utility, i.e. in order to acquire factual knowledge. Yet to this kind too belongs what we said of the preceding. — There remains to us still one kind of strength in a language. For it can still be seen from excipiring whether someone has gathered a store of words, whether he has acquired the facility of putting a Latin garment on German words and sentences, which is, however, by far not yet a Roman one. Now, this I will grant, and it is true; since from construing, where the context and the advantage that German is our mother tongue more readily put the meaning of the words into our hands, one cannot so judge the strength in the words. But to acquire this strength excipiring will certainly be of little help. Repeated reading of the books written in this language, also translating, are the means for this.

What I have said here in general about excipiring holds of all kinds of excipiring, from Latin, German, etc. Only it is more humane in the one language than in the other, namely where composing still has use and which is, at least among the learned, still a living language.

#### Conversation among Three.

1785. 30 May.

*Antonius.* Have you thought over the plan which I laid before you? Are you now resolved?

*Octavius.* I have taken it into consideration and pondered it well. Should the execution proceed as happily as the plan is wisely and cleverly arranged, something glorious would come to pass.

*Lepidus.* I have found it just so.

*Octavius.* But how? Now let us also determine the details of it and trace out the hindrances that will lie in our way.

*Antonius.* After long reflection I have found no particular difficulties.

*Octavius.* But I have. I will lay them before you. Will the

[p. 452]

free Romans consent thus to our rule? Will Brutus, will Cassius, will the others who helped kill the noble Caesar, be quiet about it? Will Sextus Pompeius let himself be satisfied?

*Antonius.* Oh! Octavius, no such scruples! Believe me, I have lived longer in the world, I have more experience than you. Do you believe that in these men a spark of love of fatherland still glows? By no means. Through luxury and debauchery they are so far debased from the greatness of soul of their forefathers that they no longer care at all about freedom. Only recently, after Caesar’s murder, when Brutus and Cassius had just before stood on the speaker’s platform and had so inflamed them to hatred against the great Julius that they would almost have laid hands, in their rage, on his sacred corpse, how much eloquence did I need to tune their tone differently! How like feathers they let themselves be blown to and fro! The soldier is already accustomed to shedding the blood of citizens just as well as of enemies, and him we have indeed on our side. With the low rabble it is done with few words, a little grain or money, and public spectacles.

*Lepidus.* This article I will see to.

*Octavius.* You are perfectly right, Antonius. One scruple is now removed. But a Brutus, a Cassius, is far above the sphere of the rabble.

*Antonius.* Oh, they have lost all weight, all love, all standing through Caesar’s murder and my speech. The people are indeed on our side. What can they therefore undertake? And up to now they are quiet.

*Octavius.* Scarcely four hours ago I received letters that they are arming quite secretly for a defense, because they fear something from us. I meant to bring you the news at once, but you were neither on the Capitol nor at home.

*Antonius.* I was on my country estate. But that Brutus and Cassius are arming for war causes me no such great anxiety. We are as good warriors as they. Only we must be on our guard, unite our forces, and for that reason summon our legates and tribunes together at once.

*Octavius.* But there is yet, besides these, a multitude of enemies who indeed let friendliness show in the face, but in the heart on the contrary conceal poisonous daggers. These should be cleared out of the way.

*Antonius.* Right, my Octavius. We have, after all, already in

[p. 453]

the last assembly spoken of it, named most of them, and sworn them death. Here I have written them down. Read it through.

*Octavius* (reads it through and suddenly exclaims:) Cicero too?

*Antonius.* Yes, Octavius. We resolved in the last assembly to leave it free to each to say whom he would gladly have sent to the realm of the dead. Cicero was my mortal enemy. His speeches and letters prove it only too well. And Lepidus has indeed even given you his brother.

*Lepidus.* Yes, that I have.

*Octavius.* My given word I can never take back, but the man pains me extraordinarily.

*Antonius.* Here, Lepidus, read it through yourself too. My uncle Lucius is also, at your desire, among the condemned. There is thus an equilibrium among us. Each has sacrificed to our common weal a man who grieves him. But let us now turn to another subject, namely the division of the lands.

*Octavius.* This point we shall, it seems to me, let rest for now. Only after the subjugation of Brutus and Cassius shall we settle it. But we must think seriously of counter-measures against these enemies.

*Antonius.* I should think you and I should leave Rome, gather our army, and then fall upon them in their provinces. Lepidus can secure the city. Do you approve?

*Octavius.* Yes, entirely.

*Lepidus.* I too. I will therefore go at once and take the necessary measures. (Lepidus exits.)

*Antonius.* So! Now you are gone, simpleton. Now I will speak more freely with you alone, Octavius. Shall we let this barren head share some day in the rule of the world?

*Octavius.* You yourself drew him into this alliance. Now it will hardly be changed any more. I think he has nonetheless shown himself in many places a brave soldier.

*Antonius.* Believe my words, I have come to know him. The man has no merits of his own, no mental capacities. He can only deliver commissions skillfully. Like a dead machine he must be set in motion by others. Believe me, had he not had powerful friends, it would never have come into my mind to take him on. Now we need him, but, I think, once we are at the goal of our career, see ourselves secure enough, we shall at once relieve him of his undeserved honorary office, fatten him with the stubble,

[p. 454]

or do away with him altogether, and we consume the ears which he has planted and harvested for us.

*Octavius.* I leave this to your discretion. Of what lies further in this matter we will speak only after the happy completion of our plans. — But now, Antonius, we must look to ourselves. Nearer and more terrible storms are gathering over our heads. Let us therefore put ourselves in all haste in good order, so that we can defy with courage the breaking, soon raging storm.

*Antonius.* Yes, that we will do. Until our departure I have still some things to put in order. This evening we shall perhaps speak again. Meanwhile farewell. (Exits.)

#### *Octavius* alone.

Imbecility went off first, and then arrogance after it. What Antonius said of Lepidus is indeed not at all false, but Antonius is proud, domineering, voluptuous, cruel. Once our enemies are defeated and Lepidus put aside, Antonius, proud of his deeds and experience, will want to lead me around, as a younger man, at his pleasure. But in me he will find no Lepidus. My unservile neck is not accustomed to bow under the condescending glances of a ruler. He will wallow in pleasures. I shall allow it for a long time and be quiet about it. But when his powers of body and soul are slackened and he stands in contempt, then at last I will raise my head, show myself to him in my greatness, and then — *aut Caesar, aut nihil* [either Caesar or nothing]. Either he shall humble himself before me in the dust, or I shall prefer death to an ignominious life! (Exits.)

#### On the Religion of the Greeks and Romans.

1787. 10 August.

As for the religion of the Greeks and Romans, they went in this the way of all nations. — The thought of a deity is so natural to man that it has developed among all peoples. In their childhood, in the primal state of nature, they thought of God as an almighty being who governs them and everything merely according to caprice. They formed their representation of him after the rulers they knew, the fathers and princes of families, who disposed of the life and death of their subordinates entirely at pleasure, whom they obeyed in everything, even in unjust and inhuman commands, blindly, and who, as

[p. 455]

human beings, could be angry, act rashly, and repent something. Just so they thought their deity, and the representations of the greatest part of the people of our so-celebrated enlightened times are not otherwise constituted. Misfortune, physical and moral evil, they regarded as a punishment from it, and concluded that they must have offended it and earned its wrath, knowingly or unknowingly, by actions that displease it. This they now sought to appease by gifts, by the best that they had, by first-fruits, indeed by the dearest thing, their children. These people did not yet see that those evils are no real evils, that fortune and misfortune depend on themselves, that the deity never sends misfortune to the harm of its creatures. Nor did they consider that the supreme being is not won by gifts from men, that men can as little increase as diminish his riches, his power, and his honor. — But how were they to bring him those sacrifices? Because they saw that only things dissolved in smoke rise to the clouds, because they supposed that he dwelt there, they let the gifts intended for him evaporate in fire up to him. This is the origin of sacrifices, which among the Greeks and Romans, as among the Israelites, made up a chief part of divine worship. Human beings, who can think everything only under sensuous representations, soon made themselves bodily images of the deity from clay, wood, or stone, each according to the ideal he had of the most fearful being; hence the hideous shapes and figures of the gods among crude peoples without feeling for the beautiful and without arts. Of necessity each had to give his god also a particular name.

When now several tribes united for a common purpose or were otherwise mixed, each kept his god. But to make the union firmer, they let their particular deities too enter into a society and set them all up together in One place, where the whole people worshiped in common. — Greece and Rome had their Pantheon and each city again its own tutelary god. That these nations were a mixture of so many kinds of peoples is the chief cause of their many deities and of the so different legends and stories of them. Polytheism was also occasioned thereby; since they did not consider the power of the deity, limited according to their concepts, mighty enough to rule alone the whole compass of the All, they assigned the government of an element, certain functions, etc., to a particular deity. They also personified, no doubt, the elements, countries, and

[p. 456]

other great objects, and ascribed their effects and alterations to them themselves as freely acting beings. It is equally well known that they transported deserving heroes after their death into the abode of the gods and venerated them like these. This great confusion in mythology was enlarged still much more by the efforts of the learned to find out the meaning of each fable. For the setting up of the images of the gods special places were chosen and temples built, which all received great sanctity, because it was believed that the god dwelt here. Heights and groves were without doubt chosen for this most gladly, because even their aspect has something sublime and their seeming nearness to heaven could most readily be a dwelling of the gods; partly also because the soul of a solitary, vividly sensing man is nowhere so much enraptured as at a splendid prospect into the distance, where one surveys at once a great piece of the beautiful creation, or as in the still, dusky woods, and there he raves and believes that he really has apparitions and sees a deity.

A man full of fear on account of something interprets all circumstances with reference to it and is put into terror by everything. So too those people without enlightenment, with a lively imagination, full of the fear of their god and firm in the belief that he works all alterations in nature immediately and thereby makes his will known to them, declared all unexpectedly occurring incidents to be such disclosures. A superstitious Greek therefore did not go over the road if a weasel had leapt past him; he asked an interpreter of signs for advice if a mouse had gnawed his meal-sack. Even in our days one prophesies from a comet the end of life of a monarch and from the cry of an owl the near death of a man.

Herewith was joined still the desire of men to look into the destinies of the future. They believed that the gods, on whom they indeed depend, might quite well lift the curtain a little for them and foretell by certain signs, or let proclaim in advance through men who stand in closer intercourse with them.

All these inclinations now the shrewder and craftier men, whom one had chosen for the service of the deity, noticed. They saw that the peoples let themselves be led by nothing so willingly as by religion. As they now could draw advantage from nothing so much, satisfy their desires and passions or also work for the common good, as through the use of this docility, they strengthened those drives, fettered the imagination, and gave it, in a certain direction, nourishment and occupation through aimed-at and accumulated

[p. 457]

sensuous ceremonies. Against all assaults of reason they armed themselves thereby, in that they combined religion with all their actions and in this way sanctified them. The images of the gods they withdrew in part from the general view and onrush of the multitude, and through this mystery gave them a greater dignity and loftiness, and gave the imagination freer play. Through the oracles the priests had influence in all important affairs. They were also in Greece one of the bonds by which the so jealous and disunited states were held together and bound to a common interest.

Thus the religions of all peoples arose, so too the religion of the Greeks and Romans. Only when a nation had attained a certain stage of culture could men of enlightened reason appear among them, attain better concepts of the deity, and communicate them to others. From this period date also most of the writings which we have remaining from antiquity. The earlier ones are important to us from this side at least on account of the history of mankind. They constantly call upon us to revere a providence and to obey its, to be sure, not arbitrary commands, by which it wisely guides everything and is kind and beneficent. Correct concepts of the condition of the whole folk religion, however, cannot be drawn exactly from their poets. They treated the religion and the history of the gods as poets, each according to his purpose; only the general opinions they had to lay at the base. And this folk belief about the attributes and the government of providence was nearly at all times alike. The rabble of all peoples ascribes to the deity sensuous and human attributes and believes in arbitrary rewards and punishments. These opinions are, moreover, the strongest bridle of their passions; the grounds of reason and of a purer religion are not effective enough against them.

The sages of Greece, on the other hand, and their pupils show us in their writings much more enlightened and sublime concepts of the deity, especially with respect to the destinies of men. They taught that it gives each sufficient means and powers for his happiness and has so laid out the nature of things that through wisdom and moral goodness true happiness is attained. — In these principles most then agreed; only in their speculations about the primal being of the deity and other things incomprehensible to man have they, to be sure, devised very different systems. Considered from these points of view, there is shown to us in the concepts of the

[p. 458]

religion, of which I have, by the way, cited only some, much that will no longer seem so incomprehensible or ridiculous, if we consider that men with the same faculties as we, in the development of these, through their unequal cultivation and oblique direction, strayed upon such errors.

The manifold striving of these men to investigate the truth convinces us of the *difficulty of attaining to the pure truth, undisfigured by errors*, and shows how man often remains standing halfway to it, often ventures farther, often strays from the right path, often, blinded by a deceptive figure, snatches a shadow-image instead of reality. The failed as well as the successful endeavors are for us already made experiences, which we, without being exposed to the dangers, can use, collect and employ the good from them, and avoid the by-ways.

From their history we learn how usual it is, through habit and long prescription, to hold, in the case of certain representations, the greatest nonsense for reason, disgraceful follies for wisdom. *This should make us attentive to our inherited and transmitted opinions, to examine even those against which neither doubt nor suspicion ever came into our mind: they can perhaps be wholly false or only half true.* It should awaken us from the slumber and inactivity that so often make us indifferent toward the most important truths. — If these experiences have taught us to hold it possible, indeed *probable*, that many of our convictions are perhaps errors, and many of those of another who thinks differently perhaps truths, we shall not hate him, not judge him uncharitably. We know how easy it is to fall into errors, and shall therefore rarely ascribe these to malice and ignorance, and thus become ever more just and humane toward others.

#### On Some Characteristic Differences of the Ancient Poets.

1788. 7 August.

The introduction, which presents cultural-historical views that had meanwhile become general, can be passed over, but the remainder is, as Hegel’s first more comprehensive utterance on an *aesthetic* subject, remarkable not only for the history of his formation but also in and for itself. After Hegel has spoken of the union of the universal

[p. 459]

interest of mankind with local interest among the ancients, and of the favor thence arising for the poet, he continues:

“In our times the poet no longer has so extensive a sphere of influence. The famous deeds of our ancient, and also more recent, Germans are neither interwoven with our constitution, nor is their memory preserved by oral transmission. Only from the history books, in part of foreign nations, do we get to know them, and even this knowledge is confined to the more polished ranks. The fairy tales that entertain the common people are adventurous traditions that have connection neither with our religious system nor with true history. Moreover, the concepts and the culture of the ranks are too different for a poet of our time to be able to promise himself to be generally understood and read. Our great German epic poet has therefore not brought the wise choice of his subject into as many hands as would have happened if our public relations were Greek. One part has already removed itself from the system on which partly the whole poem, partly the individual parts are built; the others are occupied by the cares for the so multiplied needs and comforts of life too much for them to get time and desire to raise themselves and approach the concepts of the higher ranks. — What interests us is the art of the poet, no longer the matter itself, which often makes the opposite impression. —

A particularly striking property of the works of the ancients is what we call *simplicity*, which one rather feels than can distinguish distinctly. It consists really in this, that the writers present to us the image of the matter faithfully, that they do not seek to make it more interesting by subtle side-touches, by learned allusions, or more brilliant and charming by a small deviation from the truth, as we demand today. Every feeling, even a composite one, they express only simply, without separating the manifold in it, which the understanding can distinguish, and without dissecting the obscure.

Further, since the whole system of their education and culture was so constituted that each had acquired his ideas from experience itself, and

the cold book-learning, which itself / with dead signs only presses into the brain,

had not known, but with everything that they knew could also say:

[p. 460]

How? Where? Why? they had learned it;

so each had to have a form of his own spirit and a system of thought of his own, so they had to be *original*. We learn from our youth up the current stock of words and signs of ideas, and they rest in our head without activity and without use. Only little by little through experience do we get to know our treasure and think something with the words, which, however, are for us already as it were forms after which we model our ideas and which already have their determinate extent and limitation and relations, after which we are accustomed to see everything. — On this is founded, by the way, a chief advantage that the *learning of foreign languages* has, that we now comprehend the concepts generally, now learn to separate them. From that manner of cultivating oneself in our times it comes about that in many people the *series* of self-gathered ideas and learned words run *alongside one another*, without having combined into One system, often without even touching or engaging with one another anywhere.

Something else characteristic is that the poets depicted especially the outer appearances of visible nature, falling upon the senses, with which they were intimately acquainted, whereas we are better informed about the *inner play of forces* and in general know more the causes of things than how they look. With them each learned the occupations of other ranks by himself, without having otherwise had the intention of learning them. Hence the technical terms had by no means become common. To designate the fine shadings in the alteration of visible nature we have indeed also words, but they have become current only in the low language or provincial. — In general one sees it at once in all works of the ancients that they gave themselves up calmly to the course of their representations and made their works *without regard to a public*; whereas with ours it strikes the eye that they were written by their authors with the consciousness that one would read them, and as it were with the representation as if they were conversing with their readers.

We see likewise that in the forms of poems still in use circumstances gave to the genius of the first great inventors the direction. Nowhere is this influence shown so much as in the history of *dramatic* poetry. Tragedy has its origin in crude festivities arranged in honor of Bacchus, which were accompanied with song and dance (Tib. II, 157; Horatii *ars poetica*

[p. 461]

v. 220). From the reward it received the name. They were at first interrupted by only One person, who told old stories of the gods. Aeschylus first introduced two persons, made a proper stage, instead of which one had previously made use of a hut (σκηνή) of branches, which, in order to be able to represent several scenes, was divided into several chambers. The spectator then had to wander from one to another. This the following poets avoided in the arrangement of a proper stage through the unity of place, which rule they only seldom sacrificed to greater beauties (as Sophocles in the Ajax, v. 815 ff.). From its first actual creator the language, too, received its solemn dignity, which has always distinguished it since. It is clear from this how the particular form of Greek tragedy, chiefly the peculiarity of the chorus, arose. Had the Germans refined themselves gradually without foreign culture, their spirit would doubtless have taken another course and would have German plays of its own, instead of our having borrowed the form from the Greeks. — Their comedy had a like origin, from the dirty farces (φαλλικά) of the country people, the Fescennines of the Romans (Aristot. ars poët. Cap. II, κεφ. 4. Horat. Epist. II, Ep. 1, v. 139 ff. and Wieland’s note thereon). Nature herself taught the crudest men a kind of wild poetry, out of which art then gradually made what among refined peoples is called poetry. Among the Athenians, of whom Juvenal says: [Latin] the nation is a comedian, this genre must particularly have made its fortune, whereas the serious Romans could have no feeling for fine comedy.

Only these two kinds of dramatic poetry did the ancients know. Some hybrid kinds, into which one fell in order to yield to the over-refined taste of the spectators (κατ᾽ εὐχὴν ποιοῦντες τοῖς θεαταῖς; Aristot. ars poët. VII, κεφ. 13), seem not to have maintained themselves long.” —

The conclusion, which rounds off into a eulogy of the perfection of the Greeks, can be omitted here.

[p. 462]

#### III.

#### Fragments toward a Critique of Theology from the Tübingen Period and the Theses of the Theological Dissertation.

#### Fragments toward a Critique of Theology from the Tübingen Period.

“Since religion is in general a matter of the heart, it could be a question how far reasoning may intrude if it is to remain religion. If one thinks much about the origin of the sensations, about the practices one has to take part in, by which pious feelings are supposed to be awakened, about their historical origin, their expediency, and the like, they certainly lose something of the nimbus of holiness with which we have always been accustomed to see them, just as the dogmas of theology lose their authority when we illuminate them with church history. But how little such cold reflection affords a man, we see often when he comes into situations where the despair of a torn heart often grasps again for what once afforded him comfort and what he now embraces all the more firmly and anxiously. — *Wisdom* is not science. Wisdom is an elevation of the soul which, through experience combined with reflection, has raised itself above dependence on opinions as well as on the impressions of sensuousness, and which, necessarily, if it is to be practical wisdom, not mere self-complacent or boastful wisdom, must be accompanied by a quiet warmth, a gentle fire. It reasons little. Nor has it proceeded *methodo mathematica* [by the mathematical method] from concepts and, through a series of syllogisms such as *Barbara* and *Baroco*, arrived at what it holds to be true. It has not bought its conviction in the general market, where knowledge is handed out to everyone who pays properly. — Cultivation of the understanding and its application to objects that draw our interest upon themselves, enlightenment, remains on that account a fine advantage, as does a distinct knowledge of duties, i.e. enlightenment about practical truths. But they stand infinitely back in worth against goodness and purity of the heart; they are with it properly incommensurable.” —

“*Cheerfulness* is in the character of a well-disposed youth a chief trait. If circumstances prevent him from it, he must withdraw more into himself, he forms the resolve to cultivate himself into a virtuous man, and if in this he does not yet have experience enough that

[p. 463]

books cannot make him so, he perhaps takes *Campe’s Theophron* (which Hegel had already read at the Gymnasium) in hand, in order to make these teachings of wisdom and prudence the guideline of his life. He reads morning and evening a section of it and thinks all day long about it. What will be the consequence? Perhaps knowledge of men, practical prudence? Real perfecting? That requires years of practice and experience. But the meditation on Campe and on the Campean ruler will become irksome to him in eight days. Gloomy and anxious he goes into society, where only he is welcome who knows how to cheer it up. Timidly he enjoys a pleasure that tastes good only to him who is with a cheerful heart in it. Penetrated by the feeling of his imperfection, he bows before everybody. Intercourse with womenfolk does not cheer him up, because he fears that the slightest touch of some girl might pour a kindling fire through his veins. And all this gives him an awkward, stiff appearance. He will not endure it long, however, but soon shakes off the supervision of this sullen house tutor and will fare better for it.”

“If enlightenment is to achieve what its great panegyrists claim for it, if it is to deserve its praises, then it is true wisdom. Otherwise it commonly remains pseudo-wisdom, which puffs itself up and exalts itself over its *manières* [manners], which it imagines it has over many weak brethren. This conceit is commonly found among the wise youths or men who through writings attain new insights and begin to give up their previous faith, which they shared with most of those around them, whereby vanity often has a particularly large share. He who has much to say of the incomprehensible stupidity of men; who demonstrates to one down to a hair how it is the greatest folly that a people should have such prejudices; who thereby throws about him constantly with such words as: *enlightenment*, *knowledge of men*, *history of mankind*, *happiness*, *perfection* — is nothing more than a chatterer of enlightenment, who offers stale universal medicines for sale. They feed one another with bare words and overlook the holy, delicate web of human feeling. Everyone will perhaps have heard such examples chattering around him; many a one has perhaps experienced it in himself, for in our fully written-over times such a course of culture is very frequent.”

“*On the difference of the scene of death.* The whole life of the Christian is to be a preparation for this change.

[p. 464]

His wishes even are directed to it. The daily intercourse with the images of death and the hopes of that life, against which the enjoyments and joys of this world, to which he is not attached, in which he, like a stranger, takes only a slight share, are worth no attention, is to make the leaving of this theater of his activity not only not fearful to him, but even agreeable. Still less than the moment of death is terrible to him, he is afraid neither of annihilation, of the cessation of the harmony, if the instrument were broken, nor of a future fate. His whole life was a *meditatio mortis* [meditation on death]. It seems to him only a preparatory school for the future. What after all are fifty to eighty years, spent for it, against the boundless eternity? The whole duration of our existence is against this only a moment. Who could in sixty years forget the dreadful alternative: *eternal bliss, eternal damnation*? Who should not, against the ever newly awakening fear of unworthiness of the former, flee to the means of grace offered by the very doctrine that makes us acquainted with these terrors? Who should not, at the moment of this fearful catastrophe, where he not only takes leave of everything that was in any way dear to him, but where in a few hours or minutes he will never again see the splendor of this sun — but will see shimmer the throne of the judge, before which his fate for eternity is decided, who should not for this anxious moment gather all the weapons of comfort around him? Who, at least, should not even then, in haste, like one who suddenly has a journey to undertake, still pack up of spiritual equipment what time and illness permit? Hence we see the beds of the sick surrounded by clergy and friends, who groan out to the oppressed soul of the dying man the printed and prescribed sighs. Hence we hear in all remembrance and admonition, by way of conclusion, the refrain of the *Memento mori* [remember that you must die] fetched as the mightiest of all motives from beyond the grave: to die beautifully and piously, to have presence of mind still, to be able now to recall the sayings and rhymes learned with sweat at school, etc. — The *heroes* of all nations die in like manner, for they have lived and in their life have learned to acknowledge the power of nature. But *Unlittigkeit* [impatience] (an excellent Swabian provincialism, which in this period of Hegel’s occurs also as an adjective) toward these, toward their slight evils, makes one also unskilled in bearing their greater effects. How else could it come about that peoples in whose religion preparation for death is a chief point

[p. 465]

*die so unmanly*? Whereas other nations see this moment approach unconcerned. As, for a meal, one man begins early in the morning to have his hair curled, puts on his finery, has his horses harnessed, and, full of the importance of the impending undertaking, deliberates the whole time how he is to conduct himself, how he is to carry on the conversation; another, on the contrary, goes about his business in the morning and remembers the invitation only a few minutes before the hour of the table, and thus steps up to it as plainly and unconcernedly *as if he were just at home*. How different are the images of death that have passed into the imagination of our people and into that of the Greeks! Death reminded them of the enjoyment of life, us, to make it loathsome to us. It was to them a savor unto life, to us unto death. As in respectable society we do not speak of certain natural things, do not even write of them, so they circumscribed death, softened its image. With us, on the contrary, orators and preachers paint it in all possible terrible colors, to drive terror into us.” —

“It flatters the human understanding when it contemplates its great *edifice of the knowledge of God* and of human duties. It goes on embellishing the building, or even making flourishes on it. But the more extensive, the more composite the building at which the whole of mankind labors becomes, the less does it belong to any individual. He who merely copies this general building, who does not build in himself and out of himself a little house of his own, where he is quite at home, where he has every stone, if not worked quite from the raw, yet put in place and turned about in his hands, is a *man of the letter*; he has not lived and woven for himself. — He who merely builds after that great building a palace lives in it like Louis XIV at Versailles. He scarcely knows all the chambers of his property and fills only a very small cabinet, whereas a father of a household in his little house knows his way about everywhere better, can give an account of every screw, every little cupboard, of its use and its history. Lessing’s Nathan: In most cases I can still say, How? Where? Why? I learned it.” —

“If between pure religion of reason, which worships God in spirit and in truth and places his service solely in *virtue*, and between *fetish faith*, which believes that with God one can make oneself beloved also by something other than a will good in itself, there is so wide a difference that the latter, in opposition to the former, has no worth at all, that both are of wholly different kind

[p. 466]

and if it is so important for mankind to lead this ever more toward the religion of reason and to displace fetish faith, then the question arises (since a universal spiritual church remains only an ideal of reason and since it is not well possible that a public religion could be established which would take away all possibility of drawing fetish faith from it), how a *folk religion* in general must be arranged, a. in order, negatively, to give as little occasion as possible to cling to the letter and the usages, and b. positively, that the people, in order to be led toward the religion of reason, should gain receptivity for it? — Holiness is to be only an ideal to which we have to approach and to strive after which, without sensuous springs of action, is not to be possible. Into our nature itself such sensations are woven which, though not moral, i.e. not springing from respect for the law and therefore neither wholly firm and secure nor of worth in themselves, are yet lovable, hinder evil inclinations, and promote the best of men. Of this kind are all good-natured inclinations: compassion, benevolence, friendship, etc. To this empirical character, which is enclosed within the circle of inclinations, belongs also the moral feeling, which must send out its delicate threads into the whole fabric. The basic principle of the empirical character is *love*, which has something analogous to reason, insofar as it finds itself in other men, or rather, forgetting itself, posits itself out of itself, lives, feels, and is active in others, just as reason, as the principle of universally valid laws, recognizes itself again in every rational being. Love, although a pathological principle of action, is disinterested. It does not act well for the reason that it has calculated that the joys that spring from its actions are more unmixed and longer-lasting than those of sensuousness or those that spring from the satisfaction of some passion. It is thus not the principle of refined self-love, where the I is in the end always the last end.

Empiricism is indeed absolutely unfit for the establishment of principles. But when the question is how one has to work upon men, one must take them as they are. With a folk religion especially it is of the greatest importance that *imagination* and *heart* remain not unsatisfied, that the former be filled with great, pure images and in the latter the more beneficent feelings be awakened. That both receive a good direction is all the more important in that religion whose object is so great and sublime, where both too easily make paths for themselves or let themselves be led astray;

[p. 467]

either that the *heart*, led astray by false representations and its own convenience, attaches itself to external things or finds nourishment in low, falsely humble feelings and believes it serves God therewith; or that the *imagination* links things as cause and effect whose succession is merely accidental, and promises itself, contrary to nature, extraordinary effects. Man is so many-sided a being that everything can be made of him.

Folk religion distinguishes itself from *private religion* chiefly in that the former, in that it works powerfully upon imagination and heart, breathes into the soul in general the enthusiasm that is indispensable to great and sublime virtue. The cultivation of the individual, in accordance with his character, instruction about cases of collision of duties, the particular means of furthering virtue, comfort and uplifting in individual sufferings and misfortunes, must be left to the education for private religion. That they do not qualify for a public folk religion is clear from this: a. Instruction about cases of collision of duties cannot be given in public teaching. It is too dry and will not be able to bring it about that the disposition at the moment of action let itself be determined by its casuistic rules; or an eternal scrupulosity would be produced, which is wholly opposed to the resoluteness and strength required for virtue. b. If virtue is no product of teaching and of prattle, but a plant that, though with proper care, yet is formed out of its own drive and its own strength, then the many arts which one wants to have invented, to raise it as in a hothouse, where it is, as it were, not to be able to fail, spoil more in man than if one lets him run wild. — Men, early dipped into the dead sea of moral prattle, come out, to be sure, invulnerable like Achilles, but human strength too has been drowned in it.” —

“Just as the best education of children is the good example which they daily see around them, and just as they become the more inclined to disobedience and sullen obstinacy the more one always has to command them, so it is also with the *education of men on the large scale*. They shun a religion that wants always and forever to lead them by the leading-strings, that prattles to them of a multitude of virtues and vices (from the pulpits) which they have never in their life come face to face with so. — Everyone finds it intolerable when a stranger meddles in his affairs, especially in his manner of acting. *Most intolerable of all are publicly appointed guardians of morals.* He who acts with pure

[p. 468]

heart is most readily misunderstood by the people with the moral and religious ruler.”

“How little objective religion by itself, without the corresponding institutions of the state and the government, has accomplished, its history since the origin of Christianity shows us. How little has it been able to become master over the corruption of all ranks, over the barbarism of the times, over the crude prejudices of the peoples! Opponents of the Christian religion who, with a heart full of human feeling, read the history of the Crusades, of the discovery of America, of the present slave trade, and not merely these main events, in which the Christian religion in part plays a distinguished role, but in general the whole chain of princely corruption and depravity of the nations, and then held against it the pretensions of the teachers and servants of religion to excellence, to universal usefulness, and similar declamations — their hearts must bleed over it. They had to be filled with a bitterness, with a hatred against the Christian religion, which its defenders often ascribed to a diabolical malice. To the brilliant, shuddering pictures of the atrocities and the misery that zeal for a particular religion has caused, the defenders of the Christian religion oppose that these weapons are already too worn out and the grounds that could be drawn from them already long since refuted. Above all, however, they give their opponents to understand that all this misfortune would not have happened if, for the good fortune of mankind, only their compendia had already been published. But had not the popes and cardinals, had not the parsons Moses and the prophets? Could they not hear them? Did they lack the pure source of morals? Was it not capable of moderating the lust for power of the clergy, who committed either great impudences or small baseness, since this class of men hung out spiritual humility as a shield? What vice has not been in vogue among them? What has not been forbidden by their Lord and Master? Were not the times when princes let themselves be guided by their confessors, were not the countries where the spiritual lords governed, the most unhappy? — How light, laid in one scale, is the whole order of salvation, with the most detailed and learned “What is that?” crammed into the head besides — against the other, where all the passions, the power of circumstances, of education, of example, of government, send that one flying up into the air? — In such a consideration one would have to say that through the Christian religion *one can become good* if one is already good beforehand.”

[p. 469]

“The teachings and principles of Jesus were really arranged only for the cultivation of individual men. E.g., when he told the youth who asked him: Master, what shall I do to be perfect? to sell his goods and distribute them to the poor, the case, if one imagined it carried out as a principle even of only a small community, of a petty village, leads to consequences too absurd for it ever to occur to anyone to extend it to a larger people. Or, if a small number, like that of the first Christians, unites under another people under such a law of community of goods, then the spirit of such a law has vanished precisely at the moment of its institution, since by a kind of compulsion it not only occasions the desire for concealments, as in Ananias, and restricts the beneficence of such a resignation only to its members, to the comrades of its practices and distinctive doctrines, but is also contrary to the spirit of love of mankind, which pours out its blessing upon circumcised and uncircumcised, upon baptized and unbaptized.”

#### The Theses of the Dissertation *pro candidatura examinis consistorialis* 1793.

#### *Corollaria* [Corollaries].

I. [Latin] The Smalcald Articles are normative for the Württemberg church.

II. [Latin] The notion of the symbolic books under Ulrich was not yet that which was brought about under Christopher.

III. [Latin] We owe the purism of the Lutheran formula to Schrepf and Brenz.

IV. [Latin] But we deny, against *A. de Hagen* of Mainz, that we have deviated from the purism of the Lutheran church in the doctrine of justification.

V. [Latin] Nor does the distinction between *internal* and *external* justification, which he proposes in his dissertation on the variation of the Protestants concerning the doctrine of justification, 1788, by which all discrepancy could be removed, settle every dispute.

VI. [Latin] That the Exodus is the *Catechism of Christianity* is said ambiguously.

VII. [Latin] Most true, and on many counts to be praised even today, is the maxim of Brenz: “What can nourish and confirm reverence toward the public laws more *than if men feel that they obey God, if they obey the laws*?” Which indeed is to be understood not only of the *common people*, but also of the magistrate himself.

[p. 470]

[Latin] VIII. He who neglects the *literal* and *historical* sense of Holy Scripture will easily slip into luxuriant *allegories*.

IX. To the commonplaces of Philip Melanchthon we owe the better compendia of dogmatic theology of our church.

X. A cold *liturgical* mechanism befits neither the minister nor the church.

XI. The *rights of the prince* in sacred matters can best be reconciled with the *internal rights of the church*, provided both are treated religiously and with care.

XII. With the cultivation of letters neglected, Theology itself is neglected.

XIII. The conciliators of dissenting sects, while they wash the Ethiopian, ruin a good cause.

XIV. Ulrich strove for toleration as long as he could; the public treaties made him less tolerant.

XV. The *marriage of clerics*, the Augsburg formula having conceded it, was entirely reconcilable with Catholicism.

XVI. Nor was the *administration of the Holy Supper* under both kinds, offered to laymen too, incompatible with the Catholicism of that age.

XVII. But the *Mass* is entirely *incompatible* with Lutheranism.

XVIII. Those who have maintained it to be compatible in our age were not arbiters of sufficient discernment.

IV.

#### Hegel’s Travel Journal through the Bernese Alps, 1796.

“Monday, the 25th of July 1796, I set out from Bern at 4 o’clock in the morning with three Saxon house tutors, *Thomas*, *Stolde* and *Hohenbaum*. As we stopped on the way for breakfast, we arrived at *Thun* at 10 o’clock. At 10½ o’clock we embark. The shore that we had on our right begins flat and rises only gradually to a hilly tract covered with grain fields, meadows and trees, which extends for about two hours, as far as the manor of Spiess. Half an hour before, it is cut through by the Kander, which empties here into the lake. Behind this hill there rises a partly green rock chain

[p. 471]

whose highest peak is the *Stockhorn* and which here has the appearance of a hat-crown. But the side that it presents toward Thun is cut off quite vertically, and, when one is in the upper part of the lake, appears in a wholly different shape. Between the foot of this chain and the opposite *Niesen*, whose broad foot extends almost to the lake and which tapers to a majestic pyramid, the *Siebenthal* opens, as on the other side of the Niesen, which lies farther up the lake, the *Frutigenthal*. On this side one catches sight, at the foot of the said hill, in a sort of bay, of the manor of *Spiess* and, farther up, on a larger hill, of the village of *Echi*. Behind it juts out a high snow mountain, which is also seen in Bern and is called *Blümle’s Alp*. On the side that we had on our left one comes to Oberhofen and here and there, where the otherwise wild mountain rises somewhat more gently, past vineyards, of which there are also some on the other side, at Spiess. After two hours’ sail one sees *Sigriswyl* lying on a height. One can come hither only by the lake or by a dangerous footpath. After half an hour one comes to the *Nase*, and before that one catches sight of the entrance to the *Wüstithal*. Now one gradually loses from sight the lower part of the lake, as it makes a bend here. The shores of the upper part of the lake have a wholly different shape. On both sides one travels between rocks or mountains, which are used especially on the right side for cattle pastures. The rocky mountain on our left is called the *Bratenberg*, on which a village hangs high up, and from which, farther down, a spring flows out of a cave, which is called the *Beatus cave*, after the holy *Beatus* who is said to have dwelt here. At 2½ o’clock we arrived at *Neuhaus*, went on foot via *Unterseen*, a wretched little town consisting of bizarre houses, to *Interlaken*, which consists only of the houses belonging to the former monastery and lies at the foot of a mountain on whose other, rear side the *Habcherenthal* opens. Straight ahead from here one goes toward *Brienz*, to the left to *Lauterbronnen* and *Grindelwald*. We took this road.

From here nature has a wholly altered aspect for an inhabitant of level regions. He finds himself always between high mountains, partly green, and in the distance the peaks of snow mountains show themselves to him. The valleys are quite narrow, here consisting of rich meadows, which are strewn with countless fruit trees, especially walnut and cherry trees, and which always present a refreshing, pleasing, rural sight

[p. 472]

to him. But the narrowness of the valleys, where all distant view is taken from him by the mountains, has something confining, oppressive for him. He is always longing for expansion, for extension, and his gaze constantly strikes against rock. — After about an hour’s walk one has at one’s side the two *Litschenen*, whose grey-white, turbid water rushes roughly down through a stony bed and, through an eternal noise, often, where they are squeezed in, struggling through more strongly and foamingly, makes a din which at last causes tedium to one who is not accustomed to it and who goes along beside it for several hours. Where the two Litschenen flow together there are a couple of houses, which are called *Zweilitschenen*. The one coming from the left comes from Grindelwald. We kept to the road that lay on our right and came, after 3½ hours’ journey from Interlaken, to *Lauterbronnen*, a village that consists of scattered, wretched huts, which, like all houses in these regions, are badly built of wood and covered with wooden shingles, which are weighted down with large stones so that storms may not carry them off. The valley itself is quite narrow and is roared through by one of the wild Litschenen. The lower part of the mountains, which one can survey from the valley, consists of a bare row of vertical rocks, which are overgrown here and there with firs. We went still in the evening to see the Staubbach. We had already caught sight of it in part on the way, especially from the inn, where, despite our nearness, it looked to us like a mere insignificant thread of water and seemed by no means to reward us for the trouble and expense of today, but entirely to confirm Herr *Meiners’s* judgment. Despite these prejudices against it, and although it was already beginning to grow dark, we were, when we found ourselves quite close to it and beneath it, nevertheless completely satisfied. Perhaps the circumstance contributed to this that it was the first object of this kind to which our journey led us, whereas Herr Meiners had arrived there already glutted with great natural objects. The height of the rock wall from which it plunges alone has something great, the Staubbach itself properly not. All the more has the graceful, unconstrained, free playing-down of this water-dust something lovely. Since one does not behold a might, a great force, the thought remains far removed from the compulsion, from the *must of nature*, and what is living, ever dissolving itself, springing asunder, not united in One mass, eternally stirring onward and active, brings forth rather the image of a free play.

We were too tired to watch, in the night, the enchantment of the moonlight

[p. 473]

dancing upon it. Just as little did we want to wait for the famous rainbow in it, since the sun begins to fall on it only at 7 o’clock and we wanted to use the coolness of the morning for an arduous way that lay before us. We found egg dishes, hams, some roast meat and excellent strawberries for supper. — On Tuesday we set off, before the sun had yet lit the high summits of the snow mountains in the background of the valley, on the way over the *Wengeralp* to Grindelwald. The higher we came, the more we saw ourselves confronting the mountain whose foot forms the rock wall over which the Staubbach falls. We now saw its course also as that of a little stream. The height of the rock wall vanished more and more for us and seemed at last to make up only about the eighth part of the whole height of the mountain. The whole side of the Wengeralp is sown, up to a height of 1½ to 2 hours, with houses that belong to the Lauterbronnen parish, which comprises about 200 households in all. At the height of an hour we still found pieces of land sown with barley. We did not yet meet any cows on the pasture. Everything was busy with haymaking, which is saved for the winter, as the herds move ever higher as the summer advances. Every green spot of these mountains is carefully used, and small spaces of a few square feet are climbed at peril of life in order to fetch the grass. To the most dangerous, barest places goats are always driven, which are extremely useful to these mountain dwellers. — After a most arduous climb of several hours we found ourselves on another side of the mountain, which our guide called *Scheidegg*, whereby it is to be remarked that every valley gives the mountains by which it is bounded names that one finds again in the other valleys. Thus there is a Lauterbronnen Wetterhorn, Schreckhorn, a Lauterbronnen Jungfrau and Scheidegg; names which are in turn given by the Grindelwalders to certain mountains of their valley. *Scheidegg* seems to designate one that connects two great mountains or two valleys and over which the way usually leads from one valley into the other. *Wetterhorn*, a mountain peak toward evening, around which clouds usually first gather when rain is about to set in; *Schreckhorn*, otherwise a high rock; *Jungfrau*, a still unclimbed peak. If, then, one has in Bern heard certain mountains, which one can see from there, called by these names, and one asks after them in these valleys, a different one is pointed out each time under this name, and one must know,

[p. 474]

that those mountains which one knows from afar under the name of the snow mountains are chiefly those that one has before one in Grindelwald.

On the Scheidegg now, over which we went, we stopped at a *herdsman’s hut*, drank milk, cream, cheese-milk (whey) and ate cheese. One must have provided oneself with bread, since in these huts (where the cowherds stay only during the day, make their cheese here and carry it every day into their storehouses) none is to be found. We paid for it what was demanded. Already earlier, on the way, a cowherd had offered us some of his cream, which he was carrying home, to drink, and had left it to our pleasure how much money we wanted to give him. This custom, which we met with fairly generally, has its ground not, as many good-hearted travelers think, who have formed for themselves from this pastoral life a picture of general innocence and good nature, in hospitality and unselfishness, but rather these cowherds hope, by leaving the payment to the discretion of the travelers, to receive more than their ware is worth. One can easily convince oneself of this. If one gives them perhaps only as much as their goods are just worth, they do not thank one at all, do not even return the farewell greeting, but fall silent and make a vexed face. Or if one gives them less than they value what was given at, one may be sure that they then lay aside the ignorance they earlier feigned as to what their ware is worth and demand the definite price.

Already before we arrived at the hut we had a side of that Jungfrau, which is so called in Bern, on our right, and for the hour and a half that we found ourselves opposite it we heard every moment a thunder which was caused by the falling down of *avalanches*. On our side too we let a few smaller ones pass. The snow, namely, did not fall down in masses, but welled forth out of rock-gaps, or spurted forth as dust, often for ten minutes at a time — as is commonly the case with avalanches, since we otherwise form the concept of avalanches after the way we see snow roll down from our roofs.

With the Jungfrau the two *Aiger* are joined at the same time, which form bare rock masses covered at the top with snow. Near as we were to these mountains, and although we surveyed them from their foot to their summit, they nevertheless did not at all make the impression, did not arouse the feeling of grandeur and sublimity, that we had expected. Only then does one grow dizzy at the sight of a height,

[p. 475]

when one finds oneself quite at the foot of a vertical wall, as below at a church tower, and directs one’s gaze upward; otherwise, when the eye can measure it and is at some distance, not; or, too near, it sees only a small part of the height. He who is not accustomed to estimating the height of these mountains and their distances deceives himself unceasingly, and only through experience does he find that for the ascent of a height on which he believed he could be in a quarter of an hour he often needs several hours. More toilsome than the ascent was still the descent to Grindelwald. We were rewarded for it in part by the view into the basin in which Grindelwald lies. We descended on the western side and had on our left high but green mountains, covered with pastures, huts and trees. In the background on the left one catches sight of the entrance into the valley from Zweilitschenen. From here just such green mountains again stretch across to directly before us, one of which is called the other Scheidegg. From here on, on our right hand, the whole side has a wholly different aspect. A row of quite steep rocks rises here, on whose sides, here and there between the stones, firs hang and, sparingly, a little patch of grass is discovered. Their summits are covered with eternal snow. This row is interrupted by the two famous Grindelwald glaciers, of which one, the smaller, descends between the Aiger and the Mettenberg and the Wetterhorn. They show themselves here, namely, not as ice valleys, but rise, as said, between the openings of these mountains. Only at a certain height do they draw farther into the valleys that are formed by those primeval mountains, far in, like a sea that thrusts out various arms, such as here the Grindelwald glacier, and farther on the Aar glacier, the Laut glacier, and is said to extend for about twenty hours farther. From these glacier mountains the Litschenen break forth, which in summer, because of the stronger melting of the snow, are stronger, in winter in part quite insignificant.

We saw these glaciers today only at a distance of half an hour, and their sight offers nothing further of interest. One can call it only a *new kind of seeing*, which, however, gives *the spirit absolutely no further occupation* than that it is perhaps struck at finding itself, in the strongest heat of summer, so near to ice masses which, even at a depth where the heat brings cherries, nuts and corn to ripeness, can be melted by it only insignificantly. Below, the ice is very dirty and in part wholly covered with mud, and whoever has seen a broad, downhill-going, muddy

[p. 476]

street, in which snow has begun to melt, can form a fairly good concept from the view of the lower part of the glaciers as it presents itself from afar, and at the same time admit that this sight has neither anything great nor anything lovely. — Farther up the ice appears in pyramids, which have a purer blue and which one can, in comparison with the dirty ice below, if one will, call more beautiful. At about one o’clock we arrived at *Grindelwald*, which is a considerable village and extends somewhat up the height. The valley is altogether much larger, more pleasant and more fertile than the Lauterbronnen one. The greater part of the mountains by which it is surrounded rises more gently. The cherries were beginning to ripen. One is overrun by children, who offer the travelers flowers, strawberries, etc., or even beg without offering anything of the sort. Partly our weariness, partly a rainy spell that had set in, kept us at home the rest of the day, whose tedium we alleviated by a game of l’hombre. We got here for the first time Italian red wine to drink, which was of the poorer sort and sour, but is said to be healthy especially for travelers in these regions, where they eat much rich milk.

On Wednesday at 4 o’clock, the sky overcast, we left Grindelwald in order to go over the Scheidegg to Mairingen. We set out on this way with the notion of having the most arduous part of the whole journey before us, since the picture floated before us which Meiners makes of the hardships of this way. Our guide, whom we had already brought along from Lauterbronnen, consoled us to some extent by assuring us that our day’s work today would be less arduous than yesterday’s. We let ourselves be led first, in order to have seen one of the famous *glaciers* close by, to the one that did not lie out of our way and which is the larger. To get to its foot one must pass over granite blocks and other stone masses which it has pushed forward. One then finds oneself at a mass of ice, at the top fairly smooth and rounded, which likewise has gorges and crevasses melted away at the corners. Apart from the satisfaction of being now so near such a glacier that I touched it and could look at its ice, I have found no further satisfaction, especially since from this near standpoint one can survey only little of it and the not very considerable height of the ice mass that one has before one rises not suddenly but gradually. We continued our way. The higher we came, the denser a fog we went toward, which indeed protected us from the heat,

[p. 477]

but at the same time took from us all view and exposed us to the danger of going astray. When we had been on the way about 4 hours, our guide told us we were on the summit and had from here always to descend. We could not marvel enough at Herr Meiners, how he could have given such a frightful description of this way, which we had found nowhere in the least steep and troublesome. As, with this thought, we turned a little way down to the right, because our guide wanted to lead us here into a cowherd’s hut to drink some refreshing milk, we luckily met two cowherds who were carrying home the cheese they had made today. These told us we were on the way back to Grindelwald. They showed us the region where we would find the right way again, and so we turned back, praising ourselves fortunate to have met these men, but believing at the same time that Herr Meiners’s description might now still come true. But after a quarter of an hour we really found ourselves on the height, though the fog had not let up at all and we had to give up completely the hope of enjoying a beautiful view. As we gradually came lower, the fog dissolved into a downright rain, which lasted as long as we were in the valley, which is formed on one side by the Scheidegg, on the other by a range that here too is called the Wetterhorn. The *Reichenbach* flows through it, which raged the more wildly and horribly the farther down we came. Up in the valley we stopped at a cowherd’s, who owns 18 cows, whose milk gives him every day about 30 pounds of cheese and in the spring, when the grass is still better and more abundant, yields about 40 pounds. He explained to us at the same time the *process of cheese-making* and of the use of the milk. Every morning, namely, the milk that was milked the evening before and this morning itself is put in a kettle over quite gentle fire and separated by an acid which is prepared especially from calves’ stomachs and is called *Käslab* (rennet). The mass may thereby only become lukewarm. When the separation, which is promoted by constant stirring, has taken place, the watery part is taken out, wrapped in a cloth and pressed in a round wooden mould. The remaining liquid, which is called *Käsmilch* and is not much different from milk, tastes only somewhat sourish and has already taken on a yellowish color, is now put over strong fire and separated once more by boiling. The white solid mass is called *Zieger*, is salted and saved especially for the winter. The liquid is called *Schotte* and is partly drunk by the people, partly given to the swine to guzzle.

[p. 478]

After we had left this valley under constant rain, where we still passed several granaries lying together in heaps, which, to keep cooler, usually rest a man’s height above the ground on posts, we climbed, in the fog, constantly downhill by a stony way at the side of the raging Reichenbach. Since we knew that its famous fall is to be seen on this way, we were anxious, if the Reichenbach moved farther away, that the fog might have deprived us of the sight of it and that we might already have passed it. While we thus continued our way for another half hour, still in doubt and uncertainty and in the impossibility of recognizing an object farther than 30 paces away, under a constantly stronger roaring of the stream, we heard all at once a fearful thunder and could no longer doubt that this proceeded from its fall. At the same time we could absolutely not see where we might approach it. After a few minutes that we went farther, this thunder ceased, and we now soon saw Mairingen lying in the valley and a turbid white water flowing past it, which we took for the Reichenbach, which, after its fall, now went on quietly in the valley. As the rain returned and we found no one who could have given us information, we wanted to resign ourselves to making, in hope of better weather, a walk of an hour back in the afternoon and then seeing it.

All at once, as we came nearer some houses, the upper part of the fall presented itself to us from the side, and with pleasure we went through wet meadows to meet it. On the green rise opposite it we were completely drenched by the water-dust, which the wind caused by the fall drove against us. To survey more of the fall one must climb down over slippery grass farther, to the edge of the abyss into which it sinks. From here one enjoys the sight of the fall as far as one may survey it, and the majestic spectacle indeed compensated us for the trouble of the disagreeable day. Through a narrow rocky cleft the water presses forth narrowly at the top, then falls vertically down in broader waves; in waves that draw the gaze of the beholder constantly down with them and which he yet can never fix, never follow, for their image, their shape, dissolves every moment, is in each moment displaced by a new one, and *in this case he sees eternally the same image, and sees at the same time that it is never the same*. After the waves have thus come down a considerable height, more falling than plunging, they strike rocks, where, bubbling,

[p. 479]

they force their way out in three or four openings, then flow together and now plunge thundering into an abyss, into whose depth the gaze cannot follow them, because it is stopped by rocks. Only at some distance does one see a smoke billowing out of a cleft, which one recognizes as the foam spurting up from the fall.

Meiners has rightly called attention to this fall, but a description can, as little as a painting, replace even in some degree the seeing for oneself. In description the imagination can more readily, if it already has similar images, still paint the whole for itself, but a painting, if it is not made very large, cannot but turn out meager and give only an insufficient representation. The *sensuous presence of the painting* does not permit the imagination to extend the represented object, but it grasps it just as it presents itself to the sight. It is hindered still more in its extension thereby: when we hold the painting in the hand or find it hung on a wall, the senses cannot do otherwise than measure it against our size, against the size of the surrounding objects, and find it small. Such a painting would have to be brought so near to the eye that it would have trouble surveying the whole, could not set it beside other objects and so would lose the standard entirely. Besides, even in the best painting the most attractive, the essential element of such a spectacle must be lacking: the eternal life, the mighty stirring in it. A painting can give only a part of the whole impression, namely the likeness of the picture, which it must give in definite outlines and parts; the other part of the impression, on the other hand, the eternal, unceasing change of every part, the eternal dissolution of every wave, every foam, which always draws the eye along with it, which does not permit it for a split second the same direction of the gaze: all this might, all this life is wholly lost. — Quite drenched we arrived at 1½ o’clock in Mairingen. The continuing rain hindered us from seeing the lower fall of the Reichenbach. We took our refuge again in l’hombre. My left foot had already hurt me very much on the made road. This circumstance, with the bad weather, produced in me the resolution to return from here to Bern with one of the company. But since the weather cleared up completely on the next morning and brought the other back from his resolution, I too did not want to turn back alone, but resolved, in spite of my sore foot, to continue the journey.

On Thursday at 5 o’clock we set off with a new guide, the

[p. 480]

shoemaker, who had also accompanied Herr Meiners and who carried our luggage, farther up the *Haslithal*. The inhabitants of this valley differ from the other subjects of the city of Bern partly by their pronunciation, which comes closer to High German, partly by their greater political rights. A German who in other parts of Switzerland has the greatest trouble understanding the language of the people and making himself understood to them finds here much less trouble for both. He will especially wonder to hear the endings of the verbs, -*en*, pronounced so distinctly. He will indeed still hear many words that are strange to him, but they will become the more intelligible to him the more knowledge he possesses of the *old German language*. I believe the study of the various dialects of Switzerland would be not without a rich yield for the better knowledge of many expressions occurring in Old German writings and now obscure to us. — As to their constitution, they have their own court, which consists of 15 members, and a Landammann, who is only confirmed in Bern and must be a Haslithaler. Likewise other posts may only be filled with such men. Through their own carelessness and negligence or the incompetence of these officials they claim, however, to have lost many privileges gradually. How little they now still value receiving judgments only from judges out of their midst, experience shows, in that the party usually makes nothing at all of the verdict of its native court, but in most cases turns to Bern and has justice pronounced by foreign judges.

The first place we came to was *Hasli im Grund*, which lies in a green basin and is a round plain of meadows, out of which the *Aar* presses its way through a narrow opening between rocks and, probably before it found this outlet, formed a lake here and flowed off at a higher place. From here the way ascends ever more and is in part very varied. Now it leads through fir woods, now through meadows past huts. Especially the course of the Aar, which one has now on the right, now on the left, offers manifold views. Just as much variety is given by the many brooks, which rush down to the Aar now in vertical falls, now as dust, now over a less steep stony bed, and of which one has to pass a quantity, which one however, like also some waterfalls at Mairingen itself, opposite the Reichenbach, honors with no attention, because one comes from greater spectacles of the kind or is going toward them. Often the Aar, which rages and foams in a gruesome depth, leaves

[p. 481]

only a quite narrow way between itself and the rocks, which is laid with round timbers, but can yet be trodden by mules and horses. — Not far from Hasli im Grund the *Mühlithal* opens. After about 3 hours’ way we arrived at *Guttannen*, the last Bernese village, where our midday meal consisted of white bread and Valais bread (which was only about two fingers high, in the form of a cake, and very hard), butter, honey and Italian wine. We let the greatest heat pass during another game of l’hombre, set out on the journey about 4 o’clock and, as my feet continued to grow worse, I made the journey from here on constantly with trodden-down shoes. From Guttannen the way becomes ever wilder, more desolate, monotonous. One has always the same rough, dreary rocks on both sides. Sometimes one catches sight of summits covered with snow. The ground, which is more level and sometimes forms a valley, is wholly strewn with enormous granite blocks. The Aar makes several splendid waterfalls plunging down with fearful force. Over one of them a bold bridge is sprung, on which one is quite wetted with dust. One sees here from close by the mighty raging of the waves against the projecting rocks and does not comprehend how they can withstand this fury. Nowhere does one get so pure a concept of the *must* of *nature* as at the sight of the eternally ineffectual and eternally continued raging of a driven wave against such rocks! Yet one sees that their sharp corners are gradually rounded. Farther on one sees the vegetation more and more feel the curse of a nature without warmth and strength. One meets no more fir trees, only stunted fir shrub, moss, wretched grass or none at all, some larch and arolla-pine trees; many gentians grow in one region. The roots of these latter plants are gathered by a family and distilled into gentian spirit. This family lives here in the summer in complete remoteness from men and has set up its still under piled-up granite blocks that nature threw one over another without purpose, but whose accidental position men knew how to use. *I doubt whether here the most credulous theologian would venture,* to ascribe to nature itself in these mountains, in general, *the purpose of usefulness for man,* who must wrest with trouble from it the little, needy thing he can use; who is never sure whether he will not be shattered, over his poor thefts, over the robbery of a handful of grass, by stones or avalanches; whether not the wretched work of his hands, his meager hut and his cowshed

[p. 482]

will be smashed to pieces for him in one night. In these desolate wildernesses educated people would perhaps sooner have invented all other theories and sciences, but hardly that part of physico-theology which proves to man’s pride how nature has prepared everything for his enjoyment and well-being; a pride *which at the same time characterizes our age*, in that it finds its satisfaction rather in the representation that everything has been done for it by an alien being than it would in the consciousness that it is in fact itself that has commanded all these purposes to nature. Yet the inhabitants of these regions live in the feeling of their dependence on the power of nature, and this gives them a quiet resignation to its destructive outbreaks. If their hut is shattered or buried or washed away, they build another on the same spot or near it. If on a road men have often been killed by falling rocks, they nevertheless go quietly along it, otherwise than the city dwellers, who usually find their purposes destroyed only through their own clumsiness or the ill will of others, become ill-tempered and impatient over it, even when they once feel the power of nature, then need consolation and find it perhaps in some piece of chatter that proves to them that even this misfortune may be advantageous to them, for they cannot raise themselves to giving up their utility. To demand of them that *they be willing to renounce compensation would mean robbing them of their God.*

The Aar becomes more insignificant the farther one goes. Several times we saw the cleft in which it rushes filled with snow, under which it continues on its way. Once we also went more than 200 paces across a smooth, entirely continuous rock covered with no grass and no clod of earth, where grooves a finger deep, a shoe’s width apart, are engraved for the pack animals. We met a quantity of such animals with their Valaisan and Italian drivers. They carried rice, wine and brandy. On the return they load cheese. Before we came to the hospice I had counted that from Mairingen on we had crossed the Aar seven times, the last three times on stone bridges, the preceding times on wooden ones. We arrived there almost at the onset of twilight, in a stone house which has a few rooms and lies in a desolate, dreary stone wilderness that is as wild as the regions through which we had been coming for some hours. Neither the eye nor the imagination finds on these formless masses any point on which the former with

[p. 483]

satisfaction can rest, or where the latter could find occupation or play. The mineralogist alone finds material for venturing insufficient conjectures about the revolutions of these mountains. Reason finds in the thought of the duration of these mountains, or in the kind of sublimity that is ascribed to them, nothing that imposes on it, that extorted its astonishment and admiration. The sight of these eternally dead masses gave me nothing but the monotonous and, in length, tedious representation: it is so.

At the hospice we were entertained with Italian wine, Bologna sausages, mutton and veal, which, like the bread, is brought from Mairingen. What was something new for us was partly smoked, partly fresh *marmot meat*, which seemed to us just no delicacy.
