These animals are dug out especially at the beginning of winter, about which time they are fat and already lie asleep. Arolla-pine nuts too were set before us. The house itself, together with the pastures belonging to it, belongs to the Haslithal. The tenant who is on it can inhabit it only 9 months long. From December he must move to lower regions, and only in March does he make his way up again. He pays rent for the pastures. Poor people he must lodge free. From other travelers he leaves it to them what they want to give him, and his obligingness and good will, together with the consideration of how toilsome it is to bring up all requirements here, will not easily let him come off short in this venture, reliant on the generosity of the travelers. For the costs which he has for the free maintenance of the poorer, he is compensated by contributions which he has collected yearly in various cantons. — Behind this house there lies a lake which is formed by the neighborhood of the Grimsel snow. My foot, too, now much swollen and festering, the host took obligingly in hand. — One sees the way to the rear Aar glaciers, out of which, at the foot of the dark and the white Aarhorn, the Aar melts forth. — The host keeps for travelers a kind of *album*, which usually contains remarks on the way and praises of the hospitable host. Especially several remarks about the dangerousness of the way over the Mayenwand consoled us, because of Herr Meiners’s frightful description, concerning which, among others, the following rhyme is inscribed:

Herr Meiners is a coward, / Who must let such adventures be.

On Friday we climbed in an hour, partly over snow, partly

[p. 484]

over stones on which there was no trace of vegetation any more, the rest of the way up the *Grimsel*. We saw here and there high poles set up, which are to serve the traveler as signposts at the time when snow falls again. In these regions many *accidents* have already happened in the autumn and spring season. When one is overtaken by bad weather and snow, the way is at once lost. Aimlessly the unfortunate man wanders about, finds in a cleft in the snow his death, and no one knows what has become of him. Not long ago a poor Lucerner with his wife and two children wanted to go on this way into the Valais. He is overtaken by the snow, wanders about so long until his wife collapses, powerless. His own strength forsakes him so that he can drag along only himself and one child. His wife and the other child he leaves behind in the snow, and one has learned nothing more of them. From here we saw behind us the Aarhörner, right before us the region of the valley in which Obergesteln lies around the Gehrenberg; farther to the left a part of the Gotthard; deep below us the valley in which the Rhone flows, and the Rhone glacier; from this upward to our left the Mayenwand; above the glacier the Galenstock, a Uri snow mountain, and farther in the background a part of the Furka. We went now over snow toward the *Mayenwand, i.e. Blumenwand* or green wall; it is so called because it is quite sown with a beautiful green and flowers of all kinds. The way over it is indeed so constituted that one can hardly set two feet beside each other, and for some 50—60 paces’ length the angle that it forms may amount to as much as 70 degrees. Without stooping one can comfortably hold oneself with the hand on the wall. In passing we plucked Alpine roses and beautiful forget-me-nots, of which an innumerable quantity grows here. None had the least assault of fear. From here one goes still about a quarter of an hour somewhat obliquely, and from there straight downhill toward the Rhone. This descending is infinitely more troublesome. The shrubbery of the Alpine roses, which are about 1 to 1½ feet high, allows no firm tread. It was impossible for me, especially because of the bad condition of my feet, to hold myself upright. I imitated some of my companions, sat down on my breeches, seized with both hands the Alpine roses beside me and so slid down the greatest part of the mountain. Below at the Rhone we found that we had spent over an hour on this descent, which had seemed to us very entertaining. During it we heard toward the rocks a frequent whistling, which our guide ascribed to the marmots. In the valley we found spring water, which,

[p. 485]

mixed with cherry-water, refreshed us greatly. A few such springs rise in this valley, which many want to hold, rather than the glacier water, for the true sources of the Rhone; *about which it really seems ridiculous to want to have an opinion,* since the water out of the glacier in winter is indeed insignificant, but never dries up, and the one is as much the origin of the Rhone as the other. — This region, which is enclosed by the Furka and the Grimsel, is called the *Gletsch* and surpasses in desolation and dreariness everything that we had yet seen. Without going quite up to the glacier, since its ice is just as constituted as the ice of the others, we climbed up on the right hand and could from there survey it far up, where it begins to descend between the mountains. It formed a great, rough mass. Downward its surface is cut through by deep clefts and blue crevasses. Upward it is more hollowed out and has here more a shaggy aspect, set with bluish and white pyramids and ridges. One must indeed find it singular that such an ice mass descends so deep into a valley, since from its foot on, at the height of 1—2 hours, the surrounding mountains bear grass and manifold flowers and the heat of the sun burns in such a valley with concentrated force. But one must remember that up to a considerable height the snow that has fallen on the glacier itself, and gathered in the valley from the mountains, must first be melted by the sun before it can burn on the glacier itself, and that the cold which prevails in such a mass forms an atmosphere around it which can be warmed only with difficulty. We climbed first uphill to the right and had at an hour’s distance the Rhone glacier at our side. Then we went over another glacier water, which comes from the Furka glacier lying before us, onto the left part of the *Furka* and arrived, after a climb of 2½ to 3 hours, at its summit, i.e. always at that peak over which one passes and which is never the highest of the whole mountain range, but is usually called a Lücke [gap]. In a Valais hut, in which we drank milk on the way, we met some boys who in a corner of the hut, which except for the door had no light, had made a bed of stones, on which lay some linen sheets and which was their sleeping-place. Beside it hung a kettle in which they made their cheese. The rest of the hut is possessed by the pigs. Besides these well-formed boys we had earlier met some Valais peasants, who were all dressed in Capuchin color, whereas the Hasli folk whom we had so far seen all dress in blue.

[p. 486]

The wood that those boys burn for their cheese they fetch from over an hour away. Farther up we caught sight of no shrub, no stunted fir any more. A few birds of the size of a quail and of a light grey-yellow color had twittered about us farther along and were flying around us without shyness, like the birds of all uninhabited regions. Higher up we saw nothing but rocks, snow and grass, and at a still greater height than we were at we saw a herd of cows grazing. At half past eleven we arrived at the top of the Furka, at the cross by which the Valais and Uri territory is divided. We refreshed ourselves here with the bread, which was spread inside with butter and with which the host of the Grimsel hospice had cleverly provided us, and with his red Italian wine, and our appetite thanked him most heartily for it.

At noon we began to descend toward the *Ursteren* valley. The beginning we had to make by descending and gliding for a good quarter of an hour’s distance over soft snow, which the sun made still more dazzling. When one steps out of this glare onto the likewise illuminated earth again, one thinks one is walking at first only in a faint moonlight. Gradually we came into better grass, which was intermixed with aromatic flowers of all kinds. Even those that in lower regions do not smell give here a balsamic fragrance; e.g. a common *Hieracium* or *Leontodon*, which grows on all Ursteren meadows and here at the same time has a beautiful cinnamon-brown color; likewise a quite low *sanguis orba*, which smelled like chocolate. — Farther down we found the people busy with haymaking, until at 2½ o’clock we arrived at *Realp*, where a *Capuchin hospice* received us hospitably and entertained us with red Italian wine, the best we had yet met, for it came from the cellar of the spiritual gentlemen, and with good cheese; they also left it to our pleasure how much we wanted to give them for it, whereby, as it seemed to me, our cashier did not let them find their reckoning. Notwithstanding this they were polite enough to send after me a glove which I had left lying there, by a man who was also going our road. — In the evening coolness we went through flowery meadows overgrown with tall grass and between quite green mountains, past a dilapidated tyrant’s castle, first through the village of *Imdorf*, then through the village of *Hospital*, from where the way over the Gotthard to Italy rises and which we left on the right hand. It has nothing further remarkable and is nothing but a continued stone cleft, of which we began to grow heartily weary.

[p. 487]

After two short hours we came into the village of *Ursteren* or An der Matt. We contented ourselves with looking at the snow-covered summits from here. One also drew our attention to a little fir wood which stands on the slope of a part of the Gotthard toward Ursteren and in which cutting off a branch is forbidden at loss of freedom, since the inhabitants regard it as a kind of protective wall against the avalanches, which breaks their force somewhat and holds them up. — Here we had to, notwithstanding our unbelief, submit ourselves to the commandments of the church and content ourselves today with Lenten food.

On Saturday we left Ursteren and, by entering the *Urnerloch*, the Ursteren valley as well. This famous hole is a small half hour from Ursteren and a rather dark rock vault 80 paces long. We now entered a rough rocky region, which rises shapeless and dead on both sides of the wild Reuss, and we comprehended how agreeable the surprise must be for travelers who from this wilderness, through the night of the Urnerloch, step into the cheerful, green Ursteren valley. Soon we reached the so famous *Devil’s Bridge*, which for us was at first only remarkable for its fame and which necessarily must make a greater impression on travelers coming from below, who from the depth on the bank of the raging Reuss between the wild rocks see no way out any more, now see it blasted from one to the other and hope for an exit above it. It is moreover broad enough that a small carriage, char à banc, can drive over it and 4 persons can walk comfortably beside each other, and has absolutely nothing dangerous. Toward it the Reuss plunges with gruesome foaming and raging from a considerable height through resisting rocks and forms a remarkable waterfall. On both sides of the bed of the raging Reuss rise vertical, shapeless, bare masses of stone, on which here and there a scanty green patch shows itself, which is laboriously climbed and mown. Now and then one sees snowy summits. Along these rocks winds or steals, now on the one, now on the other side, now upward, now downward, the stony road in constant serpentine windings. Between Wassen and the village of Steg there lies on a meadow beside the way an isolated enormous piece of rock, and it is comprehensible that the childlike sense of these shepherd peoples was struck long ago by its being here and attached a *myth* to it. But as ever, as also with the Devil’s Bridge, the Christian imagination has produced nothing but an *insipid legend*.

From *Wassen* we were in 3 hours in the village of *Steg*, where

[p. 488]

we dined at noon. All the innkeepers down this road have a stock of *crystals*, which they buy from shepherds who come into the high mountains, and then trade with. They understand very well how to make distinctions between pieces of greater and lesser value and to fix the prices accordingly. From Wassen on the landscape becomes somewhat milder. The valley is here and there somewhat broader. The high mountains descend below, partly with gentler slopes, into the Reuss, on which meadows planted with fruit trees and scattered dwellings are found. Nowhere did the mountains seem to me so high as here in these now lower regions, for one sees here very high summits of Uri mountains, at whose foot we ourselves found ourselves, since earlier, even when we had summits of higher mountains before us, we were mostly either too far removed from their foot or ourselves at a considerable height. Or if we were also at the foot of one of those great giants, we could see only about the summit of the first terrace, which hid from us the rest and the highest peak. After 3½ hours’ way we arrived in the evening in *Altdorf* and had thus passed comfortably through the whole canton of Uri in a single day.

On Saturday early we went to *Flüelen*, which lies half an hour from Altdorf, to embark there. To avoid the competition of the boatmen, each is taken in turn by the travelers. At the same time the fare also is fixed by the authorities. We went, partly beside high rocks, first to *Tell’s Chapel*, which seems to have been freshly painted not long ago and does not, as I expected, have something venerable about it through its age or simplicity. It is well built of stone and distinguishes itself from other Catholic chapels of the kind by nothing but the rather daubed paintings *al fresco* which are found in its portal and which relate to the history of Tell and of the other founders of the freedom of these cantons. In 2½ hours from Flüelen we were in *Brunnen*. We saw on the way, on the opposite side also, the *Grittli* (so Hegel writes, not Rütli) or the green spot where the three first Confederates swore the covenant. In Brunnen we found in Herr former Landvogt Zollner and the Stag innkeeper Ulrich a very obliging man. Here 2 of our travel companions also left us. — On the way from Brunnen to Gersau we passed the solitary *cell of a hermit*, which lies right on the shore, as also a chapel called *Kindleinmord* [Slaughter of the Innocents], a name that points to the occasion for building the chapel. The boatmen

[p. 489]

told us of it the following story, touching through its simplicity and the contrast of depravity and innocence. A minstrel had left his little girl alone on this lonely spot and had played for a dance on the other side of the lake and made merry. When in the night, late, the father came back to the abandoned child, it begged him, quite hungry, for bread. The father treated it roughly. The child begged imploringly. He promised at last to give it some if it could answer three questions, of which the last two are still in my memory. What is sweeter than honey? The child answered: mother’s milk. What harder than stone? The father’s heart, replied the child, and full of fury he struck it so that it was found dead there, and pious simplicity erected on this spot a chapel in atonement for offended innocence. — *Gersau* is a neat little place, near the shore of the lake, in a pleasant little valley, a free independent republic, which is said to have some rich silk manufacturers, who give sustenance to a quantity of people in the surrounding regions. Opposite us we already had the territory of Unterwalden. Farther on we saw in Unterwalden Beckenried, an hour from it Buochs and, in the background of the region, Stans. Pilatus closes the prospect. We left this arm of the lake on the left, passed through a narrows, had the Riggiberg in part on the right and caught sight, toward Lucerne, for the first time again over the beautiful mirror surface of the lake, of lower hills, which did our eye, which had so far had partly sublime, partly grey and dreary mountains and almost never a wide view, very good.

The trip up to here between the green, most varied shores of the lake, which mirrored themselves on the pure surface, had been very pleasant. Now a thunderstorm rose behind us. The thunder rolled and large drops fell on the lake, which nonetheless remained calm. To protect ourselves from the rain we had to step ashore for a while. Opposite us we saw the debris of the village of *Weggis*, which had slid into the lake. A year earlier, in July, several men had felt that the earth and the whole landscape was moving gently. They made the other inhabitants of the village aware of it, who fled with their belongings; the sliding lasted 14 days, during which they could save everything, even take down and carry off some houses, until finally the remainder fell one after the other into the lake. — We soon found ourselves opposite the island on which we caught sight of *Raynal’s* pyramid. We did not want to stay there, since a new thunderstorm threatened us, which

[p. 490]

still drenched us, while we flew along the shores, now pleasantly sown with country houses, before we finally arrived at *Lucerne*.” —

V.

#### Fragments of Theological Studies.

1. The History of the Jews. 2. Fate and Its Reconciliation. 3. Love and Shame. 4. The Son of God and Son of Man. 5. The Last Supper. 6. The Miracle. 7. Baptism.

#### The History of the Jews.

“The history of the Jews teaches that this people did not form itself independently of foreign nations, that the form of its state did not develop freely, without a violent wrenching out of an already assumed character. *The transition from the pastoral life to the state* took place not gradually and of itself, but through foreign influence. This condition was accompanied by a feeling of a lack, which however was not general, not extended to all sides of it. No complete or bright ideal could arise to be opposed to that condition. Only in the soul of a man who in the school of the priests and at court had run through a greater manifold of knowledge and enjoyments and then, having fallen out with them, had learned in solitude no longer to miss them and had attained a unity of being, could the plan for the liberation of his people emerge. In this he could at first use only the feeling of its oppression and a rather powerless memory of another condition of their fathers, in order to lead it to the wish for independence. For the belief in the possibility of carrying it out, the belief in his divine mission inspired them. In the carrying out itself they behaved, to be sure, almost wholly passively. They fought out a ground for themselves, and their drive for independence was properly a drive for dependence on something of their own. These changes, which other nations often run through only in millennia, had to be so rapid in the Jewish people. Each of its conditions was too violent for it to have been able to last long. *The condition of independence, tied to universal enmity*, is too much the opposite of

[p. 491]

nature. The condition of independence of other peoples is a condition of good fortune and of finer humanity. That of the independence of the Jews was to be the condition of a complete passivity, of a complete ugliness. — Because their independence assured them only eating and drinking, a needy existence, with this little everything was also lost. There remained to them, besides their animal existence, nothing the enjoyment of which would have taught them to endure many a hardship, to sacrifice much. In the oppression their miserable existence came immediately into danger, to rescue which they struck out. They believed in their God because, completely at variance with nature, they found in him the unification of it through dominion. — When the Jews introduced among themselves the *royal power*, which Moses held compatible with the theocracy, Samuel however incompatible with it, *individuals* obtained a political importance, which they had to share with the priests or defend against them. Yet when otherwise in free states the introduction of monarchy reduces all citizens to private persons, so in this state, in which each was a political nothing, it raised at least individuals to a more or less restricted something. — After the vanishing of the ephemeral but very oppressive splendor of the *Solomonic* government, the new powers which the introduction of kingship still wove into the scourge of their fate — *unbridled lust for dominion and powerless dominion* — tore the Jewish people completely apart, and turned against its own entrails precisely the raging lovelessness and godlessness that it had earlier turned against other nations. They guided its fate through its own hands upon itself. Foreign nations it at least learned to fear. From a people ruling in the Idea it became a people ruled in actuality and received the *feeling of external dependence.* For a time it preserved in continuing humiliations still a sad sort of state, until at the end — as for the politics of cunning weakness the day of misfortune never fails — it was entirely trodden to the ground, without retaining the power of rising again. — From time to time *inspired men* had sought to hold fast the old genius, to revive the dying one. Yet the fled genius cannot be conjured back by enthusiasm, the fate of a people cannot be banned under its magic: well may it call forth a new spirit from the depth of life, if it is pure and living. But the Jewish *prophets* kindled their flame at the torch of an exhausted demon. They sought to give it its old strength, and with the destruction of the manifold interests of the time

[p. 492]

to restore its old, shudderingly sublime unity to it. They could therefore become only cold and, in their meddling in politics, only restricted, ineffectual fanatics, only give a recollection of past times, thereby confuse the present still more, but not bring about other times. The admixture of the passions never again succeeded in passing over into monotonous passivity, but, out of passive dispositions, it had to rage the more horribly.”

“To flee this ghastly actuality, men sought consolation in *ideas*. The common Jew, who would give up himself indeed, but not his object, in the hope of a coming Messiah; the *Pharisees* in the pursuit of the service and doing of the present objective; the *Sadducees* in the whole manifoldness of their existence, of a changeable being; the *Essenes* in something eternal, in a brotherhood, which excluded all separating property and what hangs together with it and made one living One without manifoldness. The hope of the *Romans* that fanaticism would moderate under their moderate rule failed. It glowed once more and buried itself under its own destruction.”

“The great tragedy of the Jewish people is no Greek one. It can arouse neither fear nor pity, for both spring only from the fate of the necessary misstep of a beautiful being. It can only arouse abhorrence. The more thorough the dependence of the Jews on their law was, the greater had to be their obstinacy, in which they could still have a will, and this only thing was *their service itself, when it found an opposition*. With as light a mind as they let themselves be seduced into becoming unfaithful to their faith when they were not in need and their meager enjoyment was satisfied, when the alien did not approach them as hostile, so obstinately did they fight for their service when it was attacked. They fought for it as desperate men. They were themselves capable, in the struggle for it, of transgressing its commandments, e.g. the keeping of the Sabbath, which, at the command of others, no force could make them violate consciously. And as life was maltreated in them, as in them nothing unmastered, nothing holy was left, so their action became the most unholy raving, the most furious fanaticism. — The fate of the Jewish people is the fate of *Macbeth*, who stepped out of nature itself, hung on to alien beings, in their service trampled and murdered everything holy of human nature, was forsaken by his gods (for they were objects, he was a slave) and had to be shattered on his faith itself.” —

[p. 493]

#### Fate and Its Reconciliation.

“The law is later than life and stands lower than it. As something universal it is opposed to man and his inclinations as to the particular. Fate is only the enemy, and man stands over against it just as much as a fighting power, whereas the law as law is unapproachable. Life can therefore return again to itself and sublate the handiwork of a crime, the law and the punishment. Only through a going-out from the united life, through *killing of life*, is something alien created. The annihilation of life is not a *not-being* of it, but its *separation*, and the annihilation consists in this, that it has been transformed into an enemy. It is immortal, and, when slain, it appears as a *terrifying specter* that looses all its Eumenides. The delusion of the crime, which believes it destroys alien life and thereby extends itself, dissolves in this, that the departed spirit of the injured life steps up against it, as Banquo, who came as a friend to Macbeth, was not wiped out in his murder, but a moment afterward took his seat after all, not as a partaker of the meal, but as Macbeth’s evil spirit. The criminal meant to have to do with alien life, but he has destroyed only his own. For life is not different from life, because life is in the unified divinity. In his arrogance he has indeed destroyed, but only the friendliness of life: he has turned it into an enemy. — This law is the union in the Concept, the equality of the apparently injured life and of one’s own forfeited life. With fate a reconciliation seems still harder to conceive than with the punishing law, since, in order to reconcile fate, the annihilation seems to have to be sublated. But fate has this advantage over the punishing law with regard to reconcilability, that it is within the domain of life; a crime, however, under law and punishment, in the domain of insurmountably opposed actualities. An actuality can only be *forgotten*, i.e. lose itself, as something represented, in another weakness, whereby its being would yet be posited as abiding.”

“From the point at which the criminal feels the destruction of his own life (suffers punishment), or knows himself in the *bad conscience* as destroyed, the effect of his fate begins. This feeling of the destroyed life must become a *longing for what is lost*. What is lacking is recognized as part of him, as that which in him

[p. 494]

should be and is not in him. This gap is not a non-being, but life recognized and felt as non-existent. This fate, felt as possible, is the *fear* of it and is a wholly different feeling from the fear of punishment. The former is the fear of separation, a shying away from oneself, whereas the fear of *punishment* is the fear of something *alien*. For even if the law is recognized as one’s own law, there is yet something alien in the fear of punishment. To the unworthiness there is added in it the actuality of a misfortune, that the Concept of the human being is lost. Punishment therefore presupposes an alien master of this actuality, and the fear of punishment is fear of him. The fear of fate, on the other hand, as the power of life turned hostile, is not fear of something alien. — *Nor does punishment improve*, because it is only a suffering, a feeling of impotence against a master with whom the criminal has nothing in common and wants to have nothing in common. It can only produce *obstinacy*, stubbornness in resisting an enemy by whom to be oppressed would be a disgrace, because the human being would in so doing give himself up. In fate, however, the human being recognizes his own life, and his supplication to it is not a supplication to a master, but a returning and drawing near to himself. Fate produces a longing for the lost life. This longing can — if one is to speak of improving and being improved — already be called an improvement, because it recognizes what is lost as life, as what was once friendly to it. In this cognition there is already in itself an *enjoyment of life*, and the longing can be so *conscientious*, i.e. in the contradiction between the consciousness of its guilt and the life beheld anew, still hold itself back from the return to this life, *so as to prolong the consciousness and the feeling of pain and to provoke it at every moment*, in order to unite itself with life not lightly but from the depths of the soul, and to greet it again as a friend. In sacrifices, in penances, criminals have inflicted pains on themselves — as pilgrims in hair shirts and barefoot at every step upon the hot sand — have prolonged and multiplied the consciousness of evil, the pain, and have, on the one hand, felt through to the full their loss, their gap, and on the other hand, at the same time, beheld this life, although as a hostile one, wholly within it, and so made the resumption entirely possible; for the opposition is the possibility of reunification, and so far as it *was opposed in pain, so far is it capable of being taken up again*. Because even the hostile is felt as life, there lies in this the possibility of the reconciliation

[p. 495]

of fate. This reconciliation is thus neither the destruction, the suppression of something alien, nor a contradiction between the consciousness of oneself and the hoped-for representation of oneself in an Other; or a contradiction between the deserving according to the law and the fulfillment of it, between the human being as Concept and the human being as actual. This feeling of life that finds itself again is *love*, and in it fate is reconciled. Justice is satisfied, for the criminal has felt within himself the same life that he injured. The stings of conscience have grown blunt, for from the deed its evil spirit has departed. There is nothing hostile any more in the human being, and the deed remains at most, lying as a soulless skeleton in the charnel house of actualities, in memory.”

“But fate has a more extended domain than punishment. Even by *guilt without crime* it is provoked, and is for that very reason infinitely stricter than punishment. Its severity often seems to pass over into the most flagrant injustice, when it appears all the more fearsome in the face of the most sublime guilt, the *guilt of innocence*. For because the laws are only thought unifications of oppositions, these Concepts by far do not exhaust the manifold sidedness of life. Punishment exercises its dominion only so far as life has come to consciousness, where a separation has been united in the Concept; but over the relations of life that are not dissolved, over the sides of it that have remained vitally united, beyond the limits of the virtues it exercises no power. Fate, on the other hand, is incorruptible and unbounded, like life. It knows no given relations, no differences of standpoint, of situation, no district of virtue. Wherever life is injured, be it ever so rightfully, ever so much with self-satisfaction, there fate appears, and one can therefore say: *innocence has never suffered, every suffering is guilt*. But the honor of a pure soul is the greater, the more consciousness it has had in injuring life in order to preserve the highest; so much blacker is the crime, the more consciousness an impure soul has in injuring life. A fate *seems* to have arisen only through alien guilt. This is only the *occasion*. What it arises through, however, is the manner of reception and the reaction against the alien deed.”

“By acting, by putting himself in danger, the human being has subjected himself to fate, for he steps onto the battlefield of power against power and ventures against an Other. Courage

[p. 496]

however, is greater than painful endurance, because the former, even if it succumbs, recognized this possibility beforehand, and thus took the guilt upon itself with consciousness, whereas *painful passivity* merely clings to its lack and does not set against it a fullness of strength. The suffering of courage, however, is also a just fate, because the courageous man engaged himself in the domain of right and of power; and for that reason even the struggle for rights is already an unnatural condition, just as much as passive suffering, in which there is the contradiction between the Concept of right and its actuality; for in the struggle for right, too, there lies a contradiction. Right, which is something thought, hence a universal, is in the one who attacks no other thing thought. Thus there would here be two universals that sublate each other and yet are. Just so the combatants are opposed as actual: two kinds of living beings, life in struggle with life, which in turn contradicts itself. — The truth of both opposites, of courage and of passivity, is united in the *beauty of the soul* in such a way that from the former life remains, while the opposition drops out, and from the latter the loss of right remains, while the pain vanishes. And so a sublation of right without suffering emerges, a free elevation above the loss of right and above the struggle. — The more living the relations are from which a noble nature must withdraw because they are stained, since it could not remain in them without defiling itself, the greater is its *misfortune*. This misfortune, however, is neither unjust nor just. It becomes its fate only through its having scorned those relations with its own will, with freedom. All the pains that arise for it from this are then just, and are now its unhappy fate, which it has itself made with consciousness, and it is its honor to suffer justly, for it is so far exalted above these rights that it wanted to have them as enemies. And because this fate lies in itself, it can bear it, can stand over against it, for its pains are not a pure passivity, the superior power of an alien, but its own product. Misfortune can become so great that it drives its fate, in renunciation of life, so far that it must withdraw wholly into the void.”

“But in thus setting over against himself the most complete fate itself, the human being has at the same time *raised himself above all fate*. Life has become unfaithful to him, but he not to life. He has fled it, but not injured it, and he may long for it as for an absent friend, but it cannot pursue him as an enemy. He is vulnerable on no side. Like the bashful plant,

[p. 497]

he draws into himself at every touch, and before he made life his enemy, before he provoked a fate against himself, he flees from life. Thus *Jesus* demanded of his friends that they leave father, mother and everything, in order not to enter into a bond with the dishonored world, and so into the possibility of a fate. Further: whoever takes your coat from you, give him your cloak also; if one member offends you, cut it off. The highest freedom is the *negative* attribute of the beauty of the soul, i.e. the *possibility of renouncing everything in order to preserve oneself*. But whoever wants to save his life will lose it! Thus with the highest guiltlessness the highest guilt, with the sublimity above all fate the most unhappy fate, is compatible. — A heart that is so exalted above the legal relationships, that is entangled in no objective, has *nothing to forgive the offender*. It is open to reconciliation, for it is possible for it forthwith to take up again every living relation, to re-enter into the relationships of friendship, of love, since it has injured no life in itself. On its own side no hostile sensation stands in its way; no consciousness, no demand upon the Other that the violated right be restored; no pride that demanded of the Other the avowal of having been beneath him in a lower sphere, the legal domain. — Apart from the personal hatred that springs from the offense that has befallen the individual and which strives to bring to fulfillment the right that has arisen from it against the Other, apart from this hatred there is indeed still an *anger* of rectitude, a hating severity of conformity to duty, which has to be angry not over an injury to its individual but over its concepts, the commandments of duty. This righteous hatred, in that it recognizes and posits duties and rights for Others, and in judging about them presents them as subjected to the same, posits precisely these rights and duties *for itself*, and, in that in its just anger over the transgressors of the same it makes a fate for them and *does not forgive* them, it has thereby taken from itself the possibility of obtaining forgiveness for faults, of being reconciled with a fate that would strike it on that account; for it has fixed determinacies which do not allow it to raise itself above its actualities, above its faults.”

“*Forgiveness of sins* is therefore not sublation of the punishments, for every punishment is something positive, objective, which cannot be annihilated; not sublation of the evil conscience, for no deed can become a non-deed: but fate reconciled through love

[p. 498]

Hence the rule of Jesus: if you forgive the faults, then yours too are forgiven you by the Father. To forgive others can only be the sublation of enmity, love returned, and this is *whole*. Its forgiveness is not a fragment, not an isolated act. ‘Judge not, that you be not judged.’ Jesus’ confident utterances: ‘Your sins are forgiven you!’ wherever he found faith and love, as with Mary Magdalene. — The return to morality does not sublate the sins and their punishments, fate. The action remains. On the contrary, it becomes only the more tormenting. The greater the morality, the more deeply the immoral aspect of the action is felt.”

#### Love and Shame.

“If the cosmopolitan grasps the human race in its totality, then so much the less falls to any one person of the dominion over objects and of the favor of the ruling being. Each individual loses so much the more of his worth, of the claims of his independence, for his worth was the share in dominion. Without the pride of being the center of things, the end of the collective whole is to him the highest, and he despises himself, as so small a part, like all individuals. Because to this love, surrounded only with matter for the sake of what is dead, matter is in itself indifferent, and its essence consists in this, that the human being in his innermost nature is something opposed, something independent, that everything is to him outer world, which is therefore as eternal as he himself, so *his objects do indeed change, but they never fail him*. As certain as he is, so certain are they and his Godhead. Hence his composure at loss and his certain consolation that the loss will be replaced, because it can be replaced for him. *Matter* is in this way absolute for the human being. But admittedly, if he himself were no longer, then there would also be nothing more for him. And why should he too be? That he would like to be is very comprehensible, for apart from his collection of limitations in his consciousness there lies not the perfected, eternal union in itself, only the barren non-being. The human being is thus only as something opposed. The opposed is reciprocally condition and conditioned. None is unconditioned. None bears the root of its essence in itself. Each is only relatively necessary. The One is for the Other, and thus also for itself, only through an alien power. The Other is allotted to it only through its

[p. 499]

favor and grace. To an alien, independent being must the human being owe thanks for himself and for his immortality, for which he begs with trembling and quaking.”

“True union, genuine love, therefore takes place only among living beings who are equal in power, hence through and through living for one another, in no respect dead to one another. It excludes all oppositions. In love the separated still is, but no longer as separated, rather as united, and the living feels the living. In love the whole is not contained as in the *sum* of many particular, separated things. In it life finds itself, a doubling of itself and its oneness. Life has run through the circle, from undeveloped oneness, through culture, to a completed oneness.”

“Because love is a feeling of the living, lovers can distinguish themselves only insofar as they are *mortal*, as they think the possibility of separation, not insofar as something separated is actual, as the possible, bound up with a being, would be something actual. *In lovers there is no matter.* They are One living whole, and *their own principle of life* says only: they can die. The plant has parts of salt and earth, which bear within themselves their own laws of their mode of operation. The plant can only decay. But love strives to sublate this distinction too, this possibility as a mere possibility, and itself to unite what is mortal, *to make it immortal*. In love what is mortal has laid aside the character of separability and has become a germ of immortality, a germ of what eternally develops and begets out of itself. What is united does not separate again; the Godhead has worked, created.”

“What is separable, so long as before the complete union it is still something of its own, causes the lovers embarrassment. There is a kind of conflict between the total surrender, the only possible annihilation, the annihilation of what is opposed in the union, and the independence still present. The former feels itself hindered by the latter. Love is indignant at what is still separate, at a property. This anger of love at individuality is *shame*. It is not a twitching of the mortal, not an expression of freedom to preserve itself, to subsist. In an attack without love, a loving heart is itself offended by this hostility. Its shame becomes *anger*, which now defends only property, the right. If shame were not an effect of love,

[p. 500]

which only on account of there being something hostile has the shape of displeasure, but were by its nature itself something hostile, which wished to assert an assailable property, one would have to say of *tyrants*: they have the most shame; — as of girls who do not surrender their charms without money; — or of the vain, who want to captivate by them. Neither loves. Their defense of the mortal is the opposite of displeasure over it. They attribute to it in itself a worth, they are *shameless*. A pure heart is not ashamed of love, but it is ashamed that this is not yet perfect. It reproaches itself that there is still a power, something hostile, which is a hindrance to the perfection. Shame enters only through the recollection of the body, through personal presence, in the feeling of individuality. It is not a fear for the mortal, for what is one’s own, but of it, which, as love diminishes the separable, vanishes with it. For love is stronger than fear. It does not fear fear, but, accompanied by it, sublates separations with the apprehension of finding a resisting, indeed a fixed opposition. It is a reciprocal taking and giving. Timid lest its gifts be scorned; timid lest something opposed not yield to its taking, it tries whether hope does not deceive it, whether it wholly finds itself. That which takes does not thereby become richer than the Other; just so that which gives does not thereby become poorer. In giving to the Other, it has increased its own treasures by just as much. *Juliet* in *Romeo*:

#### The more I give, the more I have!”

#### The Son of God and Son of Man.

“One cannot call the condition of Jewish culture a condition of childhood, nor its language an undeveloped childlike language. There are still some deep, childlike sounds preserved in it, or rather restored, but the remaining heavy, forced manner of expressing itself is rather a consequence of the utmost malformation of the people, with which a pure being has to struggle and from which it suffers when it is to present itself in its forms, which it nevertheless cannot do without, since it itself belongs to this people.”

“The beginning of the Gospel of John contains a series of thetic propositions that express themselves in a more proper language about God and the divine.

[p. 501]

It is the simplest language of reflection to say: In the beginning *was* the Logos, the Logos *was* with God, and God *was* the Logos; in him *was* life, etc. But these propositions have only the deceptive semblance of judgments, for the predicates are not Concepts, universals, as the expression of a reflection in judgments necessarily contains, but the predicates are themselves again something that is, something living. This simple reflection too is not skilled at expressing the spiritual with spirit. Nowhere more than in the communication of the divine is it necessary for the recipient to grasp with his own deep spirit; nowhere is it less possible to learn, to take in passively, because immediately everything expressed about the divine in the form of reflection is nonsensical, and a passive, spiritless reception of it not only leaves the deeper spirit empty, but also unsettles the understanding that takes it in and to which it is a contradiction. This ever objective language therefore finds sense and weight solely in the spirit of the reader, and a sense and weight as various as the relations of life and the opposition of the living and the dead have come to consciousness. — Of the two extremes in grasping the opening of John, the *most objective* way is to take the Logos as something actual, an *individual*, the *most subjective* way to take it as *reason*; there as a particular, here as universality; there the most proper, most exclusive actuality, here the mere being-thought. *God and Logos* are distinguished, for reflection presupposes that to which it gives the form of the reflected at the same time as not reflected. That which is must be considered in two respects, once as the *One*, in which there is no division, no opposition, and at the same time *with the possibility of separation*, of the infinite division of the One. God and Logos are distinguished only insofar as the former is the matter in the form of the Logos; the Logos itself is with God; they are One. The manifoldness, infinity of the actual is infinite division as actual. Everything is through the Logos and, insofar, the world is not an emanation of the Godhead. Only *as something actual* is it emanation: part of the infinite division. But at the same time in the part (ἐν αὐτῷ almost better referred to the next οὐδὲ ἓν ὃ γέγονεν) or in the infinitely dividing (ἐν αὐτῷ referred to λόγος) life. Each part, apart from which there is the whole, is at the same time a whole, a life, and this life again, also as a reflected one, as subject and predicate, also in respect of the division, is life, ζώη, and life comprehended, φῶς (truth). These finite things have oppositions. For the light there is darkness. The *Baptist* John was not the light. He

[p. 502]

bore witness only to it; he felt the One, but it did not come purely, restricted only into determinate relations, to his consciousness. He believed in it, but his consciousness was not equal to life. Only *a consciousness that is equal to life* (and the two are different only in this, that the latter is that which is, the former precisely this which is as reflected) is φῶς. — Notwithstanding that John was not himself the φῶς, it was yet in every human being who comes into the world (κόσμος, the whole of human relations, of human life, more restricted than πάντα v. 3 and ὃ γέγονεν). Not merely as the human being is in the world is he φωτιζόμενος. The φῶς is also in the world. All its determinations are the work of the ἀνθρώπου φωτός, of the developing human being, without the world recognizing him. The human world is his own (τὰ ἴδια), what is most kindred to him, but the human beings do not take him up, they treat him as alien. But those who in him recognize themselves obtain thereby power, which is not a new force but only expresses the degree, the equality or inequality of life. They do not become an Other, but they recognize God and themselves as children of God, as weaker than he, *but of the same nature*, insofar as they become conscious of that relation (ὄνομα) of the ἀνθρώπου φωτιζομένου φωτὶ ἀληθινῷ, finding their essence in nothing alien but in God.”

“Hitherto there has been talk only of truth itself and of the human being in general; v. 14 the Logos appears also in the modification as individual (ἄνθρωπος ἐρχόμενος εἰς κόσμον, there is nothing else to which the αὐτόν of the tenth verse etc. could refer). Not merely of the φῶς, v. 7, but also of the individual John bore witness, v. 15. — The Idea of God may be sublimated ever so much, there always remains the Jewish principle of the opposition of thought to actuality, of the rational to the sensuous, of the tearing apart of life, a dead connection of God and the world, a bond which can truly be taken only as a living connection and in which the relations of the related can be spoken of only *mystically*. — The most frequently occurring and most characteristic expression of the relation of Jesus to God is that he calls himself *Son of God*, and, as such, sets himself in opposition to himself as the *Son of Man*. — The designation of this relation is one of the few *natural sounds* that had remained over in the Jewish language of the time and which therefore belongs among its happy expressions. The relation of a son to the father is not a unity, a Concept, as for instance unity, agreement of disposition, equality of principles, and

[p. 503]

the like, a unity which is only something thought and abstracted from the living, but *living relation of living beings*, equal life, only modifications of the same life, not a plurality of absolute substantialities; thus God’s Son *the same essence* that the Father is, but for every act of reflection, yet also only for such, *a particular one*. Also in the expression: a son of the tribe of Koresh, e.g., as the Arabs designate an individual of it, it lies that this individual is not merely a part of the whole, the whole thus not outside him, but he himself precisely the whole that the entire tribe is. This is also clear from the consequence it has for such a natural, undivided people in waging war in its own way, in that each individual is cut down in the most cruel manner; in present-day Europe, on the other hand, where each individual does not carry the whole of the state in himself, but the bond is only something thought, the equal right for all, war is for that reason not waged against the individual but against the whole lying outside him; as with every genuinely free people, among the Arabs each is a part but at the same time the whole. Only of objects, of the dead, does it hold that the whole is something other than the part, in the living by contrast the part is the same One as the whole. If the particular objects, as substances, are yet at the same time, each with its property as individual, summed up *in numbers*, then their common element, the unity, is only a Concept, not an essence, a being: but the living are essences as separated, and their unity is just as much an essence. *What is a contradiction in the realm of the dead is not so in the realm of life.* A tree that has three branches makes together with them One tree, but each son of the tree, also other children, leaves and blossoms, is itself a tree. The fibers that bring sap to the branch are of the same nature as the roots. A tree turned upside down and set into the earth will put out leaves from the roots stretched into the air, and the twigs will take root in the earth. And it is just as true that here there is only One tree as that there are three trees.”

“This unity of essence of the Father and of the Son in divinity the Jews too found in the relation that Jesus gave himself to God. They found, John V, 18, that he made himself equal to God, in that he called God his father. To the Jewish principle of the dominion of God Jesus could indeed oppose the needs of the human being, e.g. the need to satisfy hunger, to the celebration of the Sabbath, but even this only in general. A deeper development of this opposition, e.g. a primacy of practical reason, was not

[p. 504]

in the culture of those times. In his opposition he stood before the eyes only as an individual. *To remove the thought of this individuality*, Jesus appeals, especially in John, always to his unity with God, who has given the Son to have life in himself, as the Father himself has life in himself; that he and the Father are One; that he is bread, come down from heaven, etc.: hard expressions, σκληροὶ λόγοι, which do not become milder by one’s declaring them figurative and, instead of taking them with spirit as life, substituting for them unities of Concepts. To be sure, as soon as one opposes to what is figurative the concepts of the understanding and accepts the latter as the ruling element, then every image must be removed as mere play, as an accessory of the imagination without truth, and instead of the life of the image there remains only something objective.”

“Jesus calls himself, however, not only Son of God but also *Son of Man*. If Son of God expresses a modification of the divine, then Son of Man would just so be a modification of the human being. But the human being is not One nature, One essence, like the Godhead. The Son of Man here means one subsumed under the Concept human being. Jesus is a human being, is a proper judgment; the predicate is not an essence but a universal. The Son of God is also Son of Man. The divine, in a particular shape, appears as human being. The connection of the infinite and the finite is admittedly a holy mystery, because this connection is life itself. Reflection, which separates life, can distinguish it into the infinite and the finite, and only the limitation, the finite considered for itself, gives the Concept of the human being as opposed to the divine; outside reflection, in truth, it does not take place. This significance of the Son of Man emerges most brightly where the Son of Man is opposed to the Son of God, as John V, 26, 27: ‘As the Father has life in himself, so he gave also to the Son to have life in himself; and he gave him also the power to hold judgment, because he is the Son of Man,’ for v. 22: ‘the Father judges no one, but has handed judging over to the Son.’ Against this it says John III, 17 (Matt. XVIII, 11): ‘God has not sent his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world be saved.’ *Judging* is not an act of the divine; for the law that is in the judge is the universal opposed to those to be judged, and judging is a passing of judgment, an equating or unequating, the acknowledging of a thought unity or an irreconcilable opposition; the Son of God does not judge, sunder, divide, does not hold the opposed

[p. 505]

in its opposition, but the world shall be saved by the divine. *Saving* too is an expression that is not well used of spirit, for it designates the absolute powerlessness, against the danger, of the one who is in danger. Salvation is insofar the act of one alien to another alien, and the effect of the divine can be taken as salvation only insofar as the saved becomes alien only to his previous condition, not to his essence. The Father judges not; nor does the Son, insofar as he is One with the Father. But at the same time he has also received power to hold judgment, because he is Son of Man; for the modification is as such something limited, capable of opposition and of separation into universal and particular. But again the human being could not judge if he were not something divine, for only thereby is the standard of judging, the separation, possible in him. In the divine his power to bind and to loose is grounded. Judging can again be of two kinds: to master the ungodly either only in representation or in actuality. Jesus says John III, 18, 19: ‘Whoever believes in the Son of God is not judged; but whoever does not believe in him is already judged,’ because he has not recognized this relation of the human being to God, his divinity; and: ‘their judgment is their greater love of darkness than of truth.’ In their unbelief, then, the judgment itself consists. The divine human being does not approach evil as a *force* ruling and oppressing it, for the divine Son of Man has indeed received power, but not force (distinction of δύναμις and ἐξουσία). He treats, combats the world not in actuality. He brings it its judgment not as the consciousness of a punishment. What cannot live with him, cannot enjoy, what has separated itself and stands apart, whose self-set limits he recognizes as such limitations, even if they are perhaps the highest pride of the world and are not felt by it as limitations, and its suffering perhaps does not have the form of suffering, at least not the form of the retroactive offenses of a law. But their unbelief, their own judgment, is what puts them into a deeper sphere, even if in their unconsciousness of the divine, in their humiliation, they take pleasure in themselves.”

“The relation of Jesus to God as of a son to the father posits, as cognition, *two kinds of natures*, a human and a divine. Those who posit the absolute difference of both substantialities and yet at the same time demand that they be thought as One in the most intimate relation do not, in this respect, sublate the *understanding*,

[p. 506]

that they announced something that would lie outside its domain, but it is the understanding to which they ascribe the demand to grasp absolutely different substances and at the same time the absolute unity of them. They thus destroy them, in that they posit it. Those who accept the given difference of the substantialities but deny their unity are more consistent. To the former they are entitled, for what is required is to think God and human being; and thereby they are entitled to the latter as well, for to sublate the separation between God and human being would go against the first thing demanded of them. In this way they save the understanding, to be sure, but if they remain with this absolute difference of the essences, then they raise the understanding, the absolute separation, *the killing*, to the highest of spirit. — In this way the Jews received Jesus.”

#### The Last Supper.

“The parting that Jesus took from his friends was the celebration of a meal of love. Love is not yet religion, this meal thus really also no properly religious act, for only a union *objectified* by the imagination in love can be the object of a religious veneration. At a meal of love, however, love itself lives and expresses itself, and all actions in it are only expressions of love. Love itself is present only as *sensation*, not at the same time as *image*. The feeling and the representation of it are not united by fantasy. But at the meal of love something objective does occur, to which the sensation is tied, but not united into One image, and therefore this eating hovers between a communal meal of friendship and a religious act, and this hovering makes it hard to designate its spirit clearly. ‘Jesus broke the bread: Take, this is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me! Likewise he took the cup: Drink all of it, this is my blood of the new testament, shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Do this in remembrance of me!’”

“If an Arab has drunk a cup of coffee with a stranger, he has thereby made a bond of friendship with him. This communal act has linked them, and through this link the Arab is bound to him to all fidelity and help. The common eating and drinking is here not what is called a sign.

[p. 507]

Sign and signified are not themselves spiritual, not themselves life. They are alien to each other, and their connection lies outside them in a third, a thought one. To eat and drink with someone is an act of union and a felt union itself, not a conventional sign. It would be against the sensation of natural human beings who are enemies to drink a glass of wine together, for the feeling of community in this act would contradict their otherwise disposition toward one another. — The communal supper of Jesus and his disciples is in itself already an act of friendship. Still more binding is the festive eating of the *same* bread, the drinking from the same cup. This too is not a mere sign of friendship, but an act, a sensation of friendship itself. But the further element, the explanation of Jesus: this is my body, this is my blood, brings the act nearer to a religious one, but does not make it one. This explanation and the act of distributing food and drink connected with it makes the sensation in part objective. The community with Jesus, their friendship with one another, and the union of the same in their center, their teacher, is not merely felt, but, in that Jesus calls the bread to be distributed to all and the wine his body and blood given for them, the union is no longer merely *felt* but has become *visible*. It is not merely represented in an image, an allegorical figure, but tied to something actual, given and enjoyed in an actual thing, a bread. On the one hand, then, the sensation becomes objective, but on the other hand bread and wine and the act of distributing are at the same time not merely objective. *There is more in it than is seen: it is a mystical act*. The spectator who did not know their friendship and had not understood the words of Jesus would have seen nothing but the distributing of some bread and wine and the enjoying of them; as when parting friends break a ring and each keeps a piece, the spectator sees nothing but the breaking of a usable thing and the dividing of it into unusable, worthless pieces; the mystical element of the pieces he has not grasped. So, objectively considered, the bread is *mere* bread, the wine *mere* wine, but both are also something more. This *More* does not cohere with the objects as an explanation through a mere *just-as*. With a simile, a *parable*, in which what is different, compared, is set up as separate: ‘As the individual pieces that you eat are of One bread, the wine that you drink is from the same cup, so you are indeed particular,

[p. 508]

but in love, in spirit One’; but *the thing and the sensation are to unite*. Or if one said: ‘Just as you all partake of this bread and wine, so you also all partake of my sacrifice.’ Or whatever similes one may find in it, the connection would be that of the objective and the subjective, of the bread and the persons, not the connection of what is compared, whereas in the symbolic act the love made objective, this subjective become a thing, returns to its nature and in eating and drinking *becomes subjective again*. This return can in this respect be compared, say, with the *thought become a thing in the written word*, which from a dead thing, an object, in reading *obtains its subjectivity again*. The comparison would be more apt if the written word, read, vanished through the understanding as thing, as in the enjoyment of the bread and wine from these mystical objects not merely sensation is awakened, spirit becomes living, but they themselves vanish as objects. And so the act seems purer, more in keeping with its purpose, in that it gives only spirit, only sensation, and robs the understanding of its own, the matter, the soulless, annihilated. When lovers sacrifice before the altar of the goddess of love and the prayerful outpouring of their feeling inspires them to the highest flame, then the goddess herself has entered into their hearts — but the image of stone remains always standing before them; whereas in the meal of love the bodily vanishes and only living sensation is present. The heterogeneous are bound most intimately. In the expression John VI, 56: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him,’ or John X, 7: ‘I am the door,’ and similar hard juxtapositions, what is bound together must necessarily in representation be separated as different things compared, and the connection regarded as a comparison. Here, however, as with the mystical pieces of the ring, wine and bread become mystical objects. In that Jesus calls them his body and blood and a sensation, an enjoyment, immediately accompanies them, *not only the wine* is blood, the blood too is spirit. ‘The communal cup, the communal drinking, is the spirit of a new covenant, which penetrates many, in which many drink life for elevation above their sins, and of this fruit of the vine I will drink no more until that day of fulfillment, when I will drink it, a new life, with you in the kingdom of my Father.’ The connection of the shed blood is not that it, as something objective to them,

[p. 509]

had been shed for their good, for *a benefit* to them, but (as in the expression: whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood) a like feeling is in all. They are all drinkers, and all are penetrated by the same spirit of love. Were an advantage arising from a surrender of the body and a shedding of the blood, a benefaction, that in which they were put on an equal footing, they would in this respect be united only in the *same* Concept. But in that they eat the bread, drink the wine, his body and blood passes into them, Jesus is in all, and his essence has penetrated them divinely as love. Thus the bread and wine are not merely for the understanding an object; the act of eating and drinking not merely a union that occurs through the annihilation of them in oneself; nor is the sensation a mere taste of the food and drink: *the spirit of Jesus*, in which his disciples are One, *is for the outer feeling, as object, present, has become something actual*.”

“But precisely this kind of an objective union, that love is attached to something visible, to something that is to be annihilated, is what kept the act from becoming a religious one. The bread is to be *eaten*, the wine *drunk*. They can therefore be nothing divine. What they have on the one side as an advantage, that the sensation attached to them returns again from its objectivity, as it were, to its nature, the mystical object becoming again a merely subjective one, that they lose precisely thereby, that love does *not become objective enough* through them. In the parable the demand is not that the different things put together be grasped in One. Here, however, in the symbolic act, eating and drinking — and the feeling of being One in Jesus’ spirit are to flow together. But the thing and the sensation, the spirit and the actuality, do not mix. *Fantasy can never grasp them in One beautiful thing.* The beheld and enjoyed bread and wine can never awaken the sensation of love, and this sensation can never find itself in them as beheld objects, just as it also contradicts the feeling of their actual taking-in, of their subjective becoming, of eating and drinking. *Something divine, insofar as it is divine, cannot be present in the shape of something to be eaten and drunk.* There are always two things present, faith and the thing, devotion and the seeing. To faith the spirit is present, to seeing or tasting the bread and wine. There is no union for them. The understanding *contradicts* the sensation, the sensation

[p. 510]

the understanding. For the imagination, in which both are and are sublated, there is nothing to do. It has here no image to give in which intuition and feeling would unite. — In an *Apollo*, a *Venus*, one must indeed forget the marble, the breakable stone, and sees in their shape only the immortals, and in beholding them one is at the same time penetrated by the feeling of eternal youthful vigor and of love. But if one rubs the Venus, rubs the Apollo to dust and says: this is Apollo, this Venus; then indeed *the dust is before me and the image of the gods in me*, but the dust and the divine never come together into One. The merit of the dust consisted in its form. This has vanished, it is now the main thing. The merit of the bread consists in its mystical sense, but at the same time in its property that it is bread, edible. Even in veneration it is to be present as bread. Before the Apollo ground to dust devotion remains, but it cannot turn to the dust. The dust can recall devotion, but not draw it to itself. There arises a regret, the sensation of this separation, of this contradiction, like the sadness at the irreconcilability of the corpse with the representation of living forces. — After the Last Supper of the disciples there arose a grief on account of the impending loss of their Master, but after a genuinely religious act the whole soul is satisfied. After the enjoyment of the Lord’s Supper among present-day Christians there arises a devout astonishment without cheerfulness, or with a *melancholy cheerfulness*, for the divided tension of sensation and the understanding were one-sided, the devotion incomplete. Something divine was promised and it has melted away in the mouth.”

#### The Miracle.

“The dispute over the *possibility and actuality of miracles* is carried on before various courts and will not soon be able to be put out of confusion until one has come to an understanding with the contending parties on it. *About the truth for fantasy all are agreed*, and only to the fantasy of those are miracles inaccessible with whom the understanding always interferes. At least the power of judgment finds itself always drawn into it, in order to judge the purposiveness with respect to the purpose given. From the side of the aesthetic power of judgment, of the freedom of the imagination,

[p. 511]

*Herder* is the first, perhaps the only one, who has treated the Old Testament in this sense, a treatment of which the New Testament is not capable. The opponents of miracles usually draw the matter before the tribunal of the understanding. Their weapons are experience and the laws of nature. The defenders of miracles fight for their cause with the weapons of a reason, not of the independent one, which sets itself ends independently out of its essence alone, but of a reason to which ends are set from outside and which then, reflecting in accordance with them, now finds subordinate ends, now infers higher ones from them. The conflict between both parties: *whether, in founding the highest science for the human being, one must start from a history?* — reduces itself to the question: Can the highest end of reason be given to it only by itself, does it not contradict the innermost of its essence if it is posited for it from outside or through foreign authority — or is reason incapable of this? — On this point alone the opponents of miracles should pin down the defenders of them. To engage in historical and exegetical discussions, to go onto their field, means not knowing one’s right or not asserting it, and the defenders of miracles have won the game. For even if one could show of each single miracle that it can be explained naturally (whereby, however, all explanations of the kind hitherto turn out, in most cases, forced in the highest degree and as a whole can never turn out satisfying to everyone, until the principle has become general that no history, no authority can posit for reason its highest end), one has already conceded too much to the defender. If only One miracle could not be explained, reason would have lost its right. This is the highest standpoint on which we must place ourselves. To engage in the conduct of the dispute before the tribunal of the understanding already proves that we do not stand firm there, that the narrative of miraculous events has made us hesitate, that we do not venture from there alone to dismiss them out of hand, but that the facts which are given out to us as miracles could be capable of overturning that independence of reason. — If one descends with the defender of miracles onto the field of the understanding, then a long and broad dispute is conducted over possibility and impossibility. This point too is commonly left undecided, and when it comes to particulars the opponent of miracles demands either that the perceptions be raised to experiences, i.e. be explained from laws of nature,

[p. 512]

or, if he despairs of this, he denies the perceptions themselves — and both parties no longer understand one another. The defender of miracles cannot comprehend what interest the opponent can have in explaining away or denying the miracles, for by the very fact that the opponent has engaged in this, he has betrayed his indecision as to whether his reason can stand on its own or not. The ineptitude that he shows, and must show, in his anxiety, in wanting to explain everything, makes him in part hated, because one credits him in this with only evil intentions, in part betrays that he would still have to fear even the slightest remnant of a miracle, and seeks often more to stupefy himself than to acquire, through clear insight, rest and security wholly unconstrained. If the opponent, however, from a polemical intention to convert the other, places himself on a lower standpoint, he undertakes to wash a Moor white and plunges him into doubt and into a condition without hold.”

#### Baptism.

“John’s custom (no such act is known of Jesus) of immersing in water those who had been educated into his spirit is a significant symbolic one. There is no feeling so homogeneous with the longing for the infinite, with the yearning to flow over into the infinite, as the longing to bury oneself in a fullness of water. The one plunging in has before him something alien that immediately flows around him entirely, makes itself felt at every point of his body. He is taken from the world, it from him. He is only felt water that touches him, where he is, and he is only where he feels it. There is in the fullness of water no gap, no limitation, no manifoldness or determination. The feeling of it is the most undistracted, the simplest. The one submerged rises again into the air, separates from the body of water, is already parted from it, but he still drips everywhere from it. As soon as it leaves him, the world around him takes on determinacy again, and he returns strengthened into the manifoldness of consciousness. In looking out into the unshaded blue and the simple formless surface of an Oriental horizon, the surrounding air is not felt. In the submerged there is only One feeling: the *forgetfulness of the world*, a solitude that has cast off everything, wrested itself from everything. As such a withdrawal of everything hitherto,

[p. 513]

as an inspiring consecration into a new world, in which before the new spirit that which is actual hovers undecided between actuality and dream, the baptism of Jesus appears in Mark I, 9 ff.” — Similar developments Hegel applies to the *resurrection* of Christ, in that he engages at the same time with immortality. The main point here for him is the necessity that the element in which individuals with all individual inequality meet cannot be a symbol, an allegory, a personified being, but, in order to be loved, must be an actual *personality*. Hence the resurrection of Jesus had been so important to the first Christians. The union of Christians was not only an *assembly* of such as had similar representations, of those believing the same thing as merely holding it to be true; rather it was a *community*, a union in love and full of life. Yet the community, as directed only toward love, was still imperfect, because it brought with it an impoverishment of culture, an exclusion of many beautiful relations of political ethical life, an indifference toward many cheerful bonds and lofty interests. Thus Hegel came here too to the relation of the Church to the State, but he only began to make the dualism between the two clear to himself in its innermost principles, rather than having already overcome it at that time. Also, although he later recognized the State as that form of objective spirit to which the Church, insofar as it likewise assumes through its praxis an objective shape, must subordinate itself, a wavering in this has constantly attached to him, which in itself lies grounded in this, that religion as invisible Church indeed goes beyond the State, which the hierarchs too know very well, in that they strive to identify the political shape of religion as visible Church with religion itself. A critique of Hegel in this respect has been given by *Rothe* in his *Beginnings of the Christian Church and Its Constitution*, 1837, Introduction § 17, p. 126 ff. At that time Hegel grasped the position of the community toward the world thus: “Apart from the communal enjoying, praying, eating, rejoicing, believing and hoping, apart from the sole activity for the propagation of faith, the enlargement of the communality of devotion, there lies still an immense field of objectivity, which sets up a fate of the most many-sided extent and powerful might and lays claim to manifold activity. In the task of love the community scorns every union that is not the most intimate, every spirit that is not the highest. There is no need to mention the unnaturalness and shallowness of the splendid Idea of a universal love of humanity, since it is not the striving of the community,

[p. 514]

must stop at love itself. Apart from the relation of the communal faith and the presentation of this community in the religious acts relating to it, every other connection to something objective, for the purpose of a development of another side of life, to a common activity, each cooperating for something other than the propagation of faith, and presenting itself and rejoicing in itself in other modifications and partial shapes of life, in games, is alien to the spirit of the community. It would not recognize itself in it. Having left love, its only spirit, it would have become unfaithful to its God. It would also not only have abandoned love but destroyed it, for the members put themselves in danger of colliding with one another with their individualities, in that through culture they betook themselves into the domain of their various characters, into the power of their various fates, and over an interest in something trifling, over a difference of determinacy in something petty, love would turn into hatred and an apostasy from God would follow. *This danger is averted only by an inactive, undeveloped love*, in that it, the highest life, remains lifeless. Thus the unnatural extension of the scope of love entangles in a contradiction, in a false striving, which had to become the father of the most terrible suffering or active fanaticism. This restriction of love to itself, *its flight from all forms, even if its spirit was wafted in them*, this removal from all fate is precisely its greatest fate, and here is the point where Jesus is connected with fate and, though in the most sublime manner, yet suffered from it.”

Hegel concludes the whole with resignation as to the possibility of a sublation of the dualism: “Between these (previously described) extremes of friendship, of hatred or of indifference toward the world, between these extremes, which are found within the opposition of God and the world, of the divine and of life, the Christian church has run through the circle forward and backward; but it is its fate that church and state, divine service and life, piety and virtue, spiritual and worldly doing, can melt together, as it were, into One.”

[p. 515]

VI.

#### Fragments of Historical Studies.
