“*Spirit of the Orientals*: respect for actuality in actuality and embellishment of the same in fantasy. — The Orientals have firmly determined characters. As they once are, they no longer change. The direction of the road they have taken they do not leave. What lies outside their road is for them not present. But what disturbs them on the road is hostile to them. Their once firmly determined character cannot let go of itself, cannot take up into itself what is opposed to it and reconcile itself with it. The one becomes ruling, the other something ruled. Power is the Concept in which the beings are equal. Force is their relation to one another, force of strength or of genius or of speech. A firmly determined character admits nothing outside itself except what it rules or by which it, as it by him, is ruled; for there are barriers, actualities in it, which cannot be sublated, which, if they are to subsist alongside other contradicting actualities, alongside the hostile, can stand in no other relation. Since the barriers of the character give actualities that love cannot unite, they must be bound *objectively*, i.e. stand under a *law*. The sameness of actuality is necessity, hence the law that rules everything. Therefore in the Oriental character the two seemingly contradictory determinations are so intimately bound: *lust for dominion over everything and willing surrender into every slavery*. Over both rules the law of necessity. Dominion and slavery, both conditions are here just, for in both of them the same law of force governs. He is in the Orient the *fortunate* man who has *courage* to subjugate to himself that which is weaker than he, and *prudence* not to attack, and at once to submit to, that which is stronger than he. He is here a *wise man* who withdraws from actualities, is active in speech and in sayings. *Noble* is the more cultured man, who knows how to distinguish and subjugates only so far as he has been resisted, and sets himself equal to the vanquished by recognizing above himself, along with him, the law of necessity; he honors in himself, the actual victor, the possible vanquished, and in the actually subjugated at the same time the possible

[p. 516]

ruler. This possibility of the opposed, this possibility of the infinite manifoldness of the actual as possibly ruling or as possibly subjugated, this power, which appears in the *transitions* of the negative to the positive, of the positive to the negative — is the infinite Godhead of the Orientals. On the loom of its will and its government the events are woven, and from the source of its command there flow into the abyss of its might the streams of the times and centuries. — Given the firm determinacy of the Oriental character, there are very few relations in which the human being stands, and everything that offers itself soon receives its place. The human being of firmly determined character lets himself in with nothing that is not of like kind to him. Most of what can run up against him he waves aside. The rest he combats and becomes master of it, or submits to force, but his claims remain the same. This immutability, this incapacity to be moved many-sidedly by the manifoldness of things, gives the Oriental his repose. Because the world is to him a collection of actualities and these appear only in their naked shape as mere opposites, without their own soul and spirit, he must, in order to help out their poverty, necessarily seek to supply by *foreign, borrowed* splendor what they lack in their own content. The Oriental always embellishes actuality with imagination. He wraps every thing in images. These images too are, to be sure, images of actualities, and one poverty seems unable to lend splendor to another, but they become poetic through their combination. The union of the dissimilar produces a semblance of life that lies in the sameness of the combined. That wherein one knows them to be similar to each other comes, because the diverse is so dissimilar, to a dim consciousness, but a shape of pure life they cannot venture to let emerge. The sublime splendor of their images sets one in amazement, the sunshine of their paintings is dazzling. But precisely because one feels the violence in the combining of the dissimilar, one marvels; because one can make no claim to the splendor of this objective, one is dazzled; because love has not bound, the sensation comes away empty, and the preciousnesses, the pearls of the Oriental spirit, are only wildly beautiful monsters. But where the objectivity of life, stripped of the manifold, emerges as unity, it can only be a Concept, a universal, with which their paintings are filled. — The determinacy of the character admits no great manifoldness of characters. The manifoldness

[p. 517]

of the determinacies would shatter itself. But what lay beyond these determinacies, indeed of like kind in substance with it, but of greater and deeper force, that had to work *wondrously* as something invisible, higher. In the manner of composition of the Oriental empires, lasting or ephemeral, out of the system of obedience and subordination in such wild masses, there shows itself clearly the power which Oriental characters, thus of like kind, but combined with strength, depth and obstinacy, exercise on other Orientals, the blind passivity of the latter toward the former, nearly amounting to annihilation. From this too arises the importance, and therefore the *sparingness* and the *gravity of speech*, of the utterance of an invisible life, unknowable in itself. — As the Orientals adorn the naked actuality of other things with fantasy, so they, who have so incomplete a consciousness of themselves and in the presentation of their nature cannot find any satisfying unity, must overload themselves with foreign ornaments to such a degree. Their *adornment* cannot be a clothing that would receive its form and beauty from the human figure and its own free play, but wholly foreign things; and not natural wholes that one puts on more out of love and adorns oneself with more through one’s own sensation, but shining things stripped of their own life and of a form shaped by life, gold, say, clothed in borrowed forms, ornaments combined in flowers, etc. — With the Orientals, precisely nature was driven out of the natural, and it appeared for itself only as common and subjugated. The feminine heart and the *love of women* alone was no such passion whose enjoyment was dominion. Among many Oriental nations it is a great dishonor, especially among the distinguished, to mention women and what relates to them: either because here even the bravest did not feel themselves lords and were thereby reminded of their weakness; or rather, since none was ashamed of this weakness before himself, and only the mention, the utterance of all that related to this side of human nature, they held to be dishonor, because they honored the feminine as something foreign to their remaining spirit, superior to them, and shrank, through the mention, from relegating it into the class of the remaining multitude of common things. Because they feel that the relation of women can never become that which the relation of all other things is, dominion or servitude, and that they are to them something that does not let itself be treated like these and of which they can become sure, they know no other counsel than to *lock them up*! — The

[p. 518]

Jews had not that shyness. They spoke of the relations of the sexes freely and without ceremony, but everything that relates to them is for them, like everything, a mere actuality, impenetrated by the spirit of love. This, then, does not govern them in the treatment of this matter either, and the treatment is therefore, in their very laws and in the books which contain the sum of their culture, so revolting, base and shameful; for the holier and purer the animating being is, the more abominable it is to present its organs and its expressions as mere things and to treat them as such. — Among the Orientals the *beard* is very holy. Among the Jews no razor might come upon the head of a Nazirite, one consecrated to God. Every seventh year, and perhaps also every fiftieth, which were consecrated to God, no field might be tilled, no vine pruned, no vintage held. In the spontaneous produce of the earth servants, cattle and game were to be able to share freely. It is a very great arbitrariness to let the beard grow. It is, to be sure, though in a very slight degree, an organ of the body, and in this respect the cutting of nails is just as much, and the circumcision so common among the Orientals and commanded among the Jews is surely a still greater mutilation. The retention of the beard cannot therefore be regarded as a respect for the completeness of the human figure, which respect, moreover, flatly contradicts the concealment of the figure by tasteless clothing and its overloading with glittering and manifold ornament. An arbitrariness which one imposes upon oneself as law is maintained with all the greater obstinacy, just as the sacrifice has the more merit, the greater the arbitrariness to which one submits. But why did the Orientals impose upon themselves precisely this arbitrariness? Why with the importance that the beard is even something holy? Since in the Oriental spirit all worth and subsistence lie in the infinite object, since it can hold nothing of a self-subsisting thing that has a life of its own in itself, it must deck itself out from without, through glittering things in which there is no life, and make something of itself nonetheless; and so it also seeks to preserve most of all the beard, which is the most unessential thing in its organic wholeness, and to honor most the thing about it that is most indifferent.”

“*Memory* is the gallows on which the Greek gods hang strangled. To exhibit a gallery of such hanged men, to drive them round in a circle with the wind of wit, to make them tease one another

[p. 519]

and to blow them into all sorts of groups and distortions, is often called poetry. — Memory is the grave, the repository of the dead. The dead rests in it as dead. It is shown like a collection of stones. The arranging, going through, dusting, all these occupations have, to be sure, a relation to the dead, but are independent of it. — But to babble unintelligible prayers, to read masses, to say rosaries, to perform meaningless ceremonies of worship, this is the doing of the dead. Man tries to become wholly object, to let himself be governed utterly by something alien. This service is called devotion. Pharisee!”

“*Keening women* at the public funeral rites for those who fell in the first year of the Peloponnesian War. Thucydides, B, λδ: καὶ γύναικες πάρεισιν αἱ προσήκουσαι ἐπὶ τὸν τάφον ὀλοφυρόμεναι [and the women related to them are present at the tomb, lamenting]. The greatest relief of grief is to cry it out, to have said it purely in its whole extent. Through utterance grief is made objective, and the equilibrium is restored between the subjective, which alone is present, and the objective, which in grieving is nothing. Through utterance alone does it come to consciousness, and what has come to consciousness is then over. It is brought into the form of reflection and is pushed away by subsequent determinations. But when the heart is still full, grief still wholly subjective, nothing else has room in it. Tears too are such a discharge, such an utterance, an objectification of grief. Grief has then, since it is subjective and has also become objective, made itself into an image. But since grief by its nature is subjective, it is very loath to go out of itself. Only the highest distress can drive it to this. But when the distress is past, when everything is lost and it has become despair, it shuts itself up in itself, and here it is most beneficial to bring it out. This can be done by nothing heterogeneous. Only by being given to itself does it have itself as itself and as something partly outside itself. A painting does not have this effect. It only sees, but does not itself move. Speech is the purest form of objectivity for the subjective. It is not yet anything objective, but yet the movement toward objectivity. Lament in song has at the same time still more the form of the beautiful, because it moves according to a rule. Laments sung by hired women are therefore the most human thing for grief, for the need of discharging itself, in that one most deeply

[p. 520]

develops it for oneself and holds it before oneself in its whole extent. Only this holding-before-oneself alone is the balm.”

“Thucydides, B, λϛ: τὰ δὲ πλέω αὐτῆς (ὅσην ἔχομεν ἀρχὴν) αὐτοὶ ἡμεῖς· οἱ δὲ, οἳ νῦν ἔτι ὄντες μάλιστα κ. τ. λ. [but the greater part of it (the empire we hold) we ourselves, those of us who are still alive, etc.]. So only the popular assembly of a small free state can speak. Before it and from its mouth such words as *We* have complete truth. In larger republics they are always very restricted. The *We* is always the more foreign to those who utter it, the greater the multitude of their fellow citizens. The share of each individual in a deed is so slight that he can hardly speak of it at all as his deed. The share in the glory of his nation is greater, but it says only: *I belong to the nation*, not: *I am*. This whole exercises a dominion over him, under which he stands. A free great people is therefore in this respect a contradiction in itself. The people is the totality of all individuals, and all and each are always ruled by the whole. Their deed, that which is the deed of *each one*, is an infinitely small fragment of a national action.”

“Before Lycurgus, after an absence of ten years, returned to Sparta in order now to carry out the completed plan of his legislation, he consulted the oracle at Delphi about it. The Pythia called him, in the name of Apollo, a friend and favorite of the gods. She told him he was more a god than a man. She declared to him that Apollo approved the plan he had made; if he could bring about the adoption of his laws, there would be no better-ordered republic in the world than the Lacedaemonian. — After he had now gradually introduced his laws, he betook himself again to the oracle, which pronounced that he had provided sufficiently for making the Lacedaemonians as happy as they were virtuous, and that if they steadfastly kept his laws, they would enjoy eternal glory and happiness. — Had the Lacedaemonians and the other Greeks been capable of submitting to positive divine laws, indeed, of so much as having an idea of them, would not the Lacedaemonians have had to bind the other Greeks, to preach to them, to adopt likewise their constitution, which a pronouncement of the universal oracle had declared the most perfect? Would not the others, in order to be consistent, have had to adopt the same? — But the Greeks were

[p. 521]

a free nation, which *would let not even a god give them laws*. This motive, confirmation by the Deity, was foreign to them.”

I pass over a multitude of similar aphorisms, because their content has emerged again in Hegel’s later lectures, albeit altered by the context. Yet I should think I was withholding too much from the reader if I did not communicate some reflections relating to the Greek and Roman world, inasmuch as the force of the original freshness of cognition gives their form a quite special charm. Let one imagine for once that these reflections were contained in letters, and then ask oneself whether one would leave them out of a biography. Do they not present to us the process of the conquest of Ideas? That Hegel himself set store by these aphorisms is evident not only from their preservation but especially from the *care* with which he often improved the *style* in detail. Through these fragments we get, alongside the already canonical Hegel, as it were an apocryphal one for elucidation. Not to take delight in the boldness and abruptness of such effulgurations, but to take offense at them, would betray only one’s own narrow-mindedness and poverty of soul.

“After the downfall of Roman and Greek freedom, when the dominion of their Ideas over the objects had been taken from men, the genius of humanity split apart. The spirit of the *corrupted multitude* said to the objects: I am yours, take me! threw itself into their stream, let itself be swept along by them, and perished in their change. — The spirit of the *Stoics* did the opposite. It said: you are foreign to my essence, which knows nothing of you; I rule you in my Idea; you may be as you will, that is indifferent to me, you are too contemptible to me for me to want to lay hand on you. — *Other* spirits felt that the objects ought to be otherwise, but they had not the courage to seize and to shape them. Their superior power weighed upon them and left them only the feeling of their impotence. One part of these spirits formed for itself objects invisible to the senses, which it found in the delusion of the people, but it transferred its Ideas to them and implored them: take me up into your essence, appear to us, reveal yourselves to us, draw us to you, rule us! They were called *Theurgists*. — Another part of the latter spirits heard of a similar new object, fled the

[p. 522]

outer objects that were denied it, threw itself into the arms of the faith that that Invisible would rule them themselves and the outer objects — and they were called *Christians*. The developed Church has united both, the wish of the Stoics and of those inwardly broken spirits. It permits man to live in the whirl of the objects, and promises, through easy exercises, manual tricks, movements of the lips, etc., at the same time to raise himself above them. The wish of the Theurgists has properly come only here and there into the head of so-called Christian *visionaries*. This union has never actually become a trade, like the rest.”

“In the series of the revelations of God, or in the successive descent and generation of his shapes, his revelations as sun, stars, sea, air, love, preceded his revelation as *man*. The latter shape was necessary in the graded sequence of his generations. Nature was subjected, by the institution of the Roman state, which took freedom from almost the whole known earth, to a law alien to man, and the connection with it was torn. Its life became stones and woods; the gods became created and serving beings. Where force stirred, beneficence revealed itself, greatness ruled, there was man’s heart and character. For the Athenians Theseus became a hero only after his death. To Demetrius and Antigonus they sacrificed only when they were departed. The Roman Caesars were deified. Apollonius of Tyana worked miracles. The great was no longer supernatural but contrary to nature, for nature was no longer divine, therefore no longer beautiful and no longer free. In this *separation of nature and of the divine* a man became the connector of both, therefore the reconciler and redeemer. — The people of the *Jews*, however, has gone to hell in the wickedness of hatred. What of it has staggered on later upon the earth has remained as a sign. As the more recent peoples must have under them all forms of humanity, the noble ones indeed only in suffering, so this people too still stands beneath them as the ideal of the most abject. In Homer’s world the manifoldness closes at the bottom with Thersites, who has only a useless tongue. Yet after he has been beaten, a tear falls from his eye. Full of fear and silent he sits down and wipes away the tear. His fear and his silence acknowledge mightier human beings. This receptiveness at least for the better had to remain to the worst of the Homeric

[p. 523]

men. But in a more recent human world one sees, beside Amalia’s heavenly pure soul, Schufterle roasting children at the fire, and when the Captain, now becoming conscious of his fate, threatens the robbers with a fearsome muster, they think he is in a bad mood today. In such a jumble of different species, which together are called Man by the systematist, the Jew has his place. A man among the Jews good-naturedly let God say: whoever heeds not my commandments, him will I punish to the third and fourth generation. But the Furies of their religion are already lashing them into their hundredth. Yet perhaps they do not think themselves punished when the Christian throws them down the stairs because they are Jews, when for the gain of a couple of kreuzers they have let themselves be treated abjectly for hours and begin, even in the third hour, to chatter, — and when they come back the next day.”

“What a cultivated taste and a prejudice-free reason, which know how to appreciate the nobility of the Greek spirit in its whole compass, in all its modifications, still find to object to, is *the ignoble in the passion of love*, which among the nations of German descent, in more recent history, has won a quite different, more sublime shape. Should this phenomenon not also be connected with the spirit of their free life? If a knight from the times of chivalry were to relate to an *Aristides* the deeds he did for his beloved, the adventures he underwent for her, the long series of years each moment of which was devoted with iron patience solely to one purpose, which his beloved had set him; if such a one, in so doing, left Aristides in *doubt* as to who had been the object of this activity; — or if a noble young man were to paint to this same Aristides, with all the fire of imagination, in just the same indefinite way the beauty of his beloved object, to describe to him the deep regard he felt for her, the holiness and purity of his sensation, the inspiration in her nearness, how it were the sole interest of his life to work for her, to breathe; — would not Aristides, who did not know to whom all this expenditure of feelings, deeds and inspiration was devoted, reply perhaps in the following manner: I dedicated my life to my fatherland; I knew nothing higher than its freedom and its welfare; I worked for it without any claim to distinction

[p. 524]

or power or wealth, but I am conscious that I did not do so much for it, did not feel so exclusive and deep a regard; I know otherwise indeed Greeks who did more, who were more highly inspired, but I know none who had come to this height of sensation, of self-denial, on which you stand. And what was the object of this your lofty life? It must be infinitely greater, worthier, than the highest I could think of, greater than fatherland and freedom!”

“The *unbridled imagination of the women of the Middle Ages* raged about in the horrors of witchcraft, in the craving to exercise petty envy and revenge on others, and brought them to the stake. To the Greek women a permitted scope for raging themselves out was given in the *Bacchic* festivals. The exhaustion of body and imagination was followed by a quiet withdrawal into the circle of ordinary sensation and traditional life. The wild Maenad was for the rest of the time a sensible woman. There witches, here Maenads; there the object of the fantasy devilish grimaces, here a beautiful, vine-wreathed god; there, associated with it, satisfaction of envy, vindictiveness, hatred, here nothing but purposeless pleasure, often going as far as raging frenzy; there progress from isolated fits of madness to complete and lasting derangement of the mind, here return to ordinary life; there the age regarded this feigned frenzy not as an illness but as the most blasphemous outrage, which could be expiated only with the stake, here this need of many feminine fantasies and temperaments was something holy, for whose outbreaks festivals were given, sanctioned by the state, and thereby brought into the possibility of becoming harmless.”

“*Contempt of men.* Everyone is accustomed to judge others by the rule he has made for himself for *humanity*, and to demand that he be so. Only long experience of the world or an excess of goodness of heart brings us back from this. This demand is peculiarly European. It is a kind of obstinacy. Thus it is also a sign of our times and nothing further — not high culture, not approach to the purpose of humanity, to perfection — the public judgment of characters, e.g.

[p. 525]

of a *Rousseau*, by the rules of reason. Besides the fact that each should first look into his own bosom, it is only *virtue* alone, which gives itself rules, that can judge and demand, but no *man* has against another the right to put himself in the place of virtue and, representing its person, to make demands on others. Anyone can answer such a one: virtue has the right to demand this of me, but not you.”

“*In the states of the modern age security of property* is the hinge on which the whole legislation turns, to which most of the rights of citizens relate. In many a free republic of antiquity the strict right of property, the care of all our authorities, the pride of our states, has already been impaired by the very constitution of the state. In the Lacedaemonian constitution security of property and of industry was a point which hardly came into consideration at all, which, one may almost say, was forgotten. In Athens the rich citizens were usually deprived of a part of their fortune. Yet one made use of a pretext honorable for the person whom one wished to rob: namely, one entrusted him with an office that demanded enormous expense. Whoever in the tribes, into which the citizens were divided, had been chosen for a costly office, could look around among the citizens of his tribe to see whether he might not find a richer man. If he believed he had found such a one and the latter asserted that he was less rich, the former could propose to him an exchange of their fortunes, which the latter might not refuse. How greatly the disproportionate wealth of some citizens is dangerous even to the freest form of constitution and capable of destroying freedom itself, history shows in the example of a Pericles at Athens, of the patricians in Rome, whose downfall the threatening influence of the Gracchi and others sought in vain to check by proposals of agrarian laws, of the Medici at Florence — and it would be an important inquiry how much of the strict right of property would have to be sacrificed to the durable form of a republic. One has perhaps done the system of sans-culottism in France an injustice if one sought the source of the greater equality of property intended by it solely in rapacity.”

[p. 526]

“*In Italy*, where political freedom had presented itself in purer forms and fairer features, but was lost somewhat earlier than in Germany, jurisprudence rose in Bologna earlier than poetry, and the noblest of the people streamed there from all sides and contented themselves with becoming learned and exact judges in their fatherland, for *on the judgment seat alone were they still servants of an Idea*, servants of the laws, since otherwise they were only servants of a *man*. — In the medieval history of Central and Upper Italy we find the connection of men into states extremely incomplete and the bonds extremely loose. The history of Italy in this period is not really the history of a people or of several peoples, but rather that of a *multitude of individuals*, and because in this picture no great masses appear, or only for short periods and at once disperse again, it is extremely hard to find general points of view for it. The more interesting is the history of single men, since their individuality has not gone under in the general forms of state and constitution. It is usually only an interest of the moment that unites men. Seldom do we see a union that had a lasting interest as its ground. All disputes concerned the rights of single families and men, who could never be brought to give up some of their rights for the good of social union. Living together in cities was more a being-beside-one-another in the same space, within the same walls, than subjection under the same laws. The power of the magistracy was weak. Absolutely no Ideas yet ruled. The open country was not only covered with an innumerable number of castles, which each had built for his security; every palace of the families in the city too was fortified with towers and in other ways, where they besieged one another. *The administration of justice was only the victory of one faction over the other.*”

“*Public capital punishment.* Montesquieu makes, on the occasion of the Japanese, the remark that the many public and at the same time cruel executions have made the character of the people wild and indifferent to these punishments themselves, as to the crimes. Whence this phenomenon, which produces just the opposite of the purpose which legislators and judges had in view in public punishments, namely terror and fear of crimes?

[p. 527]

Is it merely habit that takes from death by the executioner, from the fearful preparations for it, from the anguish of death and the general contempt or, what is still more oppressive to many, the general pity, its loathsome, ghastly and horrible aspect? Habit would produce only indifference, as in the warrior, at whose right a thousand and at whose left ten thousand fall. What is it actually that first strikes the eye at an execution, and what sensation is occasioned by that appearance? — A defenseless man it is that strikes our eyes, bound, surrounded by a numerous guard, held by dishonorable hangman’s assistants, led out and there, quite defenseless, amid the exhortation and prayer of the clergy, which the evildoer cries out after them in order to drown the consciousness of the present moment. So he dies. The *soldier* who is cut down beside another, or, struck by an invisible bullet, falls down, does not awaken in us the sensation that the execution of the evildoer produces. I think that in this last moment we feel that a man has been deprived of *his right to defend himself for his life*. The man who dies in combat with another may be pitied by us, but it does not have for us the offensiveness that the death of the former has, for the latter has still exercised his natural right to defend himself for his life. He fell also only in that the other asserted the same right. The revolting sensation of seeing a defenseless man executed by an armed number, moreover a superior one, is kept from turning into rage in the spectators only by this: that *the pronouncement of the law is holy* to them. But this representation is not able wholly to repress that sensation, which is produced by the immediate sight. If the executioners are indeed servants of justice, yet this mere representation has not been able to suppress the general feeling which branded with the mark of *dishonor* the trade or station of these men, who here before the eyes of the whole people can kill a defenseless man in cold blood, who here, quite as blind instruments, like the wild beasts to which criminals were formerly thrown, perform their service. The enlightened understanding may decry this voice of the people and the obscure feeling on which it is grounded as prejudice as much as it likes, may repeat to it ever so urgently that in the analysis of that feeling it finds no rational ground, and on the other hand sees the executioners as servants of the state and of justice, who do their duty, in parallel with other state officials, it will, as it has happened to it with so many

[p. 528]

other feelings, be unable to suppress these either. The fair-minded man, however, will always know how to distinguish the man himself from the trade that outrages his feeling, and to let him have justice, even if he wished him another trade, just as he would not otherwise either, convinced of the shamefulness of the custom or habit of a people, on that account hold for a scoundrel an individual with whom he had to do. — A striking remark is said to have been made about the men of this station: that on the whole they are quiet, upright and for the most part pious people. Should their occupation, which shows them most immediately the punishment of crimes, have this effect, or not rather a self-feeling to save their individuality against the contempt that is shown to their station; the feeling that worthiness of the person is independent of the esteem or disesteem of the station? — Among the Greeks I do not know that there were public executions. Socrates at least drank the cup of poison in prison, and Orestes, in Euripides, was himself to carry out on himself the mode of death he had chosen. Were anyone nowadays to make the proposal to abolish the publicity of capital punishments, he would have a thousand tongues cry out against him that a principal ultimate end of punishments, *the example for others*, would thereby be lost. It seems the Greeks did not conceive this ultimate end of punishments to themselves, and their legislators did not think it necessary, by a horrible spectacle, to shake the feeling and the imagination and thereby to replace what inner morality and respect for the laws could not effect. The asserted necessity of cruel public punishments proves on the whole nothing further than the little confidence that legislators and judges could place in the ethical feeling of their people. — Just as loudly one would say against such a proposal that, if death sentences were not carried out publicly, there would be one check upon wrong the less for *unscrupulous judges*. Despotism would murder more unscrupulously in the dark than it dares to do publicly. (Are the executions in Venice all carried out privately, or only those of state criminals?) Against citizens of a state who had this to fear and who raised this objection, nothing is to be answered; and in general in every state in which a court not elected by the people from its midst — behind closed doors passes sentence on the life of a fellow citizen, nothing is so much to be wished for the subjects as that this shadow of an importance of the voice of the public be preserved, for before the public

[p. 529]

execution the court justifies itself, as it were, for its pronouncement of sentence, which is read out with reasons, in the eyes of the people. But in states in which the citizen has the right to be tried by his peers, where everyone has free access to the courtroom, this inconvenience would fall away.”

“*Hume* characterizes himself as a historian of modern times at once through the character of what happened itself. The object of his history is a state of modern times, whose inner relations are not only, as also among the ancients, determined by law, but also have their subsistence more through the form of right, less through the unconscious free life in them. The legal, the consciousness of universality and at the same time of opposition, of particularity, assigns the various estates indeed their place, but men do not act as whole men from an *Idea* that animated all. Their force and power is, invisibly to be sure, this Idea, but what comes to consciousness is first of all their external relation to their fellow-actors as *commanding or obeying, in different gradations and kinds* of business. The men who stand at the head and as whose deeds history gives us the events always have the state, with all the manifoldness of its relations, above them and outside them. It is in them as thought. It determines them; they reckon by it, let it pass before them in consciousness, and so it is not so much the *character* that we see immediately in acting, but the *considerations* according to which he acts. His actions themselves are for the greater part command or obedience. Besides the fact that the state as thought is already the determining thing, no one has done an action *wholly*. — Because the whole of an action, in which each actor has only a fragment, is splintered into so many parts, so also the whole work is a result from so many individual actions. The work is *not done as deed, but as a conceived result*. The consciousness of the deed as a whole is in none of the actors. The *historian* cognizes it from the results and has already been made attentive, in what precedes, to what brings these about. As *actors* only the commanders, or those who in some way have influence on the commanders, can be regarded; the rest helps toward it in its order. Because everything is ordered and *the power of this order* rules, most appear only as wheels of a machine. The living thing, the alteration

[p. 530]

in the organization of it is *small, gradual and invisible*. Because everything in it is determined, no great man can be adhered to by peoples, as the Sicilians to Timoleon, nor can anyone make such whole plans individual to him as Alcibiades, Themistocles, etc., which plans make up the great man, but his action is more only *conduct* in a determined, given circle.”

A special critical task Hegel undertook with *Schiller’s* History of the *Thirty Years’ War*, which, after first appearing in fragments in the Ladies’ Almanac, was printed as a whole in 1793. Hegel cites, in his glosses, according to this edition:

p. 519. “But Johann Georg’s subsequent conduct uncovered the motives which had kept him from availing himself of his advantage over the Emperor and from furthering the plans of the King of Sweden by an expedient activity.” The greater part of the period lies in “furthering,” while its purpose is to give the opposite to be understood. This opposite lies in the word “kept.” This is meant to bring about the negative sense of the whole, the greater part of which nevertheless contains the same thing expressed positively.

p. 504. “Where the way of kindness (namely toward the conversion of the Protestants) availed nothing, soldierly help was employed to frighten the strayed back into the sheepfold of the Church.” In this addition the manner of the conversion is the main idea. This manner is expressed specifically: kindness and soldierly help. Although that idea whose manner of execution is given here must necessarily already have been expressed *before* and is very prominent, its expression in this addition nevertheless takes up again almost the one whole and moreover large half. Further, it stands *at the end*. Through both circumstances it lifts itself out above the main idea, the manner of the conversion, and remains in the mind. The expression “frighten” alone still has a relation to the manner and improves the fault somewhat in that it still reproduces the main idea. — The second period after this has again for its conclusion: “to preach the gospel to the heretics.” It blurs the historical somewhat, brings the already sufficiently expressed main idea to the reader once more — and the next period ends again with: “to carry through his purpose.”

The *character portraits* are excellent. For them large periods

[p. 531]

in which many traits gather into unity, are most suitable. But this becomes mannerism when Schiller uses it for the presentation of a *situation* that is composed of many external *circumstances*, and especially when it is a situation for a circumstance that is not coordinated, as a connection of cause and effect in time and space, into one deed. The traits are then too much separated from one another, too heterogeneous. Their unity is only the point to which they are related as preceding; e.g. p. 501: “Reinforced by the troops which went over to him from the enemy garrison, the Saxon General von Arnheim directed his march to Lusatia, which province an imperial general, Rudolph von Tiefenbach, had overrun with an army, to chastise the Elector of Saxony for his going over to the party of the enemy.” What disparate things are gathered here! The “going over” should stand all the more before the “reinforced,” because this is only a subsidiary circumstance. Then the going over of the enemy garrison of Leipzig stands immediately beside the directing of the march to Lusatia, — and the end of the period is the chastising of the Elector by the imperial general — things that lie far enough apart. The grammatical connection is only for the understanding, not for the imagination. The placing of sentences beside one another without relative pronoun is the true connection, conformable to the series of events. The Romans in the historical style have often many sentences in the *infinitive*.

p. 508. “This unexpected, inexplicable lack of resistance *aroused Arnheim’s mistrust* all the more, since the hurried approach of the relief force from Silesia was no secret to him and the Saxon army, supplied with too few siege implements, was also by far too weak in number to storm so large a city. *Afraid* of an ambush, etc.” Arnheim’s mistrust is the main idea, which is still heightened by the grounds of his mistrust. These grounds are *thoughts* in Arnheim’s soul. Through their enumeration, however, they become events and *circumstances* for us. We forget to see them only in Arnheim’s soul, we see them ourselves and lose thereby the main idea, Arnheim’s mistrust. This should therefore stand at the end. Often, in order to depict the situation of a hero, the most disparate things are in this way put together in the unity of his thinking as end and means. The Greeks narrate on. One sees only the external action of the doer, not it as his thought, as his purpose. But it always characterizes very well whether *the deed was* purpose

[p. 532]

and still more important is it whether the purpose was *great*. This is recognized from the deed. If that was great and this small, the man is a small spirit. — The nesting of sentences into one another by means of the relative pronoun disrupts the natural sequence in the order of the sentences and has its ground partly in the awkwardness of the relative particles, partly in the lack of the absolute ones, etc.”

[French] “In the monarchy the people was an active power only for the moment of combat. Like a paid army it had to keep its ranks not only in the heat of the fight itself, but immediately after the victory to return into a perfect obedience. Our experience is accustomed to see a mass of armed men enter, at the word of command, into a regulated fury of carnage and into the lotteries of death and life, and at the same word return into calm. The same was demanded of a people that has armed itself. The word of command was liberty, the enemy tyranny, the commander in chief a constitution, subordination obedience toward its representatives. But there is much difference between the passivity of military subordination and the fire of an insurrection; between obedience to the order of a general and the flame of enthusiasm which liberty pours through all the veins of a living being. It is this sacred flame that strained all the nerves, it is for it, to enjoy it, that they had strained themselves. These efforts are the enjoyments of liberty, and you want it to renounce them; these occupations, this activity for the public cause, this interest is the agent, and you want the people to throw itself again into inaction, into ennui?”

#### VII.

#### The Concept of the Positivity of Religion, 1800.

The Concept of the positivity of religion has arisen and become important only in more recent times. A positive religion is opposed to the *natural* one, and thereby it is presupposed that there is only *One* natural one, because human nature is only One, but that of positive religions there can be *many*. Already from this opposition

[p. 533]

it is clear that a positive religion would be a *counter-natural or supernatural* one, which contains Concepts, items of knowledge that are transcendent for the understanding and reason; demands feelings and actions that would not proceed from the natural man, but, as concerns the *feelings*, are forced out *violently*; as concerns the *actions*, are done only on command and out of obedience, without one’s own interest.”

“One sees from this general explanation that, in order to be able to declare a religion or a part of it positive, the Concept of human nature, and with it also its relation to the Deity, must have been determined. In more recent times people have been very much occupied with this Concept. One believed oneself more or less clear about the Concept of the vocation of man, in order now, with it as standard, to go to the sifting of religion itself. A long course of culture, extending over centuries, had to run its course before a period could come in which the Concepts became so abstract that one persuaded oneself to have comprehended the infinite manifoldness of the appearances of human nature in the unity of some general Concepts. These simple Concepts, because of their generality, become at the same time necessary Concepts, characters of humanity. All the remaining manifoldness of customs, habits and opinions of peoples or of individuals becomes, through these characters being fixed, accidentalities, prejudices and errors, and thereby the religion that suited this manifoldness a positive religion, because the relation of it to accidentalities is itself an *accidentality*, but as a part of religion at the same time a *holy commandment*.”

“One has made it now a reproach, now a praise to the *Christian* religion that it adapted itself to the most diverse customs, characters and constitutions. The corruption of the *Roman* state was its cradle. The Christian religion becomes dominant when this empire was in its sinking, and one does not see that its fall was arrested by it. On the contrary, it gains thereby in extent of territory and appears at the same time as the religion of the over-refined slavish Romans and Greeks, swimming in the basest vices, as of the most ignorant, wildest, but freest barbarians. It was the religion of the *Italian* states in the fairest times of their wanton freedom in the Middle Ages, and of the earnest free *Swiss republics*, of the monarchies of modern Europe, moderated in manifold degrees, as well

[p. 534]

as the religion of the most downtrodden serfs and of their masters: both attend *One* church. With the cross going before, the *Spaniards* murdered whole generations in America, the *English* sang Christian hymns of thanks for the devastation of India. From its bosom the loftiest blossoms of the plastic arts sprang forth, the lofty edifices of the sciences rose up, and in its honor all beautiful art has also been banished, the cultivation of the sciences reckoned as godlessness. Under all climates the tree of the cross has thriven, has struck roots and borne fruit. All the joys of life peoples have tied to it, and the most unhappy gloom has found in it its nourishment and justification.”

“Infinite *modifications* the general Concept of human nature admits of, and it is not a makeshift to appeal to experience that modifications are necessary, that human nature never was present pure, but it can be strictly proved. It is sufficient only to fix what then the *pure* human nature would be? This expression is to comprise nothing in itself but the conformity to the general Concept. But *living* nature is eternally something other than the *Concept* of it, and thereby that which for the Concept was mere modification, pure accidentality, a superfluity, becomes the necessary, the living, perhaps the only natural and beautiful.”

“With this the standard set up at the beginning for the positivity of religion now acquires a quite different aspect. The general Concept of human nature will no longer be sufficient; freedom of the will becomes a one-sided criterion, for the customs and characters of men and the religion connected with them do not depend on a determination by mere Concepts. In every form of culture there would have to occur the consciousness of a higher power and with it representations that are transcendent for understanding and reason. If the ordinary life of men does not supply feelings that must occur in nature, violent arrangements become necessary to produce those feelings, to which, to be sure, something of violence always clings. Likewise, actions which the most natural religion demands, but which in times when everything has become unnatural would likewise fall away, are done only on command out of blind obedience. To be sure, religion has now become positive, but it has also *only become* so, it was not so originally. *Religion must now be positive, because otherwise there would be none at all.* It remains only as a legacy of past times

[p. 535]

remains. Its demands are then still respected and perhaps the more highly honored and feared, the more unknown its essence is. Also to tremble before an Unknown, in one’s mode of action to renounce one’s own will and to submit oneself wholly to given rules like a machine; without any understanding, through doing and renouncing, speaking and keeping silent, to lull oneself into a shorter or lifelong dullness of feeling — all this *can be natural*, and a religion that breathed that spirit would not on that account be positive, just because it was suited to the nature of its age. A nature that required such a religion would indeed be a wretched nature, but the religion would fulfill its ultimate purpose. It would give this nature something higher, such as it alone can bear and in which it finds satisfaction. Only when another courage awakens, when it acquires a self-feeling and with it demands freedom for itself, does not place it merely in the religion’s overpowering essence, can the religion it has had hitherto seem positive to it. The general Concepts of human nature are too empty for them to be able to furnish a standard for the particular and necessarily more manifold needs of religiosity.”

“One would have understood what precedes badly if one wished to see in it a justification of all the presumptions of established religions, of all superstition, of all ecclesiastical despotism, of all dullness engendered or nourished by false religious institutions. No! the most feeble-minded, the harshest superstition is for a soulless being having human shape nothing positive; but as soon as soul awakens in it and the demand of superstition remained, then it would become positive for him who otherwise stood quite unconstrained under it. For the judge, however, it is necessarily something positive, precisely because for him, as judge, an *Ideal* of humanity must hover before him. An Ideal of human nature, however, is quite something other than general Concepts about the human vocation and about the relation of man to God. The Ideal allows quite well particularity, determinacy, and demands even peculiar religious actions, feelings, usages, a superfluity, a multitude of superfluous things, which before the lantern-light of general Concepts appears only as ice and stone. Only *when the superfluous abolishes freedom*, i.e. when it makes pretension against understanding and reason and contradicts their necessary laws. The generality of this criterion must be limited by this, that *understanding and reason* can be judges only when they are appealed to; *what makes no claim to be sensible or rational*

[p. 536]

*belongs not at all to their jurisdiction*. And herein lies a main point, whose neglect produces such opposed judgments. Understanding and reason can summon everything before their judgment seat, and easily arises the presumption that everything *is to be* sensible, everything rational, and thus they certainly discover enough of the positive, and the outcry about slavery of the spirit, pressure on conscience, superstition has no end at all. The most unconstrained actions, the most innocent feelings, the most beautiful representations of fantasy, experience this rough treatment. But the effect is also suited to this unsuitable doing. The men of understanding believe they speak truth when they speak *sensibly* to the feeling, to the imagination, to religious needs, and cannot grasp how their truth is resisted, why they preach to deaf ears. The fault is, they offer stones to the child that demands bread. If a house is to be built, then their ware has usefulness. But precisely if bread made claim to fitness for house-building, they would rightly object.”

“In a religion actions, persons, memories can count as holy. Reason proves their accidentality. It demands that that which is holy be eternally imperishable. With this it has, however, not proved the positivity of those religious things, for man can and must attach imperishability and holiness to an accidental thing. In his thinking of the Eternal he attaches the Eternal to the accidentality of his thinking. It is another matter when the accidental as such, as that which it is for the understanding, makes claims to imperishability, holiness and veneration. Then the right of reason sets in to speak of positivity. The question whether a religion is positive concerns much less the content of its doctrines and commandments than the form under which it authenticates the truth of its doctrine and demands the practice of its commandments. Every doctrine, every commandment is capable of becoming positive, for each can be proclaimed in a violent manner with suppression of freedom, and there is no doctrine that would not under certain circumstances be truth, no commandment that would not under certain circumstances be duty, for even that which may count universally as the purest truth demands, for the sake of its universality, in the particular circumstances of application, *limitation*: i.e., does not have unconditional truth under all circumstances. The following treatise has therefore not the intention of investigating whether there are positive doctrines and commandments in the Christian religion? The answer to this question according to general Concepts of the

[p. 537]

human nature and the attributes of God is too empty; the dreadful twaddle in this tone has become too tedious through its endless extension and its inner emptiness, has lost all interest too much, so that it would perhaps rather be a need of the age to hear the proof of the *opposite* of that enlightening application of general Concepts; it goes without saying that the proof for this opposite would not be conducted with the principles and the method which the culture of its time furnished to the old dogmatics, but would be to derive that now rejected dogmatics from what we now recognize as the need of human nature, to show its naturalness and necessity. Such an attempt would presuppose the belief that the conviction of many centuries, that which the millions who lived and died in those centuries held for duty and holy truth — that this has not been sheer nonsense and indeed immorality, at least according to the opinions. If, according to the favorite method, by general Concepts the whole edifice of dogmatics has been declared a relic of dark centuries untenable in enlightened times, one is yet so human as to ask afterward how it can then be explained that such an edifice, which is so contrary to human reason and through and through error, could have been erected?”

On 24 September 1800.

#### VIII.

#### Aphorisms from the Jena and Berlin Periods.

#### From the Jena Period.

*Böttger* speaks of the *legend-monger* Pausanias, of the blowing Fama with the trumpeter’s cheeks; but both is he himself.

A *party* exists, then, when it falls apart within itself. So Protestantism, whose differences are now supposed to coincide in attempts at union; — a proof that it is no more. For in falling apart the inner difference constitutes itself as reality. At the origin of the

[p. 538]

Protestantism all the schisms of Catholicism had ceased. — Now the truth of the Christian religion is constantly being proved, one does not know for whom; for we surely have no dealings with the Turks.

“To stick a tobacco pipe in one’s face or in one’s physiognomy.” Is this not poetry? The wholly individual, at which the pipe is aimed, and in which it appears, is here posited quite objectively as nothing subjective that would still have something behind it, like a drawing on a wall, — and just so the hand that is to connect the pipe with it. I heard that expression from quite prosaic merchants.

What is not called science nowadays! “The terracer or the whole of the art of terracing.” So peat-cutting, chimney-building, cattle-breeding, etc., as science.

“A boy who had been subjected.” *Sommer’s* Novellas, p. 391. Is that not the *participium aoristi* [aorist participle] of the Greeks?

*Experience.* The shadow which *candlelight* projects, illuminated by the *daylight* of the morning, becomes *blue*; the shadow which daylight casts (which is weaker, and to bring it about one must move away from the light), illuminated by candlelight, becomes *red*. — The shadow cast by candlelight, held quite close to the light, shimmers toward the greenish.

*On historical logic.* It is asserted that we judge: gold is yellow. This assertion is probable. But not so probable is it that we infer: all men are mortal: Caius is a man, therefore he is mortal. I at least have never thought such flat stuff. It is supposed to go on in the interior without our having consciousness of it. To be sure, much goes on in the interior, e.g. the production of urine and something still worse, but when it becomes external, we hold our noses. Just so with such inferring.

The older Germans were really a merry people. From the venerable Ulysses, whose life is One earnestness, they made a silly Eulenspiegel; from the divine Circe, appearing in this as Nemesis, a pig. The moderns do more or less the same, only with greater earnestness. Formerly the people were the

[p. 539]

*Irony* about those divine beings, but now these are the irony about the earnest handlers and comprehenders.

As there has been a poetic period of genius, so at present there seems to be the *philosophical period of genius*. A little carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen kneaded together, and stuck into a paper inscribed by others with polarity, etc., with a wooden pigtail of vanity, etc., rockets shot into the air, they think they are presenting the Empyrean. So *Görres*, *Wagner* and others. The crudest empiricism with a formalism of matters and poles, trimmed with reasonless analogies and drunken flashes of thought.

The peasant woman lives in the circle of her Liese, which is her best cow, then of the Blackie, of the Spotty, etc.; also of Märten, her boy, also of Urschel, her girl, etc. Such familiar things are for the philosopher infinity, cognition, motion, the sensuous laws, etc. And as for the peasant woman her departed brother and uncle, so for the philosopher Plato, Spinoza, etc. The one has as much actuality as the other, but these have eternity besides.

Among the grape-husks men are already in science. From there it is not far to the *Pater peccavi* [Father, I have sinned].

Is it only the German women who let themselves be given laws by Frenchwomen? — The German gentlemen too, you will say in reply, Madame, and appeal to the *history of the Reichsdeputation*. — You do not know the story? Oh, I must tell it to you. The German Empire has been assured by the French that it is waging war with them. It has, to be sure, no hand on arms, a couple of petty burghers excepted, who count for nothing. But the French assured it of it, and since they assured it, one had accordingly to let oneself be plundered. Then the German Empire learned from the newspapers — we read them at table, and you can imagine what joy it caused that this was said of it — that it had made peace. But so that it might know in what manner the peace had been made — the French are polite people — they sent expressly an envoy to Germany to tell it so. He took it upon himself, so that one could not doubt it, to take another along. The Germans, as honest people — from the mouth of two witnesses the truth is made known —

[p. 540]

believed it naturally, when these assured it of it. They too are polite and thanked them handsomely for it.

When the Absolute slips and from the ground on which it strolls about falls into the water, it becomes a fish, an organic, living thing. If it now slips just so and falls into *pure thinking* — for pure thinking too is not to be its ground — then it is to become, plopping into it, something bad, finite, of which one really has to be ashamed to speak, if it did not happen officially and because it cannot once for all be denied that a logic exists. Water is such a cold, bad element, and life is so well in it all the same. Is thinking, then, to be a much worse element? Is the Absolute to fare so very badly in it and also to behave badly in it?

In Germany *common sense* is always taken under protection against the so-called *presumptions of philosophy*. Vain effort, for even if philosophy concedes them everything, it is of no use to them, for — they have none. True common sense is not peasant coarseness, but, in the cultivated sphere, freely and forcibly dealing with the determinacies of culture in pursuit of truth, and then immediately Rousseauesque paradox, when it expresses its contradiction to the determinacies, just like culture itself, in principles, or as experience, ratiocination, wit, like Voltaire or Helvetius. The nobility in Germany too has common sense, but precisely for that reason it uses it straight off, without proving that it may be used — which is where those others stop short.

*Wieland*, to whom one otherwise does not exactly reproach paradox, has set up the paradoxical proposition that it is serviceable to understand something about the matter on which one writes, and it has been found proven.

Fools become wise through harm; the clever, on the other hand, remain unwise despite all harm.

Be no sleepyhead, but always awake! For if you are a sleepyhead, you are blind and dumb. But if you are awake, you see everything, and say to everything what it is. This, however, is reason and the mastery of the world.

[p. 541]

On coins of Titus and Vespasian: θειότης [divinity], *aeternitas* [eternity] (Titi etc.), something common. Already *Aeternitas Augusti* too. Imperial title: *Aeternitas Vestra* [Your Eternity]. Αἰώνιος βίος [eternal life] occurs also of the Ptolemies on the Rosetta Stone; otherwise also only αἰώνιος. This αἰὼν [eon, eternity] seemed otherwise to be peculiar to the New Testament.

To a scrupulous person one can say that conscience is a moral lantern which shines only on a good road; if one goes on a bad one, one blows it out.

*In omnia alia abeunt* [they go off into everything else], who, with denial of their subjectivity, are supposed to think and accept something proved, truth. Their subjective unrest is not capable of the repose of cognition. They have stood under no discipline.

In Swabia one says of something that happened long ago: it is already so long ago that soon it will no longer be true. So Christ has already died for our sins so long ago that soon it will no longer be true.

The balls, public places, theaters are no longer much frequented. [French] One assembles in the family, one returns to *moeurs* [manners, morals]. These *moeurs* are the general boredom of the public sphere, morality.

For baseness only morality as relation to virtue is possible. As Karl Moor, after he has quite despaired, after father and beloved are gone, goes, as his punishment, through a moral action: “the man can be helped.” The truly tragic is the moral. To us it is at the same time sentimental.

The truth of science is a calm light, illuminating and gladdening all things, like a warmth in which everything at once sprouts forth thrivingly and lays out the inner treasures in the breadth of life. The *flash of thought* is the Capaneus that imitates this heavenly fire in a bad, vanishing manner, formally annihilating, and is unable to arrive at any enduring life.

If one knows the Pythagorean theorem and says: with it nothing is eaten or drunk; — another: what is that to me? it is a matter of application for life; I must find my totality expressed in it; — a third: no useful application,

[p. 542]

no maxim of wisdom for the moral life results from it; — then all this is one and the same, but we honor the expression in such a way that we call the first boorish clumsiness, the second sound common sense, the third zeal for the moral interest of humanity.

[French] “What a lot of things in a minuet!” exclaimed Marcel, the most famous dancing master of Paris, fourteen years ago, in the enthusiasm of his art. “Dancers today put it differently: *one must know the moral of the dance*, and they say this very seriously.” In Germany this is called: poetry.

[French] “The Germanic empire is a *moral being without action by itself*, and it is a body, dead by its constitution.” Germany is no monarchy, etc., no *state*, but a Reich. Reich is supposed to be a Concept or rather, if it is to be a state, an intuition which is empty.

The *Allgemeine Zeitung* reports of Frau von *Staël* in Berlin how the Queen addressed her: [French] “I hope, Madame, that you think us of too good a taste not to be flattered by your arrival in Berlin. It is a long time that I have admired you, and I have been impatient to make your acquaintance.” Here too, indeed, spirit came to spirit, and like to like, as the proverb says, gladly joins company.

In the German treatments of the sciences the content of most works is only this: *I too know* what has been discovered here or there. Thus six hundred have worked on cowpox and all repeated the same thing. They then fell into dispute with one another over plagiarism, but the fact was that they had all *copied the same thing*, just as the Evangelists are supposed not to have copied from one another, but to have had *one* Gospel before them. In free sciences, such as philosophy, each copies out the general triviality of culture.

The answer which *Robespierre* gave to everything — here someone had thought this, done that, wanted this or said that — was: [French] death! Its uniformity is extremely tedious, but it fits everything. You want the coat: here you have it; the waistcoat too: here; you give a slap in the face: here is the other cheek as well; you want the little finger: cut it off. I can kill everything, abstract from everything.

[p. 543]

So obstinacy is insurmountable and can in itself overcome everything. But the highest thing that would be to be overcome would be precisely this freedom, this death itself.

*Reading the newspaper* early in the morning is a kind of realistic morning blessing. One orients one’s attitude toward the world either by God or by what the world is. The former gives the same certainty as the latter, that one knows where one stands.

*Ora et labora!* [Pray and work!] Pray and curse! *Cursing* is otherwise, when someone says “Sacrament!”, but in religion all these things, which otherwise lie apart, fall together. “Cursed be the earth, and in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat thy bread!” To work means to annihilate the world or to curse.

The necessity of studying a system of philosophy *entirely*. The *principle* contains everything enveloped, but also only enveloped, latent: the empty formal Concept, not the thing itself. Like a miser who keeps all enjoyments in his purse as possibility and spares himself the actuality, the burdensomeness of enjoyment itself.

The questions which philosophy does not answer are answered in such a way that they are not to be posed in this fashion.

*Gellert*, *Hagedorn*, *Uz* have rhymed virtue flat: “Whoever only loves virtue,” etc. “Indeed I found it, between virtue and understanding,” etc. “Friend, virtue is no empty name,” etc. God forbid! — Nicolai, a bookseller in Berlin, thereupon invented, or preeminently urged, *uprightness*.

It is a fine trait, what contempt for *money* one has and shows in Germany. The Germans attribute to it an origin that could not be more contemptible and base. It is represented to the eye in figures called money-sh—ers. A mythological reference is said to underlie it. A bratwurst, or whatever it may be, one does not wish to think together with so base a manner of origin.

*Common thinking* does not construct: here a linden tree beside willows, cuttings, etc., and below a cow runs past. It does not prove,

[p. 544]

but takes its exertion for proof of something, its tedium for depth and its exhaustion for the result.

What has a *deep significance* is, for that very reason, good for nothing.

*Our posterity is the next fair.* As in reason everything draws together, so too in the view of a mountain range the stream comes nearer. [Latin] The feet of those who will carry you out are at the door.

*Science.* Whether an individual possesses it, he can assure himself and others. Whether it is true is decided by the nearest surroundings, the contemporary world and then posterity, once the former have given their approval. Yet consciousness has risen so far in culture, the barbaric tenacity of comprehension has become so much more fluid and rapid, that a few years already bring on *posterity*. Over *Kantian* philosophy the staff has long since been broken, while the *Wolffian* held out for fifty years and more. More hastily has the determination of its standpoint been hurried on for *Fichte’s* philosophy. What *Schelling’s* philosophy is in its essence will reveal itself in a short time. The judgment upon it stands, as it were, before the door, for many already understand it. Yet these philosophies succumbed less to proof than to empirical experience of how far one can get with them. Blindly their adherents elaborate them, but the fabric grows ever thinner, and at last they find themselves surprised by its cobweb transparency. It has melted away for them like ice and slipped like quicksilver through their fingers, without their knowing how it happened to them. They simply no longer have it, and whoever looks into the hand with which they offer their wisdom for sale sees nothing but the empty hand and goes on his way with mockery. While those, feeling the cold, still proclaim it as something, these suppose they have fathomed the matter, since they have in fact seen only its nothingness, not what it was. The one party is deceived, like the other. The truth, however, is that this vanished thing itself has brought them hither. The word of Scripture is fulfilled: when we keep silent, the stones cry out.

The first subjective thing in the study of the sciences is *honesty* toward oneself. To doubt everything is easily thought and said, but the question is whether it is true. The empty word, if the whole nature of the essence does not deny itself, is a lie, and it is appalling

[p. 545]

what people want to lie to themselves and to others, and to talk themselves and others into.

For the study of a science it is necessary not to let oneself be put off by the principles. They are general and do not mean much. As it seems, only he has their meaning who has the particular. Often, too, they are bad. They are the consciousness about the matter, and the matter is often better than the consciousness. One should study on. At first consciousness is murky. *Only one must not want to have grasped and proven step by step*; rather one throws the book away, reads on as if between waking and sleeping, resigns oneself to one’s consciousness, i.e. to one’s individuality, which is painful. In this way I studied the differential calculus and other things. So I have heard of others who studied Kant’s *Critique of Pure Reason*.

*Original*, quite wonderful works in culture are like a bomb that falls into a rotten town, in which everyone sits at the beer mug and is supremely wise and does not feel that its flat well-being has itself brought on the crash of thunder.

Most harmful is it *to want to guard oneself against errors*. The fear of actively creating error for oneself is the comfort and the companion of absolutely passive error. Thus a stone has no active error, except, e.g., lime when aqua fortis is poured over it. Then it comes quite out of itself. It positively goes astray, foams up, comes into another world. It is all Greek to it, it perishes. Not so man. He is substance, preserves himself. This stoneness or stoniness or stonenness (for the German language makes it hard to turn a substantive, a thing, a solid man, a respectable citizen who has wife and children, into a predicate!), this refractoriness is what one must renounce. *Pliability*, not the instinctive *non aridet* [it does not appeal (to me)], is the truth. Only when one understands the matter, which comes after learning, does one stand above it.

The *basic principle* of a system of philosophy is its result. As we read the last scene of a play, the last leaf of a novel, or as Sancho thought it better to tell the solution of the riddle beforehand, so the beginning of a philosophy is certainly also its outcome, which is not the case with those. But nobody will

[p. 546]

be content with the end of the former or with the word of the riddle, but the *movement* through which it comes about is held to be the essential. — That the particular is in the universal is denied by the opponents of philosophy, and they themselves practice this denial in that they merely pull hither and thither at the principle, because the whole is supposed to be in it. They possess the whole as they possess mathematics when they have bought a copy of Euclid or a slave who is a mathematician. The thing itself one cannot receive as a gift, thrown in, as it were, into the bargain, by procuring the principle or result. To remain standing, on the other hand, at the intuition of, e.g., *Jakob Böhme* is barbarism, as at the basic principles it is superficiality. The development of knowing is not a removal of those intuitions, any more than of the basic principle, but a working out of them from within or from without. *Böhme’s* intuition is a deeper one than *Jacobi’s* faith reveals. Those who take such a thing as a particular, vanishing opinion and place the barbarism in the matter itself err just as much as those who do not hold the basic principle to be essential. The former make the form of the barbarous the essence of the matter, the latter on the contrary the solidity of faith. (Jacobi: we are born in faith; pressing of hands; *dear* Mendelssohn, etc.; as empty Pietists with bowed heads and rolling eyes press one another’s hands without knowing what to say.)

The barbarian is astonished when he hears that the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the two legs. He thinks it could also be otherwise, is especially afraid of the understanding, and remains in intuition. Reason without understanding is nothing, understanding yet something without reason. Understanding cannot be given as a gift.

The words: *eternal, holy, absolute, infinite*, draw the man who feels something in them upward, warm and heat him. They are powers that govern him, pull him hither and thither, and the sign of their dominion over him is that with them he *feels* himself. They are the intuited gods of the Greeks, which for the Nordic peoples are only abstractions, words, and hence themselves in ideal form. Only comprehending kills them as power. It separates itself from them. Instead of lying in their element, it is the stepping back from them and seeing through them, a feelingless clarity. Those *words* elevate the man — how much more their knowing! But their knowing gives

[p. 547]

to man, to the I, his freedom, and the elevation is the extinguished heat or the (extinguished) feeling of the individual.

God, having become nature, has spread out into the splendor and the mute circuit of the configurations, becomes conscious of the expansion, of the lost punctuality, and grows wrathful over it. Wrath is this forming, this gathering together into the empty point. It finds itself as such, and its essence poured out into the repose-less and rest-less infinity, where there is no present but a wild rushing out beyond the limit, which ever comes to be as it is sublated. This wrath, in being this rushing out, is the destruction of nature. This going beyond the configurations is just as much an absolute going into itself, a becoming toward the center-point. In this the wrath devours its configurations into itself. Their whole extended realm must pass through this center-point; their bones are crushed by it and their flesh squashed into just this fluidity.

The wrath of God over himself in his otherness, the fallen Lucifer, fixed here, rebels against God, and his beauty makes him haughty. Nature, with the consciousness of its shape, displays it and takes pleasure in itself in it. But this its being for itself, or its being as consciousness, is not its being in an ever tranquil representation of itself, so that the thought would be only the secondary, the empty inactive space which receives its content, but this consciousness is immediately absolute activity. It is the wrath itself, the kindling of the fury in him, which wears itself out and consumes its haughty splendor. Consumed nature rises up in a new ideal shape as a realm of shadows, which has lost that first life, the appearance of its spirit after the death of its life. This new shape, however, is the overcoming of evil, the having endured in the glow of pain in the center-point, where, purified, it has left behind all the dross in the crucible, a residuum which is the pure nothing. It raises itself as free spirit, which sees this its transfiguration only in nature. —

Such myths, such intuitions are the intuitions of *barbarism*. The shape of these intuitions annihilates the individual, or rather here it is the fury against this Absolute which has come to be, itself again subsisting. For the individual is nothing in it. It does not go under, but has gone under, and that intuition must still go through a second process in order to be absolute. This is science, or the knowing, that that imagining

[p. 548]

into itself, that course of God’s life, proceeds from the knowing itself; that nature in its essence is not the otherness over which spirit — that it has thus lost itself — grows wrathful, but its intuition, it as it, which spirit is. The individual as such is itself nature, and the intuition of the divine essence a natural one, even though its content is spirit. The individual itself makes this path in the consuming of itself, or in science, for in this the natural essence of the subject perishes. And it is not only the elevation of the individual to this, or a culture of it; it is not merely a view from its side, a relation to it: but the second circuit of the Absolute itself, which, having become spirit, as such, as an outborn totality, as spirit, as consciousness, enters into that pain, so that spirit as consciousness produces that its becoming in itself as one that has become. — That intuition of religion is universal religion, and it is this only as science. Not a passing through, a producing of that first path within itself as an intuiting circuit; but science raises itself above faith and its intuiting, leaves itself as spirit and comes to itself as spirit. The culture, the scientific development of that intuition, is this: that it always remains spirit, does not lose spirit, and as this spirit not losing itself becomes an other to itself and refinds itself. Knowing makes every moment of the intuition, which for itself is an impenetrable, determinate shape that does not unlock its interior but proceeds, acts and vanishes through another acting thing, into a process in itself or into a spiritual nature.

*Bad reflection* is the fear of sinking oneself into the *matter*, always going beyond it and returning into itself.
