The analyst, as *Laplace* says, abandons himself to the calculus, and the task vanishes for him, i.e. the overview and the dependence of the individual moments of the calculation on the whole. Not only is the insight into the dependence of the individual on the whole alone what is essential, but just as much that each moment itself, independent of the whole, is the whole, and this is the sinking into the matter.

*Faust* found the limits of humanity too narrow and pushed against them with wild force, in order to move them beyond actuality. He found the noble head suppressed and neglected, the dunce and the scoundrel raised to honors. He wants the ground of the moral

[p. 549]

evil, to explore the relation of man to the Eternal, whether there is one who guides the human race and whence the contradictions that plague it arise. He wants the ground of things, the secret mainsprings of the appearances of the physical and moral world, and to have within his grasp him who has ordered everything.

In vain! He hurries onto the stage of life, where virtue and vice are intertwined, good comes from evil, evil from good. More and more the spirit grows confused. He sees the chain of necessity wound about the free creatures, gnashes his teeth that no one is master of his deeds, and cannot change it. He must let everything run its eternal course, while that power which he does not see, which seems only to mock him, deep darkness, gloomy silence envelops. To the spirit of man everything is dark; he is a riddle to himself.

*Theology* grants what speculation denies: What did I do to your God, I who only strove to fulfil the laws of humanity according to the guidance of the heart — to your God, who upon no sacrifice came to the aid of your wishes, who stilled none of your sufferings, to whom the one plagued by you calls in vain? Necessity is the name of the mighty, unknown power. This is all you grasp. Submit and die. —

Not the Godhead, but humanity itself, through abuse of its gifts, through wrong application of its capacities, through pusillanimity and sloth, bears the blame for everything. Man abuses what is given him for his happiness: religion, government and science. *Happiest* is he who, in quiet repose, far from the roaring activity of men, lives out his days without knowing how men are governed, and without inquiring why God lets things happen before our eyes such as we see happening daily. But *can* man do that? Does he determine his situation and his fate? Is he not violently swept into the whirlpool of life? The great *Why* returns.

The man who no longer accuses God, yet acknowledges his dependence, wants to know to what purpose he is there. And if he cannot force an answer, he would still like to know why nature stopped halfway with him and lets him only surmise where he demands certainty. Man is master of his fate and his vocation. He can through his action further and disturb the fair course of the moral world, and the whole human race, from the beggar to the king, is master-builder of the moral world. The

[p. 550]

man develops only the striving laid in him, like every thing of the visible world, only with the difference that his free will and his sense, comprehending bad and good, alone make him capable of punishment and reward. — I have conquered the inclination to evil. The purity of my will, the feeling of having acted according to the laws of reason, the conviction that a being cannot perish that has worked through the understanding, are what elevate me. — Restless, bold, often fruitless struggle of the noble with the specters begotten by these gods: diremption of the heart and of the understanding; the sublime dreams and the bestial, depraved ones; the pure and lofty sense, heroic deeds and crimes; prudence and madness; violence and sighing submission; the whole human society with its wonders and follies, atrocities and excellences. — *But* — is that enthusiasm perhaps more than the dream of a fanatic? Does cold understanding justify it? Do we not, following it, chase empty shadows and lose thereby essentiality? Yes, can such a dream be realized at all, such as the world once is, as its present conditions are?

*Spirit* of Nature: *Live* in me, with me! I am with you and cannot become plainer to you than I am! Blooming and withering, thriving and destroying, hang together. My friendship hides from you the near chaining-together. I have given my dear children delusion as a companion. My reward is your happiness. The source of it streams with rich flow in your heart. Only seek it there! Flee the delusion of those who seek it outside me!

Everyone wants and thinks himself to be better than this his world. Whoever *is* better only expresses this his world better than others.

The *usual royal road* in philosophy is to read the prefaces and reviews, in order to get an approximate idea of the matter.

The *last royal road* in study is thinking for oneself.

Those who speak so much against philosophical systems *overlook*, in the case of a *particular* system, the circumstance that it is a philosophy; the chief circumstance, just as that an oak is a tree.

[p. 551]

Kiesewetter has found a very great inclination among the deaf-mutes to speak in rhymes, and, what seems almost incredible, their rhymes were founded not on orthography but on sound.

To speak in *one’s own language* is one of the highest moments of culture. A people belongs to itself. Out with foreignness, down to the Latin letters!

Someone steps forward and delivers something *mediocre*. All greet him as their equal and cherish and tend him: You are one of ours, you are just not in earnest, etc.

With philosophy the public is concerned about religion, the lost one; not about science; about this only afterward. Man wants to learn where he stands, wants satisfaction for himself, the interest of the humanity of this time.

“*Fine sciences*” is no longer said, but still: *think to yourself* a house with two trunks beside it, etc., instead of: *represent* to yourself.

It is no longer so much a matter of *thoughts*. We have enough of them, good and bad, beautiful and bold. But of *Concepts*. However, since those are to be made valid immediately through themselves, whereas as Concepts they are to be made comprehensible, the form of the style thereby undergoes a change, an appearance demanding perhaps painful exertion, as in Plato, Aristotle;

The *effect* on the public is an absolute standard, over which the subject may well become furious. It has done everything; but opposed to its *insight* stands precisely the unconscious *instinct*.

*On morals*: Its highest — to bury the guilt and the sufferings of this heart within itself, to make the heart the grave of the heart.

With the *miracles* of the New Testament it is not the *content* of the miracle that matters, but that it is a *miracle*.

[p. 552]

What does it matter about the healing of a withered hand, the withering of a fig tree, or the drunkenness of the wedding guests.

A patched stocking is better than a torn one; not so self-consciousness.

*Studying* means coming to regard as true what others have thought. But if one is at first immediately done with it as with something false, one does not know the things.

Since religion is lost, one demands of philosophy that it devote itself to *edification* and stand in for the pastor.

The partition between the *terminology* of philosophy and that of ordinary consciousness is still to be broken through; the resistance to *thinking* the familiar. It is supposed to be left at that peacefully, philosophy is not to be taken seriously; but this it does when it turns to what is current and accepted.

Philosophy is not so fortunate as to have a *proposition* and to be able to say: this is, or is *nothing*.

Kant is cited with admiration for teaching *philosophizing*, not *philosophy*; as if someone taught joinery but not how to make a table, chair, door, cupboard, etc.

The *joy in the St. John’s fire* needed only to be organized. On all the mountains a multitude of fires are lit. It is the joy in the first fire, and what is the joy in such a living element other than something religious? For it is joy in it itself as an element. This joy must honor itself, order itself with consciousness, make itself lawful. This joy needs only to be taken seriously, and it is an act of worship. But it is not so taken. Man, in the religion of sorrow, despises his joy, rejects the consciousness of it. — Otherwise with the Greeks, who made even eating an act of worship, i.e. enjoyed with consciousness and will. With us boredom is at home. A company is ashamed of eating. There are no more serious men than the Greeks and none more cheerful.

[p. 553]

Formerly the lower class of the people cast out individual family members as the scapegoat, upon whom lay the burden of privation, penance and self-estrangement to the point of madness, while it itself went free and purchased reconciliation for itself through these sacrifices. Now, however, it has taken the penance itself upon itself.

Rather have ten millions taken by force, be spat in the face, trampled underfoot, cudgeled, than freely give one million, freely expose oneself to a wound by dealing out wounds: that is *the sense of the German nation*. With the tenth part of the expenditure of money and goods in kind, with the thousandth part of the sufferings, with the saving of the mountain of disgrace which the past war has cost the Germans, they could, by 9/10 of what was lost, avert 999/1000 of the sufferings and, instead of disgrace, acquire honor. But the Germans want to have the satisfaction of remaining neutral, i.e. of letting themselves be skinned by both parties, rather than adhering to one party. They have the gratification, nonetheless, of having remained for themselves. They are the Quaker nation of Europe. They let everything be taken from them, the coat, and out of good nature, so as not to get a sour face, they give the doublet as well. When they receive a slap in the face from one side, from one of the warring powers, they put themselves in the position of having to receive one from the other as well. As Tertullian describes the Christians.

By the *How* of a thing one means its manner. Four wooden legs, a board over them, is the How of a chair, i.e. precisely the chair.

Necessity of laws against *usury*. Because the individual does not know the opportunities and the individuals with whom money is to be had, it appears rarer than it is. The state, on the other hand, is supposed to know this, the scarcity or abundance of money. Its fixing of the rate of interest supplies the consequence from which that difficulty would arise, the opinion of greater scarcity and thereby the emergence of higher interest. Furthermore, as every rumor of war and peace, hailstorm, etc., has influence on the price of grain, the same fluctuation would occur with money. It is this instability that raises the price, for the hope of selling higher, or at least not lower, is stronger than the fear of the opposite, and the former brings about a stronger

[p. 554]

withholding than the latter does dumping. Hence official *price-fixing* on bread, meat, etc. is necessary.

There is no country like Germany, where every notion is at once made into something universal, built up into the idol of the day, and its exhibition driven to charlatanry, so that it is also just as quickly forgotten and the fruit is lost which it would have borne had it been confined within its limit. Thereby it would be recognized in its measure and valued and used as much as is due to it, whereas in the other way, with its undue inflation, it shrivels up entirely and, as said, is forgotten.

The South Germans have honestly pirated. The North Germans copy one another out and repeat the same thing; compendia, a chapter earlier or later; even elegant newspapers.

I remember very well how long I knocked about in the sciences, honestly supposing that what was open to view of them was not yet everything. From the turns of phrase used to conduct the matter I concluded that the essence still lay in the background and that all knew far more than they had said, namely the spirit and the grounds for advancing something of that kind. After I had long sought in vain where this was to be found, of which there was always speaking or doing as if it were the generally known, and the pursuit of the ordinary therefore the right, and could not find its justification, I found that in fact there was no more to it than I well comprehended, and besides that only this: the tone of confidence, arbitrariness and presumption.

A friend of genuine natural science proposes to invite the sufficiently well-known Herr Dr. *Gall*, who, to the greatest astonishment, has already completed one course, to give another, since it is clear from his lecture that he is inexhaustible and will always still know how to tell us new stories. Provisionally he has already shown himself not unwilling and has promised, through new arrangements, to bring his skull-emptiness still more to light. He will, namely:

1) for the display of the brain, unfold his flat skin; on a little apron for the chapeaux [gentlemen], for the ladies on a pair of trousers;

2) show the origin of the nerves from the coccyx;

[p. 555]

3) point out a great number of new senses: in ladies, besides the sense of dancing, also the sewing-sense and the cooking-sense; in peasant flails [boors] the threshing-flail sense; in others, however, the charlatan sense, all without thinking;

4) to call in the hair-combing woman from the orphanage, Barbara Sprützbein, who with her practiced manipulation of skulls and her experience will assist Herr Dr. Gall.

One enlightens the *age*, another feels it out in sonnets, educates it up, reflects it, gazes it out, prays it up. The age is for each the *truncus ficulnus* [fig-tree trunk], from whose whole each wants to fabricate a Mercury; but the devil leads the trunk away under his hands, or, to pass over into another simile, the Mont Blanc granite, and leaves him only a splinter or grain, so that when one now views his finished work by the light, he has produced a damned small little Mercury, and cannot rail enough at the badness of the time and of the devil, who left him only such crumbs, so that now a multitude of little ages are running about, all depicting differently: a Salzmannish, a Campean, a cowpox little age; — to clarify it, so that it becomes pure clear ether, from which the star-shapes spring forth freely in the middle in eternal solar beauty.

#### From the Berlin Period.

A great man condemns men to explicate him.

Russian women complain when they are not beaten by their husbands; they do not love them. That is world history.

Goethe made love poetic throughout his whole life, squandered his genius on this prose — his *Werther*; — the poetry of love he got to know in the Orientals — his *Divan*.

*Aufgeben* [to give up; also, to set as a task], like *aufheben* [to sublate], is double-sensed: 1) *aufgeben* — to regard something as lost, annihilated; 2) *aufgeben* — but precisely thereby

[p. 556]

at the same time to make it a problem, whose content is not annihilated but is to be rescued, and whose stunting, difficulty, is to be solved.

When man has once come to the point that he no longer knows better than others, i.e. that it is quite indifferent to him that others have done it badly, and only what they have done rightly interests him: then peace and affirmation have entered into him.

*One-sidedness* of philosophy is the favorite chatter, which one hears most frequently, and this category passes for a talisman that once and for all helps against any philosophy, against any demand of it, etc.; an absolute armor off which a pretension of it slides, if not as to acquaintance, then at least as to outward respect. A philosophy is one-sided because it is a particular one, and such it is because it is a determinate one — or better, in general, because there are still others differing from it. — What is to be done, then, in order not to fall into such one-sidedness? Prudence directly indicates making oneself acquainted not merely with one but with the different philosophies; only in this way does one put oneself in the position to be able *first to choose*, and thereby to be self-active and independent. Is this not prudent, is this not the homespun understanding, which has thought out for itself with deliberation such a circumspect and cautious conduct and finds itself quite well, and especially so, off in it?

Yet such conduct is not without misfortune; for after sobriety, in order to guard against one-sidedness, has resolved on a choice, that which it has chosen is itself again a determinate, a particular philosophy, — for it is immediately *different* from those from which it was chosen, or also against which it has itself produced something that it calls a philosophy. — This homespun understanding, in wanting to avoid one-sidedness, falls thereby only itself into it, and its prudence has not only helped it not at all but seduced it to that which it wants to escape. Kant knew the Wolffian, the Humean philosophy, made himself one of his own against them — thus a one-sided one, etc.

There is only one way to avoid the dreaded one-sidedness — namely, to be dispensed from philosophy, because every one is one-sided. The understanding then also refrains from choosing, from deciding. To have one’s philosophy, or indeed to know that there is nothing in philosophy, nothing in any, this negative, *empty* thing — it cannot be denied that it is *free of one-sidedness*, from the one-sidedness

[p. 557]

of some content, namely. Just with this another one-sidedness at once enters again, for *ignorance* is again only *one* side, something particular, because something other, particular, namely knowledge and science, stands over against it. In fact the understanding, with its homespun-ness, has fallen only from the mountain of its absurdity into the abyss of its stupidity. O you blessed Sancho Panza, who that has read Don Quixote has not had his pleasure in you?

There are those who hate the speculative cognition of the Christian mysteries because they lose the merit of unreason. True faith is *unprejudiced* as to whether reason is in accordance with it or not, without regard and relation to reason, but *polemical* faith wants to believe against reason.

Musical composition of *hic, haec, hoc* [this, this, this] by Carissimi, for singing, is declared excellent. Sign of the senselessness of music; let someone try to paint it or to make a poem about it!

Christ, the man, represented, is a quite different riddle from the Egyptian one. This is the animal body from which a human face breaks forth — but there the human body from which the God breaks forth.

In the year 1764 a new hymnal was prepared in Danzig. Of *Gellert* only two hymns went in, and indeed, as the clerical Ministerium expressed itself on the matter, because he was “also a comedy writer.”

*Securi adversus Deos* [secure against the gods], said Tacitus of the Germans, as *against* the Romans; — as against the superstitious Romans. *Febris* [Fever], *Pestis* [Plague], like *Cloacina*, were their gods. — From that it is not far to the devil. Raise those merely physical devilries into the spiritual, and we have devils.

*Life and Opinions* was formerly a good title, for of men some have a *life* and no opinions; others only *opinions* and no life; finally there are those who have both, life and opinions. The latter are the rarer; then the former; the most common are, as always, the middle.

[p. 558]

*Prussian State Gazette* 1819, 52nd issue, 29 June: “Public expenditures are greatest among those peoples who have for the longest time and most completely taken part in the granting of taxes.” — “The bold plans of enterprising rulers age and die with them; but the aroused pride of nations, the trust in the strength of its people imbibed with the mother’s milk, the ancestral delusion that might gives right, proliferates from the forebears to the grandchildren. Far be it from us to fail to recognize how powerfully this stirring of all individuals works on the spirit of the whole, on the education of the human race; peoples live by their faith: *but they also pay for it*.”

And *gladly* at that. Those who live by their unbelief must also pay for it.

The *Latin language* was formerly pursued in the schools from two chief points of view: 1) the sense and content of the writers, of Cornelius Nepos, Curtius, J. Caesar, Cicero, Tacitus, Horace, etc. The one chief point, *the content suited* to the young; noble, simple, firm dispositions and actions, principles of morality and of political life presented in their naive nearness and universality; 2) as language according to more general rules of grammar. *Rule* is the subsuming of the particular under the universal. The Latin language has in this the advantage over the Greek; firm rules, plastic, lapidary; simple structure of sentences and periods; — sense of obedience, of lawful procedure; — firm rule and acting according to it, without exceptions, caprices, evasions, etc. — According to these rules the pupil had to make his compositions, not according to whether a form, inflection, construction, etc. had been found. The refinement of the study of Latin, chiefly by Dutchmen and Englishmen (Drakenborch and Ruhnkenius disputed over whether *simulac ego, perinde ac ego* is correct, and it was finally settled: *simul atque ego*, and to correct everywhere accordingly — and so a multitude of subtleties, i.e. particularities), has entirely changed the nature of the study of Latin as a means of culture toward *discipline*.

The nobility of today has, as a rule, precisely *not* come from the old free *landowners*, but for the most part from the imperial, royal and ducal *vassals*. For even those free landowners themselves had to become vassals if they wished to retain some importance and not be wholly suppressed.

[p. 559]

*Vis-à-vis* the nobility the courts have been *magnifique* [magnificent], have gathered the nobility around them and ruined it. — Now *vis-à-vis* the wealth of the bankers the courts (the princes in clothing, etc.) have become simple, because wealth can at once imitate clothing, women’s adornment, dwelling, fêtes. — Facing this same wealth the courts can be stiff, full of etiquette. This is laughed at, and the courtiers are regarded as servants, as ornaments, [French] who debase themselves by putting a price on it.

In world history the division holds, as with the Greeks: *Greeks and barbarians*.

*Canova* wanted to consecrate to *God* the church which he built in his native city. This was not permitted. — Brahma had no temples in India. Protestant churches are called houses of prayer in Catholic countries. Houses of God, the name in southern Germany.

Corporations and collegial bodies are much stricter in refusing than individuals: difference between the collegial constitution and personal responsibility. As much as the latter can be more energetic, especially at the beginning, so much does its force blunt. The individual is supposed to govern like a nobleman, as an independent personality resting on itself. But the individual as merely particular is in manifold dependence; — this one or that one can or will be able to harm him. Refusing appears as a personally individual matter, and there is in fact more or less of the accidental in it.

*Walter Scott* in his *Life of Napoleon* says of the causes and purpose of the French Revolution: “Heaven, in punishment of the sins of France and of Europe, in order to give the human race a great lesson, left power and force to such men as were only the instruments of its vengeance and of its secret designs.” — What? If the sins of France and of Europe were so great that the *just* God visited the most terrible punishment on the continent, then the Revolution would indeed have been *necessary* and no new crime, but only the just chastisement of old crimes; — presumptuous phrases which could hardly be excused in a Capuchin who wants to gloss over his ignorance. — “The most intellectually gifted people of Europe, it says in vol. I, p. 47, let itself be

[p. 560]

led astray by the grossest deceptions and the most pernicious principles.” Shallow head.

IX.

#### Förster’s Birthday Poem, 1826.

Hellas’ poets sing the glory of immortal heroes, / Who by land and by sea did and endured many things. / But above all One is celebrated in myths and sagas, / Who by the gods’ decree did what no other accomplished.

For with mighty arm he wrestled with lions and dragons, / Sheltered for human diligence a securely enclosed land. / Where nature breaks in with crude violence, he conquers it, / To the Olympian circle Heracles clears his way.

And so we too, in the genuinely Germanic North, extol / A hero who has done twelve deeds and more besides. / For among us, too, the Erymanthian boar was rooting, / Poisonous dragon-brood snort with flaming rage; / True, they no longer dwelt in nocturnal woods and swamps, / But in the realm of spirit they practiced sacrilegious deeds.

Behold! there was born to us a hero, a holy George, / Whose courage never failed, whose strength never lacked. / On the winged steed of thought he rode out to battle, / Bore truth’s shield, bore faith’s banner. / And never missed its mark his lightning-bright javelin, / And with the flash of the sword his piercing word struck.

So the hero already in early years announced himself, / When the skeptics sent him serpents of doubt. / Truly! the newts he crushed as if they were Göttingen sausages, / And of skepticism there remained only the empty shell behind. —

Purring, a tomcat prowled about through valleys and mountain gorges, / Everywhere Wolffian metaphysics held the floor. / But the Wolf, the later fellows too, had / Deceitfully fetched the name from Aristotle; / Yet you recognized them well, and on dialectical hunt / You stripped the pelt for them over their ears,

[p. 561]

And you brought to honor the garment of the Greek master, / Invulnerable in it you offered defiance to your foes. / Then you soon scared away the nocturnal Stymphalian birds, / Which with stench and screeching filled the cheerful air. / With reviewers’ chatter in literary gazettes / They screech noisily about, but they bite no more. —

Had the son of Zeus to stoop to lowly labor, / You have with divine courage accomplished similar deeds. / But Augeas’ stable, that was the academies, / Truly the gentlemen therein academized mightily. / But when now the surge of philosophical sea-flood / Broke in, how all the wigs at last scattered out like dust; / And they departed with molecules and pores, / With the particles of light which they had stuffed into sacks. —

Fettered fast to the rock you saw your comrade Prometheus, / Who with daring courage stole the heavenly ray, / Who drew back the veiling veil of holy Isis / And grasped the Idea of nature meaningfully in an image, / When first he greeted the magnet as the symbol of the Concept, / Where the opposition unites, though it appear divided. / But it did not profit the seer; substance held him fettered, / Sick subjectivity gnawed his liver out. / Yet you slew the vulture; then rigid substance dissolved / And to the Idea of the Idea you pressed on, to the spirit of the world.

True, you did not carry off from the Delphic god the tripod, / But you brought back from him glorious spoil. / That “*Know thyself*,” which no mortal yet solved, / You have solved, and to the god you gave the question back. —

You slew the hydra of thousand-headed opinion, / Which raised heads swelling in state and in right; / For youth wanted, by the urging of the heart and by caprice, / To rule and lead the realm, but only not to obey. / And we dreamed, no doubt, much of old, happy times, / Looked, yearning, across the sea to the new world. / Yet through you we came to love the present and the homeland, / And with the actual world you have reconciled us again. —

Then too you led us to the gardens of the Hesperides, / Plucked for us the golden fruits of eternal art, / That we might understand the works which a Mozart, a Goethe, / Which a Phidias boldly, a Raphael created for us. —

[p. 562]

What you have won in spirit, you have made firm in spirit, / As in a star-fort you rest in your system / And the pillars bear, as firm as the columns of Heracles, / Forever the gloriously infinite edifice of science. —

Thus you created a realm of actuality and of truth, / Then descended yourself into the glow of your thoughts. / There the flame consumed what was earthly and perishable, / But the eternal remained true to you, the immortal.

Hebe approached you in divine beauty and youth, / Offered on a blooming meadow a nectar-filled goblet. / And the friends gather here for the festive games; / Once they extolled Nemea, today we extol our Berlin.

X.

#### Funeral Orations by Marheineke and Förster.

Beloved colleagues and friends!

The hard blow, the irreplaceable loss that has struck us, scarcely permits us to collect ourselves and to recover from this deep pain, and it is infinitely hard for me to express in a few words the whole wealth and depth of your feelings on this extraordinary death.

So many dear sacrifices has our young university already made: this great, world-famous man too has now been demanded of us, and what the deeply bowed widow, what the two promising sons, what we all now feel, it is so much, so heavy and deep, especially because we have to bear the grief of so many who are not present here.

Beloved friends and colleagues! What is life, if the immortal himself must die of this life? We cannot grant death any right over him; it has snatched from us of him only what was not *He himself*.

This is rather his spirit — how it shone through his whole being, the gracious, friendly, benevolent, how he made himself known in his noble, lofty disposition, how he unfolded himself in

[p. 563]

the purity and amiability, in the quiet greatness and childlike simplicity of his whole character, with which every prejudice, too, once he was known more closely, was easily reconciled; his spirit, as it lives in his writings, in his numerous admirers and pupils, and will live imperishably.

He who, like our departed friend, already in the midst of this life knew how to free himself from himself, from the I and its craving, from semblance and all vanity, to immerse himself, thinking, in the eternal truth, and who was spiritually reborn and risen from the death of this earthly life; he who, seeing thus through the semblance of knowledge, always knew how to hold solely to what is truly actual, which is the working of the eternal spirit behind all the transient appearances of life in nature and history; he who, like this king in the realm of thought, has founded a new edifice of knowledge upon the immutable rock of the spirit — he has won for himself an immortality as few have, he has added his name to the most brilliant and unforgettable names of our race, he has accomplished what he himself says in one of his works: “The easiest thing is to pass judgment on what has content and solidity; harder, to grasp it; hardest of all, what unites both: to produce its exposition.”<sup>∗)</sup>

We are now to accompany him to his resting place beside his great predecessor.<sup>∗∗)</sup> And yet he is not wholly parted from us, the dear, the unforgettable one; he himself still lives among us, indeed, released from the earthly husk, more purely than before, freed from all sensuous appearance, no longer exposed to misjudgment, transfigured in the hearts and spirit of all who recognized his imperishable worth, and who will only come to recognize it rightly in time to come.

Like our Redeemer, whose name he always glorified in all his thinking and doing, in whose divine teaching he recognized anew the deepest essence of the human spirit, and who as the Son of God gave himself up to suffering and death in order to return eternally as spirit to his community — so he too has now gone back to his true home, and has pressed on through death to resurrection and glory.

Therefore it befits us too, who are called to live in the spirit, to purify our grief for him and to transfigure it into the pure grief of the spirit, into what he willed and only intimated,

∗) *Phenomenology of Spirit*, p. 5.

∗∗) Fichte.

[p. 564]

to continue courageously and to bring it into the most general understanding; and if we cannot all reach him in the depth of his knowledge and in his extraordinary learning, yet to become like him in his love, gentleness and patience, in his humility and modesty, in his faithful following of Jesus Christ, whose disciple to be was his highest glory on earth.

Blessed, blessed are the dead who thus die in the Lord; the spirit rests from his labor and their works follow after them.

Already we might, beloved friends in mourning, give ourselves up to the hope that the storm which for months had been hanging threateningly over our city was past, and only individual flashes and scattered sheet lightning still announced its nearness to us, when suddenly and unexpectedly a quivering bolt descends and a mighty thunderclap makes us fear a misfortune. —

Yes, my friends, the lightning has struck and what a head this blow has hit! — Our friend, our teacher is no more! This lofty cedar of Lebanon, to which we looked up in astonishment, is felled; this laurel which adorned science, art, every heroism of history with its wreaths, this tree of knowledge, from whose fruits no envious prohibition forbade us to gather, is robbed of its adornment, and with moved hearts we stand at the dark chamber where the narrow resting place was allotted to the great man! —

What? This gloomy cave, this narrow grave is to shut in *him* who led us through the spaces of heaven? This handful of dust is to cover him who revealed to us the mysteries of spirit, the wonders of God and of the world? No, my friends, let the dead bury their dead; the living one belongs to us, who, casting off the earthly bonds, celebrates his transfiguration and calls to the tamed and conquered elemental powers with the voice of the master: Death, where is your sting? Hell, where is your victory? —

So let no unworthy lament be heard at his grave; but he himself, the immortalized, granted the deep feeling, the pure sensation its right; those who stood closer to him often saw the tear of melancholy and of pain gleam in his eye, and who, that knew him, that loved him as we do, could at this farewell refrain from tears? But as he has led us from the night of presentiment to the dawn

[p. 565]

of consciousness, from the sleep of inwardness to waking thought, from faith to vision, so too may grief over his loss not remain a dull brooding, nor the cry of pain, nor merely this tear of quiet sympathy; such a loss wants not merely to be felt, it wants to be spoken out, and true consolation we shall win only when we find the word for our inner soul-suffering, and become conscious of the privilege that this is *our* pain, that it is *we* who have lost him, that this star in the solar system of the world spirit has shone upon *us*!

What name would be too bold that we, his pupils, could not bestow on the beloved teacher? Was it not he who reconciled the discontented with the motley tangle of life, by showing us how to comprehend freedom in necessity? Was it not he who reconciled the unbeliever with God, by teaching us to know Jesus Christ rightly? Was it not he who led back to confidence those who despaired of the fatherland, by convincing them that the great political movements of foreign lands will not diminish Germany’s glory in having called forth the far more successful movement in the church and in science? Was it not he through whom the weary and heavy-laden, even in misfortune, came to love this earth, by erecting upon it a realm of imperishable actuality and truth? Yes, he was to us a helper, rescuer and liberator from every need and distress, by redeeming us from the bonds of delusion and selfishness.

To preserve, proclaim, establish his teaching shall henceforth be our calling. True, no Peter will arise who would have the presumption to call himself his vicar, but his realm, the realm of thought, will spread on and on, not without being contested, but without resistance; the vacated throne of Alexander no successor will mount, satraps will divide the orphaned provinces among themselves, but as Greek culture then, so this German science, as Hegel devised and created it in many a sleepless night by the quiet lamp, will become world-conquering in the domain of spirits.

His name is thus added to the other celebrated names which made Prussia famous; he was worthy to be called to the land where a great king set philosophy on the throne; where Leibniz and Kant with the plowshare of their spirit broke up the dried-up soil and planted the seed of science; where the expelled Fichte found reception and recognition. Although born in

[p. 566]

the south of Germany, our Hegel has nevertheless found only here among us his true home and now also, beside his great predecessor Fichte, as was his own wish, his grave.

Fichte and Hegel! these are the pillars of Hercules which here mark the limit, and we shall wait for him who would have the courage on this spot to pronounce the *plus ultra* [more beyond]!

Come on, then, you storms of winter, and cover this grave with rough frost and a high bed of snow; our love will not grow cold; come on, you Pharisees and scribes, who haughtily and ignorantly misjudged and slandered him, we shall know how to uphold his fame and honor; come on, folly, madness, cowardice, apostasy, hypocrisy, fanaticism; come on, servile disposition and obscurantism, we do not fear you, for his spirit will be our leader!

Freedom, joy, peace he has given us, and these three guardian spirits will be the keepers who watch over this grave. Take, dear departed teacher, our tears, take our thanks with you into the vault, from which on the day of judgment you will celebrate a glorious resurrection! —

Printed by J. Petsch in Berlin.
